title: ‘Delights await!’: Margaret Atwood and other writers on Nobel winner Anne Carson | Books | The Guardian
description: The Handmaid’s Tale author is joined by Emily Wilson, Ocean Vuong and Booker-shortlisted writer Rebecca Perry in celebrating the newly announced Nobel laureate
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Handmaid’s Tale author is joined by Emily Wilson, Ocean Vuong and Booker-shortlisted writer Rebecca Perry in celebrating the newly announced Nobel laureate
Content: Risk and vision … Anne Carson.Photograph: Peter SmithView image in fullscreenRisk and vision … Anne Carson.Photograph: Peter SmithBooks‘Delights await!’: Margaret Atwood and other writers on Nobel winner Anne CarsonThe Handmaid’s Tale author is joined by Emily Wilson, Ocean Vuong and Booker-shortlisted writer Rebecca Perry in celebrating the newly announced Nobel laureateAnne Carson wins Nobel prize in literature 2026Where to start with: Anne CarsonMargaret Atwood, Emily Wilson, Ocean Vuong and Rebecca PerryThu 8 Oct 2026 13.12 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 15.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMargaret AtwoodAnne Carson’s work has long been admired among poets of many countries. For new readers, I would recommend The Beauty of the Husband – direct and visceral, funny and angry and sad – or Men in the Off Hours. Delights await!View image in fullscreenMargaret Atwood.Photograph: Christopher Wahl/The GuardianEmily WilsonMany congratulations to Anne Carson for the well-deserved Nobel prize! This is also great news for translation, classics, poetry, the breaking of generic and disciplinary boundaries, and the fact that you don’t have to fit a pre-existing mould to have a brilliant, successful career.Ocean VuongTo see the Nobel Committee honour a mind and spirit of such immense capacity and rigour gives me hope for the role of letters in our world at an hour when the vocation’s integrity is more threatened than ever before. For decades, Carson’s unapologetically erudite work has centered strangeness and mystery as methods of human revelation. And its myriad and restless formal enactments have granted endless permissions to multiple generations of writers. Like the best work out there, it fosters others as it forges new ways to be and think for itself. I count myself lucky to write in its wake.Rebecca PerryIn 2013, I (and pretty much every writer I knew at the time) went to see Anne Carson give thePoetrySociety annual lecture. She had us gripped, of course; she was generous, smart, sharp, impeccable in cowboy boots and a suit. Her person demands undivided attention. At the end, in the Q&A, a man asked a long, self-indulgent question to which she simply replied: “No.” The audience waited, briefly, for elaboration. None came.And there lies the magic of Anne Carson – she is concurrently at play and utterly serious. She never gives many words when one will do.View image in fullscreenRebecca Perry.Photograph: Robin Christian/Waterstones Debut Fiction Prize/PAFor most of my writing life she has been the writer I go to for pretty much anything I need. I pick up The Beauty of the Husband and I fall in love with poetry again, I deal out the pamphlets of Float and remember that ambition and weirdness aregood, I teach The Glass Essay and it shows up notions of formal boundaries as an absurdity.She shows us that there is always, that there must be, room for risk and vision, for uncompromising writing. Poets everywhere are rejoicing.Explore more on these topicsBooksAnne CarsonNobel prize in literatureAwards and prizesPoetryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Not since 9/11 has the UK faced such a security crisis – and threat to our liberal principles | Gaby Hinsliff | The Guardian
description: The combination of Iranian, Russian and Chinese aggression is deeply worrying: just how much more concerned about security should the country be?, asks Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Author: Gaby Hinsliff
Headline: The combination of Iranian, Russian and Chinese aggression is deeply worrying: just how much more concerned about security should the country be?, asks Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Content: Illustration: Nate Kitch/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Nate Kitch/The GuardianOpinionIranNot since 9/11 has the UK faced such a security crisis – and threat to our liberal principlesGaby HinsliffThe combination of Iranian, Russian and Chinese aggression is deeply worrying: just how much more concerned about security should the country be?Thu 8 Oct 2026 12.55 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 17.27 EDTShareThe first time the window-rattling roar of a B-1 bomber woke me up this summer, I thought for one crazed second we were under attack. By the second time, I’d learned to recognise the sound of US planes taking off from their base at RAF Fairford for what it was: a reminder that although Britain wants no part in this war withIran, we cannot quite escape the consequences.We’ll feel themat the petrol pump, orin the supermarketthis autumn, or in thiswinter’s heating bills. But living under the flight path adds an extra edge to it. The skies finally fell silent last week, but only because the bombers have been hastilysummoned homeafter an alleged terrorist plot to attack Fairford, in which (according to the prime minister) there are “strong indications that Iran played a part”. If Fairford is now a target of war, did that threat disappear when the Americans did? Nobody knows.Rural Oxfordshire is peppered with military bases, and after 15 years here I don’t bat an eyelid at helicopters practising low-flying drills, uniforms on the school run, or the stash of Day-Glo marshmallow cereal our local supermarket used to keep for homesick Americans. But the Fairford incident follows a serioussecurity breach at RAF Brize Norton last year– and though this involved pro-Palestinian protesters rather than the Russians, it didn’t inspire confidence – and news this summer that the Manchester synagogue attacker had scoped out the security arrangements forthe nearby Shrivenham defence academy. Bases nationwide are on high alert, with two Latviansarrested on Thursdayon suspicion of trespass inside RAF Molesworth in Cambridgeshire, home to a Nato intelligence hub. At Fairford, it was a farmer who sounded the alarm, raising some difficult questions about how vigilant to be in small rural communities where strangers tend to stand out. I don’t want to become paranoid about every passing dog walker, or leap to ridiculous conclusions on hearing a Russian accent. But not since living in London in the aftermath of 9/11 have I felt more alert to anything seemingly out of the ordinary.And that, of course, is how terrorism works. It’s not just the attacks themselves, but the fear and distrust they engender. For a while after the 7/7 bombings, people would change train carriages rather than stand next to some poor kid with a rucksack. At the height of the Troubles in Northern Ireland, Irish émigrés in Britain faced hostility. Sadly, it’s usually minorities who are singled out for suspicion or – in areas prone to far-right protests or antisemitic attacks – forced to wonder which of their neighbours might have joined themarches, ordaubed graffiti on Jewish-owned shops. This time, there’s a particularly grim risk of a backlash against asylum seekers, with Reform pouncing on unproven reports thatTehran may be using small boat crossingsto smuggle covert operatives into Britain. (For the record, those arrested and released on bail in connection with the alleged Fairford plot haveBritish nationality. However, aKuwaiticitizen recently convicted of a terror plot against the Israeli embassy andtwo Iranian nationalsrecently charged with allegedly plotting to target Jews in Manchester reportedly got here in dinghies.) Whatever the truth, Tehran must be delighted to see such destabilising ideas spread.For the second time since 9/11, Britain faces a dilemma over how much of a securocracy – a country dominated by security concerns, whose citizens live at a pitch of constantly heightened anxiety – it should become in response to increasing threats. As Andy Burnham will remember, the “war on terror” forced the last Labour government, of which he was part, into a painful rolling back of civil liberties at home. Since the threat this time is less from an ideology than from three hostile nation states with domestic reach – namely Russia, Iran and China – the coming dilemmas may be more over the movement of technology, assets and people.Historically, Britain’s economy has been a relatively open one, even after Brexit. We let Gulf statesbuy our football clubs, Russian oligarchs prop up theprime London real estate market, and Chinese money bail out ourcash-strapped universitiesand build ourpower stations, despite concerns about espionage, censorship and interference in domestic politics. (Tom Tugendhat, the shadow foreign affairs minister and longstanding China hawk, revealed last week that he still gets letters from Beijing to the family home “that say, basically, ‘we know where you live’”.)London’s tech startups, expanding faster than they could hire domestically, snapped up skilledyoung Russian codersunderstandably anxious to escape a country at war. We didn’t slaptariffs on cheap Chinese EVswhen the EU did, despite concerns they could kill off domestic car manufacturing – or even that some of their software mightstill be controllable from China, because trade wars are generally bad for business. (Though the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds,suggested recentlythat that debate is not entirely closed.)We chosenotto become a fortress because for a long time, the benefits of being open to the world felt worth the risks, but perhaps also as a statement of our values. But there is an increasingly live debate in Whitehall about whether, in retrospect, autocracies saw that openness as a weakness to exploit. If nothing else, they’re certainly weaponising it now: both Iran and Russia are throttling shipping routes inthe strait of HormuzandBlack Searespectively, with consequences for oil and food prices that are now ringingserious alarm bellswithin governments.Though it’s not entirely clear yet what Burnham makes of all of this, there are early signs of attitudes hardening. The Cabinet Office recentlysummoned CEOsof critical infrastructure companies to brief them on the threat of Russian sabotage, while last week MI5 issued arare public warningto academics against working with a Chinese organisation regarded as a front for espionage. The concrete barriers hurriedly going up around Fairford last week may be a harbinger of what is to come: a signal that as the world moves closer to a war footing, our relaxed way of life may have to change.But there’s a difference between being vigilant and being paranoid, let alone xenophobic, and we are going to need to hold that line in months to come. No foreign national in the UK should ever be persecuted for the sins of their country of origin: there’s no going back to the dark days of 1939, when Jewish refugees fleeing Nazi Germany and Austria were shockingly interned in Britain as “enemy aliens”. New powers of surveillance should always come with new safeguards.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnd this government should remember that if the “war on terror” taught us anything, it’s that security crises test liberal principles to breaking point. I just hope Burnham is ready for that.Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: 50 men’s autumn fashion updates for under £100 (mostly) – some are even free | Men's fashion | The Guardian
description: Oversized coats, relaxed-fit trousers and secondhand jumpers that will last for years to come … here’s how to build an effortlessly cool autumn wardrobe on a budget
Author: Peter Bevan
Headline: Oversized coats, relaxed-fit trousers and secondhand jumpers that will last for years to come … here’s how to build an effortlessly cool autumn wardrobe on a budget
Content: Style lesson: Good Will Hunting offers plenty of inspiration for cooler-weather dressing.Photograph: United Archives GmbH/Alamy Stock PhotoView image in fullscreenStyle lesson: Good Will Hunting offers plenty of inspiration for cooler-weather dressing.Photograph: United Archives GmbH/Alamy Stock PhotoGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterMen's fashion50 men’s autumn fashion updates for under £100 (mostly) – some are even freeOversized coats, relaxed-fit trousers and secondhand jumpers that will last for years to come … here’s how to build an effortlessly cool autumn wardrobe on a budgetThe best men’s shirts for every occasionPeter BevanThu 8 Oct 2026 13.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s time to pack away your weekly rotation of T-shirts and shorts and start thinking about layers.As always, there’s no shortage of inspiration for your autumn look. The menswear shows displayed their usual styling tricks: at Prada, the exaggerated shirt cuff became this season’s unlikely focal point. Then, there are the It boys, old and new, who are always good for a sartorial steer: comedian and actor Jack Innanen is the latest addition to the roster, though Brad Pitt’s 90s looks are just as current. And that’s all before you get to the colour palette: this year, bright colours can be thrown in among the traditional rich, earthy shades.These 50 easy updates span style, grooming and the wider cultural stuff worth knowing as the leaves start to turn – and, besides a few investment pieces, they’re all less than £100.Men’sstyle updates for autumnClothingColour blockingBright colours are in for autumn, but it’s still best to keep the look restrained. All you need to update your look is a couple of colourful T-shirts – say blue, red or green – to layer beneath shirts, coats and knitwear. For a steer in the right direction, check out Japanese designerSsstein’s show.View image in fullscreenArket 170 GSMregular T-shirt£14.45 at H&M£17 at ArketChoose brown over blackThough I’m always a fan of black, autumn is when you can switch it for brown because it has a softer, lived-in feel. It could be knitwear, trousers, outerwear or shirts; just stick to the richer, darker tones that look luxurious as opposed to toffee or caramel.View image in fullscreenAbercrombie & Fitchbaggyjeans£54.99 at Asos£75 at Abercrombie & FitchCoat checkAutumn’s a good time to invest in outerwear because you can make the most of it throughout the colder months ahead – simply switch up what’s underneath as the weather gets cooler. As this is a long-term purchase, go for something you can see yourself wearing for years to come, like a big, oversized woollen overcoat. Take a look atGant’s recent campaign with Theo Jamesfor style pointers.View image in fullscreenWeekday double-breasted wool-blend coat£165 at Weekday£165 at H&MTactile trousersIt’s time for trousers that feel cosy. It could be corduroy, flannel or wool; the key is to go for a relaxed fit that looks comfy rather than anything slim or constrained – something that would look at home next to an open fire with a book in hand.View image in fullscreenAsos Designbaggy corduroy trousers£32 at AsosView image in fullscreenCoswool-blendwide-legtrousers£119 at CosSlogan T-shirtsNeed proof slogan tees are back? Look no further than Jack Innanen. The up-and-coming Adults star has been cycling through them, with phrases such as “are my lips moving?” and “horny”. The best place to get them is Idea – the rare books shop that moonlights in slogan merch, where you can find T-shirts that say everything from “Yoga Helps” to “Intern”.View image in fullscreenIdea That Band You Like T-shirt£40 at IdeaCheck matePlaids and flannels are trending this year, with checks seen everywhere from Ralph Lauren to Zegna and, of course, Burberry. Try not to go full-on lumberjack and instead keep the cut sharp: tucked into tailored trousers or layered under a blazer rather than paired with denim and boots.View image in fullscreenCarhartt WIP Todrickcheckedflannelshirt£95 at Mr Porter£95 at John LewisZip-up cardiganThanks to Callum Turner – who has worn one everywhere from the red carpet to casual dinners out – the zip-up cardigan is the latest knitwear silhouette to add to your rotation. Turner has worn versions by Axel Arigato and John Smedley, but if you’d prefer something a little more accessibly priced, try the Danish high-street brand Selected.View image in fullscreenSelected 100%cottonzipcardigan£65 at AsosTry an Aran knitView image in fullscreenHeavy weather: substantial layers at Hermès autumn/winter 2026.Photograph: Marc Piasecki/WireImageAnyone who’s seen When Harry Met Sally will appreciate the appeal of a chunky Aran knit come autumn. Hand-knitted versions tend to be expensive, so Vinted is your best bet for a good, secondhand option.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: GoodLifeStudio/Getty Images/iStockphotoShop Aran jumpers at VintedNavy sealA plain navy T-shirt is autumn’s answer to summer’s white tee. If the fabric’s premium and it fits properly, it’s a top that can elevate everything from jeans to tailored trousers. If you’re shopping luxury,Sunspel’s the spot, butCosand Uniqlo are my top high-street options.View image in fullscreenUniqlo 100% Supimacotton T-shirt£19.90 at UniqloGo indigoWhile promoting The Dog Starsin London, Jacob Elordi wore the perfect transitional outfit: a lightweight windbreaker with a pair of wide-leg indigo jeans. For structure, look for untreated denim – a good-quality pair can develop its own patina; you’ll be wearing them for years.View image in fullscreenPercivalstraightlegheritagedenimjeans£120 at PercivalHood over heelsThough hoodies are mostly relegated to the comfy drawer, some styles are appropriate to wear out and about. What you’re after is substantial fabric – natural, not synthetic – and smart shapes rather than anything too baggy. If you want to make it work for the office (at least, one with a more casual dress code), throw an oversized blazer on top. End is a great place to start, especially the retailer’s newly released own line.View image in fullscreenEnd Worn Establishedhoodie£109 at EndSports-meets-fashionRunning kit is increasingly crossing over into everyday fashion. The vibe is sportswear designed for day-to-day settings. Think 9-to-5k. Whether you actually make it to the run remains, as ever, optional.View image in fullscreenAcid Runningmen’slongsleeve T-shirt£52 at Acid Running£59.99 at SportsShoesThe leather reportView image in fullscreenPlum role: Romeo Beckham in Burberry’s fur-trimmed bomber.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/AFP/GettyEver since Burberry showed a leather bomber on Romeo Beckham this season, it’s a jacket I can’t stop thinking about. His was a rich plum shade with a fur-trimmed collar, but a more classic style will make a versatile investment piece for autumn. A loose fit is the key: you want some room through the shoulders and torso so it reads as expensive – although real leather costs more than synthetic, it can age well and last for years with proper care.View image in fullscreenZararegular-fitleatherjacket£149 at ZaraFor more, read our guide onhow to make your leather last a lifetimeFuzzy texturesView image in fullscreenGrunge stripes: Kurt Cobain performs in one of his signature tops in 1993.Photograph: KMazur/WireImageEveryone from Dries van Noten to Tom Ford and Our Legacy sent fuzzy jumpers down the runway this season. If you’re buying mohair, look for pieces with ethical credentials – the Responsible Mohair Standard, for example. Or, for a more budget-friendly alternative, find something similar that’s made with synthetics, like this Topman jumper. Keep Kurt Cobain’s knitwear in mind while you’re shopping, and you can’t go far wrong.View image in fullscreenTopmanfluffy jumper£45 at Topman£45 at AsosView image in fullscreenBound Heatongradientsweater£95 at BoundLong-sleeved layersA long-sleeved T-shirt is one of the best layers you can own as the colder months close in: a base that works under anything, from casual shirts to jumpers, adding a pop of interest and extra warmth. A stripe or hit of colour peeking out at the cuff or collar works best.View image in fullscreenH&Mrelaxedfitboxy long-sleeved T-shirt£23.80 at H&MShoes and accessoriesSole warmingIf you buy one thing, make it cosy socks, whether in soft cashmere or grey marl merino. It’s a touch that makes your outfit feel completely autumnal – and it couldn’t be easier.View image in fullscreenPairsthemerinoset£40 at PairsSling shotEvery time I’m out in London, I spot another guy wearing a sling bag – and it’s usually the best-dressed guy on the street. The style is similar to a crossbody, but with a more streamlined fit that sits diagonally across the body rather than hanging in one fixed spot. It looks easy and effortless – and, more importantly, big enough for all the essentials such as sunglasses, keys and a mini aftershave.View image in fullscreenCosmodulecrossbodybag£119 at CosMerlot modePenny loafers are a year-round staple, but this is the best time for dark merlot red because, just like the wine, it gets along so easily with everything that’s in rotation at the moment, including rich navy and earthy green. Marks & Spencer, as always, has the classic nailed down.View image in fullscreenM&Sleatherpennyloafers£65 at M&STint conditionDark sunglasses and autumn aren’t a good match – unless you’re Anna Wintour. Instead, go for a lighter tint that’s better suited to lower light levels. It could be brown, blue, yellow or orange. Theo James wears ones by Moscot – specifically the Miltzen frames with a yellow tint – but for a more affordable alternative, try Le Specs.View image in fullscreenLe Specs Heart Throb£50 at Fenwick£50 at Le SpecsSchoolboy tiesTieshave been rising in popularity for a while now and are showing no signs of slowing down. The trick is wearing them in a less formal way – with a casual-leaning shirt, without a blazer, under a hoodie. Go for something silk, striped and preppy-adjacent:vintageand charity shops are great places to look.View image in fullscreenVintageChristian Diortie£65 at RokitSole investmentWhatever boots you choose should last you for years to come, so it’s best to go with something classic and versatile. My preference? Chelsea boots. You can dress them up or down and they’ll never date.View image in fullscreenSchuh Diceleatherchelseaboots£65 at SchuhOut with stripes, in with ticksAdidas has been head honcho in the trainer world for a few years, but it feels like the tide’s turning towards Nike thanks to the Moon Shoe. It’s a style from the brand’s archives brought back in collaboration with Jacquemus and has since made it into the mainline. The brown colourway is my top pick.View image in fullscreenNike Moon shoe OG£89.99 at Nike£89.99 at AsosRing leadersView image in fullscreenSilver lining: Paul Mescal adds a small hoop to his monochrome look.Photograph: Neilson Barnard/GettyThe It boys are wearing mini hoops – Drew Starkey, Colman Domingo, Paul Mescal. Michael Jordan and Brad Pitt wore this look in the 90s, so this wave could run. You’re looking for the kind of hoop that looks like you never take it out: minimal, low-key and a size that sits close to your lobe.View image in fullscreenSerge Denimessilver huggie hoop£55 at Serge Denimes£55 at EndJewellery doesn’t need to be masculineThe men’s offering at jewellery brands can be full of dark gunmetal and chunky pieces that only really work if you’ve got measurements like Dwayne “the Rock” Johnson. But this season, it’s better if your pieces lean delicate: think thin chains, vintage bracelets and small signet rings. Don’t be afraid to shop in the women’s section – and always look for precious metals like sterling silver.View image in fullscreenMejuriovallinkchainskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion£88 at MejuriTopped offA baseball cap is always helpful: it protects from the sun, shields from the rain and helps retain warmth when it’s cold. This time of year calls for a weather-resistant finish, such as waxed cotton, or something warm like corduroy. Barbour’s Ashby hat has both.View image in fullscreenBarbour Ashbycap£29.95 at Barbour£29.95 at John LewisIntellectual glassesView image in fullscreenSmart set: Matt Damon makes the case for classic frames in The Talented Mr Ripley.Photograph: Moviestore Collection Ltd/AlamyAutumn’s the perfect time to try clear glasses – the kind you’d expect a seasoned Oxford professor to wear with a neat blazer and corduroy trousers. Think something classic, rounded and tortoiseshell à la Matt Damon’s Mr Ripley. See it as an excuse to get your eyes tested; if you’re 20/20 it’s a bonus because you won’t have to pay for prescription lenses.View image in fullscreenJimmy Fairlythe Cloud glassesFrom £100 at Jimmy FairlyRolex, eat your heart outThough we’d all love a Rolex, dropping the equivalent of a house deposit on a watch isn’t feasible. If you like the Rolex Day-Date, Casio has a great alternative with a 40mm case, a classic stainless steel bracelet, and a similar day-and-date display. All for less than £60.View image in fullscreenCasioMTP-1370D-1A1VEF£59 at AmazonVans are backStockX’s August Big Facts report suggested the marketplace is betting on an incoming “skate boom” in clothing and footwear with brands such as Vans, whose sales on the platform rose 238% in the first half of 2026. So, consider it time to dust off your Old Skools – don’t worry, you can leave the board at home.View image in fullscreenVans Old Skool platform trainersFrom £36.99 at AsosFrom £70 at VansCuff loveWith cuffs in the fashion spotlight, what better time to upgrade your cufflinks? My favourites are all vintage and tend to cost way less than anything bought new – especially when you buy a job lot on eBay.View image in fullscreenVintagecufflinks£25 at eBayCarabiner stylingView image in fullscreenKey player: charms add detail at Charles Jeffrey Loverboy.Photograph: Antoine Flament/GettyCall it the Labubu effect if you like, but the appetite for stacking your carabiner with charms has spread beyond the viral toy; at Charles Jeffrey Loverboy, for example, they were accessorised with keyrings. Whether you go for designer charms or antique keyrings picked up from eBay, clip a couple on to your carabiner and call it a day.View image in fullscreenCadillac black leatherkeyring£6.95 at eBayGroomingGo heavier on fragranceThis is the time for warm notes such as sandalwood, leather, amber or vetiver – or, if you like something aromatic, look for spices like cardamom or clove. &Horace offers the perfect balance.View image in fullscreen&Horace eau de parfum, 50ml£62 at HoraceSkin foodAs we head towards winter, it’s worth reaching for more nourishing products, as cold air and central heating can strip moisture from your skin. A facial oil is one way to help combat the effects. My favourite is Aesop’s Damascan rose formula with camellia and rosehip oils. Blend a few drops with your moisturiser at night.View image in fullscreenAesop Damascan rosefacialtreatment, 25ml£65 at John Lewis£65 at SephoraReturn to retinolRetinol can make your skin more sensitive to the sun, so you may have eased off during summer. If you did and you want to build it back into your routine, start gradually with a low-strength formula. Byoma’s retinol oil is ideal, and make sure you still don’t skip the SPF.View image in fullscreenByoma Sensitiveretinoloil, 30ml£17.99 at Cult Beauty£17.99 at SephoraSkin in the gameWinter skin can take a beating, so it’s important to replenish it with nourishing ingredients. As a bonus, fragrance tends to last longer on hydrated skin.View image in fullscreenHotel, Mike hand and body lotion, 350ml£33 at Hotel, MikeLip serviceWhile entry-level lip balms, such as Vaseline, will do the job, I find I have to reapply them much more regularly than formulas with active ingredients, such as Exist’s SpaceLip Origin, which contains a bioactive ingredient cultivated aboard the International Space Station. It’s the longest-lasting lip balm I’ve ever tried and comes in a suitably slick metal applicator.View image in fullscreenExist SpaceLip Origin, 3.2g£34 at ExistFor more, read our guide to thebest lip balms to hydrate and protect your lipsPatch upThere’s never a bad time for eye patches, but some are better than others. My recent favourites are by Grown Alchemist. The brand says caffeine and ectoin can help brighten and hydrate the undereye area and reduce puffiness – and you get eight pairs for £20.View image in fullscreenGrown Alchemist Hydra-Restoreeyepatches£20 at Lookfantastic£20 at Cult BeautyDon’t skip conditionerCold weather can be drying on hair, too, especially if you’ve got any substantial length, as the ends can be particularly vulnerable. Start with something light, as using a heavy formula on fresh hair is how you end up looking like you haven’t showered in a week.View image in fullscreenHair By Sam McKnight Light Nourishconditioner, 200ml£28 at Sephora£29 at Cult BeautyView image in fullscreenHair By Sam McKnight Light Cleansehair andscalpshampoo, 250ml£28 at Sephora£29 at Cult BeautyWho needs contour?Using a gua sha or sculpting tool every morning can help your face look more defined by reducing puffiness and boosting circulation. FaceGym’s Multi-Sculpt has six edges for 10 different moves, all explained on the product page, but if you’re new to sculpting, you could start with a facial massage using just your hands. Apply an oil after cleansing to give your skin some slip so the tool (or your fingers) can glide rather than drag.View image in fullscreenFaceGym Multi-Sculpt£39.75 at Lookfantastic£53 at Space NKFresh skinMedicube’s PDRN pink collagen gel mask is a recent addition to my rotation that’s made a big difference. Niacinamide can help brighten your skin, while the cooling gel feels soothing. It also contains salmon-derived PDRN, an ingredient being studied for its potential in skin repair. The immediate glow afterwards is unrivalled.View image in fullscreenMedicube PDRNpinkcollagengelmask£14.99 at Lookfantastic£18 at Space NKRaising eyebrowsSmall cosmetic touches like curling your eyelashes, using a touch of concealer or a liquid blush can make a huge difference. An eyebrow gel is a good entry-level product that takes less than 30 seconds to apply, helps frame your face, and tidies away strays.View image in fullscreenRefy Brow Sculpt, 8.5ml£20 at Refy£20 at Space NKInspiration for freeAdd Jack Innanen to your moodboardView image in fullscreenStreet style: Jack Innanen in New York.Photograph: TheStewartofNY/GC ImagesJacob Elordi might be the reigning menswear muse, but Adults star Innanen is the newcomer to watch. His style skews more playful than Elordi, but he’s just as fluent in the classics – think a green polo under a beige harrington or a striped breton with cream jeans.Good Will Hunting is your film homeworkView image in fullscreenBench mark: Matt Damon and Robin Williams set the scene for classic autumn layers in Good Will Hunting.Photograph: FlixPix/AlamyIf you’re familiar with my seasonal updates, you’ll know there’s always film homework; this autumn, it’s Good Will Hunting. From Matt Damon’s denim, T-shirts and jackets to Robin Williams’s tweedy academia-core, it’s full of inspiration for the months ahead.SevenView image in fullscreenCase study: Brad Pitt and Morgan Freeman in Seven.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyLook past the crime-scene horror and this film is basically a masterclass in outerwear for the transitional months, from Morgan Freeman’s trench to Brad Pitt’s leather coat.As easy as a walk in the parkView image in fullscreenAutumn inspiration: Meg Ryan and Billy Crystal in When Harry Met Sally.It might sound obvious, but the best way to get into the autumnal spirit is to go for a walk in the park. The changing leaves and moody grey skies should give you all the palette inspiration you need.Cuff itView image in fullscreenSleeve note: Prada makes a feature of oversized white cuffs.Photograph: Giovanni Giannoni/WWD/GettyWhere collars have been the main character on recent runways – worn skew-whiff, poking out of blazers and knitwear – autumn/winter 2026 is about cuffs. Look at Prada to see how it’s done: big, oversized shirting with the cuffs folded back over coats or jumpers to create a contrast pop of colour or stripe.Fighting cutsView image in fullscreenCut above: Brad Pitt’s choppy 90s style still looks sharp.Photograph: Frank Trapper/Corbis/GettyTry Brad Pitt’s Fight Club warrior cut on your next trip to the barber. It’s a choppy look that’s still got some length on the side: ask for two to three inches on top and a low taper cut with scissors – and a barber may use a razor blade to create extra texture. Style with a matte clay while it’s wet and follow with a salt spray before scrunching with your hands.On your reading listAdd Tobias Wolff’s Old School to your book pile. Set at a New England boarding school in 1960-61, it has the tweed and atmosphere of Brideshead Revisited without the indulgence.View image in fullscreenOld School by Tobias Wolff£10.99 at the Guardian Bookshop£9.85 at AmazonFor your playlist: Mk.geeGet into the new season zone by listening to Mk.gee, which mixes Bon Iver’s hazy melancholy with Frank Ocean’s slow-burn soul for a sound that’s moody but not miserable. A nice one to listen to on vinyl.View image in fullscreenMk.geeTwo Star & the Dream Policevinyl£37.99 at Rough Trade£33.63 at AmazonFor your watchlist: The BearView image in fullscreenServing looks: Jeremy Allen White in The Bear.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyIf you never got around to watching The Bearbefore it finished, now is the perfect time to binge. And not just for the high-intensity kitchen drama, but for the style: workwear jackets, gold chains and white T-shirts, including the now-famous215 by German heritage label Merz b Schwanen, which the show helped turn into a cult favourite overnight.Worn identityView image in fullscreenWear and tear: Austin Butler gives the white T-shirt a lived-in look.Photograph: John Phillips/GettyDistressed T-shirts are on the up –Gallery Dept sells them with built-in holes and stains for hundreds of pounds(not a typo), but you can get the same look for free by digging out your old tees and roughing them up a little. For style cues, see Austin Butler, whose pieces seem to be genuine vintage rather than anything bought new.For more, read thebest white T-shirts for menandthe best men’s shirts for every occasionPeter Bevan is a stylist and fashion journalist covering menswear, womenswear and beautyExplore more on these topicsMen's fashionThe FilterAccessoriesMen's topsMen's trousersMen's coats and jacketsMen's shoesWatchesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sofia Coppola: ‘I’m glad we weren’t kicked out of Tokyo making Lost in Translation’ | Sofia Coppola | The Guardian
description: The director talks about what she learnt from her mother, working with a rookie Tim Burton, and 20 years of her cult classic Marie Antoinette
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: The director talks about what she learnt from her mother, working with a rookie Tim Burton, and 20 years of her cult classic Marie Antoinette
Content: ‘Even painful memories are part of making you who you are’ … Sofia Coppola at the Venice film festival in 2025.Photograph: Abaca Press/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Even painful memories are part of making you who you are’ … Sofia Coppola at the Venice film festival in 2025.Photograph: Abaca Press/AlamyFilm & Music reader interviewSofia CoppolaInterviewSofia Coppola: ‘I’m glad we weren’t kicked out of Tokyo making Lost in Translation’As told toRich PelleyThe director talks about what she learnt from her mother, working with a rookie Tim Burton, and 20 years of her cult classic Marie AntoinetteThu 8 Oct 2026 09.16 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 12.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHello, I’m Cherry, I’m 14 and an aspiring film-maker. I love how your films capture what it feels like to be a young girl growing up. We hear so much about the famous men in your family, but how have the successful women in your family inspired and influenced you? Your films capture the experience of what it is to be a young girl in a way words often can’t.CherryEmmaThat’s nice to hear, thank you. I feel like I got a lot from my mom about being true to yourself, following what you’re interested in and seeing the beauty in your surroundings. My mom always noticed odd details in life, so a lot of my films are made up of those kinds of things.View image in fullscreenSofia Coppola behind the scenes while making Marie Antoinette.Photograph: Sofia CoppolaYour films beautifully capture the isolation of hotel rooms – spaces completely detached from a character’s past or future. If you were forced into that stillness and could choose to preserve only one cherished memory while erasing another for ever, what would they be?Malpractice1It’s hard to pick a memory, but recently we had a party in Versailles for the anniversary of Marie Antoinette and New Order played. When they started playing Ceremony [from the soundtrack] and the lights went on, I just know that in the future when I have to remember a happy memory, that’s going to be it. Even painful memories are part of making you who you are, and you learn from them, so I can’t think of anything I would erase.I heard that some ofLost in Translationwas filmed guerrilla-style due to a lack of permits. Which scene carried the biggest risk of getting you arrested? What if you had been kicked out of the country?catchytitledWe had permission for most of it, but we had to grab the scenes with Scarlett [Johansson] on the subway with real people around. The same with the overhead shot of her at that famous Shibuya crossing – we just went into Starbucks because it had this incredible view, but we would have never got permission to film there. So we stole a few things in the spirit of guerrilla film-making. And I’m glad we didn’t get kicked out, yes.View image in fullscreenThe Virgin Suicides (1999): clockwise from left, Kirsten Dunst, Leslie Hayman, Chelse Swain and AJ Cook.Photograph: American Zoetrope/AllstarWhat was the dynamic like between the five girls behind the scenes onThe Virgin Suicides? For instance, which girls were the closest, who was the loudest, who was the quietest, etc?Imogen067Their personalities did kind of emerge. We did rehearsals where we all hung out together and had them interact as a family and they cooked together. They hung out off set and they started to bond. Chelse Swain was the most eccentric one.View image in fullscreenKirsten Dunst and Jason Schwartzman in Marie Antoinette (2006).Photograph: Sofia CoppolaThe postmodern soundtrack in Marie Antoinette, all that post-punk and new romantic music, was so audacious that it took your film to a staggering level of artistry. What was the original idea behind bringing those two worlds together?Dmitry_SWhen I first started reading about Marie Antoinette in Antonia Fraser’s book, I was struck by how young she was. She was 14 when she came to Versailles and around 18 when she became queen. So I really wanted to convey that she and Louis were teenagers, and I thought back to the new romantic music I was listening to when I was a teenager. I was lucky that I had a big brother who exposed me to good music at a young age. I wanted to show it through that filter of Bow Wow Wow and Adam Ant. When the film came out, some people were offended because it just wasn’t usual to put contemporary music in a period film.Your 2003video fortheWhite Stripes’ cover of I Just Don’t Know What to Do With Myselfhas been rated byRolling Stone as one of the sexiest music videos ever. What other ideas were considered before you landed onKate Moss pole dancingfor three minutes?McScootikinsOh, wow, I didn’t know that. That’s so cool. I don’t know where it came from. It was just my idea, and I was glad that everyone was on board with it. I just asked Kate to do that, she said yes, and the band was into it.Are you aware that you’re a girlblogger icon?sleepy_nymI don’t know that much about bloggers, but that’s nice to hear. I’ll have to ask my teenage daughters. I do appreciate that my work was made a while ago, so it’s great that it connects with young women of this generation.View image in fullscreenSofia with her father, Francis Ford Coppola, at Cannes film festival in 1979.Photograph: Gilbert TOURTE/Gamma-Rapho/Getty ImagesWhat was it like working onTim Burton’s 1984 short film Frankenweenie, beforeTim Burtonwas “Tim Burton”?jasonaparkesThat was such a fun experience. I was 12 or something. I think Tim Burton was right out of school. It was an early short film, so it was really fun to meet him and be on his set – he used to do drawings for me. I’d spent a lot of time on my dad’s film sets, so it was fun to be on someone else’s. I still like to visit film sets. I’m never jaded – I’m still impressed by movie magic.Didn’t you mind having your mum filming behind the scenes for all those hours when you were making Marie Antoinette?Dr_J_A_ZoidbergMy mom always had a grounding mom presence. It was a stressful shoot, so it was nice to have her there. She also appreciated all the beauty of the costumes and the details of the food and the flowers, so it was fun to show it to her, and she was really into filming all the details and how it was made. I forgot about the footage until recently and I didn’t realise how much there was. My mom had almost 80 hours of footage, so it was a real treat to have this home movie to revisit. I never thought we would do something with it.View image in fullscreenBill Murray and Scarlett Johansson in Lost in Translation (2003).Photograph: Focus Features/AllstarYou’re not going to answer this – but someone has to ask it anyway. WhatdoesBob whisper toCharlotteat the end ofLost in Translation?rolleyesI like what Bill [Murray] always says. He says, “It’s between them,” so I’ll leave it at that.Making Marie Antoinette, directed by Eleanor Coppola, is in UK cinemas from 23 October and streams on Mubi from 6 NovemberExplore more on these topicsSofia CoppolaFilm & Music reader interviewTim BurtoninterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Supermarket shake-up: why Asda or Morrisons could vanish within a decade | Supermarkets | The Guardian
description: Talks between Sainsbury’s and Morrisons have set industry tongues wagging, with analysts saying the market is ripe for change
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: Talks between Sainsbury’s and Morrisons have set industry tongues wagging, with analysts saying the market is ripe for change
Content: Morrison’s or Asda –or both – could disappear within a decade.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMorrison’s or Asda –or both – could disappear within a decade.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianSupermarketsSupermarket shake-up: why Asda or Morrisons could vanish within a decadeTalks between Sainsbury’s and Morrisons have set industry tongues wagging, with analysts saying the market is ripe for changeTesco lifts profit forecast and says shoppers are resilientSarah ButlerThu 8 Oct 2026 06.26 EDTFirst published on Thu 8 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThey may be two of the most recognisable brands in Britain, with a combined 188 years serving shoppers, but industry watchers agree that either Asda orMorrisons– or both – could disappear within a decade.This week, it emerged that Sainsbury’s and Morrisons – the UK’s second- and sixth-largest supermarket chains – hadheld merger talksbetween last November and February, before the larger player decided to walk away.News of the potential deal has relaunched speculation that the UK grocery market is now ripe for consolidation and revealed that the Sainsbury’s boss, Simon Roberts – who has been in post for six years – is at least willing to consider the possibility of buying one of his troubled rivals.Morrisons is not a must-do deal for Sainsbury’sRead moreSainsbury’s, which has 600 supermarkets and almost 900 convenience stores, has until recently been seen as wary of trying to revive merger talks with its rivals afterits bid to buy Asda for £7bn in 2019 was blocked.However, industry experts sayAsdaand Morrisons’ owners have held informal talks with each other – and both with Sainsbury’s team – and predict that talks could restart.“The three of them, one way or another, are talking to each other,” one said. He suggested that a combination of Asda and Morrisons could happen but was likely to be a weaker deal than a Sainsbury’s takeover of either, as both businesses struggle with costs and interest on debt piles.Competition fears easeThe industry has undergone significant change since the collapse of the Sainsbury’s-Asda deal. While riding the wider retail trends towards online shopping and convenience stores, the supermarket groups have been jockeying for market share.Aldi is poised to overtake Asda to become the UK’s third-largest supermarket, with less than 1 percentage point separating them. Aldi is rapidly opening stores while Asda has struggled to find growth since a£6.8bn, debt-fuelled takeoverin 2020 and heavy price competition from the discounters and from its bigger rivals Tesco and Sainsbury’s.View image in fullscreenAldi is poised to overtake Asda to become the UK’s third-largest supermarket.Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/ReutersAnother big change could emerge this month when the UK’s competition watchdog is due to publish its final ruling on whether Aldi and Lidl should now officially be classified as “large grocery retailers” likeTesco, Sainsbury’s, Asda and Morrisons.In August, theCompetition and Markets Authority(CMA) said it had found provisionally that Aldi and Lidl no longer qualified as “limited assortment discounters” as they now carry a “full range” of groceries and operate stores larger than 1,000 sq m (10,700 sq ft) across the UK.The change means the German-owned discounters are now taken into account when assessing competition in different locations.This is the strongest hint yet that the CMA has changed its stance blocking the Sainsbury’s buyout of Asda on the basis that shoppers would be worse off.It also indicates that the CMA’s “balance of competition” – its estimation of the impact of a deal based on drive times for customers around stores – has shifted, meaning Sainsbury’s might have to dispose of dozens fewer stores to gain regulatory clearance for a merger. A figure of 150 was suggested when it tried to buy Asda.Clive Black, an analyst at Shore Capital and Sainsbury’s broker, says the CMA preliminary ruling indicates “the shape of the pitch has adjusted a little” and “the change encourages another chapter of consolidation”.It is a step-change from 2019 when analysts accused thesingingformer Sainsbury’s boss Mike Coupe and his board of directors of “arrogance” and “folly” for pursuing Asda. Now they say that consolidation is almost inevitable.That comes amid what is seen as a more welcoming regulatory environment backed by the UK government’s growth agenda combined with theappointmentof Doug Gurr, a grocery industry veteran who has spent time at Asda and Amazon, to lead the CMA.Sainsbury’s holds the cardsOne analyst described Sainsbury’s as the “kingmaker” in any industry consolidation as it uniquely has the resources to snap up a rival without the market dominance to immediately prevent any deal.Analysts agree it is unlikely to face significant competition if it opts to buy Morrisons or Asda –Tesco is too big to buy a rival, while Marks & Spencer and Waitrose appear unlikely to have the financial firepower or desire to pursue such a deal.Amazon should not be ruled out as a player in consolidation, according to one analyst, who said the online specialist might be prompted into action by any of the supermarkets announcing plans to merge.View image in fullscreenAmazon’s foray into the grocery business didn’t go welland it shutall 19 of its Fresh stores.Photograph: Zuma Press/Alamy“The last cards are coming on to the table,” he said, suggesting that Amazon might consider buying Asda, Morrisons or even Sainsbury’s, now that it had effectively disposed of Argos which may have caused competition concerns for Amazon.However, Amazon has not fared well with its dip into high street retail. Last year, itdecided to closeall 19 of its Fresh stores, with plans to convert five of them into shops under its Whole Foods Market brand.As analysts at Bernstein put it: “We believe that scale is the most important source of advantage in grocery retail, and the combined market share of Sainsbury’s and Morrisons would improve Sainsbury’s ability to take on Tesco.”The logic of a deal for Morrisons’ American private equity owner is clear. Clayton, Dubilier & Rice has few options for an exit, four years on from its £7bn acquisition of the Bradford-based chain.Private equitybidders are not likely to be lining up, as there is little room for a another debt-fuelled buyout, while pursuing a stock market flotation would require a compelling growth story to lure investors but which is now absent.The heavy debts taken on to fund CD&R’s acquisition in 2022 have left Morrisons struggling to compete as interest rates have risen, pushing up costs, while competition has toughened as pinched households look to save costs on their grocery bill.Clearly, the CD&R adviser and former Tesco boss Terry Leahy is unlikely to let Morrisons go cheaply – with price demands ultimately understood to have led Sainsbury’s Roberts to walk away from any deal.However, Morrisons hasfallen backto be the UK’s sixth-largest supermarket with an 8.4% market share, just behind Lidl on 8.7%, according to the latest data from the industry analysts Worldpanel by Numerator.A ‘sweetheart deal’Asda’s owners, led by the British investment firm TDR Capital, may also welcome a tidy exit although they are likely to be happier to wait, having largely made their money selling off various parts of the grocer’s assets, industry insiders say. Under the returning boss, Allan Leighton, there are nascentsigns of a turnaroundif the owners are willing to sit tight and hedoes not appear keenon reviving talks with Sainsbury’s.For Sainsbury’s, the appeal is cost-savings derived from larger scale. The combination of Sainsbury’s and Morrisons would hold 23.6% of the UK market and add 500 supermarkets and 1,600 conveniencestores to its portfolio – taking it closer to Tesco’s 27.8% market share. Buying Asda would take it to about 26.7%.View image in fullscreenAny motivation for Sainsbury’s comes from the potential cost-savings that a scaled-up merger would bring.Photograph: Bloomberg/GettyOne industry expert said a combination with Asda was the “sweetheart deal” because it would not only bring larger scale but involve fewer stores serving the same customers in the south of the country.The main benefit of any deal would come from cost-savings garnered from combining central operations, such as buying and property management, and aligning supplier terms.Asda’s bigger supply chain brings greater potential savings and it is arguably a less complicated acquisition than Morrisons, which operates a large food processing business which Sainsbury’s would probably want to dispose of to a variety of specialist suppliers.One issue is that businesses cannot seek pre-approval for a deal from the CMA, so launching a formal takeover offer for either Morrisons or Asda would involve an element of risk – consuming management time, and costly fees for bankers and lawyers.As one industry expert says, “the critical argument is the role of the discounters” and the CMA’s rulings do not always follow the expected path. “It’s a lottery,” he said.Analysts at Bernstein also say that “despite the benefits of a possible deal, the risk of distraction for Sainsbury’s would be high”.The industry insider says: “Sainsbury’s is best served by being patient” as Asda and Morrisons are likely to continue to struggle. “There comes a point when the CMA has no choice but to let something happen as [Asda and Morrisons] can’t compete. You could argue that is already the case.”This article was amended on 8 October 2026. An earlier version said that Sainsbury’s is unlikely to face significant competition if it opts to buy “Sainsbury’s or Asda”; that should have said Morrisons or Asda.Explore more on these topicsSupermarketsAsdaRetail industryMorrisonsAldiMergers and acquisitionsCompetition and Markets AuthoritynewsShareReuse this content

title: What would make your life easier? Martin Lewis asks public for ‘small ideas’ to improve UK | Martin Lewis | The Guardian
description: Finance expert launches Small Ideas Initiative to gather ‘practical, low-cost’ ideas to put before cross-party panel
Author: Rosie Peters-McDonald
Headline: Finance expert launches Small Ideas Initiative to gather ‘practical, low-cost’ ideas to put before cross-party panel
Content: Lewis said he wanted to ‘fix some of the frustration points’ in everyday life.Photograph: Ken McKay/ITV/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenLewis said he wanted to ‘fix some of the frustration points’ in everyday life.Photograph: Ken McKay/ITV/ShutterstockMartin LewisWhat would make your life easier? Martin Lewis asks public for ‘small ideas’ to improve UKFinance expert launches Small Ideas Initiative to gather ‘practical, low-cost’ ideas to put before cross-party panelRosie Peters-McDonaldThu 8 Oct 2026 13.29 EDTFirst published on Thu 8 Oct 2026 12.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEvery day, people run into what the finance expert Martin Lewis calls “the life-potholes of unintended consequences” – clunky systems and poorly conceived rules that make life harder than it should be. His latest project, theSmall Ideas Initiative, will attempt to address that, with a cross-party panel of politicians and policymakers crowdsourcing ideas for everyday fixes to take to government.The ideas could cover anything from health and schools to policing, tech and money. Lewis is encouraging people to submit ideas for “practical, low-cost, non-controversial ways to improve the UK” before 12 November.“If we can fix some of those frustration points, we can make people’s lives easier, save time and help everyone get on with work or the things they enjoy,” said Lewis.“There’s just a sense that there’s so many little things to fix,” said Polly Mackenzie, who worked with Lewis to come up with the idea. Mackenzie, who was director of policy to Nick Clegg during his deputy premiership, says the initiative could be an avenue to regaining trust in public institutions.“I think this is about rebuilding confidence in the idea that government can sort stuff out, rather than rebuilding confidence on any one political party having the right ideas,” she said.View image in fullscreenNo such thing as a rubbish idea: bins were on the brain for some Londoners.Photograph: UK Stock Images Ltd/AlamyMackenzie will sit on the panel, which will choose about 50 ideas to take to the government, councils and regulators. Alongside Lewis, the initiative is run by the innovation charity Nesta and the public participation charity Involve.The Reform MP Danny Kruger, the former Conservative MP Penny Mordaunt, and the Labour mayor of West Yorkshire, Tracy Brabin, are among those sitting on the panel alongside Mackenzie. She said the group had “a real interest and capability in getting involved and sweating the small stuff”.The ideas they are looking for will be “no-brainers” that are not party-political and would be easy fixes. Mackenzie said a good example was when she and Lewis first set up the Money and Mental Health Policy Institute and discovered through a survey that GPs had been charging to fill out debt and mental health evidence forms.“People in debt crisis were having to pay 80, 100, 150 quid to get forbearance for their debts, which is just wrong-headed,” she said. In 2019, two years after the Money and Mental Health Policy Institute started its campaign, the law changed.View image in fullscreenMacKenzie and Lewis in 2016, on the launch of the Money and Mental Health Policy Institute.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianBefore the initiative’s launch, people in north London shared the policies they would consider submitting. Clare, a railway worker, suggested the government should increase rubbish collections during heatwaves, saying her bins had been “a buffet for flies” this summer. Mark, who works on a market stall, said he would ask the government to put more bins in and around train stations. “There are no bins. I know it’s for security reasons, but I think they could find a way,” he said.Kwajo Tweneboa, a social housing campaigner who will also sit on the deciding panel, said relatively small changes could make a “massive difference”.“One small change I’d like to see is housing providers aiming to fix repairs properly, rather than repeatedly applying plaster fixes that don’t address the underlying problem and prolong the misery for tenants,” he says. “I’ve seen how something that should be a straightforward repair can drag on for months, with residents having to repeatedly chase their landlord while the problem gets worse.“It’s about listening to those everyday experiences and turning simple, practical ideas into policy that can make a tangible difference to people’s lives.”Explore more on these topicsMartin LewisConsumer affairsLocal governmentPublic services policynewsShareReuse this content

title: NHS at risk of ‘system failures’ as demand for ADHD and autism care soars, inquiry finds | NHS | The Guardian
description: England-focused review led by Prof Peter Fonagy returns stark warning and calls for shift to ‘needs-led’ system
Author: Denis Campbell
Headline: England-focused review led by Prof Peter Fonagy returns stark warning and calls for shift to ‘needs-led’ system
Content: The review found the number of people suffering mental distress has risen sharply across all age groups in England since the 1990s, especially under-18s.Photograph: Johner RF/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe review found the number of people suffering mental distress has risen sharply across all age groups in England since the 1990s, especially under-18s.Photograph: Johner RF/Getty ImagesNHSNHS at risk of ‘system failures’ as demand for ADHD and autism care soars, inquiry findsEngland-focused mental health review returns stark warning and calls for shift to ‘needs-led’ systemExplainer |What has the Fonagy review found and what does it recommend?Analysis |No ‘snowflakes’: mental health review says today’s youth have it harder and harms are realDenis CampbellandAnna BawdenThu 8 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 19.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe NHS inEnglandis heading into a “world of system failures” as it struggles to cope with relentlessly rising demand for mental health, ADHD and autism care, leaving those affected desperate for support, a government-commissioned inquiry has found.The stark warning was made in a review led by Prof Peter Fonagy into the sharp rise in demand over recent decades for help with mental health and neurodevelopmental conditions.It found there was an increasing risk of overdiagnosis of autism and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and urged ministers to toughen the regulation of the private clinics to which many people are turning because they cannot get assessed quickly by theNHS.The experts behind the review also called for access to care to be based primarily on a person’s needs so fewer people would have years-long waits for a formal diagnosis.NHS England mental health services review: what has it found and what does it recommend?Read moreThe review found that the number of people suffering mental distress has risen significantly across all age groups in England since the 1990s, especially the under-18s.The number of 16- to 64-year-olds with a common mental disorder increased from 15.5% in 1993 to 22.6% in 2024. However, it jumped more sharply – from about one in six to one in four – among 16- to 24-year-olds over the same period.The evidence shows that sceptics are wrong to cast doubt on young people’s struggles, the 607-page report found.“That’s sometimes been attributed to personal failures, people being told they’re making it up, it’s all in their head, which is absolute nonsense,” said Prof Simon Wessely, a leading psychiatrist and vice-chair of the review.The report’s conclusions may have significant implications for the government’s drive to reduce the number of young people in the UK not in education, employment or training – now almost 1 million – and the size of the welfare bill, with a record 2.8 million people too sick to work; and also for schools as they grapple with the demands arising from the growing number of pupils with special educational needs.Fonagy, a psychoanalyst and clinical psychologist at University College London,dismissed the notion that young people in particular were “snowflakes”who were less resilient than in previous generations. “The rise in mental health problems is real, is affecting everyday functioning and cannot be explained by greater awareness alone,” his report said.He lamented that an array of social and economic circumstances had piled unprecedented pressure on young people. “There is increased uncertainty – financial pressures, insecure work, unaffordable housing – but perhaps more important, a lack of hope among young people that their lives will be better than their parents, and that’s the first time since the second world war that surveys have noticed that.”The explosion in demand for help with mental ill-health and neurodiversity has left people stuck on waiting lists for years at a time and with worsening symptoms, Fonagy said. At the end of last year more than 560,000 people in England were waiting to be assessed for ADHD – 17 times more than were doing so in 2019. Another 254,000 people were waiting for a diagnostic assessment for autism, taking the total number waiting to more than 800,000. Almost all – 90% – had been waiting for at least three months.Chart showing percentage of UK NHS patients with an active recorded ADHD diagnosis within a five-year window, by age group and from 2000 to 2025Chart showing percentage of UK NHS patients with an active recorded autism diagnosis within a five-year window, by age group and from 2000 to 2025The number of six- to 11-year-olds being diagnosed with autism has also soared. It jumped 20-fold to 4.58% between 2000 and 2025 and by even more among those aged 12 to 17 over the same years, from 0.1% to 4.06% – a 40-fold jump. And the proportion of children aged six to 11 with an ADHD diagnosis has increased more than sixfold in five years and more than 15-fold in 12- to 17-year-olds, to 2.7% and 3.9% respectively.While 4 million children already suffer from “high psychological distress’’, if current trends continue, that could reach 4.5 million by 2030, the report warned. The number of under-18s who self-harm could also rise from 1.9 million to 2.5 million.Chart showing projected numbers of mental health cases by condition by 2030The exponential rise in diagnoses of autism and ADHD means the UK has reached a “tipping point” where people are at risk of being misdiagnosed with either condition, Wessely warned.The authors did not find that overdiagnosis was occurring at scale, but added that the evidence “suggests we are entering a phase in which the balance of risks between underdiagnosis, misdiagnosis and overdiagnosis may be changing, with the risks of misdiagnosis and overdiagnosis becoming increasingly important considerations for policy and service delivery”.The increasing tendency of young people to self-identify as neurodivergent – as many as a fifth of secondary school pupils do so – means that “the line between the social and the medical is beginning to blur”, they added.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionChart showing percentage of self-reported cases of autism, ADHD or other neurodivergence by school yearThe 10-month review found “strong concerns about the consistency and quality of ADHD and autism assessments being carried out by independent providers, and the financial incentives associated with assessment activity”.Ministers should ban direct-to-public advertising of such services and ensure that all clinics offering them are regulated by the Care Quality Commission, it said.Growing numbers of young people have a combination of mental ill-health and ADHD or autism, or both. “Co-occurence is the rule rather than the exception,” the report said. For example, 61% of 16- to 24-year-olds with a common mental health condition also had autistic traits, and 57% had ADHD symptoms.Graph showing percentages of 16- to 24-year-olds with a common mental health condition and ADHD or autism from 2007 to 2004Graph showing percentage of 16- to 64-year-olds with one, two or three mental health or neurodevelopmental conditionsThe report said their needs meant the NHS should bring together mental health and neurodevelopmental services and move to a “needs-led” system.The Royal College of Paediatrics and ChildHealthbacked Fonagy’s call for diagnosis to no longer dictate who received care.“Too often, a diagnosis is the only route to accessing meaningful help. This means that children and families can be left struggling alone while waiting for assessments, with little or no support available in the meantime,” said Dr Ronny Cheung, its officer for health services.The NHS moving to a “needs-led” approach would “ensure children and young people can seamlessly and more quickly access a robust, holistic and reliable standard of care”, he added.Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, will draw on Fonagy’s recommendations in putting together the forthcoming mental health strategy, which is due by the end of the year.In her response, she promised that the NHS would provide a “needs-led” system under which people would get much faster care. She has asked NHS England to establish how it can provide faster advice, assessments and treatment.She said: “It is clear that mental health services need to change to focus more on the early support young people need to stay in education or work or keep their lives on track.”She also pledged to ensure all private assessment clinics are regulated but did not commit to the advertising ban Fonagy said was needed.Explore more on these topicsNHSMental healthAttention deficit hyperactivity disorderAutismHealthNeurodiversityChildren's healthnewsShareReuse this content

title: A lake pilgrimage and a quiet car ride to the beach: last hours of sisters who took own lives in Brighton | Brighton | The Guardian
description: Inquest hears details of how three women spent their last days but why they ended their lives may never be known
Author: Esther Addley
Headline: Inquest hears details of how three women spent their last days but why they ended their lives may never be known
Content: Jane Adetoro (left), Christina Walters and Rebecca Walters (right) with their father, Joseph Jacobson.Photograph: PAView image in fullscreenJane Adetoro (left), Christina Walters and Rebecca Walters (right) with their father, Joseph Jacobson.Photograph: PABrightonA lake pilgrimage and a quiet car ride to the beach: last hours of sisters who took own lives in BrightonInquest hears details of how three women spent their final days but why they ended their lives may never be knownEsther AddleyThu 8 Oct 2026 13.19 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 14.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJane Adetoro and her younger sisters, Christina and Rebecca Walters, were “the closest sisters and the best friends”, according to their family. Devoted to their father, Joseph, whom they messaged every day, the adult siblings lived quiet lives in the flat they shared in westLondonand would do everything together.When they died in May this year, it was no different. Early in the morning of 13 May, the sisters’ bodies were recovered from the sea inBrighton, hours after a taxi had dropped the three women at the beachfront.On Thursday, an inquest in the city found that the women, who all drowned,died by suicidea day after making a pilgrimage together to the lake in Birmingham where their mother died by drowning 16 years earlier.In a statement, Joseph Jacobson told the inquest that the scale of his loss was indescribable. “There are no words that can adequately express the pain of losing a child. To lose all three of my precious daughters, Jane, Christina and Rebecca, is a heartbreak beyond anything I could ever have imagined.”Jacobson, who attended the inquest by video link, said he could not understand why their lives had ended so suddenly. “You were my daughters, you will always be my daughters and I will love you for the rest of my life. May your beautiful souls rest in perfect peace,” he said.Precisely why Jane, 36, Christina, known as Tina, 32, and 31-year-old Rebecca, or Becky, decided to end their lives may never be known, the senior coroner Penelope Schofield told the hearing at Woodvale coroner’s court in Brighton.“These three sisters lived very secluded lives. They were incredibly private. We don’t know why they took this course of action or indeed why they chose to do it in Brighton,” Schofield said.View image in fullscreenFlowers laid at Brighton beach in May after the sisters’ bodies were found.Photograph: Anahita Hossein-Pour/PAWhat police were able to establish, after initial public bafflement over the circumstances of the tragedy, is how the women spent the day before they died. On the night of 11 May, the sisters travelled by Uber from their home in Greenford, west London, to Birmingham, where they were dropped off at 11.36pm in Linton Walk, in the north of the city.This was the address where Jane and Rebecca, then 20 and 15, were living with their mother, Janice Adetoro, when she disappeared on 5 January 2010, prompting an anguished public appeal by family members. (Christina, then 16, was reportedly living with her father at the time.) Janice’s body was recovered a month later from Brookvale Park Lake, which runs to the end of Linton Walk. She was 43.Described as a doting mother, Janice had been suffering from “paranoid delusions”, the inquest into her death heard. She was sectioned and admitted to a psychiatric unit, the Sunday Times reported, but was discharged from a home treatment team weeks before her death.The tragedy of the sisters’ deaths “wasn’t a story that started in May”, their cousin Natalie Walters-Danieltold the newspaperlast month. “It was a story that started long before.”DCI Mark Cullimore, of Sussex police, told the inquest there was no CCTV to show what the three sisters did in the time they were in Birmingham, but less than two hours after arriving, at 1.28am on 12 May, they were picked up by taxi and driven back to their London flat.The inquest heard that Christina, who had recently graduated from Brunel University of London and worked as an accountant, had experienced anxiety and depression since her mother’s death and made “extensive searches” about suicide in the days before her own death.Jane, who was also an accountant, had paid off a loan in full on 11 May. Described as “extremely intelligent”, Jane was said by family members to have taken on a maternal role after the death of her own mother.Rebecca, “the baby” to relatives, worked in HR. She was previously described as “mischievous” and “the lively one who was always cracking jokes”.The two younger sisters had changed their names to their mother’s maiden name after her death. “Their mother’s death was a hard thing to carry and bear,” their cousin said. “They held a certain level of their feelings to themselves … I believe it was their own coping mechanism.”View image in fullscreenThe sea was particularly rough on the night of the sisters’ deaths, the inquest was told.Photograph: Charlotte Coney/Getty ImagesOn the evening on 12 May, the inquest heard, the three women caught a train to Brighton, arriving at 10.20pm, and then took a car to the beachfront near the marina. The Uber driver was struck by the lack of conversation between them, he later told police.Sussex police reviewed hundreds of hours of CCTV to establish that for at least four hours the women paced the seafront in the darkness. They were picked up periodically in snatches of footage, last being seen at 2.42am. It was a windy night and the sea was particularly rough, Cullimore told the inquest.Emergency services were called after a cyclist reported seeing a body on the beach shortly before 5.45am. Jane was brought to shore by an RNLI crew and declared dead at the scene. Christina’s body was also located by the lifeboat crew. Rebecca’s body was recovered from Brighton beach where it appeared to have been washed to shore. None of the women had been able to swim.Cullimore told the inquest he had “remained open-minded throughout and always considered whether there was third-party involvement” but he was now satisfied there had not been. There was no evidence that any of the sisters had used drugs or alcohol, and no indication of any violence.The coroner found that all three had intended to die. “I will record in respect for each of them that on 12 May they entered the sea at West Beach, Brighton, to end their lives,” she said. “They could not swim and the conditions were adverse.”In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsBrightonLondonEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Search warrants used in Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor raids were unlawful, court rules | Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor | The Guardian
description: ‘Technical errors’ are embarrassing for Thames Valley police but unlikely to affect outcome of investigation
Author: Haroon Siddique
Headline: ‘Technical errors’ are embarrassing for Thames Valley police but unlikely to affect outcome of investigation
Content: King Charles stripped Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor of his right to be a prince and of his dukedom over his association with Epstein.Photograph: ShutterstockView image in fullscreenKing Charles stripped Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor of his right to be a prince and of his dukedom over his association with Epstein.Photograph: ShutterstockAndrew Mountbatten-WindsorSearch warrants used in Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor raids were unlawful, court rules‘Technical errors’ are embarrassing for Thames Valley police but unlikely to affect outcome of investigationHaroon SiddiqueandVikram DoddThu 8 Oct 2026 12.23 EDTFirst published on Thu 8 Oct 2026 09.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndrew Mountbatten-Windsor has won his legal challenge against Thames Valley police over search warrants used to raid his home after they arrested him.The former prince brought a judicial review of the legality of the force’s actions and those of the central criminal court, which granted the warrants.On Thursday, Mr Justice Hilliard, sitting at the high court in central London, said Thames Valley police (TVP) had conceded that it obtained the search powers under the wrong statutory provision and ruled that the warrants were unlawful.The episode is embarrassing for TVP but police believe it will not affect the success of the investigation.The warrants were issued by an Old Bailey judge on 18 February and Mountbatten-Windsor was subsequentlyarrested the following day, on his 66th birthday, on suspicion of misconduct in public office.The arrest followed information that emerged from theJeffrey Epsteinfiles. It was alleged that when Mountbatten-Windsor was the UK’s trade envoy he shared sensitive information with Epstein, a convicted child sex offender.Police began searching the former Duke of York’s residence on the Sandringham estate and his former Windsor home, Royal Lodge, on the same day as his arrest. Documentary material and electronic devices were seized.Hilliard said the search warrants were quashed but police had made an application, which would be heard next year, to retain the seized property on the basis that it would have been lawful to take it under a different statutory provision. Mountbatten-Windsor opposes that application.The judge said: “The fact that the search warrants were quashed does not bring the investigation to an end or mean that the whole of the investigation is unlawful.”A senior police source said: “It’s not going to bring the investigation to a halt or affect the chances of success.”They added: “The news media might say the police messed up. But it was the judicial decision [to grant the warrant] that was incorrect.”View image in fullscreenPolice officers patrolling near to Royal Lodge, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor’s former residence in Windsor Great Park, on 19 February.Photograph: Leon Neal/GettyTVP have been in discussions with lawyers from the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) about the strength of their case and what evidence they would need for a prosecution.A TVP spokesperson said: “The agreement that led to the quashing of the warrants relates specifically to a decision made by the court regarding the legal basis for these and is not a judgment on our ongoing investigation.“We ensured the court was presented with all the necessary information and paperwork to inform their decision, following the correct legal processes throughout.“We accept the position that the initial court’s decision to issue warrants under the specific piece of legislation used was incorrect and therefore these must be legally quashed.”Hilliard told the court that the grant of a search warrant under section eight of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act (Pace) 1984 was conditional on the issuing judge being satisfied there were reasonable grounds to suspect that the material sought did not include items subject to legal privilege or special procedure material.Special procedure material includes documents in possession of a person who acquired them in the course of any trade, business, profession or other occupation – for the purpose of any paid or unpaid office – who holds it subject to an express or implied undertaking to hold it in confidence.The judge said the presence of legally privileged material was expressly envisaged in the application for the search warrants and that material was likely to be in the possession of Mountbatten-Windsor “who had acquired or created it in circumstances which would make it special procedure material”.
