He concluded that a lawful warrant could only have been issued under section nine of Pace.Nick Vamos, the former head of special crime at the CPS, said: “Given the technical nature of the errors revealed today, I expect the crown court to rule in due course that the police can keep the material, or at least as much of it as they would have been entitled to seize in the first place, so they may not ultimately pay much of a price beyond today’s red faces.”Late last year,King Charles stripped his brother of his right to be a princeand of his dukedom over his association with Epstein.Mountbatten-Windsor receives an annual stipend, the amount of which has not been disclosed, from King Charles’s private funds, but a palace source told reporters it had been made clearthis should not be used to fund the judicial review.Explore more on these topicsAndrew Mountbatten-WindsorPoliceJeffrey EpsteinMonarchyUK criminal justicenewsShareReuse this content

title: Pentagon says execution of Fort Hood shooter will be livestreamed | Pete Hegseth | The Guardian
description: Nidal Hasan, army psychiatrist who killed 13 people, will be executed by firing squad on 3 December
Author: Joseph Gedeon
Headline: Nidal Hasan, army psychiatrist who killed 13 people, will be executed by firing squad on 3 December
Content: Pete Hegseth announces a new navy shipyard in Baltimore on Tuesday.Photograph: Anna Rose Layden/EPAView image in fullscreenPete Hegseth announces a new navy shipyard in Baltimore on Tuesday.Photograph: Anna Rose Layden/EPAPete HegsethPentagon says execution of Fort Hood shooter will be livestreamedNidal Hasan, army psychiatrist who killed 13 people, will be executed by firing squad on 3 DecemberJoseph Gedeonin WashingtonThu 8 Oct 2026 19.18 EDTFirst published on Thu 8 Oct 2026 17.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePete Hegseth has said the execution of Nidal Hasan, the former army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, will be a public event when the sentence is carried out later this year. A defense department official later confirmed the execution will be livestreamed.In an interview with Real America’s Voice, the Pentagon secretary said the firing squad will carry out the sentence at Fort Hood, Texas, at 1pm on Thursday, 3 December. This would be the firstUS militaryexecution in more than 60 years.“It was a radical Islamist attack in uniform inside the ranks, and so he’s going to get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be, and we’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth said.Hasan opened fire at a medical processing center on the Texas base on 5 November 2009, killing 13 people and wounding dozens more. A military jury sentenced him to death in 2013, and he has been held at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas ever since. He exhausted his appeals last year, which cleared the way for Donald Trump to approve the sentencethis weekon a recommendation from Hegseth.Investigators had found that Hasanhad exchanged 18 emailswith Anwar al-Awlaki, a radical cleric who was subsequently killed in a US drone strike, in the months before the attack. At his court martial, Hasan said he had acted to stop American soldiers from deploying to Afghanistan to kill fellow Muslims, before his own impending deployment. A review led by William Webster, a former FBI director, concluded that the bureau should have investigated his correspondence more thoroughly.In the interview, Hegseth said Barack Obama had called the attack “workplace violence”. The Pentagon initially treated the shooting as a workplace-violence incident rather than a terrorist attack, aclassificationthat affected the victims’ eligibility for Purple Hearts and other combat-related benefits.But there is no record of Obama himself using the phrase. At a memorial days after the attack, he instead described the victims as Americans who had been unable to escape “the horror of war”, while calling the shooting a tragedy and saying the killer would face justice.The last known case of a military firing squad in the US was inNovember 1945, but the Trump administration has sought to bring it back in Trump’s second term to expedite capital punishment cases. Five US statesallow for firing squads: Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah.Abroad, Amnesty International’smost recent annual reviewlists Afghanistan, China, North Korea, Saudi Arabia, Somalia, Taiwan, the United Arab Emirates and Yemen among the countries that still use firing squads.Asked whether Hasan had made a final request or reached out to Trump, Hegseth replied: “Don’t care. We’ll see him on December 3.”Explore more on these topicsPete HegsethFort Hood shootingsUS militarynewsShareReuse this content

title: Two Latvian men arrested at RAF base in Cambridgeshire used by US military | UK news | The Guardian
description: Men aged 32 and 36 detained on suspicion of trespass, causing criminal damage and entering a prohibited place
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Men aged 32 and 36 detained on suspicion of trespass, causing criminal damage and entering a prohibited place
Content: A police car leaving RAF Molesworth after the two men were arrested.Photograph: Chris Radburn/ReutersView image in fullscreenA police car leaving RAF Molesworth after the two men were arrested.Photograph: Chris Radburn/ReutersUK newsTwo Latvian men arrested at RAF base in Cambridgeshire used by US militaryMen aged 32 and 36 detained on suspicion of trespass, causing criminal damage and entering a prohibited placeDan SabbaghDefence and security editorThu 8 Oct 2026 17.27 EDTFirst published on Thu 8 Oct 2026 11.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo Latvian men were arrested in the early hours of Thursday after they were discovered inside the perimeter of RAF Molesworth, a Cambridgeshire base used by the US military and Nato for intelligence operations.The men, 32 and 36, were picked up at 2am inside the base, in an investigation that began four hours earlier when military police discovered an abandoned vehicle outside the facility.Military police, helped by officers from Cambridgeshire police, discovered a small hole in the perimeter fence before finding and arresting the men, initially on suspicion of trespass on a prohibited site and causing criminal damage.The suspects, Latvian nationals currently resident in the UK, were then further arrested on suspicion of an offence under section 4 of the National Security Act 2023 – namely entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK.Counter-terror police are now leading the investigation due to the nature of the incident, which comes a few days after the US withdrew B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire amid concerns about a possible Iran-directed attack.Commander Helen Flanagan, head of counter-terrorism policing London, said there was nothing at this stage to suggest a connection to September’s incident near RAF Fairford, but said investigators were yet to determine what the men had been doing.“Our investigation into this incident is at its very early stages. A big part of this is looking at any potential motivation as to why the men were present at the site, but I must stress we are keeping an open mind at this stage and inquiries are very much ongoing,” she added.Investigators said it was unclear at this stage if there was a hostile state link to the men’s presence on the base, if they were criminals or whether they had ended up on the site in a misjudged state of late-night exuberance.The abandoned vehicle was taken to a nearby police location. Initial searches led concerned officers to call in explosives specialists to carry out further checks, though nothing concerning was understood to have been found.A police cordon was also briefly imposed on part of the A1 south of Peterborough and around the village of Glatton, as a precaution, but has been lifted. Officers were carrying out two searches at addresses in the Peterborough area in connection with the investigation, counter-terror police added in a statement.Both men remained in police custody on Thursday.RAF Molesworth is home to Nato’s Intelligence Fusion Centre, which provides military intelligence to Nato, and the US Joint Intelligence Operations Center, Europe, which provides similar service for the US military’s European command, though not Centcom, which is responsible for Iran.View image in fullscreenThe two Latvian nationals were arrested after breaching the perimeter fence of the military base.Photograph: Ryan Jenkinson/Getty ImagesThe head of the armed forces, Air Chief Marshal Sir Richard Knighton, said he had “confidence around the safety and security of our bases” as he visited troops on a military exercise in Wales earlier on Thursday.The chief of defence staff cited the “enormously close relationships from an intelligence perspective and operationally with the US” as reasons for his confidence, but said the US had removed its bombers from Fairford as a precaution.“The decision to remove the bombers, which don’t ordinarily live there … to take them back was an operational decision to reduce the risk,” he added. The bombers were suddenly redeployed on Sunday, amid reports that the US feared Iran could orchestrate a drone attack on B-1 planes on the ground.British sources remain sceptical that Iran would have the capability to launch an attack of such sophistication, though the investigation into why five men driving three white vans descended on a village next to Fairford continues.Mark Rowley, the Met police chief, said the public would “see more progress on this investigation”, and urged them to trust the police as they worked with spy agencies MI5, GCHQ and intelligence partners internationally.The five men arrested near RAF Fairford, all British nationals in their 20s from London, have been released on police bail without charge, as has a sixth, a dual UK-Iranian national, who was arrested subsequently.A seventh man, aged 22, who was arrested on Wednesday on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts, was also let out on bail on Thursday.Rowley acknowledged the threat landscape appeared to have changed. “We’re dealing with an increased tempo of terrorists and also of threats that are directed by foreign states such as Iran and Russia,” he said in a radio interview.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: French ministers scramble to appease students after 10 days of protests | France | The Guardian
description: Education minister promises 3,000 substitute teachers by Tuesday with schools still blockaded across France
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: Education minister promises 3,000 substitute teachers by Tuesday with schools still blockaded across France
Content: Students on the July Column in the Place de la Bastille during protests in Paris on Thursday.Photograph: Teresa Suárez/APView image in fullscreenStudents on the July Column in the Place de la Bastille during protests in Paris on Thursday.Photograph: Teresa Suárez/APFranceFrench ministers scramble to appease students after 10 days of protestsEducation minister promises 3,000 substitute teachers by Tuesday with schools still blockaded across FranceJon Henleyin ParisThu 8 Oct 2026 17.47 EDTFirst published on Thu 8 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHigh school students have again blockaded schools and marched through cities acrossFrance, promising to continue their campaign against the poor state of the national education systemin the 10th day of protests that have left hundreds injured.Large crowds took to the streets on Thursday for mainly peaceful demonstrations in cities including Lille, Rennes, Nantes, Lyon, Toulon and Marseille, while in Paris a large procession marched through the city centre to the Place de la Bastille.An estimated 25,000 students thronged the square in the east of the capital, with some climbing the monument at its centre, which commemorates France’s 1830 July revolution, while waving the tricolour flag and singing the Marseillaise.As the evening drew in, riot police fired teargas and crowd-dispersal rounds and carried out repeated baton charges to clear the protesters, some of whom hurled bottles, paving stones and other projectiles at the heavily armoured squads.View image in fullscreenA protester kicks away a teargas canister during a demonstration in the Place de la Bastille.Photograph: Julien de Rosa/AFP/Getty ImagesEliane, 16, a pupil on the Paris march, said she had come to “defend and encourage high schools in an even worse state than mine”, calling the march “magnificent”. She said she planned to continue protesting until concrete progress was achieved.The education minister, Édouard Geffray, told TF1 television on Thursday night that 3,000 substitute teachers would be deployed to about 100 high schools identified as having particularly acute teacher shortages “between tomorrow and Tuesday”.Geffray said he would also authorise the recruitment of “several hundred” new teachers. The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said the government would propose amendments to the 2027 budget to “translate some of the students’ demands into concrete measures, particularly regarding teacher replacements”.View image in fullscreenCrowds gathering at the Place de la Bastille earlier on Thursday.Photograph: Abdul Saboor/Reuters‘This is state violence’: Paris students rage at politicians and heavy-handed policingRead moreStudents earlier said the government’s reaction was not sufficient. Ryad Rani, the president of one high school students’ union, said the protesters had heard “no concrete measures whatsoever, no response to our demands”. The movement “will continue”, he said.Sabrine Kharbach, from another students’ association, said the protest, over teacher shortages, long school hours and dilapidated buildings, would last “for as long as €10bn hasn’t been put on the table”, the amount students and some leftwing politicians have said needs to be urgently invested in France’s schools.According to an Elabe poll ​for BFM TV, 72% of French people think the students’ demands are legitimate but 55% of them think the protests should stop. Unions called for another national day of action in support of the students next Tuesday.View image in fullscreenA protester reading a book as teargas is sprayed by police during a blockade near Hélène Boucher high school in Paris on Thursday.Photograph: Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP/Getty ImagesThe education ministry said fewer high schools had been forced to close than in recent days, with 224 shut on Thursday morning and 157 by lunchtime, meaning that about 95% of the country’s high schools were at least partly open.But more than 71,000 protesters took to the streets on Thursday, the interior ministry said. The demonstrations, backed by many teachers, parents and unions, involved further clashes with police around some school barricades in Paris. In Rennes riot officers used water cannon to disperse protesters.A prominent complaint on student banners and placards was the heavy-handed police response to the wave of protests. “Too young to be listened ​to, but old enough to be teargassed,” read one banner on the Paris march.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenBurning bins during a blockade of a school in Toulouse on Thursday.Photograph: Lionel Bonaventure/AFP/Getty ImagesOver the past two weeks, some demonstrators have set dustbins on fire outside their schools, destroyed bus shelters and hurled projectiles at riot police, who have responded using batons, teargas and riot-control rounds.At least 215 teenagers, 89 school staff and 761 police officers have been injured since the start of the protests, which were triggered by chronic teacher shortages, crowded classes,dilapidated buildingsand long school days.The Guardian view on the French school protests: the political class needs to heed the voice of students | EditorialRead moreThe government on Wednesdaysuspended the use of stun grenadesby police after a teenager’s hand was blown off, while saying it was “excessive” to speak of “police repression” and denying that officers had “orders to confront” the young protesters.View image in fullscreenProtesters clash with French gendarmes in Nantes on Thursday.Photograph: Stéphane Mahé/ReutersThe protests have rocked a government caught between popular demands for investment in deteriorating public services and pressure from markets to reduce France’s ballooning budget deficit and debt mountain, among the highest in the EU.The economy minister, Roland Lescure, said this week there was room to address demands for more school resources in the 2027 budget. In the current draft, schools have the second-largest funding increase after defence, with a 1.4% hike to €90.9bn.Six months away from a crucial presidential election to replace Emmanuel Macron, politicians are jockeying to exploit the protests, with the far-right frontrunner, Marine Le Pen, highlighting the damage to schools and calling for parents ⁠to foot repair bills.Her hard-left opponent, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, has praised the protesters ​as “incredible” and denounced police brutality.Explore more on these topicsFranceProtestEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: New Ofsted inspection regime damaging teachers, survey says | Ofsted | The Guardian
description: Nine in 10 school heads who responded say inspections still ‘negatively affected’ staff mental health
Author: Richard Adams
Headline: Nine in 10 school heads who responded say inspections still ‘negatively affected’ staff mental health
Content: School leaders called the survey results a ‘damning indictment’ of Ofsted’s attempts to reform.Photograph: PAView image in fullscreenSchool leaders called the survey results a ‘damning indictment’ of Ofsted’s attempts to reform.Photograph: PAOfstedNew Ofsted inspection regime damaging teachers, survey saysNine in 10 school heads who responded say inspections still ‘negatively affected’ staff mental healthRichard AdamsEducation editorThu 8 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSchool inspections inEnglandcontinue to damage the mental wellbeing of teachers and senior leaders, according to a survey commissioned by Ofsted that casts doubt on efforts to reduce the stress caused by inspectors’ visits.The independent survey of school leaders who had undergone the revised inspections since last year found that 88% said it had “negatively affected” the mental wellbeing of school staff, including 29% who said it affected them “a lot”.England school inspections to be overhauled again after barrage of complaintsRead moreSchool leaders called the results a “damning indictment” of Ofsted’s attempts to reform after a coroner’s finding in 2023 that anOfsted inspection contributedto the mental health deterioration and death of headteacher Ruth Perry.The Guardianreportedlast week that education secretary Lucy Powell wants Ofsted to “go back to the drawing board” after hearing complaints that the new format was stressful and damaging to teachers’ mental health.Martyn Oliver, Ofsted’s chief inspector, said: “The data published today shows that we are on the right track. We are inspecting first and foremost in the interests of children and maintaining high standards, while at the same time improving the experience for the hard-working professionals in our nurseries, schools and colleges.“I know that workload and wellbeing in education continue to be challenging, and I don’t take that lightly. We will keep listening to feedback from professionals and parents alike as we continue to improve what we do.”But Pepe Di’Iasio, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, said: “It is extremely serious that the health of so many educators is being undermined and we do not understand how [Ofsted’s] chief inspector Sir Martyn Oliver can then say the system is on the right track. This is clearly not the case.View image in fullscreenLucy Powell, the education secretary.“The feedback that we receive from our members shows a devastating toll on wellbeing and several have told us they will leave the profession before undergoing another Ofsted inspection. These are highly experienced and resilient professionals who will be lost to the education system.”Paul Whiteman, general secretary of the National Association of Head Teachers, said the wellbeing and workload findings “should stop everyone in their tracks”. He urged Ofsted to release the full survey data rather than a summary.“Ofsted is once again trying to put a positive spin on a truly terrible situation, showing the profession why it cannot be trusted,” he said.“The evidence is clear that the framework is still creating unacceptable levels of pressure, workload and stress. It is a damning indictment – certainly not a vindication.”Fewer than one in four schools agreed to be surveyed after their inspections, leading the authors, IFF Research, to note that its findings had limitations.View image in fullscreenDaniel Kebede, NEU general secretary.Ofsted highlighted the results from all categories, including childminders and further education providers, showing that six out of 10 respondents said their inspection would help them improve.More than three-quarters of those inspected under the new approach said it had been conducted respectfully, collaboratively and empathetically, while a similar proportion said the inspections “successfully identified” their best elements.But Daniel Kebede, general secretary of the National Education Union, described the overall results as “rose-tinted,” and added: “Lucy Powell has indicated a readiness to review.“We want to see a new system that is more supportive, but also fair and effective. It is what the profession is crying out for.”Explore more on these topicsOfstedSchoolsTeachers' workloadMental healthEnglandLucy PowellEducation policynewsShareReuse this content
