title: Israel’s downgrading of UK consulate aims to tighten its hold on Jerusalem | Israel | The Guardian
description: Consulate targeted in sanctions spat has unusual diplomatic status that clashes with Israel’s ambitions to fully annex the city
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: Consulate targeted in sanctions spat has unusual diplomatic status that clashes with Israel’s ambitions to fully annex the city
Content: The consulate general’s diplomats are part of an independent team who report directly to London.Photograph: Abir Sultan/EPAView image in fullscreenThe consulate general’s diplomats are part of an independent team who report directly to London.Photograph: Abir Sultan/EPAIsraelAnalysisIsrael’s downgrading of UK consulate aims to tighten its hold on JerusalemEmma Graham-Harrisonin JerusalemConsulate targeted in sanctions spat has unusual diplomatic status that clashes with Israel’s ambitions to fully annex the cityThu 8 Oct 2026 13.16 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 13.40 EDTShareIsrael’s attempt to close the British consulate general in Jerusalem was primarily designed to deter London from imposing sanctions on settlements in occupiedPalestine. But it also served the current government’s ambitions to fully annex Jerusalem as a national capital, diplomatic and legal experts said.The UK mission to the city has an unusual diplomatic status, which dates back to before the founding of the state ofIsrael, rooted in a vision of Jerusalem as a neutral enclave under international control.Unlike other consulates general around the world, it is not a satellite of the British embassy in Tel Aviv. Instead its diplomats are part of an independent team, who report directly to London.British consulate in East Jerusalem will stay open as UK mission, says Ed MilibandRead moreThat is anathema to those in Israel who claim all of Jerusalem as their territory. Israeli forces occupied East Jerusalem in 1967, and the Knesset passed a law annexing the city in 1980, but that status has not been recognised by most of the world.Gideon Sa’ar, the Israeli foreign minister, threatened to close the consulate general a month ago in an attempt to deter the UK government from proceeding withplans to bar trade with West Bank settlementsand put sanctions on companies that provide them with services including financing.The UK threatened to respond with amass expulsion of diplomatsbut the two countries appear to havebacked away from a full-blown diplomatic spatas Israel prepares for national elections, due on 27 October.Britain will rebrand its consulate general ⁠as a UK “mission” and reduce the number of diplomats, but it will remain independent of Tel Aviv in a compromise one source described as a temporary “ceasefire”. If Israel gets a new leader in three weeks, negotiations on the status of the consulate and its staff could resume.Maintaining a foothold in Jerusalem and the independent status of UK diplomats was important, said Daniel Seidemann, an Israeli lawyer and expert in the geopolitics of Jerusalem who hasadvisedwestern diplomats including a British foreign secretary.“The arrangement that the UK arrived at with Israel was probably the optimal among a number of options that were even worse. So I’m not faulting anybody, but this is far from a victory,” he said.“The British presence in Jerusalem after almost a century and a half has been downgraded from one of the diplomatic mission to another office. And that is a stark qualitative change.”View image in fullscreenMaintaining a foothold in Jerusalem and the independent status of UK diplomats was important, one expert said.Photograph: Mostafa Alkharouf/Anadolu/Getty ImagesThere are seven other consulates general in East Jerusalem, all opened before 1948, representing their nations’ interests in Jerusalem and occupied Palestine. Like the UK one, they are independent and report directly to their foreign ministries.They have long been a particular thorn in Israel’s side because of their unusual status, which reflects the designation of Jerusalem as “corpus separatum”, an independent body, under the UN’s 1947 partition plan for historic Palestine.Never implemented, it envisaged Jerusalem as a sort of Vatican-like independent enclave, under international administration. That clashes with Israel’s claim on the city, and Sa’ar’s attack on the consulate should be seen in that context, and not purely as a response to sanctions.“This is part of the overall attempt to establish the primacy of a very specific Jewish-Israeli Jerusalem,” Seidemann said. “Any diplomatic presence in Jerusalem that does not pay fealty to the government of Israel and Israel’s sole sovereignty is targeted.”Other countries have missions based in Ramallah to manage relations with Palestinians, but these are technically subsidiary to Tel Aviv embassies.The US had a consulate general but closed it after Donald Trump recognised Jerusalem as the capital of Israel during his first presidency.The UK sanctions plan represents the most consequential attempt by one of Israel’s allies to halt settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank. Israeli banks are rattled by a proposal they fear could affect their business, Haaretzreportedon Thursday.An assessment by Israel’s Association of Banks laid out concerns that they could be affected, and they are refusing to say whether they will provide financial guarantees needed to underpin construction contracts for theE1 settlement in the West Bank.When Ed Miliband, the UK foreign secretary, announced his plans, he said the timing was driven partly by the Israeli government’s decision to put out tenders for this project. Israel’s finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, has boasted that it will “bury” the possibility of a Palestinian state by severing parts of the occupied West Bank.Ilan Baruch, a former Israeli ambassador to South Africa, left diplomatic service to advocate for a two-state solution, including pushing foreign governments to move beyond condemnations of Israeli policy to imposing a “meaningful price”.The threats to Britain’s Jerusalem consulate were a sign the UK had finally done that. “I was relieved [by Israel’s position], realising Miliband touched a nerve,” he said.Renaming the consulate while preserving its independent status indicated Israel had stepped back from confrontation, helped by Britain making smaller “face-saving” concessions, he said.Explore more on these topicsIsraelForeign policyPalestineMiddle East and north AfricaanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Can Sánchez convince Spanish voters he is their best hope for fairer housing? | Spain | The Guardian
description: Recent death of 87-year-old woman likely to focus attention on crisis in run-up to election at end of November
Author: Sam Jones
Headline: Recent death of 87-year-old woman likely to focus attention on crisis in run-up to election at end of November
Content: A housing protest camp in Puerta del Sol in Madrid, Spain, on Thursday.Photograph: Borja Sanchez-Trillo/EPAView image in fullscreenA housing protest camp in Puerta del Sol in Madrid, Spain, on Thursday.Photograph: Borja Sanchez-Trillo/EPASpainAnalysisCan Sánchez convince Spanish voters he is their best hope for fairer housing?Sam Jonesin MadridRecent death of 87-year-old woman likely to focus attention on crisis in run-up to election at end of NovemberThu 8 Oct 2026 08.16 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 18.38 EDTShareEven beforeMaría del Carmen Abascal died on Wednesday night, a mere fortnight after hereviction from the Madrid flatwhere she had lived for most of her life, the frail 87-year-old woman had become the enduring face of Spain’s housing crisis.Her plight – and the wider issue it embodied – had led to street demonstrations, the creation ofa protest camp in the middle of the Spanish capital, and spurred the socialist-led government to propose emergency measures to facilitate and protect access to housing. Whenrightwing and far-right parties voted down those measuresin congress last week, the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, responded by announcinga snap general electionfor the end of November.View image in fullscreenFlowers and candles are placed in memory of María del Carmen Abascal at a housing protest camp in Puerta del Sol, Madrid, on Thursday.Photograph: Borja Sanchez-Trillo/EPAAbascal’s death now looks set to focus even more attention on housing in the run-up to that election and, in particular, on whather lawyer has called“the shameful violence of these types of evictions and the evident impact and consequences they can have on people’s health”.With more than42% of Spaniards identifying access to housing as their main worryand withrents having risen by 80% over the past decade, the most pertinent question may be: why has it taken the eviction of an octogenarian and the accompanying protests to shake Spain’s political class into action? To which the answer could be that, despiteyears of protests against overtourism and gentrification, the tipping point had not been reached. Now, arguably, it has.On Thursday, Spain’s state centre for sociological researchpublished pollingthat showed that 76.3% of those surveyed were in favour of the state intervening in the market “as much as necessary to guarantee everyone’s access to housing”, while 79% believed housing should be prioritised as a constitutional right.Sánchez’s socialist-led government is keen to persuade voters that it is the only political force that cares about rents and tenants’ rights – hence the emergency measures, which have been redrafted into two new decrees after their defeat in parliament last week. The 21 measures include facilitating renting or buying a new home; extending eviction protections for vulnerable residents; prohibiting speculative real estate purchases, and granting tax breaks to property owners and tenants who pay on time.View image in fullscreenPedro Sánchez: ‘a matter of simple common sense; a matter of humanity’.Photograph: Burak Akbulut/Anadolu/Getty Images“These are measures that, if I may say so, are a matter of simple common sense; a matter of humanity,” the prime minister said on Tuesday. “They unite small property owners and tenants while standing up to vulture funds, precisely because they target only those who view housing merely as a commodity for speculation.”The measures come almost three years after the prime ministerpromised to build 184,000 affordable public rental homes. His government has also sought to address soaring housing prices by introducinga law allowing authorities to cap “disproportionate” rent prices in some areas.Those who had voted down last week’s decrees, Sánchez said, had done so despite studies showing the measures enjoyed “cross-cutting support that transcends ideology”, adding that the public was in favour of regulating “a dysfunctional market”. He is now hoping that at least one of the decrees will be passed by congress’s permanent council, a special body that operates when parliament is not in session. Its approval could go some way to convincing voters that his administration is taking the housing issue seriously.View image in fullscreenThe leader of Spain’s right-wing opposition People’s party, Alberto Núñez Feijóo (centre), has promised to address the crisis despite his party voting against the proposed measures last week.Photograph: Antonio Sempere/AFP/Getty ImagesOthers disagree. Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party, which voted down the measures last week, has said it is a bit late for Sánchez, who has been prime minister since 2018, to suddenly appoint himself Spain’s housing champion.“Housing has been the big failure of this government but will be the success story of the one that follows it,” he said on Monday. Feijóo, whose party is leading the polls, added: “When a prime minister has been in power for eight years, it’s hard to blame others for what he’s failed to do.” The PP has promised to address the crisis by building 200,000 homes a year, lowering taxes and cutting down on bureaucracy.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHowever, the PP’s decision to side with the far-right Vox party and the rightwing Catalan pro-independence Junts party to fell the measures has left it looking less than committed to the issue of the day. Sánchez and his allies will be hoping that fact will not be lost on voters as the election campaign kicks off and as trade unions prepare a general strike over housing for 11 November.Mindful, perhaps, of the distance between his words and his party’s voting history in congress, Feijóo called for people not to manipulate Abascal’s death to suit their own purposes.“No campaigning, no political parties, no partisan ends, no more bricks in the wall,” he said on Wednesday night. “When a person dies there should be nothing but respect.”View image in fullscreenMigrants try to make their way past police officers in Ceuta after mass crossings on foot and by sea at the end of July from Morocco into Spanish territory.Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/ReutersAnd yet, despite the primacy of housing as an issue, Feijóo opted to start his campaign in Spain’s North African territory of Ceuta, where at least 141 people died astens of thousands tried to cross overfrom neighbouring Morocco at the end of July. The Spanish government’s handling of the mass crossing, which saw about 80,000 people enter Ceuta, has been criticised at home and abroad. Speaking in the territory on Wednesday, Feijóo promised that its safety would be at the “top of [the] in-tray” if he became prime minister.Vox, meanwhile, has responded to Absacal’s death by posting footage of a TV interview in which she said she held Sánchez responsible for what had happened to her. The far-right party accused the socialists of using “the suffering of an elderly person to stage a campaign to hide the government’s responsibility in the housing disaster”. It also suggested that Sánchez had visited “ruin and death” on Spain in the form ofthe floods that killed 230 people in Valencia two years ago, last year’snationwide power cut, thedeadly train crash in southern Spain in January, and recent events in Ceuta.Explore more on these topicsSpainEuropePedro SáncheznewsShareReuse this content

title: Rent review – Jonathan Larson’s New York bohos move into the West End and unpack their passions | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Stranger Things’ Gaten Matarazzo leads the grief-stricken 90s musical about friends living under the threat of Aids
Author: David Jays
Headline: Stranger Things’ Gaten Matarazzo leads the grief-stricken 90s musical about friends living under the threat of Aids
Content: A nebbish bearing witness … Gaten Matarazzo (centre) and the cast of Rent.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA nebbish bearing witness … Gaten Matarazzo (centre) and the cast of Rent.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianTheatreReviewRent review – Jonathan Larson’s New York bohos move into the West End and unpack their passionsTom Stoppard theatre, LondonStranger Things’ Gaten Matarazzo leads the grief-stricken 90s musical about friends living under the threat of AidsDavid JaysThu 8 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIs Rent one of the musical greats? It’s a forever fan favourite – this new production extended its run even before the official opening – and its origin story holds a special place in theatre-kid hearts.Jonathan Larson, Rent’s creator, died just before the off-Broadway premiere in 1996, aged 35 – a poignant echo of its raggle-taggle bohemians in New York, living fast and fearing death will come before their time.This production is developed by director Luke Sheppard (Paddington: The Musical) from his versionat Manchester’s Hope Mill theatre. With onstage seating circling the space, Sheppard cradles the piece in community, knitting together the story’s hopeful vagabonds. Actors watch between scenes, harmonising and dancing in their chairs. The cast even form something close to a prayer circle for the imperishable Seasons of Love.We’re in a grungy New York – even Howard Hudson’s light design looks grey and gritty. Everyone layers up against winter in thrift store coats, boots and berets, while the choreography (Tom Jackson Greaves) catches the hard-knock city in rucking elbows and weaving hips. Candles wink in jam jars, tiny lights against the harsh, dark chill.View image in fullscreenFractious situationships … Travis Ross and Lazy Violet.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianIt’s the story of La Bohème, kinda – taking a friendship circle of artists and wannabes from meet-cute in a power cut to last-act misery, riffing off Puccini’s sob-stringed melodies. Romances flare and falter, ambitions compromise, Aids is an ever-present anxiety.Gaten Matarazzo(Stranger Things) plays narrator Mark, a nebbish bearing witness to his pals’ shenanigans with a Super 8 camera (footage plays around the stage). He observes fractious situationships between his bestie Roger (a snarling Travis Ross) and lost Mimi (Alexa Lopez); between his heedless ex Maureen (Lazy Violet) and Joanne (Danielle Fiamanya, preppy, goofy).View image in fullscreenLives lost too soon … Jeevan Braich in Rent.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianLoss steals into these young lives too soon. Part of the wrench of Seasons of Love is that kids shouldn’t have to keep toll of time (“Five hundred, twenty five thousand, six hundred minutes”) – they should see the moments stretch ahead of them. Instead, when Jeevan Braich’s shining drag queen dies, her lover falls into elegy – Billy Nevers’ lost, husky growl fills the air with grief.Franz & Marie review – Woyzeck folk musical finds heart amid the horrorRead moreThis show gives good value to Larson the composer – the band gunning through the score up on a gantry, the cast unleashing some rib-shaking vocals. Larson the lyricist emerges less well, engulfed by a wall of sound. The revival is produced with devotion but, nudging three hours, also needs dramaturgical tough love. Some lachrymose ballads don’t earn their stage time, while Maureen’s dairy-based activism (“Moo for me!”) has lost its bite. Keeping eight principal characters in play is tricky – Mark too often fades from his own story.The glory of the show is its songs – the bolshie ensembles and scared solos. Larson threw everything into Rent, from wrenching anthems and witty tango to strutting pop. He must have hoped to have more musicals ahead of him, but wrote like he was running out of time – that desperate sense to write the songs, love the love and live the life is the urgent heart of the show.AtTom Stoppard theatre, London, until 29 MayExplore more on these topicsTheatreMusicalsWest EndAids and HIVreviewsShareReuse this content

title: A teen tried to navigate Canadian mountains with Claude. His trek ended in an emergency rescue | Canada | The Guardian
description: The incident is the latest to raise questions about the growing reliance on digital maps for wilderness navigation
Author: Leyland Cecco
Headline: The incident is the latest to raise questions about the growing reliance on digital maps for wilderness navigation
Content: Hiker rescued from climb of Canada’s Widowmaker Arete.Photograph: North Shore RescueView image in fullscreenHiker rescued from climb of Canada’s Widowmaker Arete.Photograph: North Shore RescueCanadaA teen tried to navigate Canadian mountains with Claude. His trek ended in an emergency rescueThe incident is the latest to raise questions about the growing reliance on digital maps for wilderness navigationLeyland Ceccoin TorontoThu 8 Oct 2026 15.31 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 18.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe route up the Widowmaker Arete, a 1,700-foot wall in British Columbia, is deceptively described as “mostly easy slab climbing”, interspersed with “short steep sections that can include finger cracks, blocky face climbing”. It requires careful planning, and the right equipment.When 16-year-old Bryce Vincent Gowryluk found himself facing its sheer headwall last week, he had neither. He did, however, ask theAIchatbot Claude for directions.Last week, Gowryluk had to be rescued after those directions proved wildly incorrect, in the latest incident to raise questions about the growing reliance on digital maps for wilderness navigation.On Saturday morning, Gowryluk took a gondola up to the top of Grouse Mountain and, while ascending,asked Claude to plan a routeto nearby Crown Mountain and back. After navigating scree and more than 2,000ft of elevation gain, the summit promises 360-degree panoramic views of Greater Vancouver, the Fraser valley and the Capilano watershed.Typically, the trek takes eight hours and hiking guides warn it is not for beginners.As Gowryluk, a keen indoor climber, navigated down the Crown Pass and up through Crater Slabs and into a boulder-strewn valley, the directions from Claude took him away from the planned course.He found himself at the final headwall of the Widowmaker Arete – a climb that requires ropes, cams and a clear plan for ascent. As he climbed, Gowryluk soon realized the terrain was far too steep and that he was stuck at the base of a cliff. He phoned his mother, then called emergency services for help.Police notified North Shore Rescue, which sent a helicopter, but Gowryluk was too close to the rock face for the rotors, so two members of the rescue team were hoisted down to lift him up. He was flown to the rescue base near the Cleveland Dam.In their debrief the rescue crew said Gowryluk was “far off” his intended route. While the incident is believed to be the first time a hiker has been lost because of AI, it isthe latest in a string of mishapsin the mountainous region of south-western British Columbia, where hikers increasingly rely on imprecise mapping directions.In July, three people were rescued after they planned a route on the Howe Sound Crest Trail using Google Maps, which gave them wildly inaccurate time estimates, suggesting a route that often takes as long as 14 hours could be done in just over five.Search manager Paul Markey warned that mountaineers should not rely on the directions of artificial intelligence, and that proper prepartion was key.“In this particular case, the boy had a headlamp. He had good clothing. He had he had a good pair of boots, spare battery and spare food. He was was pretty well equipped for hiking and scrambling. But he was certainly not prepared or equipped for rock climbing,” Markey said.“Claude in this particular situation, has never been in the area that this 16-year-old boy found himself in. Claude can only go so far with regard to describing what the area may be like.“There’s definitely a trend towards using electronic applications as opposed to map and compass skills. But is really no substitute for the good map and compass training and education.”He noted that in some cases apps give too much information. “We have found that some of the apps have identified trails in areas where, really, our preference as a rescue team would be that those trails or routes are not actually identified,” he said, adding that people see routes they think are good trails only to get into difficulty.“The main thing is: do not blindly rely on a on AI as as a route planning tool. It can never substitute for good education, good training, a good experience, good decision making in the field.”Explore more on these topicsCanadaAmericasAI (artificial intelligence)featuresShareReuse this content

title: Animals review – Ben Affleck’s dull Netflix thriller is lacking in bark and bite | Ben Affleck | The Guardian
description: Actor-director’s listless LA-set crime thriller makes for a surprisingly anonymous effort and one that feels very similar to many other, better films
Author: Jesse Hassenger
Headline: Actor-director’s listless LA-set crime thriller makes for a surprisingly anonymous effort and one that feels very similar to many other, better films
Content: Kerry Washington and Ben Affleck in Animals.Photograph: Warrick Page/NetflixView image in fullscreenKerry Washington and Ben Affleck in Animals.Photograph: Warrick Page/NetflixBen AffleckReviewAnimals review – Ben Affleck’s dull Netflix thriller is lacking in bark and biteActor-director’s listless LA-set crime thriller makes for a surprisingly anonymous effort and one that feels very similar to many other, better filmsJesse HassengerThu 8 Oct 2026 19.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 19.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBen Affleck has pushed through multiple Hollywood comebacks, at least one predicated on his facility behind the camera, directing Boston-based thrillers both artistically ambitious (Gone Baby Gone) and juicily crowd-pleasing (The Town). So now that his acting career seems particularly stable, as he works steadily and produces movies via the company he founded with longtime friend and collaborator Matt Damon, why does his directing career remain in what seems like post-Oscar doldrums? (Though he has never been nominated for a best director Oscar, his film Argo won best picture in 2013.) His new movie Animals appears perfectly situated within his wheelhouse: it’s a Los Angeles-based crime-and-politics thriller to match his earlier east coast work. The real surprise, however, is just how listless it can get.The Social Reckoning review – Aaron Sorkin’s jittery sequel with all-new evil puppet ZuckerbergRead moreAffleck himself plays Mark Kimball, a Angeleno running for mayor of his home town. His status as an independent non-party-affiliated candidate (and one who scarcely exhibits a trace of a platform in what little we see of his stump speeches and interviews) is only one element of his unlikely backstory, which also includes history as a teacher, a lawyer and a veteran of the first Gulf war. (Not sure the math on all that checks out, but let’s allow it as evidence of a fusion between Mark’s dedication to service and a rapacious ambition.) He’s leveraged his family’s wealth to take him through the home stretch of a close campaign, and tensions are medium-high with his wife, Abby, (Kerry Washington), who’s hiding some problems of her own. Things get considerably worse when, on Halloween, he receives a phone call: Kidnappers have taken his preteen son Denny (Christopher Woodley). They’re demanding $7m that Mark doesn’t have to get him back safely.Mark and Abby both panic, but still find time to disagree about how, precisely, to handle this nightmare scenario. They’re especially divided on whether or not to heed the advice of Mark’s right-hand man Sam (Steven Yeun), who advocates employing a mysterious unnamed fixer (Gillian Anderson) – which itself will also cost the Kimballs plenty of money they will not get back unless Mark wins the election (which in turn involves him attending a crucial campaign event inconveniently scheduled on Halloween night). All the ingredients – starry cast; ticking clock; complicated dilemmas centered on money, power, and ambition – are in place for a high-toned thriller, even if it is on Netflix with a few stray theatrical engagements.And then, once Affleck gets his ducks in a row … very little. For a movie that attempts to position Mark as both a product and a potential savior of Los Angeles, shockingly much of Animals takes place on Mark and Abby’s property, in a series of dull rich-folks rooms. It’s the kind of environment usually fit for a stage production, and the actors certainly play to the cheap seats – especially Washington, who can overact a whisper if called upon to do so. But the screenplay by Affleck, Billy Ray, and Connor O McIntyre doesn’t lend much substance to any of the arguments. Some secrets are revealed, then turn out not to matter. Mark, Abby and Sam talk in irritated circles. The kidnapper keeps calling, using voice modulation that makes him sound like Jigsaw. Only Anderson, resplendent in an all-white suit, has settled on whether this thriller is serious business or pulpy fun. (She chooses the latter, probably wisely though not particularly in sync with anyone else on screen.)One particular mid-movie plot turn so closely aligns Animals with another recent kidnapping thriller, Spike Lee’s Kurosawa remake Highest 2 Lowest, that those who have seen Lee’s movie may drop their jaws in disbelief. Of course, this movie was likely written and maybe even shot before Affleck would have seen that film, but someone involved in this production must have seen Kurosawa’s original High and Low, nicking just enough for the story to count as homage rather than an outright redo. There’s nothing wrong with that on its face, but Animals has shockingly few ideas about how to transpose the material into a different city, time period or milieu. It may not be an entirely fair comparison, but it’s hard to think of Lee’s bravura ransom-drop sequence set on a long subway ride traversing Manhattan without suppressing laughter at the obligatory Los Angeles river-basin standoff that serves as the newer film’s all-wet climax. If Affleck has any greater insight into Los Angeles politics than the most basic and bludgeoning messaging of the film’s final moments, he’s kept it to himself, or cut it out of a movie that runs about 100 minutes without credits.Affleck the actor is still fun to watch, especially playing a politician visibly straining to not look like one – a charismatic guy nonetheless laboring to resemble a narrative version who may be a little nicer and more down-to-earth than he really is. But despite employing ace cinematographer Robert Elswit, who shot Affleck’s The Town as well as There Will Be Blood, among many others, the look of Animals is pretty Netflix-y – slick, lacking in texture and ultimately a bit dull. In other words, Affleck has – presumably by accident – imitated his character. This is a movie that just wants to get the job done with frictionless likability, with seemingly no one inquiring about why.Animals is out on Netflix on 9 OctoberExplore more on these topicsBen AffleckKerry WashingtonGillian AndersonNetflixreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Troye Sivan: She’s the Best review – a strange, singular pop star who deserves to be multiplatinum | Troye Sivan | The Guardian
description: Adored by the A-list and filling arenas, but without huge smash hits, the Australian singer treads his own distinctive path through pop via shoegaze, Balearic and the Smiths
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: Adored by the A-list and filling arenas, but without huge smash hits, the Australian singer treads his own distinctive path through pop via shoegaze, Balearic and the Smiths
Content: Huge profile … Troye Sivan.Photograph: Marcus CooperView image in fullscreenHuge profile … Troye Sivan.Photograph: Marcus CooperAlexis Petridis's album of the weekTroye SivanReviewTroye Sivan: She’s the Best review – a strange, singular pop star who deserves to be multiplatinum(Interscope)Adored by the A-list and filling arenas, but without huge smash hits, the Australian singer treads his own distinctive path through pop via shoegaze, Balearic and the SmithsAlexis PetridisThu 8 Oct 2026 19.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 20.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfew years back, the New York Times reported on the phenomenon of the “middle-class pop star”. The feature bluntly explained that this signified “a pop star who isn’t that popular”, for whom the word signified not commercial dominance, but “a sound, an aesthetic, an attitude”. It isn’t an entirely new phenomenon: you may recall a game late 00s attempt to differentiate critically acclaimed but commercially underground pop artists – Alphabeat, Frankmusik and the Clik Clik among them – from the massed ranks of chart-topping TV talent show graduates by grouping them together under the generic banner of “wonky pop”. But the arrival of social media clearly changed things dramatically, enabling artists who seldom, if ever, encroach on the charts’ upper reaches to develop ferociously loyal – and very online – followings, reliably packed-out shows and a genuine aura of celebrity to go with their good reviews.View image in fullscreenTroye Sivan: She’s the Best album coverTroye Sivan might well be the apotheosis of this phenomenon. Over the last 12 years, his albums have shifted respectable, rather than earth-shattering quantities. Intermittently, the odd single has become a mainstream hit, but their success is vastly outstripped by his profile – arena tours, features in broadsheet newspapers and style magazines, interviews on late night US chatshows – and indeed his standing among huge stars. He has been glowingly written about in Time magazine by Kylie Minogue. Nicole Kidman appears in the video for the title track from She’s the Best. Madonna apparently gave personal approval for him to use a sample from 2000’s Music on another of the album’s singles, Party. He has duetted on hits by Dua Lipa, Ariana Grande and Charli xcx, with whom he co-headlined a US tour just after the release of Brat.The latter is also present on She’s the Best, providing backing vocals on the title track, one of a brace of songs co-produced by her husband, George Daniel. You might also detect her influence in the track’s lyrics, which offer a BFF’s approving description of a very Brat-sounding girl (stained dress, ciggie on the go, “DJs from Wednesday to Monday / Don’t ask, she’s not taking any fucking requests”) and indeed on the deadpan spoken word vocal and wilful, almost aggressive flimsiness of Party. There’s really nothing to Party beyond the aforementioned Madonna sample, and Sivan blankly intoning a list of locations in which a party might theoretically take place.But there ends the resemblance. The lyrics of the title track are set to a shuffling breakbeat, and with its misty synths, flute samples and Charli’s cooing backing vocals, it sounds a little like Foxbase Alpha-era Saint Etienne, not the last time that She’s the Best presents the listener with music that might have slipped on to Top of the Pops in 1991, in between Soho’s Hippychick and Zoë’s Sunshine on a Rainy Day.Both Canada Dry and I Do This for You’s descriptions of a fleeting – and apparently unsatisfactory – online hook-up carry a distinct flavour of the moment the post-acid house Balearic sound intruded on British pop, an intriguing off-message place for a 21st-century artist to alight. Elsewhere, Love So Big It Hurts and Lost Time balance out their straightforward pop smarts with impressively weird arrangements – a layer of abstract noise and bursts of distorted guitar disrupt the former, off-key synths decorate the latter. There’s a beautifully opaque take on acoustic pop on Embarrassingly, with a hint of the Smiths in the mix, substantially prettier than you might expect a song about – and there’s no polite way to put this – having a wank over the thought of your ex-to-be.These are uniformly great, very hooky songs, filled with lyrics that subtly pine for domestic contentment even as they’re hymning the pleasures of no-strings sex: only the drum’n’bass-influenced Troye Meets World, with its noisome sped-up vocal hook, lands flat. After the album ends you’re left feeling slightly frustrated: there seems no reason whatsoever why Troye Sivan should still be a relative cult figure within pop, rather than an actual multiplatinum star.MNEK on writing smash hits, battling self-doubt and his solo struggles: ‘I’m a fat Black gay man. Try selling that’Read moreBut equally, he seems to be using the space he occupies to his advantage, to push and experiment. If he were a huge star, would he be allowed to be as loudly, unapologetically queer as he is here? This is, after all, an album that rhymes “California” with “getting dick just how I wanna”. Would he be more hidebound by expectations that he should come up with more of the same? (There’s an intriguing sense that the more Balearic-facing tracks sound not unlike the album you might have thought Dua Lipa was about to release if you bought the stuff she said in interviews about Radical Optimism being “a pop tribute to UK rave culture” inspired by Screamadelica and Massive Attack.) Would he think twice about counterintuitively burying the choruses of FF and Le Boy under dense waves of shoegazey guitars, however thrilling doing so sounds? Perhaps he’s absolutely fine where he is.This week Alexis listened toMichael Kiwanuka – Summer ClothesThe first taste of Fudge, the swiftly recordedMichael Kiwanuka cut he made before suffering a stroke: piano-led soul that’s looser in feel than usual, but no less lovely.Explore more on these topicsTroye SivanAlexis Petridis's album of the weekPop and rockalbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: A death, a plagiarism scandal and a quest for revenge: the bizarre tale of Otto Z | Germany | The Guardian
description: The long read: After his mother died, Otto became convinced he’d been wronged by the forensic investigators – and that one of them was a fraud. The truth was even stranger
Author: Alessio Perrone
Headline: The long read: After his mother died, Otto became convinced he’d been wronged by the forensic investigators – and that one of them was a fraud. The truth was even stranger
Content: Illustration: Anaïs Mims/Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenIllustration: Anaïs Mims/Guardian DesignThe long readGermanyA death, a plagiarism scandal and a quest for revenge: the bizarre tale of Otto ZAfter his mother died, Otto became convinced he’d been wronged by the forensic investigators – and that one of them was a fraud. The truth was even strangerAlessio PerroneThu 8 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 03.15 EDTShareOn a balmy, quiet evening in June 2020, Otto’s elderly mother, Doria, was fading in her Munich apartment. As she lay with her eyes closed, her pale face, framed by her white hair, was calm.Otto, masked, gloved and draped in a sterile apron, dozed in a chair beside her. Otto, who sometimes goes by the name Rainer, and whose last name is only known as “Z” because of Germany’s strict privacy laws, was a doctor who had cared for his mother for years, ever since she had suffered a stroke and moved in with him. He described the course of that night to me. He woke to the sound of her short breath and tried to sit her upright. Her eyes were shut, and her lips pursed. She stopped breathing. Otto reached for his phone to call for help, but then Doria opened her eyes and stared into his. She smiled, drew one last deep breath, shut her eyes again, and lay still.Otto sank into his chair. As a doctor, he had seen death many times, but his own mother’s passing sent him into shock. He felt frozen, watching the windows glisten in the fading light. He was 66, and his brother and father had died years before. He had no friends. He had given all of his time, energy and attention to his mother’s care, and now that his task was suddenly over, he had no one to turn to. He mourned in solitude, with an impromptu ritual. He lit candles and set metal plates at the four corners of her bed. He sat beside her and thought about her soul.Once the rite was complete, Otto picked up the phone and called a funeral home. He knew the procedure: as a doctor, he could issue his own mother’s death certificate. After he hung up, Otto waited. It was the last calm moment he would experience for many months.After he called the funeral home, Otto told me, he waited beside his mother all night and into the next afternoon before he heard a knock at the door. He was surprised to see that, rather than doctors, the two men in the hallway were police officers. They wore bulletproof vests and carried guns. He invited them inside, where they scanned the rooms. He directed them to his mother’s bedroom and followed close behind, but the officers stopped him and asked him to take a seat.While the officers inspected his mother’s body, Otto sat in his office. Forty-five minutes passed, and then he heard someone else enter the flat without knocking. A tall, stylish woman approached and introduced herself as a coroner from the Munich Institute of Forensic Medicine, before walking off to the bedroom.Otto knew that a coroner – as opposed to a doctor or nurse – is only sent to the scenes of suspicious deaths. He followed her to the bedroom, where she had begun inspecting his mother’s body. Otto wasn’t easily rattled, but he told me that the way the coroner handled Doria threw him off. He found her elegant attire unprofessional, given the circumstances, and her bedside manner lacking. He said that he tried, however, to remain polite and helpful. As she went about her work, he offered his recollections from his mother’s final hours and an account of her long illness, which he had documented minutely over the years. Otto informed the coroner that he was a doctor, but it seemed to him that she was uninterested. She turned to the police officers and, without explanation, told them that this was a matter for law enforcement, before leaving the flat. Otto told me he wondered why nobody was listening to him, the grieving son, the doctor?More armed police officers arrived and searched the rooms. A commissioner approached Otto and told him to gather his things, as they needed to conduct their work uninterrupted. Sleep-deprived and grief-stricken, Otto was ushered on to the street and ordered not to return. He drifted along Munich’s wide, lamplit streets. As darkness fell upon the city, Otto told me he felt that he “didn’t understand the world any more”.He checked into a hotel, but found it intolerable to sit in his room. Later that night he wandered back to his flat and found the door sealed with police tape. He was desperate to check in on his mother and thought she might still be inside. He broke the police seal and entered the dark rooms, which were a chaotic mess, as if burglars had turned it over before fleeing the scene. He entered the bedroom. His mother was gone.Otto went back to his hotel but still found it impossible to sleep. He returned to his flat a second time at about 2am, and this time he found several police officers stationed there. They spotted him and put him in the back of a police car. He was taken to the Institute of Forensic Medicine, where doctors extracted samples from him: hair, urine and blood. When they had finished, Otto was taken back to the police station and found himself alone in what he described as a tiny, windowless cell with only a mattress, a stainless steel toilet and bars on the door.The next morning, two officers questioned him. How did he care for Doria? Why did he document her condition so precisely? Had he given his mother a concentrated saline injection? Only then did Otto understand: the police believed he had murdered his mother.After two nights in jail, or possibly three (his memory of this time is confused), Otto was released and allowed to return to his flat. While it was a relief to be home, he told me he still didn’t understand why he was under suspicion. He had not yet been formally charged with any crime. Otto wrote to the head of the Institute of Forensic Medicine, Prof Matthias Graw, to ask if his team had discovered anything suspicious while inspecting Doria’s body. Eager to prove his innocence, Otto offered to send Graw all of his day-to-day notes on Doria’s health. He suggested, boldly, that they co-author a paper about the cause of her death.Graw never answered Otto’s emails, and Otto fell into a depression. He told me he began blaming himself for his mother’s death. Had he made a mistake? Overlooked some critical detail? Was there some way he could have saved her? Over the years, he said, he had taken her to see 19 different specialists to ensure that she received the best care. He made sure she exercised and spent time each day in the fresh air. He had tried his best, hadn’t he?Doria was his whole world. Before the pandemic he used to take her into the city centre each night, where she was a favourite among the buskers for her generous tips. In her younger years, Doria had been an avid traveller, and Otto had taken her, in a wheelchair, on one last holiday to Italy. Now she was gone. Otto’s despair grew until he was unable to eat or sleep.In January 2021, the authorities dropped their investigation into his mother’s death, and Otto was cleared of any wrongdoing. But he still couldn’t get over her death. He checked himself into a psychiatric treatment centre, hoping to quiet his mind.Through therapy and exercise, Otto slowly regained his strength. Meanwhile, he had received a copy of the results of his mother’s toxicological report, signed by Graw and two of his institute’s specialists, but he was too disoriented to examine them carefully. Months passed. It was mid-summer, after Otto had moved back into his apartment, when he finally sat down with Doria’s medical files and the report.With two PhDs and decades of experience in medicine and chemistry, Otto knew how to interpret lab reports. He told me that something seemed off. Data seemed to him to have been highlighted selectively. Other details seemed to him to have been glossed over. In the toxicological report, he said he spotted a chemical compound – commonly associated with exposure to cold – in her bloodstream. In his telling, an impossible, unspeakable idea crept into his mind: could his mother have somehow still been alive when she was taken away and stowed in the mortuary’s freezer? Could she have actually died at the Institute of Forensic Medicine, under the coroner’s care? And if so, how? The report also mentioned unusual traces of a substance contained in the autumn crocus flower, a poison called colchicine.Otto began researching the Institute of Forensic Medicine. He started with its director, Prof Matthias Graw, and discovered that decades earlier, when Graw was a doctoral student at the University of Hamburg, he had written his dissertation on a certain naturally occurring poison found in the autumn crocus flower, called colchicine – the same poison found in Doria’s blood. Otto told me that a dark theory took shape in his mind: what if the institute had tried to frame him, to cover up the fact thattheyhad actually killed his mother?He did not go to the police – who, he reasoned, must work closely with the head of the institute of legal medicine. He would take the matter into his own hands. Hoping to perform his own examinations, Otto again wrote to the institute and requested access to his mother’s remains. Once more, his letter received no reply. In his apartment, hunched over his computer, Otto dug deeper into Graw, looking for evidence of negligence or criminality in the records of the man who oversaw his mother’s autopsy. He scoured scientific literature to research colchicine, the poison in which Graw was an expert.By mid-February 2022, Otto had on his desk a book, dated 1982. Its title was Colchicine – 100 Years of Research.One of the chapters – its experiments, findings, tables and conclusion – was nearly identical to Graw’s dissertation, published five years later.Otto was convinced that he had in his hands the evidence he needed to bring Graw down.At the end February 2022, a man named Stefan Weber was sitting in his office on the outskirts of Salzburg when an intriguing email landed in his inbox. The message claimed that Graw, the head of the Institute of Forensic Medicine at the University of Munich and one of the most respected forensic scientists in Germany, had plagiarised his doctoral thesis.View image in fullscreenStefan Weber, a plagiarism hunter.Photograph: Joachim BergauerThis was the kind of message Weber lived for. Fifty-six years old, baby-faced, broad, energetic and unrelentingly serious, Weber is the German-speaking world’s most-feared plagiarism hunter. His investigations have previously targeted Austria’s former labour and family minister Christine Aschbacher, who stepped down after Weberclaimedher master’s thesis showed “never-before-seen depths of gobbledegook, nonsense and plagiarism”, and the German politician Annalena Baerbock, whose once-promising bid for the chancellorship was torpedoed whenhe investigatedher book. The New York Timeshas called Weber the “undisputed terror of academics, politicians, [and] celebrities”.Weber does not go out of his way to be liked. A former communications professor, he failed on eight occasions at eight universities to attain tenure. His colleagues in academia often found him brusque and inflexible. He told me he was hated because of his insistence on high standards.Weber dresses in black and conducts his affairs with extreme scrupulousness. Fearing diabetes, he fasts for long periods. He spends his days in almost complete solitude, moving between his office, the library and the copy shop. He receives numerous requests for investigations each month, mostly from law firms and private individuals who want him to look into an applicant, competitor or colleague. Weber told me he charges up to €350 an hour for his work. He frequently pillories both public figures and obscure academics on his blog, where he also rails against “theWokistan ideology” and has written: “Rightwing extremistmust be understood as a title of honour!” In his spare time, he writes lofty books of philosophy and theory, with titles such as Language, Humanity, Universe.The email, sent by one Otto Z, claimed that Graw’s entire career was “built on deception”. From Otto’s description, the colchicinebook would have been an easy source to pilfer. It had been published in East Germany at the height of the cold war, which meant that it most likely wasn’t known to western academics when Graw published his dissertation. It was also, in plagiarism-hunter parlance, “grey literature”: informal material that isn’t peer-reviewed and therefore lies outside the reach of digital research platforms. Without Otto’s tip-off, it would have been impossible for Weber to discover the book’s existence.Weber accepted the case and, with the help of an assistant, got to work researching the book. The archive of the East German publisher had been lost after reunification, and the book had never been cited by another source. Weber went searching for a physical copy. At the library, the elderly archivist told him they didn’t carry it. After consulting her databases, she informed him that no other library in the world did, either. But she found a single copy on eBay, for $220, and soon Weber held the book in his hands: a bright red hardcover. When Weber sat down to read it, he discovered that the red book told an incredible story nearly lost to history.It was a record of an academic symposium held in 1981 at a hospital in the small Romanian city of Târgu Neamţ. Present were eminent experts on colchicine – biologists, pharmacists, zoologists – who gathered to present their work. Their lectures and conversations were assembled into chapters that chronicled the history of their niche field of research. Since at least the first century, the autumn crocus has been known to be toxic. Since the sixth century, the toxin responsible, colchicine, has been used to treat gout. Throughout the 20th century, new uses for colchicine were discovered: its ability to disrupt microtubules, for example, helps scientists study cell division, disease mechanisms and drug toxicity.More surprising than any discovery presented at the symposium, however, was the guest list. Experts came from both sides of the iron curtain. At least two Americans were present: zoologist John Julius Biesele and obesity researcher Jules Hirsch. Had these westerners risked their reputations, careers and possibly their freedom to take part?Perhaps the explanation had something to do with the symposium’s host, Elena Ceaușescu, the eccentric and ruthless wife of Nicolae Ceaușescu, then-dictator of Romania. Adding a bizarre twist to Weber’s investigation, Mrs Ceaușescu was, herself,an infamous academic cheat. Despite only completing elementary school, she believed that she was “born a great chemist”, and coerced the Polytechnic Institute in Bucharest into awarding her a PhD in chemistry. Throughout her husband’s reign, she forced Romanian chemists to produce work under her name. Had she somehow blackmailed western scientists into attending her conference? Or could they have been spies sent by the CIA to gather intelligence?When Romania’s Soviet-backed regime collapsed in 1989, Elena Ceaușescu, along with her husband, was executed by firing squad. Weber’s research turned up no other references to her groundbreaking conference. By 2022, most of its attendants had also passed away. The conference seemed destined to remain a footnote in the history of science. But poring over the pages of Colchicine, Weber was soon convinced that one man had not overlooked the book: Matthias Graw.After cross-referencing the red book and Graw’s dissertation, Weber and his assistant concluded that nearly 80% of Graw’s work was not original. Two of his thesis’s central chapters and many whole sections were word-for-word copies, with images and tables reproduced wholesale.On 6 June 2022, Weber finally filedhis report. In the 70-page document, which he sent to several media outlets, he claimed that Graw had plagiarised deliberately and with intent to deceive. “The case smells of severe scientific misconduct,” he declared in his blog. “The head of a forensic medicine institute … obviously has a corpse in the basement himself.”Graw was on holiday in northern Norway when word reached him. On 20 June 2022, a reporter from the investigative magazine Der Spiegel contacted the University of Munich’s Institute of Forensic Medicine, asking if Graw would like to comment on allegations that he had plagiarised his thesis. Graw, a stern man of 66, told me through his lawyer that he remembered being baffled by the call. He explained that he had gone on holiday and left his laptop behind in Munich, about 1,500 miles away. Without it, he couldn’t possibly respond to each of the many accusations, which were anyway baseless. Soon after, the legal department of Graw’s employer, the University of Munich, called Graw to say that they could not support or represent him, as they had to maintain impartiality until the end of the investigation.Der Spiegelbroke the story on 1 July 2022 with an article headlined: “Serious plagiarism allegations against Munich forensic pathologist”. The Munich-basedSüddeutsche Zeitungquoted Weber saying that Graw should be suspended while the allegations were investigated. Then came the tabloidBild, which reported that several lawyers were calling for all the institute’s reports published under Graw’s directorship – thousands – to be reviewed, and the cases re-examined, potentially causing an “earthquake in the Munich judiciary”.There were calls for Graw to resign. His underlings at the institute began speculating about his successor. The German government asked him to step down from his position as vice-president of the Society for Forensic Medicine. Finally, Graw’s alma mater, the University of Hamburg, opened an inquiry. If its investigation corroborated Weber’s report, Graw’s doctorate would be rescinded. He would lose his office, tenure and pension.View image in fullscreenProf Matthias Graw.Photograph: Fritz_Beck/Fritz BeckWhile Weber waited for the results of the Hamburg inquest, in late August he was surprised to read a follow-up story inBild. Without alerting Weber, Otto had granted the paper an interview in which he claimed that Graw had stolen a gold tooth from his mother during the autopsy. In the article, Otto also claimed that his mother, Doria, was a Jewish Holocaust survivor – which immediately evoked a parallel between the gold tooth theft and the Nazi concentration camps. It was Weber’s policy never to investigate his clients’ motives. He was only interested in the truth, not in hearsay or petty grievances. But reading the article, he began to wonder whether Otto’s interest in Graw might go beyond academic integrity.Three months after opening their investigation, the University of Hamburg’s panel of ombudsmen finished their internal inquiry. Graw’s detractors expected his disgrace to be complete. But the story was to take a new, unexpected twist.The university team did not agree with the conclusions of Weber’s report accusing Graw of plagiarism. In fact, they pointed the finger in an entirely new direction. In the university’s view, it wasn’t Graw’s dissertation that was fraudulent. The panel had examined the red book on colchicine, which Graw had supposedly plagiarised for his thesis.And in their expert opinion, it was the red book that was fake.Weber was stunned. He began looking into the university inquiry’s claims. First, it stated that the publisher’s address listed on the copyright page didn’t correspond to any real location in the former German Democratic Republic. Second, a certain technical term was translated awkwardly into English. And third, the text cited a 1983 source, which was impossible for a book printed in 1982 and based on a 1981 conference.This evidence struck Weber as weak. It could all be the result of sloppy socialist-era publishing, rather than proof of a forgery. And why would anyone go to such lengths to destroy Graw’s reputation as to create an entirely fake book with such an elaborate backstory?Still, Weber felt his abilities as an investigator had been called into question, and he set out to crush the accusations. He began by contacting Otto, who had first sent him a pdf scan of the red book, before Weber’s librarian found a print copy on sale on eBay. He asked whereexactlyhe had first found the red book. Previously, Otto had explained that he had seen it cited in a patent, then happened upon the volume he had in his possession at a Serbian flea market. Weber asked, which flea market? And could he provide the patent where it was cited?Otto, who had previously been helpful in all of his interactions with Weber, became evasive, then angry. Without answering Weber’s questions, he insisted that the University of Hamburg had performed a sham investigation designed to clear Graw’s name. Then, turning conspiratorial, he flooded Weber’s inbox with hundreds of pages of documents chronicling his mother’s death and his reasons for believing that Graw had mishandled her remains.Weber tried to make sense of Otto’s behaviour by working through the twists in the story on his blog. “If [this is a] forgery, then all this is as unlikely as researchers finding out tomorrow that the Earth is flat,” hewroteon 6 October 2022. Weber saw only two options: either the academic elite had conspired to protect Graw by conducting a shoddy investigation, or Otto had forged the book with the intention of using Weber as a pawn in a shockingly elaborate scheme to sabotage Graw. He announced that if the latter was true, he would renounce plagiarism hunting for ever.Weber cleared his schedule and turned his attention to the red book. He looked through old GDR phone books for the name of the translator – but no person under that name seemed to live in East Berlin at the time. Weber brought the book to an antiquarian, who claimed that the volume’s cloth bookmark was unusual for that era of East German publishing. A graphic designer informed him that the book’s primary font, Scotch Modern, was only released in 2008. Finally, Weber tracked down the photographer responsible for a key photo of the autumn crocus, who told him that he had uploaded the picture to Wikimedia Commons in 2005.Weber realised he had been duped. On 13 October, he publicly apologised and revoked his accusations against Graw in a blog post that called the affair “a disaster for plagiarism research”. Then, in a new blog post titled Chronology of a Failed Character Assassination, he set out to document how the book had been produced.Graw was perfectly sure he had not copied his PhD dissertation, but in a recent phone call, he told me how unsettling the accusations had been: “One thing was clear: the plagiarism hunters had been commissioned by someone, but the question was who, and why?” He spent months trying to calm people in his circles, convincing them he’d done nothing wrong. When he received a pdf of the red book he was supposed to have plagiarised, he was struck by how many glaring errors it contained – and how many people had overlooked them.During this time, Otto had initiated a series of civil proceedings against Graw, accusing him of copyright infringement. In August 2022, Graw read the interview with Otto in Bild, in which Otto further accused him of stealing a gold tooth from his dead mother. It was then he realised that Otto, the bereaved son, was behind the plot to destroy his career. In October, Graw filed a criminal complaint against Otto, asking for a police investigation of the whole affair.On 8 November 2022, police burst into Otto’s apartment. Officers found extensive literature on colchicine and several of Graw’s scientific papers. They seized correspondence and data-storage devices containing sprawling documents in which the name “Graw” appeared more than 28,000 times. Otto’s laptop contained folders named Graw and Dissertation, and images of the autumn crocus flower. Investigators also found correspondence with a Pakistani ghostwriter and a contract with a Serbian printer. Out of these disparate ingredients, it seemed, Otto had carefully assembled the red book.As investigators pored over Otto’s records, a picture emerged of his past, his mother’s final days and his strange, obsessive quest for revenge. Though he had lied about practically everything else, Otto was, in fact, a doctor – albeit one with a chequered clinical history. After practising in the US, Switzerland and Germany, he settled in the UK, but concerns raised by a pharmacist about “bizarre” prescriptions he’d written had prompted a review by Lambeth primary care trust and an investigation by the General Medical Council. In 2010, he had been barred from practising medicine in the UK, but by then, he had returned to Munich to focus on just one patient: his mother.Otto believed that movement was key to improving Doria’s health. He insisted that Doria walk every day, even when she was so exhausted she could barely get out of bed. He brought her down into the streets and observed as she hobbled along the pavement. He told me that he would leave marks on the buildings to track her progress, and took her to her favourite park bench. “Come on, Ma!” he remembered saying to cheer her on. “Just another three metres!”For years, he monitored her day and night, noting signs of progress or deterioration. Every day, he inspected her urine and weighed her faeces to make sure she was getting enough nutrition.After Doria died, Otto called the funeral home, asking for her to be picked up as late as legally possible, 36 hours after her death. When the company asked for a death certificate, Otto issued one himself, noting “rigor mortis” as a sign of death. It was then that the funeral company got suspicious and alerted the police, who sent a patrol unit and a coroner.When the coroner arrived, Otto’s erratic behaviour and desire to share his copious records of his mother’s health made her suspicious, too. “Extremely odd behaviour of the son; questionable medical treatment; extremely poor condition of care,” she noted in her report. Noting “indications of an unnatural death”, she ordered an autopsy. The examiners’ prevailing theory was that Otto had accidentally killed his mother with an overdose of insulin, then covered up his mistake by administering a glucose injection to stabilise her vitals.In the weeks after the coroner issued her report, Otto launched legal action against her, including for invoicing irregularities, but his suit was dismissed. Police opened a manslaughter investigation against Otto for the death of his mother, but dropped the case after the autopsy. Graw told me he didn’t perform the autopsy himself. His name was on the report merely as the institute’s director. The report found no conclusive evidence that Doria’s death was unnatural.During those long, uncertain months, Otto became tormented by trying to recover his mother’s corpse and discovering the exact cause of death – wondering whether it was due to a mistake he had made. He wrote to Matthias Graw to suggest they co-author a paper on the conditions that led to Doria’s passing, and recommended they perform an invasive brain exam, called a histology, which he later described in court as entailing “a circular cut with a butcher’s knife, then pulling the skin off and going at it with a saw”.Graw said he never received the letter, but if he had, he wouldn’t have responded to Otto for the same reason that Otto was kept in the dark about the examinations of his mother’s body – the ongoing criminal investigation forbade any contact with a suspect. Otto seems to have become obsessed with Graw, the keeper of his mother’s remains, and his fixation gradually twisted into a conviction that he was hiding something sinister.Barred access to Graw, Otto sought to learn everything he could about the man and find a fatal flaw. He fixated on Graw’s dissertation on the poison colchicine, hoping to undermine the foundation of the doctor’s entire career. He launched a flurry of bizarre proceedings against him, claiming that the doctor had failed to recognise inconsistencies in the colchicine levels in his mother’s blood, and accusing him of using the “flesh of the Jewish woman Mrs Z” for experiments.On 1 March 2024, the Munich public prosecutor concluded its investigation and charged Otto with document forgery, copyright infringement and multiple counts of defamation and fraud. The case came to trial in early 2025. The prosecution argued that Otto had attempted to “completely obliterate the livelihood” of Graw by commissioning the creation of the red book, inventing the 1981 conference on which it was based, and listing the book on eBay in order to fool Stefan Weber into carrying out his plan. Carbon dating corroborated these claims – the paper on which the book was printed was produced no earlier than 2015. When the furore failed to cost Graw his job, the prosecution claimed, Otto had fed the press the gold tooth accusation.View image in fullscreenOtto (centre) in court with two of his lawyers.Photograph: Dpa Picture Alliance/AlamyDuring the trial, Otto repeatedly claimed that his mother was a Holocaust survivor. Reporters forDie Zeit, the weekly magazine that published an extensive article on the case, contacted every organisation that documents survivors of the camps, and concluded that her name does not appear in the records.On 6 March 2025, Otto was sentenced to two and a half years in prison. The court cited his “almost unprecedented criminal energy”. Otto appealed against the court’s decision. When convicted, he was offered a suspended sentence if he confessed, but he maintained his innocence, claiming he and his mother were the victims of a string of bureaucratic errors, then a conspiracy to cover them up. Finally, in July 2026,he confessedto commissioning the red book and agreed to pay €210,000 in damages to Graw. He received a two-year suspended sentence.When I spoke to Graw recently, he told me he was satisfied with the outcome and hoped for peace and quiet now. But he was still coming to terms with the case, which had consumed the past few years of his life. He remained baffled by Otto’s motive in targeting him – he hadn’t performed the autopsy or started the investigation, and his institute’s report was the reason why Otto had been exonerated. He lamented that Otto had never explained, or apologised.He complained that “some of the media had no interest in investigating the allegations and carried stories before giving me a chance to respond”. And while, as a scientist, he was bound to test hypotheses before publishing them, “plagiarism hunters didn’t even check whether the source was genuine at all”. (Despite his vow, Stefan Weber has not retired from plagiarism hunting, but he has sworn to never again work with “grey literature”.)The murder that obsessed Italy | Tobias JonesRead moreAt trial, questions were raised about Otto’s mental health, but he refused to submit to psychiatric evaluation. According to experts called by the court, the assiduous attention to detail with which he carried out his forgery seems to rule out a full psychotic breakdown or a schizophrenic episode, but he may have experienced temporary delusions brought on by grief.Otto dismisses mental illness allegations as attempts to discredit him. He told me he has bought a house in Serbia to transform it into a memorial dedicated to his mother. With the slow, reverent precision with which he does everything, he has been attempting to retrace the steps of Doria’s entire life. In this memorial exhibition, he said, he will show she was a Holocaust survivor, and detail the true sequence of events that led to her death.This article is a collaboration withEpic magazineListen to our podcastshereand sign up to the long read weekly emailhere.

title: My latest discovery? You can eat the skin of a kiwifruit – and the benefits are myriad | Adrian Chiles | The Guardian
description: It turns out all that time spent peeling and paring was entirely wasted, writes Adrian Chiles. Now I’m gobbling them like apples and putting the extra fibre to good use
Author: Adrian Chiles
Headline: It turns out all that time spent peeling and paring was entirely wasted, writes Adrian Chiles. Now I’m gobbling them like apples and putting the extra fibre to good use
Content: Who knew?Photograph: Antonio Busiello/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWho knew?Photograph: Antonio Busiello/Getty ImagesOpinionFruitMy latest discovery? You can eat the skin of a kiwifruit – and the benefits are myriadAdrian ChilesIt turns out all that time spent peeling and paring was entirely wasted. Now I’m gobbling them like apples and putting the extra fibre to good useThu 8 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 06.05 EDTShareEvery day’s a school day, honestly. How on earth did I get to just short of my 60th birthday before finding out that you could eat the skin of kiwifruit? Astounding, just astounding. What a revelation. It’s odd, because of all fruit skins, it’s probably the one that looks least appetising. Nice clean oranges and bananas almost beg to be troughed, skins and all, yet we know this is a no-no. But it turns out that all of this small, hairy, boringly coloured object can go down the hatch. Admittedly, I have been slicing the ends off first, but I might start eating them, too.The first time is the hardest. You need to set aside years of prejudice against that hairy skin that you’ve been so painstakingly removing. Mind over matter. Initially, I sliced my kiwis longways and then each half into four. Now, I’m just eating them like apples. Sometimes three bites, usually two, occasionally just the one. I promise you, a lifetime’s fear of the fur evaporates in an instant. At least, for me it did. I have to report that when I talked my mum into giving it a try, she gagged alarmingly and swore at me with some venom as she fought to expel bits of skin from her mouth. Perhaps it’s not for everyone, after all.The health benefits are many, apparently. Plenty of furry fibre (I’m sure the furry type is the best) and all kinds of nutrient blah as well. This wasn’t the appeal for me, so much as the dispensing of the faff, all the peeling and paring. That said – and I apologise for oversharing – increasing the furry fibre intake made short shrift indeed of a recent bout of constipation. Highly recommend.The kiwifruit’s trade association needs to get this out there – the easy eating, that is, not the laxative effect. I think it’s possible it doesn’t even know. In Lidl in Stourbridge this week, I saw some badged up as “easy peelers”. What? No need! If there had been anywhere to give them a wash, I’d have commenced an eat-it-whole demonstration there and then. Seriously, this is marketing gold. My kiwi consumption has gone from every now and then to every other hour. Once the word gets out, all that pent-up demand will be unblocked. Get yourself out there and panic-buy, while stocks last.Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
