title: Trump’s latest attacks on the press exude desperation | Margaret Sullivan | The Guardian
description: Trump seems to invent ugly new variations on his press-bashing theme almost every day
Author: Margaret Sullivan
Headline: Trump seems to invent ugly new variations on his press-bashing theme almost every day
Content: ‘His war against the press is something of a reflex for him.’Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/APView image in fullscreen‘His war against the press is something of a reflex for him.’Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/APOpinionUS politicsTrump’s latest attacks on the press exude desperationMargaret SullivanTrump seems to invent ugly new variations on his press-bashing theme almost every dayThu 8 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 11.49 EDTShareWhen you hate the mainstream press as much asDonald Trumpdoes, nothing gets in the way of the punishment fantasy.Not court rulings. Not public opinion. Not even the dreadful consequence of less media coverage.And certainly not any awareness of how the first amendment is supposed to function in American democracy.This week, his revenge tour took yet another turn.He barred one of his most disfavored media organizations – Politico – from boarding Air Force One, where it was supposed to provide “pool coverage” to the rest of the press corps as Trump traveled to Nebraska for a campaign stop on Monday afternoon.‘Take out’ Los Angeles and San Diego? Trump is beyond irresponsible | Ted WidmerRead moreThat move was met with a strong show of solidarity by several media outlets, who decided not to fill the Politico spot.And the White House was defiantly delusional, claiming that Trump will “continue to grant an unprecedented level of access to the press”.This latest chapter came with the usual blast of venom at the mainstream media, though not specifically aimed at Politico.“The New York Times and many other Artificial Media Outlets should be arrested for their dishonesty and disservice to our Country,” he posted on Truth Social.The episode follows Trump’s effort in mid-September to ban Politico, CNN and MS Now from the White House. Those organizations quickly sued, charging that Trump’s action was unconstitutional.Trump-appointed judge Timothy Kelly came down on the side of the media, issuing a temporary restraining order that ordered the White House to reinstate the press badges that had been taken away.And since then, CNN has been kept off Air Force One repeatedly, using the rationale that access to the White House is one thing, but access to the president’s plane is another.“The law is absolutely clear,” Ted Boutrous, the first amendment lawyer who is representing the three news organizations said in astatement.“The harm to our clients, the first amendment and the public as a whole is profound.”The Trump administration’s position is that traveling with the president is a privilege not a right.The fight is not over, since Kelly will conduct a hearing later this week over the media outlets’ request for a preliminary injunction – a stopgap measure to protect press access in advance of a possible trial.Trump, of course, has been picking fights with individual journalists and entire news outlets for years. At this very moment, there are court fights involving the Associated Press, the Wall Street Journal, the New York Times and Disney, which owns ABC News and a number of local ABC affiliates.So far, there’s been a rare display of support among news organizations that are normally each other’s competition. Columbia Journalism Reviewcalledit “a striking and heartening show of solidarity from the White House Press Corps”.When the three outlets were kicked out of the White House last month, the other networks in the press pool decided not to replace CNN in the rotation, thus suspending coverage for a time.Peter Baker of the New York Times noted that for the first time in his 30 years covering the White House, “the president will not have a network TV camera covering his everyday official actions and travels”.What’s more, about 50 media organizations backed up the lawsuit by the three who had been singled out by filing an amicus brief.It’s hard to understand exactly how less coverage and this constant squabbling benefits Trump, but apparently, he is making a different calculation.His anti-press actions get a lot of attention, which is the very oxygen he requires to breathe. It doesn’t matter that much of the attention is negative.Meanwhile, he has entered a phase of saying and doing ever more outrageous things, like his statement this week at a rally that his war in Iran was necessary to protect the world. Trump appeared to suggest that Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego if it develops a nuclear weapon which prompted California’s Democratic governor, Gavin Newsom, to call the president “deranged and dangerous”.Trump exudes a sense of desperation these days, with the midterm elections only weeks away and his approval ratings underwater.His war against the press is something of a reflex for him – it’s what comes naturally, especially when he doesn’t like the shape of reality.The press corps’ newfound solidarity is encouraging. It’s been a long time coming from a group that, in the past, has responded to this president’s constant abuse with deference and dinner invitations.Trump seems to invent ugly new variations on his press-bashing theme almost every day.Standing together will be a necessity in the weeks and months ahead.Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and cultureExplore more on these topicsUS politicsOpinionDonald TrumpcommentShareReuse this content

title: Can hope save the planet? An endangered parrot that is beating the odds can help us find out | Helen Pilcher | The Guardian
description: A new global biodiversity report strikes an encouraging note. But we cannot rest on our laurels – and resilience is key, says science writer Helen Pilcher
Author: Helen Pilcher
Headline: A new global biodiversity report strikes an encouraging note. But we cannot rest on our laurels – and resilience is key, says science writer Helen Pilcher
Content: New Zealand’s kākāpō, which was once close to extinction.Photograph: Nature Picture Library/AlamyView image in fullscreenNew Zealand’s kākāpō, which was once close to extinction.Photograph: Nature Picture Library/AlamyOpinionWildlifeCan hope save the planet? An endangered parrot that is beating the odds can help us find outHelen PilcherA new global biodiversity report strikes an encouraging note. But we cannot rest on our laurels – and resilience is keyThu 8 Oct 2026 11.05 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 13.36 EDTShareThe new Living Planet Report is out. Published every two years, it assesses the health of the natural world and, historically, it’s made for gloomy reading.Take 2024’s report, which showed global wildlife populations had plummeted by 73% in 50 years and that ecosystems were being pushed toward collapse.After reading it, I retired to a dark room and drank gin, but every time I popped my head out, there was more bad news:heatwaves,floods,wildfiresandmass coral bleaching.So, when this year’s edition dropped, I braced myself. But there was a plot twist. Biodiversity is still being pummelled, but not everywhere. According to the new report, conservationists have prevented the extinction of 32 birds and 16 mammals since 1993, and the numbers of wild tigers, elephants and sea otters are stable or growing. The energy sector has historically been extremely damaging to the planet,accounting for about 75% of global greenhouse gas emissions. But the report notes we have passed a positive tipping point in the energy system, with the transition to renewables snowballing and coal use declining in many wealthy countries.I can therefore see why the report is titled The Science of Hope.But pegging it on hope is a bold move. People who write about the natural world, myself included, face a difficult choice. Focus on the bad news, and risk shouting into a void where people simply don’t want to listen. Focus on the good news and risk peddling “hopium” – stories that dull the pain briefly but do little to spur action.The report, however, isn’t talking about your average kind of hope. It’s talking about a geeky kind of hope rooted in psychological research.View image in fullscreenNumbers of South African elephants are up, the report has found.Photograph: Merten Snijders/Getty ImagesThe American psychologist Charles “Rick” Snyder spent decades studying hope and came up with asurprisingly practical definition. Hope, he argued, starts with a goal but also requires pathways, or ideas about how to get there, and agency: the belief that you can make a difference. To this, the Living Planet Report adds another ingredient: resilience – the capacity to keep going when progress stalls. Or, as British anarchist punk band Chumbawamba famously put it: you get knocked down, but you get up again.We can illustrate this point by looking at New Zealand’s kākāpō, the world’s fattest, greenest, least-able-to-fly parrot. When non-native predators drove the kākāpō to the brink of extinction, conservationists didn’t waste time wishing its numbers back up. In the mid 1990s,they moved the remaining birds to predator-free islands, and when recovery was slow, they changed tack.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionStockpile food – and wash your hands: is that really how to prepare for environmental catastrophe? | George MonbiotRead moreThey experimented with hand-rearing, foster mothers and artificial insemination. They fitted the birds with smart transmitters and monitored them almost obsessively.When new technology came along, they embraced it:the genomes of every living bird have now been sequencedto inform decisions about who should breed with whom.This is what real hope looks like. It’s not the same as optimism – the expectation that things will work out. Nor is it wishful thinking. And it’s certainly not “hopium”, which can make the problem seem smaller than it is. Real hope has its sleeves rolled up and is prepared to get messy. It leaves room for uncertainty and failure but refuses to believe that there’s nothing left to do. That’s why the opposite of hope isn’t despair. It’s inaction.Scientists who have studied hope have found it matters what we’re hopeful about.A 2023 meta-analysisfound that people who felt hopeful about their ability to make a difference were more likely to engage with the climate crisis – from seeking information and supporting climate policies to taking everyday action to reduce their environmental impact. Those whose hope rested on the belief that the climate crisis wasn’t really a problem were less likely to engage.In other words, useful hope needs to be grounded in reality. And that requires knowing what we’re up against. This was whythe Starmer government’s decision not to publish the full national security assessment on global biodiversity lossis so frustrating. The public has since seen an abridged14-page version. But the detail – and any devil within it – likely remains hidden.Produced by the Joint Intelligence Committee, it asks a stark question: what would ecosystem collapse mean for the UK?The answer is bleak: threats to national security and prosperity, havoc wroughtwith food and water supplies, a surge in irregular migration and even more geopolitical instability around the world.To find a way through the climatecrisis, we need both a clear view of the problem and the determination to tackle it. How can we find the right pathway if we don’t have the full map?In 1995, there were just 51 kākāpō. Today, there are 324, a remarkable turnaround for such a slow-breeding bird. Conservation plans are still evolving, and the species isn’t out of the woods yet. But at least it has a fighting chance.That’s the kind of hope we need: pragmatic, resilient and open to revision. We need our governments to be honest about the scale of the challenge we face. Because when they withhold information, they don’t just rob us of knowledge. They also rob us of hope.Helen Pilcher is a science writer and the author of Life Changing: How Humans Are Altering Life on Earth and This Book May Cause Side EffectsExplore more on these topicsWildlifeOpinionClimate crisisAnimalsBiodiversitycommentShareReuse this content

title: Free land for those who will build social homes on it. Is this the radical solution to the UK’s housing problem? | Phineas Harper | The Guardian
description: A bold south London initiative to give land to community groups rather than private developers could transform the system, says writer Phineas Harper
Author: Phineas Harper
Headline: A bold south London initiative to give land to community groups rather than private developers could transform the system, says writer Phineas Harper
Content: ‘To get new social housing built in their area, councils are reliant on private developers building a proportion of homes for social rent as part of larger master plans.’Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘To get new social housing built in their area, councils are reliant on private developers building a proportion of homes for social rent as part of larger master plans.’Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesOpinionSocial housingFree land for those who will build social homes on it. Is this the radical solution to the UK’s housing problem?Phineas HarperA bold south London initiative to give land to community groups rather than private developers could transform the systemThu 8 Oct 2026 07.56 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 12.53 EDTShareLewisham council, in southeast London, is developing ambitious plans to transfer public land to community groups in an attempt to get new social housing built in the borough. According topaperstabled at Wednesday’s council cabinet meeting, the local authority is devising a new housing strategy, which includes giving packages of public land worth up to £2m each to community-led organisations such as housing co-operatives, on the condition that they build social housing.The Green-controlled council is further considering placing any land it gives away through the programme intocommunity land trusts, legal instruments that lock in permanent affordability. They may also provide low-interest loans to help developments get started, and pre-approve planning permission to speed up construction. It is hoped that the proposals will take effect within a year.Together, they form the most radical suite of solutions to the housing crisis any local authority is currently putting forward. If adopted elsewhere, the approach could transform the construction of social housing not just in Lewisham, but across the entire country.Todaythree in fournew British homes are built by for-profit property developers. The rest are erected predominantly by housing associations, with just a paltry few built by local authorities.Unlike in comparable European economies, almost no new UK homes are being built by community organisations. To get new social housing built in their area, therefore, councils are reliant on private developers building a proportion of homes for social rent as part of larger master plans. But developers frequently use their strong bargaining positionto haggle downthe amount of social housing they actually deliver.“There’s a limit to how much social housing we can realistically get private property developers to build,” says Daniel Dream, cabinet member for inclusive regeneration, planning and housing delivery in Lewisham. “We’ve got to get more creative about how to deliver social housing.” Dream, a key architect of Lewisham’s evolving new strategy, says the current system of councils haggling with developers is broken and will never produce enough social housing to meet need. Instead, he hopes to use public land to empower community-led organisations to build essential housing for themselves, or as he puts it: “enabling community to deliver community”.Selling off public land is a fraught business even for well-meaning councils. Under a1972 law, public bodies are obliged to accept the highest price they are offered, regardless of the buyer’s intentions. Wealthy property developers can therefore typically swoop in and outbid community groups for land, even when the community groups have far more interesting, sustainable and socially valuable ambitions. In September, for example, Somerset councilvoted to sell a site in Frometo the London-based investment firm Newcore Capital rather than tolocal community developerswho had plans to build homes, workspaces, a riverside park and a lido.However, the 1972 law has a loophole. If a local authority is selling a site worth £2m or less,the council can chooseto sell it to whomever it likes, and at whatever price it pleases, even giving it away for free, provided doing so provides positive benefits for the area.The new strategy could be especially useful in helping support more ambitious housebuilding on tricky small sites. In London a “small site” is defined as a piece of land that isunder 2,500 sq metres, about the size of nine tennis courts. These plots are too modest for major developers to take an interest in, so often just sit empty. However, the potential to better use vacant small sites is enormous. The architecture practice RCKaestimatesthere is enough land stuck in small sites to build 850,000 new homes in the capital alone. It recentlyconducted a survey of Lewishamidentifying space for up to 9,700 new homes across more than 3,000 potential small sites.Improved use of small sites can also create better homes. As the research projectSmall Sites Londonshows, modest developments are generally more likely to produce high-quality housing that makes a positive contribution to its local neighbourhood than the swathes of anodyne towers put up by mainstream developers on larger sites.Lewisham has a long history of successful projects proving the potential of community participation in housing. Beginning in the late 1970s, families on the council housing waiting list were offered the opportunity tobuild their own homesusing an innovative construction system devised by the German architect Walter Segal. In 1997, London’s first black housing co-operative finishedbuilding Nubia Way. In 2024 a community land trust completed Church Grove, a block of36 permanently affordable homes. But more recently the borough’s reputation for housing leadership has waned. In June, The Filigree, a major new residential and commercial development in central Lewisham,was announced joint winner of the Carbuncle Cup, an award for Britain’s worst new building. These plans to revive ambitious community-led housing could not come sooner.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLewisham’s housing target is30,376 homes over 15 years. Community-led development won’t be able to meet that target alone, but it marks a clear break with the failing system of squeezing piecemeal benefits from major speculative developments. If successful, the approach could better empower the council and its constituents – and if introduced nationwide, it could catalyse a genuine revolution in social housing construction everywhere.Phineas Harper is a writer and curatorExplore more on these topicsSocial housingOpinionLocal governmentLondonHousingCommunitiesEnglandcommentShareReuse this content

title: Stockpile food – and wash your hands: is that really how to prepare for environmental catastrophe? | George Monbiot | The Guardian
description: The UK state is dumping its responsibilities on our doorsteps, while green-lighting policies that lead us closer to crisis, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Author: George Monbiot
Headline: The UK state is dumping its responsibilities on our doorsteps, while green-lighting policies that lead us closer to crisis, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Content: Illustration: Ben Jennings/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Ben Jennings/The GuardianOpinionEmergency planningStockpile food – and wash your hands: is that really how to prepare for environmental catastrophe?George MonbiotThe UK state is dumping its responsibilities on our doorsteps, while green-lighting policies that lead us closer to crisisThu 8 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 10.45 EDTShareWould you mind fixing the NHS? And while you’re at it, could you please build an anti-missile system in your garden? Then regulate the banks, replace the water mains, tax the very rich and use the proceeds to rebuild our schools. Well, come on people: what are you waiting for?I exaggerate, but this isn’t very far from the approach taken by the government’sPrepare campaign. Crucial functions, way beyond the scope of individual action, are dumped on our doorsteps while those in power fail to act. As a result, our national resilience isarguably lowerthan at any time since the second world war. At the Labour conference last week,Andy Burnham promised“a Britain where people feel the country has got their back again”. To make good on that pledge, he will have to change almost everything.It’s not that the advice offered by Prepare – a government campaign designed to promote readiness for emergencies – is irrational. But when the state is absent or working against us, households and communities cannot fill the gap.The campaign tells us, for example, to conserve water during droughts by turning off the tap while brushing teeth, or taking a shower instead of a bath. For sure. Every citizen should do their duty. But the government has at the same time declared datacentres “nationally significant infrastructure projects” that can be forced through the planning system, despite two startling facts. The first is that even Water UK – the body representing water companies, those paragons of environmental responsibility –has saidthere isn’t enough water to support the new datacentres. The second is that, as a freedom of information response reveals,the government has no ideawhat they are being used for. You could be turning off your taps so the water can be used to nudify celebrities.Talking of droughts, the government’sNational Risk Registerseems seriously out of whack. It estimates the risk of a drought with a moderate impact occurring in the next five years at just 0.2-1%. What?? It also estimates the risk of heatwaves with a “significant” impact – by which it means between 200 and 1,000 deaths – at only 1-5% over the next five years.The government estimatesthere were 2,877 heat-associated excess deaths in England during this year’s hot weather in May and June. There werea similar numberof deaths in the heatwave of 2022.But never mind: thePrepare campaign advisesthat “if you live in a home that is more likely to overheat … contact your local council, your letting agency or Citizens Advice to find out what help and support they can provide”. Good luck with that. In the meantime, the “future homes standard” is at last due tocome into forcein March 2028, but thanks to lobbying by the building sector,according to some practitionersit still won’t deliver new homes matched to the climate challenges we face. And local authoritieshave been blockedfrom demanding anything better, thanks to the same corporate pressure.Survive floods, thePrepare campaign tells us, by “packing a ‘grab bag’ of essentials in advance”, moving “valuable items upstairs” and making “changes to your property to reduce the damage flooding can do”. But one in nine new homesare being builtin areas at risk of flooding according to data from Aviva, and a recent high court judgment reveals thatthe law preventslocal authorities from blocking such developments, even if they fail a crucial safety test.These are not the starkest examples of public exhortation colliding with government failure. The Prepare campaign tells us to helpstop the spread of avian fluby washing hands “with soap and water” after feeding wild birds. Fine. But at the same time,at the behest of lobbyists, the government is pushing a “poultry sector growth plan”. This will multiply the number of super-incubators of avian flu: namely the factory farms rearing chickens. As the Scientific Task Force on Avian Influenza and Wild Birdspoints out, poultry farms are where highly pathogenic bird flu first arose. Through their growth and intensification, the spreading of their manure on fields and its runoff into rivers, we could scarcely devise a better formula for generating new variants of the virus and the attendant ecological disasters. Oh hang on, we could: the shooting industry is still allowed to breed tens of millions of pheasants and partridges in similar conditions each year, then release them into the countryside to mingle with wild birds. But do wash your hands.You’re also advised to “reduce your exposure to air pollution”. How? The government is allowing new homes to beequipped with wood-burning stoves, building huge and arguably pointlessnew roadsand consulting onradically delayingthe transition to all-electric vehicles. All, once again, in response to lobbying.As for food resilience, the Prepare campaign scarcely mentions it, except to say we should stock some “non-perishable food that doesn’t need cooking” in our homes. Last week, a group of anonymous senior food executiveswarned that, in the face of “material reductions in yield, quality and reliability of supply”, their industry was “defaulting to quick-fix crisis management” rather than taking a strategic, long-term approach. “At present, we are seeing companies either consistently lobby against necessary regulations or stay silent,” they said. The result is a likely failure toaddress an existential threat.There was much in Burnham’s speech that delighted me, especially his listing of deregulation as one of the five great evils putting Britain on “the wrong path”. That’s a break with 47 years of policy, in which all governments have dismissed essential public protections as “red tape” that must be cut. The Tories werestill at itin their own conference this week – telling us, in effect, they are here to burn it all down. But, like Keir Starmer, Burnham has tied his own hands by pledging to “stick to our fiscal rules”. These rules did not come from government. They weredeveloped by Westminster junktanksand pushed into being by the media. As Larry Elliott hasargued persuasively, they are unnecessary and self-defeating.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe threats to our resilience are the same as the threats to our democracy: what Burnham called “that sense of the powers-that-be pulling against the people, not with them”. We’ve had five decades of lobbyists shaping policy, with devastating consequences for our ability to withstand crises. Willing to play our part as we may be, we cannot do the work of government.George Monbiot is a Guardian columnistThis article was amended on 8 October 2026. The illustration was replaced as an earlier version had said to take baths instead of showers, rather than vice versa.Explore more on these topicsEmergency planningOpinionFood securityDroughtFloodingExtreme weatherWatercommentShareReuse this content

title: Here’s what connects the Cornell alleged rape case to those before: accused men not being held to serious account | Emma Brockes | The Guardian
description: There was progress after #MeToo, but not enough. Certainly not enough to shift the assumptions that still protect men and denigrate victims, says Guardian columnist Emma Brockes
Author: Emma Brockes
Headline: There was progress after #MeToo, but not enough. Certainly not enough to shift the assumptions that still protect men and denigrate victims, says Guardian columnist Emma Brockes
Content: People protest against Cornell University's handling of an alleged gang-rape on campus, in Ithaca, New York, 5 October 2026.Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPAView image in fullscreenPeople protest against Cornell University's handling of an alleged gang-rape on campus, in Ithaca, New York, 5 October 2026.Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPAOpinionRape and sexual assaultHere’s what connects the Cornell alleged rape case to those before: accused men not being held to serious accountEmma BrockesThere was progress after #MeToo, but not enough. Certainly not enough to shift the assumptions that still protect men and denigrate victimsThu 8 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 04.05 EDTShareIf the past is another country, and there is nothing so poignant as the innocence of recent history, then there is a thirdcategory of engagement with the era directly preceding our own, encapsulated by the line “that didn’t age well”.I found myself thinking about this in relation to news of the seven male students accused of gang-raping a 20-year-old woman two years ago in theirfraternity house at Cornell University, and now facing a civil suit brought by their alleged victim. Apparent failures by Cornell and the local district attorney to act appropriately at the time have triggered another round of commentary about the “death of #MeToo”, not least with thelooming anniversary on 15 October, the date in 2017 when the hashtag first went viral. But the period I find myself thinking about predates even that, when it seemed as if these questions of consent had been largely resolved.“Campus rape” – a category of sex crime historically taken even less seriously by the criminal justice system than regular rape – has always flushed out complacencies among those who otherwise consider themselves liberal.So it was in 2015, when it seemed to many liberal observers as if, after almost eight solid years of President Barack Obama in the White House, a crucial line had been crossed; conservatism had lost, liberalism had won, and the biggest threat to female students on campus was the temptation to overpunish men for minor transgressions, thanks to the sheer force of the pendulum swing to their side.This was the notion of “liberal overreach”, in which a popular president and a comfortably dominant political order allowed for what, in hindsight, looks like a load of decadently counterintuitive takes, accusing the left of going too far.The horror of the Cornell rape case is how ordinary it is | Moira DoneganRead moreTwo things pertinent to the Cornell case happened that year:Valerie Jarrett, the Obama adviser tasked with co-chairing a White House panel on women and girls, came up with the idea of using civil rights legislation known asTitle IXto prosecute sexual assault cases on campus. And, in January that year, a 22-year-old woman was sexually assaulted at a frat party at Stanford University in what would become known as the “Stanford swimmer case”. As with the Jane Doe at the centre of the Cornell rape allegations, Emily Doe had been drunk when the sexual assault occurred and much of the debate would centre on her ability to consent.The reason for bringing this up is twofold. First, Stanford’s Title IX process had yet to be introduced when Emily Doe was assaulted in 2015, but her experience foreshadowed just how inadequate the new internal complaint system would become for handling serious felonies on campus.Second, the conversation around Emily Doe’s own culpability was a stark reminder that the Obama era had ushered in neither a brave new dawn of understanding around consent, nor a period in which innocent male students were at risk of persecution. Instead, the details of the case ran along age-old lines in which a man, Brock Turner, after being discovered assaulting an unconscious Emily Doe by the bins at the back of the fraternity house, was found guilty of felony sexual assault and sentenced tosix monthsin jail,of which he served three.While the assailant was spoken of glowingly by the judge as a champion swimmer, his victim was dragged through the mud, a narrative that only changed whenChanel Miller, who would later dispense with her anonymity,read out her victim impact statementin court. “You don’t know me,” she said, addressing Turner directly, “but you’ve been inside me, and that’s why we’re here today.”If looking back at this case brings on a dismal sense that nothing changes, it also allows us to celebrate a little progress. After an initial flurry of whataboutery, it seems to me the Jane Doe in the Cornell case has been subject to considerably less public scepticism than Miller was a decade ago. The problem remains the utter pointlessness of Title IX as a mechanism for punishing serious sexual assault – two of Jane Doe’s alleged assailants were expelled from Cornell, two were suspended, one defendant was issued a persona non grata, and two were barred from campus – and some lingering fallacies about the role played by alcohol.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEspousing a popular view, in his 2019 bookTalking to Strangers, Malcolm Gladwell, over an entire chapter, presented the crime against Miller as a tragic misunderstanding between two people – a “transparency failure on steroids” – which wouldn’t have happened had alcohol not been present. This is true.Also true, but omitted from Gladwell’s analysis, is that it wouldn’t have happened if Brock Turner hadn’t been male; if parents didn’t raise their darling boys differently to how they raise their girls; if the criminal justice system prosecuted sexual assault with the enthusiasm it brings to, say, motoring offences; if “campus rape” was taken seriously as a category of crime; if two-thirds of the rapes and sexual assaults that occur in the US didn’t go unreported; if the conviction rate for those that are reported washigher than about 8%.It would seem to me that the pivotal disinhibiting agent in the sexual assault of Chanel Miller, and in the alleged assault of the latest Jane Doe, wasn’t drugs or alcohol, but entitlement, misogyny and a well-founded assumption on the part of the men accused that they would never be held to serious account.Emma Brockes is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on cancers in under-50s: the risks of obesity must be confronted | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: More research into the troubling rise in early onset cancers is needed. But we already know that food is among the culprits
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: More research into the troubling rise in early onset cancers is needed. But we already know that food is among the culprits
Content: ‘Earlier detection is thought to be one factor behind the rise in younger patients.’Photograph: Joe Giddens/PAView image in fullscreen‘Earlier detection is thought to be one factor behind the rise in younger patients.’Photograph: Joe Giddens/PAOpinionCancerThe Guardian view on cancers in under-50s: the risks of obesity must be confrontedEditorialMore research into the troubling rise in early onset cancers is needed. But we already know that food is among the culpritsThu 8 Oct 2026 13.50 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 14.31 EDTShareThe latest findings about therise in cancers in people under 50, from the World Cancer Research Fund (WCRF), are extremely concerning. While a cancer diagnosis is bad news at any time, it is a particular blow for those in younger age groups where most people are in good health. Overlapping trends observed in England, the Netherlands and the US include a troubling rise in the incidence of colorectal (or bowel) cancer. Other diseases that have increased in England include uterine and kidney cancers.These diseases are still rare in young people:10 times moreadults in their 50s, 60s and 70s are diagnosed than those in their 20s, 30s and 40s. Earlier detection is thought to be one factor behind the rise in younger patients.Diagnosing more cancers sooneris an explicit policy goal in England, where late diagnosis and lower uptake of screening are two reasons formortality ratesthat are higher than elsewhere in Europe.But diagnostic improvements are unfortunately not the main reason for increased cases. While research is ongoing and many questions remain, evidence points to obesity and poor diet causing cancers as well as heart disease and type 2 diabetes. TheProspect-UK trialis currently seeking 250,000 participants for a longitudinal study into early-onset (under-50) bowel cancer. It will scrutinise information about nutrition in more detail than has been done previously, including what people are eating less of.The success of international efforts to cut lung cancer through targeting smoking set a powerful precedent for public health campaigning. This took longer than it should have done, due to tobacco industry lobbying. But it remains the gold standard of regulation combined with messaging, to bring about behaviour change. The WCRF data shows that lung cancer rates in under-50s have continued falling.View image in fullscreenThe government has been criticised for doing ‘virtually nothing’ to alert consumers to the carcinogenic properties of the nitrites added to bacon.Photograph: Getty/iStockphotoSo far, efforts to cut obesity have had nothing like the same impact. The patterns are not the same everywhere; one recent study found that in some countries a rapid rise had been replaced by alevelling-off. But English-speaking countries have some of the worst records, and the lack of strong action in the UK is among the big disappointments of health policy in the last decade.Politicians fromBoris JohnsontoWes Streetinghave committed to obesity action plans, only to water them down in the face of opposition from the food and drink industries. Last year, scientists wrote to Mr Streeting toprotestthat the government had done “virtually nothing” to alert consumers to the carcinogenic properties of the nitrites added to bacon and ham.There is a grim irony in dramatic advances in cancer research and treatment coinciding with the rise in early-onset cancers. For many doctors and patients, this a period ofhope. But politicians and health bosses must guard against a situation in which some groups have improved prospects, while others face increased risks linked to socioeconomic disadvantages.In relation to obesity and diet, the close link with poverty points to the need for ministers to view public spending holistically, and to recognise that theNHSis not the only institution with the capacity to improve health. While more research into early-onset cancers is needed, existing data tells us a great deal. Governments should be as bold in tackling the causes of obesity as they once were in confronting big tobacco.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on Ethiopia’s return to conflict: civilian catastrophe and a spiralling regional polycrisis  | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The escalating violence reflects deep domestic rifts – but is fuelled by broader geopolitical power games
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The escalating violence reflects deep domestic rifts – but is fuelled by broader geopolitical power games
Content: Members of the Ethiopian federal police on patrol on 8 October 2026.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenMembers of the Ethiopian federal police on patrol on 8 October 2026.Photograph: ReutersOpinionEthiopiaThe Guardian view on Ethiopia’s return to conflict: civilian catastrophe and a spiralling regional polycrisisEditorialThe escalating violence reflects deep domestic rifts – but is fuelled by broader geopolitical power gamesThu 8 Oct 2026 13.49 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 14.31 EDTShareWhen the Nobel peace laureate is announced on Friday, the committee will be hoping that its choice ages better than 2019’s.Ethiopia’s prime minister, Abiy Ahmed, won the prizefor ending the 20-year border conflict with neighbouring Eritrea – signing a peace agreement with President Isaias Afwerki. A year later, their new relationship facilitated a war with the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) that killed as many as 600,000 people, displaced millions more, led to atrocities by both sides, andpushed Tigrayans into famine.Both sides bear responsibilityfor failing to properly implement the deal that ended that conflict in 2022, and the African Union and US did little to ensure that a piece of paper became a durable settlement. Now violence has resurged in northern Ethiopia, and old foes are forming bizarre new pacts. Last month, seven Ethiopian regional groupsannouncedan “Alliance for Survival” to remove the federal government. Mr Abiy’s coalition is held together by his patronage, but so far may be faring better than his rivals, united solely by shared loathing of him and riven by deep disputes. The TPLF, which controls Tigray, has previously battled the Fano militia of Amhara, and their territorial dispute endures. Ethiopia accuses Eritrea – previously accused ofatrocities against Tigrayan civilians– of backing the rebel alliance. Despite Asmara’s denials, there are multiple reports ofEritrean troops in Tigray.View image in fullscreenAbiy Ahmed.Photograph: Prime Minister Office/ReutersThe Ethiopian prime minister demands his landlocked country shouldgain access to the Red Sea, to Eritrea’s concern and anger. The Eritrean president’s control of the coastline, opposite Houthi-held stretches of Yemen, means that Washington isnow keen to engagewith his regime and unlikely to challenge him. Ethiopia’s complex internal politics are interlocking with geopolitical turmoil. Addis Ababaalso accusesEgypt and Sudan of backing the TPLF. They deny it, but Cairo is furious over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance dam on the Nile. Khartoum too fears losing water, and says Ethiopia is supporting the RSF rebels in the civil war (Addis Ababa denies it). The UAE, having lost a foothold in Yemen, has increased support for Ethiopia.The concern now is not merely the grave risk of full-scale war within Ethiopia, or between Ethiopia and Eritrea, but that a spiralling regional polycrisis is hitting already beleaguered communities. Agricultural production hasnot recoveredfrom the last war. Now the fertiliser and fuel crisis born of the Iran war, the evisceration of aid budgets and the impact of El Niño are intensifying the crisis. The UK and others must urgently provide humanitarian support.Though the escalating violence is alarming, with hundreds reportedly killed, this conflict has not yet fully ignited. In 2020, Tigrayans believed they had to unify for collective survival. This time the TPLF itself is deeply split, with veteran commandersreportedly arrestedfor questioning the new war, and soldiers and civiliansshowing little appetitefor a conflict fuelled by factionalised, self-serving and corrupt leaders. A truce is not impossible and must be a priority. Ethiopia needs relief, reconstruction and a political reconfiguration. But its conflict cannot be separated from the broader picture, as wars in Sudan, Somalia, Yemen, Iran and beyond enmesh to devastating effect. The longer that ambitious leaders convince themselves that interference elsewhere can advance their own power and resources, the deeper and more intractable it will become.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Legal rights must be retained for children with special educational needs | Special educational needs | The Guardian
description: Letter: Campaigners and Send parents including Chris Packham and Sally Phillips urge ministers to work with families and organisations to preserve individual provision and improve accountability in the system
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Campaigners and Send parents including Chris Packham and Sally Phillips urge ministers to work with families and organisations to preserve individual provision and improve accountability in the system
Content: ‘When provision is unsuitable or unavailable, legal rights are often the mechanism through which families can secure a suitable education for their child.’Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreen‘When provision is unsuitable or unavailable, legal rights are often the mechanism through which families can secure a suitable education for their child.’Photograph: AlamySpecial educational needsLettersLegal rights must be retained for children with special educational needsCampaigners and Send parents includingChris Packham, Carrie GrantandSally Phillipsurge ministers to work with families and organisations to preserve individual provision and improve accountability in the systemThu 8 Oct 2026 12.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 12.32 EDTShareThe legal rights of children and young people with special educational needs and disabilities (Send) are still under threat. The government’s proposed Send and education otherwise than at school (Eotas) reforms would significantly reduce existing legal rights to enforceable education, health and care plans (EHCPs), parental choice of educational settings and independent routes of appeal.Campaigners led by Chris Packham urge prime minister to rethink Send reformsRead moreWe support the government’s ambitions for a more inclusive education system. Better teacher training, earlier identification of need, greater specialist expertise and a properly staffed workforce are all necessary. But none of these initiatives require children and families to surrender the legal protections they currently have.The proposals impact everything from how children and young people qualify for statutory support, what can be written into EHCPs, who decides the provision delivered, where children and young people are educated, how families can challenge poor decisions, and whether children and young people who cannot attend school can secure suitable education elsewhere. TheChildrenand Families Act 2014 places children and families at the centre of decision-making, and the current proposals reverse this.This is not simply a technical change to Send law. When provision is unsuitable or unavailable, legal rights are often the mechanism through which families can secure a suitable education for their child. A promise that the system will work better cannot substitute for an enforceable right when it does not.Lucy Powell was a member of the education select committee during its 2019 Send inquiry. The committee concluded that the 2014 reforms were the right ones if problems of implementation and funding were addressed, and specifically warned the government against responding to those problems by “weakening or watering down duties”. We therefore urge ministers to work with Send families and organisations to retain existing Send legal rights, preserve individual provision, improve accountability in the system, and retain meaningful independent routes of appeal.A genuinely inclusive education system should reduce the number of families who need to enforce their rights. It should not reduce their rights when the system fails.Chris PackhamBroadcaster and campaignerCarrie GrantBroadcaster and Send parentSally PhillipsActor, campaigner and Send parentKamran MallickCEO, Disability Rights UKDaniel KebedeGeneral secretary, National Education UnionKellie BrightActor, campaigner and Send parentSimon Baron-CohenProfessor in the departments of psychology and psychiatry, University of CambridgeDr Virginia BovellFounder of Treehouse/Ambitious About Autism, author,campaigner and Send parentLuke ClementsCerebra professor of law and social justice, Leeds UniversityEliza FrickerMissing the MarkJohn HarrisJournalist, writer and Send parentRobin InceComedian, author and broadcasterPaula McGowanCampaignerDavid MitchellAuthor and Send parentRosa MoncktonPeer, and disability and Send campaignerSaba SalmanJournalist and campaignerSara RyanProfessor of social care, Manchester Metropolitan UniversityIan BirrellJournalist and disability campaignerStephen UnwinDirector, writer and Send parentGareth HitchinAutism DadcastCathy WassellCEO, Autistic Girls NetworkMarsha MartinFounder, Black SEN MamasSuzy YardleyCEO, Child Autism UKCarol BoysCEO, Downs Syndrome AssociationMadeleine CassidyCEO, IPSEA (Independent Provider of Special Education Advice)Samantha ClarkCEO, Learning Disability EnglandAlison BloomerEditor, Learning Disability TodayClaire DorerCEO, National Association of Special SchoolsAndy StevensonCEO, Reverse RettRachel FilmerFounder, Send Rights AllianceSharon PrattFounding member, Send National CrisisTania TirraoroFounder and co-director, Special Needs JungleDr Mine ConkbayirEarly years researcher, author and consultantRuth MadeleyActor and disability campaignerAnonymous co-founderMeasure What MattersTee Jay ChetwyndTeenage Send campaigner and advocateExplore more on these topicsSpecial educational needsEducation policyChildrenYoung peopleTeachingPrimary schoolsSecondary schoolslettersShareReuse this content

title: Honouring Sylvia and Emmeline Pankhurst on stage and in political action | Women's suffrage | The Guardian
description: Letter: As we approach the centenary of equal franchise in 2028, it is important to build on the rights that were won by the suffragettes, writes Helen Pankhurst
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: As we approach the centenary of equal franchise in 2028, it is important to build on the rights that were won by the suffragettes, writes Helen Pankhurst
Content: Beverley Knight as Emmeline Pankhurst, centre, in Sylvia: A Musical Revolution.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBeverley Knight as Emmeline Pankhurst, centre, in Sylvia: A Musical Revolution.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianWomen's suffrageLettersHonouring Sylvia and Emmeline Pankhurst on stage and in political actionAs we approach the centenary of equal franchise in 2028, it is important to build on the rights that were won by the suffragettes, writesHelen PankhurstThu 8 Oct 2026 12.29 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 12.55 EDTShareThere was a proud Pankhurst in the audience in Leicester as Sylvia: A Musical Revolution began its national tour (Suffragette cities: blazing Sylvia Pankhurst musical hits the road – in pictures, 3 October). A blazing show indeed – and one that, 98 years after women gained the vote on equal terms with men, asks how much remains to be done, how to do it and how women can bridge their differences to advance their common cause.As Sylvia Pankhurst’s granddaughter and Emmeline Pankhurst’s great-granddaughter, I honour both women. Their political paths diverged. I seek to reconcile their legacies through Centenary Action, the cross-party coalition that I lead, in a shared cause: dismantling the barriers to women’s participation, selection and retention in politics.Also in the audience were Philippa, a relative of Emily Wilding Davison, and Peter, a relative of Alice Hawkins. The connections endure – and so does the activism. Remembering past sacrifices means protecting the rights won and building on those struggles as we approach the centenary of equal franchise in 2028.As Emmeline said: “You must make women count as much as men.” And as Sylvia said: “Great is the work that remains to be accomplished.”Helen PankhurstConvener,Centenary ActionHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: A better way to inspect and evaluate schools  | Ofsted | The Guardian
description: Letters: Gareth Jones and Richard Hooper draw on their experience as educators to offer alternatives to the Ofsted system that is not fit for purpose
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Gareth Jones and Richard Hooper draw on their experience as educators to offer alternatives to the Ofsted system that is not fit for purpose
Content: ‘The sympathetic, supportive model of evaluation is already out there waiting to be adopted.’Photograph: Michael Austen/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘The sympathetic, supportive model of evaluation is already out there waiting to be adopted.’Photograph: Michael Austen/AlamyOfstedLettersA better way to inspect and evaluate schoolsGareth JonesandRichard Hooperdraw on their experience as educators to offer alternatives to the Ofsted system that is not fit for purposeThu 8 Oct 2026 12.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 12.32 EDTShareThe news that Ofsted inspections are to be overhauled again indicates that a fundamental rethink is required, rather than tinkering again with the grading system (England school inspections to be overhauled again after barrage of complaints, 2 October). As an educator with 30 years’ experience in international schools (21 years as head of two schools), I would suggest that when further changes are made, the first step should be to stop calling them “inspections”. The word implies an unfeeling, top-down procedure. While British curriculum international schools tend to use an Ofsted-style procedure, American international and international baccalaureate schools tend to use “evaluation” or “accreditation” procedures.In these, the school evaluates its own performance against a set of standards. The people who work in the school, including students, plus parents and board members, spend a year discussing the school’s achievements and identifying areas for improvement. They submit their report to the agency, which then puts together a team who will visit the school. The team is made up of practising educators from other international schools. So the school is evaluated by fellow professionals, which is much less threatening than a team of inspectors. Their job is to decide whether the school has accurately evaluated its own performance.My experience is that schools generally do an excellent job of self-evaluation, which means that the visitors can say: “Well done, you know your strengths and weaknesses, we can now offer our expertise in building on this report and helping you to move up to the next level.” The team visit is a positive, collegial experience whose aim is to validate the work that the school’s own staff has done. This contrasts with the seagull approach of anOfstedvisit – they fly in, make a lot of noise, disrupt everything and then take off, leaving a load of guano behind.The sympathetic, supportive model of evaluation is already out there waiting to be adopted.Gareth JonesLondonI have experienced four Ofsted inspections: as the chair of governors at a primary school, an early years group, head of a large adult learning service, and vice‑chair of governors at a further education college. Three received favourable judgments under the previous Ofsted framework; the fourth was rated “requires improvement”, severely affecting staff morale and mental wellbeing.However courteous the inspectors, the methodology in all cases created considerable pressure and anxiety. The process sometimes resembled a police search: practices and records were scrutinised, staff questioned under suspicion and the final judgment delayed.Educational institutions require rigorous inspection and poor practice must be addressed. But the current model appears to favour enforcement over constructive professional support. A more effective model would combine inspection with consultation. Inspectors would identify strengths and areas for improvement, followed by targeted support for a defined period. A shorter follow-up would assess progress. One has only to refer back to the more collaborative model adopted by the former Adult Learning Inspectorate to appreciate the difference.This would retain rigour while reducing the punitive tone, and foster a more collegiate relationship between Ofsted and institutions. It would also require inspectors to offer remedies as well as judgments.Richard HooperPenistone, South YorkshireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: To reduce reoffending, prisoners need better support after release | Prisons and probation | The Guardian
description: Letters: Pavan Dhaliwal responds to an article on the early release of prisoners. Plus a letter from a prison officer who works in a men’s open prison
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Pavan Dhaliwal responds to an article on the early release of prisoners. Plus a letter from a prison officer who works in a men’s open prison
Content: People leaving HMP Wormwood Scrubs, London: ‘A prison place without stable housing, treatment and support on release simply sends people back through the same revolving door.’Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAView image in fullscreenPeople leaving HMP Wormwood Scrubs, London: ‘A prison place without stable housing, treatment and support on release simply sends people back through the same revolving door.’Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAPrisons and probationLettersTo reduce reoffending, prisoners need better support after releasePavan Dhaliwalresponds to an article on the early release of prisoners. Plus a letter from a prison officer who works in a men’s open prisonThu 8 Oct 2026 12.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 12.31 EDTShareRegarding your article (Prisoners thank Andy Burnham as they leave jail in first wave of early releases, 1 October), Michael Bogle’s story should make us ask a bigger question than whether prisoners are being released too soon.Bogle, 38, has 100 convictions and has been jailed five times. He told the Guardian that he turned to shoplifting after becoming homeless, in order to eat. On leaving prison, he said that there was a risk he would shoplift again.At Revolving Doors, we work on systems change with people whose lives follow precisely this pattern – repeated contact with the criminal justice system, often for relatively low-level offences, driven by combinations of homelessness, addiction, poor mental health, poverty and trauma.We can keep arresting, prosecuting and imprisoning people like this. But after 100 convictions, surely we are entitled to ask whether doing the same thing for the 101st time constitutes a serious public-safety strategy. A prison place without stable housing, treatment and support on release simply sends people back through the same revolving door.Pavan DhaliwalChief executive, Revolving DoorsThere has been much in the media on the early release of prisoners, how full our prisons are and sentencing. I work at the end of the line, in a men’s open prison. It is my personal and strong opinion that we need to look at children and how we are failing to care for them. This is where a criminal life often begins, through neglect, abuse, trauma, the witnessing of violence and rape in the home, and so on.Many of the prisoners who I work with enter the care system at an early age, leave care without the support they need and end up in prison. For a large number of them, prison is the only life they know. I would urge anyone who is interested, and truly cares, to read Justice on Trial by Chris Daw KC. He suggests some radical solutions, which give hope that we might, one day, be able to prevent so many going to prison and, equally as important, reduce the number of victims of crime.Name and address suppliedHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend | Soccer | The Guardian
description: Michael Carrick is wary of ‘Dr Tottenham’, Oliver Glasner returns to Selhurst Park and will City summon a siege mentality at Anfield?
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Michael Carrick is wary of ‘Dr Tottenham’, Oliver Glasner returns to Selhurst Park and will City summon a siege mentality at Anfield?
Content: Declan Rice, Erling Haaland and Jay Dasilva will be looking forward to getting back on the pitch for varying reasons.Composite: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDeclan Rice, Erling Haaland and Jay Dasilva will be looking forward to getting back on the pitch for varying reasons.Composite: Getty ImagesTen things to look out for this weekendSoccerPremier League: 10 things to look out for this weekendMichael Carrick is wary of ‘Dr Tottenham’, Oliver Glasner returns to Selhurst Park and will Manchester City summon a siege mentality at Anfield?Premier League top scorers|View the league tableGuardian sportThu 8 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 19.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google1Rice rested and refreshed?Declan Rice’s future role in England’s midfield was questioned by Gary Lineker after Alex Scott’s impressive first senior international start in the 7-0 thrashing of Croatia. But the decision to withdraw from Thomas Tuchel’s squad in an attempt to manage his workload made sense after Rice had only three weeks off post-World Cup before returning to pre-season training. The 27-year-old has struggled with persistent back problems after suffering a hamstring injury last December and Mikel Arteta will hope that the rest has done Rice – who is thought to be close to agreeing a lucrative new contract at the Emirates – the world of good as they prepare to resume the defence of theirPremier Leaguetitle against Leeds on Saturday.Ed AaronsArsenal v Leeds, Saturday 12.30pm (all times BST)2Ready? Garnacho’s time to shineHavertz, Isak, Dorgu … spate of injuries with national teams leaves sour taste for top clubsRead moreSeveral Aston Villa players shone for their countries during the international window but one of those who stayed with the club may have made the biggest impression on Unai Emery. Villa’s remaining squad went to Spain for a mid-season training camp, including Alejandro Garnacho, whose last cap for Argentina was almost two years ago. Garnacho has been lesser-spotted in a Villa shirt, playing just 31 minutes as a substitute, but scored in both of Villa’s friendlies during the break, against Southampton and Sevilla. The 22-year-old, who joined Villa on loan from Chelsea in the summer with a conditional obligation, was an unused substitute for their past matches but is he now primed to affect games? Villa are hopeful Emery has unlocked Garnacho, who has struggled for form since leavingManchester United. “Ready now!” Garnacho posted on social media last weekend and Villa will hope that is the case.Ben FisherAston Villa v Brentford,Saturday 3pm3Toth can soothe pain of Scott’s injuryWith Eli Junior Kroupi, Amine Adli, Veljko Milosavljevic and Julián Araujo yet to feature this season due to injury, Marco Rose must have been tearing his remaining hair out upon learning Alex Scott got hurt on England duty and will be out of action for two months. Sitting 17th and still searching for their first league win, the German’s side squandered nine points from winning positions in four of their first five games – and it was the 23-year-old who was central in ensuringBournemouthhad those leads in the first place. With just 55 minutes of football behind him this season, it seems unlikely Alex Toth will get the nod to replace Scott when Bournemouth travel to Chelsea with the older, more experienced Ryan Christie available and in good form. But having forced his way into the Hungary starting lineup during the international break it would be no surprise to see the 20-year-old get more minutes with a view to being used far more often given his side’s gruelling schedule of nine matches in the next month.Barry GlendenningChelsea v Bournemouth, Saturday 3pmView image in fullscreenAlex Toth impressed for Hungary during the international break and will look to make his mark for Bournemouth.Photograph: Peter Morrison/AP4Ipswich’s calm an obstacle for FulhamIpswich’s place in mid-table, their total of six points, came via victoriesover SunderlandandCrystal Palace. Gary O’Neil’s team were presented with a tough opening schedule, and while defeated by Manchester United, Liverpool and Arsenal, their manager has not allowed those reverses to dilute team spirit. Speaking to the media following thehome defeat by Liverpool, O’Neil painted an ultra-positive picture that defied most observers’ view of a game beyond his team’s reach from the early stages. Thus far, a successful strategy, certainly by comparison to early season at winless Fulham. Like O’Neil, Álvaro Arbeloa is new to his job. An improved performance in thedraw against Uniteddid not result in a victory Fulham deserved, though there were signs of the progressive, attacking football the arrival of the former Real Madrid interim promised. Much of the burden has fallen on Josh King, the teenager building on last year’s breakthrough season.John BrewinIpswich vFulham, Saturday 3pm5Ballard’s absence a boon for BrightonStill in the Carabao Cup, with a Europa League campaign to negotiate and just four points acquired from their opening five Premier League excursions, the games are about to start coming thick and fast for a Sunderland side whose ability to cope with such a hectic schedule remains to be seen. Having lost Dan Ballard and Brian Brobbey to hamstring injuries during the international break, Régis Le Bris will have to reshuffle his pack against a free-scoring Brighton side who make the 700-mile round trip to Wearside for their first game since embarrassing Arsenal three weeks ago. While Wilson Isidor will almost certainly deputise for Brobbey, Ballard’s centre-back berth will be filled by either Omar Alderete or Nordi Mukiele. Having shipped five last time out againstManchester City, a Sunderland defence that had looked conspicuously porous in the early stages of this season will need all their focus if they are to stop the gallop of a team that have already scored 16 goals.BG.Sunderland v Brighton, Saturday 3pm6Crisis talk lingers in air at Old TraffordIf “Dr Tottenham” is a thing, Manchester United possess their own healing powers for opponents. Self-harm is a factor too. Theyrolled out the welcome matto Premier League newcomers Hull on opening day and Brighton wereushered back into a Carabao Cup tie. In United’s final game before the international break flagging Fulham were able to restore some faith, their goal via slapstick defending from Lisandro Martínez and Senne Lammens. Can Old Trafford, where fans will have regulatory matters at City to celebrate, lift the gloom for Tottenham? This season, like last season and the one before that, Spurs have assumed the mantle of crisis club, a status Michael Carrick’s January arrival temporarily removed from United. Lose to Tottenham, and the crisis prefix is likely to be reattached. Tottenham have done damage before. In September 2024, a 3-0 Spurs win at Old Trafford began Erik ten Hag’s hurtle towards the exit. Losing the Europa League final started Ruben Amorim’s downward spiral. Carrick beware?JBManchester United v Tottenham, Saturday 5.30pm7Fiery reception for Glasner at PalaceAll eyes will be on Oliver Glasner as he returns to Selhurst Park with Nottingham Forest on an afternoon that will be emotionally charged for both sets of supporters and in the boardroom. The Crystal Palace chair, Steve Parish, sought to defuse tensions last week when he urged fans to “buck the trend” by welcoming the manager who led the south London club to the first three major trophies in their history in the space of 12 months. “I would be mortified if he gets anything other than the roof blown off,” said Parish. But given the strength of feeling towards Forest and their owner, Evangelos Marinakis – who is still blamed by some for Palace’sdemotion to the Conference Leagueat the expense of Forest last season – many have still not forgiven Glasner for joining their rivals and could still make their feelings known when the Austrian takes his seat in the dugout before kick-off.EACrystal Palace vNottingham Forest, Sunday 2pmView image in fullscreenWas this the calm before the storm for Oliver Glasner?Photograph: Ritchie Sumpter/Nottingham Forest FC/Getty Images8Aerial battle of the dead-ball bossesIn Sergej Jakirovic and David Moyes,Hull Cityand Everton boast two of the more “pragmatic” managers in the Premier League. Renowned for their safety-first defensive styles, both teams are happy to surrender possession, rank among the top flight’s lowest sides in pass completion rates, and rely on rapid transitions and set pieces for a major share of their total expected goals. A game featuring two defences that pride themselves on their obduracy may well be settled by a well-delivered dead ball into a packed penalty area. While it may not be aesthetically pleasing, expect to see the massed ranks of defenders on both sides spending much of Sunday afternoon bracing themselves for rearguard action while peering towards the sky. The last time these sides met in the Premier League, Everton ran out easy 4-0 winners. A decade on, the aerial traffic is unlikely to be quite so one-way.BGHull City vEverton, Sunday 2pm9Anfield to turn up heat on besieged CityManchester City resume playing under the darkest of clouds, with a visit to their greatest rivals of a golden period now shrouded by a guilty verdict. Five Premier League wins from five under Enzo Maresca had offered hopes of success in a post-Pep Guardiola era. The dial has since moved on what constitutes success for a club where minds are consumed by legal issues but the band must play on. Can Maresca summon a siege mentality? City lifted a treble, including the Champions League, when the 100-plus charges first came to public light in 2023. The Anfield crowd will readily remind City of the infamy their club faces down. That Guardiola’s now-disputed dominance came at the cost of Jürgen Klopp’s great team will add to the ire, and very probably the pyro greeting to Anfield. Cool heads may be required in the policing and on the field, to which a return to focusing on football may offer welcome relief.JBLiverpool v Manchester City, Sunday 4.30pm10Will Coventry build on first win?International football’s incursions have curbed the adrenaline rush ofCoventry’s win at Nottingham Forestand Jay Dasilva’s brilliant goal, his club’s first in the top division since 2001. That gave Frank Lampard foundations to build on, a blueprint, where Forest were allowed to blow themselves out before Dasilva’s strike came on the counter. It was Stephen Mfuni, 18, on loan from Manchester City, who starred in that rearguard effort on his Premier League debut. Coventry now seek a first Premier League goal at a stadium opened in 2005, after the club’s long decline had set in. Newcastle this week passed five years of the ownership of a consortium led by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund. There have been two seasons of Champions League football, a trophy lifted and yet a sense of unfulfilled promise. Matthias Jaissle is leading the second phase of a jagged development process, this season’s positive signs tempered by reverses such as the4-1 defeat by Leeds, shows how far Coventry must travel.JBCoventry v Newcastle, Monday 8pmPosTeamPGDPts1Man City58152Arsenal54123Brighton511104Brentford5695Leeds5496Liverpool5397Everton5398Hull5289Newcastle50810Chelsea5-2711Ipswich5-4612Man Utd50513Nottm Forest5-1514Sunderland5-4415Crystal Palace5-5416Aston Villa5-5417AFC Bournemouth5-2318Coventry5-9319Fulham5-3220Tottenham Hotspur5-62Explore more on these topicsFootballTen things to look out for this weekendPremier LeagueManchester CityArsenalBrighton & Hove AlbionBrentfordLeeds UnitedfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Khaldoon al-Mubarak: the tightrope walker who made rare misstep over City charges | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: Manchester City’s chair is key to the project of making Abu Dhabi a secure world power but his next move may be the sale of the club
Author: Rob Draper
Headline: Manchester City’s chair is key to the project of making Abu Dhabi a secure world power but his next move may be the sale of the club
Content: Manchester City chair Khaldoon al-Mubarak appears to have driven the club’s confrontational approach with the football authorities.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAView image in fullscreenManchester City chair Khaldoon al-Mubarak appears to have driven the club’s confrontational approach with the football authorities.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAManchester CityProfileKhaldoon al-Mubarak: the tightrope walker who made rare misstep over City chargesManchester City’s chair is key to the project of making Abu Dhabi a secure world power but his next move may be the sale of the clubRob DraperThu 8 Oct 2026 08.19 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNo one better understands the precarious tightrope Abu Dhabi walks when it tries to balance its relationships with western Europe while weighing the complex geopolitics of the Gulf region than Manchester City’s chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak. He was eight when his father, ambassador Khalifa Ahmed Abdel Aziz al-Mubarak, left the family’s Paris apartment for work on 9 February 1984, and was assassinated on the street by a Palestinian terrorist.And no one outside the emirate’s royal family could be more wrapped up in the project of making and maintaining Abu Dhabi as a significant and secure world power and the dominant member of the United Arab Emirates, a nation state still only 55 years old. His paternal grandfather, Ahmad bin Abdul Aziz al-Mubarak, was chair of Abu Dhabi’s Sharia judicial department and senior adviser to Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan al-Nahyan,the founding president of the UAE. As such, Ahmad bin Abdul Aziz was the James Madison of the UAE (the founding father, not the Spurs player) in that he crafted the Islamic legal framework of the new nation in the 1970s.‘Those memories are ours and no verdict changes that’: Manchester City fans’ viewsRead moreKhaldoon’s father was assassinated by a group led by Abu Nidal which, according to the CIA, was “the most dangerous and effective of all terrorist groups [and] the best organized of the radical Palestinian terrorist groups” before the emergence of Hamas. The murder was justified in a phone call saying that the UAE “had expelled Palestinian and Arab residents and was linked with American imperialism”. In essence, they were accused of being too soft on the west, not radical enough for Palestinians.Both al-Mubarak’s grandfather and father have streets named after them in Abu Dhabi, with his father honoured as a martyr of the state. It is fair to say the City chair has honoured the family tradition as chief adviser to the UAE president and Abu Dhabi ruler, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed al-Nahyan, for whom he first worked after graduating from Tufts University in Massachusetts. Given his father’s martyrdom, the royal family is said to have looked out for al-Mubarak as a quasi-adopted son. According to a source in the Financial Times, al-Mubarak is “diplomatically in charge of the UK file as well as the China file … and he’s the main liaison with the US administration” and has diplomatic immunity in the UK. That said, he appears to have made a rare misstep with his belligerent tone on Manchester City.According to Manchester City’s lawyer Simon Cliff, it was al-Mubarak who dictated the aggressive, confrontational stance City have taken with football authorities. As far back as 2014, when City were fighting their first Uefa charge, Cliff wrote, according to leaked documents first published by Der Spiegel: “Khaldoon says he would rather spend £30m on the 50 best lawyers in the world and sue them [Uefa] for the next ten years than agree a financial penalty.”View image in fullscreenKhaldoon al-Mubarak with Pep Guardiola after Manchester City’s Premier League title win in 2021-22.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAHe backed down on that occasion, along with the co-accused Paris Saint-Germain, both clubs agreeing a small fine and minor transfer restrictions with Uefa. It is extraordinary that City kept fighting thereafter, whereas the Qatar-owned PSG accepted their punishment, cosied up to Uefa – with the club’s president, Nasser al-Khelaifi, becoming chair of the European Club Association (now European Football Clubs) and chief opponent of the breakaway Super League – and built the most exciting and successful team in Europe, bringing admiration for the Qatari brand from observers willing to ignore human rights abuses. Al-Mubarak, in fighting to the end with City, appears to have broken an ambassador’s cardinal law: don’t embarrass your boss. Should City lose their appeal against an independent commission’s finding that they wereguilty of multiple breaches of financial rules,al-Mubarak may be instructed to organise the sale of the club.“I’m sure that’s the case with Man City,” says Christopher Davidson, author of Abu Dhabi, Oil and Beyond. “More than that, I’ve been told by some [in Abu Dhabi] that it will be the case. I can’t see any reason why they would stick around and try to rebuild the reputation after this. It’s embarrassing the royal family now. I can’t think of any example where things have gone wrong [for Abu Dhabi] and they’ve just kept plugging money into it. I think they’ll play out the appeal – nothing to lose with that – but once that’s done, it’s all about how to get out before the owners are declared unfit, a far worse outcome. There are very clever people involved in Abu Dhabi who I’m led to believe will very strongly counsel this needs to be a quiet retreat because the longer they stay in the game, the more damaging it is and it will unravel any kind of soft power Abu Dhabi managed to gain.”In June al-Mubarak said “these sorts of jewels, you don’t sell” and that there was “only intention to keep growing this”. As for thewider threat to UK-Abu Dhabi relations, Davidson believes it is overstated. “Some of the reporting perhaps has portrayed Abu Dhabi as a bit monolithic. There are entire big and growing sections of Abu Dhabi state economy that are outside al-Mubarak’s remit. Some of Abu Dhabi’s biggest investments in the UK in recent years have been in renewable energy and the windfarms of Scotland from Masdar energy, which is chaired by Sultan al-Jaber, who’s another key lieutenant of the ruler.”Davidson also cites the International Holding Company (IHC), which has huge biotech, shipping, healthcare and retail investments in the UK, including the Ivy restaurants, and is chaired by Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed al-Nahyan, deputy ruler of Abu Dhabi and brother of the UAE president and Sheikh Mansour. “It’s inconceivable that these investments would be withdrawn,” says Davidson.View image in fullscreenKhaldoon al-Mubarak (left) alongside City owner Sheikh Mansour at the then City of Manchester Stadium in August 2010.Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/ReutersIn May this year the UK signed a free trade agreement with Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE which it said could beworth £3.7bn a year to the UK economy. “The UAE was a major force behind getting that and it was a major accomplishment on both sides, so there’s no prospect any of this is going to be interfered with,” Davidson says.Al-Mubarak will probably emerge from this fiasco largely untarnished, because City are a tiny part of his portfolio. “He can’t possibly have known what’s going on in every part of his empire,” says Davidson. “My gut feeling would be that it’s the layers below him. It’s all about your legal counsel. I think the Qataris had very clever people working for them.
