This has been a case of poor advice being given to the senior Emiratis involved, a misreading of UK politics and a misreading of the Premier League and its bigger picture as a rules-based institution.“I think the statements al-Mubarak has made, including the one early last summer that ‘We will not sell’, are the product of poor advice delivered to him and ultimately to Sheikh Mansour. It may be important to us in the UK but Man City has been a peripheral project [for Abu Dhabi].”Explore more on these topicsManchester CityFinancesFootball politicsprofilesShareReuse this content

title: Manchester United offer JJ Gabriel new deal but risk losing prodigy for £350,000 | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: Manchester United have made JJ Gabriel an official scholarship contract offer, but remain at risk of losing the teenage forward for as little as £350,000
Author: Sam Cunningham
Headline: Manchester United have made JJ Gabriel an official scholarship contract offer, but remain at risk of losing the teenage forward for as little as £350,000
Content: JJ Gabriel in action at youth level for Manchester United. Rivals must deal directly with the club for the player, or compensation will be set by a tribunal.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAView image in fullscreenJJ Gabriel in action at youth level for Manchester United. Rivals must deal directly with the club for the player, or compensation will be set by a tribunal.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAManchester UnitedManchester United offer JJ Gabriel new deal but risk losing prodigy for £350,000Teenager almost certain to leave despite fresh offerCompensation for move to European rival would be lowSam CunninghamThu 8 Oct 2026 10.10 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 12.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleManchester United have made JJ Gabriel an official scholarship contract offer, but remain at risk of losing the teenage forward for as little as £350,000.The prodigy, who turned 16 this week,stunned the clubwhen he asked for his registration to be cancelled last month, setting in motion a scramble among Europe’s elite clubs for his signature.Under Premier League youth rules, Gabriel would have been able to leave for a rival for nothing in January if the club had not offered him a formal scholarship for next season. The Guardian can reveal that the offer has now been lodged with the player.Next Generation 2026: 60 of the best young talents in world footballRead moreWhether he accepts it or not – and it appears unlikely he will stay at Old Trafford – any Premier League club must now negotiate a fee directly with United for the player. If one is not reached, compensation will be set by a Professional Football Compensation Committee tribunal.At a tribunal, United would expect to receive in excess of £3m, plus a clause in the deal granting them 20% of his next transfer fee. In a previous tribunal for a high-profile academy player, Liverpool were required to pay Chelsea £2.8m up front – with an additional £1.2m in performance-related add-ons – for Rio Ngumoha, and a 20% sell-on clause was inserted in the deal.A United team photograph released this week featuring Gabriel briefly raised fan hopes of a reconciliation. But a breakdown between his representatives and the club means the forward – who has been at United since he was 11 – is now almost certain to leave.He was permitted under Premier League rules to sign a pre-agreement after his 16th birthday, but his camp were not prepared to enter discussions after a disagreement over first-team minutes.His next move is yet to be decided, though it is believed he favours a move to Europe, where compensation would be significantly lower. Real Madrid are favourites to sign him, with Barcelona, Bayern Munich and Paris Saint-Germain all monitoring developments.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAccording to official Fifa compensation figures for a Category I academy, United would receive around £350,000 if he moves abroad. He would ordinarily have been prevented from transferring before his 18th birthday, but is eligible for an EU passport through his parents. The club will consider taking legal action if they believe recruitment rules have been breached.Gabriel has not appeared at training for more than three weeks and, according to sources, the club has made multiple attempts to check on his wellbeing. To fast-track his progression into the first team, Gabriel had worked with specialist staff usually reserved for senior players.Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitednewsShareReuse this content

title: Wiegman praises Toone’s attitude after late Lionesses recall for Greece playoff  | England women's football team | The Guardian
description: Sarina Wiegman hailed Ella Toone’s attitude after the midfielder was belatedly called up for England’s World Cup playoff in Greece
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: Sarina Wiegman hailed Ella Toone’s attitude after the midfielder was belatedly called up for England’s World Cup playoff in Greece
Content: Ella Toone has replaced Lucy Bronze in the England squad.Photograph: Harriet Lander/The FA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenElla Toone has replaced Lucy Bronze in the England squad.Photograph: Harriet Lander/The FA/Getty ImagesEngland women's football teamWiegman praises Toone’s attitude after late Lionesses recall for Greece playoffManchester United midfielder left out of initial squadFirst leg of World Cup playoff is on Friday in CreteTom Garryin Agia PelagiaThu 8 Oct 2026 12.33 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 15.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSarina Wiegman heaped praise on Ella Toone for her positive reaction to being left out of England’s initial squad for their Women’s World Cup playoff against Greece, after recalling the Manchester United midfielder for Friday’s first leg in Heraklion, Crete.An injury sustained by Lucy Bronze, described by Wiegman as “really small”, prompted the England right-back to return to Chelsea and Wiegman called up Toone, who travelled to Greece from Spain, where she had organised a training routine during the international window.Women’s Super League faces wait until 2029 for full-time referees despite funding boostRead moreToone has 69 caps and has scored 24 goals, including in the Euro 2022 final and 2023 World Cup semi-final, but Wiegman said when naming her squad that she had left out Toone and Chloe Kelly because “the levels weren’t what I expect from them on the pitch”. On Saturday, after startingManchester United’s victory over Liverpool, Toone took ownership of things, telling the BBC: “It’s about me now. I’ve got to keep working hard and use it as fuel to come back even better.”Wiegman, asked whether she had been impressed with Toone’s response, said: “Yes, very much. I think when I gave her the call, of course that was a hard call. But she took that straight away. Of course [she was] very disappointed, but the first thing she did [was say]: ‘OK, I’m going to get back, I’m going to do that.’ She has the support around her too.”The head coach referenced Toone’s post-match comments when she said: “That answer in the game, also the way she spoke about it, I thought that was really good. And then getting everything ready to go to Spain instead, but go for training there, I think that really impressed me. Well done, I would say.”That will be music to the ears of Toone, whose experience is also understood to have been a factor in Wiegman picking her rather than a replacement right-back. She could feature on Friday, when the European champions will hope to build a strong first-leg lead before Tuesday’s reverse fixture in Leicester.To qualify for next summer’s finals in Brazil, England must overcome Greece and win another two-leg playoff, against Slovakia or Ukraine, in December.Quick GuideGreece v England: Wiegman's probable team for visitorsShow(4-2-3-1) Hampton; Le Tissier, Morgan, Williamson, Greenwood; Stanway, Walsh; Mead, James, Hemp; RussoGreece v England, Pankritio Stadium, Friday, 5.30pm BSTWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.The draw for the World Cup will follow on 11 December and it would feel inconceivable for the 2023 runners-up to miss out. They are in the playoffs despite winning five of their six qualifiers in a group with Spain, the defending champions, who pipped England to top spot by virtue of their stronger head-to-head goal difference.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenSarina Wiegman (centre), speaks to the players during a training session in Heraklion, Greece.Photograph: Naomi Baker/The FA/Getty ImagesGreece have never qualified for a major tournament and, major underdogs against England, will probably set up in a low, defensive shape. The England defender Esme Morgan said she and her teammates would remain calm even if it takes time to break through: “It’s just [about] persistence and trying not to get drawn into being frustrated by the opposition. I think a really good example of it was the away game we played against Ukraine [in qualifying].“We couldn’t seem to break through in the first half – the keeper was making saves, I think we struck the woodwork a couple of times – but the messaging at half-time among the players and when Sarina came in to speak to us was just to keep continuing because we were creating opportunities. Not to start snatching or taking hot shots from distance, just trusting in the style of play that we have and in our ability to keep finding gaps in and around the defence. We came out for the second half after that and scored really, really quickly. So it’s just sticking to the gameplan, trusting in what we do and being patient”Explore more on these topicsEngland women's football teamSarina WiegmanWomen's World Cup 2027 qualifiersWomen's footballnewsShareReuse this content

title: Sergio Camello: ‘Rayo is the last team standing – it’s football from another time’ | Rayo Vallecano | The Guardian
description: Rayo Vallecano’s fascinating forward on his unique club, his musical passions and the goalscoring form that puts him among Europe’e elite
Author: Sid Lowe
Headline: Rayo Vallecano’s fascinating forward on his unique club, his musical passions and the goalscoring form that puts him among Europe’e elite
Content: ‘The least important thing about the football here is the football.’ Sergio Camello in the Vallecas neighbourhood.Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘The least important thing about the football here is the football.’ Sergio Camello in the Vallecas neighbourhood.Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The GuardianRayo VallecanoInterviewSergio Camello: ‘Rayo is the last team standing – it’s football from another time’Sid LoweRayo Vallecano’s fascinating forward on his unique club, his musical passions and the goalscoring form that puts him among Europe’e eliteThu 8 Oct 2026 15.20 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 16.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn 11-year-old, second-hand VW Beetle with more than 300,000km on the clock pulls over on Clown Fofó Street in the heart of Vallecas. The music goes off, the Smiths silenced and out gets Sergio Camello: movie aficionado with156 films reviewed,part-time photographer, sometime drummer, Olympic gold medallist and the second-top goalscorer in Europe’s top five leagues. Engulfed in graffiti, stickers covering the glass between metal bars in red, a single step up from the street, the small door into Rayo Vallecano’s ground is locked, but in 64 hours it will open for the first time this season. “It’s my home, it’s Vallecas,” Camello says.Forced to abandon their place, on Saturday at 2pm the tenants return. With the Madrid council declaring Estadio de Vallecas unsafe, unfit for purpose, Rayo’s home matches have instead been played in Leganés, out of the city to the south and boycotted by fans. Walking the neighbourhood that is proud of its social conscience, its community and its team, Camello can’t wait to be back again. And not just for the football; maybe not even for the football. “It’s the pre-game, the post-game, the people,” he says, passing the bar where they’ll be waiting for him after, same as always.View image in fullscreen‘I’m me, Sergio Camello, a normal person from a humble team’ – Sergio Camello at the door to Rayo Vallecano’s Vallecas ground.Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The GuardianYet the football is good too, good as it’s ever been. Across the continent’s top five leagues only Raphinha has more goals than Camello’s seven in seven league games and Camello himself has never had so many either. “I try not to think about it but my teammates keep reminding me,” he says. “‘Pichichi! Pichichi!’ It’s not Sergio any more.” Pichichi was the great Athletic Club striker whose name adorns the top-scorer award. No pressure, then. “None, I love it,” Camello replies, “and I love that they’re enjoying it.”Two months into the season, this is already his best campaign inprimerawhere the previous totals were five, three and three. And although there’s a tactical element, the new coach Beñat San José altering his movement, Camello looks deeper for an explanation. Above all he looks inside, which is where, from the beginning, another conversation starts: a simple question prompts a complex, nuanced and human discussion, the striker talking calmly, thoughtfully and with startling unexpected honesty.View image in fullscreenSergio Camello celebrates after scoring against Barcelona in August.Photograph: Pablo Rodriguez/Quality Sport Images/Getty ImagesCamello is that most unusual of footballers – prepared to speak on materialism, racism, or homophobia, social media “poison” or the housing crisis, that rare player prepared to use his platform, which he says was born of his upbringing but also learned being here in thebarrio. This is personal, but at once universal too, something in his experience that is about everyone. Who knows, maybe there is something in what he has lived that can help, some reason to share it, the goals scored offering tangible proof of an intangible process.So what has changed? “How I go on to the pitch,” he says. “I thought it would be much harder to change my mindset but I’m seeing that I can be myself: be free, connect with the Sergio I can offer Rayo. To feel liberated, to enjoy it – and it’s been a long time since I enjoyed all this like this.View image in fullscreenSergio Camello has been outscored only by Barcelona’s Raphinha so far this season.Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The Guardian“The first thing was to have many conversations with friends, people who truly know me. Especially my twin brother Gonzalo; there’s a connection that goes beyond the human. He could see I wasn’t enjoying it much, wasn’t myself. We talked and I tried to take that on to the pitch. Above all, to play without the pressure. Because pressure is horrendous. It makes it so that you don’t enjoy absolutely anything, puts you in a position where if things don’t work, that leads to frustration, frustration leads to pity, and suddenly everything is negative. There’s a point in the conversations where it’s: ‘That’s it; it’s done’.“This is a sport you chose before it was your job, because it’s what made you happiest. It’s about connecting to that kid again. I’d discussed this in therapy too; the idea of getting back to that kid.”Somewhere that can be lost – not just failure you have to live with but also success. “The pressure can come from everywhere,” Camello says. “We’re young, the change happens so fast, no one prepares you for it. If you can’t manage that it can do a lot of damage and that happened to me. [Early on], I would even get a bit paranoid, have fixations. ‘They’re looking at me.’ The first day inprimera, when I scored, the journey there had been normal – scooter, bus, metro, bus – but on the same journey home some kids followed me shouting: ‘Camello! Camello!’ It was a shock. The night we returned from the Olympics I was in the usual bar, people crowded and I had a kind of anxiety attack and had to go. And, look, I’m me, Sergio Camello, a normal person from a humble team. I can’t imagine what it is like forsomeone at Lamine Yamal’s level. I don’t envy that.”Joint-second“But it’s about seeing the balance, understanding,” Camello continues, “and football has given me so, so much. There are so many people who can’t enjoy their job, who don’t have the [financial] freedom. When you have bad moments, when the clouds come, when you feel that cycle of negativity, you talk.”Camello looks across the room: it’s quiet, 25 chairs sitting empty. “One of my friends [Dani Fernández] is a musician about to do four sellouts at the Wizink [Centre]; when I met him, he wouldn’t have sold out this room,” he says. “We both got ‘caught’ in this about the same time and we talked a lot. When he had doubts, I was there; when I did, he was. A torch in the darkness. You think: ‘I’d love to be a rock star’, and then someone you admire who is tells you how bloody shit it can be behind the scenes. You understand each other, you think: ‘Bloody hell, maybe I don’t have to analyse things so deeply.’ If in even those places you idealise, there is darkness, solitude, maybe I’m not so bad.View image in fullscreenSergio Camello says he his thriving by playing without pressure.Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The Guardian“Otherwise you could go into a very dark place where you feel you have to escape this [football]. Even then the world wouldn’t end. And fortunately, the positive in football has always weighed much more heavily. And that’s been shown to be right. Those conversations give me perspective, make me conscious of how fortunate I am.”Although Camello says doubts about the game itself are rarely shared in such depth in the dressing room – “football might be the most important thing in the entire world to your teammate” – something about this place helps. The club’s problems are significant, debilitating and should not be romanticised, he insists, and yet somehow they have made a success of it, built through solidarity. Besides, he says, “we’re also here because we want to be” and there is something about Rayo, something about breaking out of the bubble, that has been good for him, for all of them, as people as well as players. There’s a moment when he talks about everything that comes with being a footballer and says “it’s easy to be a dickhead”, but that’s diminished at a clubnot just in thebarriobut of thebarrio, one that’s “totally different” to anywhere else he knows, where “your feet are that bit more on the ground and you realise you’re not stars”.View image in fullscreenSergio Camello says the club and players have a unique connection with the Vallecas neighbourhood.Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The Guardian“Rayo is the last team standing from football from another time, that’s what I like,” Camello says. “Even just parking here on the street right in front changes things. The same faces, every time. The least important thing about the football here is the football; it’s what they stand for every weekend, what they believe in, the connection. It’s Isi in the bar on the corner. Unai and his mates in the one down the bottom there. The bar we’ve taken over. That doesn’t exist anywhere else. To have those guys you were watching half an hour ago in the same bars, doesn’t happen. I’ve built relationships that are very sincere that I never expected. I’m a normal bloke who fulfilled mine and many kids’ dream. Like a superhero when they pull on the mask; I come here, I put on the kit, I’m the most competitive, most professional person you can be. But when I leave I take it off and forget about it.”There is a release, refuge in something else. In the camera. In the drum lessons Camello admits have been slow and the guitar he’s abandoned, the ability God gave his feet denied to his fingers. In the films, in the indie rock music first heard in the family car, and the musician mates he has made. The music discouraged by reggaeton-loving teammates who control the stereo blaring out each morning– and, . They wonder, he says laughing, why he’s not so keen on the gym.View image in fullscreenSergio Camello with the Action for Music charity.Photograph: Action for MusicThe music that can make a difference, too; if there is anything that moves people, reaches them like football, it may only be that. “There’s something I’ve wanted to do for a long time and it’s really fun,” Camello says. “I joined a charity, Action for Music, which gives opportunities to kids to play music in humble neighbourhoods. They go to four hours of classes a week: percussion, strings, wind. The kids don’t pay a euro, everything’s free: the space, the teachers, the instruments. They have schools in Tetuán and Carabanchel. I’m getting involved, learning, and I want to set up a school in Vallecas next year.” He stops, grins. “Only I’m going to do it my way … with rock.“I did a session with them the other day, me trying to play the drums after six months. There was a kid on sax: wow, what a vibe he had, he was just loving it. When you don’t know where to go, there’s a place, someone who believes in you, gives you an opportunity. Forty kids: put some drum sticks in their hand, a guitar, a sax, something that will give them so much. Tell them they can be good at something, feel good about themselves. Have fun, maybe find something inside they didn’t know was there. It’s a way of giving back to Vallecas everything it gives me. I’m so excited.”View image in fullscreenSergio Camello stops to take a selfie with a fan while walking through the Vallecas neighbourhood.Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The GuardianImagine them playing the Wizink. “I can be their manager,” Camello laughs. “The ideaisto do concerts at the end of each year. Imagine those kids, coming into their first class … then going on stage. It’s good to see yourself up there, with an instrument. Their family there, people who have bought tickets to see them play, the applause. That feeling: ‘I’m worth it.’”Sounds like scoring a goal. Camello’s eyes light up. “Yes, it is,” he says. “I’m still the same guy as I was when I didn’t score, eh. But at that moment when you’re standing there, there’s nothing else in your head, just a feeling that all this makes sense. When the ball hits the net, when you get a ground on its feet, all together, when they’re celebrating, it’s like it’s all worth it. You feel important, you’re good at something.”Explore more on these topicsRayo VallecanoLa LigaEuropean club footballinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Victor Montagliani eyes re-election at Concacaf that would rule out Fifa presidency run | Fifa | The Guardian
description: Concacaf president Victor Montagliani has clarified his intentions to staff at the confederation after he was touted as a potential rival to Gianni Infantino at Fifa
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Concacaf president Victor Montagliani has clarified his intentions to staff at the confederation after he was touted as a potential rival to Gianni Infantino at Fifa
Content: Victor Montagliani (left) said he will run again for Concacaf’s presidency; Gianni Infantino (right) intends to keep the top job at Fifa.Photograph: Chris Brunskill/Fantasista/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenVictor Montagliani (left) said he will run again for Concacaf’s presidency; Gianni Infantino (right) intends to keep the top job at Fifa.Photograph: Chris Brunskill/Fantasista/Getty ImagesFifaVictor Montagliani eyes re-election at Concacaf that would rule out Fifa presidency runConfederation president clarifies his intentions to staffCanadian was eyed as potential rival to Gianni InfantinoExclusive byMatt HughesandNick AmesThu 8 Oct 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 14.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVictor Montagliani has told Concacaf staff he intends to stand for re-election as the confederation’s presidentnext year, which will rule him out of going up against Gianni Infantino for the top job atFifa.The Canadian businessman is understood to have relayed the message to most of the 41 members of Concacaf, the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation.Police occupy Djibouti FA headquarters amid attempt to oust Fifa council memberRead moreMontagliani has been widely touted as a potential candidate to take on Infantino for the Fifa presidency, particularly among Uefa member associations, who are conscious a European candidate would have no chance of beating Infantino in a ballot of Fifa’s 211 members.At a town hall meeting of Concacaf staff late last month, however, Montagliani is understood to have said that despite the Fifa governance crisis and calls for him to stand, he wants to continue serving members in the region.Concacaf’s presidential election will take place in the first quarter of next year before the Fifa vote on 18 March in Rabat, with the similar timelines leading Montagliani to clarify his intentions to staff.The 61-year-old was elected president on a reforming mandate 10 years agoafter the corruption scandalthat culminated in the arrest of then Concacaf president, Jeffrey Webb, after an FBI investigation. Webb admitted he had taken “bribes and kickbacks”.Uefa will also hold presidential elections next year, with Aleksander Ceferin confirming his intention to stand at a meeting of Uefa’s 55 member associations in Berlin on Thursday. Ceferin had said in February 2024 that he would not run for a fourth term at the helm but the likelihood that he would, after all, continue had long been an open secret. Previously, changes to the Uefa statutes had been passed that meant his first term, which began midway through the standard four-year cycle, did not count towards the standard three-term limit.It raises the prospect of Ceferin, who took the presidency in September 2016, holding power for more than 15 years in total. That is seen among most European FAs as a positive amid the turmoil engulfing football’s governance while putting to bed any perception that Ceferin, who would have had a number of proponents, might be tempted to challenge Infantino for the Fifa roleMontagliani and Ceferin are expected to continue working together to bring about governance reform at Fifa after the World Cup sell-off scandal, which will be on the agenda at next Thursday’s Fifa council meeting in Zurich.Fifa’s council has not met since Infantino’s Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) plan was exposed in July despite repeated calls from members for an extraordinary general meeting, with the summit their first meeting since Fifa congress in Vancouver last March.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMontagliani, Ceferin and the Asian Football Confederation president, Salman bin Ibrahim al-Khalifa, are expected to use the council meeting to demand an independent review of FFE and call for broader governance reforms of Fifa, which would give a greater voice to stakeholders and formalise the council’s role in decision-making.Previous calls from the trio, expressed in letters sent to Infantino last month, for Fifa to allocate a portion of its $6bn (£4.5bn) cash reserves to members will also be discussed.Delegates at Uefa’s Berlin meeting discussed a framework for Fifa reform, whose key points were made public during the afternoon. Among the points listed were the need for “a president who leads, not manages”, “stronger ethics, disciplinary, audit and compliance”, and “a clear process for major decisions”.Azerbaijan was an outlier in refusing to back Uefa’s reform proposals. The Azeri FA’s former general secretary, Elkhan Mammadov, now plays a key role at Fifa as its chief member associations officer and has been instrumental in Infantino’s attempts to keep wavering nations onside during the FFE crisis. Later this month, Azerbaijan will hold the first Fifa Under-15 World Cup, whose contestants will include Russia.Explore more on these topicsFifaFootball politicsUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Pat Cummins unfazed by prospect of Khawaja book raising sandpaper scandal: ‘Tell your story’ | Australian ball tampering | The Guardian
description: Pat Cummins has confirmed that Usman Khawaja called to inform him he would be writing a book, which will be released after Australia’s tour of South Africa
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Pat Cummins has confirmed that Usman Khawaja called to inform him he would be writing a book, which will be released after Australia’s tour of South Africa
Content: Pat Cummins and Usman Khawaja. The former Test opener is writing a book which will be the first by any Australian who played in the 2018 ‘Sandpaper’ Test.Photograph: William West/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPat Cummins and Usman Khawaja. The former Test opener is writing a book which will be the first by any Australian who played in the 2018 ‘Sandpaper’ Test.Photograph: William West/AFP/Getty ImagesAustralian ball tamperingPat Cummins unfazed by prospect of Khawaja book raising sandpaper scandal: ‘Tell your story’Former Test opener is writing a new book released next monthAustralia captain Cummins confirms conversation with KhawajaAustralian Associated PressThu 8 Oct 2026 19.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePat Cummins has suggested he is unfazed by the prospect of the sandpaper scandal being raised in Usman Khawaja’s autobiography, which will be the first from any Australian player who played in that 2018 Cape Town Test.Cummins confirmed that Khawaja had called to inform him he would be writing the book, which will be released days after the end of Australia’s first Test tour of South Africa since the infamous match.What’s left to say about Australia’s ball-tampering? The answer is everything | Geoff LemonRead moreHow much will be written about the ball-tampering scandal that rocked Australian cricket remains to be seen.Khawaja is a childhood friend of former opening partner David Warner, who was given a 12-month ban out of the ball-tampering scandal.At the time, Warner was painted as the architect of the ploy, with captain Steve Smith also suspended for a year and Cameron Bancroft nine months.There had been a report at the time that Khawaja had suggested the team should take joint responsibility over the incident, rather than just the three players.However, aCricketAustralia investigation found no other player had knowledge of the plan to apply sandpaper to the ball, a point that has long been maintained.Australia’s bowlers have also previously issued a statement denying their knowledge that “a foreign substance” would be taken onto the field.View image in fullscreenUmpires speak with Cameron Bancroft and Steven Smith at Newlands in 2018.Photograph: Gallo Images/Getty ImagesIn his autobiography next month which has been penned without a ghost writer, there is no suggestion Khawaja will suggest anything other than what investigations found.Cummins was asked ahead of Friday’s first Test in Durban if Khawaja had specified how much detail he would go into and if he would agree with his former teammates’ version of events.“You would have to ask him,” Cummins responded. “It’s obviously a long time ago. All the investigations, everything was done back then. Answered every question a million times.“It was dealt with then, all I can say is as a group we’ve moved on. Very happy with the last eight or nine years, how we’ve been as a group and evolved. He didn’t go into too much detail ... As always it was ‘no worries, you can tell your story, that’s fine’.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt has been hard to escape talk of the 2018 series in the lead up to the first Test.Cummins noted on Thursday there was a larger than normal media turn-out in Durban, with this also the battle between the world’s top-two sides.Sandpaper made Australia the story in 2018 while South Africa’s achievement faded into irrelevanceRead moreBeyond the ball-tampering scandal, the 2018 series was littered with clashes between the two teams from the middle of the pitch to dressing-room stairwells.But tensions have thawed significantly since, with neither side expecting similar dramas.“It was quite a big series that 2018, it was pretty full on,” Cummins said. “After that, I think pretty much every Test team in the world felt like they’d made some adjustments.“This group is quite a different group in how we approach playing, and I’m really proud of how the guys have been since that 2018 series.”Explore more on these topicsAustralian ball tamperingAustralia cricket teamCricketAustralia sportShareReuse this content

title: Valtteri Bottas reveals lizard-leaping, python-dodging cycling exploits on epic ride | Valtteri Bottas | The Guardian
description: Valtteri Bottas has revealed the details of an incident-packed 418km bike ride between Malaysia and Singapore
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Valtteri Bottas has revealed the details of an incident-packed 418km bike ride between Malaysia and Singapore
Content: Valtteri Bottas poses with his bike after arriving Singapore at the end of a 418km ride from Malaysia.Photograph: Simon Galloway/LAT ImagesView image in fullscreenValtteri Bottas poses with his bike after arriving Singapore at the end of a 418km ride from Malaysia.Photograph: Simon Galloway/LAT ImagesValtteri BottasValtteri Bottas reveals lizard-leaping, python-dodging cycling exploits on epic rideCadillac driver rode between Malaysia and SingaporeFour-day trip helped him acclimatise for Singapore GPGiles RichardsThu 8 Oct 2026 12.08 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 14.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleValtteri Bottas has revealed the details of an incident-packed 418km bike ride including encounters with snakes, being chased by dogs and the eerie atmosphere of riding through the jungle at night as the Cadillac driver cycled between Malaysia and Singapore this week.The 37-year-old is a keen cyclist and after a suggestion from his girlfriend, the Australian Olympic cyclist Tiffany Cromwell, he decided to take on the challenge of riding from the last round in Sepang near Kuala Lumpur to this weekend’s grand prix on the street circuit in Singapore, under his own steam.Verstappen’s victory in Sepang should serve as a warning to Red Bull’s rivals | Giles RichardsRead moreHe managed the journey, which the rest of the F1 paddock undertook in flights that last just over an hour, in four days of riding including off-road and gravel sections beginning on the Sunday after the race in Malaysia. He completed 56km on the Sunday, before putting in two big stints on Monday and Tuesday, both of 161km, before concluding with 40km to finish on Wednesday.Speaking before this Sunday’s night race in Singapore the Finn, who has won 10 grands prix, described events that included leaping over a lizard en route.“Saw some snakes, which I was a little bit worried about but actually they were pretty chill. They were just doing their thing,” he said. “I saw one cobra, saw one python just crossing the path in front of me. Saw some of those big lizards that you also see here.“One was on the path, I had to jump over it with a bike. So I saw it like last minute. Got chased by one dog. Got stuck behind a group of cows on a small track. Eventually they moved away.”He admitted it had been hard, but added that it was a unique experience. “What was the wildest part was the riding at night in the jungle. The noise in there is like … your mind starts to play games of what is out there. But then you just need to crack on and keep going. Riding with your lights at night, that was probably the most epic part in the forest.”Bottas has taken part in cycling events when he is away from F1. Earlier this year he finished fifth in his age group in a qualifying event in Czechia for the Gravel World Championships, earning him a place in the competition which he is unable to take up because it clashes with the race this weekend.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueWithCadillacin their first season in F1 the team are still very much coming up to speed. Bottas has yet to score a point and is 22nd of 23 in the drivers’ standings, with eight DNFs in what was always going to be a difficult year for the fledgling team. He observed that the heat on the journey had made his bike seat like a “cheese grinder” but that it would not impair his build up to this weekend’s race.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I obviously wouldn’t do it if I knew it hurt my preparation,” he said. “So I’m pretty good. The amount of sweat in those days was quite impressive. You get used to the heat the more time you spend in the heat, so that can help me hopefully a little bit.”Quick GuideRwanda GP expected in 2030ShowRwanda will host an F1 Grand Prix in 2030, it is understood, marking the first race in decades on the African continent. The nation has been chasing a Grand Prix race for years, having already used football, basketball and other sports to enhance its image and attract investment. A source in the country’s government told AFP: "Rwanda’s bid to host the Formula 1 race has been greenlit, an agreement has been reached." An official announcement is expected to be announced in the Rwandan capital, Kigali, next week, with Qatar supporting the project. President Paul Kagame formally announced the bid when Rwanda hosted a gathering of the FIA in December 2024. "It all comes down to respect, and giving everyone the chance to contribute, where they can," he said at the time.Seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton has long called for an African stop on the F1 circuit, backing Rwanda’s plans in 2024 and calling the country "one of my favourite places".AFPWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.The race in Sepang was a one-off to stand in for the cancelled Bahrain GP, but it is believed talks have opened about a potential return for the circuit in future, which Bottas said may prompt him to repeat the feat.“When I got to the hotel yesterday afternoon, I said to myself, no, not again. But now, today, I’m like, yeah. Let’s see.”Explore more on these topicsValtteri BottasFormula One 2026Formula OneCadillacMotor sportCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Is Prem rugby union turning into basketball? Nailbiters supply case for defence | Prem Rugby | The Guardian
description: Record try-glut in round one suggested all-out attack is en vogue, but maybe you can defend well and still concede tries in the modern game?
Author: Gerard Meagher
Headline: Record try-glut in round one suggested all-out attack is en vogue, but maybe you can defend well and still concede tries in the modern game?
Content: Louis Rees-Zammit of Bristol leaves George Hendy behind to score the Bears’ second try against Northampton on Saturday.Photograph: David Rogers/GettyView image in fullscreenLouis Rees-Zammit of Bristol leaves George Hendy behind to score the Bears’ second try against Northampton on Saturday.Photograph: David Rogers/GettyPrem RugbyIs Prem rugby union turning into basketball? Nailbiters supply case for defenceRecord try-glut in round one suggested all-out attack is en vogue, but maybe you can defend well and still concede tries in the modern game?Gerard MeagherThu 8 Oct 2026 14.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter one weekend of the Prem season the feeling was we had crossed the Rubicon. A remarkable 52 tries, eclipsing the previous record for round one despite the fact that fewer matches were played added further weight to the argument – a criticism and a compliment – that the English club game is creeping closer towards a form of basketball.Then came round two and 41 tries. A sizeable number, certainly compared with seasons of yesteryear, but equally giving a sense that defences had their day in some cases.Sale’s gritty victory over Saracenswas a dogfight,Leicester’s win over Newcastlewasn’t pretty and whileBristol ran in six tries against Northampton, their success owed everything to defensive steel.Saracens’ Brendan Venter takes aim at ‘autocratic’ Prem over media dutiesRead moreSo perhaps the shark has not been jumped just yet and defence may not be optional after all. Indeed, there was a consensus in pre-season that rugby is cyclical, trends will come and go and attacking impetus will be en vogue for a time before defences get back on top. “The game ebbs and flows,” said Exeter’s director of rugby, Rob Baxter. “There were some really high-scoring games last season but it wouldn’t surprise me at all to see some real dogfights and nailbiters this season, I think that’s the way the game is heading.”Courtney Lawes, who has returned to the Prem with Sale after two seasons in France, was of a similar opinion, having watched the English top flight from across the Channel. The manner in which Sale dug in against Saracens, despite losing Jacques Vermeulen to a 20th-minute red card, appears to support his point.“A lot of tries, 40 points, 30 points each way, that’s quite interesting,” Lawes says. “It’ll be interesting this season. It might be the team that’s got the best defence that actually wins the league. When you’ve both got 50 or 40 points on the board, that’s a pretty open game, isn’t it? So defences have got to tighten up. I understand why the attacking game is important, but if you can equally have a good defence, then you’re going to win more games than the boys that are only interested in attack.”Two rounds is not enough to draw conclusions. There have already been, and will continue to be, blowouts when teams simply try to outscore opponents. But as the Northampton director of rugby, Phil Dowson, says: “I see a lot of comments around ‘it’s becoming basketball’ but I don’t think there’s any lack of intent in defence. I don’t think we’re not defending.”Northampton’s defeat at Bristol is a fascinating case because it was far from the exhibition many thought possible given how lethal both attacks can be: yet there were still 10 tries scored. Perhaps a greater attacking intent, brought about by a number of factors including the absence of relegation, a collective drive to deliver a more entertaining product, refereeing changes and improving pitches, has all meant more tries are scored. Perhaps Bristol can defend remarkably well against Saints and still concede four tries.“I’ve no doubt in my mind that, like in the NFL, it ebbs and flows between attack and defence,” says Dowson. “Sometimes the attack is very popular and sometimes the defence comes out on top. When Shaun Edwards came in at Wasps and changed the game when I was playing, that was a step-change in defence. Everyone complains, ‘It’s 9-3, 12-6,’ now we’re going, ‘Oh it’s 48-32’ – what do people want? That’s the question isn’t it, what do we want the game to look like?”View image in fullscreenPhil Dowson, Northampton’s director of rugby, said Fitz Harding was ‘exceptional’ at the breakdown for Bristol at Ashton Gate.Photograph: Bob Bradford/CameraSport/Getty ImagesThat is indeed the question and the pre-season view of Leicester’s Geoff Parling showed it is not easy to answer. “The product on the pitch in general is decent,” Parling said. “Lots of tries scored, although I would say that doesn’t necessarily equal a good game for me. I think 9-8 can be a beautiful game, in the right way, a genuine gladiatorial contest with physicality going at each other. I think try-scoring in general is a good thing, but it doesn’t necessarily mean it is a good game.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIf rugby is naturally cyclical, the World Cup looming next year is impossible to ignore. The England head coach, Steve Borthwick, has instructed referees to alter interpretations of certain laws in an effort to better prepare his side for Australia next year. In the first two rounds the number of offside penalties was eye-catching while, according to Oval Insights, there were 15 penalties for holding on in the first round, 18 in round two. Not a massive jump, but a step in the right direction in Borthwick’s eyes given how fiercely the breakdown is contested at international level. Indeed, Fitz Harding’s performance for Bristol against Northampton will not have gone unnoticed.“We try to correct [the breakdown] every day, every minute of the game, all the time because that’s the game,” Dowson said after the match. “I don’t know how many lineouts, between 12 and 15, I don’t know how many scrums, but 200 breakdowns, so whenever you get tackled the ball is in that situation. They did a very good job, Fitz Harding was exceptional.”It is too early to tell whether Borthwick’s influence is bearing fruit, but he may have been happier after the second round of the Prem than the first.Explore more on these topicsPrem RugbyRugby unionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Astronomers detect mysterious burst of energy from a galaxy far, far away  | Astronomy | The Guardian
description: Intense flash of radio waves is more than 10bn years old and has travelled through ‘approximately 80% of cosmic history’
Author: Donna Lu
Headline: Intense flash of radio waves is more than 10bn years old and has travelled through ‘approximately 80% of cosmic history’
Content: Scientists detected the burst using the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa and subsequently identified its host galaxy using Nasa’s James Webb space telescope.Photograph: Brendon Wainwright/WikipediaView image in fullscreenScientists detected the burst using the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa and subsequently identified its host galaxy using Nasa’s James Webb space telescope.Photograph: Brendon Wainwright/WikipediaAstronomyAstronomers detect mysterious burst of energy from a galaxy far, far awayIntense flash of radio waves is more than 10bn years old and has travelled through ‘approximately 80% of cosmic history’Donna LuThu 8 Oct 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 19.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA long time ago in a galaxy far, far away, a mysterious flash of energy was released into the universe.Astronomers have now detected that flash – a burst of radio waves which travelled for more than 10bn years before reaching Earth – what they believe to be the most distant fast radio burst (FRB) ever recorded.FRBs are intense bursts of radio waves that can emit as much energy in milliseconds as the sun does inmonths or years. These mysterious pulses were firstdiscovered in 2007and havepuzzled scientists ever since, with speculation from some that they could have analien origin.In a new study published in Science, researchers have detected an FRB that originated when the universe was only about 3bn years old, meaning it has travelled through “approximately 80% of cosmic history”.Astronomers detect fastest known star in Milky WayRead moreThe burst, dubbed FRB 20240304B, is believed to be the farthest yet detected, more than double the previous distance record.The scientists detected the burst using the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa and subsequently identified its host galaxy using Nasa’sJames Webb space telescope(JWST).Dr Themiya Nanayakkara of the University of Sydney, one of the lead researchers on the paper, said when the burst was produced, “there was no Earth, there was no sun”.Data from the JWST indicated that the burst originated from a “young, very small galaxy which is forming stars at a very high speed, with not many metals around it”.There are several theories as to what the source of FRBs is, including that they originate from magnetars, neutron stars with a very powerful magnetic field.“Whatever the mechanism that causes this radio burst has to account for that fact that it can be produced in … very young galaxies with very low amount of metals,” Nanayakkara said.More than 10,000 FRBs have been detected since 2007. Some repeat continuously, Nanayakkara said, while “some of them repeat for a while and then stop … and then there are some FRBs that only go once and we never see again”.Whether the new distant burst is a one-off flash or will yield recurrent signals remains to be seen.“[But] the fun thing about FRBs is that we don’t need to know what is causing them to do some of the science we are doing now,” Nanayakkara said.This particular burst “has been travelling for 80% of the age of the universe”, he said, adding that further detections of distant FRBs would enable scientists to map unseen matter in the distant universe.Prof Matthew Bailesof Swinburne University, one of the astrophysicists whofirst discovered FRBs, described the new paper as “a validation of how powerful the FRBs are for probing the universe”.Bailes described them as “a very fundamental way of counting how many atoms there are in the universe”. FRBs are affected by the particles they travel through, enabling scientists to quantify matter that cannot be seen through optical telescopes.Dr Sara Webb, an astrophysicist also at Swinburne University who was not involved in the research, said: “You can use them essentially as a line-of-sight count for how much matter they had to go through [to get to Earth].”The discovery suggests that “FRBs might have been very common in the early universe”, she added.Explore more on these topicsAstronomySpaceJames Webb space telescopenewsShareReuse this content

title: Russian attack on bus kills at least 30 people near Ukraine frontline | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Zelenskyy says Kremlin deliberately targeted ‘ordinary public transport stop’ in Kramatorsk, with 18 wounded
Author: Luke Harding
Headline: Zelenskyy says Kremlin deliberately targeted ‘ordinary public transport stop’ in Kramatorsk, with 18 wounded
Content: The regional prosecutor’s office said the vehicle was hit at 10am on Thursday by an aerial bombPhotograph: Ukrainian State Emergency Service/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe regional prosecutor’s office said the vehicle was hit at 10am on Thursday by an aerial bombPhotograph: Ukrainian State Emergency Service/AFP/Getty ImagesUkraineRussian attack on bus kills at least 30 people near Ukraine frontlineZelenskyy says Kremlin deliberately targeted ‘ordinary public transport stop’ in Kramatorsk, with 18 woundedLuke HardingThu 8 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTFirst published on Thu 8 Oct 2026 06.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Russian missile strike on a bus in the eastern city of Kramatorsk has killed at least 30 people, officials have said, in one of the worst attacks by Moscow on Ukrainian civilians this year.The regional prosecutor’s office in the Donetsk region said on Thursday the vehicle had been hit at 10am by an aerial bomb. “As of now, the death toll from this morning’s attack has risen to 30. Eighteen people were wounded,” it said, adding that all local public transport had been suspended.Images ​posted by police ‌showed bodies ‌strewn across a street littered with debris, as well ‌as a charred shell of what appeared to be a bus. A second bus had also caught fire, officials said. The strike targeted an area next to a dental clinic on the city’s Yuvileina Street.Three people had also been killed by shelling in the village of Bilenke, outside Kramatorsk, they added.Volodymyr Zelenskyysaid the Kremlin had deliberately targeted an “ordinary public transport stop”.MapSome of those killed could not be identified because of the severity of their injuries, Ukraine’s president added.He said the number of victims could “sadly rise”, as doctors fought to save the lives of those wounded.He said: “This strike will not go unanswered. Russia is trying to destroy all life in Donbas, and a response from the world is a must. A forceful response – exactly as the Russians deserve for all the deaths they have brought. May all those killed rest in peace.”The bombing follows a gruesome Russian strike on Wednesday on a five-storey block of flats in Pryluky in the northern Chernihiv region. The building collapsed, entombing those inside. At least 22 people were killed, including five children, aged between one and eight.Visiting the scene with Ed Miliband, the British foreign secretary, Zelenskyy urged the US to expand Starlink satellite internet coverage so that Ukraine could hit targets inside Russia such as launch sites. So far, Donald Trump and Elon Musk have refused Kyiv’s request.View image in fullscreenRescuers at the site of the Russian attack on the block of flats in Pryluky.Photograph: Serhii Okunev/EPAMiliband said there was “no clearer sign of Putin’s evil, evil intent and strategy in this conflict” than this week’s murderous attacks. He said: “Putin once said that he was going to win on the battlefield. He is trying to win by terrorising civilians.”Writing earlier on social media, Zelenskyy called on western allies to take “concrete steps” to boost Ukraine’s depleted air defences, amid a round-the-clock Russian onslaught in recent weeks featuring ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones.“Supplies of anti-ballistic capabilities, ammunition for our combat aircraft, and investments in interceptors – all of this is directly helping save lives every day. Important talks with our partners will take place today and tomorrow,” Zelenskyy said.Kramatorsk and neighbouring Sloviansk form part ofa “fortress belt”. They are the last two big cities in northern Donetsk under full Ukrainian military control. Russia has been trying to capture them for more than a decade, after a brief period in which Russian forces occupied Sloviansk in 2014.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenBus on fire after the Russian missile strike.Photograph: National Police of Ukraine/ReutersThe cities are home to thousands of civilians, as well as Ukrainian soldiers. In recent months, roads have been festooned with nets to protect traffic from marauding enemy drones. These defences offer little protection, however, against aerial bombs.“These are not ‘the consequences of war’, nor dry statistics. These are people killed by the Russian army,” the Donetsk regional governor, Vadym Filashkin, said ‌on Telegram after Thursday’s strike. “Russia comes to Ukrainian land with death.”He added: “The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians. For them, a bus full of passengers is an attractive target precisely because a single strike can kill as many people as possible.“Russia deliberately flouts every conceivable rule of warfare and the norms of international humanitarian law. It selects targets where it can inflict the greatest suffering on civilians.”There was criticism of the White House’s policy of engaging with Vladimir Putin, whom Donald Trumphas invited to December’s G20 summitin Miami, Florida. The Kremlin has yet to say if Russia’s leader will take part.The former US ambassador to Moscow Michael McFaul said on social media that Russia was guilty of terrorism. “There is no other word for it. Putin is running a terrorist state. That officials from my country call this terrorist a nice guy is deeply embarrassing for me.”Putin has demanded Ukraine cede the rest ​of ​the eastern Donbas region still under its ​control. Kyiv refuses to hand over its territory, believing Russia will take any concessions and carry on fighting.Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaEuropeVolodymyr ZelenskyynewsShareReuse this content

title: Scientists discover 180,000 giant tortoises on one Seychelles island  | Wildlife | The Guardian
description: Free-roaming Aldabra population far exceeds human population of Seychelles after decades-long recovery programme
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Free-roaming Aldabra population far exceeds human population of Seychelles after decades-long recovery programme
Content: Giant tortoise population thriving as survey discovers 180,000 on one island.Photograph: Dennis Hansen/SWNSView image in fullscreenGiant tortoise population thriving as survey discovers 180,000 on one island.Photograph: Dennis Hansen/SWNSWildlifeScientists discover 180,000 giant tortoises on one Seychelles islandFree-roaming Aldabra population far exceeds human population of Seychelles after decades-long recovery programmeSouth West News ServiceThu 8 Oct 2026 16.20 EDTFirst published on Thu 8 Oct 2026 12.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA survey of the world’s largest free-roaming giant tortoise population has discovered that the once endangered species is thriving.A population of Aldabra giant tortoises lives on an island inSeychellescalled Aldabra Atoll.Themost recent survey, led by Seychelles Islands Foundation (SIF) and the University of Exeter, revealed there were approximately 180,000 tortoises living on the island. This is the highest figure ever recorded for the species and far exceeds the human population of Seychelles.The new figure was obtained by a team who analysed five years of tortoise counts between 2018 and 2022. It is the first update since a widely cited figure of 100,000 tortoises from the late 1990s.Aldabra Atoll is one of only two places in the world where giant tortoises are found in the wild, with a much smaller population living in the Galápagos.Dr Frauke Fleischer-Dogley, the CEO of SIF, said: “More than 180,000 giant tortoises roaming freely on our atoll is proof of what long-term commitment to conservation can achieve. This is wonderful news for Seychelles, for the world, and for everyone who has worked to protect Aldabra.”View image in fullscreenThere are more giant tortoises on Aldabra Atoll than humans.Photograph: Avalon.red/AlamyThe study, published in the scientific journal Ecology and Evolution, found that the population was relatively stable for this period, with a best estimate of almost 183,000 adult and sub-adult tortoises.In the 19th century, exploitation of the animals meant there were fewer than 1,000 Aldabra tortoises left on the island, but a recovery programme led to it becoming a strict nature reserve in 1981 and a Unesco site in 1982.Researchers are now saying it is one of the greatest conservation success stories of the Indian Ocean, with the new study confirming it. “Aldabra’s giant tortoise monitoring programme is one of the longest running in the region, but the atoll’s dense vegetation makes counting tortoises genuinely difficult in places,” said Dr Nancy Bunbury, one of the study’s co-authors.“By modelling what we didn’t see, as well as what we did, we’ve produced the most reliable baseline yet for this iconic Seychelles species, establishing a benchmark we can use to track the population for decades to come.”Despite the good news, the study’s authors say that vigilance is essential. Aldabra’s climate is changing, with longer and more frequent droughts predicted to reduce the shade and food available to tortoises, while rising sea levels threaten low-lying parts of the atoll.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe study authors say invasive mammals remain a threat including feral cats and black rats that prey on tortoise eggs and hatchlings. The planned eradication of these remaining invasive mammals, the authors say, could lift the last barriers to further growth of the population and help it withstand future climate pressures.Saving the Siamese crocodile: Cambodia moves to protect one of the world’s last wild populationsRead more“These results are great news for the tortoises and testament to the fantastic work done in the field,” said Dr Dave Hudson, a postdoctoral research associate at the University of Exeter’s Cornwall campus.“But it’s important to remember that the numbers provide a baseline – not an endpoint.“Hopefully we have provided the conservation managers the evidence they need to track future change and act early as the tortoises face increasing pressures from climate change, drought and invasive species.”Explore more on these topicsWildlifeConservationAnimalsSeychellesAfricaResearchBiodiversitynewsShareReuse this content

title: July 2026 was worst on record for wildfires in England, data shows | Wildfires | The Guardian
description: Devastating blaze near Sizewell B nuclear power station in Suffolk among a record 624 wildfires in July this year
Author: Pippa Neill
Headline: Devastating blaze near Sizewell B nuclear power station in Suffolk among a record 624 wildfires in July this year
Content: Smoking rising from Dunwich Heath in Suffolk, where vast areas of a nature reserve were destroyed by fire.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenSmoking rising from Dunwich Heath in Suffolk, where vast areas of a nature reserve were destroyed by fire.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAWildfiresJuly 2026 was worst on record for wildfires in England, data showsDevastating blaze near Sizewell B nuclear power station in Suffolk among a record 624 wildfires in July this yearPippa NeillEnvironment reporterThu 8 Oct 2026 06.34 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 10.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis July was the worst on record for wildfires inEngland, provisional data shows, with England experiencing a clear upward trend in the total number of wildfires recorded.This summer has been astark reminderof the vulnerability of the UK to climate breakdown, after punishingly hot and dry weather turned large parts of the countryside into a tinderbox.Provisional government data reveals 1,354 wildfires have been recorded so far this year, with 624 of these in July alone, making 2026 the second worst year on record.July’s wildfires included a devastating fire that burned close to theSizewell B nuclear power stationin Suffolk and destroyed vast areas ofa protected nature reserve.The summer of 2026 was the UK’s hottest on record, according to provisional data from the Met Office, with 40 days of temperatures above 30C (86F) recorded, smashing the previous record of 34 days.Scientists have said therecord heatof 2026 has only been possible due to the climate crisis driven by fossil-fuel burning.This year also marks the first time in the data series, which runs from 2010–26, that a death has been recorded due to a wildfire.This incidentinvolvedthe death of a 70-year-old man after a fire burned in fields behind Berrington Road and Castle Gardens in Chipping Campden, Gloucestershire.Last week,the Guardian revealedthat the government quietly scrapped plans to prepare the countryside in England for wildfires. This was despite new data showing fire crews do not have the proper protective gear to tackle them.Alistair Carmichael, the Liberal Democrat MP for Orkney and Shetland and the chair of the Commons environment food and rural affairs committee, said this raised “serious questions” about whether this summer’s wildfires could have looked different with more resources on the ground.This year is the second worst year on record in terms of total number of wildfires, with the worst being 2022, when 1,592 were recorded. 2022 was also a record year for heat, with the UK recording temperatures of 40C for the first and only time.The 2026 data covers January to August only, whereas the 2022 data covers the full 12 months. Despite this, 2026 has already had a record number of woodland and forest fires, with 88 recorded.After a wildfire spread across an areaincluding several homes in Stourbridge in the West Midlandsin August, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, convened an emergency Cobra meeting and issued atemporary ban on the sale of disposable barbecues.The data shows a clear upward trend in the number of wildfires being recorded. Between 2010 and 2017, annual totals remained consistently under 750 (ranging between 310 and 721).In contrast, four out of the last nine years exceeded 950 incidents.The environmental author and campaigner Guy Shrubsole has accused respective governments of “fiddling whilst Britain burns”. He called on the prime minister’s upcoming Wildfire Summit to include “radical changes to how we fire-proof our landscapes – by restoring peat bogs, ponds and wetlands – and cut out the fossil fuels making wildfires worse”.A government spokesperson said this summer was one of the “most challenging wildfire seasons on record”.They added: “We have to make sure we are prepared for the threat of wildfires – which is why we have invested nearly £100m to upgrade national resilience assets and we are convening a summit with fire and rescue service partners to inform decision-making and make sure we have the right equipment and resources to be as resilient as possible.”Explore more on these topicsWildfiresEnglandClimate crisisExtreme heatnewsShareReuse this content

title: This is one of Norway’s most pristine fjords. So why is it being used as a dumping site for mine waste? | Environment | The Guardian
description: The Norwegian government has given a permit to a mining company to release waste into Førde fjord despite a 17-year battle by campaigners and a supreme court ruling against it
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Norwegian government has given a permit to a mining company to release waste into Førde fjord despite a 17-year battle by campaigners and a supreme court ruling against it
Content: Førde fjord in Vestland county, Norway, where the government granted Nordic Mining a permit to dispose of waste in 2015.Photograph: Marek Slusarczyk/AlamyView image in fullscreenFørde fjord in Vestland county, Norway, where the government granted Nordic Mining a permit to dispose of waste in 2015.Photograph: Marek Slusarczyk/AlamySeascape: the state of our oceansEnvironmentThis is one of Norway’s most pristine fjords. So why is it being used as a dumping site for mine waste?The Norwegian government has given a permit to a mining company to release waste into Førde fjord despite a 17-year battle by campaigners and a supreme court ruling against itSupported byAbout this contentDaniel Shailer in Vevring, NorwayThu 8 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 12.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShortly after the Norwegian stock market closed on 17 June 2026, a few dozen local people from the small west coast town of Vevring crowded around a laptop in a school. Surrounded by children’s drawings and windows looking out over Førde fjord, they listened as news arrived from Oslo. Norway’s supreme court had ruled against its government: a permit to release mining waste directly into the fjord two miles upstream was illegal, the court said.The moment marked the end of a 17-year fight, one of Norway’s most protracted environmental battles in living memory. In Oslo, Ingvild Fonn Asmervik, the project leader forNaturvernforbundet(Friends of the Earth Norway), compared the joy she felt to giving birth to her child. For Anne-Line Thingnes Førsund, a third-generation fisher living on the banks of the fjord in Vevring and a volunteer for the charity’s local branch, it was more of a relief. Like a mountain lifting off her shoulders, she said.These feelings of elation were short-lived. While Førsund and others celebrated, a government lawyerappeared on a television debate showto set out plans for a new temporary permit, and to allow the mine to continue to release waste directly into the fjord in the meantime. Four days later, the mine applied for fresh permission, andin late September, it was grantedby Norway’s climate and environment ministry.“When we heard the pollution would continue, it was like they snatched the carpet from under us,” says Førsund. “We have answered every letter, commented on every consultation, complained whenever we could. We have been knocked down so many times and this could have been the opportunity for change.”While the government insists that it is acting lawfully, critics say the dumping threatens to foul one of Norway’smost pristine fjords. Others worry that the decision heralds a new wave of permits to pollute Norway’s fjords in the race to secure critical minerals.View image in fullscreenAnne-Line Thingnes Førsund, a third-generation fisher, has campaigned against Engebø mine for two decades.Photograph: Daniel Shailer“This is not only about the fjord and us and our lives,” says Førsund. “This is about principles. When you have a government that doesn’t respect the supreme court you’re changing the system itself.”The move comes just as a wider spotlight is being shone on the issue of polluted waters in Norway. Arecent report showedthat Norwegian fish farms are filling fjords and other coastal waters with nutrient pollution equivalent to the raw sewage of tens of millions of people each year.Meanwhile, populations of Atlantic salmon are ata historic lowin the country –155 of Norway’s 450 or so salmon riverswere closed to fishing at the start of the season this year.Submarine tailings deposition (STD) – known colloquially by Norwegian critics as “fjord dumping” – is the process of pumping crushed rocks and chemical waste into the sea through pipelines hundreds of metres underwater. Proposed as an alternative to disposing of waste on land, the Norwegian government’s own Institute of Marine Research (IMR)warns that STD releasesfine particles of toxic waste that can accumulate in smaller sea life and disrupt ecosystems at large.STD is outlawed in all of North America, Australia, Russia, Brazil, China and most ofEurope. The few countries that still permit the practice include Papua New Guinea, Indonesia and Turkey.The Engebø titanium mine, on Førde fjord near Vevring, was first proposed by Nordic Mining in 2006 and the governmentawarded a permit to release waste into the fjordless than 10 years later. In response, Friends of the Earth Norway launched legal challenges thatworked their way up the country’slegal system, arriving at a week-long supreme court hearing in spring 2026. Meanwhile, the mine came online and began releasing waste late in 2024.Nordic Mining is financed by investors including Japan’s Iwatani Corporation and the British offices of the international banks Morgan Stanley, UBS and Goldman Sachs. Other banks, includingStandard CharteredandCitigroup, explicitly banfinancing projects using STD.Nordic Mining did not respond to repeated requests for comment from the Guardian, but said in asocial media postshortly after the supreme court decision that it would continue with how it disposed of waste, with the encouragement of Norwegian officials.“It has been said that our operation is illegal, that we have to close, that our work must stop. That is not the situation,” NordicMiningsaid, adding that it was continuing “with the ambition to act responsibly, with respect for the fjords and mountains, and for the local community around us”.View image in fullscreenNordic Mining’s Engebø titanium mine, near Vevring. Its new permit allows it to deposit waste into the fjord for three years.Photograph: Daniel ShailerLegal wrangling over the permit came to focus on the EU’s water framework directive (WFD), which applies to Norway as a member of the European Economic Area. The WFD allows industrial activities to pollute water bodies only when there is an “overriding public interest”.The supreme court ruled that the reasons given when the permit was first awarded were not strong enough. However, the government argues they have grown stronger since theEU added titanium to its list of “critical minerals”in 2020.“The Norwegian government considers the Engebø project to be of significant importance for Norway and Europe,” a ministry spokesperson said, because “the Engebø mountain contains one of the world’s largest known deposits of rutile, a titanium-bearing mineral. Within Europe, Norway and Ukraine are the only countries with significant resources of this kind.”Legal scholars have questioned this logic. “That’s wrong. A permit exists or it doesn’t, and the supreme court decision is quite clear: the permit is illegal,” says Tarjei Ellingsen Røsvoll, associate professor of administrative and constitutional law at the University of Inland Norway.“The government is then openly allowing a company to dump a bunch of stuff in a fjord illegally. That is unprecedented; it damages trust and undermines a fundamental structure of constitutional and administrative law. They should take responsibility for having made an invalid and illegal decision, morally and legally.”While Nordic Mining awaited its new three-year permit, it continued to dispose of waste into Førde fjord. Økokrim, Norway’s central office for white collar and environmental crime, is now considering whether to investigate the dumping for illegality.While there have been few comprehensive studies of the impact of STD on marine ecosystems, scientists have linked heavy metal pollution now present in some fjords to STD decades earlier.View image in fullscreenTerje van der Meeren rows to work at Norway’s Institute of Marine Research. ‘What will happen with the fish spawning in this fjord? We don’t know.’Photograph: Daniel ShailerThe impact is particularly damaging when the waste is milled into small pieces, according to Terje van der Meeren, a research professor at the IMR, who co-authored the institute’s response to the Engebø mine application and testified during the supreme court hearings.“It’s like flour,” says Van der Meeren, adding that waste from Engebø includes a chemical that degrades into carbon disulphide, a neurotoxin. “Our concern is that this fine dust will pass into the rest of the fjord. What will happen with the [fish] spawning in this fjord? We don’t know.”In 2016, Van der Meeren and other IMR researchers travelled to the Arctic Repparfjord, in Hammerfest in the far north of the country, where a copper mine dumped waste for six years in the 1970s. Decades later, they found haddock with higher levels of lead, arsenic and chromium in their muscles than those in nearby waters, according toresearch published this year. Other Norwegian studies have found historic STD contamination inplankton,crabsandfish eggs.Back in Vevring, Førsund and other campaigners are now preparing for a fresh legal battle over the temporary waste permit – though dumping is likely to continue for as long as it takes for a new decision to be reached.She looks back on the first protests against the mine with nostalgia. In one photograph, taken more than a decade ago, protesters gathered for a meal on the banks of the fjord; Førsund’s daughter, now an architect, was only a child. “So many of these people are dead now,” she says.“The fjord is bigger than us. It has given us food and income and meaning and music and fish and birds for thousands of years. Now it gives us the energy to keep fighting.”Explore more on these topicsEnvironmentSeascape: the state of our oceansNorwayMining (Environment)Mining (Business)ActivismEuropePollutionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: MoD has objected to four windfarms in past year over radar interference fears | Wind power | The Guardian
description: Complaints risks putting tdefence ministry on collision course with Department for Energy Security and Net Zero
Author: Jillian Ambrose
Headline: Complaints risks putting tdefence ministry on collision course with Department for Energy Security and Net Zero
Content: The MoD has a long history of objecting to windfarm developments.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe MoD has a long history of objecting to windfarm developments.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesWind powerMoD has objected to four windfarms in past year over radar interference fearsComplaints risks putting defence ministry on collision course with Department for Energy Security and Net ZeroJillian AmbroseThu 8 Oct 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 13.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Ministry of Defence has objected to at least four planned windfarms in the past year over fears the spinning blades could cause “unacceptable interference” with radars used to detect military aircraft.MoD officials raised concerns in late June over plans for an onshore windfarm in County Durham that could result in aircraft “not being detected” within an RAF Low Flying Area, according to a letter to Britain’s planning authority.The objection to the planned Hope Moor project, which could see 23 turbines built to heights of 200m, is understood to be the latest of at least four objections made against a planned windfarm on national security grounds in the last year.The complaint risks putting the MoD on a collision course with the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ), whichended a decade-long block on onshore wind developments in Englandwhen Labour came to power in 2024 after it was put in place by the Conservatives almost 10 years earlier.The government aims to double the UK’s onshore wind power capacity by 2030, and has designated Hope Moor a nationally significant project whose fate will be decided upon by the energy secretary.The MoD has also warned against plans to build an onshore windfarm of six turbines at Burton Agnes, near Driffield in the East Yorkshire Wolds, and of the “unmanageable” risk of building a 13-turbine windfarm near the Scottish borders.Meanwhile, plans for a far larger offshore windfarm in the Irish Sea have also raised concern within the ministry on the grounds that the proposed 87-turbine array could interfere with aviation radar systems at the Warton Aerodrome base in Lancashire, on the west coast of the UK.The MoD has a long history of objecting to windfarm developments, but industry sources note that the precautionary concerns do not usually rule out development. The “well-trodden path to the negotiating table” usually leads to minor adjustments to the size or height of the turbines, which means they can move ahead, they said.However, the ministry’s “routine” interventions are often used by those opposed to windfarms to support their campaigns, the sources added.Hope Moor is one of four windfarms under fire fromthe “Not One Moor” campaign, led by former England cricketer Lord Botham. Others include the Scout Moor windfarm in Lancashire, the Walshaw Moor windfarm in West Yorkshire and Ray Fell windfarm in Northumberland.Angus Thompson, a Conservative councillor in North Yorkshire, said: “The MoD’s stark warning is the nail in the coffin for this scheme … This hopeless project should be abandoned without delay.”Alexandre Davies, the head of aviation at trade group Renewable UK, said the industry “works closely” to find solutions to radar issues, “and has done so for many years” to “deliver projects faster”.A DESNZ spokesperson said: “We work closely with the Ministry of Defence.
