All onshore wind projects are subject to a rigorous planning process in which defence and security, the views of the local community and impacts on the environment are considered.”The MoD was approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsWind powerEnergy industryEnergyRenewable energynewsShareReuse this content

title: Campaigners led by Chris Packham urge prime minister to rethink Send overhaul | Special educational needs | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Letter to government says changes will unfairly remove legal protections for children in England
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Exclusive: Letter to government says changes will unfairly remove legal protections for children in England
Content: Campaigners are calling on Andy Burnham to abandon core parts of the reforms, which were announced by Keir Starmer and Bridget Phillipson.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAView image in fullscreenCampaigners are calling on Andy Burnham to abandon core parts of the reforms, which were announced by Keir Starmer and Bridget Phillipson.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PASpecial educational needsCampaigners led by Chris Packham urge prime minister to rethink Send overhaulExclusive: Letter to government says changes will unfairly remove legal protections for children in EnglandLetter: Legal rights must be retained for children with SendKiran StaceyPolicy editorThu 8 Oct 2026 12.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 14.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCampaigners are calling onAndy Burnhamto abandon the core elements of the government’s overhaul of special educational needs provision in England, arguing they unfairly remove children’s legal protections.A group of children, parents and experts, led by the broadcaster Chris Packham,have written a lettercalling for the prime minister to gut the plans laid out under his predecessor Keir Starmer.Starmer and Bridget Phillipson, the former education secretary,announced the sweeping changesthis year, aiming to curb the increase in legally mandated education, health and care plans (EHCPs) and save money in the long term.Now campaigners are hoping the change of prime minister and education secretary may bring a change of heart from the government – even though officials say it is unlikely.In the letter, published in the Guardian, the campaigners say: “The legal rights of children and young people with special educational needs and disabilities (Send) are still under threat.“The government’s proposed … reforms would significantly reduce existing legal rights to enforceable EHCPs, parental choice of educational settings and independent routes of appeal.”They add: “We … urge ministers to work with Send families and organisations to retain existing Send legal rights, preserve individual provision, improve accountability in the system, and retain meaningful independent routes of appeal.”View image in fullscreenThe campaigners are led by the broadcaster Chris Packham.Photograph: Hugh Hastings/Getty Images for The National LotteryThe letter is signed by 36 people, including Packham, the actor Sally Phillips, the clinical psychologist Simon Baron-Cohen and the Guardian columnist John Harris.The changes were announced in February after lengthy consultation by ministers with experts and Labour MPs.Under the plans, instead of legally enforceable EHCPs, millions of pupils will be given individual support plans, which will be agreed between parents and schools but will not be subject to independent legal appeal.These support plans will be administered by schools rather than local authorities, and parents who are unhappy with them will be asked to appeal to the school rather than being given recourse to an independent tribunal.Schools will be given more resources to help support Send children, but the overall package is designed to curb the rapid escalation in costs under the current system, which has left councils in England facing aprojected £6bn financial black holein two years’ time.However, the Guardianrevealed on Thursdaythat the projected savings risk being undermined by a flood of new applications for EHCPs, as parents look to secure legal protections before the new system takes force.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe campaigners say they want significant changes to the proposals, including keeping the current threshold for EHCPs, allowing parents to appeal against decisions at a tribunal and scrapping the assessment system proposed for individual support plans.Ministers are consulting on the measures and are expected to recommend some changes to Phillipson’s proposals.Legal rights must be retained for children with special educational needs | LettersRead moreHowever, those close to the process say Burnham andLucy Powell, the new education secretary, are likely to adopt more minor modifications to reinforce legal protections rather than the wholesale changes called for by the campaign group.A spokesperson for the Department for Education said: “We inherited a Send system under immense strain. Our once-in-a-generation reforms will change that.“Legal duties on schools to identify and support children’s needs are getting stronger, not weaker. And we will never leave parents without a route to challenge decisions about their child’s support.“We have consulted on our proposals to make sure we get these reforms right, and in the meantime we’re investing in schools to improve inclusion.”Explore more on these topicsSpecial educational needsEducation policyAndy BurnhamLucy PowellBridget PhillipsonEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Entitled’ ex-police chief guilty of gross misconduct over affairs with junior officers | Police | The Guardian
description: Scott Chilton, who led Hampshire and the Isle of Wight police force, barred from becoming a police officer again
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: Scott Chilton, who led Hampshire and the Isle of Wight police force, barred from becoming a police officer again
Content: Scott Chilton, pictured in 2016, was told his behaviour showed ‘persistent dishonesty and lack of integrity’.Photograph: Steve Parsons/PAView image in fullscreenScott Chilton, pictured in 2016, was told his behaviour showed ‘persistent dishonesty and lack of integrity’.Photograph: Steve Parsons/PAPolice‘Entitled’ ex-police chief guilty of gross misconduct over affairs with junior officersScott Chilton, who led Hampshire and the Isle of Wight police, barred from becoming a police officer againSteven MorrisThu 8 Oct 2026 11.11 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 12.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA former chief constable showed a sense of entitlement, dishonesty and lack of integrity by having sexual relationships with two subordinate officers, including engaging in sexual activity while on call to lead major incidents, a misconduct hearing has ruled.The panel found that the behaviour of Scott Chilton, 53, who retired as chief constable of Hampshire and the Isle of Wight before the hearing, amounted to gross misconduct.Chiltonwas found to have had “consensual sexual relations” when he was a chief inspector or superintendent with a woman identified as Officer A, including while he was on duty. When he applied to be chief constable – and during his tenure – he “repetitively and dishonestly” denied this relationship.The hearing in Eastleigh, Hampshire, was told that a consensual relationship with another woman, Officer B, began within weeks of Chilton becoming chief constable.He was found to have “abused his position for a sexual purpose” and should have declared the relationship. When it came to light, he “behaved inappropriately” to Officer B, putting pressure on her to conceal what had happened.Chairing the panel, Michelle Skeer of His Majesty’s Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Services said Chilton’s behaviour showed “persistent dishonesty and lack of integrity”. She said his actions suggested he did not think the rules applied to him.“He was in the highest position of trust as the most senior officer in the constabulary and ought to have known the foreseeable risk of harm by having a covert relationship,” Skeer said.“He repeatedly lied by act and omission about both his relationships with Officer A and Officer B and he knew that this was wrong. His conduct was a serious, deliberate and sustained attempt to mislead … to subvert any negative impact on himself.”Skeer said Chilton had been privy to confidential and sensitive information on colleagues, security and national policing matters. “There was evidence that he was discussing issues which he shouldn’t have been discussing with Officer B during WhatsApp message exchanges.”She added that Chilton had attempted to bully Officer B into “keeping quiet” by asking her to “delete and double delete” their messages and not to go to events that his wife would attend, which showed the power imbalance between them.She said Chilton had engaged in sexual activity with Officer A while on duty and in silver command, which meant he would have been the officer in charge if a major incident had occurred.Skeer added that “his actions were driven by his own entitlement” and the “abuse of his position was for personal gain and ultimately his own sexual gratification”.She said Chilton had acted in a domineering fashion towards his colleagues in an attempt to “control the narrative” in relation to responding to press inquiries about the allegations.Attention also focused during the hearing on disciplinary proceedings against another prominent Hampshire police officer, the former DCI Roger Wood.In February 2025 a disciplinary hearing concluded Wood had inappropriate relations with two junior colleagues and would have been dismissed had he not already resigned.Before his case, Wood claimed to have “damaging information” about Chilton and during the proceedings stated that the chief had “had affairs”.John Beggs KC, who presented the case against the former chief constable, said Chilton had discussed using the force solicitor to prevent Wood from speaking to the press, adding: “He was trying to use his position as a chief constable to advance his own best interests.”Since Chilton became chief constable in February 2023, there have been about 20 misconduct cases in Hampshire in which officers were accused of various forms of sexual behaviour. About five of these haveincluded behaviour against junior officers.Chilton retired in April 2025 after a career spanning 33 years that included actingas a lead for the National Police Chiefs’ Council on national investigation standards and coordination.At the start of the hearing, James Berry KC, representing Chilton, said his client would not be attending the hearing because of “medical issues”.Chilton said in a statement that he admitted the second relationship but not the first. He said he accepted that by not disclosing that relationship he fell short of the standards police officers were judged by.He added: “These were personal matters, rather than issues affecting policing or public safety, and at no point did this relationship influence policing decisions, operational matters or the discharge of professional responsibilities.”He said his “deepest regret” was for his family “for the hurt caused by my poor judgment and actions”.Chilton would have been dismissed if he had not resigned, the panel said. He has been placed on the College of Policing barred officers list, so he can never again become a police officer.Explore more on these topicsPoliceHampshirenewsShareReuse this content

title: BBC pays compensation to PinkNews couple over false sexual misconduct allegations | BBC | The Guardian
description: Broadcaster apologises after admitting claims against Benjamin Cohen and Anthony James were defamatory
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Broadcaster apologises after admitting claims against Benjamin Cohen and Anthony James were defamatory
Content: The PinkNews founder, Benjamin Cohen (left), with his husband, Anthony James, in London, 2022.Photograph: Dave Benett/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe PinkNews founder, Benjamin Cohen (left), with his husband, Anthony James, in London, 2022.Photograph: Dave Benett/Getty ImagesBBCBBC pays compensation to PinkNews couple over false sexual misconduct allegationsBroadcaster apologises after admitting claims against Benjamin Cohen and Anthony James were defamatoryMichael SavageMedia editorThu 8 Oct 2026 11.23 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 12.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheBBChas apologised and paid “substantial” compensation to the couple behind the PinkNews website, after conceding that stories accusing them of sexual misconduct were false and defamatory.In a sweeping admission, the BBC accepted at the high court that a 2024 iPlayer documentary about the PinkNews founder Benjamin Cohen and his husband, Anthony James, called PinkNews: Behind Closed Doors, had made “a series of very serious, false, and defamatory allegations”.The corporation also accepted that an accompanying news article had made “false and extremely harmful” allegations that the pair had placed inappropriate pressure on young female staff members to act as surrogates for them.The claims were widely reported. Downing Street described the claims of sexual misconduct made against the couple behind PinkNews, the world’s largest LGBTQ+ website,as “very concerning”.The accusations also meant that the pair were subjected to investigations by the Children and Family Court Advisory and Support Service, which safeguards the interests of children involved in family court proceedings. The investigations took place before a hearing concerning the couple’s son, who was born via a surrogate.Cohen felt compelled to resign as a trustee of a global disability charity, his legal team told the court. James resigned as an associate non-executive director on the board of Bedfordshire hospitals NHS foundation trust.“These allegations were false and extremely harmful to the claimants’ reputations,” said the couple’s legal team. “They were – unsurprisingly – picked up and republished by other national media outlets and across social media.”The BBC’s barrister said: “On behalf of the defendant, I accept everything that my learned friend has said. The BBC retracts and apologises unreservedly for the defamatory allegations made in the programme and the article.”In a joint statement after the hearing, Cohen and James said the BBC still had questions to answer about how the allegations ever reached publication.“The BBC ignored warnings about the veracity of these allegations and chose to broadcast false claims to millions of people,” they said.“When this began, we were new dads and our son was just six months old. What should have been one of the happiest periods of our lives was instead thrown into chaos, impacting our business, our colleagues and our family. This included being subjected to additional investigations by social workers.“Throughout all of this, our greatest fear has been for our son’s future. We have worried about the day he goes to school and other children find these false allegations online. We have worried about what he might read about his dads, what his friends might say and what that could do to him.“Today’s apology cannot erase what happened, but it means that when that day eventually comes, the truth will be there.”Cohen and James launched legal action last year. The case will no longer go to trial after the BBC apologised and agreed to pay compensation, described as “substantial”. The couple are donating it to the Multiple Sclerosis Society and Bedfordshire Hospitals NHS Charity.The documentary and accompanying BBC article have been removed. The corporation said: “The BBC has reached a settlement with Ben Cohen and Anthony James. We will not be issuing any further comment.”Explore more on these topicsBBCDefamation lawMedia lawLGBTQ+ rightsCharitiesVoluntary sectornewsShareReuse this content

title: Israel promotes film that mimics NAZA documentary | Israel | The Guardian
description: Embassies post links to hastily produced online film echoing style of real Guardian documentary about mass killings of Gaza civilians
Author: Louisa Loveluck
Headline: Embassies post links to hastily produced online film echoing style of real Guardian documentary about mass killings of Gaza civilians
Content: The new online film mimics some of the style of the real NAZA documentary (above) which uses footage shot from rooftops in Tel AvivView image in fullscreenThe new online film mimics some of the style of the real NAZA documentary (above) which uses footage shot from rooftops in Tel AvivIsraelIsrael promotes film that mimics NAZA documentaryEmbassies post links to hastily produced online film echoing style of real Guardian documentary about mass killings of Gaza civiliansLouisa LoveluckThu 8 Oct 2026 13.52 EDTFirst published on Thu 8 Oct 2026 12.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Israeli government is promoting an online film project that mimics the style of NAZA, the award-winning documentary that details Israel’s mass killings of civilians in Gaza, in an attempt to counter the real film’s findings.Thereal documentary, directed by the Oscar-winning film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, and produced by the Guardian, is in cinemas and will be shown in more than 50 countries.The Israeli government has denounced the film andannounced plans to stripAbraham and Szor of their citizenship, accusing them of treason.In recent days, Israeli embassies have been promoting a link to a hastily produced online film entitled NAZA: The Real Story. Mimicking some of the style of the real documentary, including the use of anonymised interviews shot on rooftops in Tel Aviv, it is hosted on a website called nazadocumentary.com.Ariel Averbuch, an Israeli attorney and army reservist who made the new documentary, described it as an “offensive move” intended to shift the world’s focus from allegations about the Israeli military’s killing of civilians. The film claims that Israel has the “most moral army in the world”.Another film-maker listed on the website for NAZA: The Real Story is Roi Danino, a candidate for the rightwing Israel First party.The website domain was registered on 16 September, six days after NAZA’s premiere at the Venice international film festival, where itwon the special jury prizeafter receiving the longest ovation in the festival’s history.Initially, the website falsely presented itself as a promotional page for NAZA itself, naming Abraham and Szor as the directors, and listing film festivals where the documentary was due to be screened.1:55NAZA - official trailer“Shot at night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv, the film reveals in detail the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of terrorists in Gaza,” it said, distorting the film’sofficial synopsisby removing the reference to the deaths of Palestinian civilians.That wording was removed from recent updates of the website, once the video for NAZA: The Real Story had been added to the page.It now appears as a platform for the rival film, with a counter that implausibly suggests the short film has been watched more than 42m times. (The film’s official YouTube page is listed as having just 30,000 views.)According to a technical analysis, the discrepancy suggested the viewer counter could have been driven by requests made to the website, by humans or bots, rather than the number of people who actually watched the video. When asked about the source of the 42m claim, Averbuch said he did not know and referred the questions to his tech team.The Israeli military has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians in Gaza since the Hamas attacks of 7 October 2023, in a military campaign that a United Nations commissionhas describedas genocide.View image in fullscreenRachel Szor and Yuval Abraham speak onstage at the NAZA premiere at the New York film festival on 26 September.Photograph: Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty for FLCThe 24 interviews with Israeli military insiders in the original film NAZA detail how an AI-assisted apparatus of mass surveillance was activated during theGazawar, revealing the systems that were used to target Hamas operatives in the knowledge large numbers of Palestinian civilians would also die.The Israeli embassy to the US, which shared the new documentary on its social media, said the ministry of foreign affairs was not involved in producing the film, and that it had intended only to “amplify the message of its creators and expose wider audiences to arguments challenging and dismantling the blood libels and false allegations”.NAZA film-makers say they spoke to more than 100 sources about Israeli actions in GazaRead moreThe Israeli government said on Thursday that it wasawarding the film-makers with a certificate of appreciation“for their contribution to Israeli public diplomacy”, claiming the production had garnered tens of millions of views.A Guardian spokesperson said: “We are aware that the Israeli government has been promoting a film hosted on a website that initially – and falsely – claimed it was Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s documentary.“This was a brazen attempt to mislead audiences and distract from the urgent questions raised by NAZA.”As well as its global cinema releases, NAZA will be available free on the Guardian’s website from late November.Averbuch is the founder of an organisation that says it conducts “advocacy warfare”, including through the publication of scripts to help influencers criticise Abraham and Szor’s critically acclaimed previous film, No Other Land, which documents the destruction of the Palestinian village Masafer Yatta. The two Palestinian co-directors of No Other Land, Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal, have been harassed or detained by the Israeli military since the film won an Oscar in 2025.Israeli government officials have scrambled to discredit NAZA’s content, while far-right activists have threatened to hunt down the directors.The Israel Defense Forces’ chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, has said they will use “every tool at our disposal” against the film, while themilitary has issueda 10-page response to the film, which was based on interviews with more than 100 sources with knowledge of the military systems used in the war.Within a week of NAZA’s premiere, Israel’s ministry of culture had announced a formal investigation into the documentary, calling for Abraham and Szor to be stripped of their citizenship.Demonstrators gathered outside the home of Szor’s parents, demanding that the she face the death penalty, and a mural depicting the film-makers through the sights of a gun appeared in the Israeli city of Ashdod.View image in fullscreenSpanish film industry members show support for NAZA’s directors at the San Sebastian International film festival on 25 September.Photograph: Ander Gillenea/AFP/GettyOn Monday, the far-right Israeli activist Mordechai David announced he was fundraising in order to establish a team that would “chase” Abraham. “We’ll find him,” David said in a video posted to Instagram.Szor and Abrahamaddressed the backlashto their documentary at a Q&A after its New York premiere. “Our country is doing so much to hide these systems,” Szor told the audience. “It’s not a world that is open even to the Israeli public.”At theLondon film festivalon Thursday, one of NAZA’s producers, James Wilson, said Israeli politicians’ “hysterical, vituperative, aggressive backlash” to the documentary had not been anticipated by the team behind it.Wilson said although Abraham and Szor had “anticipated displeasure … there wasn’t an anticipation of the level of aggression leading to these threats and the rabble-rousing aspect”.He added: “To have made a film, a documentary film and be threatened by the political elites of your home country, with charges of treason and defamation … it’s been very difficult and stressful and horrible and scary for them.“I try to look at the overwhelmingly positive reaction to the film in the majority of the world.”Additional reporting byPhilip McMahonandRachel HallExplore more on these topicsIsraelNAZAGazaPalestineMiddle East and north AfricaIsrael-Gaza warDocumentary filmsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump promises not to attack Iran before November’s US midterms | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: Statement outlines pause on protracted war US president has struggled to end after almost eight months
Author: Joseph Gedeon
Headline: Statement outlines pause on protracted war US president has struggled to end after almost eight months
Content: Donald Trump speaking to reporters on the South Lawn of the White House on Wednesday.Photograph: Anna Moneymaker/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump speaking to reporters on the South Lawn of the White House on Wednesday.Photograph: Anna Moneymaker/Getty ImagesDonald TrumpTrump promises not to attack Iran before November’s US midtermsStatement outlines pause on protracted war US president has struggled to end after almost eight monthsJoseph Gedeonin WashingtonThu 8 Oct 2026 13.56 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 15.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump has promised not to attack Iran before November’s US midterm elections, outlining a pause on the protracted war he has struggled to end after almost eight months.In a Truth Socialposton Thursday, the US president said Washington was “having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran”, which he claimed was “in very bad condition, both Economically and Militarily”.The strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas passed through before the war, was all but closed after the US and Israel struck Iran in late February.On Thursday, however, Trump suggested that oil was moving through the strait in record volumes: “22 Million Barrels, last night alone”, he claimed, “with not one barrel coming from, or going to, Iran”. The figure could not be independently verified.“We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd,” Trump wrote. “IRAN WILL NOT HAVE A NUCLEAR WEAPON!”The US first imposed a blockade on the strait of Hormuz in April after talks in Islamabad collapsed, and reinstated it in July after a short-lived June deal to end the fighting. Fighting flared again in early September, when US forces struck rocket launchers on Iran’s Larak Island and Tehran responded with missiles aimed at American military bases in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates.Trump’s public position on the elections has shifted over the past month. On 2 September, as the US exchanged fire with Iran for the first time in weeks, he told reporters he was “not affected by the election”, adding that he was not on the ballot himself but intended to help his party.A week later, before heading to the Republican “midterm convention” in Dallas,he saidhe expected the war to end almost as soon as the voting was over, and accused Tehran of holding out in the hope that a change of power in Congress would leave it free to pursue a nuclear weapon. He also conceded that US oil prices were unlikely to fall before polling day.AReuters/Ipsos surveyfrom late September found that only about a third of Americans approved of the strikes on Iran, while more than four in five expected the conflict to last for an extended period, and that approval for Trump among Republicans had fallen from 82% to 73% in a week.Polling averages now show Democrats leading Republicans by roughly nine points on the generic congressional ballot, according toforecaster Nate Silver, the widest margin of this election cycle.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly, for twelve weeksSign up toHow we winBernie Sanders, Robert Reich, Stacey Abrams, Medhi Hasan, Paul Krugman and other bold thinkers on how to defeat Trumpism and build a better future. From our opinion desk.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Wall Street Journalreportedin September that JD Vance, the US vice-president, and secretary of state Marco Rubio had privately warned Trump the conflict could extend through the remainder of his presidency.Trump’s post did not say what the US would do after 3 November.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpUS-Israel war on IranUS midterm elections 2026Trump administrationUS politicsShareReuse this content

title: Anne Carson wins Nobel prize in literature 2026 | Nobel prize in literature | The Guardian
description: Most prestigious literature prize goes to Canadian known for genre-crossing works such as Autobiography of Red
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: Most prestigious literature prize goes to Canadian known for genre-crossing works such as Autobiography of Red
Content: The academy cited Anne Carson’s ‘bold and inventive oeuvre’ in its awarding of the prize.Photograph: Pontus Lundahl/TT/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe academy cited Anne Carson’s ‘bold and inventive oeuvre’ in its awarding of the prize.Photograph: Pontus Lundahl/TT/ReutersNobel prize in literatureAnne Carson wins Nobel prize in literature 2026Most prestigious literature prize goes to Canadian known for genre-crossing works such as Autobiography of Red‘Delights await!’: Margaret Atwood and other writers on Nobel winner Anne CarsonWhere to start with: Anne CarsonEmma LoffhagenandLeyland Ceccoin TorontoThu 8 Oct 2026 10.03 EDTFirst published on Thu 8 Oct 2026 07.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheNobel prize in literaturehas been awarded to the Canadian poet and essayist Anne Carson, the Swedish Academy has announced.The academy cited the author’s “bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature”.The Nobel prize, regarded as the most prestigious award in global literature, is awarded for a lifetime body of work. The winner receives 12m Swedish kronor (£900,000).Ingrid Carlberg, the permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy, said she had told Carson of the award on the phone shortly before the news broke. “She had time to tell me that she is, for the moment, in Iceland, where she is listening to the wind,” Carlberg said. “She was taken by surprise but very happy. I could hear that in her voice.”View image in fullscreenBooks by Anne Carson on display at a Waterstones bookshop in London.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersBorn in Toronto in 1950, Carson is known forwork that moves freely between poetry, prose and translation, drawing heavily on the literature and mythology of the ancient Greek world. She has been a professor of classics at various institutions including Princeton, New York University and McGill University in Montreal. She is the 19th woman to win, out of 123 literature laureates.Carson’s first book, Eros the Bittersweet, was published in 1986 and combined literary criticism with an exploration of desire and the ancient Greek tradition.Her best-known work is Autobiography of Red, a 1998 novel in verse inspired by the fragments of the ancient Greek poet Stesichorus. It reimagines the myth of Geryon, the red-winged monster killed by Herakles, as the story of a modern teenage boy navigating heartbreak and desire.In 2001, she became the first woman to win the TS Eliot prize, for her collection The Beauty of the Husband. She has also been awarded Guggenheim and MacArthur fellowships.The Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney,congratulated the poeton X after the announcement. “With wit, imagination, and a style entirely her own, Canadian poet Anne Carson has reimagined the classics. She has brought ancient stories to new audiences and transformed the way we think about literature,” he said, adding that it was a “proud moment for Canada”.David Leonard, the executive director of the Writers’ Trust ofCanada, said: “Anne is such a brilliant writer. Her work is broad, but also extremely smart.” Calling Carson’s work “intoxicating”, he said her four-decade career had resulted in a peerless collection of poems and essays. “They’re beautiful, they’re smart, they’re true and they are humane. It’s exactly what we need in our writing.”Carson’s work has attracted praise from fellow writers including Susan Sontag, who once said: “She is one of the few writers writing in English that I would read anything she wrote. If there’s a magazine that has something of hers in it, I buy it automatically.”View image in fullscreenIngrid Carlberg announcing Anne Carson as the recipient of the 2026 Nobel prize in literature in Stockholm on Thursday.Photograph: Christine Olsson/EPAAnders Olsson, the chair of the Swedish Academy’s Nobel Committee for Literature, praised Carson for work that had “broken away from lyrical poetry bound to the narrative self and inspired new forms of contemporary literature”. He said: “This method of writing leads to playful and ironic works that move not only between classical and modern poetry but also between different genres and artforms.”Carson’s books have ranged widely in form. Men in the Off Hours combined verse essays, poems, epitaphs and prose about artists and historical figures, and won the inaugural Griffin poetry prize in 2001. Decreation, another eclectic work, brought together poetry, essays and an opera.Nox, published in 2010, is particularly characteristic of Carson’s avant-garde approach to literature – the book takes the form of an accordion-fold box containing a reproduction of a notebook Carson made after the death of her brother. Her later works include Red Doc> and Float.In aGuardian reviewof Red Doc>, Sarah Crown wrote: “To engage so fluidly, so originally and compellingly, with a story first told more than 3,000 years ago, is astonishing: her ambition is one thing; the fact that it is so completely achieved is, frankly, something else.”Much of Carson’s work has emerged from her fascination with language itself. The Swedish Academy noted: “Almost all her literary production has centred upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning,” adding that Carson had identified the etymology of words as “the starting point for all her work”.Asked why she continually moved between forms, Carson said in an interview: “Boredom, I guess. There is a restlessness. There are a lot of forms to try.”She has acknowledged the difficulties that come with her experimental style. “[My work] does fall apart a lot,” she said in a 2018 interview. “It gets just too weird for anyone to care about reading, or else it gets diluted into a sort of parody of itself.”Ira Wells, the president of PEN Canada, said Carson’s win felt “particularly significant at a moment in which Canada and Europe are strengthening cultural ties amidst broader global disruption”. He added: “On an aesthetic level, Carson’s verse vibrates on profound human frequencies, at a moment in which more and more language is formulated by machines.”Carson has generally kept her personal life out of interviews. However, in an August 2024 article for the London Review of Books, she disclosed that she had been diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease.The Nobel prize in literature has been awarded on 118 previous occasions since 1901. Recent laureates include Annie Ernaux, Bob Dylan, Abdulrazak Gurnah, Louise Glück, Peter Handke and Olga Tokarczuk. Last year’s recipient was the Hungarian author László Krasznahorkai, known for his dystopic and avant-garde writing.Carson, 76, will formally receive the medal and diploma in a ceremony in Stockholm in December.To browse works by Anne Carson, visitguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsNobel prize in literatureAnne CarsonFictionPoetryAwards and prizesCanadaAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Top bosses at Goldman Sachs to share bonus pot worth up to $500m | Goldman Sachs | The Guardian
description: Eye-watering sum, to be split between 20 bankers, is one of the biggest payouts in the bank’s history
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Eye-watering sum, to be split between 20 bankers, is one of the biggest payouts in the bank’s history
Content: The bank’s chief executive, David Solomon, is due to take about $100m (£75,595) of the reward.Photograph: Aaron Schwartz/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe bank’s chief executive, David Solomon, is due to take about $100m (£75,595) of the reward.Photograph: Aaron Schwartz/ReutersGoldman SachsTop bosses at Goldman Sachs to share bonus pot worth up to $500mEye-watering sum, to be split between 20 bankers, is one of the biggest payouts in the bank’s historyKalyeena MakortoffBanking correspondentThu 8 Oct 2026 14.09 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 14.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTop bosses atGoldman Sachsare in line to share a bonus pot worth up to $500m (£378m) this year, marking one of the biggest payouts in the Wall Street bank’s history.The eye-watering sum will be shared between 20 bankers, with its chief executive, David Solomon, due to take about $100m (£75.6m) of the reward, which is made up of Goldman Sachs stock.That is more than double the value of the record $47m (£35.5m) annual pay packet he was granted last year.The $500m bonus pot is the culmination of a long-term investment plan first crafted by the bank in 2021.The final sum, which is due to be confirmed later this month, is tied to how high Goldman’s share price has climbed over the past five years, as well as how its stock price has performed compared with peers such as JP Morgan and Bank of America over that period.Goldman Sachs said the bonuses were meant to persuade bosses to stay at the bank “in an increasingly competitive market”.The bank’s president, John Waldron, who is widely expected to succeed Solomon as chief executive, is also in line for a payout, alongside other top bosses such as the co-heads of global banking and markets, Ashok Varadhan and Dan Dees.News of the bumper bonus, which was first reported by Bloomberg, comes days before Goldman is due to report third-quarter earnings on 13 October.The bonuses reflect the value of Goldman Sachs stock, which has surged roughly 146% over the past five years, and climbed about 300% since Solomon took the helm as chief executive.A spokesperson for the bank said: “The board created these awards to achieve three principal objectives: align compensation with rigorous performance thresholds, ensure leadership continuity and enhance retention of our top talent in an increasingly competitive market. It’s no secret our firm has performed exceptionally well in the years since.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe payouts are the latest in a string of large payouts for executives in the US, particularly on Wall Street.The US lender Citigroup announced earlier this year that its chief executive, Jane Fraser, had been paid a record $42m (£31.8m) for 2025. Meanwhile, JP Morgan’s chief executive, Jamie Dimon,took home a total pay package worth $43m (£32.5m) last year, up 10% from a year earlier. Dimon’s own long-term incentive award is worth about $270m (£204.1m), according to Bloomberg.Explore more on these topicsGoldman SachsBankingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Bank governor urges John Healey to use budget to allay market fears amid bond turmoil | Gilts | The Guardian
description: Andrew Bailey tells chancellor ‘whatever the stance of fiscal policy, it must be credible and be seen as such by financial markets’
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Andrew Bailey tells chancellor ‘whatever the stance of fiscal policy, it must be credible and be seen as such by financial markets’
Content: The interest rate on 10-year UK government bonds is at its highest level since July 2007, when the global financial crisis was starting to unfold.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAView image in fullscreenThe interest rate on 10-year UK government bonds is at its highest level since July 2007, when the global financial crisis was starting to unfold.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAGiltsBank governor urges John Healey to use budget to allay market fears amid bond turmoilAndrew Bailey tells chancellor ‘whatever the stance of fiscal policy, it must be credible and be seen as such by financial markets’Heather StewartandPhillip InmanThu 8 Oct 2026 12.38 EDTFirst published on Thu 8 Oct 2026 08.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Bank of England governor, Andrew Bailey, has urged the chancellor,John Healey, to agree a budget that reassures financial markets after the UK’s medium-term borrowing costs hit a fresh 19-year high.With investors offloading government bonds previously considered safe havens amid fears of rising inflation, Bailey told all governments caught in the crosshairs of financial speculators that they needed to avoid market turmoil that raises the interest paid on debt.Recentdramatic moves in government bond marketshave been driven by international factors, but will increase the pressure on Healey ahead of his tax and spending announcement on 28 October.The yield, or interest rate, on 10-year UK government bonds had risen 0.06 percentage points by lunchtime in London, to 5.515%. That was the highest level since July 2007, when the global financial crisis was starting to unfold.Yields on 20- and 30-year UK government bonds, which are known as gilts, also rose significantly, to their highest level since as long ago as 1998. Yields go up when bond prices go down.Yields later dropped back on a day of volatile trading, but analysts said further conflict in the Middle East would push them up again as concerns increased about inflation becoming embedded in many major economies.Meanwhile, the benchmarkoil price rose by more than 5%to $105.3 a barrel amid escalating tensions in the Middle East and a squeeze on production from the threat of a hurricane off the US coast.Diesel prices at UK pumpshit £2 a litre last week, leading to concerns among central banks that inflation will surge over the coming months, leading to higher interest rates and burgeoning government debt financing costs.Speaking at a conference in Istanbul, Bailey said he would not meddle in government policy, but he had one observation for Healey after the recent bond rout dramatically increased UK borrowing costs.“Whatever the stance of fiscal policy, it must be credible and be seen as such by financial markets,” he said.Realistic commitments to rein in debt would help curb demands ‌for higher returns from investors who might sell when there were shocks like the outbreak of the Iran war, he said. “In other words, such commitments are needed more than ever when these negative shocks occur.”Economists believe rising borrowing costs and a weaker growth outlook are likely to have wiped out around half of the £24bn buffer against Labour’s fiscal rules that Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves, built up at the time of her spring statement in March – perhaps significantly more.Healey is expected to raise taxes at the budget to partly rebuild that cushion, as well as paying for policy interventions including thesix-month VAT cut on electricity billsand a modestenergy support package for the poorest households.Some economists are warning the chancellor not to go too far in rebuilding the Treasury’s headroom, however. Andrew Wishart, of Berenberg Bank, said: “Raising taxes to keep the surplus close to the size it was in the March forecast (ie to ‘maintain the headroom’) would do unnecessary damage to economic incentives.”He argues that gilt yields are likely to come back down over the next year, with the Bank of England likely to make fewer rate rises than the four that investors currently expect.The Bank is widely expected to raise interest rates at its November meeting to tackle surging inflation, echoing moves already made by the European Central Bank, Federal Reserve and Bank of Japan.The bond selloff has intensified across big economies in recent days,as oil prices have soared, with no resolution of the Middle East conflict in sight.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionInvestors appear to be anxious about higher inflation and runaway government spending. France has been hardest hit, as Paris battles to pass a budget, but the selloff has been widespread.Reuters reported that European Central Bank officials and eurozone finance ministers were preparing on Thursday to make representations to the French government to pass a 2027 budget to calm bond ⁠markets.Investors are worried about the country’s large budget deficit and 2027 presidential election. Its ⁠10-year bond yield has jumped nearly 80 basis points since the start of September and hit its highest level since July 2002, just short of 5%.An EU official said finance ministers were unlikely to make a public plea, but would call for a budget that brought down annual borrowing.“That’s kind of a no-brainer. So I would expect this to be the main message,” the official said.Kristalina Georgieva, managing director of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), hasurged governments to tighten their beltsin response to rising bond yields.“My message to the world’s economic policymakers will be this: we cannot keep delaying necessary policy action – you have the tools, now have the wisdom to use them,” she said, ahead of next week’s IMF annual meeting in Bangkok.Higher yields not only push up costs for indebted governments, but have knock-on effects for borrowers across the economy, including homeowners and businesses.The US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, has tried to rein in yields on the US’s long-term debt byincreasing buybacksof its government bonds, known as treasuries, but the policy appears to have had little impact.Yields on the 30-year treasuries targeted by Bessent’s policy were about 5.235% when he announced the doubling of buybacks in August, but have since surged above 5.7%.Explore more on these topicsGiltsBondsJohn HealeynewsShareReuse this content

title: E.ON Next deal to buy Ovo Energy leaves UK with just ‘big three’ energy suppliers | E.ON | The Guardian
description: Competition watchdog clears takeover despite concerns that suppliers will have less incentive to lower bills
Author: Jillian Ambrose
Headline: Competition watchdog clears takeover despite concerns that suppliers will have less incentive to lower bills
Content: E.ON Next will now become the UK’s second-largest energy supplier, narrowly behind Octopus Energy.Photograph: Mark Richardson/AlamyView image in fullscreenE.ON Next will now become the UK’s second-largest energy supplier, narrowly behind Octopus Energy.Photograph: Mark Richardson/AlamyE.ONE.ON Next deal to buy Ovo Energy leaves UK with just ‘big three’ energy suppliersCompetition watchdog clears takeover despite concerns that suppliers will have less incentive to lower billsJillian AmbroseEnergy correspondentThu 8 Oct 2026 11.16 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 13.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlmost three-quarters of households in Great Britain are now served by just three energy suppliers, afterE.ONNext completed a deal to buy Ovo Energy despite fresh concerns about competition in the energy market.The takeover concluded on Thursday after Britain’s competition watchdog cleared it, despite concerns that the shrinking number of household energy suppliers could mean bill payers will have less choice and suppliers will have less incentive to lower bills.While there will be no immediate change for the 4 million households supplied by Ovo, the sale means that E.ON Next, which already supplies 5.6 million households, will hold 25% of the household energy market – or 13.45m gas and electricity accounts – and become Great Britain’s second-largest energy supplier.The supplier’s hold on the market is narrowly behind Octopus Energy, which holds a 26% share or 14.3m accounts, and ahead of legacy energy incumbent British Gas, which was once the top supplier but today serves about 23% of the market or 12.5m accounts.It also deals a blow to the decade-long efforts to dismantle the dominance of what were the“Big Six” energy suppliersto increase competition and lower energy prices.Tom Goswell, the energy supply lead at Cornwall Insight, a leading consultancy, said: “The big six have become the big three, and there have been questions raised over how this will impact household choice and the health of the market.”Those concerns were rebuffed by Chris Norbury, chief executive of E.ON UK, who described the market as “fiercely competitive” and said the company’s “flexibility and scale” would allow it to “deliver for customers now and to transform for the energy system to come”.The legacy big six suppliers – British Gas, EDF Energy, E.ON UK, SSE, Scottish Power and npower – dominated about 85% of the energy market in 2016 whena landmark investigation by the CMAwarned that customers were overpaying by roughly £1.4bn to £1.7bn every year due to weak market competition.As a result of the E.ON deal, about 90% of Great Britain’s household energy supply market will be held by only five suppliers when including EDF Energy and Scottish Power alongside the big three.Although there was a surge in new energy start-ups after 2016 – led by Octopus, Ovo and Bulb Energy – the market began to shrink after SSEsold its household supply business to Ovo in 2019, and dozens of supplierswent bustduring the 2021/22 energy crisis.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOctopus became the biggest supplier in the market aftertaking on 1.5 million customers from Bulb, which became the biggest casualty when it went into administration in 2022.“Larger suppliers do bring with them a degree of stability, andafter about 30 firms dropped out of the market, leaving customers wondering who would be sending their next bill, stability is not something to dismiss lightly,” Goswell said.“The concern with fewer suppliers is that the pressure to compete eases off, taking with it some of the incentive to keep prices low and offer something different. The big suppliers have the resources to give people real choice, and the test over the next few years will be whether households who shop around find a genuine range of deals waiting for them rather than three versions of the same thing,” he added.Explore more on these topicsE.ONEnergy industryUtilitiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Harvey Nichols’ Birmingham store to close in January | Retail industry | The Guardian
description: Closure will cost at least 60 jobs, while Leeds and Bristol outlets to be converted to Flannels brand
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: Closure will cost at least 60 jobs, while Leeds and Bristol outlets to be converted to Flannels brand
Content: The Mailbox, home to Birmingham’s Harvey Nichols store, which opened 25 years ago.Photograph: Arcaid Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Mailbox, home to Birmingham’s Harvey Nichols store, which opened 25 years ago.Photograph: Arcaid Images/AlamyRetail industryHarvey Nichols’ Birmingham store to close in JanuaryClosure will cost at least 60 jobs, while Leeds and Bristol outlets to be converted to Flannels brandSarah ButlerThu 8 Oct 2026 13.18 EDTFirst published on Thu 8 Oct 2026 12.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHarvey Nichols’ Birmingham store is to close in January, with the loss of at least 60 jobs, while its Leeds and Bristol outlets will be converted to the Flannels brand in a shake-up under Mike Ashley’sFrasers Group.The owner of Sports Directbought the department store chain, whose headquarters are at the Knightsbridge site in London, for £43m on the day it was put into administration in mid-August.About 1,000 of the group’s 1,200 jobs and six UK stores were saved in that deal. Harvey Nichols’ Oxo Tower restaurant was sold to a separate buyer, saving 130 jobs.The chain’s branches in London, Edinburgh,Birmingham, Leeds and Manchester and Bristol are accompanied by outlets in Riyadh, Dubai, Doha, Kuwait and two in Hong Kong. A further store in Dublin was closed by administrators in September.View image in fullscreenHouse of Fraser in Bristol will be rebranded as Flannels.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersThe Harvey Nichols Group owed about £100m to unsecured creditors at the time of its administration, including dozens of brands from Canada Goose to Victoria Beckham.Ashley previously said he would keep Harvey Nichols’ Knightsbridge and Edinburgh stores, but rebrand the four other UK stores – in Birmingham, Leeds, Manchester andBristol– as House of Fraser or Flannels.It has now emerged that Frasers plans to close the Birmingham store, which opened 25 years ago, with staff informed earlier this week, as first reported by the fashion trade journal Drapers. Frasers will rebrandLeedsand Bristol to Flannels, while the future for the Manchester, Edinburgh and London Harvey Nichols stores is unclear.Michael Murray, the chief executive of Frasers Group, recently said in a statement about the group’s luxury division: “Our ambition is clear: to continue scaling Frasers Group Luxury globally through organic expansion, acquisitions and strategic investments, creating long-term value for our brand partners, customers and the group.”Ashley has bought aseries of struggling premium brandsin recent years after starting out with a single sports shop.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFrasers bought the House of Fraser department store chain out of administration in 2018 and has since closed about 40 of its 60 stores. It has been building its interests in luxury fashion with the Flannels chain and large stakes in brands such as the British handbag maker Mulberry.The group recently celebratedlifting its stakein the German label Hugo Boss to 48%, just short of taking full control, despite opposition from the company’s board.Frasers did not respond to a request for comment.Explore more on these topicsRetail industryFrasers GroupMike AshleyBirminghamLuxury goods sectorJob lossesLeedsnewsShareReuse this content

title: The woman with the mattress: the radical, rage-fuelled history of anti-rape art | Art | The Guardian
description: A performance piece from 2014 has gone viral in response to an allegation of rape at Cornell University. But with such defiant pieces stretching back hundreds of years, will things ever change?
Author: Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Headline: A performance piece from 2014 has gone viral in response to an allegation of rape at Cornell University. But with such defiant pieces stretching back hundreds of years, will things ever change?
Content: Viral artwork … Emma Sulkowicz carries a mattress at Columbia University, as part of Mattress Performance (Carry That Weight), 2014Photograph: Andrew Burton/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenViral artwork … Emma Sulkowicz carries a mattress at Columbia University, as part of Mattress Performance (Carry That Weight), 2014Photograph: Andrew Burton/Getty ImagesArtThe woman with the mattress: the radical, rage-fuelled history of anti-rape artA performance piece from 2014 has gone viral in response to an allegation of rape at Cornell University. But with such defiant pieces stretching back hundreds of years, will things ever change?Rhiannon Lucy CosslettThu 8 Oct 2026 10.19 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 10.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn September 2014, Emma Sulkowicz began to carry a blue mattress weighing 23kg around her university campus. The mattress was similar to the ones New York’s Columbia University used in its dorm rooms, where Sulkowicz said she had been raped by a fellow student two years earlier. Her performance/endurance artwork constituted her visual art senior thesis, drawing attention to the lack of criminal charges brought against her alleged attacker and his continued presence at the university. As she hauled it across campus, others could choose to assist her with her burden. Many did. She recorded responses to the piece in a diary.“I could have taken my pillow,”she told the writer Jessica Valentiat the time. “But I want people to see how it weighs down a person to be ignored by the school administration and harassed by police.”Sulkowicz would carry the mattress, she said, for as long as her alleged attacker remained at Columbia. And so she ended up carrying it all the way to graduation where, helped by other women, she took it on stage. The university president refused to shake her hand, turning away from her instead.Footage of Mattress Performance (Carry That Weight) went viral in 2014, just as the momentum for #MeToo was building. Now the performance piece has gone viral again, in response to public fury at anotherallegation of campus rape. Jane Doe (the female pseudonym used in the US for the purposes of anonymity) is suing Cornell University in New York, and seven men, claiming they drugged her and gang-raped her when she was studying there in 2024.View image in fullscreen'An imposing force’ … In Mourning and In Rage (1977) by Suzanne Lacy and Leslie LabowitzPhotograph: Maria Karras/Suzanne Lacy and Leslie LabowitzThrough her performance work, Sulkowicz joined a long line of women who have made art in response to rape, sexual assault and domestic violence. It forms a radical, if rarely explored, canon that encompasses a huge range of responses. Paula Rego’s 2008-9 workOratoriowas an altarpiece-like triptych featuring scenes of sexual assault. Yoko Ono, in 1964’sCut Piece, invited members of an audience to remove her clothing with scissors as she knelt unmoving. Jenny Holzer used human bones in 1994’sLustmord Table, her installation about rape as a weapon of war in the former Yugoslavia.Nan Goldindocumented a violent relationship in The Ballad of Sexual Dependency. AndKara Walkermade cut-paper silhouettes that explored the brutal legacy of white male power in the American south.In fact, it’s a canon that stretches back at least as far as the 17th century, whenArtemisia Gentileschi, whose rape and subsequent torture as part of her rapist’s trial no doubt informed the rage at the heart of her Judith Slaying Holofernes (1612-13). Her earliest known work, Susanna and the Elders, painted in 1610 when she was 17, viscerally conveys an intimate knowledge of how it feels to be a young woman vulnerable to sexual abuse and harassment.That knowledge is something many of us carry around, so it’s no surprise that sexual and gender-based violence is a subject that female artists return to again and again. The current Tate Modern show examining the cult and commercialisation of Frida Kahlo provides an apposite moment to reflect that Kahlo’s most groundbreaking works are never going to make it on to coasters and tote bags.A Few Small Nips, from 1935, shows a woman’s stabbed, naked body on a bed smeared with blood. The work was inspired by a story Kahlo read in a newspaper in which a man who murdered his wife dismissed his actions with the words: “But I only gave her a few small nips.”View image in fullscreenKara Walker, Confederate Prisoners Being Conducted from Jonesborough to Atlanta from the portfolio Harper’s Pictorial History of the Civil War (Annotated), 2005.Photograph: Kara Walker. Photo by Peter Paul GeoffrionNo less bloody is Ana Mendieta’s response to the rape and murder of Sarah Ann Ottens, a female student at the University of Iowa.Rape Scene(1973) was a private performance piece that the artist staged in her apartment for fellow students. Recreating a sexual assault, she posed semi-nude, bloodied and bent over a table. She stayed in that position for over an hour, forcing her audience to confront the brutal, traumatic reality of male violence against women.It does not feature in the current Tate Modern exhibition of her work, but her film Moffitt Building Piece, made in the same year in response to the same crime, does. In it, passersby are filmed without their knowledge as they encounter a bloodstain left by Mendieta on the pavement outside her building. Their responses – to ignore, to sidestep – serve as a metaphor for how violence against women is occluded by society.This feels all the more relevant in light of the gap at the heart of the Tate show: the violent manner of Mendieta’s own death and how her fate has for many come to represent misogyny in the art world. Many believe her fall from a 34th-floor window was not suicide, but rather a murder committed by Carl Andre, her husband, who was tried and acquitted (exhibitions of his work have attracted feminist protests due to what they say is his lack of accountability andher erasure as an artist). The decision tosideline this element of an artist’s biography, perhaps in a well-meaning attempt to prevent her being part of a “victim” narrative, ended up muffling the pain and the outrage that gives her works their power, robbing them of crucial context.View image in fullscreenFrida Kahlo, A Few Small Nips, 1935.Photograph: Album/AlamyThat pain was manifest in another feminist performance piece: Suzanne Lacy and Leslie Labowitz’sIn Mourning and In Ragefrom 1977. At the time, a serial killer sensationalised by the media as “the hillside strangler” was murdering women in Los Angeles. In response, the two artists, along with feminist activists and some family members of the victims, staged a funeral motorcade to city hall. Over 60 women followed behind a hearse from which, on arrival, 10 others emerged, 7ft tall and clad in black mourning robes.These were not passive, grieving victims but an imposing, rageful force, delivering statements anda chorus of: “In memory of our sisters, we fight back!” It followed Lacy’s workThree Weeks in May, which saw her daily updating a “rape map” of the city, based on statistics given to her by police. These interventions arguably had an impact on how the police and media in the city approached sexual assault at the time.Given that one in four women have been raped or sexually assaulted,according to Rape Crisis (England and Wales), such artworks will naturally often feel emotionally heavy for the viewer. Yet at a time when equality and justice can still feel so far away, when so many women are carrying around their own proverbial mattresses, it is crucial to continue to give voice to these experiences.I know I am not the only woman who found herself in tears during A Second Life, Tracey Emin’s retrospective at Tate Modern earlier this year. This happened while I watched her 1995 short filmWhy I Never Became a Dancer, about her teenage experiences of sexual exploitation and the shaming she was subjected to during a dance competition. “Shane, Eddie, Tony, Doug, Richard … this one’s for you,” she says, before breaking into a smiling dance to You Make Me Feel (Mighty Real).As a work of art, it is defiance, strength and survival. What made me cry was Emin’s determination to be joyful despite the abuse she suffered. What’s a crying shame is that it still feels so painfully relevant.Explore more on these topicsArtRape and sexual assaultViolence against women and girlsTracey EminPaula RegoYoko OnoJenny HolzerfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Good night, and good lick: what can we expect from George Clooney’s restaurant? | Movies | The Guardian
description: The newly-official French citizen is planning to open an Italian restaurant in Provence. Will it float like his tequila brand or sink as swiftly as the Steven Spielberg submarine eatery that made one reviewer ‘embarrassed to be human’?
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: The newly-official French citizen is planning to open an Italian restaurant in Provence. Will it float like his tequila brand or sink as swiftly as the Steven Spielberg submarine eatery that made one reviewer ‘embarrassed to be human’?
Content: Ham … George Clooney in Jay Kelly.Photograph: Peter Mountain/NetflixView image in fullscreenHam … George Clooney in Jay Kelly.Photograph: Peter Mountain/NetflixMoviesGood night, and good lick: what can we expect from George Clooney’s restaurant?The newly-official French citizen is planning to open an Italian restaurant in Provence. Will it float like his tequila brand or sink as swiftly as the Steven Spielberg submarine eatery that made one reviewer ‘embarrassed to be human’?Stuart HeritageThu 8 Oct 2026 07.25 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 07.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Provençal village of Cotignac is not wanting for places to eat. Within a short drive of its pale stone houses, you can find a wealth of high-end dining options. La Table de Mentone, set within the beautiful Château Mentone wine estate, is famed for the produce it grows on site. The Michelin-starred Restaurant Bruno offers dazzling variations of truffle dishes. More locally, Picotte Provence offers the sort of charming village dining that showcases the best of what the region has to offer.However, despite all these wonderful options, there is one thing that Cotignac does not yet boast, and that’s a celebrity vanity project. But that is all about to change, thanks to the news thatGeorge Clooneyis planning to open a restaurant there.According to reports, Clooney, who lives locally, is keen to open a restaurant in partnership with the Canadian owner of a nearby hotel, with an elegant dining room and an outdoor terrace. No formal application has been submitted, but it is thought that the restaurant will open next year.Some aspects of this make more sense than others. After all, Clooney and his family have beenFrench citizens since December, so it would make perfect sense for him to want to lay deeper roots within the community. In fact Clooney is so French that he turns up for the only memorable scene in the recent Call My Agent! movie.View image in fullscreenClooney and his wife, Amal, have been French citizens since December.Photograph: Earl Gibson III/Deadline/Getty ImagesHowever, it has also been reported that Clooney’s proposed restaurant would be Italian, which seems a little odd given that Provence is one of the major food capitals of the world. Becoming a citizen of one country and then immediately building a temple to the food of the last place you lived in could be seen as a little vulgar.‘Suspension of entry into the US’, paparazzi – and wine: three other reasons George Clooney moved to FranceRead moreBut only a fool would rule Clooney out here. This is a man with a habit of making a success of himself whenever he turns his hand to something new. His tequila company was so successful that not only didhe sell it for $1bnbut now you can’t walk into a supermarket without tripping over a dozen alcoholic drink brands created by performers desperately hoping that it will make them enough money to stop acting.In fact, Clooney’s tequila money is probably his saving grace here. He could sink hundreds of millions of euros into this new restaurant and, even if it ended up being a disaster, he would still be abnormally well insulated for the rest of his life. And that is probably a good thing because, when it comes to restaurants, Hollywood figures don’t tend to have the best reputation.The true successes, such asRobert De Niro’s Nobu, are few and far between. More often than not, these things tend to end in disaster. For instance, when Hulk Hogan decided to dip his toe into hospitality in the mid-1990s, the venture lasted less than a year. Admittedly this is because it was a pasta restaurant inside a shopping mall, and all the pasta was shaped like Hulk Hogan, and the place was called Pastamania, and it had an exclamation mark on the end, which meant you couldn’t say it aloud without sounding either angry or scared, but the point still stands.View image in fullscreenNot wanting for places to eat … the Provençal village of Cotignac.Photograph: David Gabis/AlamyThere are so many others. In 2002 Jennifer Lopez opened a restaurant in Pasadena inspired by her mother’s cooking, but it never quite recovered from the moment when she hired her ex-husband as manager, then fired him after six months, then got sued by him in a case so messy that he later ended up threatening to leak their honeymoon footage. And in 2012 Eva Longoria opened a restaurant called SHe, which was a steakhouse for women complete with smaller portions, a catwalk and dessert menus with mirrors on the back so diners could retouch their makeup. It closed in 2014.Then there is the daddy of them all, a calamity of such legendary proportions that you have to assume Clooney has paid attention. I am of course referring to Steven Spielberg’s Dive! restaurant that was open for a few years in the 1990s.It is genuinely hard to know where to start here. Dive! (enough with the overexuberant punctuation already, 90s celebrities) was based on Spielberg’s obsession with submarines, to the extent that it was literally shaped like a submarine – complete with working periscope – and primarily sold submarine sandwiches. Also, at 45-minute intervals, an announcement would interrupt the meal, instructing diners to prepare for submersion. At this point red warning lights would flash and a siren would sound, and it would remain this way until the restaurant had theoretically descended into the ocean. When it opened, the LA Times review stated that: “This restaurant makes me embarrassed to be a human in the 90s.”Which isn’t to say that Clooney will fall into the same trap as these failed ventures. He is a man of style and good taste, and surely knows that the quickest way to kill a restaurant is to turn it into a museum of his career. A nice, well-run restaurant that can be enjoyed without knowing the work of its primary investor is far more likely to succeed. That said, if there isn’t a Nespresso on every table, someone should kick the windows in.Explore more on these topicsFilmGeorge ClooneyFranceRestaurantsEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Matchbox: the Movie review – as pointless as a film based on a toy car could be | Action and adventure films | The Guardian
description: John Cena and Jessica Biel collect paychecks in a soulless and synthetic slab of corporate product that hints at what we can expect from the Paramount-Warner merger
Author: Benjamin Lee
Headline: John Cena and Jessica Biel collect paychecks in a soulless and synthetic slab of corporate product that hints at what we can expect from the Paramount-Warner merger
Content: Jessica Biel, John Cena and Teyonah Parris in Matchbox: the Movie.Photograph: Apple TVView image in fullscreenJessica Biel, John Cena and Teyonah Parris in Matchbox: the Movie.Photograph: Apple TVAction and adventure filmsReviewMatchbox: the Movie review – as pointless as a film based on a toy car could beJohn Cena and Jessica Biel collect paychecks in a soulless and synthetic slab of corporate product that hints at what we can expect from the Paramount-Warner mergerBenjamin LeeThu 8 Oct 2026 14.23 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 14.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter a windy road, this weekit finally happened. The day that Hollywood, and many of those who are invested in it, had been dreading, the grimly inevitable disappearance of Warner Bros as it was consumed by what is now known as Paramount. The two once-classic studios will become one – Skydance, the David Ellison-owned company that has infinitely more money than common sense or base-level creativity.The Social Reckoning review – Aaron Sorkin’s jittery sequel with all-new evil puppet ZuckerbergRead moreThe week has seen many,including the Guardian, speculate about what we may be able to expect, what kind of films the billion-dollar behemoth might now be releasing. Warners after all has created classics such as Casablanca, The Exorcist and 2001: A Space Odyssey while Paramount has been behind The Godfather, Chinatown and Breakfast at Tiffany’s. Just imagine what the combined might of these two prestigious, industry-defining studios could achieve with the promise of 30-plus theatrical releases a year, huge amounts of money and considerable manpower at play.Arriving just days after the deal was made official, Skydance’s Matchbox: the Movie suggests that the future is even bleaker than we had anticipated.Like most of the company’s previous films, it’s an empty-headed, synthetically made action film cobbled together as if by machinery only, so lacking in personality or even vigour that it’s impossible to believe anyone involved was there for anything but an undeserved paycheck. It’s a two-hourApple TVfilm based on the Matchbox toy vehicle line, a sentence no one should have had to hear in this lifetime, and it’s exactly as disposable and dead-eyed as that would imply.How would that film make any sense, one might ask, and well it doesn’t, the toy awkwardly used as a way to bond a group of young friends in the 90s before leaping forward to present day as they reunite. One of them (John Cena) has become a super spy and after he returns home for a funeral, he accidentally involves his childhood gang (Jessica Biel, Sam Richardson, Teyonah Parris and Arturo Castro playing gay – LGBTQ+ representation in a Matchbox movie, we did it!) in a mission to save a nuclear warhead. Cue antics and vehicles and lines like “Maybe I need to think inside the box” as if a Mattel exec was on set insisting on as many nods as humanly possible.The action comedy has become the most depressingly common, and most reliably awful, streaming genre and Matchbox, despite whatever loosely defined IP it’s attached to, might not be the worst but it’s among the most aggressively anonymous. The worst remains Apple’s Chris Evans-Ana de Armas multi-vehicle pile-upGhosted(another Skydance classic!) but that film’s awfulness and utter incompetence did at least make it drunkenly entertaining, a satisfyingly punchable piñata. There’s no joy to be had in ribbing this one, it’s more competently made (by Sam Hargrave, a stuntman turned director of the Extraction franchise) but it’s just so devoid of colour, its stench the result of total no-tries blandness (thanks to a script from David Coggeshall, whose credits include hokey horrors The Deliverance and Orphan: First Kill).Dialogue feels consistently, boringly AI-generated throughout and while textured characters would have been unfair to expect here, it’s not a stretch to hope for some mild laughs along the way. But the comedy is of the predictably smug and quippy variety, the kind of film where a character is mid-action telling someone on the phone that they’re “a little busy right now”. The pairing of a slick super agent with regular civilians is also so exhaustingly overdone at this stage and despite what could have maybe been a slightly more interesting angle – young friends transplanting a playground dynamic to a globe-hopping, bomb-exploding action stage – it’s just more of the “woah, he just did that!” bumbling that even the cast seem bored with. A plasticky, unenthused Cena is stuck in autopilot once again (I think that button might actually be broken) while a similarly flat Biel, bizarrely choosing this as her first film in almost a decade, makes zero effort to convincingly play anyone but herself, styled up as if she walked to set from home (a petrol-stained small town ambulance-driving car enthusiast she is not).I wasn’t a big fan of Greta Gerwig’s overpraised Barbie but it was at least a respectably large swing, a smart enough justification for why Mattel might actually need a Hollywood arm. But this is exactly what we should more reasonably anticipate from their output (Jon M Chu’s Hot Wheels and Vin Diesel’s Rock ’Em Sock ’Em Robots are both on the way). No one needed a Matchbox movie that dissected toxic masculinity or used toy cars as a metaphor for anything, but no one really needed a Matchbox movie in the first place. As boredom swept over me during the film’s truly punishing runtime, I imagined better ways to mash the words Matchbox and movie together. I came to the natural conclusion that doing so would be obviously ungodly but even my worst idea was better than “what if another sloppy streaming action comedy but with Matchbox mentions?” Ellison and Skydance have amassed a great deal of power and capital in Hollywood but junk like this is a glum warning sign of what will be done with it.Matchbox: the Movie is out on Apple TV+ on 9 OctoberExplore more on these topicsAction and adventure filmsComedy filmsApple TVreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Below review – a killer snot-berg causes chaos for Josh Hartnett  | Television | The Guardian
description: Don your best plaid shirts for this supernatural thriller about a gang of beefy fishermen who tackle sea monsters. It is totally ridiculous – but you will have loads of daft fun
Author: Sarah Dempster
Headline: Don your best plaid shirts for this supernatural thriller about a gang of beefy fishermen who tackle sea monsters. It is totally ridiculous – but you will have loads of daft fun
Content: Embattled sea hunk … Josh Hartnett as Calvin in Below.Photograph: Netflix/PAView image in fullscreenEmbattled sea hunk … Josh Hartnett as Calvin in Below.Photograph: Netflix/PATV reviewTelevisionReviewBelow review – a killer snot-berg causes chaos for Josh HartnettDon your best plaid shirts for this supernatural thriller about a gang of beefy fishermen who tackle sea monsters. It is totally ridiculous – but you will have loads of daft funSarah DempsterThu 8 Oct 2026 03.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 06.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAbandon all hope, ye who enter Below. And jettison disbelief while ye be at it. A six-part supernatural thriller forged from industrial-grade bunkum, Below is set in Snook’s Arm, a struggling Newfoundland fishing community beset by an ancient, unknowable evil. And plaid. And sea hags, shifty conservationists, mist, motorbikes, curses, a catch-all nostalgia for the 70s-90s, galoshes, wind and, horrifyingly, the collected works of the Waterboys. But mainly an ancient, unknowable evil (and plaid).Here’s twitchy young roustabout Wade Penney (Charlie Heaton) with some combatively accented exposition. “I tells ye, these waters can be deadly,” he splutters, waggling his fish slice seawards as he prepares breakfast for his credulous Airbnb guests. “It’s been one seafarin’ tragedy after another for us.” Wade is an idiot but he is not, in this instance, wrong. First there was the seafarin’ tragedy of 1986, a splosh-based catastrophe that saw his family’s cottage – and his disconcertingly muscular grand pappy – dragged underwater by forces unknown. Then there were the fishing bans, the decades of economic uncertainty and the resettlement programme – a looming government-led scheme that threatens the town’s remaining hopes for survival. And now? “Jumpin’ Jesus,” blurts ripped paterfamilias Calvin Penney (Josh Hartnett). “Will ye look at dat!” We look at dat. It’s an iceberg. A towering wodge of inexplicable CGI menace has materialised in the harbour, bringin’ with it yet more trouble for the embattled sea hunks.View image in fullscreen‘Muscular grand pappy’ … Below on Netflix.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixBut this is no ordinary trouble. And this is no ordinary iceberg.
