Indeed, this particular “floater” stinks “of ammonia” and soon trawlermen are vanishing, bloodied body parts are bobbing ashore and something vast and vengeful is glowering up at them all from the depths of the bay. As tiny-eyed widower Calvin puts it: “What da frig is goin’ on?” Simple, says doughty Dr Fonda Howander from the Ocean Science Centre down in Seal Cove. “It’s not an iceberg.” It is, in fact, “one big frozen mucous membrane!” Calvin’s brow concertinas.Mucous? Deep within his ruggedly masculine skull, a long dormant synaptic connection flickers to life. “You mean,” he gulps, “like … snot?”Fonda (Mackenzie Davis) smiles and nods pityingly. These beefy simpletons and their innocent ways! If only nature was as sympathetic as she is. Alas, nature – in the form of a massive squid unleashed via the thawing of ancient Arctic permafrost and subsequently driven to a) rubbing itself over icebergs in a desperate act of territory marking, and b) killing everyone – is a bastard. Or is it? Could the cephalopod’s ire be justified? Its very existence be a heartrendin’ metaphor for climate breakdown and the passivity of humankind? Possibly. But then, it’s hard to tell. The eco theme is so far down in the mix as to be virtually inaudible. There are fleeting references to warming oceans and “systems breaking apart” but these are curiously apologetic things; faint and barely decipherable prophecies of doom burbling under the neon blare of revvin’ motorbikes and references to Jaws. There is the suspicion that Below’s creator, Jesse McKeown, had intended the climate stuff to be … bigger? More series-defining? That is until, one imagines, the inevitable hand landed on his shoulder and a network pep talk that included an only half-joking mention of “woke” ensured this particular element sank like a CGI stone.View image in fullscreenSquid game … Mackenzie Davis as Dr Fonda Howander.Photograph: Jan Thijs/NetflixWhat we get instead is an old-fashioned tale of sea monsters, isolation and plaid clad tenacity, replete with exploding viscera and goofy nods to such era-defining horrors as The Thing, The Fog and Stranger Things. It is, if you will, Widower’s Bay. And very enjoyable it is too, with much cable-knit daftness re sea hags and David “Lord of the Rings” Wenham having a whale of a time as a self-styled “climate change activist” whose plans for Snook’s Arm are as flagrant as his chinos.Below is hunky sea-fun that, for all its efforts to the contrary, still, quietly, #makesUthink. Come on in. The water’s ridiculous.Below is on Netflix nowExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Fierce, frantic and loaded with menace: Fontaines DC’s 20 greatest songs – ranked! | Fontaines DC | The Guardian
description: Ahead of the Irish alt-rockers’ highly anticipated fifth album, Dopamine Chamber, we count down their potent, occasionally political, catalogue
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: Ahead of the Irish alt-rockers’ highly anticipated fifth album, Dopamine Chamber, we count down their potent, occasionally political, catalogue
Content: A portrait of alienation and egotism … (left to right) Tom Coll, Conor Deegan, Grian Chatten, Conor Curley and Carlos O’Connell of Fontaines DC.Photograph: Theo CottleView image in fullscreenA portrait of alienation and egotism … (left to right) Tom Coll, Conor Deegan, Grian Chatten, Conor Curley and Carlos O’Connell of Fontaines DC.Photograph: Theo CottleRankedFontaines DCFierce, frantic and loaded with menace: Fontaines DC’s 20 greatest songs – ranked!Ahead of the Irish alt-rockers’ highly anticipated fifth album, Dopamine Chamber, we count down their potent, occasionally political, catalogueAlexis PetridisThu 8 Oct 2026 10.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 10.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google20. It’s Amazing to Be Young (2025)A single inspired by the birth of bassist Conor Deegan’s daughter, It’s Amazing to Be Young is a lovely example of Fontaines DC operating in euphoric mode, a relatively recent addition to their emotional mood board: “Sometimes,” offered frontmanGrian Chatten, “optimism is a necessary delusion.”19. Death Kink (2024)It’s often cheeringly difficult to work out exactly whatFontaines DC’s influences are, but the shadow of Pixies definitely hangs over Romance’s Death Kink, from the string-bending lead guitar line on the chorus to the fabulously wonky solo and the abrupt ending. A delight, albeit one as dark-hued as the title suggests.18. A Lucid Dream (2020)The best take on A Lucid Dream might be the radically different “live version” released as a single in 2021, which slows the tempo, drags a piano into proceedings and amps up the song’s ineffable sense of menace. That said, the original – speedy drums, abstract guitar noise, ferocious climax – is quite something, too.17. Big (2019)As introductions to a new band go, the opening track of Fontaines DC’sdebut album, Dogrel, takes some beating. Big is a fierce, snotty, swaggering, supremely exciting statement of intent (“Dublin in the rain is mine … I’m gonna be big”) that immediately lets listeners know they are in the presence of something special.View image in fullscreenIt’s cheeringly difficult to work out their influences … Fontaines DC performing at Reading festival in 2024.Photograph: Simone Joyner/Getty Images16. In the Modern World (2024)The saga of “a fictional throuple together amid Armageddon” – tale as old as time, etc – written by Chatten during a spell of isolation in Los Angeles, In the Modern World feels a little like one of Lana Del Rey’s LA noir tales shot through Fontaines’ grimy lens, with startling results.15. Skinty Fia (2022)As with a lot of songs onFontaines’ third album, the lyrics of the title track deal in ambiguity and confusion, as a recently expat Irishman grapples with different notions of Irishness among the diaspora. But there’s nothing ambiguous about the music – a muscular, funky rhythm section overlaid with eerily gothic guitar and industrial noise.14. Hurricane Laughter (2019)Fontaines’ pummelling early approach in miniature: a relentless, Krautrock-y riff – think Can’s Mother Sky – turned up to 11, frantic post-punk guitars, vocals that somehow manage to feel laconic and forceful at the same time, a remarkable sense of confidence and purpose dripping from the entire enterprise.View image in fullscreenA pummelling early approach … the band on stage in Austin, Texas, in 2019.Photograph: Travis P Ball/Getty Images for SXSW13. Big Shot (2022)In retrospect, Big Shot sounds not unlike a dry run for the widescreen, expansive sound Fontaines would explore on2024’s Romance, but it’s a fabulous track in its own right, driven by an immense, glowering guitar riff. Check the strings-and-piano live version that highlights the sombre majesty of its melody.12. I Don’t Belong (2020)A lot ofA Hero’s Death, their second album, suggested the success of its predecessor, Dogrel, sat uneasily with Fontaines DC; opener I Don’t Belong, an unflinching and remarkably affecting portrait of alienation and egotism on tour, certainly does. The music broods and wrongfoots the listener: you think it’s building to an epic climax, but it just dies away, unresolved.11. Marianne (2026)It’s hard to think of another alternative rock album in 2026 as eagerly awaited as Fontaines DC’s Dopamine Chamber, trailed as a bleaker counterpart to Romance. The slow-motion synth chug of the first single, Marianne – epic, possessed of a superb pop melody and faintly disquieting lyrically – did nothing to damp down the anticipation.10. Televised Mind (2020)Released prior to A Hero’s Death, Televised Mind is a queasy reflection on the impact of social media, its lyrics too oblique to fall into cliche. Between the fuzzed-out bass (apparently influenced by the Prodigy), the scrabbling, corrosively distorted guitars and Chatten’s dead-eyed drawl, it builds up a powerful, infectious mood of anxiety.9. Favourite (2024)You would never have imagined the punchy, dark-hued band behind Dogrel might one day come up with anything quite as sweetly irresistible as Romance’s closer, Favourite. It’s the kind of glorious, sunlit guitar jangle that could have been an indie disco floor-filler at virtually any point in the last 40 years.View image in fullscreenInitially heralded as a punk band … Fontaines DC pictured in 2024.Photograph: Simon Wheatley8. Liberty Belle (2018)Initially, at least, Fontaines DC were heralded as a punk band. They turned out to be something far less straightforward than that. But you can see how it happened from Liberty Belle, an invigorating mass of frantically thrashed guitars, thumping drums and lyrics that cast a rueful eye over Dublin street life.7. A Hero’s Death (2020)Amid the troubled album of the same name, A Hero’s Death feels like a series of notes to self – “Don’t give up too quick / You only get one line, you better make it stick” – set to music that balances darkness with flickers of light in the buoyant rhythm and backing vocals.6. Nabokov (2022)Skinty Fia’s stunning closer ends the album on a bleak note. The lyrics offer a grim view of the compromises involved in a long-term relationship, while the music is a maelstrom of guitars from the darker end of the shoegazing spectrum. There’s nothing dreamlike about their heaving din, just a disorienting claustrophobia.5. Roman Holiday (2022)As a wall of guitar drifts beguilingly along, Roman Holiday offers a brilliant evocation of the complex feelings evoked by moving to London, equal parts agog with excitement – “Baby come on, get your high heels on” – and wary and confused, the latter emotions amplified by Ireland’s problematic relationship with Britain.4. Boys in the Better Land (2019)It’s cut from a noticeably different musical cloth – a heady, intense rush of distorted guitars, the apotheosis of Dogrel’s youthful blast – but you could see Boys in the Better Land as a counterpoint to Roman Holiday: an equally complicated set of emotions evoked by Fontaines DC’s home town of Dublin.View image in fullscreenSomething special … the Dublin-raised, London-based band photographed in 2024.Photograph: Peter Joseph Smith3. Jackie Down the Line (2022)This relates the saga of an abusive relationship, told from the point of view of the unrepentant abuser – Chatten’s vocal delivers some spectacularly grim lines with a callously diffident shrug – and rendered all the more chilling by its infernally catchy melody. A genuinely amazing song.2. Starburster (2024)The song that introduced Fontaines V2.0:– image more striking, music more pop-facing without sacrificing any of their agitated urgency. Starburster’s monstrous beat, orchestral samples and guitar twang vaguely resemble trip-hop retooled for a more fretful era, with Chatten’s vocal punctuated by panic-attack gasps. Hooky but glowering and supremely powerful.1. I Love You (2022)The centrepiece of Skinty Fia starts straightforwardly enough: a cliched title, a gentle, faintly Cure-ish intro of bass and gothy guitar. But I Love You just keeps building and building, ratcheting up the tension through a lengthy kick-drum-driven interlude, as Chatten’s lyrical open letter to Ireland gets more knotty and conflicted, his voice more fraught and antagonised: “This island’s run by sharks with children’s bones stuck in their jaws.” It’s five minutes of music that leaves the listener wrung out: dense, complex, emotive and crushing. You can’t imagine any of Fontaines DC’s peers making anything remotely like it.Dopamine Chamber is released via XLon 16 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFontaines DCRankedPop and rockIndiePunkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Women and the Piano album review – Tomes brings her poetic instincts to a rewarding compilation | Classical music | The Guardian
description:
Tomes
(Hyperion)
From Marianne Martines – taught by the family lodger, Haydn, to Teresa Carreño who played for Lincoln, there’s names new and old in this fascinating and appealing collection
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: Tomes(Hyperion)From Marianne Martines – taught by the family lodger, Haydn, to Teresa Carreño who played for Lincoln, there’s names new and old in this fascinating and appealing collection
Content: Pioneering performer … Susan Tomes.Photograph: Robert PhilipView image in fullscreenPioneering performer … Susan Tomes.Photograph: Robert PhilipClassical musicReviewWomen and the Piano album review – Tomes brings her poetic instincts to a rewarding compilationSusan Tomes(Hyperion)From Marianne Martines – taught by the family lodger, Haydn, to Teresa Carreño who played for Lincoln, there’s names new and old in this fascinating and appealing collectionClive PagetThu 8 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis attractive compilation came out of Susan Tomes’ research for a book on female pianists across history. As she discovered, many wrote music as well, producing short works for the salons and domestic circles to which they were frequently restricted. Thanks to pioneering performers such as Tomes, some of the dozen women presented here are familiar names, but several will be new to many, as will their appealing compositions.View image in fullscreenSusan Tomes: Women and the Piano album cover.Photograph: HyperionTake Marianne Martines, given lessons in lieu of rent by the family lodger, Haydn. Her miniature A major sonata possesses the sparkle of Scarlatti. Marianna von Auenbrugger died aged 23, but she was taught by Salieri, who paid for the publication of the Mozartian E-flat major sonata recorded here.Music by Clara Schumann,Fanny MendelssohnandCécile Chaminadeneeds little introduction, but it’s well worth getting to know Polish virtuoso Maria Agata Szymanowska whose Caprice sur la Romance de Joconde was dedicated to her St Petersburg neighbour, John Field. Or Venezuelan pianist Teresa Carreño, who played for Abraham Lincoln and whose Un Bal en Rêve appears to channel Happy Birthday a quarter century before it was published. Raie Da Costa’s syncopated Razor Blades is pure Billy Mayerl.None of this would be half so rewarding if it were not for Tomes’ poetic instincts. Her sensitive touch, combined with Hyperion’s natural sound, give this polite and appealing music ample room to make its case.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.music.apple.com. title: Book of Lives by Margaret Atwood audiobook review – a dryly funny memoir | Margaret Atwood | The Guardian
description: The Handmaid’s Tale author reflects on her loves, losses and literary achievements in a memoir that showcases her wisdom and wit
Author: Fiona Sturges
Headline: The Handmaid’s Tale author reflects on her loves, losses and literary achievements in a memoir that showcases her wisdom and wit
Content: Leisurely narrator … Margaret Atwood.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianView image in fullscreenLeisurely narrator … Margaret Atwood.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianAudiobook of the weekMargaret AtwoodReviewBook of Lives by Margaret Atwood audiobook review – a dryly funny memoirThe Handmaid’s Tale author reflects on her loves, losses and literary achievements in a memoir that showcases her wisdom and witFiona SturgesThu 8 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMargaret Atwood had to be persuaded to write a memoir. The thought of writing about herself initially seemed “dead boring. Who wants to read about someone sitting at a desk messing up blank sheets of paper?” Yet, she continues, time passed and the possibility of a memoir took on a “lurid phosphorescent glow. ‘Wasn’t there something appealing in the idea?’ my sinister alter ego whispered … I could thank my benefactors, reward my friends, trash my enemies and pay off scores long forgotten by everyone but me.”Subtitled “A Memoir of Sorts”, Book of Lives is the Canadian author’s account of her loves, losses and literary achievements (she has written just over 50 books, including novels, short stories and poetry collections), and a fine showcase for her wisdom and wit. What little score-settling she includes is purely for the punchline. When a poet told Atwood in the early 1970s that she wrote like a man – he intended it as a compliment – she told him he forgot the punctuation. “What you meant was, ‘She writes. Like a man’.”The book is read by the author, who is 86. Her narration is leisurely, gravelly, drily funny and unmistakeably Atwood. Though she admits she can’t recall much about her early books, she remembers enough about the important ones, most notably 1986’s The Handmaid’s Tale, her landmark novel set in a dystopian future. When she showed an early draft to the novelist Valerie Martin, Atwood said: “I think I’m gonna get into trouble.” Martin read it and told her: “I think you’re gonna make a lot of money.”Available via Vintage Digital, 25hr 36minFurther listeningThe PersianDavid McCloskey, Swift Press Audio, 13hr 23minThis tense spy thriller from the CIA analyst turned author and podcaster sees Kamran, a Jewish Iranian dentist living in Sweden after being driven out of Iran, returning to his home country as a Mossad agent. Fajer Al-Kaisi is the narrator.ElementalArthur Snell, Wildfire, 12hr 28minFormer diplomat Snell reads his compelling study of the huge geopolitical problems caused by the climate crisis – including mass migration, drought, rising sea levels and food and energy shortages – and how they can be addressed.Explore more on these topicsMargaret AtwoodAudiobook of the weekAutobiography and memoirreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Spend time going down rabbit holes’: how the Avalanches created their wildest album yet | The Avalanches | The Guardian
description: The Aussie trio explain creating their new record sampling kids’ science shows and Tunisian music – and their surreal film with Haley Joel Osment
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Aussie trio explain creating their new record sampling kids’ science shows and Tunisian music – and their surreal film with Haley Joel Osment
Content: ‘What’s beautiful about what we do is the memories and the humanness in the sounds that we sample,’ the Avalanches’ Robbie Chater says.Photograph: Dean PodmoreView image in fullscreen‘What’s beautiful about what we do is the memories and the humanness in the sounds that we sample,’ the Avalanches’ Robbie Chater says.Photograph: Dean PodmoreThe AvalanchesInterview‘Spend time going down rabbit holes’: how the Avalanches created their wildest album yetJason LamphierThe Aussie trio explain creating their new record sampling kids’ science shows and Tunisian music – and their surreal film with Haley Joel OsmentThu 8 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 13.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLast December, Robbie Chater and Tony Di Blasi, the core members of the Aussie disco-pop collagiststhe Avalanches, found themselves winding through the frosty, mountainous region of Minakami, Japan, withHaley Joel Osment. The pair’s lauded debut album, 2000’sSince I Left You, has become a touchstone inplunderphonics– a genre known for its innovative use of samples – and in the years since its release, the group have amassed an ardent cult following. Osment, the former child star ofThe Sixth SenseandForrest Gump, seemed to count himself among their devotees, frequently liking their posts on Instagram, so they decided to reach out and ask him to board their latest project: a 35-minute movie that would accompany their new LP, No Bad Memories.“We’d never made a film before, so it was like, ‘This could be a complete disaster for him,’” recalls Di Blasi, who is dressed in a black tee and purple cap with the logo for the cult electronic labelтрипwhen we meet in Manhattan in mid-September. “We were like, ‘We don’t really have anyone yet … We don’t even know what we’re doing.’” To their surprise, Osment signed on.‘In the wake of death, Courtney Love was giving it her all’: Hole’s Melissa auf der Maur on her best photographRead moreJoined by their co-director Jonathan Zawada, cinematographer Andrés Arochi and a crew that flew in from Mexico, they would eventually spend three weeks braving the elements, often shooting on the fly on little sleep. “It was fucking freezing and we’re driving around in the snow to this crazy isolated location,” says Chater, seated next to his longtime bandmate at their label’s New York office. Osment, whom he describes as “one of the most knowledgable music fans ever”, was game for it all. “He was the glue that kept the whole production together, because he’s naturally very funny and was so calm.”Named after an old slogan for a 5in floppy disc,No Bad Memorieswas inspired by the ways that advertising and technology shape us – specifically how jingles, audio logos and the drones, chimes and twinkling arpeggios of outdated devices can trigger and distort our recollection of events from our past. Chater and Di Blasi’s fondness for vintage pop and soul clips remains, but here they have broadened their palette to include chipmunk chirps, gurgling hard drives and video game bleeps and bloops. Listening to the record feels like feverishly flipping through an 1980s Saturday morning cartoon lineup – or getting sucked into the TV and thrust into the cartoons themselves. Loony and tuneful, it is the Avalanches’ wildest ride yet.In the forthcoming short film of the same title – a mix of live action, collage and animation – Osment plays Ken, a man who works for the fictional companyTakumi, a digital archives service that allows clients to upload and preserve their cherished possessions (or, as Di Blasi calls them, “tangible memories”). Its tagline: “At Takumi, your memories are safe with us.” Sporting a uniform emblazoned with the brand’s flashy logo, he travels to people’s homes in his Takumi van, gathering their belongings and taking them to a mysterious storage facility.“You’re not sure if they’re deceased or what the story is, but it’s quite melancholy because he’s going in and boxing up these memories – VHS tapes, CDs, cassettes and photo albums,” Chater explains.Ken is in the middle of packing up one abandoned place when things get weird. As the tale unfolds, he starts struggling to distinguish his own memories from the imagery in commercials he’s consumed over the years. He eventually seeks refuge inside an enormous iPod that materializes in his apartment. “You don’t know whether he’s losing his mind,” Di Blasi says.Chater and Di Blasi have been blurring that line between reality and fantasy, actual reminiscence and the illusion of it, for nearly three decades. They met in the mid-90s in high school. As a teenager, Di Blasi used to sleep with his guitar andcried when he first heardthe Beatles’Strawberry Fields Forever. Coming of age in the Australian countryside, Chater was blown away by theingenious samplingonDavid Byrneand Brian Eno’s My Life in the Bush of Ghosts and early De La Soul tracks.He began experimenting with tape loops using a Tascam cassette Portastudio, and by the time Di Blasi moved to his town for his last year of school, he was laying demos with it. The two bonded immediately, relocated to Melbourne and, along with Darren Seltmann, formed the Avalanches in 1997.View image in fullscreenThe Avalanches in a press shot from 2000/2001.Photograph: Steve GullickInfluenced by the dense, cavernous arrangements of theBeach BoysandPhil Spectoras well as the sample-heavy ragers theChemical Brotherswere churning out at the time, the band set out to conjure a hazy, psychedelic blast of sonic deja vu. Since I Left Youput them on the map and changed Chater and Di Blasi’s lives forever. A meticulously crafted, stunningly cohesive patchwork of upwards of 3,500 samples – everything from neighing horses andMadonna’s Holiday to snippets from 1960s comedy sketches and Arnold Palmer’s golf instructions album – it dazzled critics and vinyl hounds and was hailed a masterpiece by outlets such asPitchfork,Pasteand theGuardian, who named it among the best albums of the 21st century.“There was a real excitement and buzz around it,” Chater recalls. “It was the turn of the century. Dance music was having a moment. It was really fortuitous timing, and the beautiful sentiment behind the music connected with people.” He pauses. “And the fact that we didn’t do anything for 16 years added to this myth.”‘A genre-defying monument’: how Sign o’ the Times captured Prince at his creative peakRead moreThe gapbetween Since I Left You and its successor became legendary. When their sophomore LP,Wildflower, finally did come out, in 2016, Chatersaidthat the process of making it was plagued by “seven shades of shit”: Seltmann left the group, their label dissolved, Chater had to contend with two autoimmune diseases and a drinking problem (he is now healthy and sober) and they hit countless hurdles clearing its myriad samples. Also at play was a crippling perfectionism as they strove to meet the insanely high expectations for their long-awaited second outing.“With Since I Left You, we were so young and free, and I remember thinking afterwards, I didn’t even try that hard,” Chater says. “We just had fun and made this thing spontaneously, and people loved it. So I thought if I tried really,reallyhard, imagine how good it could be.”“Living up to that, it’s almost like people who have really famous parents,” adds Di Blasi. “They’re in their shadow. It felt like as time developed, the shadow of Since I Left You got quite large, and then you’re sitting there going, Oh, wow, it’s got to be as good as this.”Wildflower waswell receivedand a step forward for them. To bolster all of its blissed-out sampling, they enlisted guests includingDanny Brown,MF Doom,Biz Markie,Father John Misty, Tame Impala’sKevin ParkerandDavid Berman. Their third full-length,We Will Always Love You, arrived a reasonable four years later and continued their winning formula: heaps of dusty samples and a murderer’s row of modern voices, includingBlood Orange,Johnny MarrandNeneh Cherry. A meditation on death, the cosmos and the great beyond, it was a more subdued, wistful affair. Despite its quiet release in late 2020, during the height of Covid, it stillearned raves. Delivering a follow-up that was brighter and more euphoric was “definitely a conscious decision”, Di Blasi says. “We were like, ‘Let’s do something that’s a bit more of a party and fun and more in the spirit of Since I Left You.’”“We were really excited to make up-tempo, really joyous music,” Chater adds.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat, they wondered, could be more joyous than a jingle?Their first record with new member Andy Szekeres, No Bad Memories is both joyous and delightfully unhinged. That’s partly due to the abundance of whimsical ear candy on display – chanting children, whirring computers, the crack and hiss of a soda can – and partly because of how frenetic and kinetic it is. “It’s just about energy,” Chater says. “Sometimes we’d try to figure out the song order and structure, and I’d get bored and want to go to the next song, like skipping through a playlist. I thought, ‘Why can’t the album do that? The song doesn’t have to finish properly.’”“We’d just cut it off mid-cycle,” adds Di Blasi, “not even on the beat. You think it’s going somewhere and then all of a sudden we’re cutting to somewhere else. And that’s just exciting.”View image in fullscreenThe Avalanches.Photograph: Dean PodmoreThey also cast a wide net when selecting their featured artists. Newcomers including the British rapperJohn Glacierand Tunisian footwork producer Khadija Al Hanafi rub elbows withPanda BearandHaruomi Hosono, as well as previous collaboratorsKaren O,Rivers CuomoandJamie xx. Pioneering electronic composerSuzanne Ciani, who invented Coca-Cola’s classic “pop and pour” sound effect in the 1970s, also makes a cameo. The fittingly fizzy track Our Love Is Alive samples a 1980 episode of the PBS kids’ science show 3-2-1 Contact, in which she breaks down how her signature Buchla synthesizer works.As if all that recruiting, knob twiddling and movie-making weren’t enough, Chater and Di Blasi also created two other fictional products, theSuperfun consoleand a soft drink calledEl Dorado, whipping up original jingles, logos and ads for them. After Osment’s impressive performance in the No Bad Memories short film, they tapped him to record spots for them for interludes on the album.‘I thought I would lose my career’: Orville Peck on addiction and creating his best album yetRead moreThe lofty ambition of it all, including the increasingly difficult task of trying to clear all their samples – “Now you’re dealing with companies who’ve bought up all these catalogs and just want the maximum amount of money they can get,” Chater says – nearly broke them. “We literally just handed in the album and said, ‘Sincerely, never again are we going to do this. Like, we have to find another way.’”That’s a promise they’ve failed to keep. When we speak, it is less than two months after they’ve finished the record, but they are already sampling again. “We don’t know any other way,” Di Blasi says with a laugh.Besides, isn’t the pain and pleasure of discovery the point? “What’s beautiful about what we do is the memories and the humanness in the sounds that we sample,” Chater says. “What’s beautiful is that there’s no shortcut. You’ve got to just put the hours in, spend the time looking and digging and listening and going down rabbit holes.”“Yeah,” DiBlasi adds, “it’s the journey.”No Bad Memoriesis out on 16 OctoberExplore more on these topicsThe AvalanchesPop and rockElectronic musicAustralian musicExperimental musicinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Agate Head / Stone Soup by Patricia Lockwood review – a gem of a collection | Poetry | The Guardian
description: Inspired by stones and metals, the memoirist and novelist’s first poetry collection for more than a decade is charming, whimsical and intimate
Author: Rishi Dastidar
Headline: Inspired by stones and metals, the memoirist and novelist’s first poetry collection for more than a decade is charming, whimsical and intimate
Content: From the holy to the hilarious … Patricia Lockwood.Photograph: Anna OttumView image in fullscreenFrom the holy to the hilarious … Patricia Lockwood.Photograph: Anna OttumBook of the dayPoetryReviewAgate Head / Stone Soup by Patricia Lockwood review – a gem of a collectionInspired by stones and metals, the memoirist and novelist’s first poetry collection for more than a decade is charming, whimsical and intimateRishi DastidarThu 8 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 03.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the introduction to her first book of poetry in 12 years,Patricia Lockwoodstates that, “For almost a decade … I had not been able to hear it. The poems that I wrote would not end … too much was happening, there was a different kind of attention being paid.” It wasn’t that she didn’t want them to arrive. From Cave Painting: “And does she still write poems?/ Not a whole one since I had been ill. / Five years. I kept saying I was / Doing it privately. So private even / I didn’t know about it.”In that intervening period, Lockwood’s status has jumped from interesting US poet famous for the viral sensationRape Joketo literary superstar: an acclaimed memoirist and novelist whose freewheeling, antic style is for many the internet’s maelstrom lassoed and put back on to the page. Who else can claim to have turned an audience with the pope into a biting comic essay?So her return to poetry is a genuine event, and across Agate Head / Stone Soup there are countless moments that remind you that her poetic voice is unique: charming, whimsical, intimate; able to deliver images of great beauty, piercing philosophical insights and glimpses into a creative life behind the public persona. Readers of her memoirPriestdaddywill be pleased to see her father reappear in a few poems. “That my father has been drinking … / Always something new with him, / But I must say I didn’t see / 5-600 dollars’ worth of fine olive oil coming.”Agate Head / Stone Soup is presented tête-bêche – head-to-tail in French, the volumes upside down and back-to-back. And while this might appear to be a frippery, the two collections have enough differences in texture to warrant it. Agate Head feels the more public-facing, while Stone Soup wrestles with more existential concerns, as beautifully rendered in Babies Born Remembering: “Screaming in the airport. / What do they remember – / Night flights, riding birds, / Being a set of wings / Themselves, a soul, an updraft.”double quotation markIt’s impossible to escape autobiography: some poems are a form of higher gossip, our noses against the glass of fameBoth collections are inspired by stones, gems and metals of all shapes and sorts. Lockwood has been collecting fossils and minerals from an early age, and she and her husband have spent time learning metalsmithing, too. This gives her rich territories to explore. In Margaret De Patta, “Quartz wants / To be a window, wants a woman to appear. / We have properties, we are non-precious, / Wood horn bone and hair.” In An Agate a Day, we get to see her and her husband cutting agates, a hard stone with bands of different colours: “The trick is to hold the miracle steady. / We are the first to be seeing this. Ever. / Together. What happened to you? / We croon, after each cut.” It is notable that agates are associated with a sense of grounding and balance; an attempt to counteract all that other “attention”.There is a detectable technical shift in Lockwood’s poems also. Many of the poems in 2014’s Motherland Fatherland Homelandsexuals featured long lines, allowed to run on and gather momentum to their epiphanies or punchlines. Here her lines are more staccato in feeling, jumpier in syntax, as in Not Seeing Glass Flowers: “To grow. Was it that / They looked real? I asked everyone. / Or was it something more? Max Beckmann’s painting is still a horror.”It means a spikier initial impression for many of the poems. This ultimately works in their favour, as the thoughts accrete, moving in unlikely directions, before resolving into a revelation of some force. “Artists, no one really / Knows where they come from, / They fall a long way from the sky / And land zigzag” as Forged in Fire has it.Neither collection is flawless. At one level, it is impossible to get away from the autobiographical detail, and so some of the poems become a form of higher gossip, our noses pressed up against the glass of fame. Sedarising, for example, comes across as smug rather than amusing.And there are occasions when an object under discussion cannot bear the metaphorical weight being placed upon it. Polish Flint is an offender here: “The perfect ring I had married myself with / (Of Polish flint) was pried apart as I fell. / In slow motion, it seemed, surrounded / By tourists, with enough time to think / Of everything.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut these are small bumps when time and again Lockwood leaves you with the distinct impression that she can magically make the profane into the profound, the holy into the hilarious, as she does to most brilliant effect in Monastery Icons: Windows into Heaven: “It’s sounding a little bit / Like you can order a whole husband / From this catalog, as long as his name is The Lord / And you are a PRAYING VIRGIN NIGHTLIGHT: /Just what we need in these challenging times.”Agate Head / Stone Soup by Patricia Lockwood is published by Bloomsbury, (£18.99). title: Willem de Kooning review – the artist’s lifelong rebellion against himself is thrilling to watch  | Art and design | The Guardian
description: Marking a century since the Dutch artist stowed away to New York, this vast retrospective gloriously showcases the abstract expressionist’s fierce boundary-pushing
Author: Ben Eastham
Headline: Marking a century since the Dutch artist stowed away to New York, this vast retrospective gloriously showcases the abstract expressionist’s fierce boundary-pushing
Content: ‘Knockout masterpiece’ … Excavation by Willem de Kooning, 1950.Photograph: © 2026 The Willem de Kooning Foundation/ Pictoright, AmsterdamView image in fullscreen‘Knockout masterpiece’ … Excavation by Willem de Kooning, 1950.Photograph: © 2026 The Willem de Kooning Foundation/ Pictoright, AmsterdamArt and designReviewWillem de Kooning review – the artist’s lifelong rebellion against himself is thrilling to watchRijksmuseum, AmsterdamMarking a century since the Dutch artist stowed away to New York, this vast retrospective gloriously showcases the abstract expressionist’s fierce boundary-pushingBen EasthamThu 8 Oct 2026 10.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWillem de Kooning was the last great artist who really knew how to draw. More precisely, if less provocatively, he was the last truly transformative painter to have been schooled in the academic tradition that produces what is still recognised, by most people, as “good drawing”. Accurate in the sense of a photograph but, like a filter on your cameraphone, also subtly tidying up the world to meet the ideals of classical proportion. “Draw what you see and not what you think,” the young De Kooning was told. Raw personal emotion had no place – a far cry from what this master of abstract expressionism was to become.The intense labour required to build a connection between eye, brain and hand so quick as to be instinctive is illustrated by the charcoal still life Dish With Jugs. Made when De Kooning was in his mid-teens, and so minutely rendered that you might mistake it for a sepia photograph, the catalogue estimates that it took 600 hours at the Rotterdam academy to complete. The aim of this exercise was not to produce a single picture so much as to ingrain a way of seeing and reconstructing the world to the point that it becomes inescapable.View image in fullscreenLike a sepia photograph … De Kooning’s Dish With Jugs, c.1919-21.Photograph: © 2026 The Willem de Kooning Foundation, Pictoright, AmsterdamThis brilliantly researched exhibition makes a compelling case for the success of that training. Setting a handful of standout paintings among a wider selection of drawings illustrates the artist’s lifelong rebellion against rules so thoroughly internalised that he could push fiercely at their limits without entirely breaking them. The battle is thrilling to watch.De Kooning’s formative training is apparent in an early drawing of the dancer Juliet Browner and a marvellously deft portrait of the artist’s wife, Elaine. The influence of Ingres – the Pelé of academic drawing – on these works has often been remarked upon, not least by rival New York painters for whom De Kooning’s superior draughtsmanship was a source of suspicion (too prissy, too European). And it seems that the immigrant artist placed himself under pressure to unstitch the aesthetic conventions of the old world and rework them into something more appropriate to the new: irreverent, free, immediate, expressive.View image in fullscreen‘A harbinger of women to come’ … Queen of Hearts.Photograph: © 2026 The Willem de Kooning Foundation/ Pictoright, AmsterdamIt is important to note that De Kooning’s education was not limited to the academy. A working-class kid, his evening classes had been subsidised by the design firm where he worked in the day; after stowing away to the US at 22, he scraped a living as a sign painter and commercial illustrator. These lessons made their way into his art, and the difficulty of synthesising them might explain the struggles of his early career (he didn’t have a solo show until he was nearly 44) and how revolutionarythe breakthroughwas when it did arrive.Central to that achievement was that he made no distinction between drawing and painting (the tradition being, in simple terms, that you draw the outlines and paint the space between them). In Queen of Hearts, a harbinger of women to come, he drags charcoal sticks across wet paint to create soft edges, sanding down and painting over layers like a housepainter. The big bang arrives in the seminal work on paper completed in 1949, an arrangement of white sparks against a black ground that calls to mind comets dancing through the night sky. But De Kooning was no starry-eyed mystic: at the bottom edge, transforming those white sparks into liquid spurts, is a scrawled cock and balls.Excavation, a knockout masterpiece, likewise appears at first as an abstract pattern of interlocking shapes only to reveal itself as a maelstrom of screaming faces and dismembered body parts. Completed in 1950, it conjures both Europe’s mass graves and an orgiastic ecstasy of bodies dissolving into each other. Sex and death, heaven and hell, the end of the old world and the birth of the new. In one of many intelligent arrangements, Excavation is paired with a drawing from four years earlier, the aptly titled Judgment Day.It is a quirk of the exhibition that its most famous painting, Woman I, hangs in a separate gallery normally reserved for the museum’s treasures from the Dutch golden age. Not only does this icon hold its own against Vermeer and Rembrandt, but she is also unexpectedly at home. Scandalous when first exhibited, the accusation that this cartoonish, charismatic and wild figure defames all womankind by its “monstrosity” seems now to rely on some mid-century assumptions about how women should be represented. Whatever you think about Woman I, she could never be mistaken for a submissive sex object or a Stepford wife.View image in fullscreen‘De Kooning could always rely on his line’ … inside the Rijksmuseum exhibition.Photograph: Peter Tijhuis/RijksmuseumDe Kooning’s relentless attacks on convention, which is to say on himself and everything else, took their toll. A series of black-and-white works, made in Rome in the late 1950s, mark the end of his imperial phase. While these vaguely calligraphic graphic signs illustrate a point about the convergence of painting and drawing, they feel to me slapdash and derivative of Franz Kline. From here, this exhibition does little to overturn the conventional wisdom that De Kooning struggled over the next two decades to scale the same heights. There are standouts – notably the irrepressible Clam Diggers, a woozy portrait of two women standing in shallow water rendered in ice-cream colours and buttery textures, and a gorgeously fleshy painting from the mid-70s that advertises the painter’s occasionally overlooked gift as a colourist. If the paintings are hit and miss, the drawings from this period reveal that, even hindered by alcoholism and a chaotic personal life, De Kooning could always rely on his line.That line holds to the end. The show closes with an astonishing painting from 1985, during the period when De Kooning’s cognitive decline was increasingly apparent. Sinuous blue and black lines curve across a mottled white ground, weaving a pattern suggestive of bodies and yet emptied of desire. It is serene, strange and straightforwardly beautiful, as if everything that the artist had struggled to pack into his work had been boiled down to basic principles. He is back to fitting the world to a pleasing form. The difference is that it is no longer a boilerplate inherited from the classical tradition, but shaped by his experiences and entirely his own. He doesn’t need to think about it. The battle is over.Willem de Kooning at Work is at theRijksmuseum, Amsterdam, from 9 October to 17 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsArt and designArtPaintingreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Franz & Marie review – Woyzeck folk musical finds heart amid the horror | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Büchner’s jagged masterpiece about a soldier’s descent is told with enchanting and stirring songs that occasionally defuse its stark terror
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: Büchner’s jagged masterpiece about a soldier’s descent is told with enchanting and stirring songs that occasionally defuse its stark terror
Content: Traumas and tenderness … Brenock O’Connor and Jade Oswald as Franz and Marie.Photograph: Danny KaanView image in fullscreenTraumas and tenderness … Brenock O’Connor and Jade Oswald as Franz and Marie.Photograph: Danny KaanTheatreReviewFranz & Marie review – Woyzeck folk musical finds heart amid the horrorCharing Cross theatre, LondonBüchner’s jagged masterpiece about a soldier’s descent is told with enchanting and stirring songs that occasionally defuse its stark terrorChris WiegandThu 8 Oct 2026 10.57 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 13.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Georg Büchner died aged 23 in 1837, he left behind Woyzeck as a bundle of papers that would be ordered and reordered for years to come, eventually discoloured by treatments used to decipher the playwright’s handwriting. His two dozen scenes, with a handful of extra fragments, form a tragic patchwork that is mirrored, in this musical version, by a similar number of stained pieces of cloth stitched into the stage curtains and by the 27 folk songs that thread the story together.It remains the downfall of Franz Woyzeck, a desperate soldier sinking into madness who grows suspicious of his partner, but – as the first names of its romantic title suggest – the story seeks to better understand both characters. Büchner’s Woyzeck suffers from visions and hallucinations; here they are joined by traumatic battlefield flashbacks. Franz was a war hero, says Marie admiringly, adding a courageous backstory to Büchner’s downtrodden squaddie and suggesting that she sees a glimpse of Franz’s former vigour in the drum major (here named Varg) who brazenly pursues her. In the play, that leads to an affair, but the musical’s Marie fights off Varg when he attempts to rape her and it is the rumours of infidelity that accelerate Franz’s frenzy.View image in fullscreen​Busy at work … Mark Meadows, Max Alexander-Taylor, Richard Emerson Gould, Brenock O’Connor, Tom Aubrey, Matthew Heywood and Steve Simmonds in Franz & Marie.Photograph: Danny KaanThese are spread – weaponised, really – by a doctor and a soldier who could have climbed out of George Grosz’s The Pillars of Society, with itsliterally shit-headed social elite. Büchner’s satire also gains a hint of Stephen Schwartz’s picaresquePippin, as Franz is buffeted by grotesquely buffoonish men of war and science.Michael Oakley’s production of Chris Broderick and Rob Shepherd’s musical, in a new adaptation by Teresa Howard, is staged with a cast of actor-musicians who create an inescapable heartiness that occasionally defuses the stark terror of the original play. But the book and lyrics dovetail nicely and the action is propelled by military cadences and stirring folk songs that are elemental, pungent and often sweetly enchanting.View image in fullscreenWell cast … Jade Oswald in Franz & Marie.Photograph: Danny KaanBrenock O’Connor and Jade Oswald, both well cast as Franz and Marie, balance their respective traumas and tendernesses, O’Connor’s agonised gait and deeply furrowed brow also evoking German expressionism. The show accentuates the play’s folkloric nature, with Matthew Heywood’s wolfish Varg prowling around a forest designed by Bretta Gerecke that is overseen by a wandering elder (Eve Polycarpou). Everyone is busy at work, often weaving, and even the act of boot-shining becomes a percussive flourish.What you mostly miss is the jagged disorientation of Büchner’s masterpiece as Franz’s downward spiral is interrupted by a needless interval and the faltering comedy of an overstuffed second half. A tragedy that plunges you to the depths has become a musical that instead sweeps you along.AtCharing Cross theatre, London, until 14 NovemberExplore more on these topicsTheatreMusicalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Lourdes gets a Vegas glow-up at Dublin theatre festival, where canvases are slashed | Theatre | The Guardian
description: A musical about a drama group’s pilgrimage and reflections on activist art join an intriguing show about lost languages
Author: Helen Meany
Headline: A musical about a drama group’s pilgrimage and reflections on activist art join an intriguing show about lost languages
Content: Effervescent … Danielle James, Iestyn Arwel, Molly Lynch, Nichola MacEvilly and Riain Cash in Lourdes! The Musical.Photograph: Patricio CassinoniView image in fullscreenEffervescent … Danielle James, Iestyn Arwel, Molly Lynch, Nichola MacEvilly and Riain Cash in Lourdes! The Musical.Photograph: Patricio CassinoniTheatreLourdes gets a Vegas glow-up at Dublin theatre festival, where canvases are slashedA musical about a drama group’s pilgrimage and reflections on activist art join an intriguing show about lost languagesHelen MeanyThu 8 Oct 2026 07.23 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 07.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a Dublin theatre festival programme tackling heavy themes of racism, conflict and prejudice,Lourdes! The Musical(★★★★☆) promises something effervescent.Xnthony Ltd, the creators ofOliver Cromwell Is Really Very Sorry, have turned their lightly quizzical gaze to the French pilgrimage town – “a holy Blackpool, a divine Las Vegas” and a site of hope or desperation for five unlikely travelling companions.Back in his home village in “Countryland”, in 2008, following a diagnosis of HIV that punctures his dreams of Los Angeles, singer-songwriter Matthew (Riain Cash) lends his star power to a parish drama group taking a musical about Saint Bernadette to Lourdes. Interweaving this show-within-a-show and the pilgrimage strands, Xnthony’s lyrics and Matthew Floyd Jones’s score blend pop, club beats and soulful ballads. Directed by Sarah Meadows, the supercharged ensemble joining Cash as, variously, a droll priest (Iestyn Arwel), a terminally ill mother and her transgender daughter (Nichola MacEvilly and Danielle James) and an eager tour manager (Molly Lynch) carry the music’s tonal shifts effortlessly.Instructed by neon signs to “please wait for a miracle”, characters reveal what brings them to this Marian shrine with its bizarre mix of tackiness and piety. Each has a Catholic faith of sorts – something that might have been more complicated to portray if set in the present day. Rather than settling on an archly ironic approach, Xnthony’s sensitive, often lyrical writing allows fear of death, regret and above all, grief, to seep through.View image in fullscreenClever and knowing … Alice Roots in Heroes of Tomorrow.Photograph: Ste MurrayAn aura of reverence pervades the white cube gallery setting ofHeroes of Tomorrow(★★★☆☆), the latest production from the restlessly inventiveBrokentalkers. Co-directors Feidlim Cannon and Gary Keegan are joined here by British theatre artist Andy Smith to burrow into the relationship between art and activism. Pinging through centuries and continents, they make connections between historical instances of human invention and resultant exploitation, technological breakthroughs and protest, underlining the point that progress is not linear.If this sounds abstract, it is; much of it is delivered in carefully flat, affectless narration by Alice Roots, Michael Tient and Malua Ní Chléirigh, as if making a presentation in the gallery, taking turns to outline the biography of a (fictional) Norwegian conceptual artist called Jan Hansen. His latest work, The End of It All, has been commissioned by three global tech companies, a testing moment of groupthink for an artist who has acquired cachet for financially supporting climate activists who fling paint over old masters in museums.Amid questions about whether it is possible for art to remain pure, uncompromised by its corporate sources of funding, the audience is teased into imagining what Hansen’s new artwork will be. As the performers playfully poke their heads through slashed canvases and make black imprints of their hands on the pristine gallery wall, this performance is itself a form of conceptual art, played out in a highly coded space. The result is clever and knowing but, for Brokentalkers, surprisingly tentative.Zinc(★★★★☆) fromDead Centrefocuses on a forgotten mini-state, Neutral Moresnet, on the border of Germany, Belgium and the Netherlands. A political anomaly, designated a neutral zone to protect its prized zinc mines, it was passed between European powers, its inhabitants’ nationality changing as borders shifted. Adapted froma book by Belgian political philosopher David Van Reybrouck, the production brings multiple perspectives to bear on the experience of one man, Joseph Rixen, born in Neutral Moresnet in 1903.View image in fullscreenOne of their most ambitious works to date … Timmy Creed, Fabio Godinho, Cathy Min Jung, Mila Moinzadeh and Julie Mughunda in Zinc.Photograph: Alexandre FytrakisPlaying with the idea of neutrality, co-directors Ben Kidd and Bush Moukarzel and the superb international ensemble – Julie Mughunda, Timmy Creed, Fabio Godinho, Cathy Min Jung and Mila Moinzadeh – rewind, wittily, to the 1815 Congress of Vienna. Reflecting on colonisation, annexation and the accidents of history, each actor explores their personal experience of exile, displacement and lost native languages.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA co-production withThéâtre de Liège, this is one of Dead Centre’s most ambitious works to date: multilingual, integrating video mapping, projection, layered music and sound design, and, as always with their work, commenting on the art of theatre itself. Richly allusive, it connects a performer on an empty stage, before the act of imagination begins, to the perceived neutrality of a geographical place – until it can be exploited, no longer a country but “a business”.Moving away from the cartography of loss, the performance seizes on the lost political project of Esperanto as a possible neutral language of hope – literally utopian, with its root meaning of “nowhere”.Lourdes! The Musical is atCivic theatre, Dublin, until 10 October.Dublin theatre festivalruns until 11 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreIrelandEuropeMusicalsPaintingFestivalsReligionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Can Ali G: Who Iz I? save character comedy cinema? | Comedy films | The Guardian
description: Sacha Baron Cohen’s new film risks being outdated in a more rancorous era. But could it restore the personality-driven genre to big screens or end it altogether?
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: Sacha Baron Cohen’s new film risks being outdated in a more rancorous era. But could it restore the personality-driven genre to big screens or end it altogether?
Content: Last man standing in a noble tradition … Morgana Robinson as Julie and Sacha Baron Cohen as Ali G in Ali G: Who Iz I?Photograph: Courtesy of Amazon MGM Studios/courtesy of Amazon MGM StudiosView image in fullscreenLast man standing in a noble tradition … Morgana Robinson as Julie and Sacha Baron Cohen as Ali G in Ali G: Who Iz I?Photograph: Courtesy of Amazon MGM Studios/courtesy of Amazon MGM StudiosComedy filmsCan Ali G: Who Iz I? save character comedy cinema?Sacha Baron Cohen’s new film risks being outdated in a more rancorous era. But could it restore the personality-driven genre to big screens or end it altogether?Phil HoadThu 8 Oct 2026 06.58 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 07.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor a man whose campaign slogan was once “Keep it real”, Ali G has his work cut out in the reality of 2026. The big dog of Da West Staines Massiv was the character with whomSacha Baron Cohencarved out his own niche of gonzo-gotcha comedy in the late 1990s – and now he’s back with new film, Ali G: Who Iz I? But it’s unclear if his great creation has gone sufficiently fallow in the collective consciousness to still operate well in real-life situations, the kind of lethal idiot who once pitched Donald Trump anti-drip ice-cream gloves. And more critically, is the Ali G satirical project – which poked at 90s multicultural mores – still relevant and funny in far more rancorous times?It’s not just Baron Cohen’s career as an undercover operative that’s on the line. It’s the future of character-led comedy as a going concern, now that he seems to be the last man standing in this once-noble tradition – in cinemas, at least. To be clear, character comedy isn’t merely comedy with characters; it’s comedy filtered through a central persona that overlaps with the comedian playing it and whose subversive sensibility colours the entire work.View image in fullscreenMike Myers’ swinging London exile … Myers and Heather Graham in Austin Powers: The Spy Who Shagged Me, 1999.Photograph: AJ Pics/AlamyMike Myers’ swinging London exile Austin Powers was the most commercially successful example – but the actor hasn’t made a film in that first-person style since his self-help spoof The Love Guru tanked in 2008.Will Ferrell, ruling the roost as fashion’s Dr Evil, Mugatu (in Zoolander), Buddy the Elf and Ron Burgundy, seemed the best successor. Mystifyingly, though, Ferrell has barely been able to get a film bankrolled in the last decade – and certainly not one putting him out front to that extent. Character comedy subsists on TV, from where it came, with the likes of Alan Partridge and Philomena Cunk. But unless the new Ali G can blaze a fresh hit of chronic satire into the genre’s bloodstream, it’s hard to see a future for it on the big screen.Ali G was already controversial back in the day: the regular accusation was that while he was satirising the white appropriation of black culture, he in fact enabled straight lampooning of the latter. Now those criticisms are sharpened by the notion that, in 2026, he is past his sell-by date: both out of step with a more culturally mixed Britain and, overflowing with bifter gags and mad patois, dangerously adjacent to racist caricature that won’t pass these days. British standup comedian Dane Baptisterecently told Deadline: “After Black Lives Matter and the brief humanisation of black people and black creatives, it seems very dubious that we are now regressing back, not just five years, but 25 years, to bring back a character that was able to flourish because there were no accurate portrayals of black Britishness on screen.”But it would be a shock if Baron Cohen wasn’t wise to the current sensitivities. In 2020’sBorat Subsequent Moviefilm, he mostly successfully updated the Kazakhstan reporter for the post-truth, Covid-era end times of Trump’s US. His choice of target interviewees in Who Iz I? remains to be seen, but it would be surprising if he didn’t pick a few where he can opportunistically needle both woke and anti-woke camps.These debates are tricky ones, on cultural shifting sands, and Baron Cohen undeniably skirts close to reactionary goading at times (the fact that dumb Americans might actually believe Kazakhstan is that backward doesn’t escape the fact he’s propagating the idea it’s a potassium-, incest- and antisemitism-crazed shithole). But if the new Ali G film does fall foul of the post-Black Lives Matter climate, it’ll be hard not to also conclude that our splintered, fractious era lacks the unity – or at least consensus – that makes character comedy possible at all. To a large extent, audiences have to agree on the social phenomena these big satirical beasts feed off. In the late 90s, black street culture was sufficiently new and prominent a force in the UK mainstream to make this crip-sign-throwing buffoon a direct hit.There’s no reason why character comedy can’t thrive off societal shifts, though – if the character is positioned carefully enough. In fact, this is how it originally manufactured tension, with the likes of Charlie Chaplin’s Tramp getting fed through the mangler of industrialised capitalism in Modern Times. Or Peter Sellers playing both old establishment nabob Sir John Kennaway and the trade union firebrand Fred Kite in 1959’s labour-relations satire I’m All Right Jack. With postwar Britain evolving rapidly, Tony Hancock picked up the baton in 1961’s The Rebel, both surfing and sending up boho nonconformism in his role as an accidentally successful avant garde artist. Alan Partridge’s long slide into local radio-bound insignificance has only attained glorious new parallels in the post-Brexit era.View image in fullscreenA massive influence … Peter Sellers, centre, in I’m All Right Jack, 1959.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyAnother reason why character comedy may have fallen from favour is its vaudevillian strut, a very human theatricality that seems old-fashioned in an age of frictionless CGI blockbusters. It revels in transformation and disguise (Baron Cohen now, of course, being so famous he has to layer on disguises on top of his original disguises – hence the new Rasta Ali G). The genre often compounds this ludic chaos by having its stars play multiple roles, as Sellers,Eddie Murphyand Mike Myers love to do.Somehow this protean fun allows the presiding comic genius’s essential quality to pierce through all the more clearly: in Sellers’ case, a kind of unnerving mildness that could transmute into mania, or Myers’ cheeky puerility. Mrs Doubtfire, from 1993, is one of the most revelatory uses of this ventriloquist effect. Another persona that the film’s divorced voiceover artist adopts in order to see his children more often, the Scottish nanny is really a conduit for the sentimental streak that underpinned much of Robin Williams’s work. And like the theatre, you can see the tactile human continuity between character comedy’s practitioners: Myers has often talked about his admiration for Sellers’ chameleonic powers. Dr Evil’s “one million dollars” faux pas is a lift of a similar gag near the end of Sellers’ 1959 geopolitics satire The Mouse That Roared.View image in fullscreenA sentimental streak … Robin Williams in Mrs Doubtfire, 1993.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyBy 2002, when Myers was doing silhouette gags about giving birth to Mini-Me in Austin Powers: Goldmember, this vaudevillian style was looking passe. With The Lord of the Rings and Harry Potter in full pomp, blockbuster film was firmly in the CGI era; comedy had moved on, too, to the edgier Frat Pack films and the realism of Judd Apatow.But perhaps character comedy had also lost strong moorings by this point, with social comment largely absent from the genre since the 1980s. Instead, Austin Powers was an extended riff on 60s and 90s pop-cultural overlaps and discrepancies (Jean Dujardin did something similar in his later OSS-117 series), while Eddie Murphy’s multi-character outings The Nutty Professor and Norbit seemed largely there to prop up the fat-suit industry. Only Will Ferrell – via his blowhard news anchor Burgundy, but also in his general screen persona in ensemble work such as Wedding Crashers, Step Brothers and Talladega Nights – embodied a type that spoke clearly for the times: the arrested manchild.That all changed the momentBoratand his wobbling producer Azamat Bagatov landed in New York in 2006. By injecting Borat with a raw hit of the reality format incubated on The 11 O’Clock Show and Da Ali G Show, Baron Cohen completely revitalised big-screen character comedy. Suddenly, it became thrillingly politicised as his sublimely ignorant aliases, Borat and in 2009 Brüno, flushed out American and Middle Eastern absurdities and prejudices. Not to mention the high-wire aspect of his escapades: Baron Cohen was somehow impervious to whatever peril he stirred up, whether that was desecrating the Star-Spangled Banner at a rodeo in Borat, or an interpretation of mano-a-mano quite different to what cage fighting audiences were expecting in Brüno. His gleeful brazenness was the signature quality that shone through.View image in fullscreenA type that spoke clearly for the times … Will Ferrell in Anchorman: The Legend of Ron Burgundy, 2004.Photograph: Dreamworks Skg/AllstarBut Ali G has been dormant a long time. His last big-screen outing, 2002’s hit-and-missAli G Indahouse, was a very different, fully scripted endeavour. Beyond a gag about mistaking a pregnancy test for a vape, the trailer for Ali G: Who Iz I? doesn’t give much away about how sharply the character’s been updated; judging by the small-penis outro, some things are undying.Staines’s favourite son will need to pull more out of his XXXXXL puffa. Only the current culture wars – police violence, colonialism, cultural appropriation – can supply him with appropriately charged material that he can “booyakasha” his way through. Anything less, and the character’s age will show, and the once-cutting posturing and patois will seem less than ironic. Which would be a bad thing for character comedy – then the mask really will have slipped.Ali G: Who Iz I? is released in UK cinemas on 23 OctoberExplore more on these topicsComedy filmsSacha Baron CohenComedyMike MyersWill FerrellRobin WilliamsEddie MurphyfeaturesShareReuse this content
