title: ‘He punched a polar bear on the nose!’ Ninety glorious years of Brian Blessed – by Emma Thompson, Adrian Lester and more | Brian Blessed | The Guardian
description: Peeing in the sink he shared with Derek Jacobi, making a badger video with Brian May, climbing Everest with Alan Hinkes … as the great actor blasts into his 90s, stars celebrate his ‘loudness and madness’
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Peeing in the sink he shared with Derek Jacobi, making a badger video with Brian May, climbing Everest with Alan Hinkes … as the great actor blasts into his 90s, stars celebrate his ‘loudness and madness’
Content: ‘Delightfully terrifying’ … as Sir Tunbelly Clumsey in The Relapse at the National Theatre in 2001.Photograph: Donald Cooper/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Delightfully terrifying’ … as Sir Tunbelly Clumsey in The Relapse at the National Theatre in 2001.Photograph: Donald Cooper/AlamyBrian Blessed‘He punched a polar bear on the nose!’ Ninety glorious years of Brian Blessed – by Emma Thompson, Adrian Lester and morePeeing in the sink he shared with Derek Jacobi, making a badger video with Brian May, climbing Everest with Alan Hinkes  … as the great actor blasts into his 90s, stars celebrate his ‘loudness and madness’Interviews byMark FisherThu 8 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 13.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘A mighty wind, a tree of life’Emma ThompsonI know why Brian has lasted this long in spite of falling out of helicopters and off mountains and into lakes all his life: he started the whole being-cold-keeps-you-healthy thing years before Wim Hof was doing his motivational speaking.Once, when we were shooting Ken Branagh’s Henry V at Shepperton, it was very cold out. I went to visit Brian in his dressing room. I was in my costume for the Princess of France, a lovely off-the-shoulder number. All the windows were open. It was bloody freezing. Brian started to tell me a story about Everest. I sat there, fascinated, getting colder and colder. He noticed – after some time – and said: “Thompson, why are you wearing blue lipstick?”I tried to speak but my jaw had frozen in its sockets. He bundled me out into the heated corridors where I spent a good hour getting my body up to a functioning temperature. “The cold is good for you!” he thundered. And by God he was right. I took a cold shower every day after that.View image in fullscreen‘The cold is good for you!’ … with Kenneth Branagh in Henry V.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyThe man is a legend: a force, a mighty wind and a great tree of life. He has the soul of a mountain-top. I will always love him deeply and appreciate his kindness to a young actress, his wit and fun and energy and gaiety, his loudness and his madness.‘Now get to 100!’Derek JacobiWe first worked together at Birmingham Rep in 1960 when we would do a different play every month. It was my first job and he was the star of the show. I was in awe of him. He was still in his 20s but had a huge personality even then. I ended up sharing a dressing room with him, which was an education in itself. He was not particularly restrained – not when it came to pissing in the sink!View image in fullscreen‘He was not particularly restrained’ … with Derek Jacobi in I, Claudius.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyBrian is full of bluster and bigness, but underneath it all, he is as sensitive as the rest of us. He is a true man of the theatre and it was wonderful to learn from him. The next thing we did together was I, Claudius, in which he was marvellous as Augustus. Off-stage, he’s full of bonhomie, a great companion. Everything about him is big: his laughter, everything. But he’s not ego-driven: he’s just great company. My message to him is get to 100 and we’ll all be there applauding! We’re all applauding at 90 too!‘Wow, he just says anything!’Dexter FletcherView image in fullscreen‘He had a healthy belief in being who you are’ … Blessed as Claudius and Dexter Fletcher  as the Player Queen in Hamlet in 1984.Photograph: Donald Cooper/ShutterstockI worked with Brian in the 1984 season at the Royal Shakespeare Company at Stratford-upon-Avon. I was in a couple of productions that he was in: Henry V, with Kenneth Branagh playing Young Hal and Brian playing the Duke of Exeter; and Hamlet, when Brian played Claudius and Virginia McKenna was Gertrude.He came with this energy, exuberance and lust for life. I’d never seen anybody like him. He had a healthy belief in being who you are. He would talk about his cock quite openly: “That big blue vein on the side of your dick.” Branagh would be laughing, a lot of people would be shocked and Virginia McKenna didn’t seem fazed by it at all. I was 18 thinking: “Wow, he just says anything!”Towards the end of the season, I got an offer of an acting role in a film called Revolution with Al Pacino. It was a big movie and I was only 18. Hamlet was going into the Barbican in London. I didn’t know what decision to make. It was Brian who took me aside at a rehearsal space at the back of the theatre and said: “Listen, Dexter, go and do the movie because the movie world is small and when you get into it, if you make a success of it, you’re in and it’s a great living.”It led to a lot of movies – so I have a great love and affection for him because he did me a huge favour by shoving me in that direction.‘He pinched my bottom. It was perfect for the scene’Melody AndersonI remember watching I, Claudius as I grew up and thinking Brian Blessed was an incredible actor. I was 23 and it was so exciting to meet him on the set ofFlash Gordonand hear his Shakespearean voice bellow throughout the stages.It was a tough shoot, six days a week, 12 hours a day, and to have his lightness and sense of humour to alleviate the stress of the job was a gift. He was as indefatigable off screen as he was as Prince Vultan of the Hawkmen. Brian did not have to stretch to create a character because that’s him. He is a Hawkman! He takes the space, the voice is always bellowing and there is that sly smile and twinkle in his eyes – which he still has at 90.There is nothing more exciting than to work with an actor who is so inventive. Playing Dale Arden, I was on this table when we land on his planet and he was spinning me around and he just gave me a little bottom pinch. As an actor, I loved it because it solicited such an honest response. He gave me a whole other level of energy. It was exactly right for the character because it let me act like this haughty, temper-driven girl who beats up the guards at the king’s palace. It worked perfectly for the scene. Mike Hodges, the director, was thrilled.View image in fullscreen‘It’s not his ego – it’s a life force’ … with Melody Anderson and Sam J Jones in Flash Gordon.Photograph: THA/ShutterstockWhen I was at conventions with Sam J Jones, who played Flash, we would sit back and be quiet and Brian would be off, pacing back and forth across the stage and taking over. We would smile and let it be the Brian show. He takes over any place he’s in. It’s not an ego thing: it’s a life force. I don’t think I’ve ever met anyone who has such energy and self-confidence.He also has an enormous capacity to be sensitive. It’s a form of empathy to be able to pick up on the energies of the people around him and try to uplift their state if they were a little bit down.Blessings to Brian Blessed! He is a gift in my life and I’m better for knowing him.‘He appeared in our badger crusade video’Brian MayI’m old enough to remember Brian’s first appearance on TV. He was in Z-Cars and even then he was an impressive character. Getting to work with him on theFlash Gordonfilm was the most amazing thing. I didn’t see him on set, I just saw him on footage that had been shot as the days went by. We were in the studio, playing along to it all, so I felt I knew him better than I actually did.While everyone went back to finish the album Queen was making at the time, I made the soundtrack album for Flash Gordon. I pieced together lots of dialogue, sound effects and music – and you can hear Brian loud and clear. He’s a musical part of what we achieved, like an extra member of Queen.View image in fullscreen‘He cares deeply and passionately about animals’ … Brian May at a Stop the Cull protest in 2013.Photograph: REX/Julian MakeyFor years, I used to see him around Windlesham in Surrey where my studio is. He often popped in to help us with our badger crusades. He did a great appearance in ourBadger Badger Badgervideo, doing the Brian Blessed everybody wants, very loud and distinctive, shouting: “Keep the badgers alive!”He’s blustery and apparently super-confident, but we saw a side of him that cares deeply and passionately about animals. Whenever we’ve asked him for help, he has always come straight away. I’ve seen him sit and talk movingly about the way we don’t accommodate wild animals in the world we’ve built. I see him as a very deep human being.A very happy 90th to you, Brian. What an important piece you have been in the jigsaw of my life. I’ll forever be grateful to you and will forever enjoy the humanity and individuality you bring to all your work.‘He never seems to conk out’Alan HinkesView image in fullscreenBlessed at Everest base camp.Photograph: Steve Back/ANL/REX/ShutterstockIt’s 30 years since we were on Everest – and Brian got to 7,700m before turning back. We’ve both beenYorkshireman of the Yearand have the same wicked sense of humour. He can be over the top but he doesn’t offend me, although some of the anecdotes I daren’t tell you! Brian is a caricature of himself and I mean that in a good way: he is everything you expect him to be. I can’t help but laugh when I’m with him. On Everest, at base camp, he would regale us with tales in the mess tent and I would be rolling off my stool on to the floor which was probably -15C.He wouldn’t be as ebullient as that when we were up on the mountain, because you’re gasping for oxygen in the rarefied air and suffering from acute mountain sickness, which you can die from. You wouldn’t expect anyone to be entertaining when you’re that high. But you think, “How does he keep going? Does he conk out in private?” Well, I’ve seen him in private – I spent two-and-a-half months with him and he didn’t seem to conk out.At charity events, he’ll be humble and sing my praises. He’ll say: “Alan’s saved my life and he’s carried me down on his back when I was knackered.” That’s very flattering to me. I couldn’t really carry him down on my back, but it’s a good story. He’s a great raconteur.‘His booming voice creates its own weather system’Imogen StubbsI loved Brian when I worked with him inThe Relapseat the National Theatre in 2001 – he was a delightfully terrifying figure running around on stage with a blunderbuss and his signature booming voice that creates its own weather system. But also with the sweetest, kindest personality backstage that was disarmingly quiet and contemplative at times. The perfect company member. Wonderfully playful. Taking acting seriously but not too seriously.‘A rare, brilliant, kind-hearted giant’Adrian LesterBrian is often described as having a bombastic voice and a larger-than-life presence that makes us think of his performances as being, well, just performances. But don’t let that fool you. Brian brings to his characters a charisma and charm that isn’t larger than life. It is large and full to the brim with life. Honest, powerful life in all its shades. People still quote his intonation and volume when his character in Flash Gordon realises that “Gordon’s alive?!” He can tell you a story about a trip to the Arctic where he punched a polar bear on the nose and somehow you know it’s true.Brian can be quiet, subtle and piercing. Then in the same breath he can open his mouth and shake the ground you stand on. I have had the privilege of standing opposite him in a scene and been subject to a delicate subtlety in character that many would not associate with him. A rare, brilliant, kind-hearted giant of a man. I wish there were more like him.Explore more on these topicsBrian BlessedTheatreTelevisionDerek JacobiEmma ThompsonAdrian LesterFlash GordonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: You be the judge: my friend and I bought a tent but she’s moved away. Who owns it now? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Ava shared the initial cost but Ruth has forked out for repairs. You decide who’s on the wrong side of this in-tents debate?
Author: Georgina Lawton
Headline: Ava shared the initial cost but Ruth has forked out for repairs. You decide who’s on the wrong side of this in-tents debate?
Content: Illustration: Igor Bastidas/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Igor Bastidas/The GuardianYou be the judgeLife and styleYou be the judge: my friend and I bought a tent but she’s moved away. Who owns it now?Ava shared the initial cost but Ruth has forked out for repairs. You decide who’s on the wrong side of this in-tents debate?Find out how to get a disagreement settled or become a jurorInterviews byGeorgina LawtonThu 8 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 11.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe prosecution: Avadouble quotation markI paid for half of the tent, so I deserve equal use of it, even if we no longer live in the same countryRuth and I bought a tent together when we were living together in Spain and going to festivals there. We had a good time using it, and took it to four different festivals in Spain and Portugal. And after that we used it every year for festivals and camping trips.It was alwaysourtent, not Ruth’s tent that I occasionally borrowed. I moved back to the UK in 2024 and Ruth stayed in Spain, so it made sense for the tent to stay with her. There wasn’t much point in me taking half a tent back to London, and at the time there was no reason to formally decide who owned it. We were friends, we’d always used it together so I assumed it still belonged to both of us.double quotation markI didn’t give Ruth my share of the tent when I moved away. I still have ownership over itNow we both have partners and both need the tent. I’m coming back to Spain for a festival and asked Ruth if I could use the tent with my boyfriend Michael. The problem is that she’s going to the festival too with her partner, Luis, and wants it for herself.Ruth says the tent is practically hers because it has been at her flat and she’s used it much more since I moved away. She also paid for repairs when it got a hole in it. I appreciate that she’s looked after it, but none of that changes the fact that I paid for half of it from the start.I always assumed that I’d be able to use it at some stage, or have her buy me out. She has offered exactly that but doesn’t believe she should pay the same amount that I had paid for it initially, because she’s kept it all these years. I think that’s ridiculous.Besides, I didn’t give Ruth my share of the tent when I moved away. I didn’t sell it to her or tell her she could keep it permanently. I still have ownership over it – but now that I need it, it’s suddenly not mine any more.If this was a court of law, I’d still have a stake in this tent. I hope the court of public opinion sides with me. We need to acknowledge that I still own half.The defence: Ruthdouble quotation markAva hasn’t used the tent in years, and I’ve stored it and paid for its upkeep. Surely I get first dibs?Yes, Ava and I originally split the cost of the tent. We bought it in 2018 when we lived together and used to go to festivals and camping together. Back then, calling it “our tent” made total sense because we had a shared life and actually used it together.But then Ava moved back to the UK and the tent stayed with me in Spain. Since then, I’m the person who has actually been using it. It has been stored in my flat, taking up my space, and whenever something has needed sorting out, I’ve dealt with it.double quotation markI can buy her out, but I don’t think paying her exactly half back is the answerAt one point the tent got a hole in it and needed repairing. I paid for the repairs. Ava hasn’t been contributing towards those expenses from the UK while I’ve continued maintaining and using the tent. I don’t think you can disappear from the practical ownership of something for years and then suddenly expect exactly the same access to it when you happen to want it again.She actually forgot about the tent until now, and never asked about the upkeep or storage. Now she’s coming back for a festival and wants to use it. Unfortunately, I’m going to the same festival and I need it too.I’m not refusing her because I’m being possessive or because I’ve forgotten that she originally contributed. I simply have an established use for something that has effectively been in my possession for years. I’m first in line; I get first dibs.What am I supposed to do? Hand over the tent I’ve stored, used and maintained and then go and buy myself another one? Ava thinks so.Maybe the fairest thing now is for us to formally sort out ownership rather than keep pretending one tent can belong equally to two people living in different countries. I can buy her out, but I don’t think paying her exactly half back is the answer for all the reasons above: storage, repairs. It doesn’t solve the dilemma as to who gets to use it now either. It’s unreasonable to expect me to give it up exactly when I need it myself.Names have been changedskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe jury of Guardian readersAs Ruth has managed the storage and upkeep of the tent, she deserves to keep it. If Ava is going to insist on part-ownership, then she should pay Ruth for the cost of repairs, but that seems very petty. Why not use the festival to reconnect as friends? Ava should let the tent go.Holly, 36Given the tent will have depreciated in value over this time, and Ruth has paid for repairs, the fairest solution would be for Ruth to buy out Ava at a reduced rate. Either that or they share the tent at this festival.Alden, 29I recognise Ruth has incurred costs from storing and repairing the tent, but she’s also had free usage of it for the past two years. Ruth should buy Ava out for half the price of a comparable used tent.Mark, 32Ava, you’ve been back in the UK for two years. The tent is eight years old, and you’re fighting for custody? Ruth has been storing it and repairing it, and it’s impolite to expect free storage when you don’t need it. Upgrade yourself. Buy yourself a new tent.Verity, 37They are both being very boring and possessive over this holey old tent. Do neither of their boyfriends have tents?! Surely one of the few perks of having a boyfriend is they have access to tents? But as Ruth has had this one cluttering her home then Ava just needs to be gracious and relinquish ownership.Kitty, 34Now you be the judgeIn our online poll, tell us: should Ruth accept that she’s in the losing camp?The poll closes on Wednesday 14 October at 9am BSTLast week’s resultsWe asked if Kittyshould let her boyfriend hang his football calendar on the wall.68%of you said yes –Kitty is guilty32%of you said no –Kitty is innocentExplore more on these topicsLife and styleYou be the judgefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The best beauty Advent calendars in the UK in 2026, tested – from bargain buys to cult favourites | Christmas | The Guardian
description: Christmas is getting closer, and this year’s calendars are already on sale. We tested the biggest releases to find the ones worth buying, including cruelty-free picks
Author: Sarah Matthews
Headline: Christmas is getting closer, and this year’s calendars are already on sale. We tested the biggest releases to find the ones worth buying, including cruelty-free picks
Content: View image in fullscreenGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterChristmasReviewThe best beauty Advent calendars in the UK in 2026, tested – from bargain buys to cult favouritesChristmas is getting closer, and this year’s calendars are already on sale. We tested the biggest releases to find the ones worth buying, including cruelty-free picksDon’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereSarah MatthewsThu 8 Oct 2026 10.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChristmas might feel like an age away, but the festive season has already begun for fans of beauty Advent calendars. Most of this year’s calendars are now on sale or available to preorder, and many of the most popular could sell out long beforeWhamageddonclaims its first victim.So, much as it pains me to say it, now might be a good time to buy one. Below, you’ll find my favourites, from bargain beauty Advent calendars under £50 to three-figure luxuries. I’ve tested 20 to find calendars packed with cult-favourite products suitable for a whole spectrum of skin types and preferences. I also looked at the packaging and broad appeal of each calendar to help minimise waste.If nothing tickles your fancy just yet, don’t panic. More calendars get released in the lead-up to December, and I’ll keep updating this article as they drop.At a glanceBest beauty Advent calendar overallCult BeautyAdvent calendar Signature Edition£245 at Cult BeautyBest value beauty Advent calendarLookfantasticBeauty Advent calendar£120 at LookfantasticBest beauty Advent calendar under £100Anthropologie24 Days of Beauty Advent calendar£98 at AnthropologieBest beauty Advent calendar for full-size productsSpace NKBeauty Advent calendar£275 at Space NKBest luxury beauty Advent calendarLibertyBeauty Advent calendar£285 at LibertyBest beauty Advent calendar for familiesLushAdvent calendar£210 at LushBest Advent calendar for skin and body careHolland & BarrettBeauty Advent calendar£60 at Holland & BarrettBest beauty Advent calendar for teens and tweensW7Beauty Blast Advent calendar£21.99 at AmazonWhy you should trust meI test beauty products for a living, which means I’ve worked my way through more skincare, makeup, hair care, perfume and nail care products than I dare to count. Working in this industry has shown me the very best and absolute worst of what’s out there. I know how to spot a good product when I see one, even if it’s tucked away in the corner of a beauty Advent calendar.I also have a certification in cosmetic science, so I know how to identify products suited to different skin and hair types. I’ve struggled with sensitive skin for years, so I keep a close eye out for ingredients that might irritate. The calendars below are all full of products suitable for most people to minimise waste.How I testedView image in fullscreenBehind the doors: calendars were judged on the range and usefulness of their contents, as well as the packaging they came in.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianHeaps of Advent calendars are released every year. To help find the best, I longlisted 30 before testing the 20 that offer the best range of products and value for money. I’ll continue to update this page with new options in the run-up toChristmas.Testing them lets me assess the quality of each calendar and its contents, as well as the packaging it arrives in. If the calendar itself is recyclable but arrives shrouded in plastic bags and polystyrene, it’s a non-starter. I also check that each calendar is made from packaging that is recyclable at home or genuinely reusable.It’s impossible to test every product inside every calendar – I only have one face, after all – but I judge each calendar based on the range, quality and usefulness of the products inside. Broad appeal is key to avoiding wasted products, and luckily, this is how most Advent calendars are designed.I look for a good mix of skincare, makeup, body care, hair care and nail care, unless a calendar is specifically dedicated to a certain product type. I also check how easy it is to incorporate each product into a typical routine. Too many harsh treatments or bold makeup shades would be less appealing than a calendar with a more approachable lineup.This helps me assess how broadly usable the contents are and how much is likely to go to waste. While beauty Advent calendars can’t be considered eco-friendly, it’s important to minimise waste where possible.Each year I end up with far more products than one woman can reasonably use. This year, I donated the contents of the calendars to theRedbridge Reach Outservice, which supports anyone experiencing domestic abuse.Our favourite beauty Advent calendars in 2026Best beauty Advent calendar overall:Cult Beauty Advent calendar Signature EditionCult BeautyAdvent calendar Signature Edition£245£245 at Cult BeautyWhat we loveHigh-end skincare and makeup in a beautiful designWhat we don’t loveMinimal hair care; a daring blush shadeView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£245 at Cult BeautyStatus:availableIf you’re hunting for a beauty Advent calendar filled with high-end makeup and skincare, this year’s Cult Beauty Signature Edition is my top pick. I’ve tried and recommended many of the products inside over the past year, while others are established favourites. There’s very little to dislike, and with 33 products inside, 19 of which are full-size, that’s no mean feat.What we loveWhile I’m most excited about the contents of this calendar, it’s also my favourite design. It opens like a book and features detailed illustrations of lipsticks and makeup brushes hidden among festive flowers and foliage. The white, sage green and gold colour scheme should work well with most Christmas decorations. And when the countdown is complete, the box can go in your household recycling bin, while the gold ribbon can be reused.The skincare inside also has broad appeal. I tested the Medik8 Advanced pro-collagen peptide cream for my recent roundup offace moisturisers, and its light texture and peptide formula made it my top choice for anti-ageing. You’ll also get a 15ml size of the eye-wateringly expensive Augustinus Bader the Rich Cream, which I found amazing for nourishing dry winter-stressed skin.There are just two skincare products you’ll need to be a little careful with: the Paula’s Choice Retinaldehyde treatment and the Allies of Skin Azelaic serum. Both contain ingredients used to target anti-ageing, acne and hyperpigmentation, but add them to your routine gradually and separately to reduce the risk of irritation.Makeup-wise, there’s a lot to like too, with a full-size Saie liquid blush and Westman Ateliermascara, both high-end products loved by many beauty enthusiasts. You’ll also find a travel-size Charlotte Tilbury setting spray and Milk Makeup Hydro Grip primer, both of which are top picks in my upcoming primer and setting spray tests.Topping things off with hair care, you’ll find the Fable & Mane HoliRootshair oil, which helps to promote stronger strands and increase hydration without using silicones. But the hair-care highlight for me is the travel-size Gisou Honey Gloss ceramide shampoo and conditioner, which smell divine and are from the same range as my favouritehair mask.It’s a shame that …only four of the products are hair care, and there’s no perfume included. And the Patrick Ta blush duo is almost highlighter pink; you’ll need a light hand, but the shade itself may not be for everyone.Claimed overall value:more than £1,100Number of products:19 full-size, 14 mini (33 in total)Calendar shell:recyclable card with reusable gold ribbonsStandout products:Westman Atelier Eye Want You mascara, Charlotte Tilbury Airbrush Flawless Finish setting spray,Patrick Ta Major Headlines Double-Take cream + powder blush duo, Saie Dew blush, Medik8 Advanced pro-collagen peptide cream, Augustinus Bader the Rich CreamCult BeautyAdvent calendar Signature Edition£245£245 at Cult BeautyWhat we loveHigh-end skincare and makeup in a beautiful designWhat we don’t loveMinimal hair care; a daring blush shadeBest value beauty Advent calendar:Lookfantastic Beauty Advent calendarLookfantasticBeauty Advent calendar£120£120 at LookfantasticWhat we loveA broad mix of beauty staplesWhat we don’t loveNo nail care; has a massive footprintView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£120 at LookfantasticStatus:preorderThis year’s Lookfantastic calendar packs 27 products, including 19 full-size, into its vault-style design. Each drawer has been curated by a different celebrity or influencer to include one of their favourite beauty picks, from face creams to home fragrance. It largely steers clear of pricey, specialist treatments, focusing instead on familiar beauty staples.Why we love itStarting strong with skincare, there’s a full-size Medik8 Total Moisture daily cleansing gel, which I love as a quick morning cleanse that doesn’t leave my skin feeling stripped. You’ll also find an Elemis Pro-Collagen night cream – the richer version of the day cream I tried in myface moisturisertests. One of my favouritebody moisturisersalso features: the Ameliorate Transforming body lotion, which I found good for smoothing and hydrating rough, bumpy skin.As for makeup, my top two picks are classics: there’s a full-size Benefit Roller Lash mascara in black, which is one of my long-term favourites for its curl and lift. Then there’s the Anastasia Beverly Hills Brow Freeze styling wax in clear to shape up all brow shades.For wellness, I was pleased to spot a full-size Amalfi Lemon room spray from the White Company, which has an uplifting, clean scent that’s perfect for winter. There’s also a great mix of hair care, including a full-size Aveda Cherry Almond shampoo and conditioner. Since many of us heat-style our hair more often at Christmas, I was also glad to see a leave-in strengthening treatment from Color Wow.It’s a shame that …you don’t get any nail care, and the calendar has quite a large footprint, so you’ll need a lot of space to display it.Claimed overall value:more than £665Number of products:19 full-size, 8 miniCalendar shell:recyclableStandout products:Color Wow Dream Cocktail, Aveda Cherry Almond Softening shampoo and conditioner, The White Company Amalfi Lemon luxury home spray, Anastasia Beverly Hills Brow Freeze wax, Benefit Roller lash mascara, Elemis Pro-Collagen night cream, Medik8 Total Moisture daily cleansing gel, Ameliorate Transforming body lotionLookfantasticBeauty Advent calendar£120£120 at LookfantasticWhat we loveA broad mix of beauty staplesWhat we don’t loveNo nail care; has a massive footprintBest beauty Advent calendar under £100:Anthropologie 24 Days of Beauty Advent calendarAnthropologie24 Days of Beauty Advent calendar£98£98 at AnthropologieWhat we loveClassic, usable beauty treats at a good priceWhat we don’t loveOnly one makeup product insideView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£98 at AnthropologieStatus:availableSome beauty Advent calendars cost the world and then leave you wondering what on earth to do with all the products inside. That is not true of the Anthropologie calendar for 2026. There are 25 little luxuries behind 24 doors, and all are staples that should fit easily into an existing beauty routine. Small upgrades for a sensible price.What we loveThere isn’t too much skincare in this calendar, but you will find a full-size Grown Alchemist Regenerating serum worth £60. This has a light gel texture and contains rambutan, polysaccharides and plant peptides to help smooth the appearance of fine lines, hydrate and promote smooth skin.You’ll find the Espa Clean & Green Detox mask, which has a cream clay formula containing vitamin E.There are three fragrances included: the Malin+Goetz strawberry perfume oil, Phlur Father Figure, and a 10ml bottle of Floral Street Wild Vanilla Orchid. The latter is a light, floral fragrance that’s wearable and uplifting but not sickly sweet, and it’s one of my favourite new perfumes.The hair care highlights include the Superfoods prewash oil from Hair Syrup, which I’ve tested before and enjoyed using. You’ll also find a silk scrunchie from Slip, which I found snagged less than standard hair ties, creating less breakage. Be warned – I haven’t been able to go back to normal hair ties since trying these.The calendar also includes a few wellness treats, such as the This Works Deep Sleep pillow spray, a L’Occitane hand cream and a mini candle from Plum & Ashby.It’s a shame that …there’s only one makeup item inside, and Trip electrolytes sachets don’t feel like an exciting beauty treat. The Malin+Goetz strawberry perfume oil is also an acquired taste.Claimed overall value:£400Number of products:17 full-size, 8 miniCalendar shell:recyclableStandout products:Grown Alchemist Regenerating serum, Espa Clean & Green Detox mask, Hair Syrup Superfoods prewash oil, Slip silk skinny scrunchie, Floral Street Wild Vanilla Orchid eau de parfum, This Works Deep Sleep pillow spray, Phlur Father Figure eau de parfum, L’Occitane Amande (almond) Sublime hand cream, Neal’s Yard Wild Rose beauty balm, Manucurist Active Shine polishAnthropologie24 Days of Beauty Advent calendar£98£98 at AnthropologieWhat we loveClassic, usable beauty treats at a good priceWhat we don’t loveOnly one makeup product insideBest beauty Advent calendar for full-size products:Space NK Beauty Advent calendarSpace NKBeauty Advent calendar£275£275 at Space NKWhat we loveGreat product range for treatmentsWhat we don’t loveMostly anti-ageing skincareView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£275 at Space NKStatus:availableThe Space NK calendar was my top pick last year, and this year’s curation is also strong. It was only pipped to the post because its skincare selection leans a little too heavily towards anti-ageing. Still, it’s a strong option if you’re a fan of high-end beauty and want to try a range of products.What we loveThis calendar has the most full-size products included of any here; there are 26, with nine minis. The full-size Skin Rocks cleansing balm effortlessly removed stubborn makeup. There’s also a full-size Medik8 Exo-PDRN Prismatic+ serum, which is one of the best PDRN serums I’ve tried for rejuvenating and improving skin tone, while supporting the skin’s barrier. Most of the headline skincare products are tailored toward anti-ageing, such as the La Mer moisturising cream and Caudalie Vinoperfect Brightening dark spot serum.For hair care, Space NK has skipped the basics and gone straight for treatments. There’s a K18 heat protectant, a leave-in treatment from Color Wow, and an Olaplex treatment, all of which are full-size. It’s good to see a daily essential like heat protection in there, as well as treatments that should suit a range of hair types.I’m also excited by the Kulfi lip stain oil, which is a moisturising, slightly glossy stain in a neutral rose designed to suit a range of skin tones. Likewise, the perfumes have broad appeal. I’ve tried Phlur Missing Person and the Gisou hair perfume before, but I was surprised by the velvety scent of the DS & Durga Debaser in Bloom perfume. All could be layered with the Saltair Salt Water Vanilla body oil, which has a deep, warm vanilla fragrance and feels light on the skin.It’s a shame that …all of the makeup inside is cream- or liquid-based, so if you prefer powder formulations, this won’t be for you. There’s also no nail care included. And, as mentioned above, most of the skincare is focused on anti-ageing. They’re all high-end brands, but the calendar may not include enough basics for younger people or those who prefer a simpler routine.Claimed overall value:more than £1,200Number of products:26 full-size, 9 miniCalendar shell:recyclableStandout products:La Mer Crème de la Mer moisturising cream, K18 HeatBounce conditioning heat protectant, Color Wow Carb Cocktail, Olaplex No3 Plus Complete Repair treatment, Augustinus Bader the Body Cream, Caudalie Vinoperfect Brightening Dark Spot serum, Kosas Soulgazer mascara, Kulfi Lassi lip staining oil, Medik8 Exo-PDRN Prismatic+ serum, Naturium the Booster hyaluronic acid body wash, Refy Lash Sculpt, Saltair Salt Water Vanilla body oil, Skin Rocks the Cleansing BalmSpace NKBeauty Advent calendar£275£275 at Space NKWhat we loveGreat product range for treatmentsWhat we don’t loveMostly anti-ageing skincareFor more, read Sali Hughes’s guide to thebest anti-ageing creams, serums and treatmentsBest luxury beauty Advent calendar:Liberty Beauty Advent calendarLibertyBeauty Advent calendar£285£285 at LibertyWhat we loveGreat fragrance selection and luxury productsWhat we don’t loveShampoo could do with a matching conditionerView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£285 at LibertyStatus:availableBrowsing Liberty’s beauty hall is one of my favourite things to do in between meetings in London. It isn’t cheap, but this year’s Liberty calendar brought a little taste of that luxury to my living room. If you’re hoping to try new high-end beauty products, and particularly if you like experimenting with new fragrance, this will be right up your street.Why we love itWhat immediately struck me is the wide range of perfumes inside. There are eight from fragrance houses such as DS & Durga, Bibbi, and Ex Nihilo. You’ll find classics such as Molecule 01 fragrance, which smells different on everyone, but my favourite inclusion is Tana Meadow, from Liberty’s own fragrance house. It’s been my go-to fragrance recently, with spiced woody top notes that settle into white floral mid notes and a hearty vanilla, wood and praline base.My next favourite thing about this calendar is the selection of makeup. While it’s hard to tell online, I was pleased to see a versatile range of shades, with a gorgeous dusky pink Lisa Eldridge lipstick and a conditioning mascara from Ilia. There is one daring berry-red lip stain from Violette FR that promises to hydrate lips as it stains, perfect for the festive season when we need our lipstick to last through far more feasting than usual.The calendar is also rammed with skincare and hair care from luxury brands you won’t find at most high-street retailers. I tried the Maria Nila Gloss Coat anti-frizz treatment earlier this year and found it performed brilliantly in humid weather. The MZ Skin Bio-Placenta eye cream promises to improve tired eyes in four weeks; I found it had a cool, refreshing feel and sunk in quickly. There’s also a brightening vitamin C serum from Sunday Riley, which had a lovely hydrating feel and didn’t upset my skin, and an Augustinus Bader face oil that left my skin with a healthy glow without feeling greasy.It’s a shame that …the Davines shampoo doesn’t come paired with its conditioner. There’s also no nail care, which is oddly common among this year’s calendars.Claimed overall value:more than £1,300Number of products:21 full-size, 8 miniCalendar shell:recyclable, with reusable drawstring bagStandout products:DS & Durga Debaser eau de parfum, Bibbi Vanilla Factory eau de parfum, Ex Nihilo Blue Talisman extrait de parfum, Escentric Molecules Molecule 01, LBTY Tana Meadow eau de parfum, Lisa Eldridge Baume Embrace Melting lip colour in épanoui, Ilia Beauty Limitless lash mascara in after midnight, Violette_FR Lip Nectar in bêtise, Maria Nila gloss coat, MZ Skin Intensive Bio-Placenta eye cream, Sunday Riley CEO Vitamin C 15% brightening serum, Augustinus Bader the Face OilLibertyBeauty Advent calendar£285£285 at LibertyWhat we loveGreat fragrance selection and luxury productsWhat we don’t loveShampoo could do with a matching conditionerBest beauty Advent calendar for families:Lush Advent calendarLushAdvent calendar£210£210 at LushWhat we loveGreat mix of products for all ages to enjoyWhat we don’t loveThe fragrances are characteristically sweetView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£210 at LushStatus:availableIf you know your little ones won’t be able to keep their hands off your fancy beauty Advent calendar, why not buy something you can all enjoy? Lush offers two stocked-up Advent calendars every year:one filled with bath bombs and bubble barsand another with the brand’s wider beauty offerings. This reusable hamper is the latter, filled with veganand cruelty-free festive bath bombs, creams, perfumes and a lip scrub to appeal to all ages.Why we love itThat distinctive Lush smell hits as soon as you open this hamper. This will either delight or repulse you, although presumably if you’re considering this you’re in the former camp. Inside, you’ll find 25 treats spread across two 12-day halves that save you a bit of rummaging around.Starting with bath products, you’ll find festive-food-themed bombs and bubble bars, including an orange, a candied pear, a candy cane, a carrot for Rudolph and a Christmas tree. There are also picks from Lush’s standard range, such as the Sleepy bubble bar. And the sweet theme doesn’t stop at bath time, thanks to the sticky dates, s’mores, and chocolate orange shower gels. You can even eat the Hot Chocolate Orange lip scrub, which tastes just as delicious as it sounds.Out of the bathroom, the calendar comes with two exclusive fragrances. The mini Santa’s Favourite body spray smells like soft florals and settles into a light grapefruit. Or, for something stronger, the Snowcake and Rose perfume smells like warm marzipan and feels more grownup. You’ll also find hand soaps, a dusting powder, a body butter, a candle and a cosy pair of Lush socks.Lush scores highly on sustainability: the hamper is made by a B Corp-certified manufacturer, and there’s adetailed breakdown onlineon the other packaging and how to recycle it. The packing peanuts can be placed in your food or garden waste bin, and when you’re finished with the bottles and tubs, you can return them to Lush using theBring it Back schemefor money off your next purchase.It’s a shame that …unlike previous years, there are no inserts to refill last year’s Advent calendar chest. While the new hamper design is a little more reusable day to day, this change seems counterproductive from a sustainability perspective, since part of the appeal of last year’s calendar was that you’d be able to refill it. I’m hoping this version will be refillable for years to come. For a completely refillable option, Lush is launching a fabric calendar this year for you to fill yourself, which will allow you to add products you know you love.Claimed overall value:not listedNumber of products:24 full-size, 1 miniCalendar shell:biodegradable and recyclable cardboard inserts, reusable wicker hamperStandout products:Hot Chocolate Orange lip scrub, Sleepy bubble bar, Sticky Dates shower gel, Honey Bear bath bomb, Once Upon a Time candle, Dream Cream body lotion, Honey I Washed the Kids body scrub, Christmas tree bath bomb, Snowcake and Rose perfumeLushAdvent calendar£210£210 at LushWhat we loveGreat mix of products for all ages to enjoyWhat we don’t loveThe fragrances are characteristically sweetBest Advent calendarfor skin and body careHolland & Barrett Beauty Advent calendarHolland & BarrettBeauty Advent calendar£60£60 at Holland & BarrettWhat we loveIncludes top-rated, budget-friendly productsWhat we don’t loveNo makeupView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£60 at Holland & BarrettStatus:availableAdvent calendars full of high-end products are a double-edged sword: it’s great to find new favourites, but they might become a drain on your bank account if you want to repurchase them. Holland & Barrett’s Advent calendar packs in many affordable body and skin care products that I’ve tried and wouldn’t hesitate to use in my routine. Many of the products inside are from cruelty-free brands, and, of all the options here, this calendar feels the most gender-neutral, which also makes it great to share.Why we love itThe skincare selection here is strong, with two inclusions from Dr Organic: a probiotic cream cleanser that I love, and a vitamin E moisturiser that will help with dry, winter-stressed skin. You’ll find a mini version of one of my go-to breakout-busting cleansers, the Cetaphil Exfoliating SA cleanser, with a matching mini moisturiser that’s perfect for travel. There’s also a brightening eye cream from the brilliant UpCircle, which uses repurposed ingredients.For body care, there’s a full-size version of the Weleda Skin Food body lotion; I love the hand cream from this range, and the lotion has a lighter texture while still using plant-derived squalane to hydrate and protect the skin. I was also excited to see one of myfavourite hair masksincluded; the moisturising hair mask from Faith in Nature can help increase shine, and rinses away quickly without leaving a heavy coating.It’s a shame that …there’s no makeup included, and I’m also not sold on adding health supplements to a beauty Advent calendar, even if biotin and collagen are fairly common supplements. Also, unlike previous Holland & Barrett calendars, not all the products inside are vegan – some contain beeswax, lanolin, and bovine collagen.Claimed overall value:more than £266Number of products:18 full-size, 10 miniCalendar shell:recyclableStandout products:Dr Organic Probiotic cream cleanser, Dr Organic Vitamin E Super hydrating cream, Cetaphil Gentle Exfoliating SA cleanser, Cetaphil SA Exfoliating lotion, UpCircle Brightening eye cream, Weleda Skin Food body lotion, Faith in Nature Shea & Argan hair mask, Hairburst Longer Stronger shampoo, Hairburst Longer Stronger conditionerHolland & BarrettBeauty Advent calendar£60£60 at Holland & BarrettWhat we loveIncludes top-rated, budget-friendly productsWhat we don’t loveNo makeupBest beauty Advent calendar for teens and tweens:W7 Beauty Blast Advent calendarW7Beauty Blast Advent calendarfrom£21.99£22 at W7£21.99 at AmazonWhat we loveAffordable; all the skincare and makeup basicsWhat we don’t loveMostly minis; no luxury touchesView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£22 at W7£21.99 at AmazonStatus:availableNot all beauty Advent calendars require you to take out a loan; this W7 one costs less than the average takeaway and contains 24 makeup and beauty products. Last year’s W7 calendar was brilliant, and this year’s is even better suited to beautynewcomers.Why we love itStarting with skincare, this calendar contains a gentle cleanser, hydrating toner, moisturiser, lip mask and bronzing drops. Makeup-wise, there are two primers, plus a bronzer, blush, highlight and setting powder. For eyes and lips, there are two lip glosses, a lipstick and two lip liners, as well as shiny and matt eyeshadows and an eyeliner. It’s a good starter kit for tweens and teens dipping their toes into the beauty world, or anyone starting to build a beauty routine without spending a fortune.And, while the packaging isn’t high-end, the lip liners, H2O hydrating powder and setting spray are particularly good. The bronzing drops are also a bit of fun – either used alone as a liquid bronzer or mixed with moisturiser for a healthy glow. The full-size lip mask can be used overnight to hydrate lips.It’s a shame that …most of its contents are minis and all of the product packaging feels plasticky and flimsy. That’s what you’d expect for a calendar at this price, but don’t expect a luxury finish here.Claimed overall value:not statedNumber of products:6 full-size, 3 accessories, 15 miniCalendar shell:recyclableStandout products:W7 Double Draw lip pencils, H2O hydrating powder, W7 Golden Glow Drops, Sugar Cookie overnight lip maskW7Beauty Blast Advent calendarfrom£21.99£22 at W7£21.99 at AmazonWhat we loveAffordable; all the skincare and makeup basicsWhat we don’t loveMostly minis; no luxury touchesThe best of the restView image in fullscreen‘Will fit easily into most beauty routines’: the No7 25 Days of Beauty Advent calendar.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianNo7 25 Days of Beauty Advent calendarNo725 Days of Beauty Advent calendar£55£55 at BootsWhat we loveFull-size makeup; broad skincare rangeWhat we don’t loveMainly mini skincareView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£55 at BootsBest for:breaking a beauty rut rather than the bankStatus:availableIf you want to switch things up in your beauty routine, this great-value calendar is a safe bet. It feels like the grownup equivalent of the W7 calendar above; it’s more luxurious, with a larger proportion of skincare, including products with retinoids and exfoliating ingredients.All the full-size products are makeup, aside from one lip balm. These include a cool-toned light brown matt lipstick and liner, a lip oil with a punchy fruity taste, a pink liquid blush, an eyeliner pencil and a black tubing mascara. All of this is simple to use, wearable and will fit easily into most beauty routines.The calendar includes skincare from several No7 ranges, including Radiance+ and Future Renew. There are serums, aneye cream, day and night creams, cleansers and a toner. These are all minis, but this does allow you to sample a range of products before deciding whether to buy full-size versions. There’s also a £5 voucher for selected No7 Future Renew products.It didn’t make the final cut because …while the calendar has a diverse range of things to try, it’s limited to No7, so there isn’t as much choice as other calendars. Also, it’s mostly skincare, so it may be less appealing if you already have a routine you’re happy with. None of the skincare products is full-size, either, except the lip balm.Claimed overall value:£248.93;number of products:24, including 8 full-size, plus a £5 voucher;calendar shell:recyclable;standout products:No7 Pro Artist Luxe liquid blush, Pro Artist lip shine oil, Pro Artist That’s a Wrap tubing mascara, No7 Future Renew Damage Reversal body serum, No7 Future Renew SPF40 day cream, No7 Radiance+ Vitamin C Glow tonerNo725 Days of Beauty Advent calendar£55£55 at BootsWhat we loveFull-size makeup; broad skincare rangeWhat we don’t loveMainly mini skincareLiz Earle 12 Days of Beauty Advent calendarLiz Earle12 Days of Beauty Advent calendarfrom£79£79 at Liz Earle£79 at LookfantasticWhat we loveCruelty-free; luxury skincare; generous ‘minis’What we don’t loveFragranced; only 12 daysView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£79 at Liz Earle£79 at LookfantasticBest for: cruelty-free skincareStatus:availableLiz Earle is known for affordable luxury,and this 12-day calendar brings together a selection of its skincare and body care, from facial toners to rich creams. Its presentation box is recyclable; I found everything inside useful; and the selection isn’t overwhelming. It’s also Leaping Bunny certified.Why we love itIt wouldn’t be a Liz Earle Advent calendar if it didn’t include the Cleanse & Polish hot cloth cleanser. This is massaged on to dry skin, then gently “polished” off using a warm, damp washcloth (also included). The warmth makes the cleansing ritual feel spa-like.I’ve used this cleanser many times and always find the process enjoyable and oddly meditative. Add the large 75ml Superskin moisturiser, and you’ve already got the foundations of a good routine.Unlike in larger calendars, the “mini” products don’t feel like an afterthought. The Smooth & Glow exfoliating tonic, Instant Boost Skin tonic and Eyebright soothing lotion all come in matching 50ml bottles, which are larger and more high-end-looking than typical minis. The full-size body wash, body cream and hand cream come in a limited-edition fragrance, Mandarin & Nutmeg, which smells clean and uplifting, with a touch of festive warmth.It didn’t make the cut because …much of the skincare here is fragranced, and there’s only 12 days’ worth, rather than 24. A24-day calendaris available, but it’s more than twice the price, and its vast range of skincare could easily feel overwhelming.Claimed overall value:£203.50;number of products:3 full-size, 1 supersize, 8 mini;calendar shell:recyclable;standout products:Cleanse & Polish hot cloth cleanser, Skin Repair hydrating night cream, Mandarin & Nutmeg body cream, Smooth & Glow exfoliating tonic, Eyebright soothing eye lotionLiz Earle12 Days of Beauty Advent calendarfrom£79£79 at Liz Earle£79 at LookfantasticWhat we loveCruelty-free; luxury skincare; generous ‘minis’What we don’t loveFragranced; only 12 daysNext 25 Days of Beauty Advent calendarNext25 Days of Beauty Advent calendar£150£150 at NextWhat we loveGreat skincare and accessoriesWhat we don’t loveThe minimal makeup included is quite boldView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£150 at NextBest for:tools and accessoriesStatus:availableNext has partnered with the charity Future Dreams this year, with £10 from each calendar sold going to fund its specialist support centre for people with breast cancer and their families. The calendar is also one of the few I’ve encountered that includes an LED tool, and I’m a sucker for a bit of beauty tech.I don’t usually recommend wand-like LED tools that concentrate the light on small areas; fullLED face masksare much easier to use. That said, the BeautyPro anti-ageing LED wand could be worth it for those wanting to dip their toes into LED. You’ll also find other handy extras inside, like a Flat Lay Co storage pouch that clips on to your keys and a Neom candle with lavender, chamomile and patchouli to help you drift off to sleep.For skincare, the calendar packs in a full-size Caudalie anti-ageing cream and a Clinique All About Eyes serum, which is infused with caffeine and has a soothing roller for cooling the undereyes. There’s also a mini Elemis cleansing balm, which is my go-to first cleanse in the evening; follow it up with the Liz Earle Cleanse & Polish hot cloth cleanser to get a dreamy spa-like cleanse.It didn’t make the final cut because …it’s a little thin on the ground with makeup and nail care. Also, the makeup is quite bold; the Laura Mercier pink eyeshadow stick would be more useful in a neutral shade and, even though they’re great for Christmas, the glittery Natasha Denona eyeshadows won’t be right for everyone. Similarly, the perfumes are all minis apart from the Victoria’s Secret vanilla body mist, which leans a little young.Claimed overall value:more than £576;number of products:10 full-size, 19 mini;calendar shell:recyclable;standout products:BeautyPro ALED 5-in-1 anti-ageing wand, Flat Lay Co keyring pouch, NEOM Perfect Night’s Sleep travel candle, Caudalie Resveratrol-Lift Firming Cashmere cream, Liz Earle Cleanse & Polish Hot Cloth cleanser, Elemis Pro-Collagen Rose cleansing balm, Clinique All About Eyes Serum De-Puffing Eye MassageNext25 Days of Beauty Advent calendar£150£150 at NextWhat we loveGreat skincare and accessoriesWhat we don’t loveThe minimal makeup included is quite boldLiberty men’s Advent calendarLibertyMen’s Advent calendar£270£270 at LibertyWhat we loveUseful products that add a little luxuryWhat we don’t loveWorse value than the main beauty Advent calendarView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£270 at LibertyBest for:menStatus:availableIf there’s one way to bring a man around to the idea of a beauty Advent calendar, it’s buying him a great one. This is beautifully designed and filled with genuinely useful, high-end but not fussy skin, hair and body care. And, like the main Liberty calendar featured above, it’s got a wide range of fragrances inside from the likes of Loewe, D’Orsay and Granado.The highlights inside include the Paula’s Choice ectoin, which I often use at night for intensive barrier support, since it’s fast-absorbing and doesn’t upset my sensitive skin. There’s also the Commune Seymour body cream, which uses natural oils and botanical fragrance to nourish the skin – I’m also a fan of the hand cream, as the smell is divine and the recyclable aluminium packaging is luxurious. You’ll also find upgrades of men’s daily essentials, such as Ortigia shaving gel and a Charlotte Mensah hair pomade.Topping things off, you’ve got some treats to help you unwind, such as the Verden sleep mist, Earl of East bath salts and a warming muscle gel from Aromatherapy Associates.It didn’t make the final cut because …despite the similar prices, its value is significantly lower than the main Liberty calendar. There are fewer items, fewer of which are full-size, and you also lose out on the drawstring bag made from one of Liberty’s famous prints … I think the men at least deserve a drawstring bag, don’t you?Claimed overall value:£885;number of products:14 full-size, 11 mini;calendar shell:recyclable;standout products:Paula’s Choice 7% Ectoin + Hyaluronic Acid Milky Hydrating Serum, Commune Seymour body cream, Ortigia shave gel, Charlotte Mensah Manketti Oil hair pomade, Verden Nocturne sleep mist, Earl of East bath salts, Aromatherapy Associates Warming De-Stress muscle gel, Loewe Esencia pour Homme eau de parfum, D’Orsay Vanilla Affair extrait de parfum, Granado Boemia perfumeLibertyMen’s Advent calendar£270£270 at LibertyWhat we loveUseful products that add a little luxuryWhat we don’t loveWorse value than the main beauty Advent calendarJurlique Beauty Advent calendarJurliqueBeauty Advent calendar£110£110 at JurliqueWhat we loveB Corp-certified botanical beauty; reusable boxWhat we don’t loveNearly all minis; face oils won’t suit everyoneView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£110 at JurliqueBest for: B Corp-certified botanical beautyStatus:availableAustralian B Corp-certified skincare brand Jurlique makes lovely botanical skincare. This year’s 24-day calendar features a selection of its bestsellers, many of which contain ingredients grown on the brand’s farm in Australia. So, if you’re ethically conscious and a fan of botanical beauty, this might fit the bill.There’s a blend of essential oils, including mandarin, ylang ylang and geranium, designed for use in a diffuser for some calm during the Christmas period. You’ll also find products from the brand’s rose collection, including a face cream, hand cream, face mist, body lotion and shower gel, as well as its rose face oil. There are also products from its calendula range, along with serums and a hydrating face mask and cleanser.Like last year’s calendar, this comes in a gorgeous reusable box that’s just big enough to store trinkets without taking up too much space; I’m still using my 2025 calendar to store extra makeup.It didn’t make the final cut because …there’s only one full-size product, which feels a little disappointing. The essential oil needs adiffuser, so it’s not as versatile or useful as a full-size skincare product. The four face oils won’t suit everyone, and there are two identical mini rose hand creams. I’d prefer 24 different products rather than repeats. It’s also skincare-only, so makeup fans should look elsewhere.Claimed overall value:£280;number of products:1 full-size, 23 mini;calendar shell:recyclable inserts with reusable box;standout products:Radiant Skin foaming cleanser, Purely Age-Defying Firming face oil, Nutri-Define eye balm, Rare Rose face oil, Rose body lotionJurliqueBeauty Advent calendar£110£110 at JurliqueWhat we loveB Corp-certified botanical beauty; reusable boxWhat we don’t loveNearly all minis; face oils won’t suit everyoneWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenHigh-end beauty Advent calendars tend to have more luxury and full-size products than more affordable versions.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianAre beauty Advent calendars worth it?This depends entirely on your beauty routine and how much you enjoy experimenting with new products. If you like high-end, luxury beauty, then beauty Advent calendars can be a great way to get expensive products bundled together for a lower cost. It’s also an opportunity to try luxe brands without committing to buying full-size products.The first risk is you end up spending a lot of money on products you won’t use. To avoid this, think about the elements of your beauty routine that you like to switch up. If there’s anything you’re staunchly loyal to, for example your skincare, think twice before buying a skincare Advent calendar.There’s also the environmental impact of any products you don’t use, so it’s worth considering either donating them unopened to charity or giving them to any other beauty lovers in your circle.How much should you expect to spend?There is a huge range of beauty Advent calendars available, from below £20 to over £500. That chasmic difference in cost makes a big difference to the products inside. Entry-level calendars offer mostly mini-size products from high-street beauty brands. Some more affordable calendars also offer 12 doors, for the 12 days of Christmas, rather than 24.With the £20-£60 bracket covered by budget brands, the mid-range contenders sit somewhere between £61 and £150. These calendars tend to offer more full-size products than lower-priced calendars from mid-range brands. Unless you’re a big fan of one particular brand, the best way to try lots of new skincare, makeup and hair care is to choose a calendar from a beauty retailer such as Anthropologie, which offers curated calendars with a selection of brands. Most beauty fans will find something suitable in this price bracket.Spend between £151 and £250, and you can expect to find calendars filled with mainly full-size products, whether from mid-range or luxury brands or higher-end beauty retailers such asCult BeautyandSpace NK.If you’re hoping for full-fat luxury at full-fat prices, you can spend over £250 and grab a calendar from super-high-end retailers such asSelfridgesandLiberty, or premium brands such asDiptyque. These tend to contain higher-value products, with some brands claiming a total value of more than £1,000. Just be sure to triple-check the contents all appeal to you before spending this much.Why are beauty Advent calendars released so early?Unlike edible Advent calendars, which can be packed up and filled with the same chocolates year after year, beauty Advent calendars take months of planning and coordination. As you’re opening the 2026 calendar, most brands will already be deep in planning what to include in 2027.By opening waiting lists early, brands are able to better plan the number of calendars they need to make, and ensure they have enough time to send them out before 1 December.In the US? title: The dreadful decline of hosting at home: ‘I feel shame any time a friend comes over’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: It used to be quite normal to pop next door for a coffee or invite friends over for dinner. But not any more. What’s behind this change – and just how damaging is it?
Author: Leah Harper
Headline: It used to be quite normal to pop next door for a coffee or invite friends over for dinner. But not any more. What’s behind this change – and just how damaging is it?
Content: Cheers! Hosting dinner parties was popular in the 1970s.Photograph: ClassicStock/AlamyView image in fullscreenCheers! Hosting dinner parties was popular in the 1970s.Photograph: ClassicStock/AlamyLife and styleThe dreadful decline of hosting at home: ‘I feel shame any time a friend comes over’It used to be quite normal to pop next door for a coffee or invite friends over for dinner. But not any more. What’s behind this change – and just how damaging is it?Leah HarperThu 8 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 13.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Ireally loved hosting at home years ago, before I had kids, when my house wasn’t filled with toys and I had lots of time to plan and shop,” says Rehanna, 41, from Birmingham. Now, if she’s catching up with friends, she would rather go out. “I can’t host and cook at the same time, so if I have people over it will usually be a cold buffet I have made earlier. There are so many really nice restaurants where I live that I’d prefer to go out and try something new than make an old favourite at home.”Personally, I’d never say no to a cold buffet – but Rehanna’s story is not unusual. In the US, the number of people who regularly host friends or family fell from 42% in 1975 to 12% in 2026 –a 70% drop over the last 50 years. In the UK, the numbers are not much better: last year, a poll of 2,000 adults found that more thanfour in 10 British people avoid hosting at homedue to the clean-up it requires. And while chef Nigella Lawson is back on TV screens demonstrating her culinary prowess on The Great British Bake Off, it wasn’t long ago that the self-proclaimed domestic goddess revealed even she had“got out of the habit” of hosting formal dinner parties.But why have we become so unwilling to invite others into our homes – and what do we lose by only catching up in communal “third spaces”?“When you host, quite often it feels like you’re just a spectator to your friends’ evening,” says Simon, 37, from Glasgow. In the past, he’s found that, as host, he spends so much time making sure his guests are catered for that it can be difficult to connect with them on anything other than a superficial level. “You’re not fully present because you’re either trying to anticipate their next needs or you’re not even in the same room – you’re ferrying back and forth to the fridge and you just can’t get deep in the conversation. It can feel like everybody else has more of a bond at that time, because the host is just a wee bit separate.”We haven’t always felt this way about having people over. In fact, anthropologistRobin Dunbar, best known for “Dunbar’s number” – a theory that suggests humans can only really maintain about 150 stable social connections at once – believes we would still rather entertain at home given the choice, but circumstances often conspire against it. “One reason is that our social networks may have become more scattered as cities have got larger,” he says. “If we live in smaller villages and towns, it is easy to visit for casual get-togethers. There is a thing called the 30-minute rule: if someone lives more than 30 minutes away, we pretty much stop seeing them regularly. The time/effort required becomes too great.”View image in fullscreenToo much effort?Photograph: George Marks/Getty ImagesIt’s an idea echoed byKamalyn Kaur, apsychotherapistand member of the British Association for Counselling and Psychotherapy. “I’m an 80s child and when I was younger, people used to pop over to my mum and dad’s house – just for half an hour, for a cup of tea,” she says. By the time she reached her early 20s, she noticed guests had started phoning beforehand, and home visits became more of a pre-arranged event, “which is good because you’re being respectful of someone’s time and energy and space, but the downside is that people don’t have that spontaneous checking in, everything has to require a lot of planning”.Even for those who have experienced the fun of a successful soiree, it can still feel intimidating rather than inspirational. “My boomer mother was an incredible entertainer and was always having these dramatically complicated parties,” says Caz (not her real name), who spent her childhood on the fringes of these gatherings, peeking in through the door. “Living up to that feels impossible. But also, she claimed she enjoyed hosting very much, but she was always so stressed out beforehand and she’d yell at all of us all the time, and I don’t want to do that.”There is also the expense: while most of us usually spend far less on a home-cooked meal than we might at a restaurant, it’s a different story when catering for a crowd. In 2023,Retail Times reportedon data from restaurant booking site The Fork that found cooking a three-course dinner at home for a group of six typically cost the host more than £82, compared with the average cost per head at a restaurant of just over £30.In May this year, the Spectator claimed the dinner party was also being killed off “by the modern curse of the ‘dietary requirement’”; bothfood intolerancesand voluntary restrictions appear to have increased over the past 20 years, and so cooking for others might certainly feel like more of a challenge.Expectations can often feel heightened when hosting, not just when it comes to the food, but also the home environment. I’d venture that the rise oftablescapinghas a lot to answer for – and a quick browse of Instagram reels throws up numerous other “requirements” for hosting success: elaborately garnished cocktails, trendy taper candles, handwritten menu cards, a huge dining table. Whereas hosts might once have simply given surfaces a quick wipe and emptied the bins, there are now tips for curating the perfect playlist, and rules for creating an aesthetically pleasing “theme”.View image in fullscreenSocial media has fuelled higher expectations.Photograph: Maskot/Getty Images“I think there’s a lot of pressure on people to have ‘presentable’ homes,” says Kaur. “On social media, you see everyone with these amazing mansion-style houses. It creates unrealistic expectations about how a home should look. People may start worrying about their home not meeting that standard.”Caz has two children under the age of 10 and says her house is therefore always “a complete nightmare zone”. Of course, her friends don’t actually care about the mess. “I know this deep in my heart,” she admits, “but it doesn’t stop me from feeling shame every time anyone comes over.”Sydney-based chefTherese Lumalso cites TV cooking shows as one of the reasons many may feel a dinner party has to be a perfectly curated five-course production. “Add small apartments, busy weeks and the cost of feeding a crowd, and going out starts to feel easier,” she says. “Hosting has started to feel like work.”Derek Thompson, who delved into the US data forthe Atlantic, raises the idea that more intensive parenting styles could be partly to blame for the decline in hosting at home. “Americans used to have many kids whom they cared for sparsely,” he suggests. “Now they have fewer children, to whom they devote every minute of their life.”Dunbar broadly agrees: “Until the 1960s, things like homework from school was limited, and children kind of looked after themselves – playing in the street together and turning up only when they needed to get fed. Now the little darlings are under your feet until they go away to university.” In addition, he notes that there is now an “endless stream” of extracurricular clubs and activities that children are encouraged to take part in, which means “families have to be free to do a lot of ferrying”.What’s more, since the pandemic and the rise in working from home, many people have come to think of their living space differently. Socialising at home might feel more like hosting dinner in the office. As Kaur puts it: “You want a change, otherwise it doesn’t feel like a break. It’s harder to mentally switch off.” But even before Covid, the proliferation of all thingshygge–the Danish concept centred on cosiness– encouraged much of the western world to think of home as somewhere to retreat and relax, rather than invite others in. “Your home is your cosy place, so socialising there can feel like a disruption of your private space,” says Kaur.Thompson also touches on the idea that it’s now “too much fun to be home alone”. Whereas we might once have invited friends over to stave off boredom – and faced social pressure to attend such events, even if we did not much care for the hosts – today we are “cocooned within personalised entertainment fortresses”. This does not mean we no longer benefit from social connection, though: the World Health Organization reports thatisolation and loneliness are now widespread, which in turn can have a significant impact on physical and mental health – even if we are not “bored” as such.At the opposite end of the spectrum, there’s the problem of, to put it bluntly, guests outstaying their welcome. “My wife and I do enjoy hosting under very controlled circumstances,” says Simon. “We tend to have people over for drinks before going out for dinner because it sets an end time. Hosting at home can mean you lose control of when the night ends – if someone wants to sit there drinking whisky until 3am, you kind of feel compelled to join them.” There’s clearly a reason why the phrase “Please leave by 9pm” has become something ofa recurring motifon interior decor accessories in recent years.Kaur acknowledges that, as host, it can be difficult to do anything other than wait for the evening to come to a natural end. “I’m more than happy to go to bed at half eight but, for my friends, this might be when they’re all coming to life,” she says. “It can feel really suffocating to have people in your space and not be able to ask them to leave.”Should we simply accept that it’s become far easier, less stressful and sometimes less expensive to go out? “There’s a vulnerability to letting someone see you in your own home, and by not hosting at home we reveal less of ourselves to others, which can then affect the depth of our friendship,” Kaur warns. There is certainly something more intimate about catching up with a friend on their sofa – a sneak peek behind the scenes of their life that you’d struggle to gain in a more neutral space.Kaur hosts regularly, but says that’s largely because she has known her closest friends for more than 20 years. “We’ve all grown up together; we’ve seen each other at our best and our worst,” she says. “I’ve been to my friend’s home when the floor is covered with a hundred Lego pieces because their kids have been playing with it. And my friend is like: ‘Yeah, you’re just going to have to walk through that.’” But, for some, she recognises that hosting, whether it is a well-planned evening or spontaneous get-together, may remain a source of anxiety. “I would always encourage people to do whatever suits their own energy levels and mental health,” she says. “Otherwise it becomes counter-productive.”Lum, meanwhile, believes that the effort that goes into hosting is precisely what makes it so worthwhile. “Because it’s one of the most generous things you can do, it builds a kind of connection that’s hard to get anywhere else,” she says. “In my family, food was always how we showed love, and a shared table still feels that way to me.”It’s also worth bearing in mind that going out, especially for dinner or drinks, will usually mean following the venue’s rules. “At home nobody rushes you off the table, and the conversation goes wherever it wants,” says Lum. “My best nights have nearly always happened around someone’s kitchen table. Guests don’t remember whether the napkins matched; they remember feeling looked after.”Explore more on these topicsLife and styleFoodHomesFamilyFriendshipfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Cold comforts: the most satisfying autumn whites | Wine | The Guardian
description: As summer fades and our social and dining habits adapt to the cooling weather, so, too, should the white wine we drink. Here are some options best-suited to the season
Author: Mina Holland
Headline: As summer fades and our social and dining habits adapt to the cooling weather, so, too, should the white wine we drink. Here are some options best-suited to the season
Content: Want ripeness, body and freshness?  Then you can’t go far wrong with the Atlantic-influenced wines of Galicia.Photograph: graficart.net/AlamyView image in fullscreenWant ripeness, body and freshness?  Then you can’t go far wrong with the Atlantic-influenced wines of Galicia.Photograph: graficart.net/AlamyGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.WineCold comforts: the most satisfying autumn whitesAs summer fades and our social and dining habits adapt to the cooling weather, so, too, should the white wine we drink. Here are some options best-suited to the seasonMina HollandThu 8 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe wine world is full of clubs, and I’m a member of the Just-Drink-What-You-Bloody-Like club, which makes even the thought of white wines for autumn and winter feel uncomfortably prescriptive. But, for me, as the nights draw in, there’s less standing, more sitting; less chugging, more swirling; fewer sprightly aperitifs, more wine with seasonal food that demands a little more body and complexity. After months of saying yes to rosé, I’m choosing wine with more intention – it’s time to hunker down.I’m looking for whites that are like a good cardigan, at once coddling and breathable. I want ripeness, bodyandfreshness, and the Atlantic-influenced wines of Galicia in northern Spain – a place that’s no stranger to wind and rain – deliver. Expressive, with a saline edge, albariño from the Rías Baixas appellation has become ubiquitous in supermarkets and rarely disappoints (tryAldi’s Specially Selected oneat £8.99), neither does the fuller-bodied godello from nearby Valdeorras (the Wine Society’s Exhibition rangeoffers a good one for £14.95), while the blend of both those grapes and other local varieties from Galicia’s Ribeiro DO in today’s pick is a cool-climate humdinger for the colder months.In October, soft greens and nightshades are out, roots and brassicas are in, and barbecues have given way to roasts; the season’s food slows us down. At my house, spiced stews and curries are increasingly on the menu, which invite aromatic central European wines such as a zippy, limey Mosel riesling. But these heartier meals also welcome something waxier, richer, warmer, such as the South African chenin blanc in my pick. Skin-contact whites, too, hold their own with these more robust flavours. Look out for wines made with Georgian grapes rkatsiteli or kisi, or those from Italy’s Friuli region. These are not budget wines, but if I drink less in the cooler months (which I do, with the obvious exception of December), that seems a good reason to spend a bit more per bottle.There is also a small but dependable family of wines that doesn’t care about the season, and which I’ll happily drink year-round, no matter the food or mood. Gavi is often considered a summery Italian white, but the Le Marne in today’s pick is aged on the lees (the dead yeast cells left over after fermentation) for three to four months, resulting in a rounded, biscuity wine I will never tire of. But, as I said, it’s personal; if none of these appeal, just drink what you bloody like.Five whites for the cooler monthsTesco Finest Steep Slopes Mosel Riesling £8, 11%. Hits the spot when paired with a spicy takeaway and, at this price, makes for a budget-friendly Friday night in.Pazo do Mar Blanco Ribeiro 2025£9.95 The Wine Society, 13%. Five native grapes work in harmony to make this food-friendly wine that sings of cool-climate Galicia.Gavi Marne BiancoLe Marne di Carraro Federica2023£19 Sip Wines, 13.5%. I had this at my November wedding nine years ago, and love it more now than ever. Golden, savoury and complex.David & Nadia Chenin Blanc Swartland 2024£29.58 Justerini & Brooks, 12.5%. Eight vineyards, mixed soils, old oak barrels and concrete vats produce this precise, generous Swartland chenin; find me sipping it fireside.Pheasant’s Tears Rkatsiteli Bakurtsikhe 2024£21 Vinum, 13%. A light amber beauty that brings apricotty, honeyed sunshine to the dimmest of autumn evenings.Explore more on these topicsWineFoodSpanish food and drinkItalian food and drinkEastern European food and drinkSouth African food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: SOS meals – the food to cook for friends that shows you care | Food | The Guardian
description: After the death of my beloved dog, I’m thinking a lot about the role food plays in big life events – be they happy or sad
Author: Felicity Cloake
Headline: After the death of my beloved dog, I’m thinking a lot about the role food plays in big life events – be they happy or sad
