Content: Made with love … Anna Jones’s chocolate chip cookie power bites lie somewhere between a flapjack and cookie dough.Photograph: Issy Croker/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMade with love … Anna Jones’s chocolate chip cookie power bites lie somewhere between a flapjack and cookie dough.Photograph: Issy Croker/The GuardianFeastFoodSOS meals – the food to cook for friends that shows you careAfter the death of my beloved dog, I’m thinking a lot about the role food plays in all of life’s big events – be they happy or sadSign up here for our weekly food newsletter, FeastFelicity CloakeThu 8 Oct 2026 07.40 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 07.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIlost mybeloved cairn terrier Wilfa couple of weeks ago, and when I say lost, sadly, I don’t mean I mislaid him yet again on Hampstead Heath. Rather, after 13 and a half years of (mostly) civil disobedience, we had to make the tough but ultimately kind decision to say a final goodbye. Since then, I have been bombarded with kindness. Friends and family have rallied round to take me out for breakfast, lunch, dinner and coffee, clearly worried that the bereavement might affect my appetite – well, apart from the one who responded by having a baby a week early, and who now requires me to provide for her.It got me thinking about the part food plays in big life events. We so often cook, or otherwise provide for people in the aftermath of such shocks, be they happy or sad, as a way both to offer practical help and to show them how much we love them. Such tokens of affection tend to fall into two camps. The first is high-energy food that can be easily eaten with one hand while the other is holding a baby or clutching a sodden handkerchief, or simply when you’re just too busy to sit down. Just this morning, I received a picture of the new mother tucking into my extremely wholesomefruit and nut-packed granolawith her daughter sleeping on her arm, but Melissa Hemsley’sfive-ingredient flapjacks(pictured top) would fall into this category, as would Meera Sodha’schaat masala popcornand Thomasina Miers’ dark chocolate and toasted walnutbanana bread. Like Anna Jones’schocolate chip cookie power bites, Hugh Fearnley-Whittingstall’sspiced nutsormy own kale chips, they’re full of good things, and tempting enough to compete with the less nutritious options that are so easy to reach for instead. (That said, no one should judge anyone for the choices they make at times of stress.)View image in fullscreenLoad up the portable containers … Felicity Cloake’s vegan ragù.Photograph: Robert Billington/The GuardianThe second consists of home-cooked meals that you hope will make them feel looked after, even when you can’t be there to do it yourself. I’ve already promised to make a batch ofmy massaman curryfor the new parents by special request, because I usually fall back on either myragù alla bolognese(vegan version here), orchickencacciatore. Bundle the clearly labelled plastic containers with a big bag of nice pasta, too, as well as a block of hard cheese, perhaps, and I figure the recipients are never more than 10 minutes from a good dinner – though, in this case, I’ll splash out on microwaveable sachets of rice instead. Go for a pie, however, and they don’t even have to cook any carbs to go with it. At this time of year, Nigel Slater’scauliflower cheesenumber would be delicious, as would Calum Franklin’skeema-spiced shepherd’s pieor Jeremy Lee’s classicchicken version. Thomasina’sricotta, courgette and spinach dumplings, meanwhile, come with their own tomato sauce, and freeze brilliantly, as would Blanche Vaughan’sLancashire hotpot.And, if in doubt, take round a roll or two of Tamal Ray’sfreezer cookie dough, so they’re always prepared for last-minute guests or late-night sugar crashes. After the past fortnight, I can confirm there’s very little to match the comfort of a nice cup of tea and a biscuit.My week in foodView image in fullscreen‘Perfumed with petals’ … Iranian black tea.Photograph: Jorge Fernández/LightRocket/Getty ImagesOn the subject of tea …|I found myself dogless but hungry in Henley-on-Thames on Saturday evening, after talking with wine writerOlly Smithabout our respective culinary-themed novels at the town’s literary festival (which runs until Sunday). Happy chance led me toBijan’s Kitchen, a Persian restaurant that served the most delicious and enormous lamb kebabs on naan, as well as thick, garlicky yoghurt with cucumber and mint, and olives covered in a rich paste of walnuts, pomegranate molasses and garlic, plus a lovely Iranian black tea perfumed with rose petals. Best of all (for me), it’s also dog-friendly – Wilf would have loved it.Apple turnover|A reminder, should you need it, that although the weather (at the time of writing) feels more like summer, British apple season begins to wind down towards the end of October, so if you value themore unusual varieties rarely found in supermarkets(I got some lovely Charles Ross and Blenheim Orange fruits on Sunday), now is a good time to stock up at the farmers’ market, farm shop or pick-your-own orchard. Dry the apples well, if necessary, and store them, preferably in a single layer, in a slatted crate, cardboard tray or on open shelves (air flow is vital) and keep them somewhere cool, dry and dark, where they should keep until Christmas. So long as you don’t eat them all first.Not worth dying for|The start ofCelebrity Traitorshas proved a welcome distraction for me – and, as usual, I found myself most interested in what the cast is actually eating during the dramatic daily breakfasts in the castle, and what they’re awkwardly picking at from the buffet later in the day.This articlesheds a little light on the on-set catering, and confirms that I would be a terrible contestant: there’s only so long I could put up with dry croissants and rationed wine before I confessed all just to get out of there.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFeastRecipes from all our star cooks, seasonal eating ideas and restaurant reviews. Get our best food writing every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFishy business|As a devotee of the much-maligned kipper (a cold-smoked herring), I was delighted to discover that Waitrose now does a hot-smoked version in place of the Scottish mackerel it’s removed from shelves in response to warnings of imminent population collapse in the north-east Atlantic Ocean. Herring numbers, which suffered from similar problems in the 1970s thanks to over-fishing, are now more robust in the North Sea – though check it’s been responsibly sourced, because numbers have dwindled farther west. Anything youcan do with smoked mackerel, you can do with herring, fromflaking it into potato saladsto whizzing it intopaté. Just ask any of our northern European neighbours.If you want to read the complete version of this newsletterplease subscribeto receive Feast in your inbox every Thursday.Explore more on these topicsFoodFeastnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Japan beer giants raided over suspicions they colluded to set the price of beverages | Japan | The Guardian
description: Investigators probe Asahi, Kirin, Suntory and Sapporo breweries – which together control more than 90% of Japan’s beer market
Author: Justin McCurry
Headline: Investigators probe Asahi, Kirin, Suntory and Sapporo breweries – which together control more than 90% of Japan’s beer market
Content: Officials from the Fair Trade Commission raided four major beer manufacturers in Japan over suspicions they colluded to hike beverage prices in a violation of anti-monopoly laws.Photograph: Yuichi Yamazaki/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenOfficials from the Fair Trade Commission raided four major beer manufacturers in Japan over suspicions they colluded to hike beverage prices in a violation of anti-monopoly laws.Photograph: Yuichi Yamazaki/AFP/Getty ImagesJapanJapan beer giants raided over suspicions they colluded to set the price of beveragesInvestigators probe Asahi, Kirin, Suntory and Sapporo breweries – which together control more than 90% of Japan’s beer marketJustin McCurryin TokyoWed 7 Oct 2026 23.54 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 10.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJapanese authorities have raided the country’s four biggest breweries over suspicions they colluded to set the price of beer and other beverages – a practice media reports said could have forced drinkers to pay over the odds.Officials from the Fair Trade Commission this week searched the offices of Asahi Breweries, Kirin Brewery, SuntoryBeerand Sapporo Breweries – which together control more than 90% of the domestic market. The quartet are suspected of violating the anti-monopoly law.The commission’s secretary general, Hiroo Iwanari, confirmed an investigation had begun, but declined to give details. The companies said they would cooperate with authorities.Alleged ice-cream cartel in Japan investigated as sweltering summer loomsRead moreThe commission is understood to have launched the investigation given the potential effect the alleged cartel has had on prices after wholesalers sell their products on to supermarkets,convenience stores, bars and restaurants, the Mainichi Shimbun said.Japanese media quoted sources as saying that sales managers and other executives from the breweries were suspected of meeting secretly over a prolonged period to coordinate on the timing and scale of retail price increases, which ranged from several yen to several dozen yen a time.Prices forbeerand a low-malt version calledhapposhuhave risen multiple times to reflect the rising cost of raw materials and logistics. The commission suspects the breweries bypassed proper pricing competition and collaborated to ensure they made a profit, the Mainichi said.Alcohol consumption in Japan has declined in recent decades as a result of depopulation and changes in drinking habits among younger people. But sales still reached ¥3.8tn ($24.3bn) in 2024, with beer accounting for 30% of the total, followed by happoshu and third-category beer, which contains little or no malt, with a combined 11.9%The four breweries have all raised their prices at the same time, most recently in April last year, citing the rising cost of materials and distribution. Prices also rose in October 2022 and October 2023.Shares in Asahi, Kirin, Suntory and Sapporo fell after Wednesday’s raids – the first investigation of its kind involving the food and beverage industry.Japanese media quoted sources as saying the commission had judged the case to be particularly serious given its potential impact on consumers, adding that the probe could result in a criminal complaint.The probe comes three months after the commissionraided six Japanese ice-cream makersover allegations of operating a cartel.Explore more on these topicsJapanBeerAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: A good friend brings her dogs when she stays with me. I kind of dread it. What can I do? | Australian lifestyle | The Guardian
description: People often forget social rules when dogs are involved, writes advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith. But you’ll have to say something if you want things to change
Author: Eleanor Gordon-Smith
Headline: People often forget social rules when dogs are involved, writes advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith. But you’ll have to say something if you want things to change
Content: ‘If your friend doesn’t even recognise her dogs as disruptive … then it might be time for the path of more friction,’ writes Eleanor Gordon-Smith.Painting: Two Venetian Ladies (c 1490) by Vittore Carpaccio.Illustration: Wikimedia CommonsView image in fullscreen‘If your friend doesn’t even recognise her dogs as disruptive … then it might be time for the path of more friction,’ writes Eleanor Gordon-Smith.Painting: Two Venetian Ladies (c 1490) by Vittore Carpaccio.Illustration: Wikimedia CommonsLeading questionsAustralian lifestyleA good friend brings her dogs when she stays with me. I kind of dread it. What can I do?People often forget social rules when dogs are involved, writes advice columnistEleanor Gordon-Smith.But you’ll have to say something if you want things to changeRead moreLeading questionsEleanor Gordon-SmithThu 8 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 18.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA good friend of mine stays with me regularly when she comes into town. She brings her husband and two dogs that don’t get along with my dog. They’ve “used the bathroom” in our house before. I try to be nice and help clean or pretend it doesn’t bother me so that they feel comfortable. But when she asks for a weekend to come back with everyone, I kind of dread it. I enjoy seeing her and she’s a great friend. I think our friendship would be better if she stayed somewhere else, but I would feel bad if she stayed in a hotel and I don’t think she’d visit as often. She cleans up after the dogs and whatnot, but Ilike my home to be my safe haven. This friend doesn’t handle confrontation well, but is understanding. What can I do to handle this?Eleanor says:It sounds as though you’re in the jam we all get into when we try to smooth things over: you can have the social ease of pretending something is fine; or the outcome from confessing it isn’t, but not both simultaneously.Obviously, your friend should have paid more mind to the possibility that you don’t see her dogs like she does.Using the bathroom in your house?The first rule of society is that other people’s preferences might differ from yours, and that matters for how you treat them and their stuff.I love seeing pooches in pubs. But not everyone, human or canine, understands the etiquette | Paul DaleyRead moreBut bring a dog into the equation and some otherwise intelligent people seem to forget that. They’ll trail behind on a leash giving the choreography of an apology while their dog puts paws on tables, bounds excitedly up to frightened children or treats furniture and food the way they’re allowed to at home. I’m saying this as a lifelong Dog Person, for what it’s worth: there is not a muddy paw print in the world I mind if it means I am playing with a dog. But we must admit, some dog people give the rest of us a bad name by assuming everyone sees their dog the way they do.Your friend should have seen through the polite illusion of you helping to clean up. But she hasn’t. And in fairness, acting fine with it is precisely designed to downplay the disruption.So do you want the appearance of frictionlessness, or do you want the outcome to change?Sometimes we try to have both with a white lie: “Our dog’s sick! Yours had better stay away.” But fibs unravel or invite troubleshooting: “Oh no! We’ll come a different weekend instead.”But ultimately, you can’t bear a burden invisibly and hope the person you’re concealing it from will realise, then take it away.To some extent, enduring annoying things for our friends is part of the deal. We collect them from the airport in traffic and travel for their weddings and help them move and watch their kids and change plans to help them. We do these things because it’s what it is to be a friend, and because they’d do them for us. But key to those things is the friend’s awareness and gratitude that you did something annoying for their sake. If your friend doesn’t even recognise her dogs as disruptive – if she treats this as par for the course – then it might be time for the path of more friction.What about something simple, halfway between the hotel and the full menagerie: “Would love to have you stay! I’m sorry to ask, but could this visit be without the dogs? Ours has been stressed out by having other animals in the house.”Your friend should have realised you might not be as fine with this as you’re acting. But when someone doesn’t notice something they should have, you can either point it out or decide to live with it.Ask Eleanor a questionShare your questionTell us hereYour responses, which can be anonymous, are secure as the form is encrypted and only the Guardian has access to your contributions. We will only use the data you provide us for the purpose of the feature and we will delete any personal data when we no longer require it for this purpose. For alternative ways to get in touch securely please see ourtips guide.NameWhat is your question for Eleanor?Email addressYour contact details are helpful so we can contact you for more information. They will only be seen by the Guardian.By submitting your response, you are agreeing to share your details with us for this feature.SubmitShow moreExplore more on these topicsAustralian lifestyleLeading questionsFriendshipPetsDogsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: UK motorists can now see live fuel prices on Google Maps | Petrol prices | The Guardian
description: Move expected to make pump pricing more transparent and encourage competition after diesel hits record £2 a litre
Author: Jillian Ambrose
Headline: Move expected to make pump pricing more transparent and encourage competition after diesel hits record £2 a litre
Content: Google will use data from the government’s Fuel Finder platform, which displays real-time prices at 99% of forecourts, to show Google Map users the cheapest in their local area.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAView image in fullscreenGoogle will use data from the government’s Fuel Finder platform, which displays real-time prices at 99% of forecourts, to show Google Map users the cheapest in their local area.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAPetrol pricesUK motorists can now see live fuel prices on Google MapsMove expected to make pump pricing more transparent and encourage competition after diesel hits record £2 a litreJillian AmbroseEnergy correspondentThu 8 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDrivers will be able to see live petrol prices onGoogle Mapsfor the first time from Thursday, in a move that will help motorists shop around for the cheapest fuel.Millions of motorists will be able to find the cheapest petrol and diesel prices by searching for a local forecourt in theGoogleapp, in what could prove to be “a major development” in making fuel prices more fair, according to campaigners.The tech company will use data from the government’sFuel Finderplatform, which displays real-time prices at 99% of forecourts, to show Google Map users the cheapest in their local area.It is expected to make forecourt pricing more transparent and encourage competition between fuel retailers, as millions face record-high road fuel costs due to the global squeeze on supplies prompted by the US-Israel war on Iran. Theaverage price of diesel in the UK recently hit a record £2 a litre, having risen by more than 40% since late February.Edmund King, the president of motoring group the AA, said: “Getting transparent fuel prices on to Google Maps is a massive step forward and means most drivers will have easy access to pump prices. Hopefully, this high-level pump-price transparency will also encourage more competitive prices from retailers.“More transparent prices should reduce the extent of rampant price-matching between fuel stations that is currently seen in many areas. Those competitive forecourts that break rank and offer lower fuel prices can be found if drivers look hard enough and will now stand out more.”The government’s Fuel Finder scheme was launched in February to help drivers get more competitive fuel prices after a recommendation by theCompetition and Markets Authority(CMA) in 2023. It is already available via apps including Waze, PetrolPrices, the AA, Confused.com and RAC Fuel Watch.Luke Bosdet, a spokesperson for the AA, said the Google launch would not necessarily dampen interest in the existing apps, such was “the demand for fuel price information”.However, the development could “signal trouble for the fuel trade by revealing the forecourt pricing tactics which keep local prices artificially high in their full horror, he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe CMA cautioned fuel retailers in August that many were still slow to pass on falls in wholesale diesel prices. These “passive pricing strategies” may have dented competition in the market and kept household costs higher than they needed to be, the watchdog said.Polly Billington, the minister for energy consumers, said: “Accessing the cheapest fuel should be simple, which is why it is a gamechanger for near real-time fuel prices to be shown on Google Maps for the first time in the UK, helping drivers find the best deal and save money at the pump.”Explore more on these topicsPetrol pricesGoogle MapsMotoringGoogleMapping technologiesCompetition and Markets AuthorityRegulatorsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Cancer is tripling and will keep increasing’: first African to lead global action against disease ready for battle | Global development | The Guardian
description: With cancer cases rising fastest in poorer countries, Zainab Shinkafi-Bagudu, president-elect of the Union for International Cancer Control, says Africa needs investment in research, diagnosis and prevention
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: With cancer cases rising fastest in poorer countries, Zainab Shinkafi-Bagudu, president-elect of the Union for International Cancer Control, says Africa needs investment in research, diagnosis and prevention
Content: Dr Zainab Shinkafi-Bagudu, a Nigerian paediatrician and president-elect of the Union for International Cancer Control, speaking at the recent World Cancer Congress.Photograph: UICCView image in fullscreenDr Zainab Shinkafi-Bagudu, a Nigerian paediatrician and president-elect of the Union for International Cancer Control, speaking at the recent World Cancer Congress.Photograph: UICCGlobal development‘Cancer is tripling and will keep increasing’: first African to lead global action against disease ready for battleWith cancer cases rising fastest in poorer countries, Zainab Shinkafi-Bagudu, president-elect of the Union for International Cancer Control, says Africa needs investment in research, diagnosis and preventionSupported byAbout this contentJohn MusenzeThu 8 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 05.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Dr Zainab Shinkafi-Bagudu last saw Gloria in Abuja, the young breast cancer patient was so ill that she was in hospital. The cancer had spread to her bones and lungs, and she was struggling with complications from the disease.Then, at a global conference oncancer thousands of miles away in Hong Kong last month, Bagudu saw her again. Gloria was walking with a stick because of the cancer in her hips, but she was attending sessions, speaking about her experience and advocating for other patients.“I saw her hopping on the corridor here. I was shocked,” Bagudu recalled.Bagudu was recounting this story on the sidelines of theWorld Cancer Congress in Hong Kong, attended by more than 2,000 people from 124 countries.A Nigerian paediatrician and advocate for cancer patients,Bagudu is president-elect of the Union for International Cancer Control (UICC)– the first African to lead the organisation. She takes up the role as cancer cases and deaths are projected to rise sharply, with the greatest increases expected in poorer countries.“The fact that it [the election of a black person] took so long is a reflection of the inadequacy of cancer care along the entire spectrum inAfricaand other low- and middle-income countries,” Bagudu says.Her election comes as countries across the global south face agrowing cancer burdenwhile also struggling with shortages of diagnostic equipment, medicines, radiotherapy services, trained specialists and financing.According to themost recent figuresfrom the World Health Organization’s International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), 20.6 million people were diagnosed with cancer and 9.8 million died from the disease in 2024.The IARC forecasts an annualrise in cases of 67% to more than 34m by 2050, while deaths could reach 17.5 million, an increase of 79%. Most of the additional deaths are expected to occur in low-income countries.According to Bagudu, the forecasts reinforce the need to reorientate global cancer policy towards countries where health systems are already under pressure.“Cancer is tripling and is going to keep on increasing, and the people affected by it most are those from the global south,” she says.Her ambition is to use the UICC, which represents more than 1,100 member organisations across more than 170 countries, as a bridge between countries with limited cancer services and the research, technology and treatments being developed elsewhere.“I have this opportunity to be able to bring forth a lot of the problems that the low- and middle-income countries are facing to the global north,” she says.But Bagudu says access to cancer care cannot be solved simply by building more specialist hospitals. “We keep building cancer centres and we keep seeing that it’s not enough,” she says.Cancer centres need to be supported by screening, early diagnosis, radiotherapy, medicines, trained health workers and systems that prevent families from being pushed into financial hardship by treatment, she says.“I’m trying to reduce financial toxicity for the woman in the village,” she says.That gap is already visible in basic cancer services. UICC chief executive Cary Adams told delegates that less than half of the world’s population has access to diagnostic services, while many patients in low- and middle-income countries pay for care out of pocket.Only 14% of the estimated73 million people who need palliative care each yearhave access to it, according to figures presented at the congress.View image in fullscreenZainab Shinkafi-Bagudu campaigned for Nigeria to adopt the single-dose HPV vaccine, which became part of Nigeria’s routine immunisation programme in 2023.Photograph: WHOBagudu’s own work inNigeriahas focused on some of these gaps. A paediatrician and founder of the Medicaid Cancer Foundation, she helped establish Kebbi state’s first cancer-control plan and registry during her time as first lady of the Nigerian state from 2015 to 2023.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every fortnightSign up toGlobal DispatchGet a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development teamEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHer foundation has also worked on cancer awareness and access to treatment for vulnerable patients. She has campaigned for cervical cancer prevention, including the introduction of thesingle-dose HPV vaccine into Nigeria’s routine immunisationprogramme in 2023.In 2024, she became senior adviser to Nigeria’s coordinating minister of health and social welfare with a brief that included women’s health and cancer advocacy. Bagudu now wants to take some of those lessons to the international level, including pushing for new approaches to cancer financing.She says cancer hasnever received the kind of global treatment financingmechanism that HIV, tuberculosis and malaria have benefited from. “Cancer has never directly been a beneficiary of global funding for treatment,” she says.She will support efforts to develop a global cancer financing platform modelled partly on theGlobal Fund to Fight Aids, Tuberculosis and Malaria, to mobilise resources from governments, donors and other sources to strengthen cancer prevention, diagnosis and treatment.The proposal comes as African governments face competing demands on health budgets, and international development financing is under pressure with significantcuts to foreign aid.Bagudu also wants greater attention paid to cancers that can be prevented or reduced through interventions already available. She plans to focus particularly on childhood cancers and liver cancer linked to hepatitis.That prevention must go alongside investment in diagnosis and treatment, particularly as cancer risk is shaped by factors including tobacco use, infections, alcohol, diet and obesity, she adds.She wants Africa to have a greater role in cancer research, rather than remaining primarily a recipient of discoveries and training from richer countries.“Research is a little bit more difficult because you have to have the human capacity, you have to have the interest and then you have to have the right environment,” she says.She points to emerging research centres in Nigeria, Rwanda and Kenya, as well as training programmes that bring African health workers to countries including China to develop skills in radiation therapy, cancer technology and other specialist areas.TheUICC has set targetsincluding reducing cancer mortality by 25% by 2035, reducing exposure to major cancer risk factors by 30% and ensuring that 60% of cancers are diagnosed at an early stage.Bagudu says the ultimate test of her presidency will be whether the global commitments made in conference rooms reach people far beyond them.Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentGlobal healthCancerHealthNigeriaAfricaHealth & wellbeingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Covid, Brexit and Liz Truss mini-budget led to lasting decline in mental health, study finds | Mental health | The Guardian
description: Researchers found five events, including Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, caused serious damage to mental wellbeing across UK
Author: Denis Campbell
Headline: Researchers found five events, including Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, caused serious damage to mental wellbeing across UK
Content: The study estimated that the first Covid lockdown led to an increase in mental ill-health that was equivalent to about 900,000 more people seeking a GP’s help for symptoms of depression.Photograph: Anna Gowthorpe/PAView image in fullscreenThe study estimated that the first Covid lockdown led to an increase in mental ill-health that was equivalent to about 900,000 more people seeking a GP’s help for symptoms of depression.Photograph: Anna Gowthorpe/PAMental healthCovid, Brexit and Liz Truss mini-budget led to lasting decline in mental health, study findsResearchers found five events, including Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, caused serious damage to mental wellbeing across UKDenis CampbellHealth policy editorThu 8 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBrexit, Liz Truss’s mini-budget and other “shocks” over the last 10 years have led to a serious and lasting deterioration in the UK population’s mental health,research has found.Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the first and second Covid lockdowns also triggered big rises in psychological distress, as measured by the number of people with depression and anxiety.The findings come as Prof Peter Fonagy prepares topublish the report of his long-waited government-commissioned inquiryinto the dramatic increases in recent years in diagnoses of mental illness, ADHD and autism. It will be published on Friday amid concern that those conditions help explain why a record 2.8 million Britons are too sick to work and almost 1 million young people aged 16 to 24 have become “Neets” – not in education, employment or training.Researchers led by Dr Annie Jeffery of University College London used data from the UK Household Longitudinal Study of 87,857 people aged 16 and older, which was collected every year between 2009 and 2024, to estimate the mental health impact of those five “systemic shocks”.“The past decade or so has been tumultuous, shaped by multiple overlapping shocks and ongoing uncertainty and instability that have impacted mental health in Britain,” said Jeffery.“We have shown that major government decisions and current global events can have substantial impacts on people’s mental health.”All five events caused immediate and serious damage to overall mental wellbeing across the UK. But the Brexit referendum in June 2016 and first pandemic lockdown in March 2020 caused the most damage,the research team found.Their analysis of the general health questionnaire’s GHQ-12 screening tool, which measures mental health, found that the UK’s vote to leave the European Union led to an increase in overall mental ill-health equivalent to about 120,000 more people overall seeking a GP’s help for depression.However, the first Covid lockdown, when the then prime minister, Boris Johnson, told people to “stay at home”, had a much larger impact, as measured by a much bigger rise in the UK’s GHQ-12 score. That jump equated to about 900,000 more people in total visiting a family doctor because they had developed symptoms of depression, Jeffery said.Russia’s offensive against Ukraine in February 2022 led to about 15,000 more Britons a month seeking a GP’s help for depression. AfterLiz Truss’s mini-budgetin September 2022, which proved disastrous for the UK economy, about 23,000 more people a month visited their family doctor’s surgery because they were depressed.“We observed increased psychological distress immediately after theBrexitreferendum and the first Covid-19 lockdown, with more insidious monthly increases in psychological distress after the Russian invasion of Ukraine and the 2022 mini-budget,” said Jeffrey.Andy Bell, the chief executive ofthe Centre for Mental Health thinktank, said: “There is clear evidence that Covid had a big impact on mental health. And it makes sense that the other ‘shocks’ listed here would do so, either directly, by making people feel less secure and less connected, or as after-effects, for example the cost of living crisis.“It’s also clear that rising distress in the population is not due to a single cause but the effect of all these things added together, made worse by years of austerity giving fewer buffers against ‘shocks’ like this.”Mental ill-health costs the UK £300bn a year,according to research by the thinktank.The UCL-led team’s findings have been published in the journal BMJ MentalHealth. They found that psychological distress had been increasing in the UK from 2009 to a degree that was clinically significant but accelerated from 2015 onwards. Even though the most recent of the five events occurred in 2022, the heightened distress in the population that followed them has persisted and not gone back to the much lower levels seen before 2016, they found.The total number of people in England in contact with NHS mental health services almost doubled from 2.64 million in 2016-17 to 4.13 million in 2024-25. The number of new referrals the NHS receives every month for mental ill-health has jumped from 360,000 in April 2022 to 530,000 in July 2026 – a jump of 47%.The huge rise in demand for care – driven by “shocks” causing anxiety, stress and worry – has left NHS services struggling “as more people than ever are reaching out for support”, said Tom Pollard, the mental health charity Mind’s director of policy, campaigns and public affairs.Explore more on these topicsMental healthHealthBrexitCoronavirusResearchnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s not about sex but empowerment’: why I picked a ‘naked’ frock as dress of the year | Culture | The Guardian
description: Sarah Burton’s sporty, daffodil mesh dress made me smile. But the reason I chose it for Fashion Museum Bath is because it tells a story of our times, when bodies are more political than ever
Author: Jess Cartner-Morley
Headline: Sarah Burton’s sporty, daffodil mesh dress made me smile. But the reason I chose it for Fashion Museum Bath is because it tells a story of our times, when bodies are more political than ever
Content: Telling a story … Fashion Museum Bath collections manager Elaine Uttley with Jess’s 2025 picks.Photograph: Peter J Stone/Fashion Museum BathView image in fullscreenTelling a story … Fashion Museum Bath collections manager Elaine Uttley with Jess’s 2025 picks.Photograph: Peter J Stone/Fashion Museum BathCulture‘It’s not about sex but empowerment’: why I picked a ‘naked’ frock as dress of the yearSarah Burton’s sporty, daffodil mesh dress made me smile. But the reason I chose it for Fashion Museum Bath is because it tells the story of our times, when bodies are more political than everJess Cartner-MorleyThu 8 Oct 2026 07.34 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 11.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne morning in February this year, I opened my laptop to find an email with an all-caps subject line: TOP SECRET. Being a fashion editor can be exciting but state secrets are not generally my beat, so I was intrigued. Sure enough, it was a thrill: an invitation from theFashion Museum Bathto choose their Dress of the Year for 2025.What an honour.Dress of the Yearbegan in 1963, the brainchild of the museum’s founder Doris Langley Moore, as a way of keeping a static collection perpetually current. Each year a fashion expert picks an outfit or outfits that capture the year just gone, and these become part of the permanent collection. There is a Mary Quant dress and a Katharine Hamnett slogan T-shirt, Ossie Clark chiffon and Ralph Lauren pinstripes. There is sublime beauty from the catwalks of Yves Saint Laurent and Chanel and John Galliano, and pieces of cultural history: McQueen’s bumsters, Jennifer Lopez’s internet-breaking green Versace Grammy dress, Dior’s “We Should All Be Feminists” slogan, Naomi Campbell’s pandemic hazmat suit, a Black Lives Matter T-shirt, and the dress worn by the Duchess of Sussex for her Oprah interview in 2021. “Dress” is interpreted loosely, in the sense of clothing rather than a frock: the lineup includes men’s suits. The Bath museum is currently mid-revamp, having closed its doors in 2022, with construction soon to start on a new museum set to open in the city’s old post office in 2030. Meanwhile the collection is stored in Wiltshire and can be seen online.The roll call of previous selectors is formidable. All the front row grand dames are present and correct. There are Vogue editors and Fleet Street’s most feared critics. Legendary stylists, including Grace Coddington and the late Isabella Blow, iconic retailer Joan Burstein and beloved London milliner Stephen Jones. The protocol of Dress of the Year is singular, in that the museum chooses the chooser, who then has complete freedom. The thought of my fashion verdict being preserved on a pedestal in a glass case forevermore, rather than printed on the proverbial fish and chip paper, was daunting. I experienced a swift emotional gear change from “chuffed” to “mildly panicked”. Plus the schedule – decision made in spring, selector announcement in summer, and DOTY revealed in October – gave me well over a month to make my choice, a timeframe which my daily-deadline-institutionalised brain found more overwhelming than liberating.View image in fullscreenDialogue between past and present … Sarah Burton’s acid yellow knitted mesh stitch dress for Givenchy.Photograph: INDIGITAL.TV/GivenchyBut I knew what I wanted to do. Most fashion journalists are current affairs journalists at heart, I think. Fashion expresses what it feels like to live in the world at a particular moment. An eye for fashion is essentially a curiosity about that, because the clothes we wear speak to what seems beautiful or important or valuable to us. This is where the juice is. So I wasn’t interested in making a best dressed list, or awarding a prize to the prettiest frock of the year. I wanted my choice to tell a story that would help future museum visitors understand the fashion and culture of 2025.The trouble is, once you decide you are choosing a piece of history rather than a dress, almost anything is eligible.Lauren Sánchez Bezos’ girls’ trip space suits?The Birkin that sold for $10.1m?Naomi Osaka walking on court in a kimono? A Labubu?Well, no. What I chose would form part of the permanent collection of one of Britain’s foremost fashion museums, so it needed design credentials of its own. In other words: I was looking for a great look that told a great story.2025 was the year of the “naked” dress. Dresses that made headlines did so by their virtual non-existence.Margot Robbie on the red carpet in strategically covered strings of crystals– not so much a dress as a very impressive necklace.Julia Fox in transparent mesh, her long dark hair trapped beneath it and preserving her modesty a la Botticelli’s Venus.Zoë Kravitz at the Oscarsin a black dress with a heart shaped window framing her bottom.View image in fullscreenSmart casual … Navy blue viscose jacket, trousers and waistcoat with suede leather sandals by Giorgio Armani.Photograph: Giorgio ArmaniFashion has always been partly about sex, but the naked dress is different. The naked dress is about the body, not the bedroom. Fox’s dress is not alluring: it is confronting, verging on repellent. At a moment when women’s bodily autonomy is once again fiercely contested in the US, and when cosmetic surgery and GLP-1 usage is physically transforming celebrities in front of our eyes, bodies are more political than ever.There is female empowerment here; there is also subordination to the male gaze. Both of those things are true at once. But I chose a naked dress bySarah Burton, who I have known and admired since she was Alexander McQueen’s right hand woman in the late 1990s. Burton is cherished in fashion, a woman who celebrates rather than objectifies. The daffodil coloured sporty mesh dress with visible retro underpinnings that I have chosen is from her first collection for Givenchy – a significant moment in itself, at a time when female creative directors are thin on the ground – and suggests a dialogue between fashion past and present that felt perfect for the assignment. Also, the kicker hem makes me smile, and the sunny shade will look terrific on a mannequin.Sarah Burton turns up the glamour volume at Givenchy in ParisRead moreAs for my menswear choice there was never any question. Thedeath of Giorgio Armaniin September 2025 was the loss of a giant not just of fashion, but of culture. Armani changed what it meant to look modern. He invented the smart-casual mode of menswear that dominates cities all over the world today. In so many ways, he was decades ahead of his time. He pioneered gender-fluid dressing, putting women in trouser suits and men in sensuously draped silks. He always believed that fashion should be about timeless style and clothes made to last, and deplored the churn of trends and fast-fashion. He stuck to this point of view through decades when it put him at odds with the rest of the industry; these days, everyone acknowledges that he was right all along. The ensemble I picked – soft shoulders, fluid fabrics, layering that looks effortless but immaculate – comes from the last collection Armani designed, shown on the catwalk at an emotional, elegiac show in Milan a few weeks after his death.Last year was the year of California wildfires and Zelenskyy’s Oval Office showdown; the Louvre heist and the first American pope; the rise of Reform and Euros triumph for the Lionesses; victory for Zohran Mamdani and the assassination of Charlie Kirk. But beneath the headlines, it was a year when we lived and loved, worried and argued. When we prayed for Oasis tickets and got obsessed with Celebrity Traitors. A Dress of the Year, to me, is not necessarily a look that everyone wore. It is about getting a bit further under the skin of things. (The DOTY for 1996 wasLee McQueen’s bumsters, which stands up well with hindsight, but definitely wasn’t a common sight on the street that year.) What happens in fashion captures the attitude of its time, the way fabric holds on to a lingering trace of perfume. Long after the headlines of 2025 have blurred together, I hope these clothes will retain something of how it felt to be there. That, in the end, was what I wanted to put in the glass case.Explore more on these topicsCultureDressesMuseumsSarah BurtonArmaniGivenchyWomen's dressesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The fashion industry wants women to wear bras again - but is underwire the answer? | Fashion | The Guardian
description: From Charli xcx and Rihanna to Victoria’s Secret and Prada catwalks, the fashion industry is keen to move on from the comfy, wire-free bras popularized in lockdown
Author: Hannah Marriott
Headline: From Charli xcx and Rihanna to Victoria’s Secret and Prada catwalks, the fashion industry is keen to move on from the comfy, wire-free bras popularized in lockdown
Content: Rihanna at the Matières Fécales fashion show in Paris on 28 September.Photograph: Aitor Rosas Sune/WWD/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRihanna at the Matières Fécales fashion show in Paris on 28 September.Photograph: Aitor Rosas Sune/WWD/Getty ImagesFashionThe fashion industry wants women to wear bras again - but is underwire the answer?From Charli xcx and Rihanna to Victoria’s Secret and Prada catwalks, the fashion industry is keen to move on from the comfy, wire-free bras popularized in lockdownHannah MarriottThu 8 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 14.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s a trend that might have been expected to be kept under the radar – or at least under a T-shirt. But high fashion’s recent endorsement of underwire bras could not have been more visible.This fashion month, underwear as outerwear was omnipresent on catwalks, with underwire bras inred and black satinat Prada and black andsilverat Tom Ford. At the Matieres Fecales show, Rihanna wore a bra from her own Savage X Fenty rangepeeking out of her unbuttoned jacket.Elsewhere,Anya Taylor Joywore a Balmain fuchsia underwire bra, with a cardigan and a floral jacquard skirt while promoting her new series. Model Kaia Gerber recently wore a wool crepeAlaïabra top on the red carpet, which featured an exposed underwire as part of the design.At the VMAs, Tyla wore a blue snakeskin-print by Mowalola with a matching low-rise skirt.MowalolaOgunlesi, the London-based designer behind the look, says her thinking was that “I’m finding power in femininity and treating lingerie as something complete in itself, rather than something that needs to be hidden or layered”. An underwire bra was the basis of the outfit because, she says, “it sculpts the body in a unique way”.View image in fullscreenTyla during the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards at Peacock Theater on 27 September in Los Angeles.Photograph: Kevin Winter/Getty ImagesThis latest crop of high fashion underwire bras aren’t usually push-up bras – those specially designed to squish breasts together, as during the Hello Boys heyday of the Wonderbra in the late 1990s. Rather, they appear to aim for more universal appeal, creating a somewhat lifted shape without going full Jessica Rabbit. Other advocates include Lily Allen, who has been wearing underwire bras as tops for the past couple of years, and mega-girl-group Katseye, whose recent Saturday Night Live performance wardrobe mainly consisted of bras – some of which were so skimpythey did not really have cups, but were, nevertheless, underwired.Charli xcx wore an underwire bra as a top to party with Madonna at the VMAs, having previously worn underwire bras in her live shows, on the cover of Rolling Stone and in Interview magazine. Even when she wears a shirt, her bra is part of the outfit – it might be bright purple,poking out of an unbuttoned black vest.It is a very 2004, very revealing, indie sleaze-influenced look. Unlike, say, a sporty crop top, which could enable celebrities to show off their abs – a clear driving force for the trend – it is a boudoirish look which feels like a rejection of the pilates princess crop tops and comfy bralettes, which have been on trend for the past handful of years. The omnipresence of the aesthetic suggests that something is up within visual culture.Like the rest of us, bras have been behaving strangely since Covid. Kristen Classi-Zummo, apparel industry adviser at market research firm Circana, reports just one notable bump in US bra sales in the third week of March in 2021. “We can really pinpoint it to the week vaccines rolled out,” she says. “People started replenishing bras, intimates, socks.”Since then, the market has stagnated and “we haven’t seen the industry pick up”.View image in fullscreenKatseye.Photograph: NBC/Will Heath/Getty ImagesShe puts this down to a few factors: the continuation, to some extent, of work from home culture, an “overall casualization with how we’re dressing”. This has affected bras more than some other categories, says Classi-Zummo because there is a sense that “whereas maybe before she needed five bras in rotation, now maybe she only needs two or three. Bras have consistently been struggling.”At the same time, even as bra sales have plunged, and even as many women have stayed loyal to underwire bras during that downturn (underwire bras now make up about 52% of the market, down from 57% in 2022, says Classi-Zummo), the past handful of years has been driven by wire-free comfort. This has been the case since the earliest days of the pandemic, when the market research firm NPD reported that, while overall bra sales fell 1% in the second half of 2020, sales of wireless bras were up 14%.Partly, the rise of comfortable bras came from innovation. New technologies, such as silicone gel cups, aimed to ensure that even those with large busts “can have the same features – padding, lift – without the wire”, says Classi-Zummo. It also echoed broader pandemic-accelerated trends towards comfort and casualisation in dress – seen also in the adoption of elasticated waistbands over so-called “hard trousers”.Many celebrated the rise of wire-free bras as a feminist triumph. Before that, gripes about bra discomfort were so widespread that they became common fodder for female comedians. In 2014, for example, Sarah Millican had a popular bit about always needing to know what time any night out would end, so “I know what timeI can take my fucking bra off”.Underwire bras feature two loops of hard material, usually a cord of metal or resin, under each breast. Many wearers will be familiar with the downsides: ill-fitting wires digging into the ribcage or popping out of the side of the bra, and stabbing you in the armpit, when bras are past their prime. Or the sense of constriction as the ribcage expands – but the underwires and the bra band do not – after a big meal.For all of the recent technical progress in supportive wire-free bras, however, Larissa King, FIT assistant professor of fashion design, intimate apparel, says that, in general, there is still an aesthetic difference with an underwire. “Underwires work together with the bra band to cantilever the weight of the wearer’s breasts and distribute the weight around the chest wall,” she says. “If fitted well, the wires also help reduce the pressure on the wearer’s shoulders. Wires also help to define and separate the breasts. Wireless bras can be very comfortable and supportive, but they tend to give a different shape to the bust – often rounder and less defined.”View image in fullscreenThe Prada spring/summer 2027 fashion show in Milan, on 22 September.Photograph: Nowfashion/ShutterstockFinancially speaking, the underwire bras’ current high fashion moment has yet to perk the mass bra market up. In the 12 months ending August 2026, both underwire and wire-free bra sales declined in the US, according to Circana, with underwire falling five times as fast as wire-free, continuing on its post-pandemic trajectory.The fashion industry is hoping this moment will make an underwired bra uptick happen among general shoppers, and is already promoting new styles, according to Edited, a retail intelligence platform that tracks new products arrivals at mass retailers’ websites. In August, mentions of “push” and “underwired” were up 60% and 28% month on month.Anecdotally, the sight of so many high-profile women in “proper” bras does seem to be having an impact on those of us who wear our bras the old-fashioned way – under our clothes. My friends report being underwire-curious again, finding themselves poring over the Agent Provocateur website for the first time in a decade. A recent New York feature, about one writer’s quest to find her “first (bright, flashy) underwire bra in years” was a case in point. She had been, she wrote, a “strict bralette loyalist” who “would have told you underwire bras were a prison”. Recently, though, she had started feeling “an insatiable hunger for hoisting cups” and “strict reinforcement”.Many I spoke to connected the trend with the decline of body positivity. “For a while, there was this big marketing push on body positivity and comfort, and we saw this shift away to softer fabrics. Now again, as we’re starting to see this shift back to sexy,” says Classi-Zummo.This is coupled with other aesthetic developments – the shrinking of celebrity bodies in a GLP-1-influenced era, the rise of tight, tweaked faces, paired with artificially cushiony lips; the general suggestion that one must be largely taut and thin, but also soft and cushiony in precisely the “right” places.View image in fullscreenAn attender at Copenhagen fashion week in 2025.Photograph: Edward Berthelot/Getty ImagesFor King, the return to fashion of a structured bra ties in to “the current high fashion fixation on hyper-feminine, exaggerated and super-stylized body proportions”, seen on catwalks in recent seasons. “Think corseted waists, padded hips and derrieres and prominent breasts.” It also signals that we are “moving fully away from pandemic-era aesthetics”.Thanks to AI and social media image manipulation, she says, “the bodies that we see online are bearing less resemblance to the bodies we see in person on average people, and I think the luxury fashion market is playing into that disconnect by pushing silhouettes to extremes. I think this trend will evolve from the high-fashion version into a less extreme version at other levels of the market.”In the new world of underwire bras, designers are at least trying to bake more comfort into design. According to a Victoria’s Secret spokesperson, its construction has moved on since the aughts. The company’s Body By Victoria Flex Factor bra, for example, has an underwire made of flexible titanium, designed to bend to the body.“We’ve seen her expectation of comfort evolve – she still wants lift, shape and support, but she wants it to feel incredible too,” said the spokesperson, speaking of the customer base as an individual female they were on intimate terms with – as many in the bra industry do.What remains to be seen is what “she” will do next: will the customer who gleefully shed her restrictive bra a few years ago find the new underwire trend uplifting enough to buy into?Explore more on these topicsFashionUnderwearfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Vibrant, design-led and surprisingly green’: why the Dutch city of Eindhoven is perfect for a relaxed arty break | City breaks | The Guardian
description: After electronics giant Philips left, the city reinvented itself as a multicultural hub for creativity and innovation, and the home of Dutch Design Week
Author: Sarah Rodrigues
Headline: After electronics giant Philips left, the city reinvented itself as a multicultural hub for creativity and innovation, and the home of Dutch Design Week
Content: Once home to Philips, the Strijp-S district is now a creative hotspot.Photograph: Nick BookelaarView image in fullscreenOnce home to Philips, the Strijp-S district is now a creative hotspot.Photograph: Nick BookelaarCity breaks‘Vibrant, design-led and surprisingly green’: why the Dutch city of Eindhoven is perfect for a relaxed arty breakAfter electronics giant Philips left, the city reinvented itself as a multicultural hub for creativity and innovation, and the home of Dutch Design WeekSarah RodriguesThu 8 Oct 2026 03.17 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 11.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAbaggily clad skateboarder’s wheels clatter across concrete floors, the noise bouncing off exposed pipes and iron girders. Vaulted skylights set in high ceilings illuminate the industrial space and its central kitchen, from which my main course – a silky lemon risotto, spiked with samphire, rhubarb, garlic, baby onions and basil – has just been transported.I’m in the Dutch city of Eindhoven, in North Brabant, famous for its historic connection to Philips, the one-time electronics giant. The restaurant, Radio Royaal, is housed in what was once their engine room, in the Strijp-S neighbourhood. Today, Strijp-S buzzes with concept stores, an indoor food market,MU Hybrid Art Houseand the Area 51 skatepark. The broader area, Strijp, was where the company was largely headquartered: its zones are named S, T and R. In the late 90s, Philips withdrew from the city where it had started in 1891, and the letters I, J and P were never assigned.Philips had employed about half of the region’s working population, so its departure for Amsterdam inevitably left a huge hole. Fortunately for Eindhoven, this was short-lived, and within a decade the city had reinvented itself as a multicultural hub for design and innovation – so much so thatDutch Design Week, the largest event of its kind in northern Europe, has been held here since 2005.View image in fullscreenThe innovative Trudo Tower is adorned with greenery.Photograph: Pixelbiss/AlamyThis year’s iteration, from 17 to 25 October, has a jam-packed programme of exhibitions, workshops and seminars at more than 100 locations around the city, with thousands of local and international designers involved. About 350,000 visitors are expected, with displays spanning everything from abar made from mushroomsto themanipulation of Dutch wool(which is coarser than other wools, such as merino) for wearable garments.Well beyond Design Week, however, Eindhoven packs a punch in terms of creativity. On my visit, I discovered a city that is not only vibrant and design-led, but also surprisingly green.double quotation markDespite the city’s industrial past, about 40% of Eindhoven’s landscape comprises greeneryCompletely off-limits during Philips’ heyday, Strijp-S is perhaps the liveliest example of Eindhoven’s reinvention, with innovative businesses making the most of the industrial spaces. It’s distinguished, too, by the Trudo Tower, a 19-storey building where facade planters froth with more than 70 species of greenery. Purpose-built in 2020, these eye-catching apartments were designed to provide affordable housing for low-income residents.Despite the city’s industrial past, about 40% of Eindhoven’s landscape comprises greenery. Walkways – complete with bat boxes – run alongside the Dommel river, while larger spaces, such as Karpendonkse Plas and Philips de Jongh park, provide walking and biking opportunities. This, plus an average commute time of 15 minutes, helps to explain why Eindhoven was named theworld’s least stressed citylast year.View image in fullscreenEvoluon exhibition and conference space.Photograph: Bildagentur/Joko/AlamyAs you walk from the UFO-shaped Evoluon (now functioning as an exhibition space and conference centre, and given by the company to the city on its 75th anniversary) on the edge of the Het Ven neighbourhood towards Strijp-R, the area becomes both green and residential. Ahead of the times, Philips saw the correlation between nature and healthy, happy employees. As early as 1910, the company started building workers’ accommodation with large gardens, which today are a mix of social and private housing.Strijp-R’s primary allure, however, is the RK Complex. Formerly a Philips ceramics factory, it was bought by renowned Dutch designerPiet Hein Eekand opened in 2010. Other designers have workshops here, too: the idea, said Hein Eek, was to give young creatives an affordable space to work. The concept obviously works: in more than 15 years, only five of the 25 studios have changed hands.View image in fullscreenDesigner Piet Hein Eek’s studio.Photograph: Nick BookelaarVisitors flock here year-round to check out Hein Eek’s eco-forward scrap wood furniture and for glimpses into the studios, the cavernous exhibition space and the shop, packed with smaller design objects – ceramics, books, jewellery. The onsite Green Restaurant favours local, seasonal ingredients in hearty portions; it’s attached to the boutiquePiet Hein Eek hotel, also one of the designer’s innovations. It has 14 rooms, each featuring a distinctive design style, with doubles from €135.What makes a stay in Eindhoven even more interesting, however, are the myriad ways this impulse towards repurposing spaces, reusing materials and thinking sustainably shapes the visitor experience. I stayed atHotel Mariënhge(doubles from €83) in the centre, a former monastery characterised by clean lines and cheeky art, its interiors effortlessly blending old and new.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFrom here, it’s a short walk to the retail district, where vintage stores range from the highly curatedYatva Vintageto a Salvation Army ReShare store. Near Strijp-R, I happen uponLuna & Lore, owned and run by Luna Hartogs. “Lore is about wisdom passed on from previous generations, and I learned to sew from my grandmother,” she explains, as I rifle delightedly through rails of upcycled vintage clothing. “For me, it’s also about passing things on for people to enjoy.”“Eindhoven gets called ‘Vintage Valhalla’ – a paradise,” Erik van Gerwen ofEindhoven 365tells me over dinner at Fifth NRE, itself housed in a former gas factory. “There’s the Philips legacy, but the presence of the Design Academy also ensures a lively community, passionate about innovatively making use of what already exists.”View image in fullscreenBerenkuil graffiti zone.Photograph: Nick BookelaarCreating opportunities is a recurring theme in Eindhoven. I see it again atNew Order of Fashion, a nonprofit organisation providing makers with resources to experiment with, as well as a sellers’ platform. It’s also a lab, researching the future of fashion from a regenerative perspective, and a public space aiming to inspire visitors to think about their consumer choices.I loiter outside the Muziekgebouw concert hall: since 2024, its facade has featured a massive mural of a street musician and classical concert violinist embracing. Named Echoes of Harmony, it was commissioned by Eindhoven city council to represent music’s ability to bridge barriers, and since named best mural worldwide byStreet Art Cities.On the city’s north-eastern edge, graffers can legally unleash spray cans in Berenkuil, a two-level roundabout and now the country’s largest open-air graffiti zone. Ramps and rails make it a beeline for skateboarders, too; again, I hear wheels grinding on concrete. There are no dibs here: the art lasts mere days before it’s sprayed over by someone else, but that, I’m told, is the point. In Eindhoven, perhaps more than anywhere else, the idea that everything is ephemeral, yet also renewable, seems entirely at home.The trip was provided by theNetherlands Board of Tourism and ConventionsExplore more on these topicsCity breaksNetherlands holidaysEurope holidaysDesignCultural tripsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Monkeys as service animals? The ‘bizarre’, tortured history of humans and primates | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Ape Sh*t, a new zine by writer and designer Carrie McLaren, looks at the ways monkeys and apes have communicated to humans that they’re individuals too
Author: Matthew Cantor
Headline: Ape Sh*t, a new zine by writer and designer Carrie McLaren, looks at the ways monkeys and apes have communicated to humans that they’re individuals too
Content: The zine explores the history of organ grinders, who kept capuchins in captivity.Photograph: Catherine Ledner/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe zine explores the history of organ grinders, who kept capuchins in captivity.Photograph: Catherine Ledner/Getty ImagesLife and styleMonkeys as service animals? The ‘bizarre’, tortured history of humans and primatesApe Sh*t, a new zine by writer and designer Carrie McLaren, looks at the ways monkeys and apes have communicated to humans that they’re individuals tooMatthew CantorThu 8 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 12.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleZines have always lent themselves to weird and wonderful topics, from sci-fi reflections to punk fanzines to radical political tracts. The underground, often homemade publications have offered readers and writers a way to throw themselves into niche topics since long before the internet.For Carrie McLaren, a veteran zine maker, the latest topic of choice is admittedly “bizarre”, disturbing and darkly funny: the tortured relationship between humans and monkeys.It’s all documented inApe Sh*t,a new zine by McLaren, the longtime writer and designer behind the 90s/early 2000s zineStay Free!, whichcovered“the politics and perversions of mass media and American (consumer) culture”. Ape Sh*t’s first issue, The Bizarre History of the Service Monkey, details the rise of a Boston organization that provided “helper monkeys” to people with quadriplegia, as well as the uncomfortable story of organ grinder monkeys, who were often abused into submission.Stay Free! put out its last issue in 2008, around the time when McLaren had a child. But in recent years, McLaren began mulling a return to the zine format. “It was honestly a distraction from all the crazy stuff going on in the country,” she says. “Really what I’m interested in is that kind of human-non-human interaction.”View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Carrie McLarenInitially it seemed very different from covering America’s obsession with consumerism, but eventually McLaren began to see parallels. Both worlds involve power dynamics that are so ingrained that we hardly notice them, a topic she hopes to explore in future issues.There is plenty of fascinating weirdness here – enough to fill 70 pages. McLaren, who for years ran a listserv about monkeys with an Onion writer friend, was particularly interested in the media’s presentation of the Boston non-profit, Helping Hands, as a joyful story.The idea behind Helping Hands, which emerged in the 1970s, was that capuchin monkeys, the small creatures associated with old-timey organ grinders, could assist people with everyday tasks, like picking things up and flipping light switches. The press loved the idea. But for the humans and monkeys involved, things weren’t so simple.Clients apparently showed limited interest in the monkeys, who were difficult to control and inclined to make messes: in short, McLaren writes, “helper monkeys were not actually helpful”. As for the monkeys, life in a human home seemed a cruel fate. They often lived in small cages, hadsome oftheir teeth removed, and were trained using shocks. Yet Helping Hands endured until it rebranded in 2023.“I was looking for that journalistic piece to say ‘this is a media creation’, and [that article] didn’t exist,” she says. “So I’m like: OK, well, I should write it then.”View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Carrie McLarenThat led to Ape Sh*t, whose first issue tells the “messy, complicated” story of the non-profit’s founding, its struggle to place monkeys, and the adoring international media coverage. The lengthy tale of the organization, which received federal funding, is peppered with interstitial material, including a darkly comic guide to keeping “a terrible idea alive (‘problem: all monkeys bite. Solution: remove their teeth’)” and quotes from past congressional testimony opposing funding for the group: “Many quadriplegics have trachea tubes that are easily accessible to the monkeys,” noted one critic. “In addition, all have urine bags that can be opened by the monkeys. Driving controls on the quadriplegics’ wheelchairs have been used by monkeys to drive their owners into walls.”The zine’s first issue includes an interview with Alison Pascoe, a former monkey trainer at Helping Hands who has become a critic of the organization. She describes the shock treatment used to train the monkeys and her concern that Helping Hands was fueling enthusiasm for keeping monkeys as pets. She discusses how the female monkeys, who would go into heat every month, had to have hysterectomies; a monkey she adopted, Amelia, would “hand me scissors” to push her to remove the bandage from her operation.In a statement, Envisioning Access, formerly Helping Hands, wrote that it “respects Ms McLaren’s right to her own thoughts and opinions. However, we stand by the deep human-animal bonds that we have witnessed over almost half a century between recipients and their service monkeys.” The organization added that it recognized “that what was considered acceptable care for primates in the 1970s and 80s has evolved over the decades as we have learned more about these amazing animals.“This is one of many reasons why the last monkey was born into our program in 1999, and why we are committed to the support and care of every monkey in the program through their natural lifetime.”The zine also explores the history of organ grinders in a series of blurbs and pictures. Monkeys, McLaren writes, would often bite the impoverished children who gave them coins. They’d also climb buildings, leading to accidents including when “a man in Newark accidentally shot a neighbor when trying to gun down a monkey climbing a building”; in other cases, kids fell out windows trying to hand pennies to the monkeys.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Carrie McLarenAn excerpt from an interview with an organ grinder trainer describes how to “break the monkey’s spirit by rendering it entirely helpless” using “ropes or gags … a state of weakness and depression ensues, all resistance ceases.” A “switch” is also “brought into play”. Organ grinders “ordinarily” kill five to 10 monkeys before finding one who can endure the lifestyle, according to the excerpt.Sometimes, they get revenge. A 1952 account describes Gloria the capuchin punishing her owner for a long absence by unlocking a bookcase, taking all the pages out of a pair of books, and dumping them in a fish tank. In 2007, a New York Times story described a monkey named Oliver repeatedly breaking out of a cage at a Mississippi zoo; it took him 20 minutes to evade “$300 worth of new locks”. In 2001, the Chicago Tribune described a monkey who would “grab perfume bottles and empty them into his hands and rub all over himself”. He also enjoyed running around with a knife and waving it in a kid’s face.But it’s not all mayhem and cruelty. The zine closes with a palate cleanser focused on capuchins in the wild, including research on their behavior and photography.McLaren became interested in the relationship between humans and monkeys after stumbling on a book at a thrift shop by Leonard Williams, founder of a celebrated monkey sanctuary in Cornwall, south-western England, about his interactions with the animals. Her interest in the topic led to the listserv and later to researching the history of pet monkeys and Helping Hands.Ape Sh*t’s text and layout are almost entirely McLaren’s, though several friends helped with the editing process, including collaborators from her 90s zine. Of course, things have changed since then, when a 1,000-copy print run would sell out immediately. “People aren’t used to going picking up a paper artefact and thumbing through that,” she says.Still, small, homemade zines are “alive and well”. “I follow the zines subreddit, and there’s just so many creative, amazing zines that people are doing,” McLaren says. She’s also planning to put new effort into a digital format, beyond a simple PDF. And while this is by no means a full-time job, she hopes that the user-friendly approach to telling a story can serve as a classroom teaching tool, as was the case with her earlier work. “I try to use humor and clear language to express complex ideas,” she says – in this case, our species’ strange relationship with some of our closest relatives.McLaren acknowledges that “animal rights is a dirty word” in America. “There’s an assumption that if you want to advocate for animals, that you’re some kind of crazy person who’s gonna throw a bucket of blood on everyone,” she says. But “part of the fun” of writing Ape Sh*t is “trying to look at ways that animals – monkeys and apes specifically – have tried to communicate to us that they are individuals, that they are beings with perspective”.Ape Sh*t isavailable to order nowExplore more on these topicsLife and styleMagazinesAnimalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I spent years postponing my own joy. Here’s how I learned to say yes to the juicy bits of life | Sheree Joseph | The Guardian
description: Society tells us there is one way to live a life, and joy is a byproduct on the path there. But you don’t need a reason to enjoy the act of being alive
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Society tells us there is one way to live a life, and joy is a byproduct on the path there. But you don’t need a reason to enjoy the act of being alive
Content: ‘Wander and meander and do something for no reason at all. Bring back whimsy! Pay attention to the details, to what lights you up.’Photograph: Anna Berkut/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Wander and meander and do something for no reason at all. Bring back whimsy! Pay attention to the details, to what lights you up.’Photograph: Anna Berkut/AlamyOpinionHappinessI spent years postponing my own joy. Here’s how I learned to say yes to the juicy bits of lifeSheree JosephSociety tells us there is one way to live a life, and joy is a byproduct on the path there. But you don’t need a reason to enjoy the act of being aliveThu 8 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 18.43 EDTShareIhave been dwelling on what it means to live well. Not because I have mastered it, but because I have become very comically bad at it. I have spent years rushing through my life, panicked and convinced I was running out of time. I worried constantly about work – getting it, keeping it, doing it, caring about it too much, hating it and losing it. I obsessed over being more productive. I fretted about money, mostly about not having any left after travelling too much. I poured so much energy into dating that it’s kind of impressive I haven’t had a relationship for the last six years.But most of all I became fixated on my fertility and how it dwindled in my early 30s, leaving me to make choices most women don’t have to until later. I tried to save my eggs and couldn’t. My lack of a partner in a conservative Catholic Lebanese family became a cudgel.Pleasure was something bypassed on the way to a goal of being chosen and accepted. In other words, joy was a byproduct.The secret to happiness? Finding joy in others. It’s free, simple and will gladden your heart | Nadine LevyRead moreTrying to live well in a society that doesn’t prioritise it is like filling a cup with the bottom cut off: the water just runs through, passing you by, leaving you as parched as sandpaper.A holiday was an opportunity to recover from work. In Italy, the plastic cup in my hand was solid and filled with the bitter strength of a negroni sbagliato – or a “broken negroni” – a drink whose name comes from the fact it was first made by mistake.I asked the bartender why there was an exuberant street party forming outside. What was the occasion, in other words?“Just because,” he said. “We don’t need a reason.”Why did I need a reason to enjoy myself? The question ran through me.I thought about all the ways I had been trained to postpone my life. Why did I need a reason to celebrate the very act of being alive? At that moment I pondered the many nights spent couch-bound, parked in front of a television – not in a fun and delicious single-gal-about-town-living-her-best-life way, but in a dark abyss void of nothingness. Not even eating ice-cream straight from the tub, because that would be too indulgent. I couldn’t even enjoy spending money on trinkets and flowers and dresses that brought me joy without fretting and feeling guilty for spending money during an ongoing cost-of-living crisis, thereby negating the original dopamine hit.We are told there is one way to live a life: just work harder, achieve more, be thinner, be younger, find a partner, get married, have a baby, save money, buy a house, build a career, have it all! Then, presumably, I will have made it! Made it to the part where I was allowed to relax. But when? And what if the forced veering off the path was necessary and part of my story, to show me that there are other ways to live? When the tough times tear through like a tornado, what is there left for us to do if those things don’t work out?Since that moment in Italy, I have thought deeply about how to instead live a life that makes you feel fully alive, something I have dubbed “the juicy life”. There are so many simple and uncomplicated ways to live like this. Big belly laughs, truly tasting a salted tomato in summer, baptismal swims in the sea, sitting at a long table until golden hours bleed into night. Let boredom engulf you. Wander and meander and do something for no reason at all. Bring back whimsy! Pay attention to the details, to what lights you up. What makes you feel more like yourself?Create from nothing, make things that didn’t exist before: art, meals, gardens, traditions, friendships, books, beauty, music, films, photos and spaces. To create anything at all is defiance – to give life in a world that tells us only some creation stories matter. Take long walks, but go lightly, with ease and notice everything around you. Hold someone’s hand in yours and gaze at the moon. Scrunch basil up to your face with both hands and breathe it in. It’s much harder to feel existential despair when you embody your life entirely.Nine life lessons from the happiest man in the world: from embracing tiny changes to not overthinking meditationRead moreThere will always be more of everything, an endless panopticon of slop, of tech platforms churning and burning through content, of machines trying to quench their thirst on what makes us human. But you are not a walking replicant robot. Humans need rest and balance. And everything, all of this, is fleeting and not forever.The Greeks have two words for time:chronosandkairos.Chronosis chronological time – tracking the seconds, the hours and the schedules, all adding up with nowhere to go but forward and rushed. Butkairostime is different, because it is time measured by meaning – the opportune and transcendent moment; what sits between.The ancient Pythagoreans calledkairosone of the fundamental laws of the universe, the force that wove together the dualities of existence. When you live onkairostime, you move through the world differently: you stop checking and fretting over the literal and metaphorical clock. You listen instead to the revelation, to the rhythm beneath your feet. You dip down to the earth, feel the ground, hold the pebbles and rocks, let your limbs surrender.That’s when life shuttles beyond a checklist of things to achieve or acquire and becomes a constellation of moments, meaning made and remade, steeped in pleasure, to be savoured, saturating the moment until it becomes meaning itself. That’s where life lives. Make no sbagliato mistake.Sheree Joseph is a writer, editor and the author of Juicy: How to Live a Life in the Wreckage of ExpectationsExplore more on these topicsHappinessOpinionRelationshipsAgeingHealth & wellbeingcommentShareReuse this content
