title: Japan beer giants raided over suspicions they colluded to set the price of beverages | Japan | The Guardian
description: Investigators probe Asahi, Kirin, Suntory and Sapporo breweries – which together control more than 90% of Japan’s beer market
Author: Justin McCurry
Headline: Investigators probe Asahi, Kirin, Suntory and Sapporo breweries – which together control more than 90% of Japan’s beer market
Content: Officials from the Fair Trade Commission raided four major beer manufacturers in Japan over suspicions they colluded to hike beverage prices in a violation of anti-monopoly laws.Photograph: Yuichi Yamazaki/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenOfficials from the Fair Trade Commission raided four major beer manufacturers in Japan over suspicions they colluded to hike beverage prices in a violation of anti-monopoly laws.Photograph: Yuichi Yamazaki/AFP/Getty ImagesJapanJapan beer giants raided over suspicions they colluded to set the price of beveragesInvestigators probe Asahi, Kirin, Suntory and Sapporo breweries – which together control more than 90% of Japan’s beer marketJustin McCurryin TokyoWed 7 Oct 2026 23.54 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 10.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJapanese authorities have raided the country’s four biggest breweries over suspicions they colluded to set the price of beer and other beverages – a practice media reports said could have forced drinkers to pay over the odds.Officials from the Fair Trade Commission this week searched the offices of Asahi Breweries, Kirin Brewery, SuntoryBeerand Sapporo Breweries – which together control more than 90% of the domestic market. The quartet are suspected of violating the anti-monopoly law.The commission’s secretary general, Hiroo Iwanari, confirmed an investigation had begun, but declined to give details. The companies said they would cooperate with authorities.Alleged ice-cream cartel in Japan investigated as sweltering summer loomsRead moreThe commission is understood to have launched the investigation given the potential effect the alleged cartel has had on prices after wholesalers sell their products on to supermarkets,convenience stores, bars and restaurants, the Mainichi Shimbun said.Japanese media quoted sources as saying that sales managers and other executives from the breweries were suspected of meeting secretly over a prolonged period to coordinate on the timing and scale of retail price increases, which ranged from several yen to several dozen yen a time.Prices forbeerand a low-malt version calledhapposhuhave risen multiple times to reflect the rising cost of raw materials and logistics. The commission suspects the breweries bypassed proper pricing competition and collaborated to ensure they made a profit, the Mainichi said.Alcohol consumption in Japan has declined in recent decades as a result of depopulation and changes in drinking habits among younger people. But sales still reached ¥3.8tn ($24.3bn) in 2024, with beer accounting for 30% of the total, followed by happoshu and third-category beer, which contains little or no malt, with a combined 11.9%The four breweries have all raised their prices at the same time, most recently in April last year, citing the rising cost of materials and distribution. Prices also rose in October 2022 and October 2023.Shares in Asahi, Kirin, Suntory and Sapporo fell after Wednesday’s raids – the first investigation of its kind involving the food and beverage industry.Japanese media quoted sources as saying the commission had judged the case to be particularly serious given its potential impact on consumers, adding that the probe could result in a criminal complaint.The probe comes three months after the commissionraided six Japanese ice-cream makersover allegations of operating a cartel.Explore more on these topicsJapanBeerAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Indonesia accused of ‘gross negligence’ in wildfires lawsuit as haze tests region | Indonesia | The Guardian
description: NGOs in Indonesian Borneo file class action lawsuit calling for government to better manage annual fires
Author: Oliver Holmes
Headline: NGOs in Indonesian Borneo file class action lawsuit calling for government to better manage annual fires
Content: Students conduct marching drills amid haze from forest and land fires at the courtyard of the Mujahidin Grand Mosque in Pontianak, West Kalimantan.Photograph: DITO/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenStudents conduct marching drills amid haze from forest and land fires at the courtyard of the Mujahidin Grand Mosque in Pontianak, West Kalimantan.Photograph: DITO/AFP/Getty ImagesIndonesiaIndonesia accused of ‘gross negligence’ in wildfires lawsuit as haze tests regionNGOs in Indonesian Borneo file class action lawsuit calling for government to better manage annual fires andOliver Holmesin Bangkok and agenciesWed 7 Oct 2026 23.54 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 18.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Indonesian government has been accused of “gross negligence” in a class action lawsuit over its handling of wildfires that have cloaked large parts of South-east Asia in a toxic haze, shuttered schools and caused a spike in respiratory illnesses.The lawsuit, filed by indigenous and civil society groups in the Indonesian part of Borneo, namedPresident Prabowo Subiantoand the governor of West Kalimantan among 10 defendants. The case seeks comprehensive recovery and rehabilitation measures that would include covering the healthcare costs of residents.‘The physical toll is visceral’: How Indonesia’s fire haze affects millions - visual guideRead moreNone of those named in the lawsuit attended the opening day of court in West Kalimantan’s provincial capital Pontianak on Wednesday, leading judges to adjourn the hearing until 21 October.“We feel sad and regretful about their absence … But on the other hand, we also understand that perhaps this haze condition caused them to be unable to land in Pontianak,” the plaintiffs’ lawyer, Glorio Sanen, told reporters.View image in fullscreenA resident pours water to extinguish a wildfire near a residential area in Banyuasin, South Sumatra province, Indonesia on October 7, 2026.Photograph: Abriansyah Liberto/ReutersSanen said the case was “a step to address the problem” of wildfires thatflare up annually in Indonesia, where they are often lit as a cheap way to clear land for oil palm planting.Indonesia, the world’s largest producer of palm oil, has been accused of not doing enough to stop the so-called “slash and burn” land clearances, although the government has vowed a crackdown and deployed the military to fight the fires.The blazes hit a crisis point this year due to anunusually intense El Niñoweather phenomenon, which has created drier-than-usual conditions, sending a putrid smog to Malaysia, Brunei and Singapore, and even the Philippines.The transboundary haze has angered Indonesia’s neighbours. Schools in the Malaysian state of Johor, just north of Singapore, were to be closed on Thursday and Friday due to deteriorating air quality, local authorities said.The four plaintiffs in the West Kalimantan lawsuit, which was filed last month, include a chapter of Indigenous NGO AMAN and the local branch of Catholic ​Youth.View image in fullscreenMotorists commute through thick haze caused by forest and land fires as they cross the Duplikasi Jembatan Kapuas 1 bridge in Pontianak, West Kalimantan, on October 7, 2026.Photograph: DITO/AFP/Getty ImagesYakobus Kumis, a plaintiff representing a Dayak ethnic group, indigenous to the island of Borneo, expressed disappointment that government representatives did not attend this week’s hearing, saying it was a “way of the central government teaching the people that violating the law is OK.”He said the government ignored warning signs ahead of the fires breaking out, and called for the smoke crisis to be classified as a national disaster.A similar lawsuit filed last year at a court in South Sumatra was dismissed.The presidential office did not immediately ⁠respond to a request for comment.Agence France-Presse and Reuters contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsIndonesiaWildfiresEl Niño southern oscillationAsia PacificAir pollutionPalm oilnewsShareReuse this content

title: Firmus pulls biggest ASX float since Telstra amid investor doubt about datacentre company | Datacentres - Australia | The Guardian
description: The $11-a-share offer would have been the biggest debut on the stock market since the telecommunication giant in 1997
Author: Jonathan Barrett
Headline: The $11-a-share offer would have been the biggest debut on the stock market since the telecommunication giant in 1997
Content: Firmus has pulled its plans for the biggest ASX debut in two decadesView image in fullscreenFirmus has pulled its plans for the biggest ASX debut in two decadesDatacentres - AustraliaFirmus pulls biggest ASX float since Telstra amid investor doubt about datacentre companyThe $11-a-share offer would have been the biggest debut on the stock market since the telecommunication giant in 1997Get ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJonathan BarrettBusiness editorThu 8 Oct 2026 18.33 EDTFirst published on Thu 8 Oct 2026 18.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFirmus Technologies has scrapped what was set to be Australia’s biggest company listing in decades after investor demand for its much-hyped AI datacentre business failed to materialise.A Firmus spokesperson said the board decided that proceeding with the offer was no longer in the best interests of the company and its shareholders.“Firmus will now pursue capital from the private markets and consider alternative public and private market options,” the spokesperson said on Friday morning.Australia is building a lot of new homes. But is the datacentre boom holding us back? | Greg JerichoRead more“We will provide additional information to shareholders as those options progress.”Firmus, with an anticipated $44bn valuation, was expected to be the biggest ASX listing since Telstra in 1997.But it faced mounting scepticism over its huge valuation, and forecast earnings, for a company in its startup phase with just two, small operational sites.Backed by chip maker Nvidia and Wall Street firms Blackstone, Jane Street and Coatue, Firmus’s backers believed they could raise billions of dollars by selling shares in a public float with the help of five brokers.Thelack of demandmeans Firmus will need to raise money from private investors to fund its plans to build liquid-cooled “AI factories” in Australia and across Asia.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailFrantic discussionsThe polished Firmus pitch started to unravel midweek after it became clear the company’s bankers had vastly overestimated demand in their bid to raise $7bn from investors ahead of listing on the ASX on 23 October.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis prompted discussions about a heavy reduction in the company’s proposed $11-a-share initial public offering, according to one investment manager briefed on the matter.The company ultimately decided to withdraw its application to list on the ASX altogether.Guardian Australia previously reported growing concern that early Firmus investors were going touse retail investors buying into the float as their “exit strategy”, leaving small investors exposed if the excitement dissipated.The datacentre company’s troubles have already rattled other parts of the market, with shares in Firmus investor Maas Group plunging more than 20% on Thursday.The anticipated financial worth of the founders – Oliver Curtis, who hasspent time in prison for insider trading, his cousin Tim Rosenfield, and Curtis’s former brother-in-law Jonathan Levee – will also be greatly reduced.Explore more on these topicsDatacentres - title: Astronomers detect mysterious burst of energy from a galaxy far, far away  | Astronomy | The Guardian
description: Intense flash of radio waves is more than 10bn years old and has travelled through ‘approximately 80% of cosmic history’
Author: Donna Lu
Headline: Intense flash of radio waves is more than 10bn years old and has travelled through ‘approximately 80% of cosmic history’
Content: Scientists detected the burst using the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa and subsequently identified its host galaxy using Nasa’s James Webb space telescope.Photograph: Brendon Wainwright/WikipediaView image in fullscreenScientists detected the burst using the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa and subsequently identified its host galaxy using Nasa’s James Webb space telescope.Photograph: Brendon Wainwright/WikipediaAstronomyAstronomers detect mysterious burst of energy from a galaxy far, far awayIntense flash of radio waves is more than 10bn years old and has travelled through ‘approximately 80% of cosmic history’Donna LuThu 8 Oct 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 19.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA long time ago in a galaxy far, far away, a mysterious flash of energy was released into the universe.Astronomers have now detected that flash – a burst of radio waves which travelled for more than 10bn years before reaching Earth – what they believe to be the most distant fast radio burst (FRB) ever recorded.FRBs are intense bursts of radio waves that can emit as much energy in milliseconds as the sun does inmonths or years. These mysterious pulses were firstdiscovered in 2007and havepuzzled scientists ever since, with speculation from some that they could have analien origin.In a new study published in Science, researchers have detected an FRB that originated when the universe was only about 3bn years old, meaning it has travelled through “approximately 80% of cosmic history”.Astronomers detect fastest known star in Milky WayRead moreThe burst, dubbed FRB 20240304B, is believed to be the farthest yet detected, more than double the previous distance record.The scientists detected the burst using the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa and subsequently identified its host galaxy using Nasa’sJames Webb space telescope(JWST).Dr Themiya Nanayakkara of the University of Sydney, one of the lead researchers on the paper, said when the burst was produced, “there was no Earth, there was no sun”.Data from the JWST indicated that the burst originated from a “young, very small galaxy which is forming stars at a very high speed, with not many metals around it”.There are several theories as to what the source of FRBs is, including that they originate from magnetars, neutron stars with a very powerful magnetic field.“Whatever the mechanism that causes this radio burst has to account for that fact that it can be produced in … very young galaxies with very low amount of metals,” Nanayakkara said.More than 10,000 FRBs have been detected since 2007. Some repeat continuously, Nanayakkara said, while “some of them repeat for a while and then stop … and then there are some FRBs that only go once and we never see again”.Whether the new distant burst is a one-off flash or will yield recurrent signals remains to be seen.“[But] the fun thing about FRBs is that we don’t need to know what is causing them to do some of the science we are doing now,” Nanayakkara said.This particular burst “has been travelling for 80% of the age of the universe”, he said, adding that further detections of distant FRBs would enable scientists to map unseen matter in the distant universe.Prof Matthew Bailesof Swinburne University, one of the astrophysicists whofirst discovered FRBs, described the new paper as “a validation of how powerful the FRBs are for probing the universe”.Bailes described them as “a very fundamental way of counting how many atoms there are in the universe”. FRBs are affected by the particles they travel through, enabling scientists to quantify matter that cannot be seen through optical telescopes.Dr Sara Webb, an astrophysicist also at Swinburne University who was not involved in the research, said: “You can use them essentially as a line-of-sight count for how much matter they had to go through [to get to Earth].”The discovery suggests that “FRBs might have been very common in the early universe”, she added.Explore more on these topicsAstronomySpaceJames Webb space telescopenewsShareReuse this content

title: French ministers scramble to appease students after 10 days of protests | France | The Guardian
description: Education minister promises 3,000 substitute teachers by Tuesday with schools still blockaded across France
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: Education minister promises 3,000 substitute teachers by Tuesday with schools still blockaded across France
Content: Students on the July Column in the Place de la Bastille during protests in Paris on Thursday.Photograph: Teresa Suárez/APView image in fullscreenStudents on the July Column in the Place de la Bastille during protests in Paris on Thursday.Photograph: Teresa Suárez/APFranceFrench ministers scramble to appease students after 10 days of protestsEducation minister promises 3,000 substitute teachers by Tuesday with schools still blockaded across FranceJon Henleyin ParisThu 8 Oct 2026 17.47 EDTFirst published on Thu 8 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHigh school students have again blockaded schools and marched through cities acrossFrance, promising to continue their campaign against the poor state of the national education systemin the 10th day of protests that have left hundreds injured.Large crowds took to the streets on Thursday for mainly peaceful demonstrations in cities including Lille, Rennes, Nantes, Lyon, Toulon and Marseille, while in Paris a large procession marched through the city centre to the Place de la Bastille.An estimated 25,000 students thronged the square in the east of the capital, with some climbing the monument at its centre, which commemorates France’s 1830 July revolution, while waving the tricolour flag and singing the Marseillaise.As the evening drew in, riot police fired teargas and crowd-dispersal rounds and carried out repeated baton charges to clear the protesters, some of whom hurled bottles, paving stones and other projectiles at the heavily armoured squads.View image in fullscreenA protester kicks away a teargas canister during a demonstration in the Place de la Bastille.Photograph: Julien de Rosa/AFP/Getty ImagesEliane, 16, a pupil on the Paris march, said she had come to “defend and encourage high schools in an even worse state than mine”, calling the march “magnificent”. She said she planned to continue protesting until concrete progress was achieved.The education minister, Édouard Geffray, told TF1 television on Thursday night that 3,000 substitute teachers would be deployed to about 100 high schools identified as having particularly acute teacher shortages “between tomorrow and Tuesday”.Geffray said he would also authorise the recruitment of “several hundred” new teachers. The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said the government would propose amendments to the 2027 budget to “translate some of the students’ demands into concrete measures, particularly regarding teacher replacements”.View image in fullscreenCrowds gathering at the Place de la Bastille earlier on Thursday.Photograph: Abdul Saboor/Reuters‘This is state violence’: Paris students rage at politicians and heavy-handed policingRead moreStudents earlier said the government’s reaction was not sufficient. Ryad Rani, the president of one high school students’ union, said the protesters had heard “no concrete measures whatsoever, no response to our demands”. The movement “will continue”, he said.Sabrine Kharbach, from another students’ association, said the protest, over teacher shortages, long school hours and dilapidated buildings, would last “for as long as €10bn hasn’t been put on the table”, the amount students and some leftwing politicians have said needs to be urgently invested in France’s schools.According to an Elabe poll ​for BFM TV, 72% of French people think the students’ demands are legitimate but 55% of them think the protests should stop. Unions called for another national day of action in support of the students next Tuesday.View image in fullscreenA protester reading a book as teargas is sprayed by police during a blockade near Hélène Boucher high school in Paris on Thursday.Photograph: Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP/Getty ImagesThe education ministry said fewer high schools had been forced to close than in recent days, with 224 shut on Thursday morning and 157 by lunchtime, meaning that about 95% of the country’s high schools were at least partly open.But more than 71,000 protesters took to the streets on Thursday, the interior ministry said. The demonstrations, backed by many teachers, parents and unions, involved further clashes with police around some school barricades in Paris. In Rennes riot officers used water cannon to disperse protesters.A prominent complaint on student banners and placards was the heavy-handed police response to the wave of protests. “Too young to be listened ​to, but old enough to be teargassed,” read one banner on the Paris march.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenBurning bins during a blockade of a school in Toulouse on Thursday.Photograph: Lionel Bonaventure/AFP/Getty ImagesOver the past two weeks, some demonstrators have set dustbins on fire outside their schools, destroyed bus shelters and hurled projectiles at riot police, who have responded using batons, teargas and riot-control rounds.At least 215 teenagers, 89 school staff and 761 police officers have been injured since the start of the protests, which were triggered by chronic teacher shortages, crowded classes,dilapidated buildingsand long school days.The Guardian view on the French school protests: the political class needs to heed the voice of students | EditorialRead moreThe government on Wednesdaysuspended the use of stun grenadesby police after a teenager’s hand was blown off, while saying it was “excessive” to speak of “police repression” and denying that officers had “orders to confront” the young protesters.View image in fullscreenProtesters clash with French gendarmes in Nantes on Thursday.Photograph: Stéphane Mahé/ReutersThe protests have rocked a government caught between popular demands for investment in deteriorating public services and pressure from markets to reduce France’s ballooning budget deficit and debt mountain, among the highest in the EU.The economy minister, Roland Lescure, said this week there was room to address demands for more school resources in the 2027 budget. In the current draft, schools have the second-largest funding increase after defence, with a 1.4% hike to €90.9bn.Six months away from a crucial presidential election to replace Emmanuel Macron, politicians are jockeying to exploit the protests, with the far-right frontrunner, Marine Le Pen, highlighting the damage to schools and calling for parents ⁠to foot repair bills.Her hard-left opponent, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, has praised the protesters ​as “incredible” and denounced police brutality.Explore more on these topicsFranceProtestEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Thousands march in Madrid after death of evicted pensioner Maricarmen | Spain | The Guardian
description: Rally to remember woman, 87, whose rent battle with investment firm triggered nationwide protests over housing crisis
Author: Sam Jones
Headline: Rally to remember woman, 87, whose rent battle with investment firm triggered nationwide protests over housing crisis
Content: A memorial toMaría del Carmen Abascal, whose eviction from her Madrid home of seven decades sparked housing protests across Spain.Photograph: Burak Akbulut/Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA memorial toMaría del Carmen Abascal, whose eviction from her Madrid home of seven decades sparked housing protests across Spain.Photograph: Burak Akbulut/Anadolu/Getty ImagesSpainThousands march in Madrid after death of evicted pensioner MaricarmenRally to remember woman, 87, whose rent battle with investment firm triggered nationwide protests over housing crisisSam JonesandAshifa Kassamin MadridThu 8 Oct 2026 16.11 EDTFirst published on Thu 8 Oct 2026 11.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAbout 20,000 people took part in a march through the centre of Madrid on Thursday evening in memory of María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old woman whoseeviction from her flat in the capitala fortnight before her death triggeredmass protests over Spain’s housing crisis.The pensioner, whose flat had been bought by an investment firm that sought to increase her rent by 230%, had become the public face of the crisis beforeher death in hospitalon Wednesday night.Abascal’s eviction unleashed waves of demonstrations across Spain, led to the setting up of a protest camp in the centre of the capital, and prompted the socialist-led government to propose emergency measures to try to make the rental market more equitable. When those measures were voted down by rightwing and far-right parties last week, the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, announceda snap general election, to be held on 29 November.Anger over the plight of the woman who had become known around the country as Maricarmen remained undimmed a few hours after her death. On the pavement across from the apartment building where she had lived for seven decades, a steady stream of people visited a small, steadily growing memorial. Some came to light candles or leave flowers, while others left handwritten messages such as, “You made history Maricarmen,” and “Thank you for changing Spain”.Sara, 41, who had come with her young son and a sign that read, “Maricarmen, we’ll fight for you”, said: “We’re here because I think Maricarmen’s death shows how institutions can kill a person by failing to care for them.”For many, the site was a reminder of all that Maricarmen had gone through as she tried to stay in her home,fending off three eviction attemptsbefore the investment firm succeeded in forcing her out. “When people are protected less than investors, that leads to these kinds of things happening,” Sara added. “This woman could have died – if she had died of natural causes – she could have died peacefully in her home.”Jaime, 34, pointed to all that Maricarmen had come to represent, particularly in a country like Spain, where social rights are supposedly guaranteed. “She had become a symbol, albeit one she never wanted to be, of the fight for decent housing,” he said. “So I came here because I think it’s important to restore some of the respect that Spanish society took away from Maricarmen.”Visitors included some of the housing campaigners who had helped Maricarmen fight off previous eviction attempts. “This is really hard to take,” said Miguel, 59, fighting back tears as he added a red rose to the memorial. “When money is more powerful than people’s lives, it’s unbelievable.”He said he hoped Maricarmen’s death would mark a turning point in Spain. “At least now we’re talking about this and putting names to those who are being evicted,” he said. “Because until now,there were 44 people a daybeing forced out of their homes. To the people in power, those are just numbers – now at least we’ve started putting names to those going through this.”2:50How an 87-year-old Spanish woman became the face of the fight for affordable housing – explainerThe Madrid tenants’ union announced a commemorative march at 8pm on Wednesday from the camp in the Puerta del Sol square to Abascal’s flat.“Farewell, Maricarmen!” the union said ina post on social media. “Tonight we’ll honour you with a march … to the place that was your home for 70 years, and where you just wanted to stay until the end.”Abascal’s ordeal has made housing a key issue in the forthcoming election, with Sánchez’s government seeking to push a redrafted package of measures through the council that operates when parliament has been dissolved. Meanwhile, the rightwing and far-right parties that opposed the legislation in congress last week have accused the prime minister of failing to act to address the housing crisis over the course of his eight years in office.Sánchez offered his condolences to Abascal’s family and friends on Wednesday night. “A hug also to everyone who’s feeling this loss today as their own,” he wrote on social media. “Rest in peace.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAlberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party (PP), which voted against last week’s emergency measures, also offered his condolences.“No campaigning, no political parties, no partisan ends, no more bricks in the wall,” he wrote on social media. “When a person dies, there should be nothing but respect.”The following day, however, Feijóo accused the government of trying to “manipulate the emotions of the Spanish people” by focusing on one particular eviction when there had been countless others during Sánchez’s time in office.PP politicians also joined forces with the far right on Thursday toveto attemptsto hold a minute’s silence for Maricarmen in Madrid’s regional parliament and the country’s senate. In Madrid’s municipal council, meanwhile, a rightwing attempt to block a minute’s silencewas thwartedby opposition parties.Abascal’s death has prompted reflection on how she had been treated by politicians and the media. The far-right Vox party, which also voted down the new decrees, had falsely suggested that Maricarmenwould have had a home had she been an immigrant from North Africa, while one commentator had opined that“Maricarmen was chosen during a casting call for people facing eviction”to become a leftwing saint.At least two far-right figures, including one of Vox’s MEPs, sought to sow doubt over the cause of Abascal’s death, with oneeven suggesting an autopsy should be carried out to determine whether the government had been involved. Anotherwrote: “Maricarmen was probably already made to send in her postal vote before they did her in. I expect anything from this scum.”Explore more on these topicsSpainEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Two Latvian men arrested for trespass offences at RAF airbase – as it happened | Europe | The Guardian
description: Two men arrested last night as security patrols near RAF Molesworth in Cambridgeshire found an abandoned vehicle and a breach in the fence
Author: Jakub Krupa
Headline: Two men arrested last night as security patrols near RAF Molesworth in Cambridgeshire found an abandoned vehicle and a breach in the fence
Content: 10.52 EDTTwo Latvian men arrested for trespass offences near RAF airbaseMeanwhile,we are getting a line from the UK that two Latvian nationals resident in the UK have been arrested on suspicion of trespass offences at an RAF airbase in Cambridgeshire.The two men where found last night assecurity patrols near RAF Molesworth found an abandoned vehicle and a small breach in the perimeter fence.The two men were located and arrested at 2am.In a statement, the policesaidthe matter is being investigated by officers from Counter Terrorism Policing.The incident comes just over a week after a widely reported security issue near RAF Fairford, and will raise concerns about security of UK airbases.Head of Counter Terrorism Policing London team, Helen Flanagan, said:“We’re very aware of the recent heightened interest and concern around military sites, but at this stagethere is nothing to suggest this incident is connected to the events at RAF Fairford last week.Our investigation into this incident is at its very early stages. A big part ofthis is looking at any potential motivation as to why the men were present at the site,but I must stress we are keeping an open mind at this stage and enquiries are very much ongoing.As ever, I would ask the public to remain vigilant and if you see anything of concern, then to contact police.”ShareUpdated at10.53 EDT

title: Russian attack on bus kills at least 30 people near Ukraine frontline | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Zelenskyy says Kremlin deliberately targeted ‘ordinary public transport stop’ in Kramatorsk, with 18 wounded
Author: Luke Harding
Headline: Zelenskyy says Kremlin deliberately targeted ‘ordinary public transport stop’ in Kramatorsk, with 18 wounded
Content: The regional prosecutor’s office said the vehicle was hit at 10am on Thursday by an aerial bombPhotograph: Ukrainian State Emergency Service/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe regional prosecutor’s office said the vehicle was hit at 10am on Thursday by an aerial bombPhotograph: Ukrainian State Emergency Service/AFP/Getty ImagesUkraineRussian attack on bus kills at least 30 people near Ukraine frontlineZelenskyy says Kremlin deliberately targeted ‘ordinary public transport stop’ in Kramatorsk, with 18 woundedLuke HardingThu 8 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTFirst published on Thu 8 Oct 2026 06.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Russian missile strike on a bus in the eastern city of Kramatorsk has killed at least 30 people, officials have said, in one of the worst attacks by Moscow on Ukrainian civilians this year.The regional prosecutor’s office in the Donetsk region said on Thursday the vehicle had been hit at 10am by an aerial bomb. “As of now, the death toll from this morning’s attack has risen to 30. Eighteen people were wounded,” it said, adding that all local public transport had been suspended.Images ​posted by police ‌showed bodies ‌strewn across a street littered with debris, as well ‌as a charred shell of what appeared to be a bus. A second bus had also caught fire, officials said. The strike targeted an area next to a dental clinic on the city’s Yuvileina Street.Three people had also been killed by shelling in the village of Bilenke, outside Kramatorsk, they added.Volodymyr Zelenskyysaid the Kremlin had deliberately targeted an “ordinary public transport stop”.MapSome of those killed could not be identified because of the severity of their injuries, Ukraine’s president added.He said the number of victims could “sadly rise”, as doctors fought to save the lives of those wounded.He said: “This strike will not go unanswered. Russia is trying to destroy all life in Donbas, and a response from the world is a must. A forceful response – exactly as the Russians deserve for all the deaths they have brought. May all those killed rest in peace.”The bombing follows a gruesome Russian strike on Wednesday on a five-storey block of flats in Pryluky in the northern Chernihiv region. The building collapsed, entombing those inside. At least 22 people were killed, including five children, aged between one and eight.Visiting the scene with Ed Miliband, the British foreign secretary, Zelenskyy urged the US to expand Starlink satellite internet coverage so that Ukraine could hit targets inside Russia such as launch sites. So far, Donald Trump and Elon Musk have refused Kyiv’s request.View image in fullscreenRescuers at the site of the Russian attack on the block of flats in Pryluky.Photograph: Serhii Okunev/EPAMiliband said there was “no clearer sign of Putin’s evil, evil intent and strategy in this conflict” than this week’s murderous attacks. He said: “Putin once said that he was going to win on the battlefield. He is trying to win by terrorising civilians.”Writing earlier on social media, Zelenskyy called on western allies to take “concrete steps” to boost Ukraine’s depleted air defences, amid a round-the-clock Russian onslaught in recent weeks featuring ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones.“Supplies of anti-ballistic capabilities, ammunition for our combat aircraft, and investments in interceptors – all of this is directly helping save lives every day. Important talks with our partners will take place today and tomorrow,” Zelenskyy said.Kramatorsk and neighbouring Sloviansk form part ofa “fortress belt”. They are the last two big cities in northern Donetsk under full Ukrainian military control. Russia has been trying to capture them for more than a decade, after a brief period in which Russian forces occupied Sloviansk in 2014.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenBus on fire after the Russian missile strike.Photograph: National Police of Ukraine/ReutersThe cities are home to thousands of civilians, as well as Ukrainian soldiers. In recent months, roads have been festooned with nets to protect traffic from marauding enemy drones. These defences offer little protection, however, against aerial bombs.“These are not ‘the consequences of war’, nor dry statistics. These are people killed by the Russian army,” the Donetsk regional governor, Vadym Filashkin, said ‌on Telegram after Thursday’s strike. “Russia comes to Ukrainian land with death.”He added: “The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians. For them, a bus full of passengers is an attractive target precisely because a single strike can kill as many people as possible.“Russia deliberately flouts every conceivable rule of warfare and the norms of international humanitarian law. It selects targets where it can inflict the greatest suffering on civilians.”There was criticism of the White House’s policy of engaging with Vladimir Putin, whom Donald Trumphas invited to December’s G20 summitin Miami, Florida. The Kremlin has yet to say if Russia’s leader will take part.The former US ambassador to Moscow Michael McFaul said on social media that Russia was guilty of terrorism. “There is no other word for it. Putin is running a terrorist state. That officials from my country call this terrorist a nice guy is deeply embarrassing for me.”Putin has demanded Ukraine cede the rest ​of ​the eastern Donbas region still under its ​control. Kyiv refuses to hand over its territory, believing Russia will take any concessions and carry on fighting.Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaEuropeVolodymyr ZelenskyynewsShareReuse this content

title: Italian opposition cries foul as Meloni’s electoral reform passed in secret ballot | Giorgia Meloni | The Guardian
description: Parties vow to challenge law in court, arguing that extra reward for those with 42% of support distorts public representation
Author: Angela Giuffrida
Headline: Parties vow to challenge law in court, arguing that extra reward for those with 42% of support distorts public representation
Content: Giorgia Meloni says the new, fully proportional system will ensure greater political stability.Photograph: Ludovic Marin/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGiorgia Meloni says the new, fully proportional system will ensure greater political stability.Photograph: Ludovic Marin/AFP/Getty ImagesGiorgia MeloniItalian opposition cries foul as Meloni’s electoral reform passed in secret ballotParties vow to challenge law in court, arguing that extra reward for those with 42% of support distorts public representationEurope live – latest updatesAngela Giuffridain RomeThu 8 Oct 2026 09.42 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 11.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA controversial overhaul to electoral law that critics say is aimed at boosting Giorgia Meloni’s chances of clinging on to power in elections next year has been given final approval by the Italian parliament.Meloni, the Italian prime minister, says the new system, which introduces a fully proportional model, including bonus seats for any coalition that wins the most votes, will bring about greater political stability, while opposition parties argue that it mainly serves the interests of those in power.The change was passed in a secret ballot in the lower house with 227 MPs voting in favour and 164 against.There were protests from opposition politicians who held up signs decrying the law as a “scam” and a “con” when the result was announced.Opposition parties have vowed to challenge the changes in the constitutional court, arguing that the bonus seat element, which would be granted to any coalition that reaches a vote threshold of 42% of the vote, distorts voter representation.Another contentious requirement of the changes is that parties and alliances would be required lay out their government programme and name their candidate for prime minister well before a general election.Meloni, who leads the far-rightBrothers of Italy, had made the vote a test for her ruling rightwing coalition, warning MPs from her allies, including Forza Italia and the League, that, if defeated, the government would face a crisis.While there are tensions within the coalition, which has suffered setbacks in recent months and isunder threatfrom the rise of new far-right rival Roberto Vannacci, leader of Futuro Nazionale, it has put on a show of unity and has stability on its side after becoming Italy’s longest serving government since the second world war in early September. Whereas the broad leftwing alliance, led by the Democratic party, is highly fractious with no clear leader or programme.Meloni said the victory was a response to those who wanted to see her coalition divided. “Today we respond with action: we are united, cohesive and determined to fulfil the commitments made to citizens,” she wrote on social media.Elly Schlein, theleader of the Democratic party, said Meloni’s alliance sought to change the electoral system because it feared losing the next general election, which is officially due to be held before October 2027 but could be brought forward to April or May.According to a recent survey by Ipsos Doxa, the opposition coalition could reach the 42% threshold if it overcame internal divisions and managed to convince two small radical parties to join forces.Explore more on these topicsGiorgia MeloniItalyBrothers of ItalyThe far rightEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Israel promotes film that mimics NAZA documentary | Israel | The Guardian
description: Embassies post links to hastily produced online film echoing style of real Guardian documentary about mass killings of Gaza civilians
Author: Louisa Loveluck
Headline: Embassies post links to hastily produced online film echoing style of real Guardian documentary about mass killings of Gaza civilians
Content: The new online film mimics some of the style of the real NAZA documentary (above) which uses footage shot from rooftops in Tel AvivView image in fullscreenThe new online film mimics some of the style of the real NAZA documentary (above) which uses footage shot from rooftops in Tel AvivIsraelIsrael promotes film that mimics NAZA documentaryEmbassies post links to hastily produced online film echoing style of real Guardian documentary about mass killings of Gaza civiliansLouisa LoveluckThu 8 Oct 2026 13.52 EDTFirst published on Thu 8 Oct 2026 12.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Israeli government is promoting an online film project that mimics the style of NAZA, the award-winning documentary that details Israel’s mass killings of civilians in Gaza, in an attempt to counter the real film’s findings.Thereal documentary, directed by the Oscar-winning film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, and produced by the Guardian, is in cinemas and will be shown in more than 50 countries.The Israeli government has denounced the film andannounced plans to stripAbraham and Szor of their citizenship, accusing them of treason.In recent days, Israeli embassies have been promoting a link to a hastily produced online film entitled NAZA: The Real Story. Mimicking some of the style of the real documentary, including the use of anonymised interviews shot on rooftops in Tel Aviv, it is hosted on a website called nazadocumentary.com.Ariel Averbuch, an Israeli attorney and army reservist who made the new documentary, described it as an “offensive move” intended to shift the world’s focus from allegations about the Israeli military’s killing of civilians. The film claims that Israel has the “most moral army in the world”.Another film-maker listed on the website for NAZA: The Real Story is Roi Danino, a candidate for the rightwing Israel First party.The website domain was registered on 16 September, six days after NAZA’s premiere at the Venice international film festival, where itwon the special jury prizeafter receiving the longest ovation in the festival’s history.Initially, the website falsely presented itself as a promotional page for NAZA itself, naming Abraham and Szor as the directors, and listing film festivals where the documentary was due to be screened.1:55NAZA - official trailer“Shot at night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv, the film reveals in detail the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of terrorists in Gaza,” it said, distorting the film’sofficial synopsisby removing the reference to the deaths of Palestinian civilians.That wording was removed from recent updates of the website, once the video for NAZA: The Real Story had been added to the page.It now appears as a platform for the rival film, with a counter that implausibly suggests the short film has been watched more than 42m times. (The film’s official YouTube page is listed as having just 30,000 views.)According to a technical analysis, the discrepancy suggested the viewer counter could have been driven by requests made to the website, by humans or bots, rather than the number of people who actually watched the video. When asked about the source of the 42m claim, Averbuch said he did not know and referred the questions to his tech team.The Israeli military has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians in Gaza since the Hamas attacks of 7 October 2023, in a military campaign that a United Nations commissionhas describedas genocide.View image in fullscreenRachel Szor and Yuval Abraham speak onstage at the NAZA premiere at the New York film festival on 26 September.Photograph: Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty for FLCThe 24 interviews with Israeli military insiders in the original film NAZA detail how an AI-assisted apparatus of mass surveillance was activated during theGazawar, revealing the systems that were used to target Hamas operatives in the knowledge large numbers of Palestinian civilians would also die.The Israeli embassy to the US, which shared the new documentary on its social media, said the ministry of foreign affairs was not involved in producing the film, and that it had intended only to “amplify the message of its creators and expose wider audiences to arguments challenging and dismantling the blood libels and false allegations”.NAZA film-makers say they spoke to more than 100 sources about Israeli actions in GazaRead moreThe Israeli government said on Thursday that it wasawarding the film-makers with a certificate of appreciation“for their contribution to Israeli public diplomacy”, claiming the production had garnered tens of millions of views.A Guardian spokesperson said: “We are aware that the Israeli government has been promoting a film hosted on a website that initially – and falsely – claimed it was Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s documentary.“This was a brazen attempt to mislead audiences and distract from the urgent questions raised by NAZA.”As well as its global cinema releases, NAZA will be available free on the Guardian’s website from late November.Averbuch is the founder of an organisation that says it conducts “advocacy warfare”, including through the publication of scripts to help influencers criticise Abraham and Szor’s critically acclaimed previous film, No Other Land, which documents the destruction of the Palestinian village Masafer Yatta. The two Palestinian co-directors of No Other Land, Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal, have been harassed or detained by the Israeli military since the film won an Oscar in 2025.Israeli government officials have scrambled to discredit NAZA’s content, while far-right activists have threatened to hunt down the directors.The Israel Defense Forces’ chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, has said they will use “every tool at our disposal” against the film, while themilitary has issueda 10-page response to the film, which was based on interviews with more than 100 sources with knowledge of the military systems used in the war.Within a week of NAZA’s premiere, Israel’s ministry of culture had announced a formal investigation into the documentary, calling for Abraham and Szor to be stripped of their citizenship.Demonstrators gathered outside the home of Szor’s parents, demanding that the she face the death penalty, and a mural depicting the film-makers through the sights of a gun appeared in the Israeli city of Ashdod.View image in fullscreenSpanish film industry members show support for NAZA’s directors at the San Sebastian International film festival on 25 September.Photograph: Ander Gillenea/AFP/GettyOn Monday, the far-right Israeli activist Mordechai David announced he was fundraising in order to establish a team that would “chase” Abraham. “We’ll find him,” David said in a video posted to Instagram.Szor and Abrahamaddressed the backlashto their documentary at a Q&A after its New York premiere. “Our country is doing so much to hide these systems,” Szor told the audience. “It’s not a world that is open even to the Israeli public.”At theLondon film festivalon Thursday, one of NAZA’s producers, James Wilson, said Israeli politicians’ “hysterical, vituperative, aggressive backlash” to the documentary had not been anticipated by the team behind it.Wilson said although Abraham and Szor had “anticipated displeasure … there wasn’t an anticipation of the level of aggression leading to these threats and the rabble-rousing aspect”.He added: “To have made a film, a documentary film and be threatened by the political elites of your home country, with charges of treason and defamation … it’s been very difficult and stressful and horrible and scary for them.“I try to look at the overwhelmingly positive reaction to the film in the majority of the world.”Additional reporting byPhilip McMahonandRachel HallExplore more on these topicsIsraelNAZAGazaPalestineMiddle East and north AfricaIsrael-Gaza warDocumentary filmsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Israel’s downgrading of UK consulate aims to tighten its hold on Jerusalem | Israel | The Guardian
description: Consulate targeted in sanctions spat has unusual diplomatic status that clashes with Israel’s ambitions to fully annex the city
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: Consulate targeted in sanctions spat has unusual diplomatic status that clashes with Israel’s ambitions to fully annex the city
Content: The consulate general’s diplomats are part of an independent team who report directly to London.Photograph: Abir Sultan/EPAView image in fullscreenThe consulate general’s diplomats are part of an independent team who report directly to London.Photograph: Abir Sultan/EPAIsraelAnalysisIsrael’s downgrading of UK consulate aims to tighten its hold on JerusalemEmma Graham-Harrisonin JerusalemConsulate targeted in sanctions spat has unusual diplomatic status that clashes with Israel’s ambitions to fully annex the cityThu 8 Oct 2026 13.16 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 13.40 EDTShareIsrael’s attempt to close the British consulate general in Jerusalem was primarily designed to deter London from imposing sanctions on settlements in occupiedPalestine. But it also served the current government’s ambitions to fully annex Jerusalem as a national capital, diplomatic and legal experts said.The UK mission to the city has an unusual diplomatic status, which dates back to before the founding of the state ofIsrael, rooted in a vision of Jerusalem as a neutral enclave under international control.Unlike other consulates general around the world, it is not a satellite of the British embassy in Tel Aviv. Instead its diplomats are part of an independent team, who report directly to London.British consulate in East Jerusalem will stay open as UK mission, says Ed MilibandRead moreThat is anathema to those in Israel who claim all of Jerusalem as their territory. Israeli forces occupied East Jerusalem in 1967, and the Knesset passed a law annexing the city in 1980, but that status has not been recognised by most of the world.Gideon Sa’ar, the Israeli foreign minister, threatened to close the consulate general a month ago in an attempt to deter the UK government from proceeding withplans to bar trade with West Bank settlementsand put sanctions on companies that provide them with services including financing.The UK threatened to respond with amass expulsion of diplomatsbut the two countries appear to havebacked away from a full-blown diplomatic spatas Israel prepares for national elections, due on 27 October.Britain will rebrand its consulate general ⁠as a UK “mission” and reduce the number of diplomats, but it will remain independent of Tel Aviv in a compromise one source described as a temporary “ceasefire”. If Israel gets a new leader in three weeks, negotiations on the status of the consulate and its staff could resume.Maintaining a foothold in Jerusalem and the independent status of UK diplomats was important, said Daniel Seidemann, an Israeli lawyer and expert in the geopolitics of Jerusalem who hasadvisedwestern diplomats including a British foreign secretary.“The arrangement that the UK arrived at with Israel was probably the optimal among a number of options that were even worse. So I’m not faulting anybody, but this is far from a victory,” he said.“The British presence in Jerusalem after almost a century and a half has been downgraded from one of the diplomatic mission to another office. And that is a stark qualitative change.”View image in fullscreenMaintaining a foothold in Jerusalem and the independent status of UK diplomats was important, one expert said.Photograph: Mostafa Alkharouf/Anadolu/Getty ImagesThere are seven other consulates general in East Jerusalem, all opened before 1948, representing their nations’ interests in Jerusalem and occupied Palestine. Like the UK one, they are independent and report directly to their foreign ministries.They have long been a particular thorn in Israel’s side because of their unusual status, which reflects the designation of Jerusalem as “corpus separatum”, an independent body, under the UN’s 1947 partition plan for historic Palestine.Never implemented, it envisaged Jerusalem as a sort of Vatican-like independent enclave, under international administration. That clashes with Israel’s claim on the city, and Sa’ar’s attack on the consulate should be seen in that context, and not purely as a response to sanctions.“This is part of the overall attempt to establish the primacy of a very specific Jewish-Israeli Jerusalem,” Seidemann said. “Any diplomatic presence in Jerusalem that does not pay fealty to the government of Israel and Israel’s sole sovereignty is targeted.”Other countries have missions based in Ramallah to manage relations with Palestinians, but these are technically subsidiary to Tel Aviv embassies.The US had a consulate general but closed it after Donald Trump recognised Jerusalem as the capital of Israel during his first presidency.The UK sanctions plan represents the most consequential attempt by one of Israel’s allies to halt settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank. Israeli banks are rattled by a proposal they fear could affect their business, Haaretzreportedon Thursday.An assessment by Israel’s Association of Banks laid out concerns that they could be affected, and they are refusing to say whether they will provide financial guarantees needed to underpin construction contracts for theE1 settlement in the West Bank.When Ed Miliband, the UK foreign secretary, announced his plans, he said the timing was driven partly by the Israeli government’s decision to put out tenders for this project. Israel’s finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, has boasted that it will “bury” the possibility of a Palestinian state by severing parts of the occupied West Bank.Ilan Baruch, a former Israeli ambassador to South Africa, left diplomatic service to advocate for a two-state solution, including pushing foreign governments to move beyond condemnations of Israeli policy to imposing a “meaningful price”.The threats to Britain’s Jerusalem consulate were a sign the UK had finally done that. “I was relieved [by Israel’s position], realising Miliband touched a nerve,” he said.Renaming the consulate while preserving its independent status indicated Israel had stepped back from confrontation, helped by Britain making smaller “face-saving” concessions, he said.Explore more on these topicsIsraelForeign policyPalestineMiddle East and north AfricaanalysisShareReuse this content

title: British consulate in East Jerusalem will stay open as UK mission, says Ed Miliband  | Foreign policy | The Guardian
description: UK and Israel back away from full diplomatic confrontation, though British presence in Palestine will be much reduced
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: UK and Israel back away from full diplomatic confrontation, though British presence in Palestine will be much reduced
Content: A Jerusalem municipality member stands outside the British consulate on Thursday, the deadline set by Israel for its closure.Photograph: Ammar Awad/ReutersView image in fullscreenA Jerusalem municipality member stands outside the British consulate on Thursday, the deadline set by Israel for its closure.Photograph: Ammar Awad/ReutersForeign policyBritish consulate in East Jerusalem will stay open as UK mission, says Ed MilibandUK and Israel back away from full diplomatic confrontation, though British presence in Palestine will be much reducedPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorThu 8 Oct 2026 12.43 EDTFirst published on Thu 8 Oct 2026 02.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsrael and the UK have backed away from a full-scale diplomatic confrontation, with Britain announcing it is rebranding its consulate general ⁠building in ⁠East Jerusalem ​as a UK mission, a move that will result in UK diplomats leavingIsrael, with only seven to remain in the building. Among those leaving is the consul general, Helen Winterton.The change was forced on the UK by the Israeli government as punishment for the decision by the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, last monthto ban trade with illegal settlementsand introduce a tougher sanctions regime against those who aided the building of settlements. The UK is seeking to protect the two-state solution as the best means of ending the Israel-Palestine conflict.Miliband has also backed away from athreat to expela parallel number of Israeli diplomats from London, as was once planned, arguing it would be unwise to do so during the Israeli election campaign.‘Palestinians will bear the cost’: UK consulate in East Jerusalem prepares to shut its doorsRead moreThere has been a dispute within the UK government over whether taking tough measures against Israel at such a sensitive political moment could help the re-election chances of the prime minister,Benjamin Netanyahu, before polls on 27 October if they appear to boost his standing as a leader prepared to confront the nation’s critics.Israel had ​ordered the ‌British consulate ‌in East Jerusalem to shut on Thursday, and the foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, said that it had acted on its threat, describing the consulate as closed.The consulate is separate from the UK embassy, based in Tel Aviv, and has a distinct diplomatic role, covering East Jerusalem, the rest of theWest Bankand Gaza, where it provides consular services to Palestinians. Miliband said in a statement: “The UK government reiterates its longstanding view that East Jerusalem is occupied territory.”Miliband said the mission remained independent, by which he meant it will continue to report directly to the UK Foreign Office in London rather than through the UK embassy in Tel Aviv.One former Foreign Office diplomat said: “Israel has always wanted to shut the consulates in Jerusalem […] Israel will come for the French next.”Sa’ar listed four actions to curtail UK activity in Israel, including the removal of British representatives from the International Gaza Support Center in Kiryat Gat and entry bans to Israel for 12 named individuals, including the former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn. “We established a clear principle: It is not possible to act against Israel without Israel taking appropriate measures in response,” he said. “We did not want to reach this point, but the actions of the UK Labour government brought us here.”He also accused the UK government of “hostile rhetoric, including false accusations against Israel, such as accusationsof ‘ethnic cleansing’”.View image in fullscreenEd Miliband arriving in Kyiv on Thursday.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAMiliband, who is in Kyiv, said in a statement that, having ‌withdrawn a number of staff and families in recent ​weeks partly for security reasons, it would be possible to work to build up the staffing at the mission in future months.He said Britain would ⁠not take any reciprocal action ​against Israel ​while the ​two sides engaged in ​talks, in effect suspending discussions until a new Israeli government is formed.UK sources said Sa’ar had threatened to close the whole consulate, and that it was better for Britain to retain its reduced presence in the hope it could be restored and rebuilt, regardless of the imminent election outcome.The sources emphasised that the right to take reciprocal action remained, and the UK did not accept that Israel had the legal right to close the consulate, which has stood for 200 years and is in East Jerusalem on territory that Britain and international courts recognise as occupied territory. It was thought not feasible to defy Israel since the UK diplomats would have no security protection.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMiliband said the UK mission would be independent, operational and still able to provide vital services to the Palestinian people. The value of that assertion will be tested by the small number of diplomats remaining and their reduced diplomatic status. The UK national security adviser, Jonathan Powell, travelled to Israel last week to negotiate a version of the deal.Vincent Fean, the UK consul general toPalestinebetween 2010 and 2014, said: “The term mission is a generic diplomatic term and does not of itself have any meaning … In terms of numbers, losing 20 staff is a big drop but it’s a better outcome than nothing. It leaves a space, a place and team to build up whatever the outcome of the Israeli election.”Diplomats from other western countries had been worried about any closure setting a precedent, and suggested Britain had to respond strongly to the Israeli move because it had implications beyond the immediate dispute.The ‌incident has highlighted growing frustration among Israel’s longtime allies over its settlements in the occupied West Bank, viewed by much of the world as illegal under international law. In his statement last month to the UK parliament, Miliband said settler terrorists, supported by Netanyahu’s government, werecommitting ethnic cleansingin the West Bank. Israel disputes this.The UK Foreign Office was advised informally by the former attorney general Dominic Grieve thatIsrael would be acting unlawfullyif it closed the consulate on the basis it was sited in East Jerusalem, which is recognised by the UN and most of its members as being occupied Palestinian territory.Israel has also said it will revoke the credentials of Dutch diplomats from the country’s mission toPalestinein response to the Netherlands’ ban on imports from illegal Israeli settlements. France and Canada, which joined the UK in the settlement trade ban, have not had action taken against them.UK-Israeli relations have deteriorated steadily during the war in Gaza, prompted by Hamas’s7 October 2023attack on Israel, as Britain has become increasingly critical of the way in which Netanyahu seems prepared to tolerate the deaths of thousands of Palestinians in an effort to render Hamas inoperative, a task successive Westminster governments have thought is unachievable through his methods.The UK has rescinded a large number of arms export licences to Israel, and Miliband has spoken of evidence of war crimes in Gaza. He has declined to accuse Israel of genocide on the grounds he believed this a matter for international courts to determine.Explore more on these topicsForeign policyPalestineEd MilibandIsraelMiddle East and north AfricaBenjamin NetanyahuWest BanknewsShareReuse this content

title: Florida judge allows lawsuit against Shah of Iran’s alleged ‘chief torturer’ to move forward | US justice system | The Guardian
description: Parviz Sabeti denies allegations he led Savak intelligence agency under shah and directed torture of thousands
Author: Richard Luscombe
Headline: Parviz Sabeti denies allegations he led Savak intelligence agency under shah and directed torture of thousands
Content: Parviz Sabeti in an undated picture.Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreenParviz Sabeti in an undated picture.Photograph: AlamyUS justice systemFlorida judge allows lawsuit against Shah of Iran’s alleged ‘chief torturer’ to move forwardParviz Sabeti denies allegations he led Savak intelligence agency under shah and directed torture of thousandsRichard Luscombein MiamiThu 8 Oct 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 13.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe alleged “chief torturer” for the deposed Shah of Iran is a step closer to trial for human rights abuses after aFloridafederal judge rejected his demand to halt alawsuitbrought by three former political prisoners.Parviz Sabeti, who was reportedlast yearto have lived in a quiet upscale central Florida community, is accused of being the former head of Savak, the shah’s secret police and intelligence agency. The plaintiffs say they discovered his whereabouts only after a photo of Sabeti at a 2023 protest against the Iranian government wasposted on social mediaby his daughter.He could now be made to answer as early as next year to civil claims under the Torture Victim Protection Act (TVPA) that he directed and took part in thedetention and tortureof thousands of the shah’s political opponents in jails in Tehran and elsewhere until the Islamic revolution swept the regime from power in 1979.‘A return to prison is always looming’: Iran’s Nobel laureate recounts torture in jail and hopes for the futureRead moreSabeti has denied allegations that that he was personally involved or thatSavak tortured detainees, and claimed that he “always opposed torture”.Tuesday’s sealed order by the district court judge Gregory A Presnell rejected Sabeti’s argument that a statute of limitations on the allegations should be strictly enforced and a summary judgment issued in his favor.In August 2025, Presnell rejected a motion by Sabeti’s lawyers to dismiss the case outright, ordering the parties to conduct discovery on whether the TVPA claim was time-barred, and said he would listen to arguments about why the deadline should not be extended.Sabeti’s lawyers dispute that he was difficult to find and sue before 2023, filing dozens of documents which they said proved he had lived openly in Florida under his real name, including property records, media articles, and a photograph of Sabeti with George HW Bush and his son Jeb Bush, a former governor of Florida.In May, attorneys for the three Iranian plaintiffs filed a response presenting dozens of documents and articles of their own to try to bolster their argument that there were extraordinary circumstances in the case that warranted an extension of time to bring the claim.They included the Guardian’sSeptember 2025 storythat chronicled Sabeti’s departure from Iran and his low-profile new life in Florida, where the lawsuit asserts he “has spent the last four decades out of the public eye, concealing his whereabouts and identity”.As the Guardian reported last year, Sabeti was identified as a fiercely loyal ally of the shah, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, in a secretanalysis by the US Central Intelligence Agency(CIA) written in 1978, which was not released until 2018.According to the complaint, he was “widely recognized as one of the mostpowerful and feared menin the shah’s regime … with the authority to apprehend, interrogate and prosecute opponents throughout the country”.The plaintiffs, Iranian men living in California aged 68 to 85, claim they were among thousands of people rounded up as perceived opponents of the shah bySavak, Iran’s notoriously brutal internal security and intelligence agency, and subjected to abuses at Sabeti’s personal direction.Among their claims made under the TVPA are that their captors used rape, electric shocks, near-drownings and forced nail extraction against political prisoners. They say they were abducted by Savak in Tehran, beaten into giving false confessions and served prison time.The lawsuit details the alleged use of a torture device nicknamed Apollo, an electric chair named after the early US space program, which featured a metal helmet that amplified victims’ screams into their own ears.Sabeti has previously insisted he was not involved in the detention, torture or execution of prisoners. A2023 reporton the website of the People’s Mojahedin Organization of Iran, a dissident group, cited an interview Sabeti gave to the Persian channel Manoto in which he characterized his government employment as clerical work.Court papers list seven attorneys for Sabeti. None replied to the Guardian’s request for comment by the time of publication.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionClaret Vargas, senior staff attorney for the Center for Justice and Accountability, an advocacy group representing the three Iranian plaintiffs, welcomed Presnell’s ruling, which she said allows the case to move forward towards discovery on the TVPA allegations against Sabeti. The court previously dismissed the state law claims.“I’m very glad that our clients will be able to pursue justice after all these years, and everybody deserves justice for torture regardless of who was in charge, or the regime that tortured them,” she said.“Perpetrators of torture should not escape accountability simply because the survivors were forced to live with fear for decades.“We don’t yet know the specific legal basis for the court’s decision, but it’s a really important milestone for our clients to be able to bring forth this case and really address [their allegations].”Donald Trump’s war in Iran has brought new scrutiny of the resilience of the country’s hardline Islamic regime, and the strength of the opposition to it among a sizable Iranian expat community in the US.Washington DC-based Reza Pahlavi, the former shah’s son, haspositioned himselfas a possible new leader if the current regime falls, although questions remain over his level of popular support.In June, Pahlavi, 65, was forced todistance himselffrom far-right supporters who flew banners and wore shirts with the Savak emblem at rallies.Divisions between various opposition groups of Iranians in the US were highlighted by the killing in Canada earlier this year of the Iranian activistMasood Masjoody, a critic of the US-led war and the campaign to install Pahlavi as the country’s next leader.According to the Associated Press, Masjoody’s sudden disappearance in February was followed by a threatening post on X in Farsi directed at other activists by a since-deleted account named for Savak.Explore more on these topicsUS justice systemIranTortureLaw (US)US crimeMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Oil prices jump 5% on Middle East tensions and US hurricane threat | Oil | The Guardian
description: Global bond market sell-off continues and stocks fall amid reports White House has asked to see options for more strikes against Iran
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Global bond market sell-off continues and stocks fall amid reports White House has asked to see options for more strikes against Iran
Content: Crude oil is offloaded at the Banyas terminal in Tartus, Syria.Photograph: Anadolu/GettyView image in fullscreenCrude oil is offloaded at the Banyas terminal in Tartus, Syria.Photograph: Anadolu/GettyOilOil prices jump 5% on Middle East tensions and US hurricane threatGlobal bond market sell-off continues and stocks fall amid reports White House has asked to see options for more strikes against IranLauren AlmeidaThu 8 Oct 2026 07.11 EDTFirst published on Thu 8 Oct 2026 04.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOil prices have risen sharply amid fears about escalating tensions in the Middle East and a squeeze on production from the threat of a hurricane off the US coast.Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose by 5% to $105.3 a barrel on Thursday, triggering a wave of selling in the global bond and stock markets.In the UK, the yield – or interest rate – on the 10-year government bond hit its highest level since July 2007, rising by six basis points to 5.515%. Investors appear concerned that rising oil prices could stoke higher inflation.The yield on the 30-year bond – the UK’s benchmark cost for its long-term borrowing – rose by three basis points to 6.0117%, after touching 6.036% on Wednesday, the highest since January 1998.The climbing cost of government borrowing places further pressure on John Healey, as he prepares to deliver hisfirst budget, on 28 October.The market swings came after the Atlantic reported that the White House had asked the Pentagon to draw up options for strikes againstIranbefore the US midterm elections. The report cited unnamed officials in Donald Trump’s administration who said the size and targets of potential strikes, and whether they would go ahead, were still being debated.The report has weakened hopes that Trump will refrain from escalating the conflict with Iran before the midterm polls next month. A “limited operation” could be followed up with more substantial action after the midterms, it states.Another wave of strikes against Iran represents further risk to oil supply from the Middle East, with the US-Israeli war against Tehran now entering its eighth month. Attacks on tankers in the strait of Hormuz have reached their highest levels of ⁠the war, ⁠cutting ​traffic through the waterway and deepening fears about supply.The latest attack came ⁠on Wednesday, when a tanker was hit byprojectiles off the north coast of Qatar, causing casualties, according to ​United Kingdom Maritime ‌Trade Operations.Oil prices also rose in response to a squeeze on production in the Gulf of Mexico, afterTropical Storm Isaiasstrengthened to become the first hurricane of the Atlantic season.Shell and Chevron said they were shutting down production as the storm approached the region, forecast to make landfall on Friday or Saturday.The Danish shipping group Maersk added to worries around rising energy prices on Thursday after it said it was increasing its emergency fuel surcharge on all its export collections and import deliveries. In France, which has been hit particularly hard overworries about its rising debt and growing spending, the 10-year yield rose by six basis points to 4.931%, just behind the 24-year high of 4.994% it hit last week. Yields rise when prices fall.The German 10-year yield, the benchmark for European debt, rose by two basis points to 3.504%.The yield on the US 10-year treasury, which is widely considered the best quality government debt on the market, rose by five basis points to 5.331%.Global stocks also fell, with Japan’s Nikkei share index falling 1.4% and the South Korean Kospi down 2.6%.In Europe, the Stoxx Europe 600, which tracks the biggest companies on the continent, dropped 0.9%.
