title: No ‘snowflakes’: mental health review says today’s youth have it harder and harms are real | Young people | The Guardian
description: Peter Fonagy lauds courage of young people and warns of consequences of rising prevalence of mental illness
Author: Patrick Butler
Headline: Peter Fonagy lauds courage of young people and warns of consequences of rising prevalence of mental illness
Content: Young people today face stresses exacerbated by social media and there is less belonging, more loneliness, the review says.Photograph: Maskot/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenYoung people today face stresses exacerbated by social media and there is less belonging, more loneliness, the review says.Photograph: Maskot/Getty ImagesYoung peopleAnalysisNo ‘snowflakes’: mental health review says today’s youth have it harder and harms are realPatrick ButlerSocial policy editorPeter Fonagy lauds courage of young people and warns of consequences of rising prevalence of mental illnessFull report |NHS at risk of ‘system failures’ as demand for ADHD and autism care soars, inquiry findsExplainer |What has the Fonagy review found and what does it recommend?Thu 8 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 19.09 EDTShareEighteen months ago, in anoff-the-cuff remarkduring a discussion on disability benefit cuts, Wes Streeting said mental health conditions were being “overdiagnosed”, riding headlong into another culture war.He later apologised for the comment, but at the time it seemed the then health secretary had endorsed a populist view that ordinary stresses and disappointments had become too often medicalised, resulting in a surge of bogus clinical diagnoses and creating a “snowflake generation” of fragile, avoidant and workshy young people.Prof Peter Fonagy’smammoth review of mental health conditions, autism and ADHD in England, commissioned by Streeting nine months ago, has no truck with the snowflake generation caricature: the steep rise in the prevalence of mental health problems such as anxiety and depression is real, he says, and so is the distress and difficulties they can cause.double quotation markI am in awe of their courage. Young people are contending with more powerful forces than I ever facedThe review says the drivers of this rise are cultural and social.Young peopleare exposed to Covid disruption, financial and housing insecurity, and competitive school and social stresses that are exacerbated by social media. Support services, from Sure Start to youth clubs, have been swept away. There is less belonging, it says, and more loneliness.Fonagy himself was a severely depressed teenager in 1960s London, he reveals in an unexpectedly tender foreword to the review. Today’s youth have it much harder, he writes. “I am in awe of their courage. Young people are contending with more powerful forces than I ever faced. They are not fragile. They are outnumbered.”Sceptics may yearn for a mythical time when troubled young people just had to pull their socks up, fit in and learn to deal with life’s inevitable hard knocks. Fonagy makes clear the past is another country and you cannot rewind the clock. “Simple answers are rarely adequate,” he writes.Fonagy’s brief was not explicitly to settle culture war disputes, however, and the review warns that the rising prevalence of mental illness, ADHD and autism has wider consequences: public services are overwhelmed, people suffer because they cannot get care or support, and the cost to the taxpayer is unsustainable.NHS England mental health services review: what has it found and what does it recommend?Read moreThe review is frustrated by the public debate’s focus on whether there is too much or too little diagnosis. There is a risk of overdiagnosis, Fonagy admits (though he says there is no evidence it is happening at scale), and he is scathing about the growth and reliability of unregulated private providers of diagnostic assessments.But the deeper problem, the review argues, is the disproportionate power of the diagnosis in accessing clinical care, special educational needs support in schools, or disability benefits. That encourages unfairness: those who can afford private diagnosis have a higher chance of getting support.Fonagy’s solution is to reduce the heavy reliance on diagnosis (NHSdiagnosis waiting timesare 64 weeks). An individual’s needs should be identified and triaged early with the goal of ensuring they swiftly get the support they need.The challenges Fonagy identifies are also those being grappled with by the imminentMilburn reviewof the youth jobs crisis, theTimms reviewof disability benefits, and the government’sSend changes. His solutions may not fly, but his warning is clear: “Continuing as we are is not sustainable.”Explore more on these topicsYoung peopleMental healthAnxietyDepressionAttention deficit hyperactivity disorderAutismNHSanalysisShareReuse this content

title: NHS England mental health services review: what has it found and what does it recommend? | NHS | The Guardian
description: Prof Peter Fonagy’s 607-page report is categoric that mental distress has increased substantially and ‘cannot be explained by greater awareness alone’
Author: Anna Bawden
Headline: Prof Peter Fonagy’s 607-page report is categoric that mental distress has increased substantially and ‘cannot be explained by greater awareness alone’
Content: The report says mental health and neurodiversity services should ensure those with the highest needs get specialist assessment sooner.Photograph: Pornpak Khunatorn/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenThe report says mental health and neurodiversity services should ensure those with the highest needs get specialist assessment sooner.Photograph: Pornpak Khunatorn/Getty Images/iStockphotoNHSExplainerNHS England mental health services review: what has it found and what does it recommend?Prof Peter Fonagy’s 607-page report is categoric that mental distress has increased substantially and ‘cannot be explained by greater awareness alone’Full report |NHS at risk of ‘system failures’ as demand for ADHD and autism care soars, inquiry findsAnalysis |No ‘snowflakes’: mental health review says today’s youth have it harder and harms are realAnna BawdenHealth and social affairs correspondentThu 8 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 19.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Fonagy review ofNHSEngland’s mental health, ADHD and autism services was commissioned in 2025 by Wes Streeting, then the health secretary, in response to growing concerns that spiralling waiting lists for assessment, diagnosis and care threatened the NHS’s ability to meet the demand.The 607-page report,published on Friday, says that without a radical overhaul, mental health and neurodiversity services will be overwhelmed. Here are some of its key findings and recommendations.1.Unprecedented and growing levels of distress are realThe report is categoric that mental distress has “increased substantially across the population”, is real and affects everyday functioning, and that the rise “cannot be explained by greater awareness alone”. About one in four 16- to 24-year-olds are now thought to have a common mental disorder such as anxiety and depression, up from one in six in 1993, while self-harm, eating disorders, OCD, PTSD and drug dependence have also increased.About 4 million children are in “serious distress”, and if current trends continue that could reach 4.5 million by 2030, the report says. At current rates self-harm cases could reach 2.5 million across England’s population. But rates of severe mental illness such as bipolar or schizophrenia have remained much more stable, while hazardous drinking has declined.Chart of numbers of cases of mental health need2.The system is failing everyoneWith the cost of mental ill health standing at £300bn a year, “continuing as we are is not sustainable,” the report warns. “Not for the people waiting weeks, months or years, becoming more distressed because help is locked behind waiting for a diagnosis; not for those with the most severe needs who cannot access specialist care; and not for a society paying the human and economic price of failing to support people to participate in family, community, education and working life.”3.Overdiagnosis of ADHD and autism is not yet widespread but is a growing riskWhile the proportion of the population thought to have ADHD and to be autistic has remained broadly stable at an estimated 3.8% and 1.2% respectively, the recent exponential rise in those diagnosed, as well as even larger numbers waiting to be assessed, means we have reached a tipping point where people are at risk of being misdiagnosed with ADHD and autism, said Prof Simon Wessely, the review’s vice-chair.The report finds that the proportion of children aged six to 11 with an ADHD diagnosis has increased more than sixfold in five years, and for 12- to 17-year-olds more than 15-fold, to 2.7% and 3.9% respectively. And with more than 560,000 people waiting for an ADHD assessment and more than 254,000 for an autism assessment, the proportion of people with a diagnosis of ADHD or autism is expected to rise further.ADHD diagnoses chartAutism diagnoses chart“This does not, by itself, establish that overdiagnosis is currently occurring at scale,” the report states. “However, the evidence suggests we are entering a phase in which the balance of risks between underdiagnosis, misdiagnosis and overdiagnosis may be changing, with the risks of misdiagnosis and overdiagnosis becoming increasingly important considerations for policy and service delivery.”4.Private companies should be banned from advertising ADHD and autism assessmentsThe report finds that NHS spending on independent-sector ADHD services rose by 252% over three years and that private providers accounted for more than a third of NHS-funded autism assessments in the 2025-26 financial year.Responding to the report’s call for greater regulation, the health secretary, Yvette Cooper, said the government would “make all diagnostic assessments for ADHD and autism Care Quality Commission-regulated, so people can be confident that assessments are high quality and that the NHS is not being overcharged by independent or private providers”.Chart of self-reported cases of autism, ADHD or other neurodivergenceShe stopped short of committing to banning private-sector advertising of ADHD and autism assessments to the public, instead saying the Advertising Standards Authority would be asked to review it, “to ensure people receive accurate information and are not exploited by companies encouraging them to seek assessments they may not need”.5.The NHS should provide a needs-first serviceProf Peter Fonagy, the review’s chair, said the NHS needed to shift from a diagnostic labelling model to a flexible, needs-led system. “Diagnosis remains essential and must be protected,” he said, but added: “What has to change is that it is no longer the only door through which help can be reached.”Instead, people should be able to seek help through school, GP or community services, mental health services, social care, employers and family hubs. Support should be given at the point of need, not contingent on a diagnosis. And there should be a single service for mental health and neurodevelopmental support to provide more joined-up help.In response, the Department of Health and Social Care committed to a major overhaul of services to ensure “earlier, needs-led support for children, young people and adults, without long waits for clinical diagnosis”.6.Scrap first-come-first-served waiting listsPatients waiting for a diagnosis should be prioritised. Rather than a first-come-first-served system, mental health and neurodiversity services should ensure those with the highest needs – such as self-harm, multiple difficulties or risk of imminent school exclusion or unemployment – get specialist assessment sooner.Waiting lists should be “actively reviewed” to enable that prioritisation. But the authors denied that would leave those with less acute symptoms without any route to diagnosis, stressing: “No one should be removed from a pathway without appropriate assessment, communication and discussion.”Explore more on these topicsNHSHealth policyMental healthAttention deficit hyperactivity disorderAutismAnxietyDepressionexplainersShareReuse this content

title: NHS at risk of ‘system failures’ as demand for ADHD and autism care soars, inquiry finds | NHS | The Guardian
description: England-focused review led by Prof Peter Fonagy returns stark warning and calls for shift to ‘needs-led’ system
Author: Denis Campbell
Headline: England-focused review led by Prof Peter Fonagy returns stark warning and calls for shift to ‘needs-led’ system
Content: The review found the number of people suffering mental distress has risen sharply across all age groups in England since the 1990s, especially under-18s.Photograph: Johner RF/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe review found the number of people suffering mental distress has risen sharply across all age groups in England since the 1990s, especially under-18s.Photograph: Johner RF/Getty ImagesNHSNHS at risk of ‘system failures’ as demand for ADHD and autism care soars, inquiry findsEngland-focused mental health review returns stark warning and calls for shift to ‘needs-led’ systemExplainer |What has the Fonagy review found and what does it recommend?Analysis |No ‘snowflakes’: mental health review says today’s youth have it harder and harms are realDenis CampbellandAnna BawdenThu 8 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 19.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe NHS inEnglandis heading into a “world of system failures” as it struggles to cope with relentlessly rising demand for mental health, ADHD and autism care, leaving those affected desperate for support, a government-commissioned inquiry has found.The stark warning was made in a review led by Prof Peter Fonagy into the sharp rise in demand over recent decades for help with mental health and neurodevelopmental conditions.It found there was an increasing risk of overdiagnosis of autism and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and urged ministers to toughen the regulation of the private clinics to which many people are turning because they cannot get assessed quickly by theNHS.The experts behind the review also called for access to care to be based primarily on a person’s needs so fewer people would have years-long waits for a formal diagnosis.NHS England mental health services review: what has it found and what does it recommend?Read moreThe review found that the number of people suffering mental distress has risen significantly across all age groups in England since the 1990s, especially the under-18s.The number of 16- to 64-year-olds with a common mental disorder increased from 15.5% in 1993 to 22.6% in 2024. However, it jumped more sharply – from about one in six to one in four – among 16- to 24-year-olds over the same period.The evidence shows that sceptics are wrong to cast doubt on young people’s struggles, the 607-page report found.“That’s sometimes been attributed to personal failures, people being told they’re making it up, it’s all in their head, which is absolute nonsense,” said Prof Simon Wessely, a leading psychiatrist and vice-chair of the review.The report’s conclusions may have significant implications for the government’s drive to reduce the number of young people in the UK not in education, employment or training – now almost 1 million – and the size of the welfare bill, with a record 2.8 million people too sick to work; and also for schools as they grapple with the demands arising from the growing number of pupils with special educational needs.Fonagy, a psychoanalyst and clinical psychologist at University College London,dismissed the notion that young people in particular were “snowflakes”who were less resilient than in previous generations. “The rise in mental health problems is real, is affecting everyday functioning and cannot be explained by greater awareness alone,” his report said.He lamented that an array of social and economic circumstances had piled unprecedented pressure on young people. “There is increased uncertainty – financial pressures, insecure work, unaffordable housing – but perhaps more important, a lack of hope among young people that their lives will be better than their parents, and that’s the first time since the second world war that surveys have noticed that.”The explosion in demand for help with mental ill-health and neurodiversity has left people stuck on waiting lists for years at a time and with worsening symptoms, Fonagy said. At the end of last year more than 560,000 people in England were waiting to be assessed for ADHD – 17 times more than were doing so in 2019. Another 254,000 people were waiting for a diagnostic assessment for autism, taking the total number waiting to more than 800,000. Almost all – 90% – had been waiting for at least three months.Chart showing percentage of UK NHS patients with an active recorded ADHD diagnosis within a five-year window, by age group and from 2000 to 2025Chart showing percentage of UK NHS patients with an active recorded autism diagnosis within a five-year window, by age group and from 2000 to 2025The number of six- to 11-year-olds being diagnosed with autism has also soared. It jumped 20-fold to 4.58% between 2000 and 2025 and by even more among those aged 12 to 17 over the same years, from 0.1% to 4.06% – a 40-fold jump. And the proportion of children aged six to 11 with an ADHD diagnosis has increased more than sixfold in five years and more than 15-fold in 12- to 17-year-olds, to 2.7% and 3.9% respectively.While 4 million children already suffer from “high psychological distress’’, if current trends continue, that could reach 4.5 million by 2030, the report warned. The number of under-18s who self-harm could also rise from 1.9 million to 2.5 million.Chart showing projected numbers of mental health cases by condition by 2030The exponential rise in diagnoses of autism and ADHD means the UK has reached a “tipping point” where people are at risk of being misdiagnosed with either condition, Wessely warned.The authors did not find that overdiagnosis was occurring at scale, but added that the evidence “suggests we are entering a phase in which the balance of risks between underdiagnosis, misdiagnosis and overdiagnosis may be changing, with the risks of misdiagnosis and overdiagnosis becoming increasingly important considerations for policy and service delivery”.The increasing tendency of young people to self-identify as neurodivergent – as many as a fifth of secondary school pupils do so – means that “the line between the social and the medical is beginning to blur”, they added.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionChart showing percentage of self-reported cases of autism, ADHD or other neurodivergence by school yearThe 10-month review found “strong concerns about the consistency and quality of ADHD and autism assessments being carried out by independent providers, and the financial incentives associated with assessment activity”.Ministers should ban direct-to-public advertising of such services and ensure that all clinics offering them are regulated by the Care Quality Commission, it said.Growing numbers of young people have a combination of mental ill-health and ADHD or autism, or both. “Co-occurence is the rule rather than the exception,” the report said. For example, 61% of 16- to 24-year-olds with a common mental health condition also had autistic traits, and 57% had ADHD symptoms.Graph showing percentages of 16- to 24-year-olds with a common mental health condition and ADHD or autism from 2007 to 2004Graph showing percentage of 16- to 64-year-olds with one, two or three mental health or neurodevelopmental conditionsThe report said their needs meant the NHS should bring together mental health and neurodevelopmental services and move to a “needs-led” system.The Royal College of Paediatrics and ChildHealthbacked Fonagy’s call for diagnosis to no longer dictate who received care.“Too often, a diagnosis is the only route to accessing meaningful help. This means that children and families can be left struggling alone while waiting for assessments, with little or no support available in the meantime,” said Dr Ronny Cheung, its officer for health services.The NHS moving to a “needs-led” approach would “ensure children and young people can seamlessly and more quickly access a robust, holistic and reliable standard of care”, he added.Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, will draw on Fonagy’s recommendations in putting together the forthcoming mental health strategy, which is due by the end of the year.In her response, she promised that the NHS would provide a “needs-led” system under which people would get much faster care. She has asked NHS England to establish how it can provide faster advice, assessments and treatment.She said: “It is clear that mental health services need to change to focus more on the early support young people need to stay in education or work or keep their lives on track.”She also pledged to ensure all private assessment clinics are regulated but did not commit to the advertising ban Fonagy said was needed.Explore more on these topicsNHSMental healthAttention deficit hyperactivity disorderAutismHealthNeurodiversityChildren's healthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Pentagon says execution of Fort Hood shooter will be livestreamed | Pete Hegseth | The Guardian
description: Nidal Hasan, army psychiatrist who killed 13 people, will be executed by firing squad on 3 December
Author: Joseph Gedeon
Headline: Nidal Hasan, army psychiatrist who killed 13 people, will be executed by firing squad on 3 December
Content: Pete Hegseth announces a new navy shipyard in Baltimore on Tuesday.Photograph: Anna Rose Layden/EPAView image in fullscreenPete Hegseth announces a new navy shipyard in Baltimore on Tuesday.Photograph: Anna Rose Layden/EPAPete HegsethPentagon says execution of Fort Hood shooter will be livestreamedNidal Hasan, army psychiatrist who killed 13 people, will be executed by firing squad on 3 DecemberJoseph Gedeonin WashingtonThu 8 Oct 2026 19.18 EDTFirst published on Thu 8 Oct 2026 17.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePete Hegseth has said the execution of Nidal Hasan, the former army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, will be a public event when the sentence is carried out later this year. A defense department official later confirmed the execution will be livestreamed.In an interview with Real America’s Voice, the Pentagon secretary said the firing squad will carry out the sentence at Fort Hood, Texas, at 1pm on Thursday, 3 December. This would be the firstUS militaryexecution in more than 60 years.“It was a radical Islamist attack in uniform inside the ranks, and so he’s going to get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be, and we’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth said.Hasan opened fire at a medical processing center on the Texas base on 5 November 2009, killing 13 people and wounding dozens more. A military jury sentenced him to death in 2013, and he has been held at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas ever since. He exhausted his appeals last year, which cleared the way for Donald Trump to approve the sentencethis weekon a recommendation from Hegseth.Investigators had found that Hasanhad exchanged 18 emailswith Anwar al-Awlaki, a radical cleric who was subsequently killed in a US drone strike, in the months before the attack. At his court martial, Hasan said he had acted to stop American soldiers from deploying to Afghanistan to kill fellow Muslims, before his own impending deployment. A review led by William Webster, a former FBI director, concluded that the bureau should have investigated his correspondence more thoroughly.In the interview, Hegseth said Barack Obama had called the attack “workplace violence”. The Pentagon initially treated the shooting as a workplace-violence incident rather than a terrorist attack, aclassificationthat affected the victims’ eligibility for Purple Hearts and other combat-related benefits.But there is no record of Obama himself using the phrase. At a memorial days after the attack, he instead described the victims as Americans who had been unable to escape “the horror of war”, while calling the shooting a tragedy and saying the killer would face justice.The last known case of a military firing squad in the US was inNovember 1945, but the Trump administration has sought to bring it back in Trump’s second term to expedite capital punishment cases. Five US statesallow for firing squads: Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah.Abroad, Amnesty International’smost recent annual reviewlists Afghanistan, China, North Korea, Saudi Arabia, Somalia, Taiwan, the United Arab Emirates and Yemen among the countries that still use firing squads.Asked whether Hasan had made a final request or reached out to Trump, Hegseth replied: “Don’t care. We’ll see him on December 3.”Explore more on these topicsPete HegsethFort Hood shootingsUS militarynewsShareReuse this content

title: Curtis Flowers, US man wrongfully imprisoned for 22 years, dies aged 56 | Mississippi | The Guardian
description: Flowers, tried six times over 1996 murders of four people, faced execution before supreme court tossed his conviction
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Flowers, tried six times over 1996 murders of four people, faced execution before supreme court tossed his conviction
Content: Curtis Flowers exits the Winston-Choctaw regional correctional facility with his sister Priscilla Ward in Louisville, Mississippi, in December 2019.Photograph: Rogelio V Solis/APView image in fullscreenCurtis Flowers exits the Winston-Choctaw regional correctional facility with his sister Priscilla Ward in Louisville, Mississippi, in December 2019.Photograph: Rogelio V Solis/APMississippiCurtis Flowers, US man wrongfully imprisoned for 22 years, dies aged 56Flowers, tried six times over 1996 murders of four people, faced execution before supreme court tossed his convictionAssociated PressThu 8 Oct 2026 18.36 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 18.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCurtis Flowers, a Black man who spent more than 22 years in prison and was on death row in Mississippi before theUS supreme courtthrew outhis conviction and death sentence, has died. He was 56.Flowers’ family confirmed that he died on Wednesday at his home inMississippi, attorney Rob McDuff told the Associated Press on Thursday.No cause of death was given, said McDuff, who was part of Flowers’ legal team.Flowers was 26 when he was arrested several months after the July 1996 shooting deaths of four people inside a furniture store in Winona,Mississippi.Curtis Flowers’ conviction overturned over removal of black jurorsRead moreAt the time, prosecutors described him as a disgruntled former employee who sought revenge against the store’s owner because she fired him and withheld most of his pay to cover the cost of merchandise he damaged. Nearly $300 was found missing after the killings.Flowers wastried in the killings six times. JusticeBrett Kavanaughwrote in the high court’s 7-2 decision in 2019 that the removal of Black prospective jurorsdeprivedFlowers of a fair trial.During the sixth trial in 2010, Flowers was sentenced to death. There were 11 white jurors and one Black juror who considered the case after district attorney Doug Evans struck five Black prospective jurors.Flowers remained in prison for six months after the supreme court ruling because he was still under indictment. He finally was released in December 2019 after a judge set bond.Mississippidroppedcharges against Flowers in September 2020.“Today, I am finally free from the injustice that left me locked in a box for nearly 23 years,” Flowers said in a statement. “I’ve been asked if I ever thought this day would come. I have been blessed with a family that never gave up on me and with them by my side, I knew it would.”Explore more on these topicsMississippiUS justice systemCapital punishmentUS crimeUS supreme courtUS prisonsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump made ‘clear’ that media ban was due to critical coverage, court told | Media | The Guardian
description: Lawyer for CNN, MS Now and Politico says Trump admitted he banned networks from White House over their coverage
Author: Jeremy Barr
Headline: Lawyer for CNN, MS Now and Politico says Trump admitted he banned networks from White House over their coverage
Content: The CNN booth at the White House after Donald Trump announced he would ban CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House in Washington DC on 18 September 2026.Photograph: Evan Vucci/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe CNN booth at the White House after Donald Trump announced he would ban CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House in Washington DC on 18 September 2026.Photograph: Evan Vucci/ReutersMediaTrump made ‘clear’ that media ban was due to critical coverage, court toldLawyer for CNN, MS Now and Politico says Trump admitted he banned networks from White House over their coverageJeremy Barrin WashingtonThu 8 Oct 2026 13.56 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 14.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump continues to be the strongest witness for the media companies arguing that they were unfairly barred from the White House at his direction, a lawyer representing CNN,MS Nowand Politico told a federal judge on Thursday afternoon.The media coalition was in court asking the judge to extend the temporary restraining order (TRO) he issued on 24 September requiring the White House to lift the ban for 14 days. That temporary reprieve was scheduled to expire on Thursday, but district court judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, said he would extend it until Tuesday and that he would probably rule on a motion for a preliminary injunction by that day. That means the White House will be forced to allow journalists fromCNN, MS Now and Politico to continue accessing the building until at least Tuesday.Theodore J Boutrous, who has represented numerous media companies that have sued the Trump administration over access issues, said the president made abundantly clear ina recent interview with Time magazinethat he chose to bar the three news organizations because of their critical coverage of him. (Under binding court precedent, news organizations cannot be removed from the White House for editorial or viewpoint-based reasons.)Asked by Time for the “impetus” for the ban, Trump replied: “It’s just bad story after bad story, and when I say bad story, I can handle bad stories. I’ve got a lot of bad stories. Most of them are fake, and it’s not only CNN, and it’s not only MSDNC [sic]. It’s a lot of other people.” He made no mention of national security concerns, one of the primary reasons that has been given by government lawyers as a rationale for the ban.“The case has gotten stronger for the plaintiffs thanks to President Trump,” Boutrous told the judge, citing what he said was “a confession of viewpoint discrimination and retaliation”. He added: “It’s really just absolutely clear … President Trump, to give him credit – he’s not hiding it.”While the judge didn’t give a strong indication of which direction he was leaning, he accepted Boutrous’s argument when questioning the lone lawyer representing the White House, Michael Velchik.“The decision-maker seems to have said I’m taking this action because of X and Y, and the government is saying: ‘No, it’s Z,’” the judge said. “It just seems like that fact pattern is a hard one around.”Velchik, who began his argument by saying “the White House is a sacred place,” said a failure to adhere to basic standards of journalistic conduct was also one of the precipitating factors in the decision, something he said was in line with Trump’s comments criticizing the way that these three specific news organizations operate.He also faulted the media companies for not responding to post-hoc letters giving the plaintiffs a chance to rebut the charges against them, something that Boutrous later described as a “sham process”.In his ruling granting a TRO for the media plaintiffs, Kelly said the White House had violated constitutional requirements for due process by not giving the companies adequate notice for what the standards for acceptable conduct are and not giving them a chance to protest against the potential sanction in advance.Nothing from Thursday’s hearing seemed to indicate that the judge had changed his thinking on that important standard, suggesting he is likely to adhere to his earlier decision-making and extend the lifting of the ban.The judge told the government’s lawyer that they “still have a notice problem, it seems to [him], or at least a notice issue”. Kelly said the standards for adequate advance notice laid out in a binding circuit case involving a similar White House access issue “are probably the biggest hurdle you have”.Explore more on these topicsMediaTrump administrationCNNMS NowUS politicsUS television industryTV newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Starbucks reportedly exploring Chipotle takeover | Starbucks | The Guardian
description: Move would reunite chief executive Brian Niccol with chain he led before joining coffee company two years ago
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Move would reunite chief executive Brian Niccol with chain he led before joining coffee company two years ago
Content: A Chipotle Mexican Grill restaurant inside Aventura Mall, Miami, Florida.Photograph: Jeff Greenberg/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA Chipotle Mexican Grill restaurant inside Aventura Mall, Miami, Florida.Photograph: Jeff Greenberg/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesStarbucksStarbucks reportedly exploring Chipotle takeoverMove would reunite chief executive Brian Niccol with chain he led before joining coffee company two years agoReutersThu 8 Oct 2026 13.35 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 13.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStarbucks has explored a takeover of Chipotle Mexican Grill, theFinancial Timesreported on Thursday, in a move that ⁠would reunite chief executive Brian Niccol with the burrito chain he led before joining the coffee giant two years ago.The potential deal comes as restaurant chains wrestle with uncertain demand from inflation-weary ⁠consumers and rising operating costs, prompting ⁠companies to look ​for new avenues of growth while facing pressure to improve profitability.Starbucks has worked with advisers in recent months on a takeover proposal for Chipotle, the FT reported, citing people familiar with the ⁠matter.Starbucks and Chipotle did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment.Shares of Chipotle, which has a market capitalization of nearly $39bn, were up about 6% on Thursday, while those of Starbucks were down about ⁠3%. Starbucks is worth about $107bn, according to LSEG data.Analysts said any acquisition would probably be a costly undertaking for Starbucks, which is ​still investing heavily in its turnaround efforts.“A deal could require ‌heavy borrowing or issuing shares,” said ‌Lale Akoner, global market strategist at eToro. “Without a compelling financial case, investors may view the deal as an expensive distraction.“Starbucks is in ‌the midst of a turnaround under Niccol, who has prioritized customer satisfaction through investments in staffing and store improvements aimed at reducing wait times and restoring the coffeehouse atmosphere that helped make the chain a global brand.Since Niccol joined the company in September 2024, Starbucks has committed at least $500m to labor investments as part of its reorganization, contributing to pressure on profitability. As of the fiscal third quarter, adjusted operating margin was 14.4%, down from 16.7% in the same quarter two years earlier, according to LSEG data.Starbucks ‌has reported four consecutive quarters of comparable sales growth under Niccol, but in July he said that, “We have more work to do.““The timing of this would be a little weird, given that Starbucks is in ​the middle of their transformation and hasn’t yet shown the margin improvement investors are probably hoping for. Instead of jump-starting the transformation, at first blush, this seems more like jumping the shark instead,” said Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist, Annex Wealth Management.Chipotle, meanwhile, has been contending with softer traffic as consumers pull back on discretionary spending, while higher food and labor costs have pressured margins across the restaurant industry. Its shares have ⁠nearly halved since Niccol left the company.A potential deal could accelerate Chipotle’s international expansion, some analysts said.“What ​I like about this potential is the ​opportunity CEO Brian Niccol would have to leverage ​Starbucks’ licensed partnerships in Europe to expand Chipotle more aggressively,” said Jim Sanderson, an analyst at Northcoast Research.As ​of the end of ‌last year, Chipotle had ​nearly 4,000 restaurants in the United ​States and about 100 international locations. Starbucks, meanwhile, has roughly 40,000 stores globally, including about 18,000 in North America.Niccol joined Starbucks in 2024 after spending six years at Chipotle, where he was credited with steering the company through the aftermath of its food-safety crises and building out its digital business, helping drive years of strong sales growth.Explore more on these topicsStarbucksFood & drink industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Top bosses at Goldman Sachs to share bonus pot worth up to $500m | Goldman Sachs | The Guardian
description: Eye-watering sum, to be split between 20 bankers, is one of the biggest payouts in the bank’s history
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Eye-watering sum, to be split between 20 bankers, is one of the biggest payouts in the bank’s history
Content: The bank’s chief executive, David Solomon, is due to take about $100m (£75,595) of the reward.Photograph: Aaron Schwartz/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe bank’s chief executive, David Solomon, is due to take about $100m (£75,595) of the reward.Photograph: Aaron Schwartz/ReutersGoldman SachsTop bosses at Goldman Sachs to share bonus pot worth up to $500mEye-watering sum, to be split between 20 bankers, is one of the biggest payouts in the bank’s historyKalyeena MakortoffBanking correspondentThu 8 Oct 2026 14.09 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 14.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTop bosses atGoldman Sachsare in line to share a bonus pot worth up to $500m (£378m) this year, marking one of the biggest payouts in the Wall Street bank’s history.The eye-watering sum will be shared between 20 bankers, with its chief executive, David Solomon, due to take about $100m (£75.6m) of the reward, which is made up of Goldman Sachs stock.That is more than double the value of the record $47m (£35.5m) annual pay packet he was granted last year.The $500m bonus pot is the culmination of a long-term investment plan first crafted by the bank in 2021.The final sum, which is due to be confirmed later this month, is tied to how high Goldman’s share price has climbed over the past five years, as well as how its stock price has performed compared with peers such as JP Morgan and Bank of America over that period.Goldman Sachs said the bonuses were meant to persuade bosses to stay at the bank “in an increasingly competitive market”.The bank’s president, John Waldron, who is widely expected to succeed Solomon as chief executive, is also in line for a payout, alongside other top bosses such as the co-heads of global banking and markets, Ashok Varadhan and Dan Dees.News of the bumper bonus, which was first reported by Bloomberg, comes days before Goldman is due to report third-quarter earnings on 13 October.The bonuses reflect the value of Goldman Sachs stock, which has surged roughly 146% over the past five years, and climbed about 300% since Solomon took the helm as chief executive.A spokesperson for the bank said: “The board created these awards to achieve three principal objectives: align compensation with rigorous performance thresholds, ensure leadership continuity and enhance retention of our top talent in an increasingly competitive market. It’s no secret our firm has performed exceptionally well in the years since.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe payouts are the latest in a string of large payouts for executives in the US, particularly on Wall Street.The US lender Citigroup announced earlier this year that its chief executive, Jane Fraser, had been paid a record $42m (£31.8m) for 2025. Meanwhile, JP Morgan’s chief executive, Jamie Dimon,took home a total pay package worth $43m (£32.5m) last year, up 10% from a year earlier. Dimon’s own long-term incentive award is worth about $270m (£204.1m), according to Bloomberg.Explore more on these topicsGoldman SachsBankingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Microsoft suspended from applying for green cards for H-1B workers, JD Vance says | Microsoft | The Guardian
description: Vice-president also says Adobe is barred from visa program that allows high-skilled workers to apply for US residency
Author: Johana Bhuiyan
Headline: Vice-president also says Adobe is barred from visa program that allows high-skilled workers to apply for US residency
Content: Microsoft signage at an office building in New York on 27 April 2026.Photograph: Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMicrosoft signage at an office building in New York on 27 April 2026.Photograph: Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesMicrosoftMicrosoft suspended from applying for green cards for H-1B workers, JD Vance saysVice-president also says Adobe is barred from visa program that allows high-skilled workers to apply for US residencyJohana BhuiyanThu 8 Oct 2026 14.23 EDTFirst published on Thu 8 Oct 2026 12.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMicrosoft is suspended from applying for permanent residency for workers employed through a US visa program for high-skilled workers, JD Vance announced on Thursday.The US vice-president accused the tech company of abusing the H-1B system, which allows those on the visa to work while they apply for and are in the process of obtaining a green card.“Our message to Microsoft is, you’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers,” Vance said at a press conference announcing the suspension. “You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants.”‘Someone else will do it for less’: refugees in Kenya are powering tech for dwindling payRead moreMicrosoft said the vast majority of its workers were American and 80% of the H-1B applications it filed in the last year were for extensions or status changes for people who already worked for the company.“Microsoft only files H-1B petitions for those who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category,” the company wrote in a statement. “We pay our employees some of the highest compensation in the tech sector, and our wages are among the highest of all H-1B filings. We pay our H-1B employees the same as any other employees doing comparable work.”The US labor department also said Adobe had been similarly suspended.“We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labor certification applications involving these companies,” said Keith Sonderling, the US labor secretary, in a statement.Microsoft applied for H-1B visas for nearly 3,700 workers in 2026, making it the fifth largest employer of workers on the visa. Tech companies are the biggest employers of H-1B workers across the industry. Amazon topped the list with more than 9,300 petitions this year. Sonderling said since 2009, Microsoft and Adobe had received about 230,000 approvals for H-1B visas and 100,000 “permanent labor certifications”, a step towards an employment-based green card.“If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants,” Vance said.TheTrump administrationhas set its sights on the H-1B program for some time, arguing that it is rife with abuse. Vance said that, on average, workers hired through the H-1B program were making $20,000 less than US workers in the same position.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“So I’m sure that everybody here understands the game that is being played,” Vance said. “You bring in indentured servants from outside the country, you lay off American workers and, if you’re a corporation, you make a ton of money by undercutting the wages of American workers, replacing them with people who, frankly, shouldn’t be in the United States of America to begin with.”Immigration advocacy groups have long called for reforms for the H-1B program, though for different reasons. Those in the program are often beholden to their employer because their visas are tied to the company that applied for them, making it difficult to switch jobs if things aren’t going well or if they want to find a job with a higher salary.These groups, like the National Immigration Forum, largely disagree with Vance. They argue that competing for specialized talent from around the world benefits the US economy.“The United States has long benefited from its ability to attract talent from around the world, particularly in STEM, higher education, research, and innovation,” the National Immigration Forum wrote in aSeptember 2026 blogpostdiscussing proposed changes to the H-1B program. “As countries increasingly compete for highly skilled workers, policies that make the United States less attractive could strengthen global competitors.”Explore more on these topicsMicrosoftUS immigrationJD VanceTrump administrationUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend | Soccer | The Guardian
description: Michael Carrick is wary of ‘Dr Tottenham’, Oliver Glasner returns to Selhurst Park and will City summon a siege mentality at Anfield?
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Michael Carrick is wary of ‘Dr Tottenham’, Oliver Glasner returns to Selhurst Park and will City summon a siege mentality at Anfield?
Content: Declan Rice, Erling Haaland and Jay Dasilva will be looking forward to getting back on the pitch for varying reasons.Composite: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDeclan Rice, Erling Haaland and Jay Dasilva will be looking forward to getting back on the pitch for varying reasons.Composite: Getty ImagesTen things to look out for this weekendSoccerPremier League: 10 things to look out for this weekendMichael Carrick is wary of ‘Dr Tottenham’, Oliver Glasner returns to Selhurst Park and will Manchester City summon a siege mentality at Anfield?Premier League top scorers|View the league tableGuardian sportThu 8 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 19.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google1Rice rested and refreshed?Declan Rice’s future role in England’s midfield was questioned by Gary Lineker after Alex Scott’s impressive first senior international start in the 7-0 thrashing of Croatia. But the decision to withdraw from Thomas Tuchel’s squad in an attempt to manage his workload made sense after Rice had only three weeks off post-World Cup before returning to pre-season training. The 27-year-old has struggled with persistent back problems after suffering a hamstring injury last December and Mikel Arteta will hope that the rest has done Rice – who is thought to be close to agreeing a lucrative new contract at the Emirates – the world of good as they prepare to resume the defence of theirPremier Leaguetitle against Leeds on Saturday.Ed AaronsArsenal v Leeds, Saturday 12.30pm (all times BST)2Ready? Garnacho’s time to shineHavertz, Isak, Dorgu … spate of injuries with national teams leaves sour taste for top clubsRead moreSeveral Aston Villa players shone for their countries during the international window but one of those who stayed with the club may have made the biggest impression on Unai Emery. Villa’s remaining squad went to Spain for a mid-season training camp, including Alejandro Garnacho, whose last cap for Argentina was almost two years ago. Garnacho has been lesser-spotted in a Villa shirt, playing just 31 minutes as a substitute, but scored in both of Villa’s friendlies during the break, against Southampton and Sevilla. The 22-year-old, who joined Villa on loan from Chelsea in the summer with a conditional obligation, was an unused substitute for their past matches but is he now primed to affect games? Villa are hopeful Emery has unlocked Garnacho, who has struggled for form since leavingManchester United. “Ready now!” Garnacho posted on social media last weekend and Villa will hope that is the case.Ben FisherAston Villa v Brentford,Saturday 3pm3Toth can soothe pain of Scott’s injuryWith Eli Junior Kroupi, Amine Adli, Veljko Milosavljevic and Julián Araujo yet to feature this season due to injury, Marco Rose must have been tearing his remaining hair out upon learning Alex Scott got hurt on England duty and will be out of action for two months. Sitting 17th and still searching for their first league win, the German’s side squandered nine points from winning positions in four of their first five games – and it was the 23-year-old who was central in ensuringBournemouthhad those leads in the first place. With just 55 minutes of football behind him this season, it seems unlikely Alex Toth will get the nod to replace Scott when Bournemouth travel to Chelsea with the older, more experienced Ryan Christie available and in good form. But having forced his way into the Hungary starting lineup during the international break it would be no surprise to see the 20-year-old get more minutes with a view to being used far more often given his side’s gruelling schedule of nine matches in the next month.Barry GlendenningChelsea v Bournemouth, Saturday 3pmView image in fullscreenAlex Toth impressed for Hungary during the international break and will look to make his mark for Bournemouth.Photograph: Peter Morrison/AP4Ipswich’s calm an obstacle for FulhamIpswich’s place in mid-table, their total of six points, came via victoriesover SunderlandandCrystal Palace. Gary O’Neil’s team were presented with a tough opening schedule, and while defeated by Manchester United, Liverpool and Arsenal, their manager has not allowed those reverses to dilute team spirit. Speaking to the media following thehome defeat by Liverpool, O’Neil painted an ultra-positive picture that defied most observers’ view of a game beyond his team’s reach from the early stages. Thus far, a successful strategy, certainly by comparison to early season at winless Fulham. Like O’Neil, Álvaro Arbeloa is new to his job. An improved performance in thedraw against Uniteddid not result in a victory Fulham deserved, though there were signs of the progressive, attacking football the arrival of the former Real Madrid interim promised. Much of the burden has fallen on Josh King, the teenager building on last year’s breakthrough season.John BrewinIpswich vFulham, Saturday 3pm5Ballard’s absence a boon for BrightonStill in the Carabao Cup, with a Europa League campaign to negotiate and just four points acquired from their opening five Premier League excursions, the games are about to start coming thick and fast for a Sunderland side whose ability to cope with such a hectic schedule remains to be seen. Having lost Dan Ballard and Brian Brobbey to hamstring injuries during the international break, Régis Le Bris will have to reshuffle his pack against a free-scoring Brighton side who make the 700-mile round trip to Wearside for their first game since embarrassing Arsenal three weeks ago. While Wilson Isidor will almost certainly deputise for Brobbey, Ballard’s centre-back berth will be filled by either Omar Alderete or Nordi Mukiele. Having shipped five last time out againstManchester City, a Sunderland defence that had looked conspicuously porous in the early stages of this season will need all their focus if they are to stop the gallop of a team that have already scored 16 goals.BG.Sunderland v Brighton, Saturday 3pm6Crisis talk lingers in air at Old TraffordIf “Dr Tottenham” is a thing, Manchester United possess their own healing powers for opponents. Self-harm is a factor too. Theyrolled out the welcome matto Premier League newcomers Hull on opening day and Brighton wereushered back into a Carabao Cup tie. In United’s final game before the international break flagging Fulham were able to restore some faith, their goal via slapstick defending from Lisandro Martínez and Senne Lammens. Can Old Trafford, where fans will have regulatory matters at City to celebrate, lift the gloom for Tottenham? This season, like last season and the one before that, Spurs have assumed the mantle of crisis club, a status Michael Carrick’s January arrival temporarily removed from United. Lose to Tottenham, and the crisis prefix is likely to be reattached. Tottenham have done damage before. In September 2024, a 3-0 Spurs win at Old Trafford began Erik ten Hag’s hurtle towards the exit. Losing the Europa League final started Ruben Amorim’s downward spiral. Carrick beware?JBManchester United v Tottenham, Saturday 5.30pm7Fiery reception for Glasner at PalaceAll eyes will be on Oliver Glasner as he returns to Selhurst Park with Nottingham Forest on an afternoon that will be emotionally charged for both sets of supporters and in the boardroom. The Crystal Palace chair, Steve Parish, sought to defuse tensions last week when he urged fans to “buck the trend” by welcoming the manager who led the south London club to the first three major trophies in their history in the space of 12 months. “I would be mortified if he gets anything other than the roof blown off,” said Parish. But given the strength of feeling towards Forest and their owner, Evangelos Marinakis – who is still blamed by some for Palace’sdemotion to the Conference Leagueat the expense of Forest last season – many have still not forgiven Glasner for joining their rivals and could still make their feelings known when the Austrian takes his seat in the dugout before kick-off.EACrystal Palace vNottingham Forest, Sunday 2pmView image in fullscreenWas this the calm before the storm for Oliver Glasner?Photograph: Ritchie Sumpter/Nottingham Forest FC/Getty Images8Aerial battle of the dead-ball bossesIn Sergej Jakirovic and David Moyes,Hull Cityand Everton boast two of the more “pragmatic” managers in the Premier League. Renowned for their safety-first defensive styles, both teams are happy to surrender possession, rank among the top flight’s lowest sides in pass completion rates, and rely on rapid transitions and set pieces for a major share of their total expected goals. A game featuring two defences that pride themselves on their obduracy may well be settled by a well-delivered dead ball into a packed penalty area. While it may not be aesthetically pleasing, expect to see the massed ranks of defenders on both sides spending much of Sunday afternoon bracing themselves for rearguard action while peering towards the sky. The last time these sides met in the Premier League, Everton ran out easy 4-0 winners. A decade on, the aerial traffic is unlikely to be quite so one-way.BGHull City vEverton, Sunday 2pm9Anfield to turn up heat on besieged CityManchester City resume playing under the darkest of clouds, with a visit to their greatest rivals of a golden period now shrouded by a guilty verdict. Five Premier League wins from five under Enzo Maresca had offered hopes of success in a post-Pep Guardiola era. The dial has since moved on what constitutes success for a club where minds are consumed by legal issues but the band must play on. Can Maresca summon a siege mentality? City lifted a treble, including the Champions League, when the 100-plus charges first came to public light in 2023. The Anfield crowd will readily remind City of the infamy their club faces down. That Guardiola’s now-disputed dominance came at the cost of Jürgen Klopp’s great team will add to the ire, and very probably the pyro greeting to Anfield. Cool heads may be required in the policing and on the field, to which a return to focusing on football may offer welcome relief.JBLiverpool v Manchester City, Sunday 4.30pm10Will Coventry build on first win?International football’s incursions have curbed the adrenaline rush ofCoventry’s win at Nottingham Forestand Jay Dasilva’s brilliant goal, his club’s first in the top division since 2001. That gave Frank Lampard foundations to build on, a blueprint, where Forest were allowed to blow themselves out before Dasilva’s strike came on the counter. It was Stephen Mfuni, 18, on loan from Manchester City, who starred in that rearguard effort on his Premier League debut. Coventry now seek a first Premier League goal at a stadium opened in 2005, after the club’s long decline had set in. Newcastle this week passed five years of the ownership of a consortium led by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund. There have been two seasons of Champions League football, a trophy lifted and yet a sense of unfulfilled promise. Matthias Jaissle is leading the second phase of a jagged development process, this season’s positive signs tempered by reverses such as the4-1 defeat by Leeds, shows how far Coventry must travel.JBCoventry v Newcastle, Monday 8pmPosTeamPGDPts1Man City58152Arsenal54123Brighton511104Brentford5695Leeds5496Liverpool5397Everton5398Hull5289Newcastle50810Chelsea5-2711Ipswich5-4612Man Utd50513Nottm Forest5-1514Sunderland5-4415Crystal Palace5-5416Aston Villa5-5417AFC Bournemouth5-2318Coventry5-9319Fulham5-3220Tottenham Hotspur5-62Explore more on these topicsFootballTen things to look out for this weekendPremier LeagueManchester CityArsenalBrighton & Hove AlbionBrentfordLeeds UnitedfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘One of one’: A’ja Wilson stands alone with record fifth WNBA MVP award | A'ja Wilson | The Guardian
description: The Las Vegas Aces star becomes the first player to win three straight WNBA MVP awards, moving clear of Sheryl Swoopes, Lisa Leslie and Lauren Jackson
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: The Las Vegas Aces star becomes the first player to win three straight WNBA MVP awards, moving clear of Sheryl Swoopes, Lisa Leslie and Lauren Jackson
Content: A’ja Wilson celebrates after hitting a three-pointer during the Las Vegas Aces’ 101-91 win over the Seattle Storm in June.Photograph: Ethan Miller/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA’ja Wilson celebrates after hitting a three-pointer during the Las Vegas Aces’ 101-91 win over the Seattle Storm in June.Photograph: Ethan Miller/Getty ImagesA'ja Wilson‘One of one’: A’ja Wilson stands alone with record fifth WNBA MVP awardAces star wins record fifth WNBA MVP awardWilson becomes first player to win three straightOlivia Miles finishes second in MVP votingGuardian sportand agenciesThu 8 Oct 2026 17.05 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 19.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA’ja Wilson fine-tunes her shooting touch following every practice. That little bit of extra work has defined her greatness since being drafted first overall in 2018.On Thursday, she received a voice message from former US vice-president Kamala Harris congratulating her onredefining greatness leaguewideafter she was named WNBA MVP for a third straight year and for the fifth time overall.“Obviously, that is an honor,” Wilson said. “A woman of our history, and I’m so appreciative to be able to share that moment with her through the phone call and the message of her delivering that I won my fifth MVP.”2026 WNBA MVP voting resultsIn addition to becoming the first player to three-peat, Wilson won the award in 2020 and 2022.Commissioner Cathy Engelbert, Aces owner Mark Davis and team president Nikki Fargas accompanied Wilson’s mother, Eva, who presented her daughter with the trophy.“Each one of these has not been taken lightly,” Wilson said, flanked by all five of her MVP trophies. “In my heart, they’ve always been so special. But this one here, I cried a little bit harder. This one here is just a little bit different, and whatever that may look like, or whatever that may feel, my fifth one, I think, is one that’s just ... when you dream as a young girl, your dream so big and you write your goals out, and you just never imagine that you were able to just check them off.“And when you’re able to check them off – small wins, big wins – it truly means a lot. And so I think that’s why I cried a little bit harder on this one, because 15-year-old A’ja wasn’t sitting up here dreaming about being a five-time MVP. She wasn’t dreaming about being a three-time champion. She was dreaming about surviving this world.”The peerless A’ja Wilson may already be the WNBA’s greatest ever player | Bryan Armen GrahamRead moreThe 30-year-old Wilson once again led the league in scoring (26.2) while shooting nearly 53% from the field. She averaged 9.4 rebounds, a career-best 3.2 assists and 1.9 blocks.The 6ft 4in center-forward continued to expand her offensive repertoire, shooting a career-best 40.4% from three-point range while making a personal-high 38 three-pointers. Her career scoring average of 22.1 points per game is now the highest in league history.Wilson scored at least 30 points in 13 games, tying the single-season record she established last year, and recorded 33 games of at least 20 points. She also led the league with 19 double-doubles featuring at least 20 points and 10 rebounds.Her season included a 45-point performance against Connecticut on 15 May, making her the first player inWNBAhistory with multiple games of at least 45 points. She climbed from 21st to 11th on the league’s all-time scoring list and now stands just 12 points from overtaking Sue Bird for 10th.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly for the 2026 WNBA seasonSign up toWNBA 30A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWilson has helped the defending champion Las Vegas Aces reach the WNBA semi-finals for the eighth consecutive season after finishing the regular season with a 31-13 record. But their pursuit of a fourth championship in five years is in jeopardy, with the third-seeded Acestrailing Golden State 2-0 in their best-of-five series. Las Vegas will host Game 3 on Friday night, needing a victory to keep their season alive.“This is great, I love it, not going to take for granted, shine her up, let’s do it,” Wilson said. “But tomorrow, when it comes to hoisting it in front of the fans, I love the fans ... but I doubt I will be doing that. I’ll be warming up with my team. ... Everyone in this room knows the competitor that I am. Everyone knows what my main focus is, and that is to get a game.”View image in fullscreenAces star A’ja Wilson has been named the WNBA’s most valuable player for a record fifth time, becoming the first player in league history to win the award in three consecutive seasons.Photograph: Ethan Miller/Getty ImagesWilson received 65 of 74 first-place votes and nine second-place votes for 713 points from a national panel of sportswriters and broadcasters. Minnesota rookieOlivia Milesfinished second with 442 points and six first-place votes, followed by Indiana guards Kelsey Mitchell (287 points) and Caitlin Clark (212). New York’s Breanna Stewart rounded out the top five with 171 points.No other WNBA player has won more than three MVP awards, with Sheryl Swoopes, Lisa Leslie and Lauren Jackson each claiming the honor three times. In the NBA, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar holds the record with six MVP awards, while Michael Jordan and Bill Russell each won five.“A’ja Wilson is one of one,” Fargas said. “She’s now standing in a category that no other WNBA player in the history of the league has accomplished. She’s in the conversations with the Michael Jordans and the Wayne Gretzkys of the world – where she belongs.”Explore more on these topicsA'ja WilsonWNBALas Vegas AcesKamala HarrisCaitlin ClarkShareReuse this content

title: With no Pulisic and good results, have the USMNT moved on from their savior complex?  | USA | The Guardian
description: The US have been defined for so long by the next singular player. This past perfect window shows that era may be over
Author: Leander Schaerlaeckens
Headline: The US have been defined for so long by the next singular player. This past perfect window shows that era may be over
Content: The US team huddle before facing Canada.Photograph: Taylor Banner/USSF/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe US team huddle before facing Canada.Photograph: Taylor Banner/USSF/Getty ImagesSoccer with Jonathan WilsonUSAWith no Pulisic and good results, have the USMNT moved on from their savior complex?Leander SchaerlaeckensThe US have been defined for so long by the next singular player. This past perfect window shows that era may be overSign up for our free newsletter hereThu 8 Oct 2026 11.45 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 11.55 EDTShareIn 1990, then-United States men’s national team manager Bob Gansler made a critical and somewhat controversial choice. He left three of the program’s laureled veterans at home and brought a young and little-tested team to the World Cup in Italy, the USA’s first in 40 years.As Gansler recalled later: “I was thinking not only for ’90, but I was thinking about the 90s.”In 1998, Steve Sampson was looking to the future as well. He had lucked into the USMNT’s managerial gig and had barely clung on to it going into that year’s World Cup, but he nevertheless made a confident proclamation. “In 10 to 15 years, we’ll win the title, there’s no doubt about it,” he told the Washington Post. “When we Americans decide to do something, we’ll see it through.”A sense took hold sometime during that period, while never really acknowledged or said out loud, that the USMNT were the team of the future.Justin Ellis helps US cap a perfect international window with 1-0 win over CanadaRead moreThey never really stopped being that. And this bullishness on the hazily outlined not-right-now-but-definitely-sometime-later-on tended to coalesce around one player, maybe two. The USMNT made their modern World Cup breakthrough powered by the energy and unfettered talent of 20-year-olds Landon Donovan and DaMarcus Beasley in 2002. When those two foundered at the 2006 World Cup, another young player, Clint Dempsey, emerged. That year, a 16-year-old Freddy Adu made his USMNT debut.And so a pattern formed: the US soccer community waited to be lifted to the next plane by a savior. The next kid. Or maybe the one after that. He’ll do it for us. Or else the next one will.Dempsey outlasted Donovan and faded just as Christian Pulisic emerged. Because even as a golden-ish generation coalesced around him, Pulisic was seen as the player expected to make something happen at the 2026 World Cup, the culmination of an eight-year project of rebuilding the national team. He was expected to activate Hero Mode, the way he briefly had in Qatar in 2022, throwing himself in front of a cross at the expense of a pelvic contusion butbundling the make-or-break winnerinto the Iranian goal.View image in fullscreenCavan Sullivan celebrates scoring against Mexico.Photograph: Patrick Mulligan/USSF/Getty ImagesHe never did it in 2026. Aside from a great first half in the tournament opener, Pulisic’s home World Cup was a bust, and the USMNT’s campaign ended with a whimper.On its face, it felt odd thatMauricio Pochettinoshould launch a youth movement in the first camp after the World Cup. The core of his team had hardly aged out; all but defender Tim Ream are comfortably on the right side of 30. All the same, he called in 13 debutants and eight teenagers.If results in the months after a World Cup count for anything at all, they have vindicated the Argentinian’s decision to freshen things up. The kids, sprinkled in among a robust base of veterans, reeled off4-1and4-2victories over Peru and Chile, respectively, before dispatching Mexico in amerciless 3-0 walloping. On Tuesday, they concluded this jumbo-sized international window with amature 1-0 win over Canadain a scruffy, scrappy game, vanquishing a team whose fierceness and physicality had given the US agreat deal of troublein the recent past.What was startling, however, wasn’t just how much young talent is waiting down the depth chart – or now, perhaps, very much on the surface of it – but how little Pulisic, the latest savior, was missed in his absence. You easily might have forgotten that he wasn’t even there while watching a composed and polished team reel off four straight wins. The same was true for Weston McKennie, one of the USMNT’s load-bearing players for the last half decade. They both stayed with their Italian clubs, either hoping to use the time off to get back in favor with their manager (Pulisic at Milan) or to heal up an injury (McKennie at Juventus).skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe USMNT’s kids are thriving, and ‘they have a bit of swag to them’Read moreIn their absence, so many players carried the load, contributing in ways big and small, taking turns coming up with the big play, that the burden was never on any one player. Cavan Sullivan may well be next in line in the succession of the USMNT’s star players – or maybe it will be Julian Hall, or Adri Mehmeti, or Zavier Gozo, or Justin Ellis, or Mathis Albert – but there was no intimation that this was his ship to propel under his own power. This was not Sullivan’s team now, as then-manager Bruce Arena told Pulisic after the US failed to reach the 2018 World Cup in Russia.The big takeaway from this mega-pack of an international break – which encompassed more games than the USMNT’s run at several big tournaments – is that this team may, at long last, no longer be so dependent on one player, or even a small handful of them.If this program is entering into a post-savior age – moving on from Pulisic-pendencia, as it were, or whoever-pendencia– that’s a clearer sign of progress than the emergence of some new prodigy, or indeed a cluster of them.What this team, and this soccer country writ large, appear to have grown instead, is the kind of depth US fans used to envy in other, more developed soccer nations. If at the 2030 World Cup, the US TV commercials don’t all feature the same player, in the way Pulisic largely hogged the commercial blocks this past summer, it will represent another step forward.Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: USMen’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts,which is out now. He teaches at Marist University.This is an extract from Soccer Desk, a newsletter from the Guardian US.Subscribe for free here.Explore more on these topicsUSASoccer with Jonathan WilsonUS sportsChristian PulisicMauricio PochettinocommentShareReuse this content

title: Valtteri Bottas reveals lizard-leaping, python-dodging cycling exploits on epic ride | Valtteri Bottas | The Guardian
description: Valtteri Bottas has revealed the details of an incident-packed 418km bike ride between Malaysia and Singapore
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Valtteri Bottas has revealed the details of an incident-packed 418km bike ride between Malaysia and Singapore
Content: Valtteri Bottas poses with his bike after arriving Singapore at the end of a 418km ride from Malaysia.Photograph: Simon Galloway/LAT ImagesView image in fullscreenValtteri Bottas poses with his bike after arriving Singapore at the end of a 418km ride from Malaysia.Photograph: Simon Galloway/LAT ImagesValtteri BottasValtteri Bottas reveals lizard-leaping, python-dodging cycling exploits on epic rideCadillac driver rode between Malaysia and SingaporeFour-day trip helped him acclimatise for Singapore GPGiles RichardsThu 8 Oct 2026 12.08 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 14.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleValtteri Bottas has revealed the details of an incident-packed 418km bike ride including encounters with snakes, being chased by dogs and the eerie atmosphere of riding through the jungle at night as the Cadillac driver cycled between Malaysia and Singapore this week.The 37-year-old is a keen cyclist and after a suggestion from his girlfriend, the Australian Olympic cyclist Tiffany Cromwell, he decided to take on the challenge of riding from the last round in Sepang near Kuala Lumpur to this weekend’s grand prix on the street circuit in Singapore, under his own steam.Verstappen’s victory in Sepang should serve as a warning to Red Bull’s rivals | Giles RichardsRead moreHe managed the journey, which the rest of the F1 paddock undertook in flights that last just over an hour, in four days of riding including off-road and gravel sections beginning on the Sunday after the race in Malaysia. He completed 56km on the Sunday, before putting in two big stints on Monday and Tuesday, both of 161km, before concluding with 40km to finish on Wednesday.Speaking before this Sunday’s night race in Singapore the Finn, who has won 10 grands prix, described events that included leaping over a lizard en route.“Saw some snakes, which I was a little bit worried about but actually they were pretty chill. They were just doing their thing,” he said. “I saw one cobra, saw one python just crossing the path in front of me. Saw some of those big lizards that you also see here.“One was on the path, I had to jump over it with a bike. So I saw it like last minute. Got chased by one dog. Got stuck behind a group of cows on a small track. Eventually they moved away.”He admitted it had been hard, but added that it was a unique experience. “What was the wildest part was the riding at night in the jungle. The noise in there is like … your mind starts to play games of what is out there. But then you just need to crack on and keep going. Riding with your lights at night, that was probably the most epic part in the forest.”Bottas has taken part in cycling events when he is away from F1. Earlier this year he finished fifth in his age group in a qualifying event in Czechia for the Gravel World Championships, earning him a place in the competition which he is unable to take up because it clashes with the race this weekend.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueWithCadillacin their first season in F1 the team are still very much coming up to speed. Bottas has yet to score a point and is 22nd of 23 in the drivers’ standings, with eight DNFs in what was always going to be a difficult year for the fledgling team. He observed that the heat on the journey had made his bike seat like a “cheese grinder” but that it would not impair his build up to this weekend’s race.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I obviously wouldn’t do it if I knew it hurt my preparation,” he said. “So I’m pretty good. The amount of sweat in those days was quite impressive. You get used to the heat the more time you spend in the heat, so that can help me hopefully a little bit.”Quick GuideRwanda GP expected in 2030ShowRwanda will host an F1 Grand Prix in 2030, it is understood, marking the first race in decades on the African continent. The nation has been chasing a Grand Prix race for years, having already used football, basketball and other sports to enhance its image and attract investment. A source in the country’s government told AFP: "Rwanda’s bid to host the Formula 1 race has been greenlit, an agreement has been reached." An official announcement is expected to be announced in the Rwandan capital, Kigali, next week, with Qatar supporting the project. President Paul Kagame formally announced the bid when Rwanda hosted a gathering of the FIA in December 2024. "It all comes down to respect, and giving everyone the chance to contribute, where they can," he said at the time.Seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton has long called for an African stop on the F1 circuit, backing Rwanda’s plans in 2024 and calling the country "one of my favourite places".AFPWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.The race in Sepang was a one-off to stand in for the cancelled Bahrain GP, but it is believed talks have opened about a potential return for the circuit in future, which Bottas said may prompt him to repeat the feat.“When I got to the hotel yesterday afternoon, I said to myself, no, not again. But now, today, I’m like, yeah. Let’s see.”Explore more on these topicsValtteri BottasFormula One 2026Formula OneCadillacMotor sportCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Indiana Fever and the Magasphere: a WNBA team’s dangerous path to popularity | Indiana Fever | The Guardian
description: Teams have always symbolized division within America. And the Fever have come to prominence during a time of dark political intensity
Author: Howard Bryant
Headline: Teams have always symbolized division within America. And the Fever have come to prominence during a time of dark political intensity
Content: The Indiana Fever made the playoffs this season before their exit to the Las Vegas Aces.Photograph: Jeff Haynes/NBAE/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Indiana Fever made the playoffs this season before their exit to the Las Vegas Aces.Photograph: Jeff Haynes/NBAE/Getty ImagesIndiana FeverIndiana Fever and the Magasphere: a WNBA team’s dangerous path to popularityHoward BryantTeams have always symbolized division within America. And the Fever have come to prominence during a time of dark political intensityThu 8 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 07.43 EDTShareIt’s over for now, but no professional sports team spent more time receiving and drawing attention to itself than did theIndiana Feverthis season. The Fever has broken, the team eliminated by the defending champion Las Vegas Aces for the second straight season, but Indiana succeeded in being the WNBA’s canary in the coal mine, embodying both the obvious and unintended consequences of rapid growth, while also allowing themselves to be a season-long distraction: part-time professional basketball team, part-time right-wing culture war centerpiece. Less than a decade ago, Atlanta and Minneapolis were praised for their unified political stances.
