Today, Trumpism has replaced social justice as the defining characteristic of the league – and as the curtain closed on the 2026 WNBA regular season, Indiana stood at its epicenter.The Fever were the most polarizing team in professional sports, known less for their basketball than their culpability in pulling the league from its old cultural identity as a Black/queer league into its current climate of political divisiveness – a calculated and dangerous path to popularity. This season, there was the basketball of theWNBA, and then there was the Indiana Fever, the league’s Maga-friendly option.Their two most recognizable players, Caitlin Clark and Sophie Cunningham, were in a constant state of churn, always in the news, always embroiled against another,symbolizing and pandering to America’s fractures. Their best and longest-tenured player, Kelsey Mitchell,hasn’t been able to concentrate fullyon basketball the past two seasons as the Clark-Cunningham sideshow devours the oxygen and may end her time in Indiana that began as the second overall pick in 2018.Clark remains the league’s biggest name and its chief avatar – mildly reluctant orwilling pawn, but an avatar nevertheless. She is an avatar for the money at a time when broadcasters and venture capitalists are making their bets on women’s sports. She represented a certain type of hope, that the day had arrived where women’s team sports would enjoy the same visibility as female stars such as Serena Williams and Lindsey Vonn.She was an avatar of weaponization, the speculator’s proof that the WNBA is doomed by its own hand for not recognizing her overall importance to its future, a future bizarrely framed as bright only if Clark succeeds – an odd framework for sports, where the final score and holders of the trophies determines who wins.Most obviously and explosively, Clark was an avatar for whiteness, a Christian, hetero whiteness that holds the pervasive belief that it is straight, white America – already the overwhelming and unchallenged dominant cultural and financial force in this country – that is under assault. Any struggle Clark showed on the court – a foul call, a non-call – was treated as if it were an urban crime statistic, unmistakable proof that Black people had even turned basketball lawless. The opportunistic and racist White House and the Trump administration repeated this fiction. Republican members of Congress earlier this season insinuated Clark was being discriminated against by the league because she is white. The Congressmen threatened the WNBAwith a Department of Justice investigationif the league did not take steps to protect her. Clark and the Fever did little to dispel the notion.Whenever Clark did succeed, her partisans saw it as proof of how much better the league would be if only it stopped persecuting her. Through Clark, and how she navigated playing basketball in a league largely comprised of Black women – even as Breanna Stewart, Paige Bueckers and a host of other white women thrive without incident – was how the government (as well as many fans and journalists) framed the state of women’s professional basketball. She is half of what all the fuss has been about.The other half is Cunningham, who spent much of the seasonbuilding the scaffoldingfor her second act by driving a wedge into heart of the league, positioning herself at the center of the attention-fueled culture war against trans women, being the blonde, blue-eyed foil to the league’s unruly Black women, and providing an entry point for the bros, their money and misogyny to show up,for men such an Enes Kanter Freedomto do what they have always done to women’s sport – find a way to denigrate it and be rewarded with attention. While it was all very tired and calculating, framed asspeaking her truth,designed to reach the very group of white male sports fans that have either criticized or ignored women’s sports but are now bringing their toxicity to the tent under the guise of “growth,” Cunningham has been the subject of more attention than she’s ever had in her decade-long career, with public appearancesand lengthy profiles. She knows exactly to whom she is talking, and why.The Fever carrying these burdens – or wearing them proudly until having to answer for them – is how Clark’s career has shifted from starting her first season a phenom joining a team that hadn’t had a winning season in seven years to ending her third in daily controversy, with her as the signature, aggrieved face of Maga’s team.With the avatars mercifully tabled, Clark emerged as an excellent player with enormous upside and serious deficiencies. She is a volume scorer but not yet a great one – her career field-goal percentage is just 42.3, below the league average, and for all her dazzle, her career three-point percentage is a below-average 34.2. She shot 36.1% from three this season, below the Fever team average of 38.6%. She is an adept playmaker whose true skill may be less in creating offense for herself and more in controlling the tempo of the game and involving her teammates. She was second in the league in assists and first in turnovers, fitting considering she constantly has the ball – similar to James Harden in a way. She is an apathetic defender.As a basketball presence, she is wholly unlikeable. She does not play the game with her teammates as much as beyond them – a common affliction of many superstars that in victory is touted as a virtue but looks selfish following first-round defeats. She does not appear to play the game with joy or intensity, but carries a childish outrage, not only confronting officials on virtually every trip downcourt, but sprinting to berate them in dead-ball situations. Clark plays with grievance, an entitled grievance that recalls the White House grievance, the same grievance shared by much of the white electorate that uncoincidentally claims her as their champion – they’re all unfairly under attack.For all the criticism, WNBA officials have actually shown remarkable restraint toward her. She exaggerates most calls and outwardly flops on others to steal calls – call it European gamesmanship, but the true nature of flopping is to receive something undeserved and is the worst example of immoral basketball. Even during timeouts Clark finds a way to spar with someone, be it a cameraman or an assistant coach.Like Cunningham, however, Clark has mastered the key component of the so-called attention economy – she sees to it the camera is always on her. A more professional Clark, with fewer outbursts and deeper concentration on basketball would lower the temperature on the league, her team, herself, and would probably win her more trips to the foul line – but there was virtually no evidence this season that is what she wants.Superstar petulance is nothing new, and if Stephanie White doesn’t return as coach, it won’t be the first time a star player will be accused of getting the coach fired. Nor is it the first time a sports team has reflected a national political mood or been pulled into its vortex. Usually reflection marks triumph – Black and Jewish America loved the Dodgers because of Jackie Robinson and Sandy Koufax just as the Yankee teams of Tony Lazzeri, Frankie Crosetti, Joe DiMaggio, and Phil Rizzuto made them beloved in Italian-American homes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly for the 2026 WNBA seasonSign up toWNBA 30A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTeams have also symbolized division. In the 1980s, the Boston Celtics were often considered white America’s team because of Larry Bird, the high number of white players the Celtics routinely signed, and the perception that the Celtics did not play with the flamboyant Blackness that defined the rest of the league, which allowed white fans to see themselves in their no-nonsense, blue-collar ethic.Despite the presence of James White, Dont’a Hightower, the McCourty twins and Stephon Gilmore, the late-stage Brady/Belichick Patriots wereadopted by certain white supremacistsbecause the Patriots were led offensively by a handful of white players – Tom Brady, Rob Gronkowski and Julian Edelman. The supposedly colorblind whites had found their ideal.None of those examples, however, have existed within the combination of today’s dark political intensity where the federal government has positioned itself as the legal guardian of whitenessandthe precarious political footing of the league. The nation has effectively closed its borders to everyone except white South Africans, while Cunningham encourages the right to use the WNBA for anti-trans fodder and the DOJ believes Clark needs its protection.In a feeble attempt to distance itself from the obvious racism, the Fever periodically made bland, unconvincing statements –there’s no room for hate in the game –but their actions undermined their sentiments. Cunningham knows exactly who her fans view as the enemy, which fires to stoke on her podcasts, which dog whistles to sound. As does Clark, for her constant on-court histrionics elicit the right sympathy from the right people. They both know exactly what they’re doing.The season over, the Fever closed 2026 not by celebrating their best record since 2015, or by marking the first time since the 2009-2012 season the franchise posted three-straight 20-win seasons and have momentum as a potential title contender, but with more grievance. General manager Amber Cox read a ridiculous, gaslighting statement blaming outside media for the odious reputation of Fever fans. “The attacks on our fan base have no basis in reality, and must stop,” she read from the podium.Mitchell’s own wordspainfully contradicted Cox, as did rival players around the league.Maybe they just want it this way.This article originally appeared on Howard Bryant’s Substack.You can subscribe here.Explore more on these topicsIndiana FeverWNBABasketballUS sportscommentShareReuse this content

title: Senegalese college basketball player freed from ICE as another is detained | College basketball | The Guardian
description: Aminata Seck was released on bond after two months in custody, while Mississippi Valley State’s Qingfang Pang remains detained pending removal from the US
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Aminata Seck was released on bond after two months in custody, while Mississippi Valley State’s Qingfang Pang remains detained pending removal from the US
Content: Kentucky State University basketball player Aminata Seck, 26, was released on bond after spending two months in Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody.Photograph: Brian Sevald/NBAE/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKentucky State University basketball player Aminata Seck, 26, was released on bond after spending two months in Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody.Photograph: Brian Sevald/NBAE/Getty ImagesCollege basketballSenegalese college basketball player freed from ICE as another is detainedAminata Seck released on $2,500 bond after two monthsChinese player Qingfang Pang detained since SeptemberMississippi Valley State express concern for playerAgenciesThu 8 Oct 2026 12.43 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 17.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAKentuckyState University women’s basketball player from Senegal who was detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has been released after spending two months in custody.At a hearing on Tuesday, a judge granted Aminata Seck a $2,500 bond, which was posted on Wednesday after ICE declined to appeal, according to Hishem Alsalman, managing attorney of Alsalman Law Office.Meanwhile, a men’s basketball player fromMississippiValley State University has been taken into ICE custody. Qingfang Pang, who is from China, was detained on 29 September and is being held at the Richwood Correctional Facility in Richwood, Louisiana, according to ICE’s detainee database.ICE has abducted a college athlete. What are the NCAA and universities going to do about it?Read more“Mississippi Valley State University is aware of the situation involving one of our students and is deeply concerned for the student’s well-being,” the school said in a statement. “The student is registered as a full-time student at Mississippi Valley State University. University officials are closely monitoring the situation and are committed to providing appropriate support as circumstances develop.”A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, said in an email that Pang entered the US legally on 17 November 2023, with authorization to remain until 5 September 2024, but stayed beyond that date.“He accepted voluntary departure and will remain in ICE custody pending removal,” the spokesperson said. “This administration will not ignore the rule of law.”Pang spent the past two seasons at Monroe University in New York before transferring to Mississippi Valley State. The 6ft 9in forward averaged 7.3 points and 3.8 rebounds per game at Monroe.In Seck’s case, the judge found that she was neither a danger to the community nor a flight risk, Alsalman said on Thursday. The judge also ruled that she could continue working toward her degree and praised her academic and athletic achievements.Seck, 26, was detained on 7 August at Louisville’s Muhammad Ali International Airport as she prepared to travel with her team to a tournament.DHS previously said in a statement that Seck legally entered the US in 2019, then “chose to overstay her welcome in violation of our nation’s laws”. The agency said an immigration judge had ordered her removed a year earlier after she failed to appear at an immigration hearing.Alsalman previously said an immigration judge had found that Seck did not receive notice of those proceedings.Seck, who is from Dakar, Senegal’s capital, was named to the Southern Intercollegiate Athletic Conference (SIAC) all-conference third team last season after leading Kentucky State with 11.7 points and 7.3 rebounds per game.The 6ft 4in center recorded five double-doubles and scored a season-high 30 points against Lane College on 14 January.Seck also received the SIAC Women’s Basketball Elite 16 award, the conference’s highest academic honor, which recognizes student-athletes who demonstrate exemplary achievement in both athletics and the classroom.Explore more on these topicsCollege basketballCollege sportsUS sportsICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)KentuckyMississippiShareReuse this content

title: Inside NBA Europe’s $10bn plan that has football clubs queueing to join | NBA | The Guardian
description: Some of the biggest names in European football will bid for a franchise in ESL-style league, now due to launch in 2028
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Some of the biggest names in European football will bid for a franchise in ESL-style league, now due to launch in 2028
Content: Ignas Sargiunas of Fenerbahce Tarfin Istanbul, Théo Maledon of Real Madrid.Composite: GettyView image in fullscreenIgnas Sargiunas of Fenerbahce Tarfin Istanbul, Théo Maledon of Real Madrid.Composite: GettyNBAInside NBA Europe’s $10bn plan that has football clubs queueing to joinSome of the biggest names in European football will bid for a franchise in ESL-style league, now due to launch in 2028Matt HughesThu 8 Oct 2026 11.08 EDTFirst published on Thu 8 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe launch ofNBAEurope will be delayed 12 months until 2028, with a pre-qualifying competition planned for next year to find four temporary members to join the 16-team league’s inaugural season alongside 12 permanent franchises.The NBA is planning to invest about $10bn (£7.6bn) over 10 years in what sources have described as the sporting world’s biggest-ever startup competition. It is understood to have received multiple offers for the 12 franchises that exceed their targets, with prices expected to range from $500m to more than $1bn for the London franchise.Many of the winning bids are expected to come from the owners of football clubs that compete in the Champions League, with the deputy commissioner, Mark Tatum, holding talks with senior executives from Barcelona, Real Madrid, Paris Saint-Germain, Bayern Munich and Milan last week.‘It’s sad seeing players promote it’: Wembanyama says he will never endorse gambling companiesRead moreLondon, Manchester, Rome, Athens, Istanbul and Lyon will also get permanent franchises, topped up by four qualifiers from within European basketball’s existing structure.The London franchise is understood to have attracted several bids in excess of $1bn from some eye-catching investors including the former Chelsea chair Todd Boehly, a consortium involving the former Tottenham chair Daniel Levy and MSP Sports Capital, as well as Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund.Buss Sports Capital, the US investment group thatsold its 17.8% stake in the Los Angeles Lakersto Joshua Kushner this year, is believed to have submitted an offer for the Manchester franchise, but City Football Group (CFG) has not bid despite having close links with the NBA, which has agreed to set up a new global academy in Abu Dhabi as part of a $300m partnership.While the NBA has not committed to a timeframe, it is understood it hopes to announce the identity of the new franchise owners this year.The NBA managing director George Aivazoglou told the Leaders in Sport conference on Thursday that “we’re moving ahead with plans for a launch next year,” although it remains unclear what the soft launch will look like.“We’ve got people who are well-capitalised investors who don’t own any basketball franchise, but they want to get into basketball,” Tatum said at last week’s general assembly of European Football Clubs.“We’ve got existing basketball clubs in the ecosystem that have submitted bids and we have football clubs, some that have their own basketball teams today, and some that don’t and want to get involved in basketball.”The level of the bids indicates that the NBA has succeeded in winning over some of Europe’s biggest football clubs and powerful US institutional investors, but it is continuing to encounter resistance from within basketball.At a meeting at Lake Como this week, the EuroLeague clubs voted to reject the NBA’s initial offer of investment in favour of pursuing their plans to expand from 20 to 24 clubs, although NBA sources insist talks will continue.“Our vision for basketball is to bring everybody with us – EuroLeague, the governing body, Fiba and the clubs – to revamp the European basketball scene,” Tatum said. “One of the things that we’ve learned from European football is the power of the pyramid. In football every single club understands the clear pathway to play at the top level. That doesn’t exist in basketball.”View image in fullscreenLeft to right: Stephon Castle, De’Aaron Fox and Dylan Harper of the San Antonio Spurs, who will play the New Orleans Pelicans in Manchester in January.Photograph: Ronald Cortes/Getty ImagesThe NBA’s decision to seek a partnership with EuroLeagues rather than go it alone was taken during the summer, when it settled on a hybrid model representing Europe and North America’s sporting cultures.In a structure that echoes football’s toxic and swiftly abandonedEuropean Super League (ESL), NBA Europe will have 12 permanent members, with four temporary members admitted annually.While the mechanism for promotion is to be confirmed, NBA sources say there will be two entry routes: the top two ranked sides from a new second-tier European competition called theBasketballChampions League, and two finalists in a separate tournament for all of Europe’s domestic champions.In another nod to greater upward mobility, the highest ranked non-franchise club that reaches the nd-of-season playoffs would keep their place in NBA Europe the next season, with the other three sent back to the play-in competition, so there would probably be a regular turnover of entrants outside the permanent 12.While there are billions of reasons that big European football clubs want a slice of the NBA, there are suspicions that some may have ulterior motives.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSeveral sources involved in the discussions said Real Madrid’s president, Florentino Pérez, seems particularly invested in NBA Europe, eager to establish the principle of a semi-closed league in Europe in case the prospect of a breakaway football league returns.Ironically, Pérez had previously cited EuroLeague, which has 13 permanent voting members supplemented by seven additional clubs on an annual basis, as a model for the ESL. NBA Europe sources insist the proposed new competition would be more open, by providing a direct mechanism for all domestic champions to qualify.Real formally withdrew from theESLonly last year, four years after the project collapsed, and their commercial partner A22 continues to pursue Fifa and Uefa in the courts for allegedly abusing their dominant position by banning clubs from signing up.The Madrid commercial court and Spain’s high court of justice have both ruled in Real’s favour over the past two years, with Pérez seemingly determined to keep the club’s options open.“Florentino has been very involved in NBA Europe,” a senior source at a EuroLeague club said. “He wants it to happen quickly and is constantly asking for updates.“The Super League may be dead for now, but it’s not difficult to imagine a world where the biggest Champions League clubs demand permanent qualification and try to restrict access. A semi-closed Champions League would protect them from domestic failure, so NBA Europe could be very useful.”Despite the club staying out of the auction, theManchester City issueremains a potential complication for the NBA, however, as CFG are 50% owners alongside Oak View Group of Manchester’s biggest arena, the 23,000-capacity Co-op Live, which has been earmarked as the most likely venue. A regular-season NBA game between San Antonio Spurs and New Orleans Pelicans will be staged there in January.View image in fullscreenFlorentino Pérez, the Real Madrid president, is taking a keen interest in NBA Europe.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images“We want to bring on partners who are going to invest in basketball development,” Tatum said. “Academies, indoor arenas. When you think about all of Europe there’s probably only a handful of what I would consider world-class indoor arenas. These arenas provide an economic engine to cities, but we don’t have that in Europe. And so that is the investment that we’re looking to create.”Tatum has close relations with CFG, whose chair, Khaldoon al‑Mubarak, has been a basketball fan since attending a Boston Celtics’ game while studying at Tufts University in the 1990s.Al-Mubarak has played an important role in forging a relationship between the NBA and Abu Dhabi’s department of culture and tourism, culminating in a nine-year partnership that for the last four years has led to NBA pre-season games in Abu Dhabi.That deal will remain in place despite the fallout from Manchester City being found guilty by an independent commission of more than 100 charges of financial cheating, although the NBA may be slightly relieved that the club is not part of the franchise bidding process.Explore more on these topicsNBABasketballUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rays sweep Yankees out of playoffs after ‘crazy’ fan interference downgrades New York home run | MLB | The Guardian
description: Tampa Bay completed a stunning sweep of New York after a disputed fan interference call, while the Dodgers reached the NLCS and Cleveland avoided elimination
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Tampa Bay completed a stunning sweep of New York after a disputed fan interference call, while the Dodgers reached the NLCS and Cleveland avoided elimination
Content: Rays outfielder Victor Mesa Jr is unable to make a catch as fans interfere with a ball hit by the Yankees’ Anthony Volpe during the sixth inning of Game 3 of the ALDS at Yankee Stadium on Wednesday.Photograph: Caleb Bowlin/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRays outfielder Victor Mesa Jr is unable to make a catch as fans interfere with a ball hit by the Yankees’ Anthony Volpe during the sixth inning of Game 3 of the ALDS at Yankee Stadium on Wednesday.Photograph: Caleb Bowlin/Getty ImagesMLBRays sweep Yankees out of playoffs after ‘crazy’ fan interference downgrades New York home runRays sweep Yankees 3-0 after fan interference callDodgers eliminate Braves to keep three-peat bid aliveRamírez leads Guardians past Sox to avoid sweepAgenciesThu 8 Oct 2026 07.39 EDTFirst published on Wed 7 Oct 2026 22.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnthony Volpe rounded the bases, touched home plate and then waited out the uncertainty like everyone else.“Just hoping for the best,” the New York Yankees infielder said. “Crazy.”With the Yankees’ season at stake, Volpe was denied a tying home run against the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 3 of their American League Division Series when a replay review determined a fan interfered with his drive to deep left field Wednesday night.Will Venable: the White Sox manager who used basketball tactics to transform a baseball loserRead moreThe swing of emotions came nearly 30 years to the day after young fan Jeffrey Maier reached over the right-field wall at Yankee Stadium on a ball hit by Derek Jeter in the 1996 AL Championship Series against Baltimore. With no replay system in place back then, the home team benefited from umpires calling it a home run instead of interference, and New York went on to win the World Series.This time, the Yankees wound up losing 4-3 by the very run that was taken off the board and had their season end in a three-game sweep.“I mean, we lost,” Volpe said. “That’s what we’re dealing with now. That’s just what happened.”Replay umpire Malachi Moore made the call on Volpe’s sixth-inning drive in Major League Baseball’s Replay Center, and players and managers on both sides mostly agreed the right decision was made.“I thought they got it right,” New York skipper Aaron Boone said. “When he hit it, to my eye looking out there, I was a little concerned right away because it felt like something – I wasn’t sure. And then seeing the replay and seeing it unfold, I thought they did the right thing.”With George Lombard Jr on base – Austin Wells would have been as well if not for a successful ABS challenge by the Rays – Volpe turned on Griffin Jax’s 96-mph sinker and hit it 357ft to left field. A few feet further and fan interference would have been out of the question.“He almost had a big home run,” Yankees star Aaron Judge, who missed the series through injury, said. “Off the bat, I liked the chances.”The play was initially called a two-run homer that would have tied the score at 4 with two outs in the sixth. But a lengthy video review determined a fan reached over the wall to catch the ball as Rays left fielder Victor Mesa Jr tried in vain for a leaping grab.“It was interference,” Mesa said in Spanish. “I believe I might have even been able to get to that ball. Not that it matters whether we won or lost. Well, it’s in the past now. I think they could have even called an out, because I was right there. Everything happens for a reason. It was kind of an in-between call.”Spectator interference became the ruling, and Volpe was awarded an RBI double that scored Lombard from first base, trimming Tampa Bay’s lead to 4-3.“I don’t know if he would have caught it or not caught it, the guy would have scored or not,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said. “Our replay official Nick [Rogers] said the runner had passed second base at the point where the ball hit the fan’s wrist or hand, and makes sense why they awarded him home.”There was another slight delay after some fans in left threw debris on to the field, and Spencer Jones then struck out against Jax to end the inning.The fan who reached out to catch the ball was escorted out of Yankee Stadium by security and police.“After viewing all relevant angles, the Replay Official definitively determined the spectator interfered with the ball over the field of play. The ball would not have left the playing field nor would it have been caught. The call is OVERTURNED, there was spectator interference and no home run. Additionally, the Replay Official scored one run and placed the batter-runner at 2B,”MLBsaid in a statement from the Replay Center.Judge knew once he saw the side-angle replay that it was fan interference.“You go from a tie game to down one,” said starting pitcher Max Fried, who gave up a two-run homer to Mesa in the top of the sixth. “[Volpe] made a great swing, and it’s just the way the game goes sometimes. It’s unfortunate because that changes the game.”Tampa Bay, who haveone of the lowest payrolls in MLB, will play either the Chicago White Sox or Cleveland Guardians for a place in the World Series.LA Dodgers 4-1 Atlanta BravesAndy Pages drove in two runs with a bases-loaded single in the seventh inning to give Los Angeles the lead as the Dodgers beat theAtlanta Bravesto clinch their National League Division Series.The Dodgers won back-to-back games in Atlanta to take the best-of-five series 3-1 and advance to the NL Championship Series as they seek to become the first NL team to win three consecutive World Series titles.“We’ve got our work cut out,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said, adding extra rest will be important for such players as Shohei Ohtani and Freddie Freeman.“So kind of enjoy this one, get Shohei a couple of days to get back,” Roberts said. “Freddie, he had a big series, but, again a couple of days will help him. Give our guys in the pen a little reset. So we’ll be ready to go Game 1.”View image in fullscreenThe Los Angeles Dodgers celebrate after defeating the Atlanta Braves in Game 4 of their National League Division Series at Truist Park in Atlanta on Wednesday.Photograph: Kevin C Cox/Getty ImagesPages lined a 3-2 pitch from Robert Suárez up the middle to drive in Teoscar Hernández, who had singled off starter Tyler Mahle, and pinch-runner Tommy Edman for a 3-1 lead. Didier Fuentes had walked pinch-hitter Josue De Paula and Kyle Tucker to load the bases, with Edman running for De Paula.Max Muncy’s solo homer off Raisel Iglesias in the ninth padded the lead and gave the slugger 19 postseason home runs with the Dodgers, extending his franchise record.Dodgers right-hander Tyler Glasnow, making his first start since 24 September, allowed just one hit but walked five batters in four and two-thirds innings. After he issued two walks in the fifth, left-hander Alex Vesia ended the inning by inducing a groundout to second base from Matt Olson.The missed opportunity left the Braves with 18 walks in the series, none of which resulted in a run.Milwaukee Brewers 3-1 San Diego PadresGarrett Mitchell tripled and scored the go-ahead run in the fifth inning before making a pivotal catch on Manny Machado’s drive to the wall in the eighth, and the Milwaukee Brewers advanced to the NLCS for the second straight season with victory over the San Diego Padres.Mitchell also drove in Sal Frelick with Milwaukee’s first run as the Brewers snapped their 12-game postseason road losing streak dating to 2018 and reached the franchise’s fifth league Championship Series.Machado nearly tied Game 4 with a 406ft drive off reliever Abner Uribe, but Mitchell coolly tracked it down and reached just above the short wall in right-center field to keep it in the park.Second baseman Brice Turang then ended the eighth with an acrobatic catch of Ty France’s tailing pop-up in foul territory.After fending off the surging Padres in four tight games decided by a combined five runs, the 103-win Brewers will get an NLCS rematch with the Dodgers, who swept Milwaukee last October on their way to a second consecutive World Series title.View image in fullscreenMilwaukee Brewers pitcher Trevor Megill celebrates after closing out a 3-1 victory over the San Diego Padres.Photograph: Sean M Haffey/Getty ImagesFernando Tatis Jr hit a 429ft homer on an otherwise tepid offensive night for the Padres, who repeatedly tested the majors’ best regular-season team before falling short of what would have been the fourth NLCS appearance in franchise history.One night after the Padres avoided elimination in Game 3, Milwaukee claimed their first road playoff win since the 2018 NLCS by sticking to their season-long formula for success.Four Brewers pitchers combined on a three-hitter and the defense made nearly every big play, while Milwaukee’s lineup patiently worked counts, collected 10 hits against the Padres’ defense and manufactured enough runs to head home with a victory.Game 2 hero Jackson Chourio capped his impressive series by driving in Mitchell to become the Brewers’ career leader in postseason RBIs at just 22 years old. Chourio has 17 RBIs, including six in this series, in 16 playoff games.Cleveland Guardians 9-3 Chicago White SoxView image in fullscreenThe Guardians’ José Ramírez steals third base against the White Sox.Photograph: Michael Reaves/Getty ImagesJo Adell and José Ramírez powered Cleveland with a pair of two-out triples, and the Guardians avoided an ALDS sweep by cooling off the Chicago White Sox with a 9-3 victory in Game 3 on Wednesday.Adell’s three-run triple gave Cleveland a 4-1 lead in the third inning. Ramírez’s three-bagger drove in Travis Bazzana and Patrick Bailey for a 7-3 advantage in the eighth.“We continued to pile on,” Cleveland manager Stephen Vogt said. “I think that’s been the difference of the first couple games to today was Game 2, we were able to get a couple runs but weren’t able to add on. But really good job by our guys today.”The Guardians hit two triples in a postseason game for the first time in franchise history. They became the first major league team to accomplish the feat since theLos Angeles Dodgersin Game 1 of the 2024 World Series against the New York Yankees.Adell, Ramírez, Bailey and Brayan Rocchio each had two of the team’s 11 hits – a complete turnaround for the AL Central champions after they managed just three runs and seven hits in the first two games of the series combined.Game 4 is Thursday in Chicago, with the White Sox leading 2-1 in the best-of-five matchup. Once again, they’ll try to clinch a postseason series at home for the first time since the 1906 World Series against the Chicago Cubs.Explore more on these topicsMLBLos Angeles DodgersAtlanta BravesBaseballUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: Maresca believes City players ‘don’t care about the noise’ as Haaland calls for unity | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: Enzo Maresca said he is ‘very calm’ despite the storm engulfing Manchester City and with a trip to Liverpool coming on Sunday
Author: Will Unwin
Headline: Enzo Maresca said he is ‘very calm’ despite the storm engulfing Manchester City and with a trip to Liverpool coming on Sunday
Content: Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca arrives for training on Thursday.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAView image in fullscreenManchester City manager Enzo Maresca arrives for training on Thursday.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAManchester CityMaresca believes City players ‘don’t care about the noise’ as Haaland calls for unityCity travel to Liverpool for first game since guilty verdictManager ‘very calm’ despite storm engulfing clubWill UnwinThu 8 Oct 2026 14.29 EDTFirst published on Thu 8 Oct 2026 03.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEnzo Maresca says his players “don’t care about the noise” surroundingManchester City, while Erling Haaland has called for unity after the club were found guilty of serious breaches of Premier League financial rules.The manager and players reconvened on Thursday after spending the international break apart when thenews of the club’s predicamentwas made public.City maintain their innocence and have launched an appeal against the ruling, but if that fails could face a severe punishment. In the meantime, the staff and players are showing a strong front as they prepare for their first game in three weeks when they face Liverpool on Sunday.“Personally I’m very calm to be honest,” Maresca told the club’s official website. “The club has been quite clear. We trust completely the club. We understand the noise but the focus for us is just what we can control and we can control just the football side.”‘Those memories are ours and no verdict changes that’: Manchester City fans’ viewsRead moreCity have started life under Maresca with five straight Premier League wins and sit top of the table but the on-field success has been overshadowed by the off-field matters. Players have sought reassurance about the future of the club and were able were to sit down collectively for the first time since the news was announced, as they begin preparations for what is expected to be a fiery visit to Anfield.“The feeling is fantastic, to be honest,” said the Italian. “The players are excited for the next two games. But especially they are excited because in this moment we are top of the league. The players are just focused on that. They know what we can control is the football side – they are not worried at all about different things.“They know their profession and they know that the noise is there but they don’t care too much about the noise. They are just focused in this moment on how we can beat Liverpool and how, together with the fans, we can try to win in Anfield.”Haaland, meanwhile, has spoken of the need for everyone associated with City to unite in this difficult period for the embattled club.“We have to stick together,” the striker told Sky Sports News. “We have to stay with each other, and we have to stay positive. No matter what happens in life, we always have to have a smile. So we have to stay positive, look ahead, and try to win football games and try to enjoy the situation and win the game. We have to stick together; we have to spread the love to each other. So yeah: stick together, and enjoy the ride and smile.”The Norwegian is following in the footsteps of his father, Alf-Inge, who played for City in a less successful era, so has witnessed the changes that have come since the takeover in 2008. “I care a lot about City, I have to say,” he said. “I care a lot about the fans because I’m a fan myself and I feel with them as well.”View image in fullscreenErling Haaland said of Manchester City’s predicament: ‘No matter what happens in life, we always have to have a smile.’Photograph: Richard Sellers/Getty Images/AllstarPep Guardiola is expected to attend City’s first home match since they werefound guiltywhen they face Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League on Wednesday.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt would be the former head coach’s first return since leaving in the summer after 10 years. Guardiola’s attendance is regarded as a show of support for City’s hierarchy after the guilty verdict that has rocked the club.Guardiola wrote on social media last week: “I want every single fan to knowI am here; more than ever. I am, always have been, always will, be behind my club, my owner, my chairman, Ferran [Soriano, the chief executive], the players, staff, Enzo [Maresca] and you, our unique supporters. Let me be clear: we will get through this together. I love you all.”The Catalan took on a role as a City Football Group ambassador when he departed as head coach. Guardiola was a close ally of Soriano, who brought him to Manchester, the pair having worked together at Barcelona.Guardiola faced regular questions during his tenure over City’s financial conduct after they were charged by the Premier League in 2023 and always reiterated his belief in what he was told by those above him.Meanwhile, his former Real Madrid rival José Mourinho joked that he may not live to see the end of City’s legal battle. Mourinho managed Manchester United from 2016 and led them to a second-placed Premier League finish behind Pep Guardiola’s City in 2018.“I would rather ‌laugh about it,” Mourinho said, when asked about the case in an interview with Italy’s Corriere dello Sport. “I ​think we will eventually get an ending, but we are both in our 60s [Guardiola is actually 55] and we’ll need to be lucky enough to still be around when the final verdict arrives. There will be a verdict, then appeals, then more appeals.”Explore more on these topicsManchester CityPep GuardiolanewsShareReuse this content

title: Khaldoon al-Mubarak: the tightrope walker who made rare misstep over City charges | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: Manchester City’s chair is key to the project of making Abu Dhabi a secure world power but his next move may be the sale of the club
Author: Rob Draper
Headline: Manchester City’s chair is key to the project of making Abu Dhabi a secure world power but his next move may be the sale of the club
Content: Manchester City chair Khaldoon al-Mubarak appears to have driven the club’s confrontational approach with the football authorities.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAView image in fullscreenManchester City chair Khaldoon al-Mubarak appears to have driven the club’s confrontational approach with the football authorities.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAManchester CityProfileKhaldoon al-Mubarak: the tightrope walker who made rare misstep over City chargesManchester City’s chair is key to the project of making Abu Dhabi a secure world power but his next move may be the sale of the clubRob DraperThu 8 Oct 2026 08.19 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNo one better understands the precarious tightrope Abu Dhabi walks when it tries to balance its relationships with western Europe while weighing the complex geopolitics of the Gulf region than Manchester City’s chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak. He was eight when his father, ambassador Khalifa Ahmed Abdel Aziz al-Mubarak, left the family’s Paris apartment for work on 9 February 1984, and was assassinated on the street by a Palestinian terrorist.And no one outside the emirate’s royal family could be more wrapped up in the project of making and maintaining Abu Dhabi as a significant and secure world power and the dominant member of the United Arab Emirates, a nation state still only 55 years old. His paternal grandfather, Ahmad bin Abdul Aziz al-Mubarak, was chair of Abu Dhabi’s Sharia judicial department and senior adviser to Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan al-Nahyan,the founding president of the UAE. As such, Ahmad bin Abdul Aziz was the James Madison of the UAE (the founding father, not the Spurs player) in that he crafted the Islamic legal framework of the new nation in the 1970s.‘Those memories are ours and no verdict changes that’: Manchester City fans’ viewsRead moreKhaldoon’s father was assassinated by a group led by Abu Nidal which, according to the CIA, was “the most dangerous and effective of all terrorist groups [and] the best organized of the radical Palestinian terrorist groups” before the emergence of Hamas. The murder was justified in a phone call saying that the UAE “had expelled Palestinian and Arab residents and was linked with American imperialism”. In essence, they were accused of being too soft on the west, not radical enough for Palestinians.Both al-Mubarak’s grandfather and father have streets named after them in Abu Dhabi, with his father honoured as a martyr of the state. It is fair to say the City chair has honoured the family tradition as chief adviser to the UAE president and Abu Dhabi ruler, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed al-Nahyan, for whom he first worked after graduating from Tufts University in Massachusetts. Given his father’s martyrdom, the royal family is said to have looked out for al-Mubarak as a quasi-adopted son. According to a source in the Financial Times, al-Mubarak is “diplomatically in charge of the UK file as well as the China file … and he’s the main liaison with the US administration” and has diplomatic immunity in the UK. That said, he appears to have made a rare misstep with his belligerent tone on Manchester City.According to Manchester City’s lawyer Simon Cliff, it was al-Mubarak who dictated the aggressive, confrontational stance City have taken with football authorities. As far back as 2014, when City were fighting their first Uefa charge, Cliff wrote, according to leaked documents first published by Der Spiegel: “Khaldoon says he would rather spend £30m on the 50 best lawyers in the world and sue them [Uefa] for the next ten years than agree a financial penalty.”View image in fullscreenKhaldoon al-Mubarak with Pep Guardiola after Manchester City’s Premier League title win in 2021-22.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAHe backed down on that occasion, along with the co-accused Paris Saint-Germain, both clubs agreeing a small fine and minor transfer restrictions with Uefa. It is extraordinary that City kept fighting thereafter, whereas the Qatar-owned PSG accepted their punishment, cosied up to Uefa – with the club’s president, Nasser al-Khelaifi, becoming chair of the European Club Association (now European Football Clubs) and chief opponent of the breakaway Super League – and built the most exciting and successful team in Europe, bringing admiration for the Qatari brand from observers willing to ignore human rights abuses. Al-Mubarak, in fighting to the end with City, appears to have broken an ambassador’s cardinal law: don’t embarrass your boss. Should City lose their appeal against an independent commission’s finding that they wereguilty of multiple breaches of financial rules,al-Mubarak may be instructed to organise the sale of the club.“I’m sure that’s the case with Man City,” says Christopher Davidson, author of Abu Dhabi, Oil and Beyond. “More than that, I’ve been told by some [in Abu Dhabi] that it will be the case. I can’t see any reason why they would stick around and try to rebuild the reputation after this. It’s embarrassing the royal family now. I can’t think of any example where things have gone wrong [for Abu Dhabi] and they’ve just kept plugging money into it. I think they’ll play out the appeal – nothing to lose with that – but once that’s done, it’s all about how to get out before the owners are declared unfit, a far worse outcome. There are very clever people involved in Abu Dhabi who I’m led to believe will very strongly counsel this needs to be a quiet retreat because the longer they stay in the game, the more damaging it is and it will unravel any kind of soft power Abu Dhabi managed to gain.”In June al-Mubarak said “these sorts of jewels, you don’t sell” and that there was “only intention to keep growing this”. As for thewider threat to UK-Abu Dhabi relations, Davidson believes it is overstated. “Some of the reporting perhaps has portrayed Abu Dhabi as a bit monolithic. There are entire big and growing sections of Abu Dhabi state economy that are outside al-Mubarak’s remit. Some of Abu Dhabi’s biggest investments in the UK in recent years have been in renewable energy and the windfarms of Scotland from Masdar energy, which is chaired by Sultan al-Jaber, who’s another key lieutenant of the ruler.”Davidson also cites the International Holding Company (IHC), which has huge biotech, shipping, healthcare and retail investments in the UK, including the Ivy restaurants, and is chaired by Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed al-Nahyan, deputy ruler of Abu Dhabi and brother of the UAE president and Sheikh Mansour. “It’s inconceivable that these investments would be withdrawn,” says Davidson.View image in fullscreenKhaldoon al-Mubarak (left) alongside City owner Sheikh Mansour at the then City of Manchester Stadium in August 2010.Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/ReutersIn May this year the UK signed a free trade agreement with Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE which it said could beworth £3.7bn a year to the UK economy. “The UAE was a major force behind getting that and it was a major accomplishment on both sides, so there’s no prospect any of this is going to be interfered with,” Davidson says.Al-Mubarak will probably emerge from this fiasco largely untarnished, because City are a tiny part of his portfolio. “He can’t possibly have known what’s going on in every part of his empire,” says Davidson. “My gut feeling would be that it’s the layers below him. It’s all about your legal counsel. I think the Qataris had very clever people working for them. This has been a case of poor advice being given to the senior Emiratis involved, a misreading of UK politics and a misreading of the Premier League and its bigger picture as a rules-based institution.“I think the statements al-Mubarak has made, including the one early last summer that ‘We will not sell’, are the product of poor advice delivered to him and ultimately to Sheikh Mansour. It may be important to us in the UK but Man City has been a peripheral project [for Abu Dhabi].”Explore more on these topicsManchester CityFinancesFootball politicsprofilesShareReuse this content

title: Sergio Camello: ‘Rayo is the last team standing – it’s football from another time’ | Rayo Vallecano | The Guardian
description: Rayo Vallecano’s fascinating forward on his unique club, his musical passions and the goalscoring form that puts him among Europe’e elite
Author: Sid Lowe
Headline: Rayo Vallecano’s fascinating forward on his unique club, his musical passions and the goalscoring form that puts him among Europe’e elite
Content: ‘The least important thing about the football here is the football.’ Sergio Camello in the Vallecas neighbourhood.Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘The least important thing about the football here is the football.’ Sergio Camello in the Vallecas neighbourhood.Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The GuardianRayo VallecanoInterviewSergio Camello: ‘Rayo is the last team standing – it’s football from another time’Sid LoweRayo Vallecano’s fascinating forward on his unique club, his musical passions and the goalscoring form that puts him among Europe’e eliteThu 8 Oct 2026 15.20 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 16.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn 11-year-old, second-hand VW Beetle with more than 300,000km on the clock pulls over on Clown Fofó Street in the heart of Vallecas. The music goes off, the Smiths silenced and out gets Sergio Camello: movie aficionado with156 films reviewed,part-time photographer, sometime drummer, Olympic gold medallist and the second-top goalscorer in Europe’s top five leagues. Engulfed in graffiti, stickers covering the glass between metal bars in red, a single step up from the street, the small door into Rayo Vallecano’s ground is locked, but in 64 hours it will open for the first time this season. “It’s my home, it’s Vallecas,” Camello says.Forced to abandon their place, on Saturday at 2pm the tenants return. With the Madrid council declaring Estadio de Vallecas unsafe, unfit for purpose, Rayo’s home matches have instead been played in Leganés, out of the city to the south and boycotted by fans. Walking the neighbourhood that is proud of its social conscience, its community and its team, Camello can’t wait to be back again. And not just for the football; maybe not even for the football. “It’s the pre-game, the post-game, the people,” he says, passing the bar where they’ll be waiting for him after, same as always.View image in fullscreen‘I’m me, Sergio Camello, a normal person from a humble team’ – Sergio Camello at the door to Rayo Vallecano’s Vallecas ground.Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The GuardianYet the football is good too, good as it’s ever been. Across the continent’s top five leagues only Raphinha has more goals than Camello’s seven in seven league games and Camello himself has never had so many either. “I try not to think about it but my teammates keep reminding me,” he says. “‘Pichichi! Pichichi!’ It’s not Sergio any more.” Pichichi was the great Athletic Club striker whose name adorns the top-scorer award. No pressure, then. “None, I love it,” Camello replies, “and I love that they’re enjoying it.”Two months into the season, this is already his best campaign inprimerawhere the previous totals were five, three and three. And although there’s a tactical element, the new coach Beñat San José altering his movement, Camello looks deeper for an explanation. Above all he looks inside, which is where, from the beginning, another conversation starts: a simple question prompts a complex, nuanced and human discussion, the striker talking calmly, thoughtfully and with startling unexpected honesty.View image in fullscreenSergio Camello celebrates after scoring against Barcelona in August.Photograph: Pablo Rodriguez/Quality Sport Images/Getty ImagesCamello is that most unusual of footballers – prepared to speak on materialism, racism, or homophobia, social media “poison” or the housing crisis, that rare player prepared to use his platform, which he says was born of his upbringing but also learned being here in thebarrio. This is personal, but at once universal too, something in his experience that is about everyone. Who knows, maybe there is something in what he has lived that can help, some reason to share it, the goals scored offering tangible proof of an intangible process.So what has changed? “How I go on to the pitch,” he says. “I thought it would be much harder to change my mindset but I’m seeing that I can be myself: be free, connect with the Sergio I can offer Rayo. To feel liberated, to enjoy it – and it’s been a long time since I enjoyed all this like this.View image in fullscreenSergio Camello has been outscored only by Barcelona’s Raphinha so far this season.Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The Guardian“The first thing was to have many conversations with friends, people who truly know me. Especially my twin brother Gonzalo; there’s a connection that goes beyond the human. He could see I wasn’t enjoying it much, wasn’t myself. We talked and I tried to take that on to the pitch. Above all, to play without the pressure. Because pressure is horrendous. It makes it so that you don’t enjoy absolutely anything, puts you in a position where if things don’t work, that leads to frustration, frustration leads to pity, and suddenly everything is negative. There’s a point in the conversations where it’s: ‘That’s it; it’s done’.“This is a sport you chose before it was your job, because it’s what made you happiest. It’s about connecting to that kid again. I’d discussed this in therapy too; the idea of getting back to that kid.”Somewhere that can be lost – not just failure you have to live with but also success. “The pressure can come from everywhere,” Camello says. “We’re young, the change happens so fast, no one prepares you for it. If you can’t manage that it can do a lot of damage and that happened to me. [Early on], I would even get a bit paranoid, have fixations. ‘They’re looking at me.’ The first day inprimera, when I scored, the journey there had been normal – scooter, bus, metro, bus – but on the same journey home some kids followed me shouting: ‘Camello! Camello!’ It was a shock. The night we returned from the Olympics I was in the usual bar, people crowded and I had a kind of anxiety attack and had to go. And, look, I’m me, Sergio Camello, a normal person from a humble team. I can’t imagine what it is like forsomeone at Lamine Yamal’s level. I don’t envy that.”Joint-second“But it’s about seeing the balance, understanding,” Camello continues, “and football has given me so, so much. There are so many people who can’t enjoy their job, who don’t have the [financial] freedom. When you have bad moments, when the clouds come, when you feel that cycle of negativity, you talk.”Camello looks across the room: it’s quiet, 25 chairs sitting empty. “One of my friends [Dani Fernández] is a musician about to do four sellouts at the Wizink [Centre]; when I met him, he wouldn’t have sold out this room,” he says. “We both got ‘caught’ in this about the same time and we talked a lot. When he had doubts, I was there; when I did, he was. A torch in the darkness. You think: ‘I’d love to be a rock star’, and then someone you admire who is tells you how bloody shit it can be behind the scenes. You understand each other, you think: ‘Bloody hell, maybe I don’t have to analyse things so deeply.’ If in even those places you idealise, there is darkness, solitude, maybe I’m not so bad.View image in fullscreenSergio Camello says he his thriving by playing without pressure.Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The Guardian“Otherwise you could go into a very dark place where you feel you have to escape this [football]. Even then the world wouldn’t end. And fortunately, the positive in football has always weighed much more heavily. And that’s been shown to be right. Those conversations give me perspective, make me conscious of how fortunate I am.”Although Camello says doubts about the game itself are rarely shared in such depth in the dressing room – “football might be the most important thing in the entire world to your teammate” – something about this place helps. The club’s problems are significant, debilitating and should not be romanticised, he insists, and yet somehow they have made a success of it, built through solidarity. Besides, he says, “we’re also here because we want to be” and there is something about Rayo, something about breaking out of the bubble, that has been good for him, for all of them, as people as well as players. There’s a moment when he talks about everything that comes with being a footballer and says “it’s easy to be a dickhead”, but that’s diminished at a clubnot just in thebarriobut of thebarrio, one that’s “totally different” to anywhere else he knows, where “your feet are that bit more on the ground and you realise you’re not stars”.View image in fullscreenSergio Camello says the club and players have a unique connection with the Vallecas neighbourhood.Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The Guardian“Rayo is the last team standing from football from another time, that’s what I like,” Camello says. “Even just parking here on the street right in front changes things. The same faces, every time. The least important thing about the football here is the football; it’s what they stand for every weekend, what they believe in, the connection. It’s Isi in the bar on the corner. Unai and his mates in the one down the bottom there. The bar we’ve taken over. That doesn’t exist anywhere else. To have those guys you were watching half an hour ago in the same bars, doesn’t happen. I’ve built relationships that are very sincere that I never expected. I’m a normal bloke who fulfilled mine and many kids’ dream. Like a superhero when they pull on the mask; I come here, I put on the kit, I’m the most competitive, most professional person you can be. But when I leave I take it off and forget about it.”There is a release, refuge in something else. In the camera. In the drum lessons Camello admits have been slow and the guitar he’s abandoned, the ability God gave his feet denied to his fingers. In the films, in the indie rock music first heard in the family car, and the musician mates he has made. The music discouraged by reggaeton-loving teammates who control the stereo blaring out each morning– and, . They wonder, he says laughing, why he’s not so keen on the gym.View image in fullscreenSergio Camello with the Action for Music charity.Photograph: Action for MusicThe music that can make a difference, too; if there is anything that moves people, reaches them like football, it may only be that. “There’s something I’ve wanted to do for a long time and it’s really fun,” Camello says. “I joined a charity, Action for Music, which gives opportunities to kids to play music in humble neighbourhoods. They go to four hours of classes a week: percussion, strings, wind. The kids don’t pay a euro, everything’s free: the space, the teachers, the instruments. They have schools in Tetuán and Carabanchel. I’m getting involved, learning, and I want to set up a school in Vallecas next year.” He stops, grins. “Only I’m going to do it my way … with rock.“I did a session with them the other day, me trying to play the drums after six months. There was a kid on sax: wow, what a vibe he had, he was just loving it. When you don’t know where to go, there’s a place, someone who believes in you, gives you an opportunity. Forty kids: put some drum sticks in their hand, a guitar, a sax, something that will give them so much. Tell them they can be good at something, feel good about themselves. Have fun, maybe find something inside they didn’t know was there. It’s a way of giving back to Vallecas everything it gives me. I’m so excited.”View image in fullscreenSergio Camello stops to take a selfie with a fan while walking through the Vallecas neighbourhood.Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The GuardianImagine them playing the Wizink. “I can be their manager,” Camello laughs. “The ideaisto do concerts at the end of each year. Imagine those kids, coming into their first class … then going on stage. It’s good to see yourself up there, with an instrument. Their family there, people who have bought tickets to see them play, the applause. That feeling: ‘I’m worth it.’”Sounds like scoring a goal. Camello’s eyes light up. “Yes, it is,” he says. “I’m still the same guy as I was when I didn’t score, eh. But at that moment when you’re standing there, there’s nothing else in your head, just a feeling that all this makes sense. When the ball hits the net, when you get a ground on its feet, all together, when they’re celebrating, it’s like it’s all worth it. You feel important, you’re good at something.”Explore more on these topicsRayo VallecanoLa LigaEuropean club footballinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Wiegman praises Toone’s attitude after late Lionesses recall for Greece playoff  | England women's football team | The Guardian
description: Sarina Wiegman hailed Ella Toone’s attitude after the midfielder was belatedly called up for England’s World Cup playoff in Greece
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: Sarina Wiegman hailed Ella Toone’s attitude after the midfielder was belatedly called up for England’s World Cup playoff in Greece
Content: Ella Toone has replaced Lucy Bronze in the England squad.Photograph: Harriet Lander/The FA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenElla Toone has replaced Lucy Bronze in the England squad.Photograph: Harriet Lander/The FA/Getty ImagesEngland women's football teamWiegman praises Toone’s attitude after late Lionesses recall for Greece playoffManchester United midfielder left out of initial squadFirst leg of World Cup playoff is on Friday in CreteTom Garryin Agia PelagiaThu 8 Oct 2026 12.33 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 15.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSarina Wiegman heaped praise on Ella Toone for her positive reaction to being left out of England’s initial squad for their Women’s World Cup playoff against Greece, after recalling the Manchester United midfielder for Friday’s first leg in Heraklion, Crete.An injury sustained by Lucy Bronze, described by Wiegman as “really small”, prompted the England right-back to return to Chelsea and Wiegman called up Toone, who travelled to Greece from Spain, where she had organised a training routine during the international window.Women’s Super League faces wait until 2029 for full-time referees despite funding boostRead moreToone has 69 caps and has scored 24 goals, including in the Euro 2022 final and 2023 World Cup semi-final, but Wiegman said when naming her squad that she had left out Toone and Chloe Kelly because “the levels weren’t what I expect from them on the pitch”. On Saturday, after startingManchester United’s victory over Liverpool, Toone took ownership of things, telling the BBC: “It’s about me now. I’ve got to keep working hard and use it as fuel to come back even better.”Wiegman, asked whether she had been impressed with Toone’s response, said: “Yes, very much. I think when I gave her the call, of course that was a hard call. But she took that straight away. Of course [she was] very disappointed, but the first thing she did [was say]: ‘OK, I’m going to get back, I’m going to do that.’ She has the support around her too.”The head coach referenced Toone’s post-match comments when she said: “That answer in the game, also the way she spoke about it, I thought that was really good. And then getting everything ready to go to Spain instead, but go for training there, I think that really impressed me. Well done, I would say.”That will be music to the ears of Toone, whose experience is also understood to have been a factor in Wiegman picking her rather than a replacement right-back. She could feature on Friday, when the European champions will hope to build a strong first-leg lead before Tuesday’s reverse fixture in Leicester.To qualify for next summer’s finals in Brazil, England must overcome Greece and win another two-leg playoff, against Slovakia or Ukraine, in December.Quick GuideGreece v England: Wiegman's probable team for visitorsShow(4-2-3-1) Hampton; Le Tissier, Morgan, Williamson, Greenwood; Stanway, Walsh; Mead, James, Hemp; RussoGreece v England, Pankritio Stadium, Friday, 5.30pm BSTWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.The draw for the World Cup will follow on 11 December and it would feel inconceivable for the 2023 runners-up to miss out. They are in the playoffs despite winning five of their six qualifiers in a group with Spain, the defending champions, who pipped England to top spot by virtue of their stronger head-to-head goal difference.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenSarina Wiegman (centre), speaks to the players during a training session in Heraklion, Greece.Photograph: Naomi Baker/The FA/Getty ImagesGreece have never qualified for a major tournament and, major underdogs against England, will probably set up in a low, defensive shape. The England defender Esme Morgan said she and her teammates would remain calm even if it takes time to break through: “It’s just [about] persistence and trying not to get drawn into being frustrated by the opposition. I think a really good example of it was the away game we played against Ukraine [in qualifying].“We couldn’t seem to break through in the first half – the keeper was making saves, I think we struck the woodwork a couple of times – but the messaging at half-time among the players and when Sarina came in to speak to us was just to keep continuing because we were creating opportunities. Not to start snatching or taking hot shots from distance, just trusting in the style of play that we have and in our ability to keep finding gaps in and around the defence. We came out for the second half after that and scored really, really quickly. So it’s just sticking to the gameplan, trusting in what we do and being patient”Explore more on these topicsEngland women's football teamSarina WiegmanWomen's World Cup 2027 qualifiersWomen's footballnewsShareReuse this content

title: Glasner urges quick end to Manchester City saga and fears damage to Premier League | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: Oliver Glasner has said Manchester City being found guilty of arranging “sham contracts” has damaged the Premier League brand globally and believes the integrity of the English top flight is under threat
Author: Ben Fisher
Headline: Oliver Glasner has said Manchester City being found guilty of arranging “sham contracts” has damaged the Premier League brand globally and believes the integrity of the English top flight is under threat
Content: Nottingham Forest's manager Oliver Glasner is acutely aware how the legal processes can drag after time at Crystal Palace.Photograph: Darren Staples/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNottingham Forest's manager Oliver Glasner is acutely aware how the legal processes can drag after time at Crystal Palace.Photograph: Darren Staples/AFP/Getty ImagesManchester CityGlasner urges quick end to Manchester City saga and fears damage to Premier LeagueForest manager believes football fans may ‘switch off’‘The most important thing is the integrity of the league’Ben FisherThu 8 Oct 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 13.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOliver Glasner has said Manchester City being foundguilty of arranging “sham contracts”has damaged the Premier League brand globally and believes the integrity of the English top flight is under threat.TheNottingham Foresthead coach said the league faces a job to repair its image and suggested supporters might switch off after City were found to have artificially inflated their income by more than £900m.City have appealedagainst last week’s seismic judgment of an independent commission that they broke financial rules across a nine-year period. If City’s appeal fails, the panel could determine a range of sporting sanctions, including expulsion from the league and point deductions. Glasner said the case must be finalised “as soon as possible” to protect the competition’s integrity.Khaldoon al-Mubarak: the tightrope walker who made rare misstep over City chargesRead moreGlasner cited his experience ofCrystal Palace being demoted from the Europa Leagueat the court of arbitration for sport (Cas) last year for breaking Uefa’s multi-club ownership rules as an example of how legal processes can drag.“Let’s wait until the final verdict is spoken, but my wish is just that this is quick,” Glasner said. “Because we didn’t know with Palace if we were in the Europa League or Conference League and then it was ‘you will hear on Thursday’ and then that became Monday, because it was always delayed. Then we got the final verdict 10 days before the Conference League started.“And that’s why I think this must be [completed] as soon as possible. There is still damage for the Premier League, not just in England. It’s a big topic all over the world, especially in Europe. The most important thing is the integrity of the league because as soon as the fans can’t trust it, they won’t watch it any more.”View image in fullscreenManchester City are appealing against last week’s seismic judgment of an independent commission that they broke financial rules across a nine-year period.Photograph: Loannis Alexopoulos/Anadolu/Getty ImagesLast week Aston Villa’s Unai Emery became the first Premier League manager to discuss the City case. “If other clubs had been artificially inflated and that were now coming to light, there would obviously be some damage,” Emery said, in an interview published with Spanish outlet Diario de Sevilla. “That is something for the courts and the relevant authorities to decide.“I feel sorry because of the way that [City] team played. Under [Pep] Guardiola, there were times when they were unmatched.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCity deny wrongdoing and formally lodged an appeal last Thursday. “The club’s firm position is that, on multiple grounds, the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe,” a City statement read.“The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case. We will continue to respect due process and are necessarily restricted in what we can say further until all proceedings are complete.”Explore more on these topicsManchester CityNottingham ForestnewsShareReuse this content

title: Manchester United offer JJ Gabriel new deal but risk losing prodigy for £350,000 | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: Manchester United have made JJ Gabriel an official scholarship contract offer, but remain at risk of losing the teenage forward for as little as £350,000
Author: Sam Cunningham
Headline: Manchester United have made JJ Gabriel an official scholarship contract offer, but remain at risk of losing the teenage forward for as little as £350,000
Content: JJ Gabriel in action at youth level for Manchester United. Rivals must deal directly with the club for the player, or compensation will be set by a tribunal.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAView image in fullscreenJJ Gabriel in action at youth level for Manchester United. Rivals must deal directly with the club for the player, or compensation will be set by a tribunal.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAManchester UnitedManchester United offer JJ Gabriel new deal but risk losing prodigy for £350,000Teenager almost certain to leave despite fresh offerCompensation for move to European rival would be lowSam CunninghamThu 8 Oct 2026 10.10 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 12.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleManchester United have made JJ Gabriel an official scholarship contract offer, but remain at risk of losing the teenage forward for as little as £350,000.The prodigy, who turned 16 this week,stunned the clubwhen he asked for his registration to be cancelled last month, setting in motion a scramble among Europe’s elite clubs for his signature.Under Premier League youth rules, Gabriel would have been able to leave for a rival for nothing in January if the club had not offered him a formal scholarship for next season. The Guardian can reveal that the offer has now been lodged with the player.Next Generation 2026: 60 of the best young talents in world footballRead moreWhether he accepts it or not – and it appears unlikely he will stay at Old Trafford – any Premier League club must now negotiate a fee directly with United for the player. If one is not reached, compensation will be set by a Professional Football Compensation Committee tribunal.At a tribunal, United would expect to receive in excess of £3m, plus a clause in the deal granting them 20% of his next transfer fee. In a previous tribunal for a high-profile academy player, Liverpool were required to pay Chelsea £2.8m up front – with an additional £1.2m in performance-related add-ons – for Rio Ngumoha, and a 20% sell-on clause was inserted in the deal.A United team photograph released this week featuring Gabriel briefly raised fan hopes of a reconciliation. But a breakdown between his representatives and the club means the forward – who has been at United since he was 11 – is now almost certain to leave.He was permitted under Premier League rules to sign a pre-agreement after his 16th birthday, but his camp were not prepared to enter discussions after a disagreement over first-team minutes.His next move is yet to be decided, though it is believed he favours a move to Europe, where compensation would be significantly lower. Real Madrid are favourites to sign him, with Barcelona, Bayern Munich and Paris Saint-Germain all monitoring developments.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAccording to official Fifa compensation figures for a Category I academy, United would receive around £350,000 if he moves abroad. He would ordinarily have been prevented from transferring before his 18th birthday, but is eligible for an EU passport through his parents. The club will consider taking legal action if they believe recruitment rules have been breached.Gabriel has not appeared at training for more than three weeks and, according to sources, the club has made multiple attempts to check on his wellbeing. To fast-track his progression into the first team, Gabriel had worked with specialist staff usually reserved for senior players.Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitednewsShareReuse this content

title: Victor Montagliani eyes re-election at Concacaf that would rule out Fifa presidency run | Fifa | The Guardian
description: Concacaf president Victor Montagliani has clarified his intentions to staff at the confederation after he was touted as a potential rival to Gianni Infantino at Fifa
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Concacaf president Victor Montagliani has clarified his intentions to staff at the confederation after he was touted as a potential rival to Gianni Infantino at Fifa
Content: Victor Montagliani (left) said he will run again for Concacaf’s presidency; Gianni Infantino (right) intends to keep the top job at Fifa.Photograph: Chris Brunskill/Fantasista/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenVictor Montagliani (left) said he will run again for Concacaf’s presidency; Gianni Infantino (right) intends to keep the top job at Fifa.Photograph: Chris Brunskill/Fantasista/Getty ImagesFifaVictor Montagliani eyes re-election at Concacaf that would rule out Fifa presidency runConfederation president clarifies his intentions to staffCanadian was eyed as potential rival to Gianni InfantinoExclusive byMatt HughesandNick AmesThu 8 Oct 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 14.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVictor Montagliani has told Concacaf staff he intends to stand for re-election as the confederation’s presidentnext year, which will rule him out of going up against Gianni Infantino for the top job atFifa.The Canadian businessman is understood to have relayed the message to most of the 41 members of Concacaf, the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation.Police occupy Djibouti FA headquarters amid attempt to oust Fifa council memberRead moreMontagliani has been widely touted as a potential candidate to take on Infantino for the Fifa presidency, particularly among Uefa member associations, who are conscious a European candidate would have no chance of beating Infantino in a ballot of Fifa’s 211 members.At a town hall meeting of Concacaf staff late last month, however, Montagliani is understood to have said that despite the Fifa governance crisis and calls for him to stand, he wants to continue serving members in the region.Concacaf’s presidential election will take place in the first quarter of next year before the Fifa vote on 18 March in Rabat, with the similar timelines leading Montagliani to clarify his intentions to staff.The 61-year-old was elected president on a reforming mandate 10 years agoafter the corruption scandalthat culminated in the arrest of then Concacaf president, Jeffrey Webb, after an FBI investigation. Webb admitted he had taken “bribes and kickbacks”.Uefa will also hold presidential elections next year, with Aleksander Ceferin confirming his intention to stand at a meeting of Uefa’s 55 member associations in Berlin on Thursday. Ceferin had said in February 2024 that he would not run for a fourth term at the helm but the likelihood that he would, after all, continue had long been an open secret. Previously, changes to the Uefa statutes had been passed that meant his first term, which began midway through the standard four-year cycle, did not count towards the standard three-term limit.It raises the prospect of Ceferin, who took the presidency in September 2016, holding power for more than 15 years in total.
