That is seen among most European FAs as a positive amid the turmoil engulfing football’s governance while putting to bed any perception that Ceferin, who would have had a number of proponents, might be tempted to challenge Infantino for the Fifa roleMontagliani and Ceferin are expected to continue working together to bring about governance reform at Fifa after the World Cup sell-off scandal, which will be on the agenda at next Thursday’s Fifa council meeting in Zurich.Fifa’s council has not met since Infantino’s Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) plan was exposed in July despite repeated calls from members for an extraordinary general meeting, with the summit their first meeting since Fifa congress in Vancouver last March.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMontagliani, Ceferin and the Asian Football Confederation president, Salman bin Ibrahim al-Khalifa, are expected to use the council meeting to demand an independent review of FFE and call for broader governance reforms of Fifa, which would give a greater voice to stakeholders and formalise the council’s role in decision-making.Previous calls from the trio, expressed in letters sent to Infantino last month, for Fifa to allocate a portion of its $6bn (£4.5bn) cash reserves to members will also be discussed.Delegates at Uefa’s Berlin meeting discussed a framework for Fifa reform, whose key points were made public during the afternoon. Among the points listed were the need for “a president who leads, not manages”, “stronger ethics, disciplinary, audit and compliance”, and “a clear process for major decisions”.Azerbaijan was an outlier in refusing to back Uefa’s reform proposals. The Azeri FA’s former general secretary, Elkhan Mammadov, now plays a key role at Fifa as its chief member associations officer and has been instrumental in Infantino’s attempts to keep wavering nations onside during the FFE crisis. Later this month, Azerbaijan will hold the first Fifa Under-15 World Cup, whose contestants will include Russia.Explore more on these topicsFifaFootball politicsUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Mikel Arteta’s new contract reflects where the power now lies at Arsenal | Mikel Arteta | The Guardian
description: From transfers to stadium works and even the training-ground dog, there is no doubting the Spaniard’s influence at the club
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: From transfers to stadium works and even the training-ground dog, there is no doubting the Spaniard’s influence at the club
Content: Mikel Arteta signed a new contract at Arsenal this week, making him the highest paid manager in English football.Photograph: Stuart MacFarlane/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMikel Arteta signed a new contract at Arsenal this week, making him the highest paid manager in English football.Photograph: Stuart MacFarlane/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesMikel ArtetaAnalysisMikel Arteta’s new contract reflects where the power now lies at ArsenalEd AaronsFrom transfers to stadium works and even the training-ground dog, there is no doubting the Spaniard’s influence at the clubThu 8 Oct 2026 05.49 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 11.59 EDTShareIf anyone doubts Mikel Arteta’s status as No 1 at Arsenal in the week hecommitted his future to the club until 2030, just ask Win the dog. The chocolate labrador who played a starring role in the celebrations when Arsenal were crowned Premier League champions in May has become part of the family at the training ground in Hertfordshire since being introduced by Arteta in May 2023.Kai Havertz, David Raya and Mikel Merino, who issues commands in Spanish and has spoken about spending time with Win when out for three months with a foot injury, are particular favourites. But, according to sources close to Win, a therapy dog trained not to bark, there is no contest when it comes to her preferred human: Arteta.Havertz, Isak, Dorgu … spate of injuries with national teams leaves sour taste for top clubsRead moreThe manager is understood to have taken Win home for Christmas last year, having been instrumental in her arrival a few days after his side had finished as runners-up to Manchester City for the first time. Cuddly replicas are available in the club shop. The real version spends most days at Arsenal’s training centre, with her primary carer a full-time member of staff based there.“I carefully chose the dog and in my opinion it’s the perfect representative of who we are right now,” said Arteta in 2023. “Win needs accountability from us because we have to look after her as well; her emotions and what she needs.”It is an example of Arteta’s attention to detail that has helped to transform Arsenal from also-rans into champions. Ominously for the rest, the Spaniard promised on Wednesday, when he signed a new four-year contract understood to be worth more than £20m a season, that this “is only the beginning” of what Arsenal hope could be a trophy-laden dynasty under his leadership.View image in fullscreenMikel Arteta ended Arsenal’s wait for a Premier League title last season and has designs on further silverware.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianThe length of deal was significant given that it would take Arteta, who will mark his seventh anniversary in the job in December, past a decade at the helm – even if he still has some way to go to match Arsène Wenger’s record of almost 22 years in charge. Wenger’s first day was30 years ago last weekand he quickly assumed control at the club. The influence of Arteta, made Arsenal captain by Wenger in 2014, has grown steadily since he was appointed after a stint as Pep Guardiola’s assistant at Manchester City.Arteta, upgraded from head coach to manager in September 2020 having won the FA Cup six months after replacing Unai Emery, has seen various executives depart as his power has increased. The 44-year-old, who became the second-youngest manager after José Mourinho to win the Premier League, has a direct line to the co-chair Josh Kroenke and is able to exert a major say over most big decisions – on and off the pitch.Arsenal’s announcement this week that they had decidedagainst a major expansion of the Emirates Stadiumcame after Arteta is believed to have expressed concern over the disruption that would be caused by a temporary move to Wembley or elsewhere. The owner, Kroenke Sports & Entertainment (KSE), is also thought to have been put off proposals to increase the capacity to 70,000 owing to the cost, despite agreeing a record $4bn (£3bn) deal to buy the MLB side Los Angeles Angels last month.That did not stop KSE from making Arteta the best-paid manager in the Premier League with a hefty salary increase from the £10m plus £5m bonus for reaching the Champions League that he agreed in 2024. Only Atlético Madrid’s Diego Simeone is thought to earn more.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionArteta is understood to have had the final say in the decision not to pursue interest in Malick Fofana after the Belgium forward was offered in the final days of the transfer window because he wanted to ensurethe 16-year-old phenomenon Max Dowmanwould not be denied opportunities. He may regret not bringing in another forward after Christos Tzolis sustained a hamstring injury with Greece that is expected to keep him out for at least three weeks, but it is clear Arteta has been calling the shots even since the arrival of Andrea Berta as the sporting director in March 2025.Such is the intensity Arteta brings to the job that it remains to be seen whether he can last as long as Wenger, although there are few signs that operating in such a high-pressure environment has affected him physically.The odd grey hair aside, he barely looks different from the day he was announced in his first managerial role. With the twin motivations of making Arsenal back-to-back league title winners for the first time since the 1930s and European champions after coming so close last season when they lost to PSG in the final on penalties, Arteta appears to be here to stay.Explore more on these topicsMikel ArtetaArsenalanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Women’s Super League faces wait until 2029 for full-time referees despite funding boost | Women's Super League | The Guardian
description: Women’s Super League clubs have agreed to a major funding increase but the wait for full-time referees in the English top tier is set to continue until 2029
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: Women’s Super League clubs have agreed to a major funding increase but the wait for full-time referees in the English top tier is set to continue until 2029
Content: Referee Sophie Dennington officiates a WSL match. There is disappointment in the elite game over the timeline for officials going full-time.Photograph: Keeran Marquis/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenReferee Sophie Dennington officiates a WSL match. There is disappointment in the elite game over the timeline for officials going full-time.Photograph: Keeran Marquis/NurPhoto/ShutterstockWomen's Super LeagueWomen’s Super League faces wait until 2029 for full-time referees despite funding boostExtra investment agreed at latest WSL board meetingCalls for fully professional match officials have grownExclusive byTom GarryThu 8 Oct 2026 05.34 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 09.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWomen’s Super League clubs have agreed to a major funding increase for match officials but the wait for full-time referees in the English top tier is set to continue until 2029, the Guardian has learned.The extra investment, decided at the latest WSL Football board meeting, will focus on enhancing officials’ education, analysis and physical performance, it is understood.Although none of the parties involved are ruling out progressing to full-time WSL referees earlier, 2029-30 is the campaign that has been agreed for when the officials will be employed by Pro Ref, the official body, formerly known as PGMOL, responsible for match officials across English professional football.Arsenal and Chelsea set to miss a month of next WSL season due to Club World CupRead moreCalls for fully professional WSL match officials have grown since the English women’s top tier became full-time for players in 2018-19 and more so since the top two divisions were taken over by the independent WSL Football in 2024. A further three-year wait is likely to divide opinion.According to multiple sources, WSL and WSL 2 clubs – the primary shareholders of WSL Football – were told at the all-club meeting this month of the three-year funding plan to transition to full-time match officials for the 2029-30 campaign. Insiders have told the Guardian there was initially a mixed response, with some clubs hoping the move would happen sooner, before the funding plan was voted on and approved.One WSL club’s senior executive, who did not want to be named, told the Guardian it was “about time” that there was a specific timeframe but that they were disappointed it was three seasons away.Another senior WSL club source welcomed the commitment to funding the education and training needed to improve the qualityof officiating.At the board meeting, it is believed clubs the league and clubs discussed balancing the desire to have full-time officials as quickly as possible with a need to enhance standards and provisions.Many of the officials working in the WSL hold other full-time or part-time jobs. It is understood the new deal followed extensive discussions between WSL Football, the Foootball Association and Pro Ref.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe WSL has repeatedly stated its “intention” to move to having full-time officials but this is believed to be the first time a timeline has been agreed.In 2021, the FA said it had no immediate plans to introduce full-time referees to the top two divisions of English women’s football.Referees in the English men’s game became full-time professionals in 2001 across the Premier League and the EFL.There is a seat for a WSL representative on the Pro Ref board for the first time this season, after the launch of Pro Ref this summer, giving the WSL a greater say in the decision-making processes, alongside Premier League and EFL representatives.Explore more on these topicsWomen's Super LeagueRefereesWomen's footballnewsShareReuse this content

title: London Broncos graded below Barrow but still set for Super League place | Super League | The Guardian
description: Runaway Championship winners London Broncos have been graded only 16th for 2027 behind Barrow Raiders
Author: Aaron Bower
Headline: Runaway Championship winners London Broncos have been graded only 16th for 2027 behind Barrow Raiders
Content: London players celebrate winning the Championship Grand Final against Doncaster.Photograph: Olly Hassell/SWpix.com/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenLondon players celebrate winning the Championship Grand Final against Doncaster.Photograph: Olly Hassell/SWpix.com/ShutterstockSuper LeagueLondon Broncos graded below Barrow but still set for Super League placeChampionship winners only 16th in new IMG gradingsNRL money contingent on London Super League sideAaron BowerThu 8 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 12.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe runaway Championship winnersLondon Broncoshave been graded below even Barrow Raiders for next season – but they are still set to become the 15th team in an expanded Super League, the Guardian can reveal.The Broncos haveswept aside the second tier in 2026, winning all three domestic trophies on offer after assembling a squad filled with NRL talent. Under the ownership of the Kangaroos great Darren Lockyer, London’s goal was two-fold this year: to dominate on the pitch as well as making a push for the top 14 in the Rugby Football League’s gradings system.Wakefield’s wondrous Super League fairytale a victory for loyalty and logic | Aaron BowerRead moreThat system determines which teams play inSuper Leagueevery year, with the highest-ranked 14 clubs across a variety of metrics including attendances, on-field performance and finance being admitted. However, London have finished 16th – below Barrow, who are deemed the best-performing Championship club.Ordinarily that would mean another season in the Championship, but London look increasingly likely to be given a reprieve. That is because as a partnership between theNRLand Super League nears completion, the Australian governing body has insisted any deal to invest in the British game is conditional on London being in the top flight.Super League officials initially pushed back, the Guardian understands, when it became clear several weeks ago that London would not be in the top 14 of the gradings. However, the NRL returned serve and made it clear they want a London presence in the competition no matter what to increase their chances of the partnership being a success.That means Super League is poised to expand again. This time last year, the competition went from 12 teams to 14 but an increase to 15 is now on the cards, with London granted access despite officially not being the best Championship team in the system used to determine promotion and relegation.Super League would need to rapidly implement plans to become a 15-team competition. That includes introducing bye rounds for teams, as well as deciding how central distribution will be shared and whether the current fixture format of everyone playing one another home and away – plus a game at Magic Weekend – needs to change, as that would mean an increase in fixtures from 27 to 29.But talks between the two leagues are accelerating towards a conclusion, with hopes high an agreement can be struck during the upcoming World Cup in Australia. The NRL would then take administrative control of Super League’s fortunes, removing power from the club owners in return for a significant financial investment.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe new Super League champions, Wakefield Trinity, have topped the gradings for 2026 with a score of 17.85 out of a possible 20. They are the fourth different team to finish top of the system since it began in 2023 with Leeds Rhinos second, one of eight clubs to achieve Grade A status after scoring 15 points or more.With the top 14 unchanged from this time last year, all are guaranteed a spot in Super League in 2027 and they look set to be joined by London.Explore more on these topicsSuper LeagueLondon BroncosRugby leagueNRLAustralia sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Laos footballer arrested in connection with alleged match-fixing for betting syndicate | Match-fixing | The Guardian
description: Laos’ national football federation have referred Soukphachan Lueanthala, who is accused of helping a betting syndicate during the summer’s Asean Championship, to the country’s police
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: Laos’ national football federation have referred Soukphachan Lueanthala, who is accused of helping a betting syndicate during the summer’s Asean Championship, to the country’s police
Content: Soukphachan Lueanthala was arrested after Laos’ final game at the Asean Championships.Photograph: ZUMA Press Inc/AlamyView image in fullscreenSoukphachan Lueanthala was arrested after Laos’ final game at the Asean Championships.Photograph: ZUMA Press Inc/AlamyMatch-fixingLaos footballer arrested in connection with alleged match-fixing for betting syndicateNational FA refers Soukphachan Lueanthala to policeAccused of helping group during summer tournamentEd AaronsandRomain MolinaThu 8 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleALaosinternational has been arrested in connection with allegations of match-fixing during the 2026 Asean Championship after the country’s football federation referred suspected bribery, illegal gambling and match manipulation to the authorities.Soukphachan Lueanthala, a winger who featured for Laos during the tournament and plays in his homeland for Salavan United, is understood to have been accused of helping to organise the alleged operation on behalf of a betting syndicate believed to be from Vietnam.Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.According to sources close to the Laos team, he was arrested after several squad members were questioned by police after returning from their last match at the tournament for south-east Asian nations, away to Myanmar, at the start of August. The arrest has not been confirmed by the federation (LFF) or Lao police, but the Guardian has established that the player is in custody.The game against Myanmar ended in a 7-2 defeat and followed three other heavy losses during the group stage: 5-0 to Thailand, 4-0 to Malaysia and 4-1 to the Philippines.The LFF confirmed in a statement on 7 August that it had opened an investigation before referring the case to police. According to a source familiar with the allegations, who did not want to be named, Lueanthala was suspected of giving instructions to other squad members and acting as a link between those involved.Laos, managed by the Serb Vladica Grujic, failed to match the results achieved two years earlier when they scored seven goals and conceded 11 in four games, pulling off surprise draws against Indonesia and the Philippines, who both sit far higher in the Fifa rankings. The case comes against a background of previous match-fixing scandals involving Laos that led the Asian Football Confederationto impose a life ban on Thipphonexay Inthavongsain 2020 after finding him guilty of conspiring to manipulate the result of a 2017 international against Hong Kong.The AFC was contacted for comment about the latest allegations and whether it was assisting the Lao authorities, but did not respond. Neither did the LFF.The source, who has extensive experience inside Lao football, has alleged that match-fixing has been a long-running problem involving players and potentially officials. Players are particularly vulnerable because of their financial circumstances. “Until last year, they were getting $10 per day when they were joining the national team,” he said.One player allegedly told him he had fixed three matches for “$10,000” each time. He claimed suspected fixing had damaged Lao football more broadly, with experienced players disappearing from the national team and younger players taking their places. “There is such talent,” he said. “They deserve so much better than this.”Explore more on these topicsMatch-fixingLaosnewsShareReuse this content

title: New Australian Open boss Andrew Abdo throws shade at critics: ‘I’m not an outsider’ | Australian Open | The Guardian
description: Launch event marred by former NRL CEO calling world No 1 ‘Jacob’ Sinner, while announcing the grand slam will add 700 seats in 2027
Author: Jack Snape
Headline: Launch event marred by former NRL CEO calling world No 1 ‘Jacob’ Sinner, while announcing the grand slam will add 700 seats in 2027
Content: Tennis Australia CEO Andrew Abdo speaks in front of an image of Jannik Sinner during a 2027 Australian Open launch event in Melbourne.Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAPView image in fullscreenTennis Australia CEO Andrew Abdo speaks in front of an image of Jannik Sinner during a 2027 Australian Open launch event in Melbourne.Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAPAustralian OpenNew Australian Open boss Andrew Abdo throws shade at critics: ‘I’m not an outsider’Launch event marred by former NRL CEO calling world No 1 ‘Jacob’ SinnerGrand slam to add 700 seats amid focus on comfort as well as growthJack SnapeThu 8 Oct 2026 01.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 01.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNew Tennis Australia chief executive Andrew Abdo pledged more shade and more seats for outer courts at theAustralian Openin 2027, as the former rugby league administrator believes his background as a tennis outsider will fuel the tournament’s “relentless pursuit of growth”.The first tennis grand slam of 2027 will include the largest temporary grandstand constructed at Melbourne Park, adding 700 seats, and there will be “triple the amount of shade” for fans, as Abdo plans to cap day pass sales to better manage visitor comfort.Djokovic ends title drought with China Open triumph while Alcaraz claims glory in JapanRead moreHe has appointed himself tournament director – replicating thedual role held by his predecessor Craig Tiley– but his launch address to tennis staff, partners and media in Melbourne on Thursday was marred by a gaffe when he referred to men’s world No 1 Jannik Sinner as “Jacob Sinner”.Abdo told press afterwards “of course I know that it’s Jannik Sinner”, and flagged the Italian – who is recovering from a knee injury – plans to play in theOne Point Slam promotionat Melbourne Park which pits amateurs against professionals.Those in tennis accustomed to the experienced Tiley are still coming to terms with the appointment of Abdo, who has not enjoyed a smooth beginning to his tenure.In a speech at the SportNXT conference last month, Abdo raised the possibility of shortening men’s grand slam matches from best-of-five sets. The idea sparked an immediate backlash from tennis traditionalists, prompting a post on Australian Open social media accounts saying “five-set tennis is here to stay”.On Thursday, Abdo said there were benefits he brings as a tennis outsider. “I think I bring a fresh perspective, energy and new ideas,” he said.“I’m not an outsider to leading in sport, and I’m not an outsider to understanding how to surround myself with incredibly talented, hard-working people to get the best outcome.“One thing that you’ll get with from me is relentless pursuit of growth and relentless pursuit of value for our stakeholders.”More than 1.3 million tickets were sold for the 2026 tournament, up more than 100,000 on the previous year. The tournament faces growing pains however, and long queues to get into courts are common especially on the weekends.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“You never want to turn fans away, but we are ultimately really cognisant of the fan experience,” Abdo said.“We’ve broken records every year in the last few years, and 1.3 million people into the precinct, clearly for us, space is a constraint we don’t want to have.”In addition to the temporary grandstand on court six, Grand Slam Oval will include a two-storey structure around the shaded lawn. Abdo said it is a “delicate trade-off” between fan experience and selling tickets.“We want to continue working with the government to create more space in this precinct so that we don’t have to cap crowds, but it is an important element to ensure that the fans that do come have a good experience, that the queues are manageable and they’re able to actually see what they’re here for, that is tennis, and obviously get the overall community experience and the fun and the festivities.”Explore more on these topicsAustralian OpenTennisAustralia sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Wallabies back Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii on wing for first Bledisloe Cup Test against All Blacks | Australia rugby union team | The Guardian

Content: Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii is named on a wing as Australia’s Wallabies announce their team to play New Zealand’s All Blacks in a Bledisloe Cup Test at Eden Park.Photograph: Janelle St Pierre/Getty title: NFL today: How to watch Buccaneers v Cowboys, TV channels & live stream Thursday 8 October | NFL | The Guardian
description: How will the Buccaneers and Cowboys fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options
Author: Alex Kirshner
Headline: How will the Buccaneers and Cowboys fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options
Content: Dak Prescott will lead out the Cowboys against the Bucs.Photograph: Erik Williams/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenDak Prescott will lead out the Cowboys against the Bucs.Photograph: Erik Williams/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockNFL watching and streaming guideNFLNFL today: How to watch Buccaneers v Cowboys, TV channels & live stream Thursday 8 OctoberHow will the Buccaneers and Cowboys fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream optionsAlex KirshnerThu 8 Oct 2026 13.41 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 13.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe bad news for the Buccaneers: Their 0-4 start has been an unmitigated disaster that, in normal circumstances, would have already evaporated their playoff chances. The good news for Tampa Bay, however, is that they play in the NFC South, meaning they’re still just two games out of a tie for the lead in what is often the worst division in theNFL. All is not quitelost yet.If the Bucs want to join the 1992 Chargers and become the second team to make the postseason after an 0-4 opening, they’ll need to stop the bleeding on Thursday night in north Texas. They’ll have to do it without Baker Mayfield, who continues to nurse an injury to his throwing thumb.They’ll face a challenge against the Cowboys, who are just 2-2 but look like slim favorites in the NFC East while the Eagles struggle to get out of neutral. The Cowboys have gotten an excellent first four games from Dak Prescott, who has paced one of the most efficient offenses in football. No team is scoring more than Dallas’ 3.4 points per offensive series, and it’s been Prescott and the passing game doing most of that work. (Nearly 75%t of Dallas’ yards have come through the air, compared to a league average of two-thirds.) A big outing against Tampa Bay would solidify the Cowboys’ path to a division title.Buccaneers at CowboysTime:8.15pm ET/1.15am BST (Friday)Stadium:AT&T Stadium (Arlington, Texas)How to watchUnited States:Stream onPrime VideoCanada:Stream onDAZNandFuboUnited Kingdom:Watch onSky Sports NFLorSky Sports Main Event, or stream withNOWorNFL Game Pass on DAZN.What to watch forJerry Jones loves a splashy deal, and he made one before last week’s win over the Texans. The Cowboys sent out a package built around a second-round draft choice to bring in Steelers cornerback Joey Porter, who didn’t make a Pro Bowl in his first four seasons but established himself as one of the league’s tougher man-to-man cover players all the same. The next touchdown Porter surrenders as the primary defender on a target will be the first of his career. Dallas made the deal without giving Porter the new contract that had eluded him in Pittsburgh, suggesting Jones saw his acquisition as a win-now endeavor.The Bucs will ride for another week, at least, with rookie QB Jalon Daniels. The Kansas product made his debut in Week 4 and finished 27th of the league’s 32 QBs in passer rating that week, and dead last in yardage per attempt. He sprinkled in a pair of interceptions — not an ideal start for a rookie who is about to turn 24 and whosesix yearsof collegiate experience might have suggested a less rocky debut. Will Daniels find it hospitable to go up against the team that is dead-last in the NFL in net yards allowed per passing attempt (8) through the first four weeks? Tampa Bay’s last flickers of hope depend on it.Explore more on these topicsNFLNFL watching and streaming guideDallas CowboysTampa Bay BuccaneersUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Dystopian’: Co-op becomes latest firm to put staff under AI surveillance | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Whistleblower says recording and analysis of all probate calls in Co-op Legal Services is oppressive
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Whistleblower says recording and analysis of all probate calls in Co-op Legal Services is oppressive
Content: One employee says the system can mean their work is monitored by AI for seven hours a day as they handle inquiries, often from bereaved customers.Photograph: Maskot/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenOne employee says the system can mean their work is monitored by AI for seven hours a day as they handle inquiries, often from bereaved customers.Photograph: Maskot/Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)‘Dystopian’: Co-op becomes latest firm to put staff under AI surveillanceWhistleblower says recording and analysis of all probate calls in Co-op Legal Services is oppressiveRobert BoothUK technology editorThu 8 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 07.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Co-op has become the latest employer to place workers under AI surveillance with an automated listening technology that rates every phone call some of them make to customers.In a system described as “oppressive and dystopian” by a whistleblower, Co-op Legal Services is using AI models to record, analyse and award a percentage score for interactions between agents and customers seeking advice about probate, wills and estates.A model fromOpenAIhas been trained to assess more than 50 discrete aspects of each phone call and provide pass and fail scores to managers who use the data to analyse employee performance. One worker said the system can mean their work is monitored by AI for several hours a day as they handle inquiries often from recently bereaved customers.It comes after the Guardian last week revealed Euan Blair’s AI training company, Multiverse, has startedusing an AI for blanket monitoring of online classroom sessions, which teachers called “remorseless” and “unnerving”, while Multiverse said it was “using AI to improve the experience of learners and customers”. Experts have voiced fears that increasing AI monitoring of workers risks increasing stress.“You are being watched,” said a Co-op worker who spoke to the Guardian on condition of anonymity and said the AI created a sense of distrust. “It’s different from occasionally being listened to for compliance purposes. [You are] being monitored absolutely every word that you say and every time that you utter something … It just feels really dystopian. It’s the thin end of the wedge.”The Co-op, which operates supermarkets, undertakers, insurance and legal services companies, said it did not recognise the criticism and said its probate advisers were highly engaged. It said it supported colleagues with AI, which is a “key aspect of our quality assurance processes” and helps ensure “our clients consistently receive empathetic expert guidance”.The AI monitoring is understood to have been introduced in the last couple of months into the work of dozens of legal services staff. It is used in part to identify ways they can boost their sales performance.The Co-op said the AI is used solely as a support tool, is not a decision-maker, and helps leaders “support colleagues and continuously improve the experience we provide to clients”.Trade unions have begun pushing back against the spread of AI monitoring. In FebruaryBurger King in the US announced it would be using the technology to track restaurant workers’ customer interactions, and this summer,Meta paused tracking of employees’ computer keystrokesamid data privacy concerns and a staff backlash.“AI is sold as the solution to every problem, but examples like this make it clear that it can diminish sensible workplace practices and intensify working lives for no reason,” said John Chadfield, the national officer of the Communication Workers Union. “Unaccountable computer systems should not be people’s managers, and these hard-working employees demand far more respect.”“The office is becoming more like a factory now our performance feedback can be given in a more structured way,” said Hayfa Mohdzaini, a senior policy and practice adviser at the Chartered Institute of Professional Development. “Clearly some people have a problem with it. It will be interesting to see how it develops and how much managers need to adjust their approach.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis year, the International Labour Organizationwarned about the “psychosocial” risks of AI monitoring, including increasing work-related stress.“AI systems are being deployed in workplaces in the absence of a comprehensive regulatory framework,” it said. “Preventing the risk of harm by AI use and operation in this context may not be straightforward.”Caoilionn Hurley, the managing director of Co-op Life Services, which includes legal services, said: “The efficiency of AI over traditional methods allows us to review all customer conversations to ensure we consistently deliver high standards of service, while enabling more informed support, coaching and development for colleagues … Put simply, our goal is to provide expert support combined with empathy and understanding for every client at what can be a difficult time. AI helps us deliver that more consistently, while human judgment, accountability, care and kindness remain at the heart of every client relationship.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Co-operative GroupOpenAInewsShareReuse this content

title: Molly Russell’s father to tell UK cinemagoers: ‘Instagram helped kill my daughter’ | Social media | The Guardian
description: In ad to be shown before The Social Reckoning, Ian Russell will say ‘too little has changed’ since death of Molly, 14
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: In ad to be shown before The Social Reckoning, Ian Russell will say ‘too little has changed’ since death of Molly, 14
Content: Molly Russell took her own life in 2017 after viewing harmful content on Instagram.Photograph: Family handout/PAView image in fullscreenMolly Russell took her own life in 2017 after viewing harmful content on Instagram.Photograph: Family handout/PASocial mediaMolly Russell’s father to tell UK cinemagoers: ‘Instagram helped kill my daughter’In ad to be shown before The Social Reckoning, Ian Russell will say ‘too little has changed’ since death of Molly, 14Dan MilmoGlobal technology editorThu 8 Oct 2026 04.03 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 12.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMolly Russell’s father will tell UK cinemagoers that “Instagram helped kill my daughter” in an advert to be shown before screenings of a new film about Mark Zuckerberg’s social media empire.In the30-second adbefore The Social Reckoning, released on Friday, Ian Russell says “too little has changed” since the death of his 14-year-old daughter, who took her own life in 2017after viewing harmful contenton Instagram.He will ask viewers to donate to the Molly Rose Foundation (MRF) to “stop companies like Meta endangering young people like Molly”. The Aaron Sorkin film focuses on theFacebookwhistleblower Frances Haugen.View image in fullscreenIan Russell says in the ad that ‘algorithms still force streams of toxic content on to children’.Photograph: The Molly Rose FoundationThe ad will be screened at Everyman, Curzon, Showcase and AMC cinemas showing the film in the UK after the cinema advertising company Pearl & Dean offered space to MRF for free.Speaking directly to the audience, Russell will say: “I’ve said it for years:Instagramhelped kill my daughter. Too little has changed. Promises to deliver safety have failed. Algorithms still force streams of toxic content on to children. So if you agree harmful tech is unacceptable and bosses like Mark Zuckerberg should be held accountable, please support Molly Rose Foundation to stop companies like Meta endangering young people like Molly.”Kathryn Jacob, the chief executive of Pearl & Dean, said: “We know that audiences appreciate advertising that is contextually relevant. The team at the Molly Rose Foundation worked hard to deliver a campaign that works with the film.”Bauer Media Audio, the owner of the Absolute Radio, Kiss and Jazz FM brands, is also donating free advertising space to MRF for a separate advert, also voiced by Russell, in which he asks parents seeking advice to contact the charity.Haugen’s revelations about Facebook and Instagram’s approach to online safety, detailed in the Sorkin film, included internal research showing that Instagram contenthad a negative impact on teenage girls’ mental health. At the time Zuckerberg’s company said the coverage of the research “focused on a limited set of findings and casts them in a negative light”.View image in fullscreenJeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.Photograph: Leah Gallo/Sony Pictures/APThe film also covers Haugen’s testimony to the US Congress, in which she said the social media corporation put “astronomical profits before people”, harmed children and destabilised democracies.Haugen is played by the Oscar winner Mikey Madison, while Zuckerberg is played by Succession’s Jeremy Strong. The Guardian’sreview of the film, a quasi-sequel to the Sorkin-scripted The Social Network, says it “rattles along at an entertaining clip”, adding that Strong – taking over from Jesse Eisenberg in Social Network – gives a “very interesting Zuckerberg impersonation, standing and sitting like a Thunderbird puppet”.The2022 inquestinto Molly’s death was a landmark moment for online safety. The coroner ruled that she “died from an act of self-harm while suffering from depression and the negative effects of online content” and that algorithms had pushed harmful content to Molly that she had not requested.At the time, Russellaccused Meta, the owner of Facebook and Instagram, of guiding his daughter on a “demented trail of life-sucking content” that included material related to self-harm, suicide and depression. Meta later made a donation to MRF in lieu of a legal settlement to Molly’s family.In a statement issued after the release of the documentaryMolly vs the Machinesthis year, which recreates moments from the inquest, Meta said its thoughts “remain with Molly’s friends and her family”. The company said it had introduced safety measures since Molly’s death, making private accounts the default for all under-18s, and restricting who could message them and the content they saw.Explore more on these topicsSocial mediaMetaFacebookInstagramDigital mediaSocial networkingInternet safetynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Someone else will do it for less’: refugees in Kenya are powering tech for dwindling pay | Kenya | The Guardian
description: Refugee gig workers for tech companies don’t know how much they’ll be paid – if AI hasn’t already taken their jobs
Author: Claire Wilmot
Headline: Refugee gig workers for tech companies don’t know how much they’ll be paid – if AI hasn’t already taken their jobs
Content: Digital freelancers work at the Generation Aid center at the Kakuma refugee camp in Kenya.Photograph: Thabit Radjabu/The GuardianView image in fullscreenDigital freelancers work at the Generation Aid center at the Kakuma refugee camp in Kenya.Photograph: Thabit Radjabu/The GuardianReworkedKenya‘Someone else will do it for less’: refugees in Kenya are powering tech for dwindling payRefugee gig workers for tech companies don’t know how much they’ll be paid – if AI hasn’t already taken their jobsSupported byAbout this contentClaire WilmotThu 8 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 16.38 EDTShareIn a portable building in Kakuma, a refugee camp nearKenya’s northern border withSouth Sudan, Grace usedChatGPTto research translations of Christian hymns in languages she doesn’t speak. She didn’t know the client, the purpose of her work or whether she would be paid, but as a refugee unable to legally work in Kenya, she needed any opportunity she could get.Grace, who requested anonymity due to a nondisclosure agreement, prompted ChatGPT to translate the hymn’s English text into the assigned east Asian language. She then used the translation to search for existing versions and find information about its translator, author and Christian denomination. She fed those details to AOP Connect, a crowdsourced research platform owned by British AI enterprise software company RWS.If RWS deems her work high quality based on six listed criteria, it could award her up to $500 as a “discretionary reward”, according to RWS researcher documents and manuals reviewed by the Guardian. But refugees aren’t guaranteed wages, and most earn significantly less than the maximum without being told why, said Asha Luka Abdallah, a mentor at the Solidarity Initiative forRefugees(SIR), an organization that trains refugees to work in the tech outsourcing industry.The AI industry is booming. Women are getting left behindRead moreRemote jobs such as content moderation and data annotation have beenpromotedas awin-winby United Nations agencies as well as global tech companies: refugees get income opportunities, AI and social media companies get a source of cheap labor.But interviews with more than two dozen refugees in Kakuma show that only one side has clearly benefited. Tech companies have built some of their most powerful tools on datasets handled byprecarious workers, including refugees, in low-income countries. But their pay, which was never high, appears to be vanishing as entry-level tech work disappears. The shrinking number of opportunities is driving some to accept gigs for potential “rewards” rather than guaranteed wages, many said.“It’s one of the things that keeps me awake at night,” Bahana Hydrogene, a Congolese refugee who set up the SIR’s digital skills programs in 2016, said of the increasingly opaque arrangements for refugees. “They can’t get transparent answers from these companies.”A spokesperson for AOP Connect said the company offers researchers, regardless of location or background, the opportunity to participate in a wide range of projects. The reward structure is communicated “transparently upfront”, as is the nature of the copyright research work, but confidentiality is critical to AOP’s clients, the spokesperson said.Pay is based on the quality, relevance and timeliness of research submitted, and the AOP Connect platform is “not AI-enabled or used for AI-model training work”, the spokesperson added.The ‘invisible architects’Before Grace could become a qualified researcher, she filled out a questionnaire, agreeing to keep her work confidential and complete tasks by herself. Then she was able to potentially earn money through so-called “microwork”, digital tasks broken off of large confidential projects and distributed to remote workers via online platforms.She logged into AOP Connect to see a list of opportunities and found the hymns research project advertised at $9,000 in rewards available. That figure, however, would be divided among an unknown number of contributors as discretionary “rewards” rather than guaranteed wages, according to a notice displayed on the listing. RWS said higher-quality work leads to higher pay, but there is little transparency about how assessments are made, according to program participants and payment notices reviewed by the Guardian.View image in fullscreenThe Solidarity Initiative for Refugees center in the Kakuma refugee camp on 28 September 2026.Photograph: Thabit Radjabu/The GuardianChatbot-assisted research on behalf of mysterious clients offering the chance to win rewards was not what Hydrogene had in mind for when he set up the SIR’s digital skills programs in 2016. He hoped the booming global outsourcing industry would help refugees earn a guaranteed income.Some highly skilled refugees in Kakuma have found remote work through outsourcing and freelancer platforms to be a gamechanger. Those who did say they worked as web developers and software engineers interacting directly with clients. But most refugees found themselves limited to performing low-paid microwork such as data annotation for anonymous clients abroad, mediated through platforms like Remotasks, the Scale AI subsidiary that leftKenyain 2024.Life online in KakumaKakuma was originally established as a temporary home for people forced to flee the second Sudanese civil war, later expanding to accommodate people fleeing Somalia, Ethiopia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. More than 30 years later, it is one of the world’s largest refugee camps, with sprawling networks of tin-roofed buildings that make it look more like a permanent town.On a Thursday afternoon in June, temperatures topped 95F at the SIR’s compound, about 20 minutes away from Kakuma’s main entrance. The arid landscape and severe water shortages around the camp make farming unfeasible, so the more than 300,000 residents are almost entirely dependent on humanitarian aid.Inside an air-conditioned shipping container computer lab, five students practiced everything from basic digital literacy to full-stack programming. Nearby, three SIR graduates built websites and apps for clients outside the camp in a co-working space where they can access Starlink internet service and reliable electricity.View image in fullscreenFreelancers explore digital platforms at the SIR center in the Kakuma refugee camp on 28 September 2026.Photograph: Thabit Radjabu/The GuardianOne South Sudanese software engineer said that, while he has managed to get well-paid work through the SIR and Konexio, a French organization that sources remote opportunities for refugees, he worries about future workers. Entry-level work is disappearing due to AI, he said.“Senior engineers … are not hiring interns or junior roles,” he added.The SIR has trained more than 2,000 refugees, connecting more than half with remote tech work ranging from long-term employment to short-term gig work. A few years ago, SIR staff said they could easily find data annotation, transcription and translation work for their students on platforms like Remotasks. Hydrogene said workers regularly took home 500 to 1,000 Kenyan shillings, or $3 to $6, a day before Remotasks shuttered in 2024. While pay was low, it was valued in a place where less than half of households have income, and those that do earn less than $50 a month.But the microwork economy is often exploitative, said Joan Kinyua, founding president of the Data Labelers Association. The Nairobi-based organization advocates for the rights of what it calls the tech sector’s “invisible architects”, workers foundational to the industry but hidden by opaque supply chains.View image in fullscreenAction for Refugee Life staff at work on 29 September 2026.Photograph: Thabit Radjabu/The GuardianKinyua, who worked many of these jobs, said she noticed wages and conditions for entry-level data annotation eroding as early as 2018. On some platforms, she noticed that even making a small mistake, like outlining an object imperfectly, could cost her pay. Further reductions in pay and opportunities for data labeling in 2020 meant that Kinyua had to work faster for less, and had to be available anytime gigs appeared on outsourcing platforms. Eventually, she was sleeping only a few hours a night.“You can’t afford to stay away from your computer,” she said.In Kakuma, refugee data annotators said that at times they were tasked with labeling images and videos of weapons, gruesome bodily wounds and pornography on various outsourcing platforms. As a result, some workers, especially those fleeing wars, experienced post-traumatic stress disorder symptoms after annotating violent material, Hydrogene said. And the opacity of some arrangements meant workers often unknowingly contributed to products they were opposed to. The Bureau of Investigative Journalismfoundthat Somali speakers in Kakuma had done transcription work probably used by the US military, which refugees told the bureau they didn’t consent to.A spokesperson for RWS said that AOP Connect doesn’t offer data annotation work. Scale AI did not respond to the broader findings on the industry as a whole, saying it was not in a position to comment on the practices of other companies.Dwindling opportunitiesWork became more scarce between 2022 and 2024 as Remotasks closed and automated tools such as ChatGPT took off. Na’amal, a non-profit that links refugees with global employers, noticed clients requesting skilled specialists rather than workers with basic digital literacy.“As AI became mainstream, some jobs started to dry up,” said Lorraine Charles, Na’amal’s founder.View image in fullscreenThe Kakuma-Lodwar highway, with Kakuma in the background, on 29 September 2026.Photograph: Thabit Radjabu/The GuardianThe International Trade Centre (ITC), a joint World Trade Organization and United Nations agency that has trained digital workers in Kakuma, estimates jobs such as transcription, data entry, translation and web research have declined by about 50% since 2022, said an ITC spokesperson, Susanna Pak. Oxford Internet Instituteresearchsimilarly shows that growth of popular AI tools coincided with a measurable drop in many of the tech jobs promoted as paths to refugee self-sufficiency.Merci Biamungu, a refugee trained in 3D modeling, said he regularly received opportunities with guaranteed pay throughout 2023 and 2024.However, in one of his final projects, he and 20 other workers competed in teams of five to design a 3D model of a potato. The best-performing group received a reward of 15,000 Kenyan shillings, or about $116, split among the five. Now, the AI tools that Biamungu believes he helped train can build 3D images faster, eliminating the need for workers like him, he said.It’s now been two years since Biamungu has found remote work in tech.View image in fullscreenA learner using a laptop to practice image annotation at the Action for Refugee Life center.Photograph: Thabit Radjabu/The Guardian“We used to get three to five jobs per month,” he said. “Now you cannot get one.”Hubert Sanga, a Congolese refugee who established Generation Aid, another social enterprise that trains and helps refugees find work in tech, said he was seeing entry-level work for refugees collapse as AI expands.“One hundred per cent of the jobs we are doing right now are really at risk,” Sanga said.Rewards, not wagesFor many, the alternative to these precarious, lower-paid remote gigs is no income at a time when many families in Kakuma facestarvation– partly the result of Donald Trump and Elon Musk’s dismantling of USAID last year.“The language of ‘rewards’ instead of wages shifts risk entirely on to workers, who invest their time and expertise without any guarantee of fair compensation,” said Mark Graham, professor of internet geography at the Oxford Internet Institute.Hydrogene, of the SIR, said clients within the microwork economy routinely threaten to take jobs to the Philippines or India if he tries to negotiate higher pay.“AI is taking some of these jobs … and you have more talent available than there are jobs,” he said. “They say, ‘Someone else will do it for less.’”View image in fullscreenThe Kakuma refugee camp on 29 September 2026.Photograph: Thabit Radjabu/The GuardianNa’amal’s Charles has also noticed declines in wages, and as a result is shifting the organization away from microwork entirely. Graphic design, web design and search engine optimization trainings are also being phased out in favor of software engineering, digital marketing and e-commerce, and other jobs believed to be less vulnerable to automation.But most refugees will struggle to become competitive candidates for such highly skilled jobs, said Konexio’s director, Fabien de Castilla, due to disruptions to their schooling and work experience. If annotation jobs are becoming obsolete, Castilla still believes that other entry-level jobs, such as data cleaning and reviewing AI outputs, might provide opportunities for refugees in the future.Building better protectionsAs AI speeds up the refugees’ work, it’s also diminishing their pay. Jobs that used to take days now take hours, reducing billable time, Sanga said.“If I’m going to take three days to do a job, [the client] says, ‘I’m going to find someone who can do it in two hours,’” he said. “It’s killing us” on pricing, he added.Diminishing pay has prompted the SIR, Generation Aid and Action for Refugee Life, another organization that trains refugees and sources tech jobs, to push companies to offer higher wages and better conditions. But tech workers told the Guardian they feared pushing for more over concerns they’d be replaced by AI or another worker desperate for a job.Multilateral organizations like the ITC are trying to understand how digital workers can be better protected. Pamela Coke-Hamilton, the ITC’s executive director, told the Guardian that the loss of the digital economy’s lower- and middle-level workers demands new ways of thinking about collective bargaining.“We are at a tipping point,” she said. “AI has taken people by surprise with its speed and impact, and we need to ask what labor organizing looks like now. We need guardrails to prevent mass exploitation.”View image in fullscreenThe Action for Refugee Life center in Kakuma.Photograph: Thabit Radjabu/The GuardianThough workers and advocates are trying to build those guardrails, they said power ultimately rests with global tech companies, which benefit from an oversupply of cheap labor. But a “race to the bottom” is not inevitable, Graham argues. He’s pointed to the textile industry as a precedent for how pressure can change industry conditions. There, “sweatshop” scandals prompted many companies at the top of the supply chain to commit to responsible business practices at every level.Sanga believes one practical fix is simple transparency: workers need to know who they are working for so they can understand the value of their labor. When Generation Aid sources work directly from companies, it puts workers in direct contact with the client – a sharp contrast to anonymous platform work.Milagros Miceli, principal investigator at Data Workers’ Inquiry and research lead at the Distributed AI Research Institute, argues that the supposed choice between no job and a poorly paid one is false.“Without data workers, tech companies do not have a product,” she said. “So there should be space for bargaining power.”

title: Firmus pulls biggest ASX float since Telstra amid investor doubt about datacentre company | Datacentres - Australia | The Guardian
description: The $11-a-share offer would have been the biggest debut on the stock market since the telecommunication giant in 1997
Author: Jonathan Barrett
Headline: The $11-a-share offer would have been the biggest debut on the stock market since the telecommunication giant in 1997
Content: Firmus has pulled its plans for the biggest ASX debut in two decadesView image in fullscreenFirmus has pulled its plans for the biggest ASX debut in two decadesDatacentres - AustraliaFirmus pulls biggest ASX float since Telstra amid investor doubt about datacentre companyThe $11-a-share offer would have been the biggest debut on the stock market since the telecommunication giant in 1997Get ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJonathan BarrettBusiness editorThu 8 Oct 2026 18.33 EDTFirst published on Thu 8 Oct 2026 18.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFirmus Technologies has scrapped what was set to be Australia’s biggest company listing in decades after investor demand for its much-hyped AI datacentre business failed to materialise.A Firmus spokesperson said the board decided that proceeding with the offer was no longer in the best interests of the company and its shareholders.“Firmus will now pursue capital from the private markets and consider alternative public and private market options,” the spokesperson said on Friday morning.Australia is building a lot of new homes. But is the datacentre boom holding us back? | Greg JerichoRead more“We will provide additional information to shareholders as those options progress.”Firmus, with an anticipated $44bn valuation, was expected to be the biggest ASX listing since Telstra in 1997.But it faced mounting scepticism over its huge valuation, and forecast earnings, for a company in its startup phase with just two, small operational sites.Backed by chip maker Nvidia and Wall Street firms Blackstone, Jane Street and Coatue, Firmus’s backers believed they could raise billions of dollars by selling shares in a public float with the help of five brokers.Thelack of demandmeans Firmus will need to raise money from private investors to fund its plans to build liquid-cooled “AI factories” in Australia and across Asia.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailFrantic discussionsThe polished Firmus pitch started to unravel midweek after it became clear the company’s bankers had vastly overestimated demand in their bid to raise $7bn from investors ahead of listing on the ASX on 23 October.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis prompted discussions about a heavy reduction in the company’s proposed $11-a-share initial public offering, according to one investment manager briefed on the matter.The company ultimately decided to withdraw its application to list on the ASX altogether.Guardian Australia previously reported growing concern that early Firmus investors were going touse retail investors buying into the float as their “exit strategy”, leaving small investors exposed if the excitement dissipated.The datacentre company’s troubles have already rattled other parts of the market, with shares in Firmus investor Maas Group plunging more than 20% on Thursday.The anticipated financial worth of the founders – Oliver Curtis, who hasspent time in prison for insider trading, his cousin Tim Rosenfield, and Curtis’s former brother-in-law Jonathan Levee – will also be greatly reduced.Explore more on these topicsDatacentres - title: OpenAI used AI to help write email warning Australian government AI had hacked its websites | OpenAI | The Guardian
description: Revelation comes after executive told parliamentary inquiry he did not believe AI had been used to write message, but was ‘happy to go and confirm’
Author: Josh Butler
Headline: Revelation comes after executive told parliamentary inquiry he did not believe AI had been used to write message, but was ‘happy to go and confirm’
Content: Jason Kwon, chief strategy officer for OpenAI, appeared at the joint select committee on AI on Tuesday.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersView image in fullscreenJason Kwon, chief strategy officer for OpenAI, appeared at the joint select committee on AI on Tuesday.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersOpenAIOpenAI used AI to help write email warning Australian government AI had hacked its websitesExclusive:Revelation comes after executive told parliamentary inquiry he did not believe AI had been used to write message, but was ‘happy to go and confirm’Get ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJosh ButlerWed 7 Oct 2026 22.05 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 09.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOpenAI used AI to help write the email to the Australian government advising that its AI agent had hacked into key departmental websites, Guardian Australia can reveal.On Tuesday, one of the company’s executivestold a parliamentary inquiry that he didn’t believethat its own technology had been used to create the email, but said the company needed to confirm this.Guardian Australia understands AI was used by OpenAI’s legal and security teams to generateparts of the wording of the email, including word selection and formatting of the message. But a source with knowledge of the incident said humans reviewed the final email, and humans were responsible for actually sending the communication to the Services Australia inbox.OpenAI came to Australia to apologise. It will leave without answering these key questions | Toby WalshRead moreOpenAI was contacted for comment.An artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAIaccessed Services Australia data and three othersystems in June. The company notified Australia on 10 September despite becoming aware of the incident in August.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe company’s first notification to Australia came in a five-paragraph email to a Services Australia inbox, publicdisclosures@servicesaustralia.gov.au, which was only checked once per day.OpenAI has come under fire for not raising the issue in a more formal or direct way, including during a face-to-face meeting between the company’s CEO, Sam Altman, and Australia’s deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, on 1 September, nine days before the company emailed Services Australia but nearly a month after it first learned of the 18 June intrusion.Jason Kwon, OpenAI’s chief strategy officer, admitted in a parliamentary hearing on Tuesday that the company’s “response was not good enough, and we should have informed the impacted parties much sooner”.During the hearing, Liberal MP Aaron Violi – the shadow minister for technology – had asked Kwon specifically about the email and whether AI had been involved in its creation.“I appreciate that, to get the data and have a review, you’ve got to use AI agents, and obviously your business uses AI. When you notified Services Australia via email, did your staff use AI to construct that email?” Violi asked.Kwon responded: “I don’t believe so, but we’re happy to go and confirm.”Kwon indicated during the hearing that OpenAI would provide specific responses to more technical queries in answers to questions on notice.OpenAI is expected to provide more information about the email once its own investigation has concluded.The email, obtained by Guardian Australia in September, advised Services Australia: “We are notifying you of a security vulnerability identified during our review of OpenAI model activity involving Services Australia’s Medicare Statistics service at medicarestatistics.humanservices.gov.au.“An OpenAI model identified a way to make the server carry out instructions sent through the public reporting interface, without a private account or password. It was able to access this to read portions of internal program files and settings, obtain a list of files, and create and read back a small test file on the server.”The email advised that OpenAI’s review “found no evidence that the model accessed patient-level records, personal information or credentials; deleted data; or established ongoing access”, and sent information about the “affected URL” and “affected report”.“We recommend that the team responsible for the service investigate the vulnerability and assess the changes needed to prevent it. We would be glad to brief your security team and provide supporting evidence as available.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Best, OpenAI Security Team.”Andrew Charlton, the assistant minister for science and technology, spoke about the OpenAI incident in a speech in Sydney on Thursday, describing the company’s agent as having “hacked into an Australian government system”.“As a starting point, no company should release a frontier AI model that is not safe,” he said.OpenAI safety leader quits, warning AI company’s culture is ‘broken’Read more“Yet the fact that has occurred, and the fact that the labs did not detect or prevent it, prompts important questions about the role of new regulation in the National AI Standards.”Charlton said frontier AI “pushes the limits” of existing government conventions and protocols around assessing safety risks, and went beyond “conventional” approaches.The assistant minister said “the market will not fix” issues with AI development, a contrast to the United States’ approach of letting companies operate with a degree of self-regulation. Charlton raised concerns that “frontier labs are putting capability ahead of safety”, positing that Australia can have the most impact on the development of AI by hosting and influencing frontier labs.“AI needs regulating because its harms are severe, hard to undo, borne by people who never chose them, and sometimes invisible until they arrive,” he said.“The market will not fix this alone, because the incentives reward speed and capability, and even the people at the top of the industry cannot slow down by themselves.”Do you know more?
