title: Trump hosts awards party for tech billionaires, almost as if he doesn’t care about ordinary Americans | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: Amid a cost-of-living crisis, with US midterms a month away, the president held a ceremony to celebrate our tech overlords – again
Author: David Smith
Headline: Amid a cost-of-living crisis, with US midterms a month away, the president held a ceremony to celebrate our tech overlords – again
Content: From left, Satya Nadella (Microsoft), Michael Dell (Dell Technologies), Lisa Su (Advanced Micro Devices), Elon Musk (Tesla and SpaceX), Jensen Huang (Nvidia), Sergey Brin (Google) and Donald Trump at the Donald J Trump Institute of Peace in Washington DC on Thursday.Photograph: Evan Vucci/ReutersView image in fullscreenFrom left, Satya Nadella (Microsoft), Michael Dell (Dell Technologies), Lisa Su (Advanced Micro Devices), Elon Musk (Tesla and SpaceX), Jensen Huang (Nvidia), Sergey Brin (Google) and Donald Trump at the Donald J Trump Institute of Peace in Washington DC on Thursday.Photograph: Evan Vucci/ReutersThe US politics sketchDonald TrumpTrump hosts awards party for tech billionaires, almost as if he doesn’t care about ordinary AmericansAmid a cost-of-living crisis, with US midterms a month away, the president held a ceremony to celebrate our tech overlords – againDavid Smithin WashingtonThu 8 Oct 2026 18.28 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 18.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHe stands accused of beingout of touch, enriching himself and his family, building a lavish White House ballroom and, with elections looming, neglecting the hardships of the voters who brought him to power.Time forDonald Trumpto show he still has the common touch? Nope.On Thursday, the US president went to a building he named after himself, dished out awards to the world’s richest person – his old frenemyElon Musk– and other tech billionaires and even received an award that belonged to his late uncle.Given Trump’s gold fetish, the event was naturally entitled theGolden Age of American Innovationsummit, which will be news to the many agencies and academies suffering billions of dollars in cuts to scientific research on his watch.“We have an extremely high-IQ audience for a change,”the president told about 300 invited guestsat the Donald J Trump Institute of Peace in Washington, a compliment he never pays to the crowds who line up for hours to attend his campaign rallies.Standing on a podium with a white backdrop and series of US flags, the president gave a perfunctory speech, sticking unusually close to his teleprompter. He made references toartificialsuperintelligence but steered clear of the datacentres these tech overlords are erecting all over the country and, in the process, achieving the unique feat of getting Democrats and Republicans to agree on how much they hate them.Michael Kratsios, director of the White House office of science and technology policy, then treated Trump to a video about his uncle, Dr John Trump, an electrical engineer and professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology who received the National Medal of Science in 1983.The short film’s claims that John Trump’s research produced X-ray generators “used for the first radiation treatments for cancer” and that “his radars jammed German defences” on D-day in 1944 owe something to his nephew’s fondness for “truthful hyperbole”.Six years ago, the president, whobelieves in “good genes” and “racehorse theory”, suggested that his uncle’s legacy would help him fight the Covid-19 pandemic: “He was a great super genius. Dr John Trump. I like this stuff. I really get it. People are surprised that I understand it. Every one of these doctors said: ‘How do you know so much about this?’ Maybe I have a natural ability. Maybe I should have done that instead of running for president.”Kratsios had a surprise for the boss. He presented Trump with his uncle’s National Medal of Science in a handsome frame as the audience clapped. He looked happy enough, though it was clear this won’t displace the gaudy Fifa peace prize from his trophy cabinet.Among the six tech leaders who came up on stage to receive an award for scientific and technological achievement, five were immigrants.The “America first” president gave the National Medal of Science to SpaceX chief executive Musk (born in South Africa); Google co-founder Sergey Brin (Russia); Jensen Huang (Taiwan), whoseAI chip maker Nvidiais the world’s most valuable company; and Lisa Su (Taiwan), head of the semiconductor company Advanced Micro Devices.Trump also handed the National Medal of Technology and Innovation to Microsoft supremo Satya Nadella (India) and Dell Technologies chief executive Michael Dell (Texas). Hours earlier, JD Vance hadannounced Microsoft’s suspensionfrom a programme allowing companies to sponsor foreign workers for green cards.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly, for twelve weeksSign up toHow we winBernie Sanders, Robert Reich, Stacey Abrams, Medhi Hasan, Paul Krugman and other bold thinkers on how to defeat Trumpism and build a better future. From our opinion desk.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe trillionaire Musk was wearing a dark suit, white shirt and white tie. Trump gave him a pat on the back, handed him the medal and gave him another pat, then showed him a certificate and patted him once more.In earlier remarks, the president called Musk an “industrial titan”, “brilliant engineer”, “national treasure” and “modern-day Thomas Edison”. He observed: “It all works out well for Elon, right?”These guys’ relationship is more complicated thanRhett Butler and Scarlett O’Hara. Musk helped buy the 2024 election for Trump and found Doge a useful vehicle to gut the federal agencies investigating his companies. The president considered Musk’s Grok chatbot ingenious after it accurately predicted that ordinary Venezuelans would celebrate the removal of leader Nicolás Maduro,according to Time magazine.Then came their explosive falling out, with Musk tweeting on his own X platform: “Time to drop the really big bomb: [Trump] is in the Epstein files. That is the real reason they have not been made public.” It turned out both men were in the files.Vancereportedly brokered a trucebetween the two titanic egos. The bromance has never been fully rekindled, but Thursday was proof that power and wealth can’t live without each other – especially with elections less than a month away and Trump’s approval rating in the doldrums.When the ceremony was over, however, it was AI king Huang who remained on stage alongside Trump as the familiar strains of theVillage People’s YMCAblasted from loudspeakers (“Young man, when you’re short on your dough,” did not resonate with this crowd). The pair were pointing and directing people, presumably for a photo op, and looking pleased with themselves. It was a fitting closing image of two men who rule the world and may yet find aartificialsuper intelligent way to destroy it.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpThe US politics sketchUS midterm elections 2026US politicsAI (artificial intelligence)featuresShareReuse this content

title: Lourdes gets a Vegas glow-up at Dublin theatre festival, where canvases are slashed | Theatre | The Guardian
description: A musical about a drama group’s pilgrimage and reflections on activist art join an intriguing show about lost languages
Author: Helen Meany
Headline: A musical about a drama group’s pilgrimage and reflections on activist art join an intriguing show about lost languages
Content: Effervescent … Danielle James, Iestyn Arwel, Molly Lynch, Nichola MacEvilly and Riain Cash in Lourdes! The Musical.Photograph: Patricio CassinoniView image in fullscreenEffervescent … Danielle James, Iestyn Arwel, Molly Lynch, Nichola MacEvilly and Riain Cash in Lourdes! The Musical.Photograph: Patricio CassinoniTheatreLourdes gets a Vegas glow-up at Dublin theatre festival, where canvases are slashedA musical about a drama group’s pilgrimage and reflections on activist art join an intriguing show about lost languagesHelen MeanyThu 8 Oct 2026 07.23 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 07.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a Dublin theatre festival programme tackling heavy themes of racism, conflict and prejudice,Lourdes! The Musical(★★★★☆) promises something effervescent.Xnthony Ltd, the creators ofOliver Cromwell Is Really Very Sorry, have turned their lightly quizzical gaze to the French pilgrimage town – “a holy Blackpool, a divine Las Vegas” and a site of hope or desperation for five unlikely travelling companions.Back in his home village in “Countryland”, in 2008, following a diagnosis of HIV that punctures his dreams of Los Angeles, singer-songwriter Matthew (Riain Cash) lends his star power to a parish drama group taking a musical about Saint Bernadette to Lourdes. Interweaving this show-within-a-show and the pilgrimage strands, Xnthony’s lyrics and Matthew Floyd Jones’s score blend pop, club beats and soulful ballads. Directed by Sarah Meadows, the supercharged ensemble joining Cash as, variously, a droll priest (Iestyn Arwel), a terminally ill mother and her transgender daughter (Nichola MacEvilly and Danielle James) and an eager tour manager (Molly Lynch) carry the music’s tonal shifts effortlessly.Instructed by neon signs to “please wait for a miracle”, characters reveal what brings them to this Marian shrine with its bizarre mix of tackiness and piety. Each has a Catholic faith of sorts – something that might have been more complicated to portray if set in the present day. Rather than settling on an archly ironic approach, Xnthony’s sensitive, often lyrical writing allows fear of death, regret and above all, grief, to seep through.View image in fullscreenClever and knowing … Alice Roots in Heroes of Tomorrow.Photograph: Ste MurrayAn aura of reverence pervades the white cube gallery setting ofHeroes of Tomorrow(★★★☆☆), the latest production from the restlessly inventiveBrokentalkers. Co-directors Feidlim Cannon and Gary Keegan are joined here by British theatre artist Andy Smith to burrow into the relationship between art and activism. Pinging through centuries and continents, they make connections between historical instances of human invention and resultant exploitation, technological breakthroughs and protest, underlining the point that progress is not linear.If this sounds abstract, it is; much of it is delivered in carefully flat, affectless narration by Alice Roots, Michael Tient and Malua Ní Chléirigh, as if making a presentation in the gallery, taking turns to outline the biography of a (fictional) Norwegian conceptual artist called Jan Hansen. His latest work, The End of It All, has been commissioned by three global tech companies, a testing moment of groupthink for an artist who has acquired cachet for financially supporting climate activists who fling paint over old masters in museums.Amid questions about whether it is possible for art to remain pure, uncompromised by its corporate sources of funding, the audience is teased into imagining what Hansen’s new artwork will be. As the performers playfully poke their heads through slashed canvases and make black imprints of their hands on the pristine gallery wall, this performance is itself a form of conceptual art, played out in a highly coded space. The result is clever and knowing but, for Brokentalkers, surprisingly tentative.Zinc(★★★★☆) fromDead Centrefocuses on a forgotten mini-state, Neutral Moresnet, on the border of Germany, Belgium and the Netherlands. A political anomaly, designated a neutral zone to protect its prized zinc mines, it was passed between European powers, its inhabitants’ nationality changing as borders shifted. Adapted froma book by Belgian political philosopher David Van Reybrouck, the production brings multiple perspectives to bear on the experience of one man, Joseph Rixen, born in Neutral Moresnet in 1903.View image in fullscreenOne of their most ambitious works to date … Timmy Creed, Fabio Godinho, Cathy Min Jung, Mila Moinzadeh and Julie Mughunda in Zinc.Photograph: Alexandre FytrakisPlaying with the idea of neutrality, co-directors Ben Kidd and Bush Moukarzel and the superb international ensemble – Julie Mughunda, Timmy Creed, Fabio Godinho, Cathy Min Jung and Mila Moinzadeh – rewind, wittily, to the 1815 Congress of Vienna. Reflecting on colonisation, annexation and the accidents of history, each actor explores their personal experience of exile, displacement and lost native languages.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA co-production withThéâtre de Liège, this is one of Dead Centre’s most ambitious works to date: multilingual, integrating video mapping, projection, layered music and sound design, and, as always with their work, commenting on the art of theatre itself. Richly allusive, it connects a performer on an empty stage, before the act of imagination begins, to the perceived neutrality of a geographical place – until it can be exploited, no longer a country but “a business”.Moving away from the cartography of loss, the performance seizes on the lost political project of Esperanto as a possible neutral language of hope – literally utopian, with its root meaning of “nowhere”.Lourdes! The Musical is atCivic theatre, Dublin, until 10 October.Dublin theatre festivalruns until 11 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreIrelandEuropeMusicalsPaintingFestivalsReligionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: With no Pulisic and good results, have the USMNT moved on from their savior complex?  | USA | The Guardian
description: The US have been defined for so long by the next singular player. This past perfect window shows that era may be over
Author: Leander Schaerlaeckens
Headline: The US have been defined for so long by the next singular player. This past perfect window shows that era may be over
Content: The US team huddle before facing Canada.Photograph: Taylor Banner/USSF/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe US team huddle before facing Canada.Photograph: Taylor Banner/USSF/Getty ImagesSoccer with Jonathan WilsonUSAWith no Pulisic and good results, have the USMNT moved on from their savior complex?Leander SchaerlaeckensThe US have been defined for so long by the next singular player. This past perfect window shows that era may be overSign up for our free newsletter hereThu 8 Oct 2026 11.45 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 11.55 EDTShareIn 1990, then-United States men’s national team manager Bob Gansler made a critical and somewhat controversial choice. He left three of the program’s laureled veterans at home and brought a young and little-tested team to the World Cup in Italy, the USA’s first in 40 years.As Gansler recalled later: “I was thinking not only for ’90, but I was thinking about the 90s.”In 1998, Steve Sampson was looking to the future as well. He had lucked into the USMNT’s managerial gig and had barely clung on to it going into that year’s World Cup, but he nevertheless made a confident proclamation. “In 10 to 15 years, we’ll win the title, there’s no doubt about it,” he told the Washington Post. “When we Americans decide to do something, we’ll see it through.”A sense took hold sometime during that period, while never really acknowledged or said out loud, that the USMNT were the team of the future.Justin Ellis helps US cap a perfect international window with 1-0 win over CanadaRead moreThey never really stopped being that. And this bullishness on the hazily outlined not-right-now-but-definitely-sometime-later-on tended to coalesce around one player, maybe two. The USMNT made their modern World Cup breakthrough powered by the energy and unfettered talent of 20-year-olds Landon Donovan and DaMarcus Beasley in 2002. When those two foundered at the 2006 World Cup, another young player, Clint Dempsey, emerged. That year, a 16-year-old Freddy Adu made his USMNT debut.And so a pattern formed: the US soccer community waited to be lifted to the next plane by a savior. The next kid. Or maybe the one after that. He’ll do it for us. Or else the next one will.Dempsey outlasted Donovan and faded just as Christian Pulisic emerged. Because even as a golden-ish generation coalesced around him, Pulisic was seen as the player expected to make something happen at the 2026 World Cup, the culmination of an eight-year project of rebuilding the national team. He was expected to activate Hero Mode, the way he briefly had in Qatar in 2022, throwing himself in front of a cross at the expense of a pelvic contusion butbundling the make-or-break winnerinto the Iranian goal.View image in fullscreenCavan Sullivan celebrates scoring against Mexico.Photograph: Patrick Mulligan/USSF/Getty ImagesHe never did it in 2026. Aside from a great first half in the tournament opener, Pulisic’s home World Cup was a bust, and the USMNT’s campaign ended with a whimper.On its face, it felt odd thatMauricio Pochettinoshould launch a youth movement in the first camp after the World Cup. The core of his team had hardly aged out; all but defender Tim Ream are comfortably on the right side of 30. All the same, he called in 13 debutants and eight teenagers.If results in the months after a World Cup count for anything at all, they have vindicated the Argentinian’s decision to freshen things up. The kids, sprinkled in among a robust base of veterans, reeled off4-1and4-2victories over Peru and Chile, respectively, before dispatching Mexico in amerciless 3-0 walloping. On Tuesday, they concluded this jumbo-sized international window with amature 1-0 win over Canadain a scruffy, scrappy game, vanquishing a team whose fierceness and physicality had given the US agreat deal of troublein the recent past.What was startling, however, wasn’t just how much young talent is waiting down the depth chart – or now, perhaps, very much on the surface of it – but how little Pulisic, the latest savior, was missed in his absence. You easily might have forgotten that he wasn’t even there while watching a composed and polished team reel off four straight wins. The same was true for Weston McKennie, one of the USMNT’s load-bearing players for the last half decade. They both stayed with their Italian clubs, either hoping to use the time off to get back in favor with their manager (Pulisic at Milan) or to heal up an injury (McKennie at Juventus).skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe USMNT’s kids are thriving, and ‘they have a bit of swag to them’Read moreIn their absence, so many players carried the load, contributing in ways big and small, taking turns coming up with the big play, that the burden was never on any one player. Cavan Sullivan may well be next in line in the succession of the USMNT’s star players – or maybe it will be Julian Hall, or Adri Mehmeti, or Zavier Gozo, or Justin Ellis, or Mathis Albert – but there was no intimation that this was his ship to propel under his own power. This was not Sullivan’s team now, as then-manager Bruce Arena told Pulisic after the US failed to reach the 2018 World Cup in Russia.The big takeaway from this mega-pack of an international break – which encompassed more games than the USMNT’s run at several big tournaments – is that this team may, at long last, no longer be so dependent on one player, or even a small handful of them.If this program is entering into a post-savior age – moving on from Pulisic-pendencia, as it were, or whoever-pendencia– that’s a clearer sign of progress than the emergence of some new prodigy, or indeed a cluster of them.What this team, and this soccer country writ large, appear to have grown instead, is the kind of depth US fans used to envy in other, more developed soccer nations. If at the 2030 World Cup, the US TV commercials don’t all feature the same player, in the way Pulisic largely hogged the commercial blocks this past summer, it will represent another step forward.Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: USMen’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts,which is out now. He teaches at Marist University.This is an extract from Soccer Desk, a newsletter from the Guardian US.Subscribe for free here.Explore more on these topicsUSASoccer with Jonathan WilsonUS sportsChristian PulisicMauricio PochettinocommentShareReuse this content

title: I’m the attorney general of Washington state. Here’s how we’re protecting the midterm elections | Nick Brown | The Guardian
description: A coalition of Democratic attorneys general is working to make sure voters across the spectrum have their voices heard
Author: Nick Brown
Headline: A coalition of Democratic attorneys general is working to make sure voters across the spectrum have their voices heard
Content: ‘We don’t doubt the administration will continue its lawless blitz against voters.’Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘We don’t doubt the administration will continue its lawless blitz against voters.’Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesOpinionUS midterm elections 2026I’m the attorney general of Washington state. Here’s how we’re protecting the midterm electionsNick BrownA coalition of Democratic attorneys general is working to make sure voters across the spectrum have their voices heardThu 8 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 13.30 EDTShareElections have consequences. So do the Trump administration’s exhaustive efforts to undermine them.Voters will be confident in their choices, but less certain whose voice will count in the face of myriad intrusions by the executive branch. A coalition of Democratic attorneys general are working to make sure voters across the political spectrum have their say.Led by the attorneys general of Washington, California, Massachusetts and Nevada, 24 states sued to block President Donald Trump’s US Postal Service plot to interfere with voting by mail. Last month, the supreme court upheld our lower court victories and blocked the administration’s unconstitutional power grab, at least for this election.The law says states decide who receives a mail ballot. The USPS has never had the final say and, according to the American Postal Workers Union, until this year had never in its 250-year history tried to put such arbitrary restrictions on what mail it will deliver.The case we brought was an important victory in every state, and particularly Washington, where more than 99% of voters cast their ballot by mail. States such as Colorado, Hawaii and Oregon have similarly high mail voting rates. But mail voting is not confined to blue states; it is widely used in red states as well, particularly those like Nebraska and the Dakotas, with large rural populations. It’s also the president’s preferred way to cast his own ballot.The case of the postal service is just part of the multi-pronged federal attack states are pushing back against. The administration has abandoned the federal government’s traditional role of supporting election security and defending voting rights, work I participated in first-hand as a US attorney.Recall, in 2020, Trump’s own administration – and particularly the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency – worked to protect the vote and defend the election. Then, efforts to misuse the Department of Justice were thwarted, and Trump relied on insurrectionists to do his bidding. In return for serving honorably, many public servants were sent packing upon Trump’s return to office, and the convicted insurrectionists were pardoned.Now we have a US solicitor general who described the postal service’s attempt to deprive the rights of millions of eligible voters as only a “modest” use of federal authority.The Trump administration is not known for its discretion or consistency. While the administration was in court purportedly concerned about election integrity, the president publicly demanded his supporters “cheat like hell” in midterm voting. I don’t think Republican voters want that any more than Democrats do.We don’t doubt the administration will continue its lawless blitz against voters. Democratic state attorneys general are prepared, and have undertaken the largest multi-state effort to protect the vote in modern American history.Recent rulings keep state elections on track and show the law is on our side. If Trump attempts to intimidate or discourage eligible voters, or to obstruct the counting of votes or certification of the election, Democratic state attorneys general will take swift action. States have decades of experience countering these threats when lodged by private actors, and they are just as illegal when attempted by the federal government.Voters can do their part by exercising the right to elect their representatives. The president’s scheming benefits from public doubt and uncertainty. Democracy depends on the participation of its citizens, and every eligible voter should have the opportunity to render a verdict on their elected representatives.That verdict is unlikely to favor President Trump, who ran on lowering costs, preserving peace, and economic stability, but instead delivered higher prices, hollowed out critical public services, engaged in unprecedented self-dealing, and began a globally destabilizing war with no end in sight.Presidents don’t decide elections. State attorneys general and the millions of eligible voters we represent will exercise our constitutional powers to help keep it that way.Nick Brown is the attorney general of the state of WashingtonExplore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026OpinionTrump administrationUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s latest attacks on the press exude desperation | Margaret Sullivan | The Guardian
description: Trump seems to invent ugly new variations on his press-bashing theme almost every day
Author: Margaret Sullivan
Headline: Trump seems to invent ugly new variations on his press-bashing theme almost every day
Content: ‘His war against the press is something of a reflex for him.’Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/APView image in fullscreen‘His war against the press is something of a reflex for him.’Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/APOpinionUS politicsTrump’s latest attacks on the press exude desperationMargaret SullivanTrump seems to invent ugly new variations on his press-bashing theme almost every dayThu 8 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 11.49 EDTShareWhen you hate the mainstream press as much asDonald Trumpdoes, nothing gets in the way of the punishment fantasy.Not court rulings. Not public opinion. Not even the dreadful consequence of less media coverage.And certainly not any awareness of how the first amendment is supposed to function in American democracy.This week, his revenge tour took yet another turn.He barred one of his most disfavored media organizations – Politico – from boarding Air Force One, where it was supposed to provide “pool coverage” to the rest of the press corps as Trump traveled to Nebraska for a campaign stop on Monday afternoon.‘Take out’ Los Angeles and San Diego? Trump is beyond irresponsible | Ted WidmerRead moreThat move was met with a strong show of solidarity by several media outlets, who decided not to fill the Politico spot.And the White House was defiantly delusional, claiming that Trump will “continue to grant an unprecedented level of access to the press”.This latest chapter came with the usual blast of venom at the mainstream media, though not specifically aimed at Politico.“The New York Times and many other Artificial Media Outlets should be arrested for their dishonesty and disservice to our Country,” he posted on Truth Social.The episode follows Trump’s effort in mid-September to ban Politico, CNN and MS Now from the White House. Those organizations quickly sued, charging that Trump’s action was unconstitutional.Trump-appointed judge Timothy Kelly came down on the side of the media, issuing a temporary restraining order that ordered the White House to reinstate the press badges that had been taken away.And since then, CNN has been kept off Air Force One repeatedly, using the rationale that access to the White House is one thing, but access to the president’s plane is another.“The law is absolutely clear,” Ted Boutrous, the first amendment lawyer who is representing the three news organizations said in astatement.“The harm to our clients, the first amendment and the public as a whole is profound.”The Trump administration’s position is that traveling with the president is a privilege not a right.The fight is not over, since Kelly will conduct a hearing later this week over the media outlets’ request for a preliminary injunction – a stopgap measure to protect press access in advance of a possible trial.Trump, of course, has been picking fights with individual journalists and entire news outlets for years. At this very moment, there are court fights involving the Associated Press, the Wall Street Journal, the New York Times and Disney, which owns ABC News and a number of local ABC affiliates.So far, there’s been a rare display of support among news organizations that are normally each other’s competition. Columbia Journalism Reviewcalledit “a striking and heartening show of solidarity from the White House Press Corps”.When the three outlets were kicked out of the White House last month, the other networks in the press pool decided not to replace CNN in the rotation, thus suspending coverage for a time.Peter Baker of the New York Times noted that for the first time in his 30 years covering the White House, “the president will not have a network TV camera covering his everyday official actions and travels”.What’s more, about 50 media organizations backed up the lawsuit by the three who had been singled out by filing an amicus brief.It’s hard to understand exactly how less coverage and this constant squabbling benefits Trump, but apparently, he is making a different calculation.His anti-press actions get a lot of attention, which is the very oxygen he requires to breathe. It doesn’t matter that much of the attention is negative.Meanwhile, he has entered a phase of saying and doing ever more outrageous things, like his statement this week at a rally that his war in Iran was necessary to protect the world. Trump appeared to suggest that Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego if it develops a nuclear weapon which prompted California’s Democratic governor, Gavin Newsom, to call the president “deranged and dangerous”.Trump exudes a sense of desperation these days, with the midterm elections only weeks away and his approval ratings underwater.His war against the press is something of a reflex for him – it’s what comes naturally, especially when he doesn’t like the shape of reality.The press corps’ newfound solidarity is encouraging. It’s been a long time coming from a group that, in the past, has responded to this president’s constant abuse with deference and dinner invitations.Trump seems to invent ugly new variations on his press-bashing theme almost every day.Standing together will be a necessity in the weeks and months ahead.Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and cultureExplore more on these topicsUS politicsOpinionDonald TrumpcommentShareReuse this content

title: Sam Altman says AI will make ‘bad things’ happen. Exhibit A: needless death | Moustafa Bayoumi | The Guardian
description: AI is already implicated in violent deaths and nearly started world war three. Those bad things? They only happen to other people
Author: Moustafa Bayoumi
Headline: AI is already implicated in violent deaths and nearly started world war three. Those bad things? They only happen to other people
Content: ‘Why were we never consulted about any of this in the first place?’Photograph: Heather Diehl/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Why were we never consulted about any of this in the first place?’Photograph: Heather Diehl/Getty ImagesOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)Sam Altman says AI will make ‘bad things’ happen. Exhibit A: needless deathMoustafa BayoumiAI is already implicated in violent deaths and nearly started world war three. Those bad things? They only happen to other peopleThu 8 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 13.57 EDTShareSam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, has some words for you about his company and the future of artificial intelligence.“One of the differences between us and some of the stricter AI safety people is that we believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency [to use it],” Altman told Politico’s new technology podcast and newsletterDecoded.Yikes. This statement – and the approach it represents – is, well, problematic, to say the least. It’s also emblematic of precisely the kind of world-building and world-destroying that is happening with today’s technology in front of all our eyes, with precious little input from the rest of us.Altman’s mention of the “bad things” that AI might bring makes it sound like AI’s failures mistakenly create innocent, minor problems or even silly little episodes, such as the time when Google’s “AI Overviews” told users to putnon-toxic glue on pizzaso the cheese will be less likely to slide off. Good advice is helpful. Bad advice? Chalk it up to being a bad thing.Stop worrying about my AI, says multibillionaire Sam Altman. So we bear the risks and he keeps the money | Chris Stokel-WalkerRead moreBut culinary adventurism is hardly the only realm that AI operates in and the damage AI is inflicting has already and repeatedly proven itself to be dangerous and even potentially deadly to humans.OpenAI is embroiled in a lawsuit after the tragic suicide of Adam Raine, a 16-year-old student who initially began using OpenAI’s ChatGPT for homework help. Thefamily’s lawsuit allegesthat the teenager took his own life with the chatbot’s encouragement. (OpenAI has claimedRaine misused the platform.)And Raine’s action is hardly the only one. OpenAI is facingmultiple lawsuitsfiled by different families of victims of suicide and self-harm.Nor is suicide the only “bad thing” to emerge in the AI universe. In February of this year, on the first day of the war in Iran, two Tomahawk missiles struck the Shajareh Tayyebeh elementary school in the city of Minab,killing at least 120 children. (AUN fact-finding mission concludedthat the US was probably responsible for the strike.)In a recent investigation into the attack,Bloomberg Newsreported that an AI-linked system was used to target the school. In this case, the system is called Maven, and it is made by Palantir.Unnamed defense officialstold Bloombergthat “inside Centcom, which conducted the US attack, some personnel relied too much on the artificial intelligence embedded in Maven Smart System”. The report alsoaddsthat “in the past year, the Defense Department has rapidly made Maven a cornerstone of the US military apparatus”.AI is helping to produce these tragic and needless deaths, but bad things happen, I guess.Or there’s the little detail that the US may have come within a hair’s breadth of starting a major war against a superpower, all due to an AI error.In September,CNN reportedthat an unidentified AI chatbot used by the US military decided that a Chinese ship in Middle Eastern waters was carrying components of a nuclear weapons program. According to CNN, US planes took off on an interception mission and US military personnel were preparing to board the ship.Only then did the military look more closely at the report they were basing the mission on and realize the chatbot’s mistakes.Also found in CNN’s frightening story is that the analyst who used the chatbot to come up with the shoddy analysis then used AI again to write the report, which set the whole thing in motion. A twofer of bad things, I suppose.Why does it seem that these technologies, which, in the words of Trump’s White House, are “empowering Americans to achieve what was previously impossible across science, medicine, and nearly every other domain of human endeavor”, get such serious stuff so wrong and so often?And isn’t it true that the more we rely on AI, the more dangerous these little mistakes become? And why were we never consulted about any of this in the first place?Could it be that what’s behind the artificial intelligence revolution may be less about the utopian or dystopian future (take your pick) that’s just around the corner and more about the enormous amount of money that is being poured into these companies in the present?AI may be the only thingkeeping Trump’s economy afloatright now. And it’s paying dividends. According to theNew Yorker, OpenAI “is reportedly preparing for an initial public offering at a potential valuation of a trillion dollars” and Sam Altman “may become one of the wealthiest and most powerful people on the planet”.Those bad things? They only happen to other people.Meanwhile, we are beingwarnedalmost every day that AI systems are getting so smart that they’ll end humanity.But maybe the real worry here is not that the machines are taking over.It’s that the humans are giving up, ceding control and responsibility in the name of hyping up a product that has shown itself as being really good attaking jobsaway from people,stealing the intellectual propertyof others, writing somepiss-poor undergraduate essays,spying on you and your license platesand bringing us to the brink ofworld war threebecause God forbid humans should actually question the output from machines. Or the makers of those machines.What we need is real, tangible and enforceable government oversight over these technologies, which are quickly becoming a dominating force in all our lives. We must collectively have the right to decide how AI should be used. Anddespite what you may hear, Chinaalready regulatesits AI companies quite aggressively.Instead, Donald Trump, Mark Zuckerberg, CEO of Meta and Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidiabelievethat the AI companies should simply regulate themselves, so they have come up with something called the AI Accords.Signed by leaders of Meta, Nvidia, Google, Anthropic, xAI and OpenAI,the accordsask tech companies to “implement robust internal controls and monitor the capabilities and alignment of its models”, among other things. “Over time,” the agreement states, “it may make sense to codify these steps into laws or regulations.”I’m not holding my breath.Trump, who hasorderedthe term artificial intelligence be discarded for “super intelligence”, posted the accord on social media on 29 September. The document, titled The White House Accord on Super Intelligence, can still be seen onhisaccount and theWhite House’sofficial account. It’s signed by all six tech leaders and Trump, who in the document is labeled “President of theUnitesStates.”Super intelligence, indeed.In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgMoustafa Bayoumi is the author of the award-winning books How Does It Feel to Be a Problem?: Being Young and Arab in America and This Muslim American Life: Dispatches from the War on Terror. He is professor of English at Brooklyn College, City University of New York, and a Guardian US columnistExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionSam AltmanOpenAIMetaNvidiaMark ZuckerbergcommentShareReuse this content

title: Indiana Fever and the Magasphere: a WNBA team’s dangerous path to popularity | Indiana Fever | The Guardian
description: Teams have always symbolized division within America. And the Fever have come to prominence during a time of dark political intensity
Author: Howard Bryant
Headline: Teams have always symbolized division within America. And the Fever have come to prominence during a time of dark political intensity
Content: The Indiana Fever made the playoffs this season before their exit to the Las Vegas Aces.Photograph: Jeff Haynes/NBAE/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Indiana Fever made the playoffs this season before their exit to the Las Vegas Aces.Photograph: Jeff Haynes/NBAE/Getty ImagesIndiana FeverIndiana Fever and the Magasphere: a WNBA team’s dangerous path to popularityHoward BryantTeams have always symbolized division within America. And the Fever have come to prominence during a time of dark political intensityThu 8 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 07.43 EDTShareIt’s over for now, but no professional sports team spent more time receiving and drawing attention to itself than did theIndiana Feverthis season. The Fever has broken, the team eliminated by the defending champion Las Vegas Aces for the second straight season, but Indiana succeeded in being the WNBA’s canary in the coal mine, embodying both the obvious and unintended consequences of rapid growth, while also allowing themselves to be a season-long distraction: part-time professional basketball team, part-time right-wing culture war centerpiece. Less than a decade ago, Atlanta and Minneapolis were praised for their unified political stances. Today, Trumpism has replaced social justice as the defining characteristic of the league – and as the curtain closed on the 2026 WNBA regular season, Indiana stood at its epicenter.The Fever were the most polarizing team in professional sports, known less for their basketball than their culpability in pulling the league from its old cultural identity as a Black/queer league into its current climate of political divisiveness – a calculated and dangerous path to popularity. This season, there was the basketball of theWNBA, and then there was the Indiana Fever, the league’s Maga-friendly option.Their two most recognizable players, Caitlin Clark and Sophie Cunningham, were in a constant state of churn, always in the news, always embroiled against another,symbolizing and pandering to America’s fractures. Their best and longest-tenured player, Kelsey Mitchell,hasn’t been able to concentrate fullyon basketball the past two seasons as the Clark-Cunningham sideshow devours the oxygen and may end her time in Indiana that began as the second overall pick in 2018.Clark remains the league’s biggest name and its chief avatar – mildly reluctant orwilling pawn, but an avatar nevertheless. She is an avatar for the money at a time when broadcasters and venture capitalists are making their bets on women’s sports. She represented a certain type of hope, that the day had arrived where women’s team sports would enjoy the same visibility as female stars such as Serena Williams and Lindsey Vonn.She was an avatar of weaponization, the speculator’s proof that the WNBA is doomed by its own hand for not recognizing her overall importance to its future, a future bizarrely framed as bright only if Clark succeeds – an odd framework for sports, where the final score and holders of the trophies determines who wins.Most obviously and explosively, Clark was an avatar for whiteness, a Christian, hetero whiteness that holds the pervasive belief that it is straight, white America – already the overwhelming and unchallenged dominant cultural and financial force in this country – that is under assault. Any struggle Clark showed on the court – a foul call, a non-call – was treated as if it were an urban crime statistic, unmistakable proof that Black people had even turned basketball lawless. The opportunistic and racist White House and the Trump administration repeated this fiction. Republican members of Congress earlier this season insinuated Clark was being discriminated against by the league because she is white. The Congressmen threatened the WNBAwith a Department of Justice investigationif the league did not take steps to protect her. Clark and the Fever did little to dispel the notion.Whenever Clark did succeed, her partisans saw it as proof of how much better the league would be if only it stopped persecuting her. Through Clark, and how she navigated playing basketball in a league largely comprised of Black women – even as Breanna Stewart, Paige Bueckers and a host of other white women thrive without incident – was how the government (as well as many fans and journalists) framed the state of women’s professional basketball. She is half of what all the fuss has been about.The other half is Cunningham, who spent much of the seasonbuilding the scaffoldingfor her second act by driving a wedge into heart of the league, positioning herself at the center of the attention-fueled culture war against trans women, being the blonde, blue-eyed foil to the league’s unruly Black women, and providing an entry point for the bros, their money and misogyny to show up,for men such an Enes Kanter Freedomto do what they have always done to women’s sport – find a way to denigrate it and be rewarded with attention. While it was all very tired and calculating, framed asspeaking her truth,designed to reach the very group of white male sports fans that have either criticized or ignored women’s sports but are now bringing their toxicity to the tent under the guise of “growth,” Cunningham has been the subject of more attention than she’s ever had in her decade-long career, with public appearancesand lengthy profiles. She knows exactly to whom she is talking, and why.The Fever carrying these burdens – or wearing them proudly until having to answer for them – is how Clark’s career has shifted from starting her first season a phenom joining a team that hadn’t had a winning season in seven years to ending her third in daily controversy, with her as the signature, aggrieved face of Maga’s team.With the avatars mercifully tabled, Clark emerged as an excellent player with enormous upside and serious deficiencies. She is a volume scorer but not yet a great one – her career field-goal percentage is just 42.3, below the league average, and for all her dazzle, her career three-point percentage is a below-average 34.2. She shot 36.1% from three this season, below the Fever team average of 38.6%. She is an adept playmaker whose true skill may be less in creating offense for herself and more in controlling the tempo of the game and involving her teammates. She was second in the league in assists and first in turnovers, fitting considering she constantly has the ball – similar to James Harden in a way. She is an apathetic defender.As a basketball presence, she is wholly unlikeable. She does not play the game with her teammates as much as beyond them – a common affliction of many superstars that in victory is touted as a virtue but looks selfish following first-round defeats. She does not appear to play the game with joy or intensity, but carries a childish outrage, not only confronting officials on virtually every trip downcourt, but sprinting to berate them in dead-ball situations. Clark plays with grievance, an entitled grievance that recalls the White House grievance, the same grievance shared by much of the white electorate that uncoincidentally claims her as their champion – they’re all unfairly under attack.For all the criticism, WNBA officials have actually shown remarkable restraint toward her. She exaggerates most calls and outwardly flops on others to steal calls – call it European gamesmanship, but the true nature of flopping is to receive something undeserved and is the worst example of immoral basketball. Even during timeouts Clark finds a way to spar with someone, be it a cameraman or an assistant coach.Like Cunningham, however, Clark has mastered the key component of the so-called attention economy – she sees to it the camera is always on her. A more professional Clark, with fewer outbursts and deeper concentration on basketball would lower the temperature on the league, her team, herself, and would probably win her more trips to the foul line – but there was virtually no evidence this season that is what she wants.Superstar petulance is nothing new, and if Stephanie White doesn’t return as coach, it won’t be the first time a star player will be accused of getting the coach fired. Nor is it the first time a sports team has reflected a national political mood or been pulled into its vortex. Usually reflection marks triumph – Black and Jewish America loved the Dodgers because of Jackie Robinson and Sandy Koufax just as the Yankee teams of Tony Lazzeri, Frankie Crosetti, Joe DiMaggio, and Phil Rizzuto made them beloved in Italian-American homes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly for the 2026 WNBA seasonSign up toWNBA 30A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTeams have also symbolized division. In the 1980s, the Boston Celtics were often considered white America’s team because of Larry Bird, the high number of white players the Celtics routinely signed, and the perception that the Celtics did not play with the flamboyant Blackness that defined the rest of the league, which allowed white fans to see themselves in their no-nonsense, blue-collar ethic.Despite the presence of James White, Dont’a Hightower, the McCourty twins and Stephon Gilmore, the late-stage Brady/Belichick Patriots wereadopted by certain white supremacistsbecause the Patriots were led offensively by a handful of white players – Tom Brady, Rob Gronkowski and Julian Edelman. The supposedly colorblind whites had found their ideal.None of those examples, however, have existed within the combination of today’s dark political intensity where the federal government has positioned itself as the legal guardian of whitenessandthe precarious political footing of the league. The nation has effectively closed its borders to everyone except white South Africans, while Cunningham encourages the right to use the WNBA for anti-trans fodder and the DOJ believes Clark needs its protection.In a feeble attempt to distance itself from the obvious racism, the Fever periodically made bland, unconvincing statements –there’s no room for hate in the game –but their actions undermined their sentiments. Cunningham knows exactly who her fans view as the enemy, which fires to stoke on her podcasts, which dog whistles to sound. As does Clark, for her constant on-court histrionics elicit the right sympathy from the right people. They both know exactly what they’re doing.The season over, the Fever closed 2026 not by celebrating their best record since 2015, or by marking the first time since the 2009-2012 season the franchise posted three-straight 20-win seasons and have momentum as a potential title contender, but with more grievance. General manager Amber Cox read a ridiculous, gaslighting statement blaming outside media for the odious reputation of Fever fans. “The attacks on our fan base have no basis in reality, and must stop,” she read from the podium.Mitchell’s own wordspainfully contradicted Cox, as did rival players around the league.Maybe they just want it this way.This article originally appeared on Howard Bryant’s Substack.You can subscribe here.Explore more on these topicsIndiana FeverWNBABasketballUS sportscommentShareReuse this content

title: Not since 9/11 has the UK faced such a security crisis – and threat to our liberal principles | Gaby Hinsliff | The Guardian
description: The combination of Iranian, Russian and Chinese aggression is deeply worrying: just how much more concerned about security should the country be?, asks Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Author: Gaby Hinsliff
Headline: The combination of Iranian, Russian and Chinese aggression is deeply worrying: just how much more concerned about security should the country be?, asks Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Content: Illustration: Nate Kitch/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Nate Kitch/The GuardianOpinionIranNot since 9/11 has the UK faced such a security crisis – and threat to our liberal principlesGaby HinsliffThe combination of Iranian, Russian and Chinese aggression is deeply worrying: just how much more concerned about security should the country be?Thu 8 Oct 2026 12.55 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 17.27 EDTShareThe first time the window-rattling roar of a B-1 bomber woke me up this summer, I thought for one crazed second we were under attack. By the second time, I’d learned to recognise the sound of US planes taking off from their base at RAF Fairford for what it was: a reminder that although Britain wants no part in this war withIran, we cannot quite escape the consequences.We’ll feel themat the petrol pump, orin the supermarketthis autumn, or in thiswinter’s heating bills. But living under the flight path adds an extra edge to it. The skies finally fell silent last week, but only because the bombers have been hastilysummoned homeafter an alleged terrorist plot to attack Fairford, in which (according to the prime minister) there are “strong indications that Iran played a part”. If Fairford is now a target of war, did that threat disappear when the Americans did? Nobody knows.Rural Oxfordshire is peppered with military bases, and after 15 years here I don’t bat an eyelid at helicopters practising low-flying drills, uniforms on the school run, or the stash of Day-Glo marshmallow cereal our local supermarket used to keep for homesick Americans. But the Fairford incident follows a serioussecurity breach at RAF Brize Norton last year– and though this involved pro-Palestinian protesters rather than the Russians, it didn’t inspire confidence – and news this summer that the Manchester synagogue attacker had scoped out the security arrangements forthe nearby Shrivenham defence academy. Bases nationwide are on high alert, with two Latviansarrested on Thursdayon suspicion of trespass inside RAF Molesworth in Cambridgeshire, home to a Nato intelligence hub. At Fairford, it was a farmer who sounded the alarm, raising some difficult questions about how vigilant to be in small rural communities where strangers tend to stand out. I don’t want to become paranoid about every passing dog walker, or leap to ridiculous conclusions on hearing a Russian accent. But not since living in London in the aftermath of 9/11 have I felt more alert to anything seemingly out of the ordinary.And that, of course, is how terrorism works. It’s not just the attacks themselves, but the fear and distrust they engender. For a while after the 7/7 bombings, people would change train carriages rather than stand next to some poor kid with a rucksack. At the height of the Troubles in Northern Ireland, Irish émigrés in Britain faced hostility. Sadly, it’s usually minorities who are singled out for suspicion or – in areas prone to far-right protests or antisemitic attacks – forced to wonder which of their neighbours might have joined themarches, ordaubed graffiti on Jewish-owned shops. This time, there’s a particularly grim risk of a backlash against asylum seekers, with Reform pouncing on unproven reports thatTehran may be using small boat crossingsto smuggle covert operatives into Britain. (For the record, those arrested and released on bail in connection with the alleged Fairford plot haveBritish nationality. However, aKuwaiticitizen recently convicted of a terror plot against the Israeli embassy andtwo Iranian nationalsrecently charged with allegedly plotting to target Jews in Manchester reportedly got here in dinghies.) Whatever the truth, Tehran must be delighted to see such destabilising ideas spread.For the second time since 9/11, Britain faces a dilemma over how much of a securocracy – a country dominated by security concerns, whose citizens live at a pitch of constantly heightened anxiety – it should become in response to increasing threats. As Andy Burnham will remember, the “war on terror” forced the last Labour government, of which he was part, into a painful rolling back of civil liberties at home. Since the threat this time is less from an ideology than from three hostile nation states with domestic reach – namely Russia, Iran and China – the coming dilemmas may be more over the movement of technology, assets and people.Historically, Britain’s economy has been a relatively open one, even after Brexit. We let Gulf statesbuy our football clubs, Russian oligarchs prop up theprime London real estate market, and Chinese money bail out ourcash-strapped universitiesand build ourpower stations, despite concerns about espionage, censorship and interference in domestic politics. (Tom Tugendhat, the shadow foreign affairs minister and longstanding China hawk, revealed last week that he still gets letters from Beijing to the family home “that say, basically, ‘we know where you live’”.)London’s tech startups, expanding faster than they could hire domestically, snapped up skilledyoung Russian codersunderstandably anxious to escape a country at war. We didn’t slaptariffs on cheap Chinese EVswhen the EU did, despite concerns they could kill off domestic car manufacturing – or even that some of their software mightstill be controllable from China, because trade wars are generally bad for business. (Though the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds,suggested recentlythat that debate is not entirely closed.)We chosenotto become a fortress because for a long time, the benefits of being open to the world felt worth the risks, but perhaps also as a statement of our values. But there is an increasingly live debate in Whitehall about whether, in retrospect, autocracies saw that openness as a weakness to exploit. If nothing else, they’re certainly weaponising it now: both Iran and Russia are throttling shipping routes inthe strait of HormuzandBlack Searespectively, with consequences for oil and food prices that are now ringingserious alarm bellswithin governments.Though it’s not entirely clear yet what Burnham makes of all of this, there are early signs of attitudes hardening. The Cabinet Office recentlysummoned CEOsof critical infrastructure companies to brief them on the threat of Russian sabotage, while last week MI5 issued arare public warningto academics against working with a Chinese organisation regarded as a front for espionage. The concrete barriers hurriedly going up around Fairford last week may be a harbinger of what is to come: a signal that as the world moves closer to a war footing, our relaxed way of life may have to change.But there’s a difference between being vigilant and being paranoid, let alone xenophobic, and we are going to need to hold that line in months to come. No foreign national in the UK should ever be persecuted for the sins of their country of origin: there’s no going back to the dark days of 1939, when Jewish refugees fleeing Nazi Germany and Austria were shockingly interned in Britain as “enemy aliens”. New powers of surveillance should always come with new safeguards.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnd this government should remember that if the “war on terror” taught us anything, it’s that security crises test liberal principles to breaking point. I just hope Burnham is ready for that.Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Can hope save the planet? An endangered parrot that is beating the odds can help us find out | Helen Pilcher | The Guardian
description: A new global biodiversity report strikes an encouraging note. But we cannot rest on our laurels – and resilience is key, says science writer Helen Pilcher
Author: Helen Pilcher
Headline: A new global biodiversity report strikes an encouraging note. But we cannot rest on our laurels – and resilience is key, says science writer Helen Pilcher
Content: New Zealand’s kākāpō, which was once close to extinction.Photograph: Nature Picture Library/AlamyView image in fullscreenNew Zealand’s kākāpō, which was once close to extinction.Photograph: Nature Picture Library/AlamyOpinionWildlifeCan hope save the planet? An endangered parrot that is beating the odds can help us find outHelen PilcherA new global biodiversity report strikes an encouraging note. But we cannot rest on our laurels – and resilience is keyThu 8 Oct 2026 11.05 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 13.36 EDTShareThe new Living Planet Report is out. Published every two years, it assesses the health of the natural world and, historically, it’s made for gloomy reading.Take 2024’s report, which showed global wildlife populations had plummeted by 73% in 50 years and that ecosystems were being pushed toward collapse.After reading it, I retired to a dark room and drank gin, but every time I popped my head out, there was more bad news:heatwaves,floods,wildfiresandmass coral bleaching.So, when this year’s edition dropped, I braced myself. But there was a plot twist. Biodiversity is still being pummelled, but not everywhere. According to the new report, conservationists have prevented the extinction of 32 birds and 16 mammals since 1993, and the numbers of wild tigers, elephants and sea otters are stable or growing. The energy sector has historically been extremely damaging to the planet,accounting for about 75% of global greenhouse gas emissions. But the report notes we have passed a positive tipping point in the energy system, with the transition to renewables snowballing and coal use declining in many wealthy countries.I can therefore see why the report is titled The Science of Hope.But pegging it on hope is a bold move. People who write about the natural world, myself included, face a difficult choice. Focus on the bad news, and risk shouting into a void where people simply don’t want to listen. Focus on the good news and risk peddling “hopium” – stories that dull the pain briefly but do little to spur action.The report, however, isn’t talking about your average kind of hope. It’s talking about a geeky kind of hope rooted in psychological research.View image in fullscreenNumbers of South African elephants are up, the report has found.Photograph: Merten Snijders/Getty ImagesThe American psychologist Charles “Rick” Snyder spent decades studying hope and came up with asurprisingly practical definition. Hope, he argued, starts with a goal but also requires pathways, or ideas about how to get there, and agency: the belief that you can make a difference. To this, the Living Planet Report adds another ingredient: resilience – the capacity to keep going when progress stalls. Or, as British anarchist punk band Chumbawamba famously put it: you get knocked down, but you get up again.We can illustrate this point by looking at New Zealand’s kākāpō, the world’s fattest, greenest, least-able-to-fly parrot. When non-native predators drove the kākāpō to the brink of extinction, conservationists didn’t waste time wishing its numbers back up. In the mid 1990s,they moved the remaining birds to predator-free islands, and when recovery was slow, they changed tack.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionStockpile food – and wash your hands: is that really how to prepare for environmental catastrophe? | George MonbiotRead moreThey experimented with hand-rearing, foster mothers and artificial insemination. They fitted the birds with smart transmitters and monitored them almost obsessively.When new technology came along, they embraced it:the genomes of every living bird have now been sequencedto inform decisions about who should breed with whom.This is what real hope looks like. It’s not the same as optimism – the expectation that things will work out. Nor is it wishful thinking. And it’s certainly not “hopium”, which can make the problem seem smaller than it is. Real hope has its sleeves rolled up and is prepared to get messy. It leaves room for uncertainty and failure but refuses to believe that there’s nothing left to do. That’s why the opposite of hope isn’t despair. It’s inaction.Scientists who have studied hope have found it matters what we’re hopeful about.A 2023 meta-analysisfound that people who felt hopeful about their ability to make a difference were more likely to engage with the climate crisis – from seeking information and supporting climate policies to taking everyday action to reduce their environmental impact. Those whose hope rested on the belief that the climate crisis wasn’t really a problem were less likely to engage.In other words, useful hope needs to be grounded in reality. And that requires knowing what we’re up against. This was whythe Starmer government’s decision not to publish the full national security assessment on global biodiversity lossis so frustrating. The public has since seen an abridged14-page version. But the detail – and any devil within it – likely remains hidden.Produced by the Joint Intelligence Committee, it asks a stark question: what would ecosystem collapse mean for the UK?The answer is bleak: threats to national security and prosperity, havoc wroughtwith food and water supplies, a surge in irregular migration and even more geopolitical instability around the world.To find a way through the climatecrisis, we need both a clear view of the problem and the determination to tackle it. How can we find the right pathway if we don’t have the full map?In 1995, there were just 51 kākāpō. Today, there are 324, a remarkable turnaround for such a slow-breeding bird. Conservation plans are still evolving, and the species isn’t out of the woods yet. But at least it has a fighting chance.That’s the kind of hope we need: pragmatic, resilient and open to revision. We need our governments to be honest about the scale of the challenge we face. Because when they withhold information, they don’t just rob us of knowledge. They also rob us of hope.Helen Pilcher is a science writer and the author of Life Changing: How Humans Are Altering Life on Earth and This Book May Cause Side EffectsExplore more on these topicsWildlifeOpinionClimate crisisAnimalsBiodiversitycommentShareReuse this content

title: I spent years postponing my own joy. Here’s how I learned to say yes to the juicy bits of life | Sheree Joseph | The Guardian
description: Society tells us there is one way to live a life, and joy is a byproduct on the path there. But you don’t need a reason to enjoy the act of being alive
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Society tells us there is one way to live a life, and joy is a byproduct on the path there. But you don’t need a reason to enjoy the act of being alive
Content: ‘Wander and meander and do something for no reason at all. Bring back whimsy! Pay attention to the details, to what lights you up.’Photograph: Anna Berkut/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Wander and meander and do something for no reason at all. Bring back whimsy! Pay attention to the details, to what lights you up.’Photograph: Anna Berkut/AlamyOpinionHappinessI spent years postponing my own joy. Here’s how I learned to say yes to the juicy bits of lifeSheree JosephSociety tells us there is one way to live a life, and joy is a byproduct on the path there. But you don’t need a reason to enjoy the act of being aliveThu 8 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 18.43 EDTShareIhave been dwelling on what it means to live well. Not because I have mastered it, but because I have become very comically bad at it. I have spent years rushing through my life, panicked and convinced I was running out of time. I worried constantly about work – getting it, keeping it, doing it, caring about it too much, hating it and losing it. I obsessed over being more productive. I fretted about money, mostly about not having any left after travelling too much. I poured so much energy into dating that it’s kind of impressive I haven’t had a relationship for the last six years.But most of all I became fixated on my fertility and how it dwindled in my early 30s, leaving me to make choices most women don’t have to until later. I tried to save my eggs and couldn’t. My lack of a partner in a conservative Catholic Lebanese family became a cudgel.Pleasure was something bypassed on the way to a goal of being chosen and accepted. In other words, joy was a byproduct.The secret to happiness? Finding joy in others. It’s free, simple and will gladden your heart | Nadine LevyRead moreTrying to live well in a society that doesn’t prioritise it is like filling a cup with the bottom cut off: the water just runs through, passing you by, leaving you as parched as sandpaper.A holiday was an opportunity to recover from work. In Italy, the plastic cup in my hand was solid and filled with the bitter strength of a negroni sbagliato – or a “broken negroni” – a drink whose name comes from the fact it was first made by mistake.I asked the bartender why there was an exuberant street party forming outside. What was the occasion, in other words?“Just because,” he said. “We don’t need a reason.”Why did I need a reason to enjoy myself? The question ran through me.I thought about all the ways I had been trained to postpone my life. Why did I need a reason to celebrate the very act of being alive? At that moment I pondered the many nights spent couch-bound, parked in front of a television – not in a fun and delicious single-gal-about-town-living-her-best-life way, but in a dark abyss void of nothingness. Not even eating ice-cream straight from the tub, because that would be too indulgent. I couldn’t even enjoy spending money on trinkets and flowers and dresses that brought me joy without fretting and feeling guilty for spending money during an ongoing cost-of-living crisis, thereby negating the original dopamine hit.We are told there is one way to live a life: just work harder, achieve more, be thinner, be younger, find a partner, get married, have a baby, save money, buy a house, build a career, have it all! Then, presumably, I will have made it! Made it to the part where I was allowed to relax. But when? And what if the forced veering off the path was necessary and part of my story, to show me that there are other ways to live? When the tough times tear through like a tornado, what is there left for us to do if those things don’t work out?Since that moment in Italy, I have thought deeply about how to instead live a life that makes you feel fully alive, something I have dubbed “the juicy life”. There are so many simple and uncomplicated ways to live like this. Big belly laughs, truly tasting a salted tomato in summer, baptismal swims in the sea, sitting at a long table until golden hours bleed into night. Let boredom engulf you. Wander and meander and do something for no reason at all. Bring back whimsy! Pay attention to the details, to what lights you up. What makes you feel more like yourself?Create from nothing, make things that didn’t exist before: art, meals, gardens, traditions, friendships, books, beauty, music, films, photos and spaces. To create anything at all is defiance – to give life in a world that tells us only some creation stories matter. Take long walks, but go lightly, with ease and notice everything around you. Hold someone’s hand in yours and gaze at the moon. Scrunch basil up to your face with both hands and breathe it in. It’s much harder to feel existential despair when you embody your life entirely.Nine life lessons from the happiest man in the world: from embracing tiny changes to not overthinking meditationRead moreThere will always be more of everything, an endless panopticon of slop, of tech platforms churning and burning through content, of machines trying to quench their thirst on what makes us human. But you are not a walking replicant robot. Humans need rest and balance. And everything, all of this, is fleeting and not forever.The Greeks have two words for time:chronosandkairos.Chronosis chronological time – tracking the seconds, the hours and the schedules, all adding up with nowhere to go but forward and rushed. Butkairostime is different, because it is time measured by meaning – the opportune and transcendent moment; what sits between.The ancient Pythagoreans calledkairosone of the fundamental laws of the universe, the force that wove together the dualities of existence. When you live onkairostime, you move through the world differently: you stop checking and fretting over the literal and metaphorical clock. You listen instead to the revelation, to the rhythm beneath your feet. You dip down to the earth, feel the ground, hold the pebbles and rocks, let your limbs surrender.That’s when life shuttles beyond a checklist of things to achieve or acquire and becomes a constellation of moments, meaning made and remade, steeped in pleasure, to be savoured, saturating the moment until it becomes meaning itself. That’s where life lives. Make no sbagliato mistake.Sheree Joseph is a writer, editor and the author of Juicy: How to Live a Life in the Wreckage of ExpectationsExplore more on these topicsHappinessOpinionRelationshipsAgeingHealth & wellbeingcommentShareReuse this content

title: Tell us: have you been monitored or assessed by AI at work? | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: We’d like to hear from people who have been monitored or assessed by AI at work and what they thought about the experience
