title: Free land for those who will build social homes on it. Is this the radical solution to the UK’s housing problem? | Phineas Harper | The Guardian
description: A bold south London initiative to give land to community groups rather than private developers could transform the system, says writer Phineas Harper
Author: Phineas Harper
Headline: A bold south London initiative to give land to community groups rather than private developers could transform the system, says writer Phineas Harper
Content: ‘To get new social housing built in their area, councils are reliant on private developers building a proportion of homes for social rent as part of larger master plans.’Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘To get new social housing built in their area, councils are reliant on private developers building a proportion of homes for social rent as part of larger master plans.’Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesOpinionSocial housingFree land for those who will build social homes on it. Is this the radical solution to the UK’s housing problem?Phineas HarperA bold south London initiative to give land to community groups rather than private developers could transform the systemThu 8 Oct 2026 07.56 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 12.53 EDTShareLewisham council, in southeast London, is developing ambitious plans to transfer public land to community groups in an attempt to get new social housing built in the borough. According topaperstabled at Wednesday’s council cabinet meeting, the local authority is devising a new housing strategy, which includes giving packages of public land worth up to £2m each to community-led organisations such as housing co-operatives, on the condition that they build social housing.The Green-controlled council is further considering placing any land it gives away through the programme intocommunity land trusts, legal instruments that lock in permanent affordability. They may also provide low-interest loans to help developments get started, and pre-approve planning permission to speed up construction. It is hoped that the proposals will take effect within a year.Together, they form the most radical suite of solutions to the housing crisis any local authority is currently putting forward. If adopted elsewhere, the approach could transform the construction of social housing not just in Lewisham, but across the entire country.Todaythree in fournew British homes are built by for-profit property developers. The rest are erected predominantly by housing associations, with just a paltry few built by local authorities.Unlike in comparable European economies, almost no new UK homes are being built by community organisations. To get new social housing built in their area, therefore, councils are reliant on private developers building a proportion of homes for social rent as part of larger master plans. But developers frequently use their strong bargaining positionto haggle downthe amount of social housing they actually deliver.“There’s a limit to how much social housing we can realistically get private property developers to build,” says Daniel Dream, cabinet member for inclusive regeneration, planning and housing delivery in Lewisham. “We’ve got to get more creative about how to deliver social housing.” Dream, a key architect of Lewisham’s evolving new strategy, says the current system of councils haggling with developers is broken and will never produce enough social housing to meet need. Instead, he hopes to use public land to empower community-led organisations to build essential housing for themselves, or as he puts it: “enabling community to deliver community”.Selling off public land is a fraught business even for well-meaning councils. Under a1972 law, public bodies are obliged to accept the highest price they are offered, regardless of the buyer’s intentions. Wealthy property developers can therefore typically swoop in and outbid community groups for land, even when the community groups have far more interesting, sustainable and socially valuable ambitions. In September, for example, Somerset councilvoted to sell a site in Frometo the London-based investment firm Newcore Capital rather than tolocal community developerswho had plans to build homes, workspaces, a riverside park and a lido.However, the 1972 law has a loophole. If a local authority is selling a site worth £2m or less,the council can chooseto sell it to whomever it likes, and at whatever price it pleases, even giving it away for free, provided doing so provides positive benefits for the area.The new strategy could be especially useful in helping support more ambitious housebuilding on tricky small sites. In London a “small site” is defined as a piece of land that isunder 2,500 sq metres, about the size of nine tennis courts. These plots are too modest for major developers to take an interest in, so often just sit empty. However, the potential to better use vacant small sites is enormous. The architecture practice RCKaestimatesthere is enough land stuck in small sites to build 850,000 new homes in the capital alone. It recentlyconducted a survey of Lewishamidentifying space for up to 9,700 new homes across more than 3,000 potential small sites.Improved use of small sites can also create better homes. As the research projectSmall Sites Londonshows, modest developments are generally more likely to produce high-quality housing that makes a positive contribution to its local neighbourhood than the swathes of anodyne towers put up by mainstream developers on larger sites.Lewisham has a long history of successful projects proving the potential of community participation in housing. Beginning in the late 1970s, families on the council housing waiting list were offered the opportunity tobuild their own homesusing an innovative construction system devised by the German architect Walter Segal. In 1997, London’s first black housing co-operative finishedbuilding Nubia Way. In 2024 a community land trust completed Church Grove, a block of36 permanently affordable homes. But more recently the borough’s reputation for housing leadership has waned. In June, The Filigree, a major new residential and commercial development in central Lewisham,was announced joint winner of the Carbuncle Cup, an award for Britain’s worst new building. These plans to revive ambitious community-led housing could not come sooner.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLewisham’s housing target is30,376 homes over 15 years. Community-led development won’t be able to meet that target alone, but it marks a clear break with the failing system of squeezing piecemeal benefits from major speculative developments. If successful, the approach could better empower the council and its constituents – and if introduced nationwide, it could catalyse a genuine revolution in social housing construction everywhere.Phineas Harper is a writer and curatorExplore more on these topicsSocial housingOpinionLocal governmentLondonHousingCommunitiesEnglandcommentShareReuse this content

title: Stockpile food – and wash your hands: is that really how to prepare for environmental catastrophe? | George Monbiot | The Guardian
description: The UK state is dumping its responsibilities on our doorsteps, while green-lighting policies that lead us closer to crisis, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Author: George Monbiot
Headline: The UK state is dumping its responsibilities on our doorsteps, while green-lighting policies that lead us closer to crisis, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Content: Illustration: Ben Jennings/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Ben Jennings/The GuardianOpinionEmergency planningStockpile food – and wash your hands: is that really how to prepare for environmental catastrophe?George MonbiotThe UK state is dumping its responsibilities on our doorsteps, while green-lighting policies that lead us closer to crisisThu 8 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 10.45 EDTShareWould you mind fixing the NHS? And while you’re at it, could you please build an anti-missile system in your garden? Then regulate the banks, replace the water mains, tax the very rich and use the proceeds to rebuild our schools. Well, come on people: what are you waiting for?I exaggerate, but this isn’t very far from the approach taken by the government’sPrepare campaign. Crucial functions, way beyond the scope of individual action, are dumped on our doorsteps while those in power fail to act. As a result, our national resilience isarguably lowerthan at any time since the second world war. At the Labour conference last week,Andy Burnham promised“a Britain where people feel the country has got their back again”. To make good on that pledge, he will have to change almost everything.It’s not that the advice offered by Prepare – a government campaign designed to promote readiness for emergencies – is irrational. But when the state is absent or working against us, households and communities cannot fill the gap.The campaign tells us, for example, to conserve water during droughts by turning off the tap while brushing teeth, or taking a shower instead of a bath. For sure. Every citizen should do their duty. But the government has at the same time declared datacentres “nationally significant infrastructure projects” that can be forced through the planning system, despite two startling facts. The first is that even Water UK – the body representing water companies, those paragons of environmental responsibility –has saidthere isn’t enough water to support the new datacentres. The second is that, as a freedom of information response reveals,the government has no ideawhat they are being used for. You could be turning off your taps so the water can be used to nudify celebrities.Talking of droughts, the government’sNational Risk Registerseems seriously out of whack. It estimates the risk of a drought with a moderate impact occurring in the next five years at just 0.2-1%. What?? It also estimates the risk of heatwaves with a “significant” impact – by which it means between 200 and 1,000 deaths – at only 1-5% over the next five years.The government estimatesthere were 2,877 heat-associated excess deaths in England during this year’s hot weather in May and June. There werea similar numberof deaths in the heatwave of 2022.But never mind: thePrepare campaign advisesthat “if you live in a home that is more likely to overheat … contact your local council, your letting agency or Citizens Advice to find out what help and support they can provide”. Good luck with that. In the meantime, the “future homes standard” is at last due tocome into forcein March 2028, but thanks to lobbying by the building sector,according to some practitionersit still won’t deliver new homes matched to the climate challenges we face. And local authoritieshave been blockedfrom demanding anything better, thanks to the same corporate pressure.Survive floods, thePrepare campaign tells us, by “packing a ‘grab bag’ of essentials in advance”, moving “valuable items upstairs” and making “changes to your property to reduce the damage flooding can do”. But one in nine new homesare being builtin areas at risk of flooding according to data from Aviva, and a recent high court judgment reveals thatthe law preventslocal authorities from blocking such developments, even if they fail a crucial safety test.These are not the starkest examples of public exhortation colliding with government failure. The Prepare campaign tells us to helpstop the spread of avian fluby washing hands “with soap and water” after feeding wild birds. Fine. But at the same time,at the behest of lobbyists, the government is pushing a “poultry sector growth plan”. This will multiply the number of super-incubators of avian flu: namely the factory farms rearing chickens. As the Scientific Task Force on Avian Influenza and Wild Birdspoints out, poultry farms are where highly pathogenic bird flu first arose. Through their growth and intensification, the spreading of their manure on fields and its runoff into rivers, we could scarcely devise a better formula for generating new variants of the virus and the attendant ecological disasters. Oh hang on, we could: the shooting industry is still allowed to breed tens of millions of pheasants and partridges in similar conditions each year, then release them into the countryside to mingle with wild birds. But do wash your hands.You’re also advised to “reduce your exposure to air pollution”. How? The government is allowing new homes to beequipped with wood-burning stoves, building huge and arguably pointlessnew roadsand consulting onradically delayingthe transition to all-electric vehicles. All, once again, in response to lobbying.As for food resilience, the Prepare campaign scarcely mentions it, except to say we should stock some “non-perishable food that doesn’t need cooking” in our homes. Last week, a group of anonymous senior food executiveswarned that, in the face of “material reductions in yield, quality and reliability of supply”, their industry was “defaulting to quick-fix crisis management” rather than taking a strategic, long-term approach. “At present, we are seeing companies either consistently lobby against necessary regulations or stay silent,” they said. The result is a likely failure toaddress an existential threat.There was much in Burnham’s speech that delighted me, especially his listing of deregulation as one of the five great evils putting Britain on “the wrong path”. That’s a break with 47 years of policy, in which all governments have dismissed essential public protections as “red tape” that must be cut. The Tories werestill at itin their own conference this week – telling us, in effect, they are here to burn it all down. But, like Keir Starmer, Burnham has tied his own hands by pledging to “stick to our fiscal rules”. These rules did not come from government. They weredeveloped by Westminster junktanksand pushed into being by the media. As Larry Elliott hasargued persuasively, they are unnecessary and self-defeating.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe threats to our resilience are the same as the threats to our democracy: what Burnham called “that sense of the powers-that-be pulling against the people, not with them”. We’ve had five decades of lobbyists shaping policy, with devastating consequences for our ability to withstand crises. Willing to play our part as we may be, we cannot do the work of government.George Monbiot is a Guardian columnistThis article was amended on 8 October 2026. The illustration was replaced as an earlier version had said to take baths instead of showers, rather than vice versa.Explore more on these topicsEmergency planningOpinionFood securityDroughtFloodingExtreme weatherWatercommentShareReuse this content

title: Germany is right to rearm. But Europe has well-founded fears about that | Paul Taylor | The Guardian
description: Berlin’s allies are right to be wary of a sudden surge in German military spending that shuns cooperation with them, says the European Policy Centre’s Paul Taylor
Author: Paul Taylor
Headline: Berlin’s allies are right to be wary of a sudden surge in German military spending that shuns cooperation with them, says the European Policy Centre’s Paul Taylor
Content: The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, at a press conference after a visit to the German-Dutch Corps in Münster, 1 October 2026.Photograph: ANP/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, at a press conference after a visit to the German-Dutch Corps in Münster, 1 October 2026.Photograph: ANP/ShutterstockOpinionGermanyGermany is right to rearm. But Europe has well-founded fears about thatPaul TaylorBerlin’s allies are right to be wary of a sudden surge in German military spending that shuns cooperation with themThu 8 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 09.57 EDTShareWhen the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, visited the White House earlier this year for a high-stakes meeting with Donald Trump, he invited a Washington-based German researcher little known outside expert circles to a private dinner.Liana Fix had caught his eye with aforthright essayin the journal Foreign Affairs warning of the perils of Germany becoming “Europe’s next hegemon”, whose military dominance may come to scare its neighbours and divide Europe once again. That concern might seem far-fetched after three decades since the fall of the Berlin Wall, during which a peace-loving reunited Germany let its armed forces wither and rust, prided itself on being a “civil power” and preached a gospel of military restraint.Yet the combination of a sudden surge in German rearmament, growing doubts over the United States’ willingness to remain the guarantor of European security through Nato, and the rise of the far-right nationalist Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party, currently leading in opinion polls, has reignited old anxieties among Berlin’s neighbours, especially Poland and France.Fix, a historian and senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, has built her argument into a timely and incisive book,Germany Rearmed: The Return of War and the End of Illusions. Among the fallen myths she skewers are not just the delusion that economic interdependence would make Russia a benign partner for Europe, which collapsed with Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, but also the end of what she calls “the illusion of the west”, which had been central to Germany’s identity and foreign policy since 1945. “It is not that Germany wants to leave the west, but the west seems to be abandoning Germany, in particular the US-led western order,” Fix told me in an interview.To guard against any hegemonic temptation, she urges Berlin to anchor its future military power in closer European unification by helping to finance European defence through joint defence bonds, embracing a Europeanisation of the continent’s national arms industries, and deepening the integration of the Bundeswehr into European armed forces.There is little sign so far that Merz, whose first defence strategy, released in April, vowed to make Germany Europe’sstrongest conventional army by 2039, is heeding her advice.Struggling with unpopularity, economic stagnation and a rising cost of living, the conservative chancellor has ruled out issuing eurobonds to fund European defence. His government scrapped two big arms cooperation projects with France – anext-generation fighter aircraftand a tank. Planned arms purchases worth €123.3bn notified to parliament last month are overwhelmingly from national and US industries, with only scraps for European partners.To be sure, all Berlin’s armed forces are committed to Nato, unlike France’s, and it has invited allies to join itsEuropean Sky Shieldair and missile defence programme. Germany is the biggest donor of financial and military assistance to Ukraine. It is working with the UK on deep precision strike weapons. And it has stationed a brigade in Lithuania to help protect Europe’s eastern flank in thefirst permanent deploymentoutside its territory since 1945.Defence industrial nationalism is by no means confined to Germany. France and the UK are equally protective of their national arms makers. The EU’s defence commissioner, Andrius Kubilius, laments that up to 80% of European defence purchases are made by direct awards with national prime contractors without a competitive tender, exploiting asecurity exemption in the EU treaty.The fact that German rearmament coincides with a severe slump in core manufacturing industries such as cars, chemicals and machinery is an extra reason to “buy national”. But Berlin, once on the frontline of east-west confrontation, is now cushioned by a buffer zone of central European allies and should have an interest in helping them invest in their own defence. For practical reasons, it’s better to help equip friends and neighbours to intercept drones and missiles before they reachGermanyrather than waiting to shoot them all down over Berlin and Frankfurt.Fix is right to argue that because of its dark history and its weight in the middle of Europe, Germany must do more than others to reassure its neighbours and to embed its rearmament in common European industrial, political and military structures. AsTimothy Garton Ash has arguedin the Guardian, that is what Helmut Kohl achieved a generation ago by anchoring German reunification in a common European currency.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOtherwise, the question of German power and its political uses is bound to return sooner or later, especially if the Russia-friendly AfD, which opposes assistance for Ukraine and advocates withdrawal from the EU, continues to gain ground in German elections.“The German question is not dead,” Fix told me. “It’s dead in the sense that a militaristic Germany will not re-emerge under a centralised government. But the German question can also just be a question of dominance and of balance. And this is the thinking we unfortunately have to revive.”Paul Taylor is a senior visiting fellow at the European Policy CentreExplore more on these topicsGermanyOpinionEuropeArms tradeAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)European UnioncommentShareReuse this content

title: Has the high court set Australia’s fossil fuel producers shaking in their boots? They should be  | Jacqueline Peel | The Guardian
description: A high court victory sets a new baseline for coal and gas projects in New South Wales – and potentially for the rest of Australia
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A high court victory sets a new baseline for coal and gas projects in New South Wales – and potentially for the rest of Australia
Content: Extending the Mount Pleasant open-cut coalmine’s life by 22 years would have doubled its output to 21m tonnes a year until 2048.Photograph: Jessica Hromas/The GuardianView image in fullscreenExtending the Mount Pleasant open-cut coalmine’s life by 22 years would have doubled its output to 21m tonnes a year until 2048.Photograph: Jessica Hromas/The GuardianOpinionFossil fuelsHas the high court set Australia’s fossil fuel producers shaking in their boots? They should beJacqueline PeelA high court victory sets a new baseline for coal and gas projects in New South Wales – and potentially for the rest of AustraliaWed 7 Oct 2026 20.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 02.44 EDTShareFossil fuel producers across the country are shifting uncomfortably, after the high court of Australia handed down its first climate casedecisionin MACH Energy v Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group on Wednesday.For the climate conscious, the outcome was largely what was hoped for: the court ruled that the Independent Planning Commission, the body that approved the extension of Mount Pleasant open-cut coalmine’s life by 22 years – doubling its output to 21m tonnes a year until 2048 – did not do enough to consider the mine’s scope 3 greenhouse gas emissions or how they might be mitigated.Scope 3 emissions, which cover broad indirect emissions, include those that are produced downstream when the mine’s coal is burned by customers. In the case of the Mount Pleasant mine extension, these emissions accounted for 98% of its estimated climate footprint.If this welcome news conjures ideas of a unified judicial manifesto against the climate harms of fossil fuel production, I’ll encourage you to consider it more moderately. It was a restrained and technical decision, split between three judges in favour and two against.View image in fullscreenDenman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group president Wendy Wales (centre), treasurer Tony Lonergan (right), Johnson Legal director Elaine Johnson (left) and Johnson Legal principal lawyer Anita O’Hart after their high court win in Sydney.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPBut even so, it sets a new baseline for coal and gas projects in New South Wales and potentially Australia-wide. Where the law requires decision-makers to consider a fossil fuel project’s greenhouse gas emissions, that should mean all of them, including scope 3.The majority ruling rejected the idea that scope 3 emissions are someone else’s problem when they are emitted overseas. Scopes of emissions, as Justice Gordon noted, are just an accounting concept. “The impact of greenhouse gas emissions is the same, regardless of how they categorised.”A majority of the judges also ruled that how emissions are counted under international treaties like the Paris agreement doesn’t answer the question whether the decision-maker should try to mitigate them. In essence, the entire carbon footprint of these projects needs to be assessed, including their downstream emissions.The decision provides Australia with some much-needed climate credibility, as it faces pressure from Pacific neighbours over fossil fuel approvals at the pre-COP31 negotiations in Fiji and Tuvalu this week. This also brings us in line with recent judicial findings elsewhere in the world.In the UK and Norway, for instance, courts have required decision-makers to deal with the emissions from burning fossil fuels, wherever that happens, rather than looking only at the emissions from the project site.And in its landmark Advisory Opinion issued last year, the International Court of Justice found that countries’ international climate obligations require proper assessment of the downstream effects of fossil fuel projects in their territories.But the outcome of this case reaches further than this one mine.For every NSW coal and gas approval, decision-makers must now consider whether conditions are needed to deal with scope 3 emissions, such as requiring the company involved to purchase offsets – a questionable solution in itself.And while the high court’s ruling is focused on NSW law, courts and decision-makers across the country are taking note. The case has the potential to provide a legal template for future climate litigation against fossil fuel projects.So, what’s next for the Mount Pleasant mine?The case will now return to the Land and Environment court, which can suspend the mine extension’s approval or set conditions on its scope 3 emissions. If conditions are imposed, requiring the buying of offsets, this is potentially a very expensive option for MACH, with carbon credits cosing around $A38 per tonne and the extension’s lifetime emissions estimated at 860m tonnes.If fossil fuel proponents have to take scope 3 emissions into account and pay to reduce them, it could drastically shift the economic case for continuing fossil fuel production in the country.Where concern for human and planetary wellbeing won’t move the needle, financial pain may well do.For climate litigation in Australia, the decision signals a hopeful path forward. Community groups now have a clear, high court-endorsed basis to challenge fossil fuel projects where decision-makers haven’t properly considered their full climate impacts.Prof Jacqueline Peel is a climate litigation expert at the University of MelbourneExplore more on these topicsFossil fuelsOpinionGreenhouse gas emissionsCoalMiningcommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Ethiopia’s return to conflict: civilian catastrophe and a spiralling regional polycrisis  | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The escalating violence reflects deep domestic rifts – but is fuelled by broader geopolitical power games
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The escalating violence reflects deep domestic rifts – but is fuelled by broader geopolitical power games
Content: Members of the Ethiopian federal police on patrol on 8 October 2026.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenMembers of the Ethiopian federal police on patrol on 8 October 2026.Photograph: ReutersOpinionEthiopiaThe Guardian view on Ethiopia’s return to conflict: civilian catastrophe and a spiralling regional polycrisisEditorialThe escalating violence reflects deep domestic rifts – but is fuelled by broader geopolitical power gamesThu 8 Oct 2026 13.49 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 14.31 EDTShareWhen the Nobel peace laureate is announced on Friday, the committee will be hoping that its choice ages better than 2019’s.Ethiopia’s prime minister, Abiy Ahmed, won the prizefor ending the 20-year border conflict with neighbouring Eritrea – signing a peace agreement with President Isaias Afwerki. A year later, their new relationship facilitated a war with the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) that killed as many as 600,000 people, displaced millions more, led to atrocities by both sides, andpushed Tigrayans into famine.Both sides bear responsibilityfor failing to properly implement the deal that ended that conflict in 2022, and the African Union and US did little to ensure that a piece of paper became a durable settlement. Now violence has resurged in northern Ethiopia, and old foes are forming bizarre new pacts. Last month, seven Ethiopian regional groupsannouncedan “Alliance for Survival” to remove the federal government. Mr Abiy’s coalition is held together by his patronage, but so far may be faring better than his rivals, united solely by shared loathing of him and riven by deep disputes. The TPLF, which controls Tigray, has previously battled the Fano militia of Amhara, and their territorial dispute endures. Ethiopia accuses Eritrea – previously accused ofatrocities against Tigrayan civilians– of backing the rebel alliance. Despite Asmara’s denials, there are multiple reports ofEritrean troops in Tigray.View image in fullscreenAbiy Ahmed.Photograph: Prime Minister Office/ReutersThe Ethiopian prime minister demands his landlocked country shouldgain access to the Red Sea, to Eritrea’s concern and anger. The Eritrean president’s control of the coastline, opposite Houthi-held stretches of Yemen, means that Washington isnow keen to engagewith his regime and unlikely to challenge him. Ethiopia’s complex internal politics are interlocking with geopolitical turmoil. Addis Ababaalso accusesEgypt and Sudan of backing the TPLF. They deny it, but Cairo is furious over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance dam on the Nile. Khartoum too fears losing water, and says Ethiopia is supporting the RSF rebels in the civil war (Addis Ababa denies it). The UAE, having lost a foothold in Yemen, has increased support for Ethiopia.The concern now is not merely the grave risk of full-scale war within Ethiopia, or between Ethiopia and Eritrea, but that a spiralling regional polycrisis is hitting already beleaguered communities. Agricultural production hasnot recoveredfrom the last war. Now the fertiliser and fuel crisis born of the Iran war, the evisceration of aid budgets and the impact of El Niño are intensifying the crisis. The UK and others must urgently provide humanitarian support.Though the escalating violence is alarming, with hundreds reportedly killed, this conflict has not yet fully ignited. In 2020, Tigrayans believed they had to unify for collective survival. This time the TPLF itself is deeply split, with veteran commandersreportedly arrestedfor questioning the new war, and soldiers and civiliansshowing little appetitefor a conflict fuelled by factionalised, self-serving and corrupt leaders. A truce is not impossible and must be a priority. Ethiopia needs relief, reconstruction and a political reconfiguration. But its conflict cannot be separated from the broader picture, as wars in Sudan, Somalia, Yemen, Iran and beyond enmesh to devastating effect. The longer that ambitious leaders convince themselves that interference elsewhere can advance their own power and resources, the deeper and more intractable it will become.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
