title: Fierce, frantic and loaded with menace: Fontaines DC’s 20 greatest songs – ranked! | Fontaines DC | The Guardian
description: Ahead of the Irish alt-rockers’ highly anticipated fifth album, Dopamine Chamber, we count down their potent, occasionally political, catalogue
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: Ahead of the Irish alt-rockers’ highly anticipated fifth album, Dopamine Chamber, we count down their potent, occasionally political, catalogue
Content: A portrait of alienation and egotism … (left to right) Tom Coll, Conor Deegan, Grian Chatten, Conor Curley and Carlos O’Connell of Fontaines DC.Photograph: Theo CottleView image in fullscreenA portrait of alienation and egotism … (left to right) Tom Coll, Conor Deegan, Grian Chatten, Conor Curley and Carlos O’Connell of Fontaines DC.Photograph: Theo CottleRankedFontaines DCFierce, frantic and loaded with menace: Fontaines DC’s 20 greatest songs – ranked!Ahead of the Irish alt-rockers’ highly anticipated fifth album, Dopamine Chamber, we count down their potent, occasionally political, catalogueAlexis PetridisThu 8 Oct 2026 10.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 10.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google20. It’s Amazing to Be Young (2025)A single inspired by the birth of bassist Conor Deegan’s daughter, It’s Amazing to Be Young is a lovely example of Fontaines DC operating in euphoric mode, a relatively recent addition to their emotional mood board: “Sometimes,” offered frontmanGrian Chatten, “optimism is a necessary delusion.”19. Death Kink (2024)It’s often cheeringly difficult to work out exactly whatFontaines DC’s influences are, but the shadow of Pixies definitely hangs over Romance’s Death Kink, from the string-bending lead guitar line on the chorus to the fabulously wonky solo and the abrupt ending. A delight, albeit one as dark-hued as the title suggests.18. A Lucid Dream (2020)The best take on A Lucid Dream might be the radically different “live version” released as a single in 2021, which slows the tempo, drags a piano into proceedings and amps up the song’s ineffable sense of menace. That said, the original – speedy drums, abstract guitar noise, ferocious climax – is quite something, too.17. Big (2019)As introductions to a new band go, the opening track of Fontaines DC’sdebut album, Dogrel, takes some beating. Big is a fierce, snotty, swaggering, supremely exciting statement of intent (“Dublin in the rain is mine … I’m gonna be big”) that immediately lets listeners know they are in the presence of something special.View image in fullscreenIt’s cheeringly difficult to work out their influences … Fontaines DC performing at Reading festival in 2024.Photograph: Simone Joyner/Getty Images16. In the Modern World (2024)The saga of “a fictional throuple together amid Armageddon” – tale as old as time, etc – written by Chatten during a spell of isolation in Los Angeles, In the Modern World feels a little like one of Lana Del Rey’s LA noir tales shot through Fontaines’ grimy lens, with startling results.15. Skinty Fia (2022)As with a lot of songs onFontaines’ third album, the lyrics of the title track deal in ambiguity and confusion, as a recently expat Irishman grapples with different notions of Irishness among the diaspora. But there’s nothing ambiguous about the music – a muscular, funky rhythm section overlaid with eerily gothic guitar and industrial noise.14. Hurricane Laughter (2019)Fontaines’ pummelling early approach in miniature: a relentless, Krautrock-y riff – think Can’s Mother Sky – turned up to 11, frantic post-punk guitars, vocals that somehow manage to feel laconic and forceful at the same time, a remarkable sense of confidence and purpose dripping from the entire enterprise.View image in fullscreenA pummelling early approach … the band on stage in Austin, Texas, in 2019.Photograph: Travis P Ball/Getty Images for SXSW13. Big Shot (2022)In retrospect, Big Shot sounds not unlike a dry run for the widescreen, expansive sound Fontaines would explore on2024’s Romance, but it’s a fabulous track in its own right, driven by an immense, glowering guitar riff. Check the strings-and-piano live version that highlights the sombre majesty of its melody.12. I Don’t Belong (2020)A lot ofA Hero’s Death, their second album, suggested the success of its predecessor, Dogrel, sat uneasily with Fontaines DC; opener I Don’t Belong, an unflinching and remarkably affecting portrait of alienation and egotism on tour, certainly does. The music broods and wrongfoots the listener: you think it’s building to an epic climax, but it just dies away, unresolved.11. Marianne (2026)It’s hard to think of another alternative rock album in 2026 as eagerly awaited as Fontaines DC’s Dopamine Chamber, trailed as a bleaker counterpart to Romance. The slow-motion synth chug of the first single, Marianne – epic, possessed of a superb pop melody and faintly disquieting lyrically – did nothing to damp down the anticipation.10. Televised Mind (2020)Released prior to A Hero’s Death, Televised Mind is a queasy reflection on the impact of social media, its lyrics too oblique to fall into cliche. Between the fuzzed-out bass (apparently influenced by the Prodigy), the scrabbling, corrosively distorted guitars and Chatten’s dead-eyed drawl, it builds up a powerful, infectious mood of anxiety.9. Favourite (2024)You would never have imagined the punchy, dark-hued band behind Dogrel might one day come up with anything quite as sweetly irresistible as Romance’s closer, Favourite. It’s the kind of glorious, sunlit guitar jangle that could have been an indie disco floor-filler at virtually any point in the last 40 years.View image in fullscreenInitially heralded as a punk band … Fontaines DC pictured in 2024.Photograph: Simon Wheatley8. Liberty Belle (2018)Initially, at least, Fontaines DC were heralded as a punk band. They turned out to be something far less straightforward than that. But you can see how it happened from Liberty Belle, an invigorating mass of frantically thrashed guitars, thumping drums and lyrics that cast a rueful eye over Dublin street life.7. A Hero’s Death (2020)Amid the troubled album of the same name, A Hero’s Death feels like a series of notes to self – “Don’t give up too quick / You only get one line, you better make it stick” – set to music that balances darkness with flickers of light in the buoyant rhythm and backing vocals.6. Nabokov (2022)Skinty Fia’s stunning closer ends the album on a bleak note. The lyrics offer a grim view of the compromises involved in a long-term relationship, while the music is a maelstrom of guitars from the darker end of the shoegazing spectrum. There’s nothing dreamlike about their heaving din, just a disorienting claustrophobia.5. Roman Holiday (2022)As a wall of guitar drifts beguilingly along, Roman Holiday offers a brilliant evocation of the complex feelings evoked by moving to London, equal parts agog with excitement – “Baby come on, get your high heels on” – and wary and confused, the latter emotions amplified by Ireland’s problematic relationship with Britain.4. Boys in the Better Land (2019)It’s cut from a noticeably different musical cloth – a heady, intense rush of distorted guitars, the apotheosis of Dogrel’s youthful blast – but you could see Boys in the Better Land as a counterpoint to Roman Holiday: an equally complicated set of emotions evoked by Fontaines DC’s home town of Dublin.View image in fullscreenSomething special … the Dublin-raised, London-based band photographed in 2024.Photograph: Peter Joseph Smith3. Jackie Down the Line (2022)This relates the saga of an abusive relationship, told from the point of view of the unrepentant abuser – Chatten’s vocal delivers some spectacularly grim lines with a callously diffident shrug – and rendered all the more chilling by its infernally catchy melody. A genuinely amazing song.2. Starburster (2024)The song that introduced Fontaines V2.0:– image more striking, music more pop-facing without sacrificing any of their agitated urgency. Starburster’s monstrous beat, orchestral samples and guitar twang vaguely resemble trip-hop retooled for a more fretful era, with Chatten’s vocal punctuated by panic-attack gasps. Hooky but glowering and supremely powerful.1. I Love You (2022)The centrepiece of Skinty Fia starts straightforwardly enough: a cliched title, a gentle, faintly Cure-ish intro of bass and gothy guitar. But I Love You just keeps building and building, ratcheting up the tension through a lengthy kick-drum-driven interlude, as Chatten’s lyrical open letter to Ireland gets more knotty and conflicted, his voice more fraught and antagonised: “This island’s run by sharks with children’s bones stuck in their jaws.” It’s five minutes of music that leaves the listener wrung out: dense, complex, emotive and crushing. You can’t imagine any of Fontaines DC’s peers making anything remotely like it.Dopamine Chamber is released via XLon 16 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFontaines DCRankedPop and rockIndiePunkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sofia Coppola: ‘I’m glad we weren’t kicked out of Tokyo making Lost in Translation’ | Sofia Coppola | The Guardian
description: The director talks about what she learnt from her mother, working with a rookie Tim Burton, and 20 years of her cult classic Marie Antoinette
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: The director talks about what she learnt from her mother, working with a rookie Tim Burton, and 20 years of her cult classic Marie Antoinette
Content: ‘Even painful memories are part of making you who you are’ … Sofia Coppola at the Venice film festival in 2025.Photograph: Abaca Press/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Even painful memories are part of making you who you are’ … Sofia Coppola at the Venice film festival in 2025.Photograph: Abaca Press/AlamyFilm & Music reader interviewSofia CoppolaInterviewSofia Coppola: ‘I’m glad we weren’t kicked out of Tokyo making Lost in Translation’As told toRich PelleyThe director talks about what she learnt from her mother, working with a rookie Tim Burton, and 20 years of her cult classic Marie AntoinetteThu 8 Oct 2026 09.16 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 12.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHello, I’m Cherry, I’m 14 and an aspiring film-maker. I love how your films capture what it feels like to be a young girl growing up. We hear so much about the famous men in your family, but how have the successful women in your family inspired and influenced you? Your films capture the experience of what it is to be a young girl in a way words often can’t.CherryEmmaThat’s nice to hear, thank you. I feel like I got a lot from my mom about being true to yourself, following what you’re interested in and seeing the beauty in your surroundings. My mom always noticed odd details in life, so a lot of my films are made up of those kinds of things.View image in fullscreenSofia Coppola behind the scenes while making Marie Antoinette.Photograph: Sofia CoppolaYour films beautifully capture the isolation of hotel rooms – spaces completely detached from a character’s past or future. If you were forced into that stillness and could choose to preserve only one cherished memory while erasing another for ever, what would they be?Malpractice1It’s hard to pick a memory, but recently we had a party in Versailles for the anniversary of Marie Antoinette and New Order played. When they started playing Ceremony [from the soundtrack] and the lights went on, I just know that in the future when I have to remember a happy memory, that’s going to be it. Even painful memories are part of making you who you are, and you learn from them, so I can’t think of anything I would erase.I heard that some ofLost in Translationwas filmed guerrilla-style due to a lack of permits. Which scene carried the biggest risk of getting you arrested? What if you had been kicked out of the country?catchytitledWe had permission for most of it, but we had to grab the scenes with Scarlett [Johansson] on the subway with real people around. The same with the overhead shot of her at that famous Shibuya crossing – we just went into Starbucks because it had this incredible view, but we would have never got permission to film there. So we stole a few things in the spirit of guerrilla film-making. And I’m glad we didn’t get kicked out, yes.View image in fullscreenThe Virgin Suicides (1999): clockwise from left, Kirsten Dunst, Leslie Hayman, Chelse Swain and AJ Cook.Photograph: American Zoetrope/AllstarWhat was the dynamic like between the five girls behind the scenes onThe Virgin Suicides? For instance, which girls were the closest, who was the loudest, who was the quietest, etc?Imogen067Their personalities did kind of emerge. We did rehearsals where we all hung out together and had them interact as a family and they cooked together. They hung out off set and they started to bond. Chelse Swain was the most eccentric one.View image in fullscreenKirsten Dunst and Jason Schwartzman in Marie Antoinette (2006).Photograph: Sofia CoppolaThe postmodern soundtrack in Marie Antoinette, all that post-punk and new romantic music, was so audacious that it took your film to a staggering level of artistry. What was the original idea behind bringing those two worlds together?Dmitry_SWhen I first started reading about Marie Antoinette in Antonia Fraser’s book, I was struck by how young she was. She was 14 when she came to Versailles and around 18 when she became queen. So I really wanted to convey that she and Louis were teenagers, and I thought back to the new romantic music I was listening to when I was a teenager. I was lucky that I had a big brother who exposed me to good music at a young age. I wanted to show it through that filter of Bow Wow Wow and Adam Ant. When the film came out, some people were offended because it just wasn’t usual to put contemporary music in a period film.Your 2003video fortheWhite Stripes’ cover of I Just Don’t Know What to Do With Myselfhas been rated byRolling Stone as one of the sexiest music videos ever. What other ideas were considered before you landed onKate Moss pole dancingfor three minutes?McScootikinsOh, wow, I didn’t know that. That’s so cool. I don’t know where it came from. It was just my idea, and I was glad that everyone was on board with it. I just asked Kate to do that, she said yes, and the band was into it.Are you aware that you’re a girlblogger icon?sleepy_nymI don’t know that much about bloggers, but that’s nice to hear. I’ll have to ask my teenage daughters. I do appreciate that my work was made a while ago, so it’s great that it connects with young women of this generation.View image in fullscreenSofia with her father, Francis Ford Coppola, at Cannes film festival in 1979.Photograph: Gilbert TOURTE/Gamma-Rapho/Getty ImagesWhat was it like working onTim Burton’s 1984 short film Frankenweenie, beforeTim Burtonwas “Tim Burton”?jasonaparkesThat was such a fun experience. I was 12 or something. I think Tim Burton was right out of school. It was an early short film, so it was really fun to meet him and be on his set – he used to do drawings for me. I’d spent a lot of time on my dad’s film sets, so it was fun to be on someone else’s. I still like to visit film sets. I’m never jaded – I’m still impressed by movie magic.Didn’t you mind having your mum filming behind the scenes for all those hours when you were making Marie Antoinette?Dr_J_A_ZoidbergMy mom always had a grounding mom presence. It was a stressful shoot, so it was nice to have her there. She also appreciated all the beauty of the costumes and the details of the food and the flowers, so it was fun to show it to her, and she was really into filming all the details and how it was made. I forgot about the footage until recently and I didn’t realise how much there was. My mom had almost 80 hours of footage, so it was a real treat to have this home movie to revisit. I never thought we would do something with it.View image in fullscreenBill Murray and Scarlett Johansson in Lost in Translation (2003).Photograph: Focus Features/AllstarYou’re not going to answer this – but someone has to ask it anyway. WhatdoesBob whisper toCharlotteat the end ofLost in Translation?rolleyesI like what Bill [Murray] always says. He says, “It’s between them,” so I’ll leave it at that.Making Marie Antoinette, directed by Eleanor Coppola, is in UK cinemas from 23 October and streams on Mubi from 6 NovemberExplore more on these topicsSofia CoppolaFilm & Music reader interviewTim BurtoninterviewsShareReuse this content

title: The woman with the mattress: the radical, rage-fuelled history of anti-rape art | Art | The Guardian
description: A performance piece from 2014 has gone viral in response to an allegation of rape at Cornell University. But with such defiant pieces stretching back hundreds of years, will things ever change?
Author: Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Headline: A performance piece from 2014 has gone viral in response to an allegation of rape at Cornell University. But with such defiant pieces stretching back hundreds of years, will things ever change?
Content: Viral artwork … Emma Sulkowicz carries a mattress at Columbia University, as part of Mattress Performance (Carry That Weight), 2014Photograph: Andrew Burton/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenViral artwork … Emma Sulkowicz carries a mattress at Columbia University, as part of Mattress Performance (Carry That Weight), 2014Photograph: Andrew Burton/Getty ImagesArtThe woman with the mattress: the radical, rage-fuelled history of anti-rape artA performance piece from 2014 has gone viral in response to an allegation of rape at Cornell University. But with such defiant pieces stretching back hundreds of years, will things ever change?Rhiannon Lucy CosslettThu 8 Oct 2026 10.19 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 10.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn September 2014, Emma Sulkowicz began to carry a blue mattress weighing 23kg around her university campus. The mattress was similar to the ones New York’s Columbia University used in its dorm rooms, where Sulkowicz said she had been raped by a fellow student two years earlier. Her performance/endurance artwork constituted her visual art senior thesis, drawing attention to the lack of criminal charges brought against her alleged attacker and his continued presence at the university. As she hauled it across campus, others could choose to assist her with her burden. Many did. She recorded responses to the piece in a diary.“I could have taken my pillow,”she told the writer Jessica Valentiat the time. “But I want people to see how it weighs down a person to be ignored by the school administration and harassed by police.”Sulkowicz would carry the mattress, she said, for as long as her alleged attacker remained at Columbia. And so she ended up carrying it all the way to graduation where, helped by other women, she took it on stage. The university president refused to shake her hand, turning away from her instead.Footage of Mattress Performance (Carry That Weight) went viral in 2014, just as the momentum for #MeToo was building. Now the performance piece has gone viral again, in response to public fury at anotherallegation of campus rape. Jane Doe (the female pseudonym used in the US for the purposes of anonymity) is suing Cornell University in New York, and seven men, claiming they drugged her and gang-raped her when she was studying there in 2024.View image in fullscreen'An imposing force’ … In Mourning and In Rage (1977) by Suzanne Lacy and Leslie LabowitzPhotograph: Maria Karras/Suzanne Lacy and Leslie LabowitzThrough her performance work, Sulkowicz joined a long line of women who have made art in response to rape, sexual assault and domestic violence. It forms a radical, if rarely explored, canon that encompasses a huge range of responses. Paula Rego’s 2008-9 workOratoriowas an altarpiece-like triptych featuring scenes of sexual assault. Yoko Ono, in 1964’sCut Piece, invited members of an audience to remove her clothing with scissors as she knelt unmoving. Jenny Holzer used human bones in 1994’sLustmord Table, her installation about rape as a weapon of war in the former Yugoslavia.Nan Goldindocumented a violent relationship in The Ballad of Sexual Dependency. AndKara Walkermade cut-paper silhouettes that explored the brutal legacy of white male power in the American south.In fact, it’s a canon that stretches back at least as far as the 17th century, whenArtemisia Gentileschi, whose rape and subsequent torture as part of her rapist’s trial no doubt informed the rage at the heart of her Judith Slaying Holofernes (1612-13). Her earliest known work, Susanna and the Elders, painted in 1610 when she was 17, viscerally conveys an intimate knowledge of how it feels to be a young woman vulnerable to sexual abuse and harassment.That knowledge is something many of us carry around, so it’s no surprise that sexual and gender-based violence is a subject that female artists return to again and again. The current Tate Modern show examining the cult and commercialisation of Frida Kahlo provides an apposite moment to reflect that Kahlo’s most groundbreaking works are never going to make it on to coasters and tote bags.A Few Small Nips, from 1935, shows a woman’s stabbed, naked body on a bed smeared with blood. The work was inspired by a story Kahlo read in a newspaper in which a man who murdered his wife dismissed his actions with the words: “But I only gave her a few small nips.”View image in fullscreenKara Walker, Confederate Prisoners Being Conducted from Jonesborough to Atlanta from the portfolio Harper’s Pictorial History of the Civil War (Annotated), 2005.Photograph: Kara Walker. Photo by Peter Paul GeoffrionNo less bloody is Ana Mendieta’s response to the rape and murder of Sarah Ann Ottens, a female student at the University of Iowa.Rape Scene(1973) was a private performance piece that the artist staged in her apartment for fellow students. Recreating a sexual assault, she posed semi-nude, bloodied and bent over a table. She stayed in that position for over an hour, forcing her audience to confront the brutal, traumatic reality of male violence against women.It does not feature in the current Tate Modern exhibition of her work, but her film Moffitt Building Piece, made in the same year in response to the same crime, does. In it, passersby are filmed without their knowledge as they encounter a bloodstain left by Mendieta on the pavement outside her building. Their responses – to ignore, to sidestep – serve as a metaphor for how violence against women is occluded by society.This feels all the more relevant in light of the gap at the heart of the Tate show: the violent manner of Mendieta’s own death and how her fate has for many come to represent misogyny in the art world. Many believe her fall from a 34th-floor window was not suicide, but rather a murder committed by Carl Andre, her husband, who was tried and acquitted (exhibitions of his work have attracted feminist protests due to what they say is his lack of accountability andher erasure as an artist). The decision tosideline this element of an artist’s biography, perhaps in a well-meaning attempt to prevent her being part of a “victim” narrative, ended up muffling the pain and the outrage that gives her works their power, robbing them of crucial context.View image in fullscreenFrida Kahlo, A Few Small Nips, 1935.Photograph: Album/AlamyThat pain was manifest in another feminist performance piece: Suzanne Lacy and Leslie Labowitz’sIn Mourning and In Ragefrom 1977. At the time, a serial killer sensationalised by the media as “the hillside strangler” was murdering women in Los Angeles. In response, the two artists, along with feminist activists and some family members of the victims, staged a funeral motorcade to city hall. Over 60 women followed behind a hearse from which, on arrival, 10 others emerged, 7ft tall and clad in black mourning robes.These were not passive, grieving victims but an imposing, rageful force, delivering statements anda chorus of: “In memory of our sisters, we fight back!” It followed Lacy’s workThree Weeks in May, which saw her daily updating a “rape map” of the city, based on statistics given to her by police. These interventions arguably had an impact on how the police and media in the city approached sexual assault at the time.Given that one in four women have been raped or sexually assaulted,according to Rape Crisis (England and Wales), such artworks will naturally often feel emotionally heavy for the viewer. Yet at a time when equality and justice can still feel so far away, when so many women are carrying around their own proverbial mattresses, it is crucial to continue to give voice to these experiences.I know I am not the only woman who found herself in tears during A Second Life, Tracey Emin’s retrospective at Tate Modern earlier this year. This happened while I watched her 1995 short filmWhy I Never Became a Dancer, about her teenage experiences of sexual exploitation and the shaming she was subjected to during a dance competition. “Shane, Eddie, Tony, Doug, Richard … this one’s for you,” she says, before breaking into a smiling dance to You Make Me Feel (Mighty Real).As a work of art, it is defiance, strength and survival. What made me cry was Emin’s determination to be joyful despite the abuse she suffered. What’s a crying shame is that it still feels so painfully relevant.Explore more on these topicsArtRape and sexual assaultViolence against women and girlsTracey EminPaula RegoYoko OnoJenny HolzerfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Franz & Marie review – Woyzeck folk musical finds heart amid the horror | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Büchner’s jagged masterpiece about a soldier’s descent is told with enchanting and stirring songs that occasionally defuse its stark terror
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: Büchner’s jagged masterpiece about a soldier’s descent is told with enchanting and stirring songs that occasionally defuse its stark terror
Content: Traumas and tenderness … Brenock O’Connor and Jade Oswald as Franz and Marie.Photograph: Danny KaanView image in fullscreenTraumas and tenderness … Brenock O’Connor and Jade Oswald as Franz and Marie.Photograph: Danny KaanTheatreReviewFranz & Marie review – Woyzeck folk musical finds heart amid the horrorCharing Cross theatre, LondonBüchner’s jagged masterpiece about a soldier’s descent is told with enchanting and stirring songs that occasionally defuse its stark terrorChris WiegandThu 8 Oct 2026 10.57 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 13.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Georg Büchner died aged 23 in 1837, he left behind Woyzeck as a bundle of papers that would be ordered and reordered for years to come, eventually discoloured by treatments used to decipher the playwright’s handwriting. His two dozen scenes, with a handful of extra fragments, form a tragic patchwork that is mirrored, in this musical version, by a similar number of stained pieces of cloth stitched into the stage curtains and by the 27 folk songs that thread the story together.It remains the downfall of Franz Woyzeck, a desperate soldier sinking into madness who grows suspicious of his partner, but – as the first names of its romantic title suggest – the story seeks to better understand both characters. Büchner’s Woyzeck suffers from visions and hallucinations; here they are joined by traumatic battlefield flashbacks. Franz was a war hero, says Marie admiringly, adding a courageous backstory to Büchner’s downtrodden squaddie and suggesting that she sees a glimpse of Franz’s former vigour in the drum major (here named Varg) who brazenly pursues her. In the play, that leads to an affair, but the musical’s Marie fights off Varg when he attempts to rape her and it is the rumours of infidelity that accelerate Franz’s frenzy.View image in fullscreen​Busy at work … Mark Meadows, Max Alexander-Taylor, Richard Emerson Gould, Brenock O’Connor, Tom Aubrey, Matthew Heywood and Steve Simmonds in Franz & Marie.Photograph: Danny KaanThese are spread – weaponised, really – by a doctor and a soldier who could have climbed out of George Grosz’s The Pillars of Society, with itsliterally shit-headed social elite. Büchner’s satire also gains a hint of Stephen Schwartz’s picaresquePippin, as Franz is buffeted by grotesquely buffoonish men of war and science.Michael Oakley’s production of Chris Broderick and Rob Shepherd’s musical, in a new adaptation by Teresa Howard, is staged with a cast of actor-musicians who create an inescapable heartiness that occasionally defuses the stark terror of the original play. But the book and lyrics dovetail nicely and the action is propelled by military cadences and stirring folk songs that are elemental, pungent and often sweetly enchanting.View image in fullscreenWell cast … Jade Oswald in Franz & Marie.Photograph: Danny KaanBrenock O’Connor and Jade Oswald, both well cast as Franz and Marie, balance their respective traumas and tendernesses, O’Connor’s agonised gait and deeply furrowed brow also evoking German expressionism. The show accentuates the play’s folkloric nature, with Matthew Heywood’s wolfish Varg prowling around a forest designed by Bretta Gerecke that is overseen by a wandering elder (Eve Polycarpou). Everyone is busy at work, often weaving, and even the act of boot-shining becomes a percussive flourish.What you mostly miss is the jagged disorientation of Büchner’s masterpiece as Franz’s downward spiral is interrupted by a needless interval and the faltering comedy of an overstuffed second half. A tragedy that plunges you to the depths has become a musical that instead sweeps you along.AtCharing Cross theatre, London, until 14 NovemberExplore more on these topicsTheatreMusicalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Willem de Kooning review – the artist’s lifelong rebellion against himself is thrilling to watch  | Art and design | The Guardian
description: Marking a century since the Dutch artist stowed away to New York, this vast retrospective gloriously showcases the abstract expressionist’s fierce boundary-pushing
Author: Ben Eastham
Headline: Marking a century since the Dutch artist stowed away to New York, this vast retrospective gloriously showcases the abstract expressionist’s fierce boundary-pushing
Content: ‘Knockout masterpiece’ … Excavation by Willem de Kooning, 1950.Photograph: © 2026 The Willem de Kooning Foundation/ Pictoright, AmsterdamView image in fullscreen‘Knockout masterpiece’ … Excavation by Willem de Kooning, 1950.Photograph: © 2026 The Willem de Kooning Foundation/ Pictoright, AmsterdamArt and designReviewWillem de Kooning review – the artist’s lifelong rebellion against himself is thrilling to watchRijksmuseum, AmsterdamMarking a century since the Dutch artist stowed away to New York, this vast retrospective gloriously showcases the abstract expressionist’s fierce boundary-pushingBen EasthamThu 8 Oct 2026 10.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWillem de Kooning was the last great artist who really knew how to draw. More precisely, if less provocatively, he was the last truly transformative painter to have been schooled in the academic tradition that produces what is still recognised, by most people, as “good drawing”. Accurate in the sense of a photograph but, like a filter on your cameraphone, also subtly tidying up the world to meet the ideals of classical proportion. “Draw what you see and not what you think,” the young De Kooning was told. Raw personal emotion had no place – a far cry from what this master of abstract expressionism was to become.The intense labour required to build a connection between eye, brain and hand so quick as to be instinctive is illustrated by the charcoal still life Dish With Jugs. Made when De Kooning was in his mid-teens, and so minutely rendered that you might mistake it for a sepia photograph, the catalogue estimates that it took 600 hours at the Rotterdam academy to complete. The aim of this exercise was not to produce a single picture so much as to ingrain a way of seeing and reconstructing the world to the point that it becomes inescapable.View image in fullscreenLike a sepia photograph … De Kooning’s Dish With Jugs, c.1919-21.Photograph: © 2026 The Willem de Kooning Foundation, Pictoright, AmsterdamThis brilliantly researched exhibition makes a compelling case for the success of that training. Setting a handful of standout paintings among a wider selection of drawings illustrates the artist’s lifelong rebellion against rules so thoroughly internalised that he could push fiercely at their limits without entirely breaking them. The battle is thrilling to watch.De Kooning’s formative training is apparent in an early drawing of the dancer Juliet Browner and a marvellously deft portrait of the artist’s wife, Elaine. The influence of Ingres – the Pelé of academic drawing – on these works has often been remarked upon, not least by rival New York painters for whom De Kooning’s superior draughtsmanship was a source of suspicion (too prissy, too European). And it seems that the immigrant artist placed himself under pressure to unstitch the aesthetic conventions of the old world and rework them into something more appropriate to the new: irreverent, free, immediate, expressive.View image in fullscreen‘A harbinger of women to come’ … Queen of Hearts.Photograph: © 2026 The Willem de Kooning Foundation/ Pictoright, AmsterdamIt is important to note that De Kooning’s education was not limited to the academy. A working-class kid, his evening classes had been subsidised by the design firm where he worked in the day; after stowing away to the US at 22, he scraped a living as a sign painter and commercial illustrator. These lessons made their way into his art, and the difficulty of synthesising them might explain the struggles of his early career (he didn’t have a solo show until he was nearly 44) and how revolutionarythe breakthroughwas when it did arrive.Central to that achievement was that he made no distinction between drawing and painting (the tradition being, in simple terms, that you draw the outlines and paint the space between them). In Queen of Hearts, a harbinger of women to come, he drags charcoal sticks across wet paint to create soft edges, sanding down and painting over layers like a housepainter. The big bang arrives in the seminal work on paper completed in 1949, an arrangement of white sparks against a black ground that calls to mind comets dancing through the night sky. But De Kooning was no starry-eyed mystic: at the bottom edge, transforming those white sparks into liquid spurts, is a scrawled cock and balls.Excavation, a knockout masterpiece, likewise appears at first as an abstract pattern of interlocking shapes only to reveal itself as a maelstrom of screaming faces and dismembered body parts. Completed in 1950, it conjures both Europe’s mass graves and an orgiastic ecstasy of bodies dissolving into each other. Sex and death, heaven and hell, the end of the old world and the birth of the new. In one of many intelligent arrangements, Excavation is paired with a drawing from four years earlier, the aptly titled Judgment Day.It is a quirk of the exhibition that its most famous painting, Woman I, hangs in a separate gallery normally reserved for the museum’s treasures from the Dutch golden age. Not only does this icon hold its own against Vermeer and Rembrandt, but she is also unexpectedly at home. Scandalous when first exhibited, the accusation that this cartoonish, charismatic and wild figure defames all womankind by its “monstrosity” seems now to rely on some mid-century assumptions about how women should be represented. Whatever you think about Woman I, she could never be mistaken for a submissive sex object or a Stepford wife.View image in fullscreen‘De Kooning could always rely on his line’ … inside the Rijksmuseum exhibition.Photograph: Peter Tijhuis/RijksmuseumDe Kooning’s relentless attacks on convention, which is to say on himself and everything else, took their toll. A series of black-and-white works, made in Rome in the late 1950s, mark the end of his imperial phase. While these vaguely calligraphic graphic signs illustrate a point about the convergence of painting and drawing, they feel to me slapdash and derivative of Franz Kline. From here, this exhibition does little to overturn the conventional wisdom that De Kooning struggled over the next two decades to scale the same heights. There are standouts – notably the irrepressible Clam Diggers, a woozy portrait of two women standing in shallow water rendered in ice-cream colours and buttery textures, and a gorgeously fleshy painting from the mid-70s that advertises the painter’s occasionally overlooked gift as a colourist. If the paintings are hit and miss, the drawings from this period reveal that, even hindered by alcoholism and a chaotic personal life, De Kooning could always rely on his line.That line holds to the end. The show closes with an astonishing painting from 1985, during the period when De Kooning’s cognitive decline was increasingly apparent. Sinuous blue and black lines curve across a mottled white ground, weaving a pattern suggestive of bodies and yet emptied of desire. It is serene, strange and straightforwardly beautiful, as if everything that the artist had struggled to pack into his work had been boiled down to basic principles. He is back to fitting the world to a pleasing form. The difference is that it is no longer a boilerplate inherited from the classical tradition, but shaped by his experiences and entirely his own. He doesn’t need to think about it. The battle is over.Willem de Kooning at Work is at theRijksmuseum, Amsterdam, from 9 October to 17 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsArt and designArtPaintingreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Anne Carson wins Nobel prize in literature 2026 | Nobel prize in literature | The Guardian
description: Most prestigious literature prize goes to Canadian known for genre-crossing works such as Autobiography of Red
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: Most prestigious literature prize goes to Canadian known for genre-crossing works such as Autobiography of Red
Content: The academy cited Anne Carson’s ‘bold and inventive oeuvre’ in its awarding of the prize.Photograph: Pontus Lundahl/TT/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe academy cited Anne Carson’s ‘bold and inventive oeuvre’ in its awarding of the prize.Photograph: Pontus Lundahl/TT/ReutersNobel prize in literatureAnne Carson wins Nobel prize in literature 2026Most prestigious literature prize goes to Canadian known for genre-crossing works such as Autobiography of Red‘Delights await!’: Margaret Atwood and other writers on Nobel winner Anne CarsonWhere to start with: Anne CarsonEmma LoffhagenandLeyland Ceccoin TorontoThu 8 Oct 2026 10.03 EDTFirst published on Thu 8 Oct 2026 07.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheNobel prize in literaturehas been awarded to the Canadian poet and essayist Anne Carson, the Swedish Academy has announced.The academy cited the author’s “bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature”.The Nobel prize, regarded as the most prestigious award in global literature, is awarded for a lifetime body of work. The winner receives 12m Swedish kronor (£900,000).Ingrid Carlberg, the permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy, said she had told Carson of the award on the phone shortly before the news broke. “She had time to tell me that she is, for the moment, in Iceland, where she is listening to the wind,” Carlberg said. “She was taken by surprise but very happy. I could hear that in her voice.”View image in fullscreenBooks by Anne Carson on display at a Waterstones bookshop in London.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersBorn in Toronto in 1950, Carson is known forwork that moves freely between poetry, prose and translation, drawing heavily on the literature and mythology of the ancient Greek world. She has been a professor of classics at various institutions including Princeton, New York University and McGill University in Montreal. She is the 19th woman to win, out of 123 literature laureates.Carson’s first book, Eros the Bittersweet, was published in 1986 and combined literary criticism with an exploration of desire and the ancient Greek tradition.Her best-known work is Autobiography of Red, a 1998 novel in verse inspired by the fragments of the ancient Greek poet Stesichorus. It reimagines the myth of Geryon, the red-winged monster killed by Herakles, as the story of a modern teenage boy navigating heartbreak and desire.In 2001, she became the first woman to win the TS Eliot prize, for her collection The Beauty of the Husband. She has also been awarded Guggenheim and MacArthur fellowships.The Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney,congratulated the poeton X after the announcement. “With wit, imagination, and a style entirely her own, Canadian poet Anne Carson has reimagined the classics. She has brought ancient stories to new audiences and transformed the way we think about literature,” he said, adding that it was a “proud moment for Canada”.David Leonard, the executive director of the Writers’ Trust ofCanada, said: “Anne is such a brilliant writer. Her work is broad, but also extremely smart.” Calling Carson’s work “intoxicating”, he said her four-decade career had resulted in a peerless collection of poems and essays. “They’re beautiful, they’re smart, they’re true and they are humane. It’s exactly what we need in our writing.”Carson’s work has attracted praise from fellow writers including Susan Sontag, who once said: “She is one of the few writers writing in English that I would read anything she wrote. If there’s a magazine that has something of hers in it, I buy it automatically.”View image in fullscreenIngrid Carlberg announcing Anne Carson as the recipient of the 2026 Nobel prize in literature in Stockholm on Thursday.Photograph: Christine Olsson/EPAAnders Olsson, the chair of the Swedish Academy’s Nobel Committee for Literature, praised Carson for work that had “broken away from lyrical poetry bound to the narrative self and inspired new forms of contemporary literature”. He said: “This method of writing leads to playful and ironic works that move not only between classical and modern poetry but also between different genres and artforms.”Carson’s books have ranged widely in form. Men in the Off Hours combined verse essays, poems, epitaphs and prose about artists and historical figures, and won the inaugural Griffin poetry prize in 2001. Decreation, another eclectic work, brought together poetry, essays and an opera.Nox, published in 2010, is particularly characteristic of Carson’s avant-garde approach to literature – the book takes the form of an accordion-fold box containing a reproduction of a notebook Carson made after the death of her brother. Her later works include Red Doc> and Float.In aGuardian reviewof Red Doc>, Sarah Crown wrote: “To engage so fluidly, so originally and compellingly, with a story first told more than 3,000 years ago, is astonishing: her ambition is one thing; the fact that it is so completely achieved is, frankly, something else.”Much of Carson’s work has emerged from her fascination with language itself. The Swedish Academy noted: “Almost all her literary production has centred upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning,” adding that Carson had identified the etymology of words as “the starting point for all her work”.Asked why she continually moved between forms, Carson said in an interview: “Boredom, I guess. There is a restlessness. There are a lot of forms to try.”She has acknowledged the difficulties that come with her experimental style. “[My work] does fall apart a lot,” she said in a 2018 interview. “It gets just too weird for anyone to care about reading, or else it gets diluted into a sort of parody of itself.”Ira Wells, the president of PEN Canada, said Carson’s win felt “particularly significant at a moment in which Canada and Europe are strengthening cultural ties amidst broader global disruption”. He added: “On an aesthetic level, Carson’s verse vibrates on profound human frequencies, at a moment in which more and more language is formulated by machines.”Carson has generally kept her personal life out of interviews. However, in an August 2024 article for the London Review of Books, she disclosed that she had been diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease.The Nobel prize in literature has been awarded on 118 previous occasions since 1901. Recent laureates include Annie Ernaux, Bob Dylan, Abdulrazak Gurnah, Louise Glück, Peter Handke and Olga Tokarczuk. Last year’s recipient was the Hungarian author László Krasznahorkai, known for his dystopic and avant-garde writing.Carson, 76, will formally receive the medal and diploma in a ceremony in Stockholm in December.To browse works by Anne Carson, visitguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsNobel prize in literatureAnne CarsonFictionPoetryAwards and prizesCanadaAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s not about sex but empowerment’: why I picked a ‘naked’ frock as dress of the year | Culture | The Guardian
description: Sarah Burton’s sporty, daffodil mesh dress made me smile. But the reason I chose it for Fashion Museum Bath is because it tells a story of our times, when bodies are more political than ever
Author: Jess Cartner-Morley
Headline: Sarah Burton’s sporty, daffodil mesh dress made me smile. But the reason I chose it for Fashion Museum Bath is because it tells a story of our times, when bodies are more political than ever
Content: Telling a story … Fashion Museum Bath collections manager Elaine Uttley with Jess’s 2025 picks.Photograph: Peter J Stone/Fashion Museum BathView image in fullscreenTelling a story … Fashion Museum Bath collections manager Elaine Uttley with Jess’s 2025 picks.Photograph: Peter J Stone/Fashion Museum BathCulture‘It’s not about sex but empowerment’: why I picked a ‘naked’ frock as dress of the yearSarah Burton’s sporty, daffodil mesh dress made me smile. But the reason I chose it for Fashion Museum Bath is because it tells the story of our times, when bodies are more political than everJess Cartner-MorleyThu 8 Oct 2026 07.34 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 11.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne morning in February this year, I opened my laptop to find an email with an all-caps subject line: TOP SECRET. Being a fashion editor can be exciting but state secrets are not generally my beat, so I was intrigued. Sure enough, it was a thrill: an invitation from theFashion Museum Bathto choose their Dress of the Year for 2025.What an honour.Dress of the Yearbegan in 1963, the brainchild of the museum’s founder Doris Langley Moore, as a way of keeping a static collection perpetually current. Each year a fashion expert picks an outfit or outfits that capture the year just gone, and these become part of the permanent collection. There is a Mary Quant dress and a Katharine Hamnett slogan T-shirt, Ossie Clark chiffon and Ralph Lauren pinstripes. There is sublime beauty from the catwalks of Yves Saint Laurent and Chanel and John Galliano, and pieces of cultural history: McQueen’s bumsters, Jennifer Lopez’s internet-breaking green Versace Grammy dress, Dior’s “We Should All Be Feminists” slogan, Naomi Campbell’s pandemic hazmat suit, a Black Lives Matter T-shirt, and the dress worn by the Duchess of Sussex for her Oprah interview in 2021. “Dress” is interpreted loosely, in the sense of clothing rather than a frock: the lineup includes men’s suits. The Bath museum is currently mid-revamp, having closed its doors in 2022, with construction soon to start on a new museum set to open in the city’s old post office in 2030. Meanwhile the collection is stored in Wiltshire and can be seen online.The roll call of previous selectors is formidable. All the front row grand dames are present and correct. There are Vogue editors and Fleet Street’s most feared critics. Legendary stylists, including Grace Coddington and the late Isabella Blow, iconic retailer Joan Burstein and beloved London milliner Stephen Jones. The protocol of Dress of the Year is singular, in that the museum chooses the chooser, who then has complete freedom. The thought of my fashion verdict being preserved on a pedestal in a glass case forevermore, rather than printed on the proverbial fish and chip paper, was daunting. I experienced a swift emotional gear change from “chuffed” to “mildly panicked”. Plus the schedule – decision made in spring, selector announcement in summer, and DOTY revealed in October – gave me well over a month to make my choice, a timeframe which my daily-deadline-institutionalised brain found more overwhelming than liberating.View image in fullscreenDialogue between past and present … Sarah Burton’s acid yellow knitted mesh stitch dress for Givenchy.Photograph: INDIGITAL.TV/GivenchyBut I knew what I wanted to do. Most fashion journalists are current affairs journalists at heart, I think. Fashion expresses what it feels like to live in the world at a particular moment. An eye for fashion is essentially a curiosity about that, because the clothes we wear speak to what seems beautiful or important or valuable to us. This is where the juice is. So I wasn’t interested in making a best dressed list, or awarding a prize to the prettiest frock of the year. I wanted my choice to tell a story that would help future museum visitors understand the fashion and culture of 2025.The trouble is, once you decide you are choosing a piece of history rather than a dress, almost anything is eligible.Lauren Sánchez Bezos’ girls’ trip space suits?The Birkin that sold for $10.1m?Naomi Osaka walking on court in a kimono? A Labubu?Well, no. What I chose would form part of the permanent collection of one of Britain’s foremost fashion museums, so it needed design credentials of its own. In other words: I was looking for a great look that told a great story.2025 was the year of the “naked” dress. Dresses that made headlines did so by their virtual non-existence.Margot Robbie on the red carpet in strategically covered strings of crystals– not so much a dress as a very impressive necklace.Julia Fox in transparent mesh, her long dark hair trapped beneath it and preserving her modesty a la Botticelli’s Venus.Zoë Kravitz at the Oscarsin a black dress with a heart shaped window framing her bottom.View image in fullscreenSmart casual … Navy blue viscose jacket, trousers and waistcoat with suede leather sandals by Giorgio Armani.Photograph: Giorgio ArmaniFashion has always been partly about sex, but the naked dress is different. The naked dress is about the body, not the bedroom. Fox’s dress is not alluring: it is confronting, verging on repellent. At a moment when women’s bodily autonomy is once again fiercely contested in the US, and when cosmetic surgery and GLP-1 usage is physically transforming celebrities in front of our eyes, bodies are more political than ever.There is female empowerment here; there is also subordination to the male gaze. Both of those things are true at once. But I chose a naked dress bySarah Burton, who I have known and admired since she was Alexander McQueen’s right hand woman in the late 1990s. Burton is cherished in fashion, a woman who celebrates rather than objectifies. The daffodil coloured sporty mesh dress with visible retro underpinnings that I have chosen is from her first collection for Givenchy – a significant moment in itself, at a time when female creative directors are thin on the ground – and suggests a dialogue between fashion past and present that felt perfect for the assignment. Also, the kicker hem makes me smile, and the sunny shade will look terrific on a mannequin.Sarah Burton turns up the glamour volume at Givenchy in ParisRead moreAs for my menswear choice there was never any question. Thedeath of Giorgio Armaniin September 2025 was the loss of a giant not just of fashion, but of culture. Armani changed what it meant to look modern. He invented the smart-casual mode of menswear that dominates cities all over the world today. In so many ways, he was decades ahead of his time. He pioneered gender-fluid dressing, putting women in trouser suits and men in sensuously draped silks. He always believed that fashion should be about timeless style and clothes made to last, and deplored the churn of trends and fast-fashion. He stuck to this point of view through decades when it put him at odds with the rest of the industry; these days, everyone acknowledges that he was right all along. The ensemble I picked – soft shoulders, fluid fabrics, layering that looks effortless but immaculate – comes from the last collection Armani designed, shown on the catwalk at an emotional, elegiac show in Milan a few weeks after his death.Last year was the year of California wildfires and Zelenskyy’s Oval Office showdown; the Louvre heist and the first American pope; the rise of Reform and Euros triumph for the Lionesses; victory for Zohran Mamdani and the assassination of Charlie Kirk. But beneath the headlines, it was a year when we lived and loved, worried and argued. When we prayed for Oasis tickets and got obsessed with Celebrity Traitors. A Dress of the Year, to me, is not necessarily a look that everyone wore. It is about getting a bit further under the skin of things. (The DOTY for 1996 wasLee McQueen’s bumsters, which stands up well with hindsight, but definitely wasn’t a common sight on the street that year.) What happens in fashion captures the attitude of its time, the way fabric holds on to a lingering trace of perfume. Long after the headlines of 2025 have blurred together, I hope these clothes will retain something of how it felt to be there. That, in the end, was what I wanted to put in the glass case.Explore more on these topicsCultureDressesMuseumsSarah BurtonArmaniGivenchyWomen's dressesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Can Ali G: Who Iz I? save character comedy cinema? | Comedy films | The Guardian
description: Sacha Baron Cohen’s new film risks being outdated in a more rancorous era. But could it restore the personality-driven genre to big screens or end it altogether?
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: Sacha Baron Cohen’s new film risks being outdated in a more rancorous era. But could it restore the personality-driven genre to big screens or end it altogether?
Content: Last man standing in a noble tradition … Morgana Robinson as Julie and Sacha Baron Cohen as Ali G in Ali G: Who Iz I?Photograph: Courtesy of Amazon MGM Studios/courtesy of Amazon MGM StudiosView image in fullscreenLast man standing in a noble tradition … Morgana Robinson as Julie and Sacha Baron Cohen as Ali G in Ali G: Who Iz I?Photograph: Courtesy of Amazon MGM Studios/courtesy of Amazon MGM StudiosComedy filmsCan Ali G: Who Iz I? save character comedy cinema?Sacha Baron Cohen’s new film risks being outdated in a more rancorous era. But could it restore the personality-driven genre to big screens or end it altogether?Phil HoadThu 8 Oct 2026 06.58 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 07.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor a man whose campaign slogan was once “Keep it real”, Ali G has his work cut out in the reality of 2026. The big dog of Da West Staines Massiv was the character with whomSacha Baron Cohencarved out his own niche of gonzo-gotcha comedy in the late 1990s – and now he’s back with new film, Ali G: Who Iz I? But it’s unclear if his great creation has gone sufficiently fallow in the collective consciousness to still operate well in real-life situations, the kind of lethal idiot who once pitched Donald Trump anti-drip ice-cream gloves. And more critically, is the Ali G satirical project – which poked at 90s multicultural mores – still relevant and funny in far more rancorous times?It’s not just Baron Cohen’s career as an undercover operative that’s on the line. It’s the future of character-led comedy as a going concern, now that he seems to be the last man standing in this once-noble tradition – in cinemas, at least. To be clear, character comedy isn’t merely comedy with characters; it’s comedy filtered through a central persona that overlaps with the comedian playing it and whose subversive sensibility colours the entire work.View image in fullscreenMike Myers’ swinging London exile … Myers and Heather Graham in Austin Powers: The Spy Who Shagged Me, 1999.Photograph: AJ Pics/AlamyMike Myers’ swinging London exile Austin Powers was the most commercially successful example – but the actor hasn’t made a film in that first-person style since his self-help spoof The Love Guru tanked in 2008.Will Ferrell, ruling the roost as fashion’s Dr Evil, Mugatu (in Zoolander), Buddy the Elf and Ron Burgundy, seemed the best successor. Mystifyingly, though, Ferrell has barely been able to get a film bankrolled in the last decade – and certainly not one putting him out front to that extent. Character comedy subsists on TV, from where it came, with the likes of Alan Partridge and Philomena Cunk. But unless the new Ali G can blaze a fresh hit of chronic satire into the genre’s bloodstream, it’s hard to see a future for it on the big screen.Ali G was already controversial back in the day: the regular accusation was that while he was satirising the white appropriation of black culture, he in fact enabled straight lampooning of the latter. Now those criticisms are sharpened by the notion that, in 2026, he is past his sell-by date: both out of step with a more culturally mixed Britain and, overflowing with bifter gags and mad patois, dangerously adjacent to racist caricature that won’t pass these days. British standup comedian Dane Baptisterecently told Deadline: “After Black Lives Matter and the brief humanisation of black people and black creatives, it seems very dubious that we are now regressing back, not just five years, but 25 years, to bring back a character that was able to flourish because there were no accurate portrayals of black Britishness on screen.”But it would be a shock if Baron Cohen wasn’t wise to the current sensitivities. In 2020’sBorat Subsequent Moviefilm, he mostly successfully updated the Kazakhstan reporter for the post-truth, Covid-era end times of Trump’s US. His choice of target interviewees in Who Iz I? remains to be seen, but it would be surprising if he didn’t pick a few where he can opportunistically needle both woke and anti-woke camps.These debates are tricky ones, on cultural shifting sands, and Baron Cohen undeniably skirts close to reactionary goading at times (the fact that dumb Americans might actually believe Kazakhstan is that backward doesn’t escape the fact he’s propagating the idea it’s a potassium-, incest- and antisemitism-crazed shithole). But if the new Ali G film does fall foul of the post-Black Lives Matter climate, it’ll be hard not to also conclude that our splintered, fractious era lacks the unity – or at least consensus – that makes character comedy possible at all. To a large extent, audiences have to agree on the social phenomena these big satirical beasts feed off. In the late 90s, black street culture was sufficiently new and prominent a force in the UK mainstream to make this crip-sign-throwing buffoon a direct hit.There’s no reason why character comedy can’t thrive off societal shifts, though – if the character is positioned carefully enough. In fact, this is how it originally manufactured tension, with the likes of Charlie Chaplin’s Tramp getting fed through the mangler of industrialised capitalism in Modern Times. Or Peter Sellers playing both old establishment nabob Sir John Kennaway and the trade union firebrand Fred Kite in 1959’s labour-relations satire I’m All Right Jack. With postwar Britain evolving rapidly, Tony Hancock picked up the baton in 1961’s The Rebel, both surfing and sending up boho nonconformism in his role as an accidentally successful avant garde artist. Alan Partridge’s long slide into local radio-bound insignificance has only attained glorious new parallels in the post-Brexit era.View image in fullscreenA massive influence … Peter Sellers, centre, in I’m All Right Jack, 1959.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyAnother reason why character comedy may have fallen from favour is its vaudevillian strut, a very human theatricality that seems old-fashioned in an age of frictionless CGI blockbusters. It revels in transformation and disguise (Baron Cohen now, of course, being so famous he has to layer on disguises on top of his original disguises – hence the new Rasta Ali G). The genre often compounds this ludic chaos by having its stars play multiple roles, as Sellers,Eddie Murphyand Mike Myers love to do.Somehow this protean fun allows the presiding comic genius’s essential quality to pierce through all the more clearly: in Sellers’ case, a kind of unnerving mildness that could transmute into mania, or Myers’ cheeky puerility. Mrs Doubtfire, from 1993, is one of the most revelatory uses of this ventriloquist effect. Another persona that the film’s divorced voiceover artist adopts in order to see his children more often, the Scottish nanny is really a conduit for the sentimental streak that underpinned much of Robin Williams’s work. And like the theatre, you can see the tactile human continuity between character comedy’s practitioners: Myers has often talked about his admiration for Sellers’ chameleonic powers. Dr Evil’s “one million dollars” faux pas is a lift of a similar gag near the end of Sellers’ 1959 geopolitics satire The Mouse That Roared.View image in fullscreenA sentimental streak … Robin Williams in Mrs Doubtfire, 1993.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyBy 2002, when Myers was doing silhouette gags about giving birth to Mini-Me in Austin Powers: Goldmember, this vaudevillian style was looking passe. With The Lord of the Rings and Harry Potter in full pomp, blockbuster film was firmly in the CGI era; comedy had moved on, too, to the edgier Frat Pack films and the realism of Judd Apatow.But perhaps character comedy had also lost strong moorings by this point, with social comment largely absent from the genre since the 1980s. Instead, Austin Powers was an extended riff on 60s and 90s pop-cultural overlaps and discrepancies (Jean Dujardin did something similar in his later OSS-117 series), while Eddie Murphy’s multi-character outings The Nutty Professor and Norbit seemed largely there to prop up the fat-suit industry. Only Will Ferrell – via his blowhard news anchor Burgundy, but also in his general screen persona in ensemble work such as Wedding Crashers, Step Brothers and Talladega Nights – embodied a type that spoke clearly for the times: the arrested manchild.That all changed the momentBoratand his wobbling producer Azamat Bagatov landed in New York in 2006. By injecting Borat with a raw hit of the reality format incubated on The 11 O’Clock Show and Da Ali G Show, Baron Cohen completely revitalised big-screen character comedy. Suddenly, it became thrillingly politicised as his sublimely ignorant aliases, Borat and in 2009 Brüno, flushed out American and Middle Eastern absurdities and prejudices. Not to mention the high-wire aspect of his escapades: Baron Cohen was somehow impervious to whatever peril he stirred up, whether that was desecrating the Star-Spangled Banner at a rodeo in Borat, or an interpretation of mano-a-mano quite different to what cage fighting audiences were expecting in Brüno. His gleeful brazenness was the signature quality that shone through.View image in fullscreenA type that spoke clearly for the times … Will Ferrell in Anchorman: The Legend of Ron Burgundy, 2004.Photograph: Dreamworks Skg/AllstarBut Ali G has been dormant a long time. His last big-screen outing, 2002’s hit-and-missAli G Indahouse, was a very different, fully scripted endeavour. Beyond a gag about mistaking a pregnancy test for a vape, the trailer for Ali G: Who Iz I? doesn’t give much away about how sharply the character’s been updated; judging by the small-penis outro, some things are undying.Staines’s favourite son will need to pull more out of his XXXXXL puffa. Only the current culture wars – police violence, colonialism, cultural appropriation – can supply him with appropriately charged material that he can “booyakasha” his way through. Anything less, and the character’s age will show, and the once-cutting posturing and patois will seem less than ironic. Which would be a bad thing for character comedy – then the mask really will have slipped.Ali G: Who Iz I? is released in UK cinemas on 23 OctoberExplore more on these topicsComedy filmsSacha Baron CohenComedyMike MyersWill FerrellRobin WilliamsEddie MurphyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Dafydd Owain’s second album wins the 2026 Welsh music prize | Music | The Guardian
description: Ymarfer Byw, which was praised for its ‘musical excellence’, beat 14 other albums to the prize of £10,000
Author: Michael Cragg
Headline: Ymarfer Byw, which was praised for its ‘musical excellence’, beat 14 other albums to the prize of £10,000
Content: ‘It’s such a privilege to win’ … Dafydd Owain receives his award at the Wales Millennium Centre in Cardiff.Photograph: Welsh Music PrizeView image in fullscreen‘It’s such a privilege to win’ … Dafydd Owain receives his award at the Wales Millennium Centre in Cardiff.Photograph: Welsh Music PrizeMusicDafydd Owain’s second album wins the 2026 Welsh music prizeYmarfer Byw, which was praised for its ‘musical excellence’, beat 14 other albums to the prize of £10,000Michael CraggThu 8 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 08.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSinger-songwriter Dafydd Owain has won the 2026 Welsh music prize with his second album Ymarfer Byw.The emotionally charged record, which also won Welsh language album of the year in August, beat albums by the likes of Gruff Rhys, the Royston Club and Art School Girlfriend to the prize of £10,000.Receiving the award at Wales Millennium Centre in Cardiff on Wednesday, Owain, from Caernarfon, north-west Wales, told theBBC: “It’s just amazing, isn’t it? Such talented, amazing artists on the shortlist. There’s a multitude of people that contribute to creating any album, and it’s not a solo project, even though we call it a solo project … I just hope, if anything, this album and this award mean I’m able to create more music. But it’s such a privilege to win in such esteemed company.”During his acceptance speech Owain spoke of his first performance at the same Cardiff venue as a 16-year-old choir member: “I mimed the whole thing because I was ... scared of making a bum note,”he recalled. “It’s weird to have an award for what’s essentially singing now.”Huw Stephens, who co-founded the prize in 2011, praised Ymarfer Byw’s “musical excellence” and Owain’s “very personal and moving lyrics”.Past winners of the award, now in its 16th year, include Gwenno, Kelly Lee Owens and Deyah. Producer Don Leisure took home last year’s award for his album, Tyrchu Sain.Swansea singer Mary Hopkin, who was one of the first artists signed to the Beatles’ label Apple Records in 1968, was also honoured at this year’s ceremony, receiving the Welsh music inspiration award for her contribution to music.The Welsh music prize 2026 shortlist:ADJUA – Everything Is BeautifulAleighcia Scott – TaithAni Glass – PhantasmagoriaArt School Girlfriend – Lean InCerys Hafana – AngelChroma – 25 ForeverDafydd Owain – Ymarfer BywDewin – Dan y DderwenGruff Rhys – Dim ProbsGwenifer Raymond – Last Night I Heard the Dog Star BarkLocal – Too Broke to Be This BusyMari Mathias – CyfarwyddSkindred – You Got ThisThe Bug Club – Every Single MuscleThe Royston Club – Songs for the SpineExplore more on these topicsMusicAwards and prizesWalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Below review – a killer snot-berg causes chaos for Josh Hartnett  | Television | The Guardian
description: Don your best plaid shirts for this supernatural thriller about a gang of beefy fishermen who tackle sea monsters. It is totally ridiculous – but you will have loads of daft fun
Author: Sarah Dempster
Headline: Don your best plaid shirts for this supernatural thriller about a gang of beefy fishermen who tackle sea monsters. It is totally ridiculous – but you will have loads of daft fun
Content: Embattled sea hunk … Josh Hartnett as Calvin in Below.Photograph: Netflix/PAView image in fullscreenEmbattled sea hunk … Josh Hartnett as Calvin in Below.Photograph: Netflix/PATV reviewTelevisionReviewBelow review – a killer snot-berg causes chaos for Josh HartnettDon your best plaid shirts for this supernatural thriller about a gang of beefy fishermen who tackle sea monsters. It is totally ridiculous – but you will have loads of daft funSarah DempsterThu 8 Oct 2026 03.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 06.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAbandon all hope, ye who enter Below. And jettison disbelief while ye be at it. A six-part supernatural thriller forged from industrial-grade bunkum, Below is set in Snook’s Arm, a struggling Newfoundland fishing community beset by an ancient, unknowable evil. And plaid. And sea hags, shifty conservationists, mist, motorbikes, curses, a catch-all nostalgia for the 70s-90s, galoshes, wind and, horrifyingly, the collected works of the Waterboys. But mainly an ancient, unknowable evil (and plaid).Here’s twitchy young roustabout Wade Penney (Charlie Heaton) with some combatively accented exposition. “I tells ye, these waters can be deadly,” he splutters, waggling his fish slice seawards as he prepares breakfast for his credulous Airbnb guests. “It’s been one seafarin’ tragedy after another for us.” Wade is an idiot but he is not, in this instance, wrong. First there was the seafarin’ tragedy of 1986, a splosh-based catastrophe that saw his family’s cottage – and his disconcertingly muscular grand pappy – dragged underwater by forces unknown. Then there were the fishing bans, the decades of economic uncertainty and the resettlement programme – a looming government-led scheme that threatens the town’s remaining hopes for survival. And now? “Jumpin’ Jesus,” blurts ripped paterfamilias Calvin Penney (Josh Hartnett). “Will ye look at dat!” We look at dat. It’s an iceberg. A towering wodge of inexplicable CGI menace has materialised in the harbour, bringin’ with it yet more trouble for the embattled sea hunks.View image in fullscreen‘Muscular grand pappy’ … Below on Netflix.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixBut this is no ordinary trouble. And this is no ordinary iceberg. Indeed, this particular “floater” stinks “of ammonia” and soon trawlermen are vanishing, bloodied body parts are bobbing ashore and something vast and vengeful is glowering up at them all from the depths of the bay. As tiny-eyed widower Calvin puts it: “What da frig is goin’ on?” Simple, says doughty Dr Fonda Howander from the Ocean Science Centre down in Seal Cove. “It’s not an iceberg.” It is, in fact, “one big frozen mucous membrane!” Calvin’s brow concertinas.Mucous? Deep within his ruggedly masculine skull, a long dormant synaptic connection flickers to life. “You mean,” he gulps, “like … snot?”Fonda (Mackenzie Davis) smiles and nods pityingly. These beefy simpletons and their innocent ways! If only nature was as sympathetic as she is. Alas, nature – in the form of a massive squid unleashed via the thawing of ancient Arctic permafrost and subsequently driven to a) rubbing itself over icebergs in a desperate act of territory marking, and b) killing everyone – is a bastard. Or is it? Could the cephalopod’s ire be justified? Its very existence be a heartrendin’ metaphor for climate breakdown and the passivity of humankind? Possibly. But then, it’s hard to tell. The eco theme is so far down in the mix as to be virtually inaudible. There are fleeting references to warming oceans and “systems breaking apart” but these are curiously apologetic things; faint and barely decipherable prophecies of doom burbling under the neon blare of revvin’ motorbikes and references to Jaws. There is the suspicion that Below’s creator, Jesse McKeown, had intended the climate stuff to be … bigger? More series-defining? That is until, one imagines, the inevitable hand landed on his shoulder and a network pep talk that included an only half-joking mention of “woke” ensured this particular element sank like a CGI stone.View image in fullscreenSquid game … Mackenzie Davis as Dr Fonda Howander.Photograph: Jan Thijs/NetflixWhat we get instead is an old-fashioned tale of sea monsters, isolation and plaid clad tenacity, replete with exploding viscera and goofy nods to such era-defining horrors as The Thing, The Fog and Stranger Things. It is, if you will, Widower’s Bay. And very enjoyable it is too, with much cable-knit daftness re sea hags and David “Lord of the Rings” Wenham having a whale of a time as a self-styled “climate change activist” whose plans for Snook’s Arm are as flagrant as his chinos.Below is hunky sea-fun that, for all its efforts to the contrary, still, quietly, #makesUthink. Come on in. The water’s ridiculous.Below is on Netflix nowExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewreviewsShareReuse this content
