Content: Bold tactics … Rob Beckett (left) and Richard E Grant at breakfast on The Celebrity Traitors.Photograph: BBC/Studio Lambert/Euan Cherry/PAView image in fullscreenBold tactics … Rob Beckett (left) and Richard E Grant at breakfast on The Celebrity Traitors.Photograph: BBC/Studio Lambert/Euan Cherry/PATV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: has Richard E Grant blown it in The Celebrity Traitors?The game is in full swing, as we find out the first famous face to be banished. Plus: The Paper finale gets emosh. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Phil HarrisonandJack SealeThu 8 Oct 2026 01.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Celebrity Traitors8pm, BBC OneWe’ve had our first round table – and incredibly frustrating cliffhanger ending – so now it’s time to find out which celebrity is the first to be banished. After confessing he is a traitor minutes after being chosen, surely it will beRichard E Grant? But that’s what’s so delicious about this game: you just never know what twist will come next. Continues on Friday with another murder.Hollie RichardsonTaskmaster9.05pm, Channel 4Richard Ayoade’s stagey (but convincing) disdain for the show he’s agreed to appear on reaches new heights as he threatens to destroy the whole set. Things aren’t much better for the other contenders, with Chloe Petts suffering a day of setbacks. No wonder Alex just wants to lie quietly in a box for a while.Phil HarrisonAll Creatures Great and Small9.05pm, Channel 5While a stray pekingese needs a new home and Siegfried (Samuel West) becomes indignant with a car mechanic, a trip out to help a stuck calf looks initially like standard hand-up-a-cow fare. But it’s a whopper! Is it time for the Dales’ inaugural bovine caesarean?Jack SealeNot Going Out9.30pm, BBC OneNigel Planer cameos in Lee Mack’s easy-going, long-running family sitcom this week. After seeing a play together, Lee (Mack) and Lucy (Sally Bretton) bump into Nigel in a fancy restaurant. Cue a night of awkward introductions, farcical mix-ups and a few laughs.HRBreak ClauseView image in fullscreenCheat detective … Lil (Lara Ricote, left) with Kira (Assa Kanoute) in Break Clause.Photograph: Vishal Sharma/Channel 410.05pm, Channel 4More from the housing crisis comedy, where a couple split up on their first night in London but are stuck in a six-month contract. After Lil’s (Lara Ricote) excruciating first rebound date, she and Ben (Samuel Bottomley) head back to Leeds for their mates’ baby’s christening – the perfect opportunity for Lil to find the woman with whom Ben cheated on her.HRThe Paper11pm, Sky OneThe Office spin-off prints out an efficient double bill to conclude season two. Editor Ned (Domhnall Gleeson) is still trying to land his haymaker investigative piece, but should he and reporter Mare (Chelsea Frei) prioritise love over journalism? The finale has a nice amount of weakness for open-hearted emotion.JSExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightRichard E GrantLee MackTaskmasterfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Book of Lives by Margaret Atwood audiobook review – a dryly funny memoir | Margaret Atwood | The Guardian
description: The Handmaid’s Tale author reflects on her loves, losses and literary achievements in a memoir that showcases her wisdom and wit
Author: Fiona Sturges
Headline: The Handmaid’s Tale author reflects on her loves, losses and literary achievements in a memoir that showcases her wisdom and wit
Content: Leisurely narrator … Margaret Atwood.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianView image in fullscreenLeisurely narrator … Margaret Atwood.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianAudiobook of the weekMargaret AtwoodReviewBook of Lives by Margaret Atwood audiobook review – a dryly funny memoirThe Handmaid’s Tale author reflects on her loves, losses and literary achievements in a memoir that showcases her wisdom and witFiona SturgesThu 8 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMargaret Atwood had to be persuaded to write a memoir. The thought of writing about herself initially seemed “dead boring. Who wants to read about someone sitting at a desk messing up blank sheets of paper?” Yet, she continues, time passed and the possibility of a memoir took on a “lurid phosphorescent glow. ‘Wasn’t there something appealing in the idea?’ my sinister alter ego whispered … I could thank my benefactors, reward my friends, trash my enemies and pay off scores long forgotten by everyone but me.”Subtitled “A Memoir of Sorts”, Book of Lives is the Canadian author’s account of her loves, losses and literary achievements (she has written just over 50 books, including novels, short stories and poetry collections), and a fine showcase for her wisdom and wit. What little score-settling she includes is purely for the punchline. When a poet told Atwood in the early 1970s that she wrote like a man – he intended it as a compliment – she told him he forgot the punctuation. “What you meant was, ‘She writes. Like a man’.”The book is read by the author, who is 86. Her narration is leisurely, gravelly, drily funny and unmistakeably Atwood. Though she admits she can’t recall much about her early books, she remembers enough about the important ones, most notably 1986’s The Handmaid’s Tale, her landmark novel set in a dystopian future. When she showed an early draft to the novelist Valerie Martin, Atwood said: “I think I’m gonna get into trouble.” Martin read it and told her: “I think you’re gonna make a lot of money.”Available via Vintage Digital, 25hr 36minFurther listeningThe PersianDavid McCloskey, Swift Press Audio, 13hr 23minThis tense spy thriller from the CIA analyst turned author and podcaster sees Kamran, a Jewish Iranian dentist living in Sweden after being driven out of Iran, returning to his home country as a Mossad agent. Fajer Al-Kaisi is the narrator.ElementalArthur Snell, Wildfire, 12hr 28minFormer diplomat Snell reads his compelling study of the huge geopolitical problems caused by the climate crisis – including mass migration, drought, rising sea levels and food and energy shortages – and how they can be addressed.Explore more on these topicsMargaret AtwoodAudiobook of the weekAutobiography and memoirreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Starving Bride by Catherine Chidgey review – a girl wastes away in a gothic near-future | Fiction | The Guardian
description: The New Zealand author’s ninth novel is gorgeously written, but feels tame and almost quaint against the real world of GLP-1 drugs and looksmaxxing
Author: Beejay Silcox
Headline: The New Zealand author’s ninth novel is gorgeously written, but feels tame and almost quaint against the real world of GLP-1 drugs and looksmaxxing
Content: ‘Hazel fasts and the crowds gather’ in Catherine Chidgey’s latest novel The Starving Bride.Composite: Ebony Lamb / Penguin Random HouseView image in fullscreen‘Hazel fasts and the crowds gather’ in Catherine Chidgey’s latest novel The Starving Bride.Composite: Ebony Lamb / Penguin Random HouseAustralian book reviewsFictionReviewThe Starving Bride by Catherine Chidgey review – a girl wastes away in a gothic near-futureThe New Zealand author’s ninth novel is gorgeously written, but feels tame and almost quaint against the real world of GLP-1 drugs and looksmaxxingSupported byAbout this contentBeejay SilcoxThu 8 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 19.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCatherine Chidgey’s new novel was inspired by a magnificent piece of archival flotsam: a 1930s newspaper report of a bizarre pay dispute. A young woman had “undertaken to fast for 40 days and 40 nights in a lion’s den” as an attraction in Blackpool – a prowling spectacle of hunger artistry – but abandoned the feat partway. Her employer claimed she had broken the contract; the woman claimed the lion was at fault – it had been set loose. It’s a little hard to skip dinner when you might become one. What writerly catnip: the lion, the kitsch and the wage-probe.The Starving Bride restages this big-cat sideshow act in a near-future where old-timey attractions are being revived in the hope of reviving something else: “A sense of nostalgia, that was the thing. A sense of innocence. Even if the stags and hens still vomited in the gutters.” It’s bread-and-circus misdirection: the sea is rising; the buildings are crumbling; the city is beset by poverty; and the bureaucrats are masters of denial and delay. But at night, on the boardwalk, the lights are shining and the past is alive again – England in its imagined prime (the tourist board hashtag: #Asimplertime).The Long Cloud by Hector MacKenzie review – there’s only so much depth to a himboRead moreVisitors can play a game of bingo, have a slice of tearoom cake, enjoy the minstrels and their blackface antics, and – if they’re feeling a little gothic – watch a pretty girl in a wedding dress waste away in a glass coffin, while a male lion waits, patient as death. The story the showmen tell punters is that the bride is saving for her dream wedding; starving for love. But the world Chidgey conjures offers darker possibilities. Choose your allegory: climate inaction, extractive economics, the beauty industrial complex, the baying hungers of Brexit, coercive control.Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best readsThe bride in the box is Hazel. She’s newly dumped and carrying a mortifying secret, a deep and corrosive shame. That’s the attraction of the Blackpool gig: a chance to emerge from the coffin as someone else. Shed the weight on her soul. The starvation is just for show; after hours, Hazel can do – and eat – whatever she likes, as long as she stays backstage to keep up the ruse. But there’s something intoxicating about making the fairytale true. Hazel fasts and the crowds gather: mostly mothers and daughters, come to worship at this silent altar of erasure (“They don’t want chit-chat from you,” Hazel is warned. “They want suffering”). The skinnier she gets, the sleeker and more restless the lion.Chidgey has created a gauzy version of the near future. A nebulous almost. But we live in a cruelly specific time for bodies: a world of GLP-1 drugs and looksmaxxing, where the stories we tell about flesh are being twisted into all kinds of grotesque new knots. The Starving Bride is set in the aftermath (or next incarnation) of these Insta-noxious years, but the world it conjures is almost quaint in its self-hatred (and certainly myopic when it comes to gender). The plot feels tethered to a version of life – particularly online life – that already belongs to the past.Best Australian books out in October: Magda Szubanski, delicious recipes and a picture book ‘masterpiece’Read moreAnd so we have a nostalgic novel about nostalgia; or perhaps just a naive novel about the present. The Starving Bride begs comparisons, as did Chidgey’s last novel,The Book of Guilt. By the end, I had a list of books I was itching to revisit: Margaret Atwood’s The Edible Woman (1969), Marian Engel’s Bear (1976), Patrick Süskind’s Perfume: The Story of a Murderer (1985), Angela Carter’s Wise Children (1991), Don DeLillo’s The Body Artist (2001). All of them decades old, and all of them far stranger than this one: more sensual, more feral, more meat on their bones.For all its leonine rumble, the great surprise of theNew Zealandauthor’s ninth novel is how tame it all feels, especially given her capacity for top-shelf weirdness (see The Axeman’s Carnival and Pet). This vaudeville gothic is gorgeously written, but it has arrived at a moment when literary hunger has been set loose. The last decade has seen a glut in greedy novels: tales of perimenopausal wolf-women (Nightbitch, Rachel Yoder); ravenous lovers (A Certain Hunger, Chelsea G Summers); marrow-sucking aliens (Earthlings, Sayaka Murata); new sources of meat (Tender is the Flesh, Agustina Bazterrica); culture-shaking refusals (The Vegetarian, Han Kang). Cannibal-lit has become its own sub-genre: all crunch and munch and gizzards and guzzle. Books in which our appetites are allowed to become truly monstrous, where bodies leak and rot.Against this feasting, festering backdrop, The Starving Bride is positively decorous. Chidgey’s epigraph reads: “For our younger selves, who were beautiful already.” The impulse is kind: a counter to all that wild and weighted shame. But it’s also possible to read the novel as a fable about conquering your unruly hungers – mastering your inner lion.The Starving Brideby Catherine Chidgey is out now in Australia (Penguin; $34.99) and will be published in the UK on 14 January 2027 (John Murray Press)Explore more on these topicsFictionAustralian book reviewsNew ZealandreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Agate Head / Stone Soup by Patricia Lockwood review – a gem of a collection | Poetry | The Guardian
description: Inspired by stones and metals, the memoirist and novelist’s first poetry collection for more than a decade is charming, whimsical and intimate
Author: Rishi Dastidar
Headline: Inspired by stones and metals, the memoirist and novelist’s first poetry collection for more than a decade is charming, whimsical and intimate
Content: From the holy to the hilarious … Patricia Lockwood.Photograph: Anna OttumView image in fullscreenFrom the holy to the hilarious … Patricia Lockwood.Photograph: Anna OttumBook of the dayPoetryReviewAgate Head / Stone Soup by Patricia Lockwood review – a gem of a collectionInspired by stones and metals, the memoirist and novelist’s first poetry collection for more than a decade is charming, whimsical and intimateRishi DastidarThu 8 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 03.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the introduction to her first book of poetry in 12 years,Patricia Lockwoodstates that, “For almost a decade … I had not been able to hear it. The poems that I wrote would not end … too much was happening, there was a different kind of attention being paid.” It wasn’t that she didn’t want them to arrive. From Cave Painting: “And does she still write poems?/ Not a whole one since I had been ill. / Five years. I kept saying I was / Doing it privately. So private even / I didn’t know about it.”In that intervening period, Lockwood’s status has jumped from interesting US poet famous for the viral sensationRape Joketo literary superstar: an acclaimed memoirist and novelist whose freewheeling, antic style is for many the internet’s maelstrom lassoed and put back on to the page. Who else can claim to have turned an audience with the pope into a biting comic essay?So her return to poetry is a genuine event, and across Agate Head / Stone Soup there are countless moments that remind you that her poetic voice is unique: charming, whimsical, intimate; able to deliver images of great beauty, piercing philosophical insights and glimpses into a creative life behind the public persona. Readers of her memoirPriestdaddywill be pleased to see her father reappear in a few poems. “That my father has been drinking … / Always something new with him, / But I must say I didn’t see / 5-600 dollars’ worth of fine olive oil coming.”Agate Head / Stone Soup is presented tête-bêche – head-to-tail in French, the volumes upside down and back-to-back. And while this might appear to be a frippery, the two collections have enough differences in texture to warrant it. Agate Head feels the more public-facing, while Stone Soup wrestles with more existential concerns, as beautifully rendered in Babies Born Remembering: “Screaming in the airport. / What do they remember – / Night flights, riding birds, / Being a set of wings / Themselves, a soul, an updraft.”double quotation markIt’s impossible to escape autobiography: some poems are a form of higher gossip, our noses against the glass of fameBoth collections are inspired by stones, gems and metals of all shapes and sorts. Lockwood has been collecting fossils and minerals from an early age, and she and her husband have spent time learning metalsmithing, too. This gives her rich territories to explore. In Margaret De Patta, “Quartz wants / To be a window, wants a woman to appear. / We have properties, we are non-precious, / Wood horn bone and hair.” In An Agate a Day, we get to see her and her husband cutting agates, a hard stone with bands of different colours: “The trick is to hold the miracle steady. / We are the first to be seeing this. Ever. / Together. What happened to you? / We croon, after each cut.” It is notable that agates are associated with a sense of grounding and balance; an attempt to counteract all that other “attention”.There is a detectable technical shift in Lockwood’s poems also. Many of the poems in 2014’s Motherland Fatherland Homelandsexuals featured long lines, allowed to run on and gather momentum to their epiphanies or punchlines. Here her lines are more staccato in feeling, jumpier in syntax, as in Not Seeing Glass Flowers: “To grow. Was it that / They looked real? I asked everyone. / Or was it something more? Max Beckmann’s painting is still a horror.”It means a spikier initial impression for many of the poems. This ultimately works in their favour, as the thoughts accrete, moving in unlikely directions, before resolving into a revelation of some force. “Artists, no one really / Knows where they come from, / They fall a long way from the sky / And land zigzag” as Forged in Fire has it.Neither collection is flawless. At one level, it is impossible to get away from the autobiographical detail, and so some of the poems become a form of higher gossip, our noses pressed up against the glass of fame. Sedarising, for example, comes across as smug rather than amusing.And there are occasions when an object under discussion cannot bear the metaphorical weight being placed upon it. Polish Flint is an offender here: “The perfect ring I had married myself with / (Of Polish flint) was pried apart as I fell. / In slow motion, it seemed, surrounded / By tourists, with enough time to think / Of everything.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut these are small bumps when time and again Lockwood leaves you with the distinct impression that she can magically make the profane into the profound, the holy into the hilarious, as she does to most brilliant effect in Monastery Icons: Windows into Heaven: “It’s sounding a little bit / Like you can order a whole husband / From this catalog, as long as his name is The Lord / And you are a PRAYING VIRGIN NIGHTLIGHT: /Just what we need in these challenging times.”Agate Head / Stone Soup by Patricia Lockwood is published by Bloomsbury, (£18.99). To support the Guardian buy a copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsPoetryBook of the dayPatricia LockwoodreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Animals review – Ben Affleck’s dull Netflix thriller is lacking in bark and bite | Ben Affleck | The Guardian
description: Actor-director’s listless LA-set crime thriller makes for a surprisingly anonymous effort and one that feels very similar to many other, better films
Author: Jesse Hassenger
Headline: Actor-director’s listless LA-set crime thriller makes for a surprisingly anonymous effort and one that feels very similar to many other, better films
Content: Kerry Washington and Ben Affleck in Animals.Photograph: Warrick Page/NetflixView image in fullscreenKerry Washington and Ben Affleck in Animals.Photograph: Warrick Page/NetflixBen AffleckReviewAnimals review – Ben Affleck’s dull Netflix thriller is lacking in bark and biteActor-director’s listless LA-set crime thriller makes for a surprisingly anonymous effort and one that feels very similar to many other, better filmsJesse HassengerThu 8 Oct 2026 19.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 19.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBen Affleck has pushed through multiple Hollywood comebacks, at least one predicated on his facility behind the camera, directing Boston-based thrillers both artistically ambitious (Gone Baby Gone) and juicily crowd-pleasing (The Town). So now that his acting career seems particularly stable, as he works steadily and produces movies via the company he founded with longtime friend and collaborator Matt Damon, why does his directing career remain in what seems like post-Oscar doldrums? (Though he has never been nominated for a best director Oscar, his film Argo won best picture in 2013.) His new movie Animals appears perfectly situated within his wheelhouse: it’s a Los Angeles-based crime-and-politics thriller to match his earlier east coast work. The real surprise, however, is just how listless it can get.The Social Reckoning review – Aaron Sorkin’s jittery sequel with all-new evil puppet ZuckerbergRead moreAffleck himself plays Mark Kimball, a Angeleno running for mayor of his home town. His status as an independent non-party-affiliated candidate (and one who scarcely exhibits a trace of a platform in what little we see of his stump speeches and interviews) is only one element of his unlikely backstory, which also includes history as a teacher, a lawyer and a veteran of the first Gulf war. (Not sure the math on all that checks out, but let’s allow it as evidence of a fusion between Mark’s dedication to service and a rapacious ambition.) He’s leveraged his family’s wealth to take him through the home stretch of a close campaign, and tensions are medium-high with his wife, Abby, (Kerry Washington), who’s hiding some problems of her own. Things get considerably worse when, on Halloween, he receives a phone call: Kidnappers have taken his preteen son Denny (Christopher Woodley). They’re demanding $7m that Mark doesn’t have to get him back safely.Mark and Abby both panic, but still find time to disagree about how, precisely, to handle this nightmare scenario. They’re especially divided on whether or not to heed the advice of Mark’s right-hand man Sam (Steven Yeun), who advocates employing a mysterious unnamed fixer (Gillian Anderson) – which itself will also cost the Kimballs plenty of money they will not get back unless Mark wins the election (which in turn involves him attending a crucial campaign event inconveniently scheduled on Halloween night). All the ingredients – starry cast; ticking clock; complicated dilemmas centered on money, power, and ambition – are in place for a high-toned thriller, even if it is on Netflix with a few stray theatrical engagements.And then, once Affleck gets his ducks in a row … very little. For a movie that attempts to position Mark as both a product and a potential savior of Los Angeles, shockingly much of Animals takes place on Mark and Abby’s property, in a series of dull rich-folks rooms. It’s the kind of environment usually fit for a stage production, and the actors certainly play to the cheap seats – especially Washington, who can overact a whisper if called upon to do so. But the screenplay by Affleck, Billy Ray, and Connor O McIntyre doesn’t lend much substance to any of the arguments. Some secrets are revealed, then turn out not to matter. Mark, Abby and Sam talk in irritated circles. The kidnapper keeps calling, using voice modulation that makes him sound like Jigsaw. Only Anderson, resplendent in an all-white suit, has settled on whether this thriller is serious business or pulpy fun. (She chooses the latter, probably wisely though not particularly in sync with anyone else on screen.)One particular mid-movie plot turn so closely aligns Animals with another recent kidnapping thriller, Spike Lee’s Kurosawa remake Highest 2 Lowest, that those who have seen Lee’s movie may drop their jaws in disbelief. Of course, this movie was likely written and maybe even shot before Affleck would have seen that film, but someone involved in this production must have seen Kurosawa’s original High and Low, nicking just enough for the story to count as homage rather than an outright redo. There’s nothing wrong with that on its face, but Animals has shockingly few ideas about how to transpose the material into a different city, time period or milieu. It may not be an entirely fair comparison, but it’s hard to think of Lee’s bravura ransom-drop sequence set on a long subway ride traversing Manhattan without suppressing laughter at the obligatory Los Angeles river-basin standoff that serves as the newer film’s all-wet climax. If Affleck has any greater insight into Los Angeles politics than the most basic and bludgeoning messaging of the film’s final moments, he’s kept it to himself, or cut it out of a movie that runs about 100 minutes without credits.Affleck the actor is still fun to watch, especially playing a politician visibly straining to not look like one – a charismatic guy nonetheless laboring to resemble a narrative version who may be a little nicer and more down-to-earth than he really is. But despite employing ace cinematographer Robert Elswit, who shot Affleck’s The Town as well as There Will Be Blood, among many others, the look of Animals is pretty Netflix-y – slick, lacking in texture and ultimately a bit dull. In other words, Affleck has – presumably by accident – imitated his character. This is a movie that just wants to get the job done with frictionless likability, with seemingly no one inquiring about why.Animals is out on Netflix on 9 OctoberExplore more on these topicsBen AffleckKerry WashingtonGillian AndersonNetflixreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Good night, and good lick: what can we expect from George Clooney’s restaurant? | Movies | The Guardian
description: The newly-official French citizen is planning to open an Italian restaurant in Provence. Will it float like his tequila brand or sink as swiftly as the Steven Spielberg submarine eatery that made one reviewer ‘embarrassed to be human’?
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: The newly-official French citizen is planning to open an Italian restaurant in Provence. Will it float like his tequila brand or sink as swiftly as the Steven Spielberg submarine eatery that made one reviewer ‘embarrassed to be human’?
Content: Ham … George Clooney in Jay Kelly.Photograph: Peter Mountain/NetflixView image in fullscreenHam … George Clooney in Jay Kelly.Photograph: Peter Mountain/NetflixMoviesGood night, and good lick: what can we expect from George Clooney’s restaurant?The newly-official French citizen is planning to open an Italian restaurant in Provence. Will it float like his tequila brand or sink as swiftly as the Steven Spielberg submarine eatery that made one reviewer ‘embarrassed to be human’?Stuart HeritageThu 8 Oct 2026 07.25 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 07.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Provençal village of Cotignac is not wanting for places to eat. Within a short drive of its pale stone houses, you can find a wealth of high-end dining options. La Table de Mentone, set within the beautiful Château Mentone wine estate, is famed for the produce it grows on site. The Michelin-starred Restaurant Bruno offers dazzling variations of truffle dishes. More locally, Picotte Provence offers the sort of charming village dining that showcases the best of what the region has to offer.However, despite all these wonderful options, there is one thing that Cotignac does not yet boast, and that’s a celebrity vanity project. But that is all about to change, thanks to the news thatGeorge Clooneyis planning to open a restaurant there.According to reports, Clooney, who lives locally, is keen to open a restaurant in partnership with the Canadian owner of a nearby hotel, with an elegant dining room and an outdoor terrace. No formal application has been submitted, but it is thought that the restaurant will open next year.Some aspects of this make more sense than others. After all, Clooney and his family have beenFrench citizens since December, so it would make perfect sense for him to want to lay deeper roots within the community. In fact Clooney is so French that he turns up for the only memorable scene in the recent Call My Agent! movie.View image in fullscreenClooney and his wife, Amal, have been French citizens since December.Photograph: Earl Gibson III/Deadline/Getty ImagesHowever, it has also been reported that Clooney’s proposed restaurant would be Italian, which seems a little odd given that Provence is one of the major food capitals of the world. Becoming a citizen of one country and then immediately building a temple to the food of the last place you lived in could be seen as a little vulgar.‘Suspension of entry into the US’, paparazzi – and wine: three other reasons George Clooney moved to FranceRead moreBut only a fool would rule Clooney out here. This is a man with a habit of making a success of himself whenever he turns his hand to something new. His tequila company was so successful that not only didhe sell it for $1bnbut now you can’t walk into a supermarket without tripping over a dozen alcoholic drink brands created by performers desperately hoping that it will make them enough money to stop acting.In fact, Clooney’s tequila money is probably his saving grace here. He could sink hundreds of millions of euros into this new restaurant and, even if it ended up being a disaster, he would still be abnormally well insulated for the rest of his life. And that is probably a good thing because, when it comes to restaurants, Hollywood figures don’t tend to have the best reputation.The true successes, such asRobert De Niro’s Nobu, are few and far between. More often than not, these things tend to end in disaster. For instance, when Hulk Hogan decided to dip his toe into hospitality in the mid-1990s, the venture lasted less than a year. Admittedly this is because it was a pasta restaurant inside a shopping mall, and all the pasta was shaped like Hulk Hogan, and the place was called Pastamania, and it had an exclamation mark on the end, which meant you couldn’t say it aloud without sounding either angry or scared, but the point still stands.View image in fullscreenNot wanting for places to eat … the Provençal village of Cotignac.Photograph: David Gabis/AlamyThere are so many others. In 2002 Jennifer Lopez opened a restaurant in Pasadena inspired by her mother’s cooking, but it never quite recovered from the moment when she hired her ex-husband as manager, then fired him after six months, then got sued by him in a case so messy that he later ended up threatening to leak their honeymoon footage. And in 2012 Eva Longoria opened a restaurant called SHe, which was a steakhouse for women complete with smaller portions, a catwalk and dessert menus with mirrors on the back so diners could retouch their makeup. It closed in 2014.Then there is the daddy of them all, a calamity of such legendary proportions that you have to assume Clooney has paid attention. I am of course referring to Steven Spielberg’s Dive! restaurant that was open for a few years in the 1990s.It is genuinely hard to know where to start here. Dive! (enough with the overexuberant punctuation already, 90s celebrities) was based on Spielberg’s obsession with submarines, to the extent that it was literally shaped like a submarine – complete with working periscope – and primarily sold submarine sandwiches. Also, at 45-minute intervals, an announcement would interrupt the meal, instructing diners to prepare for submersion. At this point red warning lights would flash and a siren would sound, and it would remain this way until the restaurant had theoretically descended into the ocean. When it opened, the LA Times review stated that: “This restaurant makes me embarrassed to be a human in the 90s.”Which isn’t to say that Clooney will fall into the same trap as these failed ventures. He is a man of style and good taste, and surely knows that the quickest way to kill a restaurant is to turn it into a museum of his career. A nice, well-run restaurant that can be enjoyed without knowing the work of its primary investor is far more likely to succeed. That said, if there isn’t a Nespresso on every table, someone should kick the windows in.Explore more on these topicsFilmGeorge ClooneyFranceRestaurantsEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Big Girls Don’t Cry review – a New Zealand teenager finds herself in tender coming-of-age tale | Movies | The Guardian
description: Writer-director Paloma Schneideman’s wonderful film follows a 14-year-old in 2006 who pretends to be someone else in a chat room, with real-world consequences
Author: Luke Buckmaster
Headline: Writer-director Paloma Schneideman’s wonderful film follows a 14-year-old in 2006 who pretends to be someone else in a chat room, with real-world consequences
Content: Ani Palmer (left) as Sid in Big Girls Don’t Cry.Photograph: Jen RaoultView image in fullscreenAni Palmer (left) as Sid in Big Girls Don’t Cry.Photograph: Jen RaoultMoviesReviewBig Girls Don’t Cry review – a New Zealand teenager finds herself in tender coming-of-age taleWriter-director Paloma Schneideman’s wonderful film follows a 14-year-old in 2006 who pretends to be someone else in a chat room, with real-world consequencesGet our weekend culture and lifestyle emailLuke BuckmasterWed 7 Oct 2026 22.23 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 18.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAll coming-of-age films face the challenge of how to convey that intermediary period between childhood and adulthood, with all the confusion, awkwardness and self-searching that entails. Writer-director Paloma Schneideman’s drama Big Girls Don’t Cry meets that challenge, resulting in a tenderly drawn story about the slow process of a 14-year-old in ruralNew Zealandfinding herself.Schneideman’s film has a wonderfully unforced quality, unfolding in a deeply satisfying yet seemingly effortless way. It’s as if the cameras are simply recording events organically unfolding in front of them, which of course isn’t the case at all: a drama like this requires immense thought and preparation. (The film is the first to be produced under the auspices of the Jane Campion-led film-making courseA Wave in the Ocean.)The best coming-of-age stories tend to follow rebellious characters (like Antoine Doinel inThe 400 Blowsand Jim Stark inRebel Without a Cause), outsiders (like Mia Williams inFish Tankand Sybylla Melvyn inMy Brilliant Career), or the more experimental and vulnerable kind (like Heidi inSomersaultand Lidia in Kristen Stewart’s magnificent directorial debutThe Chronology of Water).Now there’s Sid (Ani Palmer), who is a difficult person to categorise. She’s a bit of an introvert, a bit of a tough nut to crack: rarely outwardly friendly, but not exactly standoffish either.It’s 2006, pre-smartphones and more or less pre-social media. During a six-week summer break, Sid starts hanging out with other teenagers – including Lana (Beatrix Rain Wolfe) and Stevie (Sophia Kirkwood Smith) – and doing very teenager-type stuff: attending house parties, drinking booze on the sly, and awkwardly interacting with the opposite sex. Sid’s father, Leo (Noah Taylor, so good recently inThou Shalt Not Steal), is a straight-talking layabout and her best friend is Tia (Ngātaitangirua Hita), whom she doesn’t treat very well.View image in fullscreen‘The film captures Sid coming to terms with her queerness, though that too is handled quite subtly.’Photograph: Jen RaoultSchneideman gets the small moments just right. When Sid shotguns a beer, then deals with sleazy teenage boys; when she smokes weed for the first time; when she simply lounges about with friends or looks at herself in the mirror. At times she goes online, visiting seedy chatrooms and pretending to be other people for shits and giggles – an act that has real-world consequences, reflecting the new dangers and challenges presented by the internet in the 21st century. The film captures Sid coming to terms with her queerness, though that too is handled quite subtly.None of the above scenarios are revelatory from a narrative perspective, and perhaps they seem insignificant when reduced to words. But theyareevergreen – the kinds of moments and scenes that remain eternally relevant to the human experience, particularly the experience of being young.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSaved for SundayEase your Sunday scaries with the best of Guardian Australia’s culture and lifestyle journalism.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘Rip it open’: Big Girls Don’t Cry director explores wounds of early love in film festival hitRead moreBig Girls Don’t Cry is a class act aesthetically, with an autumnal colour scheme and intuitive-feeling editing. Cinematographer María Inés Manchego has a good eye for interesting depictions of everyday objects and occurrences, making domestic scenes look polished, though never in an overtly showy way.The drama is boosted by highly captivating and layered performances, especially from Palmer as Sid. She’s restrained and yet so emotive, powerfully conveying a person going through profound growth and change. It’s unclear what aspects of her personality will fade away or remain across the course of her life.Like the film itself, Palmer’s performance is not remotely didactic: we’re not told what to think or how to respond, particularly when it comes to moral perspectives. And again, like many excellent coming-of-age films, there’s a curious sense of open-endedness: a feeling that this story just keeps going, well beyond the final frame.Big Girls Don’t Cry is out in New Zealand and select US cinemas now, on 27 November in the UK and on 10 December in AustraliaExplore more on these topicsFilmNew ZealandDrama filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘He punched a polar bear on the nose!’ Ninety glorious years of Brian Blessed – by Emma Thompson, Adrian Lester and more | Brian Blessed | The Guardian
description: Peeing in the sink he shared with Derek Jacobi, making a badger video with Brian May, climbing Everest with Alan Hinkes … as the great actor blasts into his 90s, stars celebrate his ‘loudness and madness’
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Peeing in the sink he shared with Derek Jacobi, making a badger video with Brian May, climbing Everest with Alan Hinkes … as the great actor blasts into his 90s, stars celebrate his ‘loudness and madness’
Content: ‘Delightfully terrifying’ … as Sir Tunbelly Clumsey in The Relapse at the National Theatre in 2001.Photograph: Donald Cooper/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Delightfully terrifying’ … as Sir Tunbelly Clumsey in The Relapse at the National Theatre in 2001.Photograph: Donald Cooper/AlamyBrian Blessed‘He punched a polar bear on the nose!’ Ninety glorious years of Brian Blessed – by Emma Thompson, Adrian Lester and morePeeing in the sink he shared with Derek Jacobi, making a badger video with Brian May, climbing Everest with Alan Hinkes  … as the great actor blasts into his 90s, stars celebrate his ‘loudness and madness’Interviews byMark FisherThu 8 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 13.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘A mighty wind, a tree of life’Emma ThompsonI know why Brian has lasted this long in spite of falling out of helicopters and off mountains and into lakes all his life: he started the whole being-cold-keeps-you-healthy thing years before Wim Hof was doing his motivational speaking.Once, when we were shooting Ken Branagh’s Henry V at Shepperton, it was very cold out. I went to visit Brian in his dressing room. I was in my costume for the Princess of France, a lovely off-the-shoulder number. All the windows were open. It was bloody freezing. Brian started to tell me a story about Everest. I sat there, fascinated, getting colder and colder. He noticed – after some time – and said: “Thompson, why are you wearing blue lipstick?”I tried to speak but my jaw had frozen in its sockets. He bundled me out into the heated corridors where I spent a good hour getting my body up to a functioning temperature. “The cold is good for you!” he thundered. And by God he was right. I took a cold shower every day after that.View image in fullscreen‘The cold is good for you!’ … with Kenneth Branagh in Henry V.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyThe man is a legend: a force, a mighty wind and a great tree of life. He has the soul of a mountain-top. I will always love him deeply and appreciate his kindness to a young actress, his wit and fun and energy and gaiety, his loudness and his madness.‘Now get to 100!’Derek JacobiWe first worked together at Birmingham Rep in 1960 when we would do a different play every month. It was my first job and he was the star of the show. I was in awe of him. He was still in his 20s but had a huge personality even then. I ended up sharing a dressing room with him, which was an education in itself. He was not particularly restrained – not when it came to pissing in the sink!View image in fullscreen‘He was not particularly restrained’ … with Derek Jacobi in I, Claudius.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyBrian is full of bluster and bigness, but underneath it all, he is as sensitive as the rest of us. He is a true man of the theatre and it was wonderful to learn from him. The next thing we did together was I, Claudius, in which he was marvellous as Augustus. Off-stage, he’s full of bonhomie, a great companion. Everything about him is big: his laughter, everything. But he’s not ego-driven: he’s just great company. My message to him is get to 100 and we’ll all be there applauding! We’re all applauding at 90 too!‘Wow, he just says anything!’Dexter FletcherView image in fullscreen‘He had a healthy belief in being who you are’ … Blessed as Claudius and Dexter Fletcher  as the Player Queen in Hamlet in 1984.Photograph: Donald Cooper/ShutterstockI worked with Brian in the 1984 season at the Royal Shakespeare Company at Stratford-upon-Avon. I was in a couple of productions that he was in: Henry V, with Kenneth Branagh playing Young Hal and Brian playing the Duke of Exeter; and Hamlet, when Brian played Claudius and Virginia McKenna was Gertrude.He came with this energy, exuberance and lust for life. I’d never seen anybody like him. He had a healthy belief in being who you are. He would talk about his cock quite openly: “That big blue vein on the side of your dick.” Branagh would be laughing, a lot of people would be shocked and Virginia McKenna didn’t seem fazed by it at all. I was 18 thinking: “Wow, he just says anything!”Towards the end of the season, I got an offer of an acting role in a film called Revolution with Al Pacino. It was a big movie and I was only 18. Hamlet was going into the Barbican in London. I didn’t know what decision to make. It was Brian who took me aside at a rehearsal space at the back of the theatre and said: “Listen, Dexter, go and do the movie because the movie world is small and when you get into it, if you make a success of it, you’re in and it’s a great living.”It led to a lot of movies – so I have a great love and affection for him because he did me a huge favour by shoving me in that direction.‘He pinched my bottom. It was perfect for the scene’Melody AndersonI remember watching I, Claudius as I grew up and thinking Brian Blessed was an incredible actor. I was 23 and it was so exciting to meet him on the set ofFlash Gordonand hear his Shakespearean voice bellow throughout the stages.It was a tough shoot, six days a week, 12 hours a day, and to have his lightness and sense of humour to alleviate the stress of the job was a gift. He was as indefatigable off screen as he was as Prince Vultan of the Hawkmen. Brian did not have to stretch to create a character because that’s him. He is a Hawkman! He takes the space, the voice is always bellowing and there is that sly smile and twinkle in his eyes – which he still has at 90.There is nothing more exciting than to work with an actor who is so inventive. Playing Dale Arden, I was on this table when we land on his planet and he was spinning me around and he just gave me a little bottom pinch. As an actor, I loved it because it solicited such an honest response. He gave me a whole other level of energy. It was exactly right for the character because it let me act like this haughty, temper-driven girl who beats up the guards at the king’s palace. It worked perfectly for the scene. Mike Hodges, the director, was thrilled.View image in fullscreen‘It’s not his ego – it’s a life force’ … with Melody Anderson and Sam J Jones in Flash Gordon.Photograph: THA/ShutterstockWhen I was at conventions with Sam J Jones, who played Flash, we would sit back and be quiet and Brian would be off, pacing back and forth across the stage and taking over. We would smile and let it be the Brian show. He takes over any place he’s in. It’s not an ego thing: it’s a life force. I don’t think I’ve ever met anyone who has such energy and self-confidence.He also has an enormous capacity to be sensitive. It’s a form of empathy to be able to pick up on the energies of the people around him and try to uplift their state if they were a little bit down.Blessings to Brian Blessed! He is a gift in my life and I’m better for knowing him.‘He appeared in our badger crusade video’Brian MayI’m old enough to remember Brian’s first appearance on TV. He was in Z-Cars and even then he was an impressive character. Getting to work with him on theFlash Gordonfilm was the most amazing thing. I didn’t see him on set, I just saw him on footage that had been shot as the days went by. We were in the studio, playing along to it all, so I felt I knew him better than I actually did.While everyone went back to finish the album Queen was making at the time, I made the soundtrack album for Flash Gordon. I pieced together lots of dialogue, sound effects and music – and you can hear Brian loud and clear. He’s a musical part of what we achieved, like an extra member of Queen.View image in fullscreen‘He cares deeply and passionately about animals’ … Brian May at a Stop the Cull protest in 2013.Photograph: REX/Julian MakeyFor years, I used to see him around Windlesham in Surrey where my studio is. He often popped in to help us with our badger crusades. He did a great appearance in ourBadger Badger Badgervideo, doing the Brian Blessed everybody wants, very loud and distinctive, shouting: “Keep the badgers alive!”He’s blustery and apparently super-confident, but we saw a side of him that cares deeply and passionately about animals. Whenever we’ve asked him for help, he has always come straight away. I’ve seen him sit and talk movingly about the way we don’t accommodate wild animals in the world we’ve built. I see him as a very deep human being.A very happy 90th to you, Brian. What an important piece you have been in the jigsaw of my life. I’ll forever be grateful to you and will forever enjoy the humanity and individuality you bring to all your work.‘He never seems to conk out’Alan HinkesView image in fullscreenBlessed at Everest base camp.Photograph: Steve Back/ANL/REX/ShutterstockIt’s 30 years since we were on Everest – and Brian got to 7,700m before turning back. We’ve both beenYorkshireman of the Yearand have the same wicked sense of humour. He can be over the top but he doesn’t offend me, although some of the anecdotes I daren’t tell you! Brian is a caricature of himself and I mean that in a good way: he is everything you expect him to be. I can’t help but laugh when I’m with him. On Everest, at base camp, he would regale us with tales in the mess tent and I would be rolling off my stool on to the floor which was probably -15C.He wouldn’t be as ebullient as that when we were up on the mountain, because you’re gasping for oxygen in the rarefied air and suffering from acute mountain sickness, which you can die from. You wouldn’t expect anyone to be entertaining when you’re that high. But you think, “How does he keep going? Does he conk out in private?” Well, I’ve seen him in private – I spent two-and-a-half months with him and he didn’t seem to conk out.At charity events, he’ll be humble and sing my praises. He’ll say: “Alan’s saved my life and he’s carried me down on his back when I was knackered.” That’s very flattering to me. I couldn’t really carry him down on my back, but it’s a good story. He’s a great raconteur.‘His booming voice creates its own weather system’Imogen StubbsI loved Brian when I worked with him inThe Relapseat the National Theatre in 2001 – he was a delightfully terrifying figure running around on stage with a blunderbuss and his signature booming voice that creates its own weather system. But also with the sweetest, kindest personality backstage that was disarmingly quiet and contemplative at times. The perfect company member. Wonderfully playful. Taking acting seriously but not too seriously.‘A rare, brilliant, kind-hearted giant’Adrian LesterBrian is often described as having a bombastic voice and a larger-than-life presence that makes us think of his performances as being, well, just performances. But don’t let that fool you. Brian brings to his characters a charisma and charm that isn’t larger than life. It is large and full to the brim with life. Honest, powerful life in all its shades. People still quote his intonation and volume when his character in Flash Gordon realises that “Gordon’s alive?!” He can tell you a story about a trip to the Arctic where he punched a polar bear on the nose and somehow you know it’s true.Brian can be quiet, subtle and piercing. Then in the same breath he can open his mouth and shake the ground you stand on. I have had the privilege of standing opposite him in a scene and been subject to a delicate subtlety in character that many would not associate with him. A rare, brilliant, kind-hearted giant of a man. I wish there were more like him.Explore more on these topicsBrian BlessedTheatreTelevisionDerek JacobiEmma ThompsonAdrian LesterFlash GordonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Lourdes gets a Vegas glow-up at Dublin theatre festival, where canvases are slashed | Theatre | The Guardian
description: A musical about a drama group’s pilgrimage and reflections on activist art join an intriguing show about lost languages
Author: Helen Meany
Headline: A musical about a drama group’s pilgrimage and reflections on activist art join an intriguing show about lost languages
Content: Effervescent … Danielle James, Iestyn Arwel, Molly Lynch, Nichola MacEvilly and Riain Cash in Lourdes! The Musical.Photograph: Patricio CassinoniView image in fullscreenEffervescent … Danielle James, Iestyn Arwel, Molly Lynch, Nichola MacEvilly and Riain Cash in Lourdes! The Musical.Photograph: Patricio CassinoniTheatreLourdes gets a Vegas glow-up at Dublin theatre festival, where canvases are slashedA musical about a drama group’s pilgrimage and reflections on activist art join an intriguing show about lost languagesHelen MeanyThu 8 Oct 2026 07.23 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 07.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a Dublin theatre festival programme tackling heavy themes of racism, conflict and prejudice,Lourdes! The Musical(★★★★☆) promises something effervescent.Xnthony Ltd, the creators ofOliver Cromwell Is Really Very Sorry, have turned their lightly quizzical gaze to the French pilgrimage town – “a holy Blackpool, a divine Las Vegas” and a site of hope or desperation for five unlikely travelling companions.Back in his home village in “Countryland”, in 2008, following a diagnosis of HIV that punctures his dreams of Los Angeles, singer-songwriter Matthew (Riain Cash) lends his star power to a parish drama group taking a musical about Saint Bernadette to Lourdes. Interweaving this show-within-a-show and the pilgrimage strands, Xnthony’s lyrics and Matthew Floyd Jones’s score blend pop, club beats and soulful ballads. Directed by Sarah Meadows, the supercharged ensemble joining Cash as, variously, a droll priest (Iestyn Arwel), a terminally ill mother and her transgender daughter (Nichola MacEvilly and Danielle James) and an eager tour manager (Molly Lynch) carry the music’s tonal shifts effortlessly.Instructed by neon signs to “please wait for a miracle”, characters reveal what brings them to this Marian shrine with its bizarre mix of tackiness and piety. Each has a Catholic faith of sorts – something that might have been more complicated to portray if set in the present day. Rather than settling on an archly ironic approach, Xnthony’s sensitive, often lyrical writing allows fear of death, regret and above all, grief, to seep through.View image in fullscreenClever and knowing … Alice Roots in Heroes of Tomorrow.Photograph: Ste MurrayAn aura of reverence pervades the white cube gallery setting ofHeroes of Tomorrow(★★★☆☆), the latest production from the restlessly inventiveBrokentalkers. Co-directors Feidlim Cannon and Gary Keegan are joined here by British theatre artist Andy Smith to burrow into the relationship between art and activism. Pinging through centuries and continents, they make connections between historical instances of human invention and resultant exploitation, technological breakthroughs and protest, underlining the point that progress is not linear.If this sounds abstract, it is; much of it is delivered in carefully flat, affectless narration by Alice Roots, Michael Tient and Malua Ní Chléirigh, as if making a presentation in the gallery, taking turns to outline the biography of a (fictional) Norwegian conceptual artist called Jan Hansen. His latest work, The End of It All, has been commissioned by three global tech companies, a testing moment of groupthink for an artist who has acquired cachet for financially supporting climate activists who fling paint over old masters in museums.Amid questions about whether it is possible for art to remain pure, uncompromised by its corporate sources of funding, the audience is teased into imagining what Hansen’s new artwork will be. As the performers playfully poke their heads through slashed canvases and make black imprints of their hands on the pristine gallery wall, this performance is itself a form of conceptual art, played out in a highly coded space. The result is clever and knowing but, for Brokentalkers, surprisingly tentative.Zinc(★★★★☆) fromDead Centrefocuses on a forgotten mini-state, Neutral Moresnet, on the border of Germany, Belgium and the Netherlands. A political anomaly, designated a neutral zone to protect its prized zinc mines, it was passed between European powers, its inhabitants’ nationality changing as borders shifted. Adapted froma book by Belgian political philosopher David Van Reybrouck, the production brings multiple perspectives to bear on the experience of one man, Joseph Rixen, born in Neutral Moresnet in 1903.View image in fullscreenOne of their most ambitious works to date … Timmy Creed, Fabio Godinho, Cathy Min Jung, Mila Moinzadeh and Julie Mughunda in Zinc.Photograph: Alexandre FytrakisPlaying with the idea of neutrality, co-directors Ben Kidd and Bush Moukarzel and the superb international ensemble – Julie Mughunda, Timmy Creed, Fabio Godinho, Cathy Min Jung and Mila Moinzadeh – rewind, wittily, to the 1815 Congress of Vienna. Reflecting on colonisation, annexation and the accidents of history, each actor explores their personal experience of exile, displacement and lost native languages.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA co-production withThéâtre de Liège, this is one of Dead Centre’s most ambitious works to date: multilingual, integrating video mapping, projection, layered music and sound design, and, as always with their work, commenting on the art of theatre itself. Richly allusive, it connects a performer on an empty stage, before the act of imagination begins, to the perceived neutrality of a geographical place – until it can be exploited, no longer a country but “a business”.Moving away from the cartography of loss, the performance seizes on the lost political project of Esperanto as a possible neutral language of hope – literally utopian, with its root meaning of “nowhere”.Lourdes! The Musical is atCivic theatre, Dublin, until 10 October.Dublin theatre festivalruns until 11 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreIrelandEuropeMusicalsPaintingFestivalsReligionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Spend time going down rabbit holes’: how the Avalanches created their wildest album yet | The Avalanches | The Guardian
description: The Aussie trio explain creating their new record sampling kids’ science shows and Tunisian music – and their surreal film with Haley Joel Osment
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Aussie trio explain creating their new record sampling kids’ science shows and Tunisian music – and their surreal film with Haley Joel Osment
Content: ‘What’s beautiful about what we do is the memories and the humanness in the sounds that we sample,’ the Avalanches’ Robbie Chater says.Photograph: Dean PodmoreView image in fullscreen‘What’s beautiful about what we do is the memories and the humanness in the sounds that we sample,’ the Avalanches’ Robbie Chater says.Photograph: Dean PodmoreThe AvalanchesInterview‘Spend time going down rabbit holes’: how the Avalanches created their wildest album yetJason LamphierThe Aussie trio explain creating their new record sampling kids’ science shows and Tunisian music – and their surreal film with Haley Joel OsmentThu 8 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 13.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLast December, Robbie Chater and Tony Di Blasi, the core members of the Aussie disco-pop collagiststhe Avalanches, found themselves winding through the frosty, mountainous region of Minakami, Japan, withHaley Joel Osment. The pair’s lauded debut album, 2000’sSince I Left You, has become a touchstone inplunderphonics– a genre known for its innovative use of samples – and in the years since its release, the group have amassed an ardent cult following. Osment, the former child star ofThe Sixth SenseandForrest Gump, seemed to count himself among their devotees, frequently liking their posts on Instagram, so they decided to reach out and ask him to board their latest project: a 35-minute movie that would accompany their new LP, No Bad Memories.“We’d never made a film before, so it was like, ‘This could be a complete disaster for him,’” recalls Di Blasi, who is dressed in a black tee and purple cap with the logo for the cult electronic labelтрипwhen we meet in Manhattan in mid-September. “We were like, ‘We don’t really have anyone yet … We don’t even know what we’re doing.’” To their surprise, Osment signed on.‘In the wake of death, Courtney Love was giving it her all’: Hole’s Melissa auf der Maur on her best photographRead moreJoined by their co-director Jonathan Zawada, cinematographer Andrés Arochi and a crew that flew in from Mexico, they would eventually spend three weeks braving the elements, often shooting on the fly on little sleep. “It was fucking freezing and we’re driving around in the snow to this crazy isolated location,” says Chater, seated next to his longtime bandmate at their label’s New York office. Osment, whom he describes as “one of the most knowledgable music fans ever”, was game for it all. “He was the glue that kept the whole production together, because he’s naturally very funny and was so calm.”Named after an old slogan for a 5in floppy disc,No Bad Memorieswas inspired by the ways that advertising and technology shape us – specifically how jingles, audio logos and the drones, chimes and twinkling arpeggios of outdated devices can trigger and distort our recollection of events from our past. Chater and Di Blasi’s fondness for vintage pop and soul clips remains, but here they have broadened their palette to include chipmunk chirps, gurgling hard drives and video game bleeps and bloops. Listening to the record feels like feverishly flipping through an 1980s Saturday morning cartoon lineup – or getting sucked into the TV and thrust into the cartoons themselves. Loony and tuneful, it is the Avalanches’ wildest ride yet.In the forthcoming short film of the same title – a mix of live action, collage and animation – Osment plays Ken, a man who works for the fictional companyTakumi, a digital archives service that allows clients to upload and preserve their cherished possessions (or, as Di Blasi calls them, “tangible memories”). Its tagline: “At Takumi, your memories are safe with us.” Sporting a uniform emblazoned with the brand’s flashy logo, he travels to people’s homes in his Takumi van, gathering their belongings and taking them to a mysterious storage facility.“You’re not sure if they’re deceased or what the story is, but it’s quite melancholy because he’s going in and boxing up these memories – VHS tapes, CDs, cassettes and photo albums,” Chater explains.Ken is in the middle of packing up one abandoned place when things get weird. As the tale unfolds, he starts struggling to distinguish his own memories from the imagery in commercials he’s consumed over the years. He eventually seeks refuge inside an enormous iPod that materializes in his apartment. “You don’t know whether he’s losing his mind,” Di Blasi says.Chater and Di Blasi have been blurring that line between reality and fantasy, actual reminiscence and the illusion of it, for nearly three decades. They met in the mid-90s in high school. As a teenager, Di Blasi used to sleep with his guitar andcried when he first heardthe Beatles’Strawberry Fields Forever. Coming of age in the Australian countryside, Chater was blown away by theingenious samplingonDavid Byrneand Brian Eno’s My Life in the Bush of Ghosts and early De La Soul tracks.He began experimenting with tape loops using a Tascam cassette Portastudio, and by the time Di Blasi moved to his town for his last year of school, he was laying demos with it. The two bonded immediately, relocated to Melbourne and, along with Darren Seltmann, formed the Avalanches in 1997.View image in fullscreenThe Avalanches in a press shot from 2000/2001.Photograph: Steve GullickInfluenced by the dense, cavernous arrangements of theBeach BoysandPhil Spectoras well as the sample-heavy ragers theChemical Brotherswere churning out at the time, the band set out to conjure a hazy, psychedelic blast of sonic deja vu. Since I Left Youput them on the map and changed Chater and Di Blasi’s lives forever. A meticulously crafted, stunningly cohesive patchwork of upwards of 3,500 samples – everything from neighing horses andMadonna’s Holiday to snippets from 1960s comedy sketches and Arnold Palmer’s golf instructions album – it dazzled critics and vinyl hounds and was hailed a masterpiece by outlets such asPitchfork,Pasteand theGuardian, who named it among the best albums of the 21st century.“There was a real excitement and buzz around it,” Chater recalls. “It was the turn of the century. Dance music was having a moment. It was really fortuitous timing, and the beautiful sentiment behind the music connected with people.” He pauses. “And the fact that we didn’t do anything for 16 years added to this myth.”‘A genre-defying monument’: how Sign o’ the Times captured Prince at his creative peakRead moreThe gapbetween Since I Left You and its successor became legendary. When their sophomore LP,Wildflower, finally did come out, in 2016, Chatersaidthat the process of making it was plagued by “seven shades of shit”: Seltmann left the group, their label dissolved, Chater had to contend with two autoimmune diseases and a drinking problem (he is now healthy and sober) and they hit countless hurdles clearing its myriad samples. Also at play was a crippling perfectionism as they strove to meet the insanely high expectations for their long-awaited second outing.“With Since I Left You, we were so young and free, and I remember thinking afterwards, I didn’t even try that hard,” Chater says. “We just had fun and made this thing spontaneously, and people loved it. So I thought if I tried really,reallyhard, imagine how good it could be.”“Living up to that, it’s almost like people who have really famous parents,” adds Di Blasi. “They’re in their shadow. It felt like as time developed, the shadow of Since I Left You got quite large, and then you’re sitting there going, Oh, wow, it’s got to be as good as this.”Wildflower waswell receivedand a step forward for them. To bolster all of its blissed-out sampling, they enlisted guests includingDanny Brown,MF Doom,Biz Markie,Father John Misty, Tame Impala’sKevin ParkerandDavid Berman. Their third full-length,We Will Always Love You, arrived a reasonable four years later and continued their winning formula: heaps of dusty samples and a murderer’s row of modern voices, includingBlood Orange,Johnny MarrandNeneh Cherry. A meditation on death, the cosmos and the great beyond, it was a more subdued, wistful affair. Despite its quiet release in late 2020, during the height of Covid, it stillearned raves. Delivering a follow-up that was brighter and more euphoric was “definitely a conscious decision”, Di Blasi says. “We were like, ‘Let’s do something that’s a bit more of a party and fun and more in the spirit of Since I Left You.’”“We were really excited to make up-tempo, really joyous music,” Chater adds.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat, they wondered, could be more joyous than a jingle?Their first record with new member Andy Szekeres, No Bad Memories is both joyous and delightfully unhinged. That’s partly due to the abundance of whimsical ear candy on display – chanting children, whirring computers, the crack and hiss of a soda can – and partly because of how frenetic and kinetic it is. “It’s just about energy,” Chater says. “Sometimes we’d try to figure out the song order and structure, and I’d get bored and want to go to the next song, like skipping through a playlist. I thought, ‘Why can’t the album do that? The song doesn’t have to finish properly.’”“We’d just cut it off mid-cycle,” adds Di Blasi, “not even on the beat. You think it’s going somewhere and then all of a sudden we’re cutting to somewhere else. And that’s just exciting.”View image in fullscreenThe Avalanches.Photograph: Dean PodmoreThey also cast a wide net when selecting their featured artists. Newcomers including the British rapperJohn Glacierand Tunisian footwork producer Khadija Al Hanafi rub elbows withPanda BearandHaruomi Hosono, as well as previous collaboratorsKaren O,Rivers CuomoandJamie xx. Pioneering electronic composerSuzanne Ciani, who invented Coca-Cola’s classic “pop and pour” sound effect in the 1970s, also makes a cameo. The fittingly fizzy track Our Love Is Alive samples a 1980 episode of the PBS kids’ science show 3-2-1 Contact, in which she breaks down how her signature Buchla synthesizer works.As if all that recruiting, knob twiddling and movie-making weren’t enough, Chater and Di Blasi also created two other fictional products, theSuperfun consoleand a soft drink calledEl Dorado, whipping up original jingles, logos and ads for them. After Osment’s impressive performance in the No Bad Memories short film, they tapped him to record spots for them for interludes on the album.‘I thought I would lose my career’: Orville Peck on addiction and creating his best album yetRead moreThe lofty ambition of it all, including the increasingly difficult task of trying to clear all their samples – “Now you’re dealing with companies who’ve bought up all these catalogs and just want the maximum amount of money they can get,” Chater says – nearly broke them. “We literally just handed in the album and said, ‘Sincerely, never again are we going to do this. Like, we have to find another way.’”That’s a promise they’ve failed to keep. When we speak, it is less than two months after they’ve finished the record, but they are already sampling again. “We don’t know any other way,” Di Blasi says with a laugh.Besides, isn’t the pain and pleasure of discovery the point? “What’s beautiful about what we do is the memories and the humanness in the sounds that we sample,” Chater says. “What’s beautiful is that there’s no shortcut. You’ve got to just put the hours in, spend the time looking and digging and listening and going down rabbit holes.”“Yeah,” DiBlasi adds, “it’s the journey.”No Bad Memoriesis out on 16 OctoberExplore more on these topicsThe AvalanchesPop and rockElectronic musicAustralian musicExperimental musicinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Women and the Piano album review – Tomes brings her poetic instincts to a rewarding compilation | Classical music | The Guardian
description:
Tomes
(Hyperion)
From Marianne Martines – taught by the family lodger, Haydn, to Teresa Carreño who played for Lincoln, there’s names new and old in this fascinating and appealing collection
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: Tomes(Hyperion)From Marianne Martines – taught by the family lodger, Haydn, to Teresa Carreño who played for Lincoln, there’s names new and old in this fascinating and appealing collection
Content: Pioneering performer … Susan Tomes.Photograph: Robert PhilipView image in fullscreenPioneering performer … Susan Tomes.Photograph: Robert PhilipClassical musicReviewWomen and the Piano album review – Tomes brings her poetic instincts to a rewarding compilationSusan Tomes(Hyperion)From Marianne Martines – taught by the family lodger, Haydn, to Teresa Carreño who played for Lincoln, there’s names new and old in this fascinating and appealing collectionClive PagetThu 8 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis attractive compilation came out of Susan Tomes’ research for a book on female pianists across history. As she discovered, many wrote music as well, producing short works for the salons and domestic circles to which they were frequently restricted. Thanks to pioneering performers such as Tomes, some of the dozen women presented here are familiar names, but several will be new to many, as will their appealing compositions.View image in fullscreenSusan Tomes: Women and the Piano album cover.Photograph: HyperionTake Marianne Martines, given lessons in lieu of rent by the family lodger, Haydn. Her miniature A major sonata possesses the sparkle of Scarlatti. Marianna von Auenbrugger died aged 23, but she was taught by Salieri, who paid for the publication of the Mozartian E-flat major sonata recorded here.Music by Clara Schumann,Fanny MendelssohnandCécile Chaminadeneeds little introduction, but it’s well worth getting to know Polish virtuoso Maria Agata Szymanowska whose Caprice sur la Romance de Joconde was dedicated to her St Petersburg neighbour, John Field. Or Venezuelan pianist Teresa Carreño, who played for Abraham Lincoln and whose Un Bal en Rêve appears to channel Happy Birthday a quarter century before it was published. Raie Da Costa’s syncopated Razor Blades is pure Billy Mayerl.None of this would be half so rewarding if it were not for Tomes’ poetic instincts. Her sensitive touch, combined with Hyperion’s natural sound, give this polite and appealing music ample room to make its case.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.music.apple.com.
