title: Severed hands, crushed bones and a ‘monstrous mermaid with sharp teeth’: Reece Shearsmith on his dark obsessions | Reece Shearsmith | The Guardian
description: The League of Gentlemen and Inside No 9 co-creator has always displayed a sense of gothic unease, and his new book combines myth, memoir – and his own disquieting drawings
Author: Fiona Sturges
Headline: The League of Gentlemen and Inside No 9 co-creator has always displayed a sense of gothic unease, and his new book combines myth, memoir – and his own disquieting drawings
Content: ‘A monstrous, wizened thing’ … The FeeJee mermaid.Photograph: Reece ShearsmithView image in fullscreen‘A monstrous, wizened thing’ … The FeeJee mermaid.Photograph: Reece ShearsmithReece ShearsmithInterviewSevered hands, crushed bones and a ‘monstrous mermaid with sharp teeth’: Reece Shearsmith on his dark obsessionsFiona SturgesThe League of Gentlemen and Inside No 9 co-creator has always displayed a sense of gothic unease, and his new book combines myth, memoir – and his own disquieting drawingsThu 8 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 07.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhenReece Shearsmithwas a boy, he overheard relatives chatting at a New Year gathering. “One of them was talking about [the ghost of] a woman they’d seen standing on the village green at three in the morning,” he recalls. “Another knew a woman who woke up and found a figure sitting at the end of her bed. It’s my first recollection of being properly scared and loving it.”From then on, the Yorkshire-born Shearsmith was fascinated by all things uncanny. He would stay up late to watch Hammer horror films – his mother allowed it because she loved them, too – and immerse himself in books including the Hamlyn Book of Horror, Conan Doyle’s Sherlock Holmes stories and the works of Edgar Allan Poe. His obsession carried through into adulthood and his work: Shearsmith is best known as the co-creator of the surreal comedy series The League of Gentlemen,Psychovilleand the horror anthologyInside No 9. “I’ve managed to forge a career from the things I loved as a kid,” he says.View image in fullscreenCreep show … Reece Shearsmith.Photograph: Rory LewisNow 57, Shearsmith has written a book, Things I Took from the Dark, about his love of the macabre. It is a compendium of ghoulish stories, with accompanying illustrations by himself, and a memoir of his early years when he would scare his neighbours by wearing a glow-in-the-dark Dracula mask, with a soundtrack of thunderclaps and wolf howls, as they returned home from work.The book is structured around an imaginary museum in which Shearsmith places the legends and artefacts that have terrified and shaped him: these include the Beast of Bodmin, the Highgate Vampire and the monster that stalks Glamis Castle in Scotland. Shearsmith has an attic room in his north London home where he keeps his eerie ephemera, including antique books, props, costumes from his TV shows and a Gottlieb Haunted House pinball machine: “The room is behind a door that looks like a bookcase,” he says, gleefully.The book is stuffed with childhood anecdotes, such as the time he and his brother were in their grandad’s Reliant Robin and the car clipped the pavement, flipped over and slid down the road on its roof, sparks flying everywhere. Somehow, all emerged from the crash without injury. He also recalls the time that his dad tried to burn a toy fire engine in their fireplace, sending bits of melted plastic up the chimney which then lodged in the flue and caught fire. Eventually, the fire brigade was called to put out the blaze.double quotation markWe are chilled by the creepiness but take hope from the idea that death isn’t necessarily the endAlong with his Dracula routine, Shearsmith’s childhood extracurricular activities included practising magic tricks, making models of his favourite monsters and recreating film scenes. He even struck up a correspondence with Christopher Tucker, the special effects and makeup supremo who worked on The Company of Wolves and The Elephant Man. After Shearsmith left school, Tucker invited him to do work experience at his studio, where he created latex masks for The Phantom of the Opera.Eventually, Shearsmith’s love of acting overtook his desire to work in special effects and he studied drama at Bretton Hall College near Wakefield (since merged with the University of Leeds). There, he met Steve Pemberton, Mark Gatiss and Jeremy Dyson, with whom he would work onThe League of Gentlemen.Shearsmith has never stopped drawing and making things, so he was thrilled to provide the illustrations for Things I Took from the Dark. He says the creepy characters in his TV projects were nearly always conceived as drawings which he would show to the makeup and costume departments.It is a measure of our collective fascination with the uncanny that the tales in Shearsmith’s book have endured – in some cases for centuries. For Shearsmith, the lure of the supernatural lies not just in the storytelling but “the black horror of our own mortality. We are chilled by the creepiness, but we cling to the idea that death isn’t necessarily the end, and there’s comfort in that.”Things I Took from the Darkby Reece Shearsmith isout now.Reece’s pieces: ‘There’s always the possibility of truth piercing the myth’The FeeJee mermaid (main image)“The American showman and philanthropist PT Barnum was behind this hoax mermaid, which he put in a New York museum. It had the mummified head and torso of a monkey and the tail of a fish. Rather than a beautiful siren with long hair, it was a monstrous, wizened thing with sharp teeth.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe Beast of Bodmin Moor.Photograph: Reece ShearsmithThe beast of Bodmin Moor“On family holidays in Cornwall, we would cross Bodmin Moor to get there and back,” says Shearsmith. “The beast is a big cat: a lynx or a lion, maybe escaped from a zoo. There’s the possibility of truth piercing the myth and it’s all the more terrifying for it.”View image in fullscreenHandy, man … TheHand of Glory.Illustration: Reece ShearsmithThe Hand of Glory“If you sever and pickle a dead man’s hand and perform some incantations, you can use the hand in witchcraft. It’s said it can unlock any property and, when you light the fingertips, it will put anyone living there to sleep while you rob their house. It sounds mythical, yet there is one in Whitby Museum.”View image in fullscreenNuns on the run … The unfortunate Urbain Grandier.Illustration: Reece ShearsmithUrbain Grandier“This is a story about a French priest who was a notorious womaniser. To get rid of him, a group of nuns pretended to be possessed by the devil, and said he had bewitched them. It’s essentially a story of a cancelling, except that this man was doused in holy water and crushed until the marrow leaked from his pulverised bones.”View image in fullscreenVamping it up … The terror of Croglin Grange.Illustration: Reece ShearsmithThe terror of Croglin Grange“This is a centuries-old vampire tale about a family staying in a house near Carlisle. A monstrous man climbed in through a window and bit a woman on the neck. Hearing her screams, her brothers came in and shot the creature in the leg. Locals subsequently discovered a body in a coffin with a bullet hole in its leg, and burned it.”Explore more on these topicsReece ShearsmithHorror booksInside No 9The League of GentlemenTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Vibrant, design-led and surprisingly green’: why the Dutch city of Eindhoven is perfect for a relaxed arty break | City breaks | The Guardian
description: After electronics giant Philips left, the city reinvented itself as a multicultural hub for creativity and innovation, and the home of Dutch Design Week
Author: Sarah Rodrigues
Headline: After electronics giant Philips left, the city reinvented itself as a multicultural hub for creativity and innovation, and the home of Dutch Design Week
Content: Once home to Philips, the Strijp-S district is now a creative hotspot.Photograph: Nick BookelaarView image in fullscreenOnce home to Philips, the Strijp-S district is now a creative hotspot.Photograph: Nick BookelaarCity breaks‘Vibrant, design-led and surprisingly green’: why the Dutch city of Eindhoven is perfect for a relaxed arty breakAfter electronics giant Philips left, the city reinvented itself as a multicultural hub for creativity and innovation, and the home of Dutch Design WeekSarah RodriguesThu 8 Oct 2026 03.17 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 11.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAbaggily clad skateboarder’s wheels clatter across concrete floors, the noise bouncing off exposed pipes and iron girders. Vaulted skylights set in high ceilings illuminate the industrial space and its central kitchen, from which my main course – a silky lemon risotto, spiked with samphire, rhubarb, garlic, baby onions and basil – has just been transported.I’m in the Dutch city of Eindhoven, in North Brabant, famous for its historic connection to Philips, the one-time electronics giant. The restaurant, Radio Royaal, is housed in what was once their engine room, in the Strijp-S neighbourhood. Today, Strijp-S buzzes with concept stores, an indoor food market,MU Hybrid Art Houseand the Area 51 skatepark. The broader area, Strijp, was where the company was largely headquartered: its zones are named S, T and R. In the late 90s, Philips withdrew from the city where it had started in 1891, and the letters I, J and P were never assigned.Philips had employed about half of the region’s working population, so its departure for Amsterdam inevitably left a huge hole. Fortunately for Eindhoven, this was short-lived, and within a decade the city had reinvented itself as a multicultural hub for design and innovation – so much so thatDutch Design Week, the largest event of its kind in northern Europe, has been held here since 2005.View image in fullscreenThe innovative Trudo Tower is adorned with greenery.Photograph: Pixelbiss/AlamyThis year’s iteration, from 17 to 25 October, has a jam-packed programme of exhibitions, workshops and seminars at more than 100 locations around the city, with thousands of local and international designers involved. About 350,000 visitors are expected, with displays spanning everything from abar made from mushroomsto themanipulation of Dutch wool(which is coarser than other wools, such as merino) for wearable garments.Well beyond Design Week, however, Eindhoven packs a punch in terms of creativity. On my visit, I discovered a city that is not only vibrant and design-led, but also surprisingly green.double quotation markDespite the city’s industrial past, about 40% of Eindhoven’s landscape comprises greeneryCompletely off-limits during Philips’ heyday, Strijp-S is perhaps the liveliest example of Eindhoven’s reinvention, with innovative businesses making the most of the industrial spaces. It’s distinguished, too, by the Trudo Tower, a 19-storey building where facade planters froth with more than 70 species of greenery. Purpose-built in 2020, these eye-catching apartments were designed to provide affordable housing for low-income residents.Despite the city’s industrial past, about 40% of Eindhoven’s landscape comprises greenery. Walkways – complete with bat boxes – run alongside the Dommel river, while larger spaces, such as Karpendonkse Plas and Philips de Jongh park, provide walking and biking opportunities. This, plus an average commute time of 15 minutes, helps to explain why Eindhoven was named theworld’s least stressed citylast year.View image in fullscreenEvoluon exhibition and conference space.Photograph: Bildagentur/Joko/AlamyAs you walk from the UFO-shaped Evoluon (now functioning as an exhibition space and conference centre, and given by the company to the city on its 75th anniversary) on the edge of the Het Ven neighbourhood towards Strijp-R, the area becomes both green and residential. Ahead of the times, Philips saw the correlation between nature and healthy, happy employees. As early as 1910, the company started building workers’ accommodation with large gardens, which today are a mix of social and private housing.Strijp-R’s primary allure, however, is the RK Complex. Formerly a Philips ceramics factory, it was bought by renowned Dutch designerPiet Hein Eekand opened in 2010. Other designers have workshops here, too: the idea, said Hein Eek, was to give young creatives an affordable space to work. The concept obviously works: in more than 15 years, only five of the 25 studios have changed hands.View image in fullscreenDesigner Piet Hein Eek’s studio.Photograph: Nick BookelaarVisitors flock here year-round to check out Hein Eek’s eco-forward scrap wood furniture and for glimpses into the studios, the cavernous exhibition space and the shop, packed with smaller design objects – ceramics, books, jewellery. The onsite Green Restaurant favours local, seasonal ingredients in hearty portions; it’s attached to the boutiquePiet Hein Eek hotel, also one of the designer’s innovations. It has 14 rooms, each featuring a distinctive design style, with doubles from €135.What makes a stay in Eindhoven even more interesting, however, are the myriad ways this impulse towards repurposing spaces, reusing materials and thinking sustainably shapes the visitor experience. I stayed atHotel Mariënhge(doubles from €83) in the centre, a former monastery characterised by clean lines and cheeky art, its interiors effortlessly blending old and new.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFrom here, it’s a short walk to the retail district, where vintage stores range from the highly curatedYatva Vintageto a Salvation Army ReShare store. Near Strijp-R, I happen uponLuna & Lore, owned and run by Luna Hartogs. “Lore is about wisdom passed on from previous generations, and I learned to sew from my grandmother,” she explains, as I rifle delightedly through rails of upcycled vintage clothing. “For me, it’s also about passing things on for people to enjoy.”“Eindhoven gets called ‘Vintage Valhalla’ – a paradise,” Erik van Gerwen ofEindhoven 365tells me over dinner at Fifth NRE, itself housed in a former gas factory. “There’s the Philips legacy, but the presence of the Design Academy also ensures a lively community, passionate about innovatively making use of what already exists.”View image in fullscreenBerenkuil graffiti zone.Photograph: Nick BookelaarCreating opportunities is a recurring theme in Eindhoven. I see it again atNew Order of Fashion, a nonprofit organisation providing makers with resources to experiment with, as well as a sellers’ platform. It’s also a lab, researching the future of fashion from a regenerative perspective, and a public space aiming to inspire visitors to think about their consumer choices.I loiter outside the Muziekgebouw concert hall: since 2024, its facade has featured a massive mural of a street musician and classical concert violinist embracing. Named Echoes of Harmony, it was commissioned by Eindhoven city council to represent music’s ability to bridge barriers, and since named best mural worldwide byStreet Art Cities.On the city’s north-eastern edge, graffers can legally unleash spray cans in Berenkuil, a two-level roundabout and now the country’s largest open-air graffiti zone. Ramps and rails make it a beeline for skateboarders, too; again, I hear wheels grinding on concrete. There are no dibs here: the art lasts mere days before it’s sprayed over by someone else, but that, I’m told, is the point. In Eindhoven, perhaps more than anywhere else, the idea that everything is ephemeral, yet also renewable, seems entirely at home.The trip was provided by theNetherlands Board of Tourism and ConventionsExplore more on these topicsCity breaksNetherlands holidaysEurope holidaysDesignCultural tripsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: SOS meals – the food to cook for friends that shows you care | Food | The Guardian
description: After the death of my beloved dog, I’m thinking a lot about the role food plays in big life events – be they happy or sad
Author: Felicity Cloake
Headline: After the death of my beloved dog, I’m thinking a lot about the role food plays in big life events – be they happy or sad
Content: Made with love … Anna Jones’s chocolate chip cookie power bites lie somewhere between a flapjack and cookie dough.Photograph: Issy Croker/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMade with love … Anna Jones’s chocolate chip cookie power bites lie somewhere between a flapjack and cookie dough.Photograph: Issy Croker/The GuardianFeastFoodSOS meals – the food to cook for friends that shows you careAfter the death of my beloved dog, I’m thinking a lot about the role food plays in all of life’s big events – be they happy or sadSign up here for our weekly food newsletter, FeastFelicity CloakeThu 8 Oct 2026 07.40 EDTLast modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 07.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIlost mybeloved cairn terrier Wilfa couple of weeks ago, and when I say lost, sadly, I don’t mean I mislaid him yet again on Hampstead Heath. Rather, after 13 and a half years of (mostly) civil disobedience, we had to make the tough but ultimately kind decision to say a final goodbye. Since then, I have been bombarded with kindness. Friends and family have rallied round to take me out for breakfast, lunch, dinner and coffee, clearly worried that the bereavement might affect my appetite – well, apart from the one who responded by having a baby a week early, and who now requires me to provide for her.It got me thinking about the part food plays in big life events. We so often cook, or otherwise provide for people in the aftermath of such shocks, be they happy or sad, as a way both to offer practical help and to show them how much we love them. Such tokens of affection tend to fall into two camps. The first is high-energy food that can be easily eaten with one hand while the other is holding a baby or clutching a sodden handkerchief, or simply when you’re just too busy to sit down. Just this morning, I received a picture of the new mother tucking into my extremely wholesomefruit and nut-packed granolawith her daughter sleeping on her arm, but Melissa Hemsley’sfive-ingredient flapjacks(pictured top) would fall into this category, as would Meera Sodha’schaat masala popcornand Thomasina Miers’ dark chocolate and toasted walnutbanana bread. Like Anna Jones’schocolate chip cookie power bites, Hugh Fearnley-Whittingstall’sspiced nutsormy own kale chips, they’re full of good things, and tempting enough to compete with the less nutritious options that are so easy to reach for instead. (That said, no one should judge anyone for the choices they make at times of stress.)View image in fullscreenLoad up the portable containers … Felicity Cloake’s vegan ragù.Photograph: Robert Billington/The GuardianThe second consists of home-cooked meals that you hope will make them feel looked after, even when you can’t be there to do it yourself. I’ve already promised to make a batch ofmy massaman curryfor the new parents by special request, because I usually fall back on either myragù alla bolognese(vegan version here), orchickencacciatore. Bundle the clearly labelled plastic containers with a big bag of nice pasta, too, as well as a block of hard cheese, perhaps, and I figure the recipients are never more than 10 minutes from a good dinner – though, in this case, I’ll splash out on microwaveable sachets of rice instead. Go for a pie, however, and they don’t even have to cook any carbs to go with it. At this time of year, Nigel Slater’scauliflower cheesenumber would be delicious, as would Calum Franklin’skeema-spiced shepherd’s pieor Jeremy Lee’s classicchicken version. Thomasina’sricotta, courgette and spinach dumplings, meanwhile, come with their own tomato sauce, and freeze brilliantly, as would Blanche Vaughan’sLancashire hotpot.And, if in doubt, take round a roll or two of Tamal Ray’sfreezer cookie dough, so they’re always prepared for last-minute guests or late-night sugar crashes. After the past fortnight, I can confirm there’s very little to match the comfort of a nice cup of tea and a biscuit.My week in foodView image in fullscreen‘Perfumed with petals’ … Iranian black tea.Photograph: Jorge Fernández/LightRocket/Getty ImagesOn the subject of tea …|I found myself dogless but hungry in Henley-on-Thames on Saturday evening, after talking with wine writerOlly Smithabout our respective culinary-themed novels at the town’s literary festival (which runs until Sunday). Happy chance led me toBijan’s Kitchen, a Persian restaurant that served the most delicious and enormous lamb kebabs on naan, as well as thick, garlicky yoghurt with cucumber and mint, and olives covered in a rich paste of walnuts, pomegranate molasses and garlic, plus a lovely Iranian black tea perfumed with rose petals. Best of all (for me), it’s also dog-friendly – Wilf would have loved it.Apple turnover|A reminder, should you need it, that although the weather (at the time of writing) feels more like summer, British apple season begins to wind down towards the end of October, so if you value themore unusual varieties rarely found in supermarkets(I got some lovely Charles Ross and Blenheim Orange fruits on Sunday), now is a good time to stock up at the farmers’ market, farm shop or pick-your-own orchard. Dry the apples well, if necessary, and store them, preferably in a single layer, in a slatted crate, cardboard tray or on open shelves (air flow is vital) and keep them somewhere cool, dry and dark, where they should keep until Christmas. So long as you don’t eat them all first.Not worth dying for|The start ofCelebrity Traitorshas proved a welcome distraction for me – and, as usual, I found myself most interested in what the cast is actually eating during the dramatic daily breakfasts in the castle, and what they’re awkwardly picking at from the buffet later in the day.This articlesheds a little light on the on-set catering, and confirms that I would be a terrible contestant: there’s only so long I could put up with dry croissants and rationed wine before I confessed all just to get out of there.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFeastRecipes from all our star cooks, seasonal eating ideas and restaurant reviews. Get our best food writing every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFishy business|As a devotee of the much-maligned kipper (a cold-smoked herring), I was delighted to discover that Waitrose now does a hot-smoked version in place of the Scottish mackerel it’s removed from shelves in response to warnings of imminent population collapse in the north-east Atlantic Ocean. Herring numbers, which suffered from similar problems in the 1970s thanks to over-fishing, are now more robust in the North Sea – though check it’s been responsibly sourced, because numbers have dwindled farther west. Anything youcan do with smoked mackerel, you can do with herring, fromflaking it into potato saladsto whizzing it intopaté. Just ask any of our northern European neighbours.If you want to read the complete version of this newsletterplease subscribeto receive Feast in your inbox every Thursday.Explore more on these topicsFoodFeastnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Cold comforts: the most satisfying autumn whites | Wine | The Guardian
description: As summer fades and our social and dining habits adapt to the cooling weather, so, too, should the white wine we drink. Here are some options best-suited to the season
Author: Mina Holland
Headline: As summer fades and our social and dining habits adapt to the cooling weather, so, too, should the white wine we drink. Here are some options best-suited to the season
Content: Want ripeness, body and freshness?  Then you can’t go far wrong with the Atlantic-influenced wines of Galicia.Photograph: graficart.net/AlamyView image in fullscreenWant ripeness, body and freshness?  Then you can’t go far wrong with the Atlantic-influenced wines of Galicia.Photograph: graficart.net/AlamyGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.WineCold comforts: the most satisfying autumn whitesAs summer fades and our social and dining habits adapt to the cooling weather, so, too, should the white wine we drink. Here are some options best-suited to the seasonMina HollandThu 8 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe wine world is full of clubs, and I’m a member of the Just-Drink-What-You-Bloody-Like club, which makes even the thought of white wines for autumn and winter feel uncomfortably prescriptive. But, for me, as the nights draw in, there’s less standing, more sitting; less chugging, more swirling; fewer sprightly aperitifs, more wine with seasonal food that demands a little more body and complexity. After months of saying yes to rosé, I’m choosing wine with more intention – it’s time to hunker down.I’m looking for whites that are like a good cardigan, at once coddling and breathable. I want ripeness, bodyandfreshness, and the Atlantic-influenced wines of Galicia in northern Spain – a place that’s no stranger to wind and rain – deliver. Expressive, with a saline edge, albariño from the Rías Baixas appellation has become ubiquitous in supermarkets and rarely disappoints (tryAldi’s Specially Selected oneat £8.99), neither does the fuller-bodied godello from nearby Valdeorras (the Wine Society’s Exhibition rangeoffers a good one for £14.95), while the blend of both those grapes and other local varieties from Galicia’s Ribeiro DO in today’s pick is a cool-climate humdinger for the colder months.In October, soft greens and nightshades are out, roots and brassicas are in, and barbecues have given way to roasts; the season’s food slows us down. At my house, spiced stews and curries are increasingly on the menu, which invite aromatic central European wines such as a zippy, limey Mosel riesling. But these heartier meals also welcome something waxier, richer, warmer, such as the South African chenin blanc in my pick. Skin-contact whites, too, hold their own with these more robust flavours. Look out for wines made with Georgian grapes rkatsiteli or kisi, or those from Italy’s Friuli region. These are not budget wines, but if I drink less in the cooler months (which I do, with the obvious exception of December), that seems a good reason to spend a bit more per bottle.There is also a small but dependable family of wines that doesn’t care about the season, and which I’ll happily drink year-round, no matter the food or mood. Gavi is often considered a summery Italian white, but the Le Marne in today’s pick is aged on the lees (the dead yeast cells left over after fermentation) for three to four months, resulting in a rounded, biscuity wine I will never tire of. But, as I said, it’s personal; if none of these appeal, just drink what you bloody like.Five whites for the cooler monthsTesco Finest Steep Slopes Mosel Riesling £8, 11%. Hits the spot when paired with a spicy takeaway and, at this price, makes for a budget-friendly Friday night in.Pazo do Mar Blanco Ribeiro 2025£9.95 The Wine Society, 13%. Five native grapes work in harmony to make this food-friendly wine that sings of cool-climate Galicia.Gavi Marne BiancoLe Marne di Carraro Federica2023£19 Sip Wines, 13.5%. I had this at my November wedding nine years ago, and love it more now than ever. Golden, savoury and complex.David & Nadia Chenin Blanc Swartland 2024£29.58 Justerini & Brooks, 12.5%. Eight vineyards, mixed soils, old oak barrels and concrete vats produce this precise, generous Swartland chenin; find me sipping it fireside.Pheasant’s Tears Rkatsiteli Bakurtsikhe 2024£21 Vinum, 13%. A light amber beauty that brings apricotty, honeyed sunshine to the dimmest of autumn evenings.Explore more on these topicsWineFoodSpanish food and drinkItalian food and drinkEastern European food and drinkSouth African food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for cheese and bread balls | Food | The Guardian
description: These highly crunchable cheesy bread balls are a great way to use up odds and ends
Author: Rachel Roddy
Headline: These highly crunchable cheesy bread balls are a great way to use up odds and ends
Content: Crunch bunch: Rachel Roddy’s cheese and bread balls.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The GuardianView image in fullscreenCrunch bunch: Rachel Roddy’s cheese and bread balls.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The GuardianA kitchen in RomeFoodRachel Roddy’s recipe for cheese and bread ballsThese highly crunchable cheesy bread balls are a great way to use up odds and endsRachel RoddyThu 8 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSadly, I’m never going to be able to recreate thecheese and bread ballsI made a few weeks ago, because, of the four cheeses used, I recognised only two of them: a bit of gorgonzola and a slice of precious Montgomery cheddar, bought from Da Corrado, a stall on Testaccio market. The other two lumps of cheese, both wrapped in white waxed paper and both quite dry, were, I think, a piece of grana padano and the end of the pecorino we brought back from Umbria. But I can’t be sure, because I didn’t really examine them. Even if I had, it would have been hard to guess; the description “heels of cheese” is appropriate here. What I do know, however, is that the combination of those four grated cheeses with two eggs and enough breadcrumbs to turn the mix into a soft, malleable dough made for fantastic deep-fried balls.The inspiration for using up the uncertain contents of the cheese box waspallotte cacio e ova,which translates as “little cheese and egg balls”,a typical and much-loved thing in both Molise and Abruzzo, which were, in fact, one region until 1964. Pallotte are resourceful, and were surely invented as a way of using up scraps of cheese (almost certainly local pecorino) and bread. Whatever combination of cheese you use, though, the important thing is to add enough soft white breadcrumbs – anything from 80g to 120g – to turn the mixture into a soft dough that you can then mould into balls, but not so compactly that the tenderness is lost. Like meatballs, cheese balls benefit from a rest in the fridge, so they can firm up before frying. The rest in the fridge also ensures that they are cold, which is important, because the thermal shock of the cold surface meeting the hot oil helps create a crisp shell.It’s not just my fridge that was (and remains) chaotic; our whole kitchen, which is still missing four cabinets since they fell off the wall, is disorderly to say the least. One of my various justifications is that I am in a suspended state until I finish editing my next book, an exuberant regional recipe book that includes a fair bit of frying. Editing and testing means I’m also feeling pretty fluent in my frying advice. I fry in a smallish, high-sided frying pan, so a litre and a half of oil comes 8cm up the sides; I use a mixture of one-third olive oil (which gives great flavour) and two-thirds neutral peanut or sunflower oil, and keep the temperature around 180C (and certainly not much hotter). Goodfrittineed a good set-up, too: the pan with oil positioned safely at the back of the stove; a slotted spoon and pair of tongs; a plate lined with kitchen towel to blot excess oil, or a wire rack set over a tray to catch drips; and a big serving plate.Pollette are a perfect pre-dinner snack, or turn them into a light meal by serving with a mixed salad. Either way, just-fried and steaming-hot cheese and bread balls call for a drink: beer, lemonade, wine. Just make sure it’s cold.Cheese and bread ballsMakes24 smallor 12 larger balls2 eggs150g grated cheese(whatever you have)Nutmeg80-120gsoft white breadcrumbs1½ litressunflower or peanut oil, or 1 litre sunflower or peanut oil and ½ litre olive oilWorking in a bowl, beat the eggs lightly, then add the cheese and a good grating of nutmeg, and mix well for a sticky mixture. Add enough breadcrumbs to turn the mix into a soft dough that you can mould into balls.It pays to weigh the dough, then weigh the first “example” lump as a guide – the lumps need to be about 15g if you are making 24 marble-sized balls, or 30g if your plan is to make 12 ping-pong balls). Roll the lumps of dough between your palms to make smooth, compact balls, then put in the fridge to rest and chill for at least an hour.Fry in batches in hot oil (180C) until deep golden, then use a slotted spoon to lift them on to the kitchen towel to blot.Explore more on these topicsFoodA kitchen in RomeItalian food and drinkSnacksStarterBreadCheeseEggsrecipesShareReuse this content
